docs.title: Cookie Agent
docs.text:
Cookie Agent is a subagent-first coding harness. A daemon owns your provider connections, sessions, agents, permissions, and memory, and runs the models. Runtimes give its sessions their tools: the files and shell of a workspace on this machine or another one. Clients, the terminal UI, the web page, and the command line, all speak one versioned protocol to the daemon, so several of them can work in the same session at once.

flowchart LR
    subgraph clients [Clients]
        tui[Terminal UI]
        web[Web page]
        cli[Command line]
    end
    daemon["Daemon<br/>sessions, agents, providers,<br/>permissions, memory"]
    subgraph runtimes [Runtimes]
        global["global<br/>memory, MCP servers, plugins"]
        local["local<br/>coding on this machine"]
        remote["templates and dial-in<br/>coding on other machines"]
    end
    tui <-->|client protocol| daemon
    web <-->|client protocol| daemon
    cli <-->|client protocol| daemon
    daemon <-->|tools| global
    daemon <-->|tools| local
    daemon <-->|runtime protocol| remote

Concepts explains each piece, and Architecture shows how the code implements them.

docs.title: Three ways to start
docs.text:
Just run it in a project. Install cookie, change to the repository, and run cookie. With no daemon running it starts one inside the process, opens the terminal UI, and works on that directory. The quickstart walks through a first session.

cd ~/src/my-project
cookie

Keep a daemon running. cookie daemon serves its sessions until you stop it, for example as a service. A plain cookie in any directory on the same machine then opens the terminal UI on it, and cookie web --open opens the same sessions in a browser once the page's origin is allowed. See Persistent daemon and Web.

cookie daemon          # in one terminal, or as a service
cookie                 # in any project: the TUI on that daemon
cookie web --open      # the browser client, with the token

Use tools on another machine. A [runtimes.<id>] template starts cookie runtime serve --stdio on another machine over ssh, so a session can read, edit, and run commands in a repository there; or that machine dials in with cookie runtime serve --daemon. See Runtimes.

[runtimes.labpc]
command = ["ssh", "-o", "BatchMode=yes", "labpc", "cookie", "runtime", "serve", "--stdio"]

Keep credentials out of Git

Prefer /connect or ${env:NAME} interpolation. Do not commit .env, a credential-bearing config, or provider-store data.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Get started: install, then a first session end to end.
  • Concepts: the daemon, clients, runtimes, machines, sessions, agents, permissions, and memory, and how they relate.
  • Clients: the terminal UI, the web page, and the command line, with every command.
  • Daemon: as its own process, reached from elsewhere, and its security boundaries.
  • Runtimes: templates the daemon starts, such as over ssh, runtimes that dial in and run as a service, and the MCP servers and ACP agents they host.
  • Working with sessions: media, compaction, goal mode, memory, scheduled prompts, and usage.
  • Extend: agents and presets, skills, providers, MCP servers, and plugins.
  • Configuration: every key of config.toml and tui.toml.
  • Reference: tools, the client protocol, events, errors, and the compatibility promise: the client, plugin, and runtime protocols and session history are frozen semver surfaces.
  • Build on cookie: architecture, building and testing, writing a client, writing a runtime, plugin development, and the Rust API.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page is the contributor's view of Cookie Agent: how the Rust workspace's fifteen crates implement the pieces the Concepts pages describe. The daemon, the engine crate served by the server crate, owns provider connections, sessions, agents, model execution, permissions, memory, and persistence. Runtimes provide its tools over the runtime protocol. Clients, the terminal UI, the web page, and the CLI, reach it over the client protocol, JSON-RPC on a WebSocket or an in-memory stream. The client, plugin, and runtime protocols and session history are versioned with semver and frozen at their major; see Compatibility.

docs.title: Process model
docs.text:
The cookie binary (crates/cookie_agent) is a thin composition root. The command reference lists every subcommand and option; in outline:

Command Behavior (none) Open the TUI on the daemon [server] describes on this machine when one answers; otherwise start an in-process daemon and open the TUI over an in-memory stream. --standalone never looks for one run [options] <prompt> Run one prompt headlessly through the local engine daemon [--port \| --listen] [--tls-cert --tls-key] Run only the daemon, listening on ws://127.0.0.1:7419/ws by default; --port 0 picks an ephemeral port attach [--url] [--token] Attach the TUI to an existing daemon WebSocket web [--url] [--token] [--open] Print (or open) the daemon's web page with its token in the fragment connect [provider_id] Interactive durable managed-provider connection (TTY only) disconnect [provider_id] Interactive durable managed-provider disconnection (TTY only) runtime serve --stdio \| --daemon [url] Serve this machine's coding runtime to a daemon, as a template starts it or by dialing in mcp list List the MCP servers of every runtime with their state and hosting runtime mcp auth <server> Start OAuth authorization for a remote MCP server config edit [path], config set <key> <value>, config unset <key>, config remove <path>, config reload, config status Read and change the daemon's config.toml and agent documents; see config.toml machine list, rename, assign, unassign, merge, forget List and regroup the machines the daemon's runtimes run on memory list, edit, rm List, edit, and delete the daemon's memories sessions upgrade [--all] Convert stored sessions to this build's history format, without a daemon

The daemon authenticates every WebSocket with a bearer token kept in [server] token of config.toml, which it writes at its first start when there is none. attach, web, connect, disconnect, mcp, config, machine, memory, and runtime serve --daemon take the token from --token, COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN, or the same configuration, and accept ws/wss URLs whose path is exactly /ws. Those that connect use the same shared protocol client as the TUI, so the CLI keeps working even when built without the tui feature.

Tools run in runtimes (see the runtimes specification). The daemon itself hosts the base layer and the global runtime (MCP servers, plugins, and memory). The local coding runtime, with read, write, edit, bash, and webfetch in the daemon's working directory, runs on a task of the daemon process and is reached over the runtime protocol through an in-memory frame pair. A configured [runtimes.<id>] template starts runtimes in child processes (typically cookie runtime serve --stdio on another machine over ssh) that speak the same protocol over stdio. A runtime can also dial in to the daemon's /runtime WebSocket route, as cookie runtime serve --daemon does, and a TUI attached to a daemon on another machine dials in its own directory as client_<host name>. The daemon groups runtimes into machines by the machine ID they report (crates/engine/src/machines.rs).

Any number of clients may attach to one daemon at once. Each sees every session's events live, can submit input to any of them, and is told of the others' changes (see the protocol). Plain cookie uses a daemon already listening at [server] on its machine and otherwise keeps an in-process daemon private to its own TUI (see A daemon already running). An attached TUI that loses its connection redials the daemon with backoff under the same client identity, then rebuilds the viewed session from a full replay, which also restores output that streamed while it was away. When the client gives up recovering the viewed session's subscription, the TUI subscribes it afresh after a short pause.

docs.title: Crate layering
docs.text:
The workspace is layered bottom-up by dependency:

identity
  └─ protocol        (wire types + session layer: transports, client, serve)
       ├─ plugin_sdk
       ├─ client_state  (reducer and client policy; also builds for wasm32)
       │    ├─ tui      (never on the engine)
       │    └─ web      (browser client; wasm32, also compiles natively)
       ├─ runtime_api   (tool contract + runtime protocol; never on the engine)
       ├─ models
       │    └─ config
       │         └─ mcp     (also on runtime_api; never on the engine)
       │              ├─ coding_runtime  (never on the engine)
       │              └─ engine  (enables mcp's `oauth` feature)
       │                   └─ server  (also on web_assets, the built page)
       └─ cookie_agent (binary: composes every layer)

The TUI deliberately sits beside the engine rather than above it: it speaks only the protocol, receives an already-connected Client, and the cookie_agent binary does the in-process wiring to server. Engine edits therefore never rebuild the TUI library, and the two compile in parallel. The TUI's own tests still drive a real server through a dev-dependency.

Crate Responsibility identity Strict shared identities: agent IDs, provider IDs, model keys, variants, wildcard patterns, revisions. The bottom of the stack with no cookie_agent_* dependencies. protocol The versioned wire contracts (semver per protocol, see Compatibility) and the protocol session layer: RPC roots, events, session metadata, agent snapshots, JSON Schema bindings, the frame-level Transport trait, the in-memory InProcessStream pair, the ServerProtocol trait, the shared Client, ServerContext, protocol-owned serve, and shared setup-value parsing. The opt-in websocket feature adds the daemon client transport (WebSocketTransport, Client::connect_websocket_with_token, validate_websocket_url). The client side also builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown: there the server, the stdio peer, paths, StopSignals, and the OAuth callback are left out, tasks and timers run on the browser's event loop, and websocket is the browser's WebSocket (Client::connect_browser_websocket, with the token in the handshake). Re-exports identity and hosts the unified wire types. client_state The client state every client shares: StateStore and SessionState, reduced from stored and transient events (attribution, pending and queued lanes, approvals, goal, live tool display deltas), the runtime snapshot revision chain, model display names, and markdown kept renderer-neutral as source plus pulldown-cmark events per top-level block, parsed incrementally while text streams; a client keeps its own rendering of a block in that block's RendererCache. Also the client policy that is not rendering: the session subscription state machine (which returns the events.subscribe requests to send and takes their outcomes back), which trees stay subscribed, session ownership from session.resume, the debounced model-selection draft, the approval list, the permission-mode cycle, the complete content of cut blocks, the retry and redial waits, and the chunked upload. It also holds the rules both clients' panels share, which render nothing: permission, runtime and machine, MCP, provider, configuration, memory, and plugin rows and their requests, the credential projection a provider connect sends, tool header text, and producer and goal row labels. The client drives every timer. Depends only on protocol and plain crates, nothing renders, and it builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown. plugin_sdk Official Rust SDK for out-of-process plugins, on the protocol crate's JSON-RPC peer: handler registration, tools over the runtime protocol's tool messages, interception hooks, event and bus handlers, and producers. models Dynamic provider/model runtime: models.dev catalog, family recipe registry, provider store, Oven adapters, compiled model manifests. Re-exports the capability wire types from protocol. config Strict runtime configuration and Markdown agent documents from the user layer, with secret zeroization; also the SKILL.md parser and project skill discovery that coding runtimes use. Re-exports AgentMode, PermissionAction, PermissionEffect, PermissionRule, and AgentDocumentSource from protocol. runtime_api The contract between the engine and the tools it runs: ToolProvider, ToolSpec, prepared calls, preparation and execution contexts, progress, the traits through which the engine provides output capture and artifact retention, the detach point through which a background-capable tool says when it may be backgrounded, runtime identity (ToolOrigin, RuntimeInfo, WorkspaceContext), tool attachment validation, and the AGENTS.md lookup. It re-exports the runtime protocol's wire types (protocol) and the symmetric JSON-RPC peer both ends run with a newline-delimited stdio transport (rpc), which live in the protocol crate so the plugin SDK shares them, and holds RuntimeConnector, which starts a runtime for a requested workspace and returns its transport with a bounded DiagnosticTail of what it writes outside the protocol. Depends on protocol only. mcp The MCP client (cookie_agent_mcp): an McpRegistry per runtime that connects its servers eagerly over stdio or Streamable HTTP, publishes their tools as <server>_<tool> with untrusted-output markings, maps result media to attachments, reconnects dropped servers with the shared reconnect policy, and reports status and failures to subscribers and an McpObserver. The oauth feature, which only the engine enables, adds OAuth for remote servers and the mcp-oauth.json credential store. Depends on runtime_api and config, never on the engine. engine Session actors, run loops, permissions, approvals, delegation, compaction, internal agents, persistence, the base layer tools (delegation: delegate_subagent, get_subagent_result; messaging: send_message; skill; goals; read_artifact; stop_background), background calls (runtime/background_tasks.rs), subagent reports (runtime/subagent_reports.rs), and the runtime registry with the runtime protocol client (runtimes::remote), the child-process connector of configured templates (runtimes::process), instance reconnects, and the global runtime's McpRegistry with the TUI's runtime-layer MCP edits and their write-back (config_store). coding_runtime The coding runtime: its read, write, edit, bash, and webfetch tools, working in the runtime's workspace, the global runtime's fallback webfetch, and the runtime protocol server (server::serve) that answers a daemon with them, the workspace's project skills, and its AGENTS.md, plus the in-process connector the daemon's local runtime uses and server::serve_stdio, which cookie runtime serve --stdio runs. The server hosts its template's MCP servers with an McpRegistry without OAuth. Depends on runtime_api, mcp, and config (the skill parser), never on the engine. server The ServerProtocol implementation over Engine, the axum WebSocket accept path for clients (/ws), dial-in runtimes (/runtime), and the web page, with TLS (load_tls), Server::connect_in_process, and token generation and the ready line. Server side only. web The browser client: a Leptos page rendered client-side, built with Trunk and styled with Tailwind, over protocol's browser transport and client_state, with the TUI's features (see Web), and a web app manifest and network-only service worker that make it installable as an app. Compiles natively too, so the workspace builds without the wasm target; its native tests cover the pure logic, and headless-Firefox scenarios (scripts/test-web-page.sh) cover the page against a real daemon. Not published. web_assets The built page (scripts/build-web.sh writes crates/web_assets/bundle/), embedded at compile time for server to serve, with a content type, cache rule, and ETag per file; a placeholder page when no bundle was built. tui ratatui terminal client: composer, transcript, approvals, sessions, provider connect flow, rendering and highlighting the shared markdown. Keeps its state in client_state and runs over a protocol::Client it is handed. cookie_agent CLI and composition root wiring every crate together, cookie runtime serve, which serves a coding runtime to a daemon over stdio or by dialing in, and cookie sessions upgrade, which converts session history to this build's format. The only binary.

docs.title: Type unification
docs.text:
The refactor consolidated shared wire types in protocol:

  • Unified: config re-exports AgentMode, PermissionAction, PermissionEffect, PermissionRule, and AgentDocumentSource from protocol; models re-exports Modality, MediaKind, MimeType, MediaCapability, ReplayCapability, CancellationCapability, FiniteF32, and ReasoningEffort from protocol.
  • Deliberately separate: Sha256Digest, ModelCapabilities, ToolChoice, RequestDefaults, ResolvedRequestDefaults, and ProviderOptions stay models-side. Their decoding is intentionally more lenient so compiled model state and manifests written by earlier versions keep loading.

docs.title: Client/server protocol flow
docs.text: The session layer lives in the protocol crate so every frontend shares one implementation of the protocol mechanics.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text: protocol::Transport is a frame-level channel: send(MessageFrame) / recv() -> Option<MessageFrame>, with MessageFrame a Text string, the Bytes of received JSON text, or a Value. It has no JSON-RPC semantics. The protocol crate also provides the concrete client transports: InProcessStream (an in-memory mpsc pair used by the local frontend and tests) and, behind the websocket feature, WebSocketTransport (tokio-tungstenite, used by the TUI, the CLI, and dial-in runtimes to reach a daemon) natively and BrowserWebSocketTransport (the browser's WebSocket, used by the web page) on wasm32. The server crate's axum WebSocket accept path implements MessageStream (the Transport alias) server-side.

docs.title: Server side
docs.text:
protocol::ServerProtocol is the server contract: one async method per RPC method plus connected and subscribe_events (which receives a ServerContext). The server crate implements it in service/routes.rs, delegating every call to Engine.

protocol::serve drives one complete server-side session over a Transport:

  • Handshake gating. Every request before a valid handshake is rejected with -32003 (a connection that has not authenticated) or -32001; a handshake of a compatible version is answered with ServerHello, then connected is invoked on the implementation. The handshake's client identity fixes the connection's origin, which ServerContext::client_origin hands to every mutating method.
  • Request dispatch. Incoming requests are correlated by JSON-RPC id and dispatched to the ServerProtocol implementation; runtime.snapshot.get, provider.connect, and provider.disconnect additionally require a request id.
  • Notification demux. ServerContext::notify queues one JSON-RPC notification per connection; the session loop interleaves it with incoming frames. The server implementation uses this for runtime.changed, event tails, and plugin bus events.
  • Shutdown. A per-connection cancellation token ends the loop and drops outstanding state.

docs.title: Client side
docs.text:
The shared concrete protocol::Client runs over any Transport. A connection task owns the stream and handles:

  • Request/response correlation by id, with a bounded command queue and a sole ordered delivery channel.
  • Notification demux into ClientDelivery variants: live events.subscription, events.plugin, runtime.changed, and the daemon-wide change notifications (sessions.changed, runtimes.changed, mcp.changed, background.changed, plugins.changed, machines.changed, memory.changed).
  • Replay and gap recovery. events.subscribe runs a cursor replay that is injected into the delivery stream before buffered live notifications; a recovery worker re-subscribes with backoff and emits RecoveryFailed when it exhausts its attempts. Replays are fetched in pages, and the connection task holds the pages until the final one so the UI still sees one replay. Each page must be answered within 5 seconds of its request being written; time spent in the client's own queue does not count. A replay runs to completion even if the caller stops waiting for it.
  • Sensitive-frame wiping. provider.connect and other secret-bearing calls serialize into a zeroizing buffer that is wiped on dispatch or cancellation.
  • Shutdown via a cancellation token that fails outstanding calls with ClientError::Closed.

Connections are made with Client::connect_stream over any transport, Client::connect_websocket_with_token (the websocket feature), or Server::connect_in_process in the server crate. The TUI, the web page, and the CLI use this same protocol::Client directly, with client_state above it for the TUI and the web page; there is no per-frontend wrapper.

Each events.subscribe costs a paged replay and replaces the connection's live tail for that session, so the TUI subscribes a session at most once per connection while that subscription is healthy. Opening, reselecting, or watching a session it already follows live only switches the view. What replays a session again is a recovery, reopening a foreign read-only snapshot (which has no tail to keep it current), a session adopted after a snapshot subscription (which needs its first live tail), and a new connection.

docs.title: Configuration and layering
docs.text:
The config crate reads built-in defaults and one optional authored layer, the user layer:

~/.cookie-agent/config.toml
~/.cookie-agent/agents/<agent-id>.md
~/.cookie-agent/agents/<preset>/<agent-id>.md

There is no workspace configuration layer: <cwd>/.cookie-agent/config.toml and <cwd>/.cookie-agent/agents/ are never opened. The working directory is the local coding runtime's workspace and only contributes context, AGENTS.md files and project skills. Unknown keys, leftover schema/version fields, wrong types, and malformed values are rejected without migration or silent ignores. The TUI additionally reads an independent ~/.cookie-agent/tui.toml.

See Configuration and the configuration reference for every key.

docs.title: Provider and model runtime
docs.text:
crates/models owns the full dynamic provider pipeline:

  1. Catalog. The daemon starts from the validated catalog cache, or the bundled bootstrap (its size and digest are pinned and checked by tests) when there is none, without waiting on the network. It then refreshes the fixed models.dev catalog (https://models.dev/catalog.json) in the background: once right away, then hourly, with an ETag, accepting gzip (the 64 MiB cap applies to the decoded body). A 304 Not Modified rewrites only the cache metadata and reuses the catalog already parsed in memory while the on-disk metadata still names the same body revision, and models are recompiled only when the catalog revision or availability changes. A new body is installed by atomically replacing the body and then the metadata that names its SHA-256 revision; a pair torn by a crash fails validation, so startup falls back to the bootstrap and the next refresh repairs it. A refresh that would replace a cache validated within the last seven days with fewer than half of its usable models is refused: the cache stays in use, marked stale with a catalog_model_loss_rejected error. Catalog selection is network, cache, or bootstrap.
  2. Family registry. A code-owned recipe registry (schema 1) maps the catalog's npm package names to protocol families: OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible chat, Anthropic, Google, Vertex, Bedrock, Azure, and Cohere. Each recipe declares a default endpoint, allowed authentication methods, and credential shapes.
  3. Compiler. DynamicCompiler compiles managed catalog rows (with optional authored overrides) and authored custom providers into CompiledDynamicModel entries with concrete endpoints, validated setup, authentication, capabilities, request defaults, and variants.
  4. Executable adapters. The Oven crates (oven-sdk, oven-sdk-openai, oven-sdk-anthropic, oven-sdk-google, oven-sdk-google-vertex, oven-sdk-bedrock, oven-sdk-azure, oven-sdk-cohere, and the reqwest HTTP transport) provide normalized language-model implementations. The models crate selects the adapter for each compiled model and freezes it into user manifests.
  5. Provider store. Managed connections live in a global per-user provider store (~/.cookie-agent/providers/store-v3.json) and are shared across workspaces. Credentials are checked on first use, not at connect time.

Each accepted run freezes its model bindings against the runtime it was admitted with and keeps that runtime in memory until it ends, so configuration, catalog, or store changes cannot change a run's model behavior midway. Nothing is persisted beyond the run's events, which record the bindings as a description of what ran. A later turn resolves afresh and best-effort: a history-derived selection whose agent, model, or variant is gone falls back to the default agent (primary, else the first root-runnable one) or the agent's default model, while earlier turns keep showing what they actually used.

Local selection/pricing identity is distinct from the effective provider wire model ID. Model and variant overrides resolve before execution; frozen bindings retain the selected wire ID and endpoint. Concrete SDK constructors provide their own request and capture attribution, including unauthenticated OpenAI Chat; no attribution-rewriting wrapper is used.

History reconstruction validates saved provenance against its original turn, then leaves block eligibility to the target codec. Standard supported blocks are not restricted by source provider, header, or model fingerprints. Encrypted reasoning requires equal known effective wire model IDs and target support; required continuation evidence survives persistence so missing native state cannot silently normalize away. Integrity markers alone do not establish a required continuation. Native-compaction scopes are a separate contract. See Providers for operational effects.

docs.title: Engine
docs.text:
crates/engine runs one actor per session. Actors serialize all mutations to a session and drive the run loop:

  • Run loop. Each run walks the agent's model fallback chain. The frozen model_retry policy defaults to three retries (four total attempts) for ordinary retryable failures and five retries (six total attempts) for overload errors or retryable HTTP 429/503 responses. Zero disables retries for a class; a negative count retries indefinitely. Both classes use exponential backoff from one second and 25% jitter. The configurable local ceiling defaults to 60 seconds; a longer provider Retry-After may exceed it without a cap, while remaining promptly cancellable. Every failed attempt emits attempt_abandoned, which is visible in the TUI. When its budget is exhausted, the loop advances to the next fallback and emits model_fallback; the fallback position is sticky. Before each request the loop compacts when the latest turn's reported usage reaches the threshold (see Compaction).
  • Permissions. Every prepared tool call is matched against one merged rule list per run, the daemon's defaults, the agent document's rules, and the session overlay's (see Permissions): the most specific matching rule wins, and unmatched checks deny by default. Tool visibility reads the same list: a tool is advertised to the model only when its action has an allow or ask rule in it. The permission pipeline is stateless; approvals and tree grants live in an in-memory ApprovalStore rebuilt from durable events.
  • Approvals. The approval reviewer (the approval internal agent) decides asks in the three auto_approve modes; its escalations go to the user, reject automatically, or approve once automatically according to the mode, and a failed review (internal_agent_failed) is never approved for the user. Each session has one append-only reviewer conversation (crates/engine/src/runtime/approval_context.rs), rendered from the event log alone: the session's labelled user messages, the agent's tool calls with their outcomes, users' decisions, the root's AGENTS.md, the reviewer's earlier verdicts, and a request block per call, bounded by budgets and restarted as a new epoch when it outgrows the reviewer's window. Each request ends with a rolling cache marker whose lifetime is [approval] cache_ttl. ask skips the reviewer, and yolo approves immediately. A doom-loop guard rejects repeated identical approvals. The tree's permission mode is recorded in the root's log (permission_mode_set).
  • Tool layers and runtimes. The engine composes each session's tool list from the base layer and the session's runtime attachments (crates/engine/src/runtimes; see the runtimes specification):
  • the base layer: the daemon's own orchestration tools (delegation, send_message, skill, goals, read_artifact), which the engine implements and registers itself when it opens (crates/engine/src/base_tools). It has no workspace and every session has it.
  • runtime instances, started from templates by a registry that keeps one instance per (runtime ID, canonical workspace) and shares it with every session attached to it. The built-in templates are global (top-level MCP servers, plugins, the memory tools, and a webfetch that is only a fallback; no workspace) and local (kind coding: read, write, edit, bash, and webfetch in the daemon's working directory, and the [runtimes.local.mcp] servers). A coding runtime hosts its template's MCP servers itself, on its own machine: it connects them before it answers runtime/initialize, declares their tools next to its built-in ones, and reports their status (mcp/changed). Both instances start with the daemon (Engine::open_async). Each configured [runtimes.<id>] adds a protocol template whose ProcessConnector runs the template's command (runtimes/process.rs); its instances start when a session needs them and are keyed by the canonical workspace the runtime reports, never by a path the daemon resolved. The global runtime is called in-process. local and the configured runtimes run behind the runtime protocol: a protocol template starts an instance with a RuntimeConnector and initializes it, and the client publishes the tools it declared, proxies preparation and execution, routes its progress into the daemon's output capture, retains the media it sends, and hands tool/detachable to the call's detach point. When a protocol connection is lost, calls in flight, backgrounded ones included, fail with runtime_unavailable; the instance reconnects (1 s, 2 s, 4 s) with its tools still published, and a restart revives it under a new generation. When every attempt fails it becomes failed and its tools are dropped.
  • attachments: a session records the instances it uses with runtime_attached and runtime_detached events. New sessions attach global and local; a log with neither event reads the same way. Each attachment has a session-unique name, the name its instance reports (local_<workspace basename>, sanitized to [a-z0-9_] and capped at 32 bytes, for a coding runtime), suffixed _2, _3, ... on a clash.
  • connections: everything a session uses is connected before its first run. The global runtime's MCP servers connect eagerly when the daemon starts, and the first run waits for those attempts; a coding runtime's servers have finished theirs when its instance starts. Creating or opening a session starts its attached instances and retries the failed MCP servers of every attached instance (mcp/reconnect for a coding runtime); its next run waits for them. A connected MCP server that drops is restarted by the shared reconnect policy (cookie_agent_runtime_api::reconnect: three attempts after 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s) in the runtime that hosts it; meanwhile its tools stay published and calls fail fast with runtime_unavailable, and when every attempt fails its tools are dropped. Connect failures, exhausted reconnects, and failed instance starts are broadcast by the runtime registry and the MCP hub, which merges the global runtime's servers with those coding runtimes report; the server turns them into mcp.changed and runtimes.changed notifications that name the affected sessions each connection subscribes to.

Every published tool records which layer or attachment offers it, and the instance generation it came from. Preparation, permission decisions, and visibility use that runtime's workspace: a tool without one never matches a ${workspace_dir} rule or a rule for a relative path, and its operations digest the runtime ID instead of a path. Names are recomputed every model turn: a name offered by one source is published bare; when several runtime tools offer one name, or a runtime tool takes a base-layer name, each runtime tool is published as <attachment>_<name> (the base tool keeps its name); a fallback tool is hidden whenever a regular tool offers its name, so the global webfetch only appears without a coding runtime; and a published name longer than 64 bytes is dropped with a diagnostic. A call to a published name runs on its attachment under the runtime's own name for the tool, and fails as operation_changed when that attachment, instance, or declaration changed since publication. The daemon's working directory itself only locates the session store and stamps each session's cwd_identity. - Tool dispatch. Calls from one committed model turn are prepared and started in model order, then all permission decisions and serialized approval prompts resolve before execution begins. Tools explicitly marked parallel are dispatched together without a fan-out limit; exclusive tools run sequentially after that set. Prepared serialization keys still prevent conflicting mutations from overlapping. Terminal events commit as calls finish. - Delegation. The delegate_subagent tool reserves a child session by appending lifecycle events to the parent session, then runs the target subagent with an inherited model suffix. Each session is assigned a short, tree-unique handle (<agent_type>_<8 hex>) recorded on its creation event, and the model-facing delegation tools accept that handle interchangeably with the full session UUID. Depth and concurrency limits come from delegation configuration. - Internal agents. The approval, context-compaction, and session-title agents run with no tools and a strict text-only output contract, normally on the parent run's model via ${parent_model}. See Internal agents.

docs.title: Sessions and persistence
docs.text: Sessions are append-only event logs. A new session exists only in memory until its first user message, when its directory, events.jsonl, and metadata cache are published atomically while its ownership lock is held. Revert truncates the log after its target, closes whatever the cut left open, and deletes the subagent sessions the removed delegations created; live subscribers get a rewound notification. Fork copies a persisted prefix under a new session ID.

docs.title: Work-dir layout
docs.text:
Session data lives under the user data directory in one store per canonical working directory:

~/.cookie-agent/
  providers/store-v3.json          # durable managed connections
  catalog/                         # validated models.dev cache
  sessions/<workdirkey>/           # one store per canonical cwd
    layout.json                    # {"version":2}
    cwd                            # canonical work-dir path
    runtime-revisions-v8.jsonl     # runtime revision index
    <root-session-id>/             # root sessions live directly inside
      metadata                     # derived session cache
      events.jsonl                 # append-only root log
      grant-invalidations.jsonl    # this tree's grant invalidation journal
      owner.lock                   # Unix in-directory lock for the whole tree
      artifacts/                   # artifacts owned by this root's tree
      <root-session-id>.owner.lock # Windows sidecar, also for the whole tree
      subagents/
        index.json                 # child-summary cache, {"version":1,...}
        <child-session-id>/        # metadata, events.jsonl — no lock file

<workdirkey> is <16-hex-hash>-<sanitized-basename>, where the hash is the DefaultHasher of the canonical path string and the suffix is the lowercased final path component with every character outside [a-z0-9._-] replaced by -, repeats collapsed, length capped at 32, and edge -/_ trimmed. The suffix exists for browsability only and is computed once at directory creation: resolution scans sessions/ for the entry equal to the hash or prefixed by <hash>-, so the hash alone is the addressing key and a stale suffix after a cwd rename is harmless. An empty suffix leaves the bare hash as the whole key.

Directories and files are created private (0o700 / 0o600 on Unix).

docs.title: Metadata-only listing and lazy trees
docs.text:
Opening a store reads nothing under the work dir. Listing root sessions parses each root's metadata once, or answers from memory for a root this process holds; it never opens an events.jsonl and keeps no cache of its own, so the next listing sees roots other processes created or changed. Everything else about a tree — its children, usage, delegations, and grants — is read when the tree is first used (see Tree-local sessions). subagents/index.json carries each child's SessionSummary and terminal run statuses for that tree only. It is a cache: a missing, corrupt, or stale entry simply means the children are unknown until the tree is loaded, and metadata remains authoritative per session.

A root directory whose metadata is absent is skipped silently, so the next listing retries it. That shape is transient rather than faulty: <root>/subagents/ exists on its own whenever a child publishes before its root, and the same shape appears while a prepared directory is merged into it. Every other failure to read a root metadata — a corrupt cache, an ID that disagrees with its directory name — still reports a diagnostic and leaves the root uncached for the next pass.

When a root first comes into use — resume, open for mutation, fork source, tree or child access — the root and every descendant are read and folded exactly once in a single bulk pass. That pass assembles the tree, harvests the artifact digests the tree references, and produces the tree's delegation-registry, approval-grant, and goal-producer records; nothing produces them for a tree that was never used. The children then leave the pass without ever entering residency, so residency caps and janitor pressure are unaffected; a child that actually runs becomes resident through the ordinary write path and later evicts like any other session.

docs.title: Artifacts
docs.text: Tool output is content-addressed under a digest-named file, and every artifact belongs to exactly one tree: output written by a root or one of its descendants lands in that root's artifacts/. A session reads only its own tree's artifacts, so a read_artifact digest naming content another tree stored does not resolve there. read_artifact therefore needs no permission rule: it is a base-layer tool that declares no permission, always published and always allowed. A fork of a root hard-links every artifact its history references — and the streams a named-stream manifest lists — into the new tree before the fork is published, so it never depends on its source; a link that fails fails the fork. Collection is therefore per tree and needs nothing from any other tree. It runs only on revert: a digest the reverted events referenced is unlinked unless the tree's remaining root or child logs still reference it, and the sweep is skipped while the tree runs or a capture is publishing. Other orphans stay until the tree is deleted.

docs.title: Delegation and ownership
docs.text:
Delegation reservations, child publication, run start/attachment, and terminal state use the parent session's events.jsonl. The engine projects a tree's records during that tree's single load pass, root log included, and rebuilds only that tree's registry entries; opening the engine projects nothing. The reservation fingerprint is recomputed from the replayed request, child agent snapshot, selected model suffix, and staged-skill provenance; a mismatch rejects recovery. A background delegation the durable facts leave nonterminal is recovered by adopting the child, whose own reconciliation terminalizes the run that died with the previous process; the completion monitor then releases the parent's slot and promotes whatever was queued behind it. A delegation event skipped by best-effort reading is absent from the recovery projection and appears in the session's skipped-event diagnostics, while other delegations continue to load.

Multiple cookie processes may share this project data directory. Ownership is per root session tree, not per session and not per work dir: one owner.lock guards a root and every delegated session filed under it, and the process that locks it is the only writer anywhere inside that root's directory. It retains the lock until process exit, including while every session in the tree is evicted from memory. On Unix the lock is <root-dir>/owner.lock; on Windows it is the adjacent <root-session-id>.owner.lock sidecar, so its open handle does not prevent directory renames. Children have no lock file of their own in either layout, and locks an older build wrote under subagents/ are ignored and swept away by the tree's load pass. New-root and fork publication acquire the Windows sidecar derived from the final directory path before renaming the temporary directory; publishing a child takes no lock, because its tree is already held. Session discovery ignores the sidecar because it scans only directories. Session listing reads metadata without locking, which is safe because every rewrite of that cache stages a sibling temporary and publishes it with a replacement that keeps the name resolvable throughout: rename on Unix, and a superseding POSIX rename on Windows.

One tree lock does not make a whole tree writable. Opening a session for mutation resolves its root and attempts that root's lock — which is where an adoption reached through a child starts — and then adopts the session itself: success enters a non-writable adoption state, reconciles only that session's interrupted work, and then publishes ownership. Taking the tree through a child therefore does not reconcile the root; the root reconciles when it is first written, through its own adoption, which needs no second lock. A session is writable only once its tree is held by this process and the session was created here or adopted here. Adoption also schedules delegation recovery for the session's tree, and a resume waits — bounded, a few seconds — for that recovery to settle before it returns, so background-delegation capacity never reads transiently over-counted; if the bound expires the resume still succeeds and recovery finishes in the background. A clean shutdown is the other half of that contract: it cancels its in-flight runs and then waits, under its own bound, for those run tasks to record RunCancelled while the actors and the store are still up. Only a crash, or a task still wedged when that bound expires and is aborted, leaves a run for the next startup to repair as interrupted by daemon restart. Reconciliation failure revokes the tree's write capability for that session and, when the failed adoption is the only thing holding the tree, releases the tree lock so a later attempt can retry. Because one authority serves the whole tree, dropping it invalidates every log in the tree at once: a retained event-log projection cannot append after its store drops ownership. A live foreign owner produces session is owned by another cookie process for every session in its tree. Classification failures fail closed as foreign-owned.

Foreign sessions remain inspectable as read-only snapshots. The TUI disables input for them and refreshes the snapshot when reopened; there is no live event tail. Forking a foreign root is allowed because the fork is a new root with a tree and lock of its own; forking a delegated session publishes into its source's tree and therefore needs that tree's lock, taking it when it is free and failing as foreign-owned when it is not. Grants and grant invalidations committed by another process become visible after restart. Concurrent MCP configuration edits remain last-writer wins. An ownership failure is the registry error session_owned_elsewhere.

The data directory must be on a local filesystem with correct flock or LockFileEx semantics. NFS-class and other network filesystems are unsupported for this directory because they cannot guarantee single-writer ownership.

Legacy project-level delegations.jsonl files are ignored. In-flight delegations that existed only in that pre-release journal are not recovered; their child directories remain ordinary sessions available for inspection.

docs.title: Event bus
docs.text:
The durable session append path publishes raw events to independent bounded plugin streams only after the JSONL append and projection publication complete. These streams are best-effort observers and never participate in consistency or backpressure. The non-durable engine bus accepts plugin sources as EngineEvent::PluginEvent; it fans out to RPC frontends and other subscribed plugins with session identity but without replay or cursor semantics. RPC fan-out is connection-local and requires a successful event subscription for that session. A plugin never receives its own bus events.

Plugin diagnostics use a mutex-protected coalescing counter rather than a message queue. Producers only increment a normalized key and wake a periodic flusher; detailed message cardinality is capped and excess keys use exact per-session/plugin/kind overflow counters. Appends and shutdown draining have deadlines, with incomplete drains surfaced on plugin status before the flusher is aborted. Plugin publish contexts are expiring one-shot grants activated at outbound delivery, so a token cannot be replayed or retargeted to another session.

See Plugins for installation and configuration, and Plugin development for SDK and extension-protocol details.

docs.title: Protocol surface
docs.text:
The wire protocol is unchanged by the session-layer refactor: JSON-RPC 2.0 over an authenticated WebSocket at /ws, client protocol 1.37 (a client of another major is refused), handshake first. Discovery is a single runtime.snapshot.get call that returns one coherent catalog view with one opaque revision. Session events stream through events.subscribe and plugin bus events through events.plugin. Raw tool output is not streamed to clients: displays come from live-only tool_call_progress and durable terminal events, and retained output is read back through artifacts.

What moved is where the mechanics live: handshake, request/response correlation, notification demux, replay/gap recovery, and shutdown are now implemented once in the protocol crate and shared by the server, the TUI, and the CLI.

See Protocol, Events, and Schemas for the wire details.

docs.title: Shell installer
docs.text:
On Linux or macOS, install the latest stable release with the cargo-dist installer:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/cookie-agent/cookie-agent/releases/latest/download/cookie_agent-installer.sh | sh

The installer selects the archive for the current platform, verifies its SHA256 checksum, and installs cookie under $CARGO_HOME/bin (normally ~/.cargo/bin).

docs.title: PowerShell installer
docs.text:
On Windows x86_64 or ARM64, install the latest stable release with the cargo-dist PowerShell installer:

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://github.com/cookie-agent/cookie-agent/releases/latest/download/cookie_agent-installer.ps1 | iex"

The installer selects the matching MSVC ZIP archive, verifies its SHA256 checksum, and installs cookie.exe under %CARGO_HOME%\bin (normally %USERPROFILE%\.cargo\bin).

docs.title: Release archives
docs.text:
Stable and nightly GitHub releases provide an archive and .sha256 checksum for:

  • Linux x86_64 with glibc
  • Linux x86_64 with musl
  • Linux aarch64 with glibc
  • macOS Apple silicon
  • macOS Intel
  • Windows x86_64 (MSVC), as a ZIP archive
  • Windows ARM64 (MSVC), as a ZIP archive

Linux and macOS archives use tar; Windows archives use ZIP. Download the archive for your platform, verify its checksum, extract it, and place cookie or cookie.exe on your PATH.

docs.title: Nightly builds
docs.text:
Once a day, when main changed since the last nightly and passes every check, CI publishes it as a timestamped v*-alpha.<timestamp> prerelease with archives for all seven targets. Nightly prereleases are retained for about two weeks, with at least the newest three always kept. They are intended for testing; run cookie --version to see the source commit hash embedded in the binary.

Open the prerelease list and select a nightly to download an archive or use its generated installer command. Each prerelease provides PowerShell (irm ... | iex) and shell (curl ... | sh) installers pinned to that prerelease.

docs.title: Connect a model
docs.text: Run cookie in a project and connect a provider with /connect; the quickstart walks through it and a first session. To remove cookie again, see Uninstall.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text: Remove cookie in the order below: services first, so nothing restarts the binary you are about to delete; then the binary and what the installer set up around it; then, only if you want it, your data. The steps for the installers are written for the default install under Cargo's home; if you extracted a release archive yourself, delete the cookie or cookie.exe you placed and skip the PATH and receipt steps.

docs.title: 1. Stop and remove services
docs.text:
Quit any running cookie. Then undo whatever you set up to keep cookie running or reachable, each in its own page:

  • The daemon as a service: remove the Linux systemd unit, the macOS LaunchAgent, or the Windows scheduled task.
  • A runtime service on this or another machine: the removal steps at the end of each platform's section of Running a runtime as a service, including the token file or COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN user variable that earlier versions of that page set up.
  • Tailscale Serve or a tunnel pointing at the daemon: run tailscale serve reset; see Remote access.
  • The web client as an installed app: uninstall it in the browser.

A daemon you started by hand stops with Ctrl-C in its terminal.

docs.title: 2. Remove the binary
docs.text:
The installers put cookie in Cargo's home and nothing else on disk besides an install receipt (below). Delete it:

Linux and macOSWindows (PowerShell) 
rm ~/.cargo/bin/cookie

Remove-Item "$env:USERPROFILE\.cargo\bin\cookie.exe"

If CARGO_HOME was set when you installed, the binary is in $CARGO_HOME/bin (%CARGO_HOME%\bin) instead. command -v cookie (Get-Command cookie) shows which cookie your shell runs.

The installers write an install receipt, cookie_agent-receipt.json, which the cargo-dist updater reads. Cookie's release archives contain no updater, so nothing reads it, but delete it:

Linux and macOSWindows (PowerShell) 
rm -f "${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/cookie_agent/cookie_agent-receipt.json"
rmdir "${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/cookie_agent" 2>/dev/null

$receipts = if ($env:XDG_CONFIG_HOME) { "$env:XDG_CONFIG_HOME\cookie_agent" } else { "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\cookie_agent" }
Remove-Item "$receipts\cookie_agent-receipt.json" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Remove-Item $receipts -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

The last line of each fails harmlessly if the folder still holds something else.

If you installed cookie with cargo install instead, cargo uninstall cookie_agent removes the binary.

docs.title: 3. Undo the PATH changes
docs.text:
The installer put Cargo's bin folder on your PATH only if it was not on it already. That folder is shared with Rust, so leave this step out if you use Cargo or rustup.

On Linux and macOS the shell installer appended a line that sources ~/.cargo/env to the shell startup files that existed (it creates ~/.profile if none did): . "$HOME/.cargo/env" in ~/.profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.zshrc, and ~/.zshenv, and source "$HOME/.cargo/env.fish" in ~/.config/fish/conf.d/cookie_agent.env.fish. Remove those lines (or that file), and ~/.cargo/env and ~/.cargo/env.fish if nothing else uses them. Open a new shell afterwards. grep -n 'cargo/env' ~/.profile ~/.bashrc ~/.bash_profile ~/.bash_login ~/.zshrc ~/.zshenv finds the lines. The installer adds them only if cargo's bin was not already on PATH, and not at all when COOKIE_AGENT_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 was set at install time.

On Windows the PowerShell installer added the bin folder to your user Path (the Path value in HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Environment). Remove it:

$bin = "$env:USERPROFILE\.cargo\bin"
$path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path', 'User') -split ';' | Where-Object { $_ -and $_ -ne $bin }
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('Path', ($path -join ';'), 'User')

Use your CARGO_HOME instead of $env:USERPROFILE\.cargo if you set one. The change applies to shells you open afterwards. (This rewrites the value as plain text; a Path that held %VARIABLE% entries has them expanded.)

docs.title: 4. Remove your data (optional, destructive)
docs.text:
Everything cookie keeps for you lives in one folder, ~/.cookie-agent (%USERPROFILE%\.cookie-agent on Windows), apart from the logs of the services above. Deleting it is permanent and cannot be undone:

  • config.toml and tui.toml, with the daemon's token ([server] token);
  • providers/, your connected providers' credentials;
  • mcp-oauth.json, the OAuth credentials of remote MCP servers;
  • acp-agents.json, what ACP agents last offered (options, file kinds), which drafts show;
  • native-compaction.json, the providers native compaction stopped being tried for;
  • deferred-tools.json, the models that refused deferred tools;
  • sessions/, every session's history;
  • memory/, projects/, and machines.json;
  • agents/ and skills/ you wrote there;
  • catalog/, a cache of the model catalog that cookie downloads again;
  • machine-id, when the machine has none of its own.

Cookie keeps no data, cache, or credential outside this folder, and uses no system keychain. Copy out what you want to keep first, such as config.toml, agents/, skills/, and memory/. To forget a provider's credentials but keep the rest, use cookie disconnect before you delete the binary.

Linux and macOSWindows (PowerShell) 
rm -rf ~/.cookie-agent

Remove-Item "$env:USERPROFILE\.cookie-agent" -Recurse -Force

Projects have their own .cookie-agent/ folder only if you made one there (project configuration, agents, and skills); delete it in each project that has one. A daemon on another machine keeps its own ~/.cookie-agent there.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This page takes you through a first session in the terminal UI: setting cookie up with a provider and its models, asking for a change, approving the tools it calls, reading the transcript, and coming back to the session later. It assumes cookie is installed.

docs.title: Start in a project
docs.text:
Change to the repository the agent should work on and start cookie:

cd ~/src/my-project
cookie

No configuration file is needed. With no daemon running on this machine, cookie runs one inside the process; the left of the bottom bar says standalone, and the runtime and directory the session will work in follow it. Sessions you create here work in this directory.

docs.title: Set up: a provider, two models, and the starter kit
docs.text:
Cookie is set up once it has a connected model provider and two models: default_model, which agents run on, and small_model, which runs the quick internal jobs (approval reviews and session titles) and the explore subagent. Until then the TUI shows a notice offering Set up (or Not now, which it remembers for this machine), and /onboard opens the same panel at any time. It walks four steps:

  1. Provider. Pick a managed provider and its sign-in: an API key, typed hidden, or a browser login. The connection is stored for your user and shared by every workspace. Several may be connected.
  2. Default model. A searchable list of the connected providers' models, with their context size; choosing one offers its variants, the model's own default preselected.
  3. Small model. The same list, nothing suggested; its variant picker preselects the model's first listed variant, the cheapest. It may be the same model as the default.
  4. Starter kit (optional). A commented config.toml, three agents (primary, which runs sessions, and its subagents explore and worker), downloaded from the release of your cookie version. Each file is marked new, same as yours (skipped), or differs: an existing file is never overwritten; the kit's version is written beside it as <name>.new.

The daemon also keeps cookie's official skills up to date by itself, such as customize-cookie-agent for changing cookie and add-cookie-runtime for adding another machine; they need no step.

Finish writes the settings and the kit together, and stays disabled, with the reason, until a provider and both models are chosen.

The same steps run from a terminal against a running daemon, here or on another machine (--url and --token, as for cookie config):

cookie daemon &                 # once; or the persistent daemon service
cookie onboard                  # numbered questions; `/` searches the lists
cookie onboard --diff           # what the kit would change, changing nothing
cookie onboard --yes --default-model anthropic/claude-opus-4-1:high \
               --small-model deepseek/deepseek-chat

The web page offers the same as a first-run sheet, and Settings → Set up Cookie reopens it. Whether the daemon is set up comes from its configuration alone: setting default_model and small_model in config.toml by hand counts the same, and disconnecting the last provider makes it ask again. See cookie onboard, default models, and agents.

To use a model the catalog does not list, configure a custom model in config.toml. /model chooses the model and its variant for the next run, and /agent the agent: primary once the kit is installed, else the built-in default agent, which runs on default_model.

docs.title: Ask for something
docs.text: Type a request in the composer and press Enter; Shift-Enter inserts a newline. The agent reads files, edits them, and runs commands through its tools, and the transcript shows each call as it happens. While it works, Enter sends another message into the running conversation, and Alt-Enter queues one for after the run (see Steering and queueing). Esc twice, or /cancel, stops the run.

docs.title: Approve tools
docs.text:
The built-in default agent reads freely but asks before it writes a file, runs a command, or delegates, and never reads files such as .env or SSH keys. A session starts in the auto-approve permission mode: the approval reviewer answers these asks against your task and passes to you, with its reason, the ones it will not decide. Click the mode in the bottom bar to cycle it; in ask every ask comes to you.

An approval appears above the status bar in place of the composer, showing the command or the diff the call will make. Press y to allow it once, a to allow it for the whole session tree, n to reject it, or e to reject it with a note telling the agent what to do instead. See Approvals and Permissions.

docs.title: Read the transcript
docs.text: Click a tool row to expand it: its arguments, then its output, such as a command's terminal output or an edit's diff with line numbers. The system prompt, the AGENTS.md files the session loaded, and skills appear as collapsed rows you can open the same way, so everything that went into the model's context can be read. /usage shows the tokens and estimated cost of the session and of the subagents it started. See Transcript details.

docs.title: Come back later
docs.text: Quit with /quit, or Ctrl-C twice when nothing is running. Sessions are kept: start cookie in the same directory again, open /sessions, and choose the session to continue it. A past message's menu (click it) copies it, reverts the session to before it, or forks a new session from it. See Sessions.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• In a browser. Run cookie daemon, then cookie web --open; see Web.
  • A daemon that keeps running. With cookie daemon running, every cookie on this machine opens on it and shares its sessions; see Persistent daemon.
  • Without the TUI. cookie run "…" runs one prompt for scripts and CI; see Command line.
  • Your own agents. Write agent documents with their own prompts, models, and permissions; see Agents and presets.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: This page is the reference for the cookie command: every subcommand and option, how commands find a daemon, and how they exit, then headless runs with cookie run in detail. Interactive work happens in the terminal UI or the web client, and Persistent daemon covers running cookie daemon and attaching clients to it.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command What it does cookie The terminal UI, on a daemon already running on this machine or in this process cookie run Run one prompt without the TUI cookie daemon Serve the client protocol, the web page, and dial-in runtimes cookie daemon restart Restart a running daemon, once idle or at once cookie attach The terminal UI on a running daemon, here or elsewhere cookie web Print the daemon's web page address with its token cookie onboard Set up a daemon: a provider, the default and small models, the starter kit cookie connect, cookie disconnect Store or remove a managed provider connection cookie runtime serve Serve this machine's coding runtime over stdio or by dialing in cookie runtime mcp-bridge Connect an ACP agent's MCP client to cookie's tools (run by a runtime) cookie config Read and change the daemon's config.toml and agent documents cookie machine List and regroup the machines the daemon's runtimes run on cookie memory List, edit, and delete the daemon's memories cookie project List, create, rename, delete, and edit the daemon's projects cookie cron List, create, edit, run, and delete the daemon's cron jobs cookie skills List the daemon's skills, refresh the official ones, and check skills cookie sessions upgrade Convert stored sessions to this build's history format cookie mcp List MCP servers and authorize a remote one

cookie --help, and --help after any subcommand, prints clap's usage; cookie --version prints the version.

docs.title: Global options
docs.text: Option Meaning --error-details Accepted by every command. When the daemon refuses a request, also print the technical detail of its error, such as the upstream cause or a path (see Error details). --standalone Plain cookie only: run the engine in this process, without looking for a running daemon. With a subcommand it is a usage error. --project <NAME> Plain cookie only: start a new session in this project. With a subcommand it is a usage error.

docs.title: Reaching a daemon
docs.text:
attach, web, connect, disconnect, daemon restart, config, machine, memory, project, cron, mcp, and runtime serve --daemon talk to a running daemon. Each takes --url and --token; for config, machine, memory, project, and cron the two may also follow the nested subcommand. They resolve the daemon this way:

  • URL: --url, else [server] url in this machine's config.toml, else the local daemon that table describes, ws://<host>:<port>/ws. The URL must be ws:// or wss:// with the path /ws.
  • Token: --token, else the COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN environment variable, else [server] token. With none of them the command fails with no daemon token. cookie removes COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN from its environment at startup, so the processes it starts do not inherit it.

When both --url and a token are given, config.toml is not read. See Server for the [server] keys and Remote access for daemons on other machines.

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text: A command that succeeds exits 0. One that fails prints cookie: and the error on standard error and exits 1; when the error is a daemon refusal that has technical detail, it adds that detail with --error-details, or a line saying to run again with it. Command-line usage errors, such as an unknown option or a missing argument, exit 2 with clap's message. cookie run has its own exit codes.

docs.title: cookie
docs.text:
cookie [--standalone] [--project <NAME>] [--error-details]

Opens the terminal UI for the current directory. Unless --standalone is given, it first looks for a daemon on this machine, as A daemon already running describes, and opens the TUI on it; otherwise it runs the engine in this process and the TUI with it. Quitting the TUI exits 0. See Terminal UI.

With --project <NAME> the TUI starts on a new session in that project: it takes the project's default agent and preset, with the agent's own default model, and, when the project's defaults name runtimes, the daemon attaches those instead of the TUI's usual ones. An agent that is gone or cannot run as root leaves the usual agent, and the status line says so. A new session belongs to no project otherwise; nothing is picked from the current directory.

docs.title: cookie run
docs.text:
cookie run [OPTIONS] <PROMPT | -p PROMPT | -f PATH>

Runs one prompt through an engine in this process, without the TUI, and never looks for a running daemon. Headless runs below describes each option.

Option Default Meaning PROMPT, -p, --prompt <PROMPT> The prompt; - reads standard input. Exactly one prompt source is required. -f, --prompt-file <PATH> Read the prompt from a file; - reads standard input. -a, --agent <AGENT> see Selection and limits Root-runnable agent ID. --preset <PRESET> Agent preset for a new session. -m, --model <MODEL> see Selection and limits provider/model to run. --variant <VARIANT> Named model variant, or base for none. --permission-mode <MODE> auto-approve auto-approve, auto-approve-n, auto-approve-y, ask, or yolo; the underscore spellings are aliases. --allowed-tools <ACTION,...> Permission actions, or skill:<name>, to allow; repeatable and comma-delimited. --skill <NAME> Load a user-invocable skill before the prompt. --skill-args <TEXT> Arguments of --skill; requires it. --max-turns <N> 100 Most committed root model turns, at least 1. --timeout <SECONDS> 600 Run timeout, at least 1. --resume-session <ID> Continue this session instead of creating one. --data-dir <PATH> ~/.cookie-agent Session and artifact store. -o, --output <FORMAT> text text, json, or none. --json Alias for --output json; conflicts with --output. --output-file <PATH> Write output to a file; not with --output none. --verbose Progress on standard error and, in JSON mode, tool-output records.

docs.title: cookie daemon
docs.text:
cookie daemon [--port <PORT> | --listen <ADDR:PORT>] [--tls-cert <PATH> --tls-key <PATH>]

Serves the client protocol on /ws, the web page, and dial-in runtimes on /runtime, for sessions of any directory; the sessions are stored for the directory it starts in. It prints the ready line, then its address and client protocol version, its process ID, and the web page's address, and runs until a stop signal or a restart. Without a [server] token it writes a fresh one to config.toml first. See Persistent daemon.

Option Default Meaning --port <PORT> [server] port Loopback port to bind; 0 lets the OS pick one, which the ready line reports. Conflicts with --listen. --listen <ADDR:PORT> 127.0.0.1, the port above Address and port to bind, such as 0.0.0.0:7419, for clients and runtimes on other machines. --tls-cert <PATH> PEM certificate chain to serve wss with; requires --tls-key. --tls-key <PATH> PEM private key of --tls-cert; requires --tls-cert.

See Remote access before listening off loopback.

docs.title: cookie daemon restart
docs.text:
cookie daemon restart [--now] [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Asks a running daemon to restart (daemon.restart): it relaunches its own executable with the same arguments and environment, which applies the configuration cookie config status lists as needing a restart and runs a binary upgraded on disk. Without --now the daemon waits until no turn is running in any session and refuses new turns meanwhile; the command prints what it waits for and how many turns are left. It then waits for the daemon to come back, up to a minute, and says whether its version changed. Ctrl-C stops waiting; the restart stays scheduled. See Restarting the daemon.

Option Meaning --now Restart at once; running turns end as interrupted. Also turns a restart already waiting into an immediate one. --url <URL> The daemon's client URL (see Reaching a daemon). --token <TOKEN> The daemon's token (see Reaching a daemon). 
cookie daemon restart --url ws://127.0.0.1:7419/ws --token <token>

A daemon not started by cookie daemon, such as an engine embedded in another program, answers restart_unsupported.

docs.title: cookie attach
docs.text:
cookie attach [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Opens the terminal UI on a running daemon, found as Reaching a daemon says. It never runs an engine of its own: a daemon it cannot reach or use is an error. A dropped connection is redialed, and quitting leaves the daemon running. See Persistent daemon.

docs.title: cookie web
docs.text:
cookie web [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>] [--open]

Prints the daemon's web page with the token in its fragment, http://127.0.0.1:7419/#token=<token>: the client URL with ws turned into http (wss into https) and the final ws dropped. It does not contact the daemon. --open also opens the page in the system browser (open on macOS, start on Windows, xdg-open elsewhere). See Web.

docs.title: cookie onboard
docs.text:
cookie onboard [--from <FILE>] [--diff] [--yes]
               [--default-model <KEY[:VARIANT]>] [--small-model <KEY[:VARIANT]>]
               [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Sets up the daemon that --url and --token name, here or on another machine, through its onboarding API; cookie onboard writes nothing itself. The steps, as numbered questions:

  1. Provider: connects one, as cookie connect does, when none is connected; otherwise offers to connect another.
  2. Default model (default_model): a numbered list of the connected providers' available models, grouped by provider; /text searches it. Its variant question preselects the model's default variant.
  3. Small model (small_model): the same list with nothing suggested; its variant question preselects the model's first listed variant, the cheapest. It may be the same model.
  4. Starter kit: shows what installing it would do to each file (new, same as yours and skipped, or differs and written beside yours as <name>.new) and asks whether to install it.

The kit comes from the daemon's own release (v<version>), else its newest nightly of the same version that carries one (v<version>-alpha.<n>, from GitHub's release list), else the latest stable release; --from takes a downloaded cookie-agent-defaults.tar.gz instead. Its manifest's hashes are checked before anything is written. --diff prints what installing the kit would change, with a diff of each changed file, and changes nothing. --default-model and --small-model answer those questions (provider/model, or provider/model:variant); --yes answers the rest with their defaults (keep what is set, install the kit) and refuses rather than guess a model or connect a provider. Without --yes or --diff it needs an interactive terminal. Running it again on a set-up daemon shows the current provider and models and offers the kit again. See Getting started.

docs.title: cookie connect
docs.text:
cookie connect [PROVIDER_ID] [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Creates or updates the daemon's durable, global connection to a managed provider: pick the provider (or name it), confirm, choose the auth method, then type its setup values and credentials. It needs an interactive terminal on standard input, output, and error: credentials are never accepted as arguments. Answering anything but y or yes to the confirmation cancels it with an error. See Providers.

A provider connected by a browser sign-in, such as chatgpt, prints the sign-in address instead of asking for credentials. The redirect returns to a listener this command opens on 127.0.0.1; when the browser runs on another machine, paste the address it fails to load, or forward the printed port over SSH first. See ChatGPT.

docs.title: cookie disconnect
docs.text:
cookie disconnect [PROVIDER_ID] [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Removes a managed provider connection after a [y/N] confirmation; it needs an interactive terminal like connect. Disconnecting chatgpt signs out and revokes the sign-in.

docs.title: cookie runtime serve
docs.text:
cookie runtime serve --stdio [--root <DIR>]...
cookie runtime serve --daemon [<URL>] [--id <RUNTIME_ID>] [--token <TOKEN>] [--root <DIR>]...

Serves this machine's runtime, the coding capability (read, write, edit, bash, webfetch), over the runtime protocol. It needs no provider configuration. One of --stdio and --daemon is required.

Option Meaning --stdio Speak the runtime protocol on standard input and output, one JSON-RPC message per line, as a [runtimes.<id>] template starts it. Exits when the daemon sends runtime/shutdown or closes standard input. --daemon [<URL>] Dial in to a daemon and stay connected: this client URL, or, without one, the daemon Reaching a daemon finds. After a drop it connects again, waiting 1 second, doubling up to 30 seconds. Its machine's [runtimes.local.mcp] servers and [runtimes.local.acp.agents] come along, and it reports changed agents as its configuration changes. --id <RUNTIME_ID> The runtime ID to dial in as; this machine's host name, sanitized, when omitted. Not with --stdio. --token <TOKEN> The daemon's token, for --daemon; also COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN. --root <DIR> Limit coding to workspaces under this directory; repeat for several. A leading ~ is expanded; a root that is not a directory is an error. Any workspace when omitted.

It runs until a stop signal. See Runtimes that dial in.

docs.title: cookie runtime mcp-bridge
docs.text:
cookie runtime mcp-bridge --socket <PATH>

Copies standard input to a runtime's bridge socket and the socket to standard output: the stdio MCP server cookie a runtime hands the ACP agents it hosts, through which they call cookie's tools (see the ACP agents spec). The runtime starts it for each ACP session; it is not meant to be run by hand.

Option Meaning --socket <PATH> The bridge socket the runtime opened for the agent's session: a Unix socket, or a named pipe on Windows.

docs.title: cookie config
docs.text:
cookie config <COMMAND> [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Reads and changes the daemon's configuration documents, config.toml and the agent documents, through the daemon, which applies each change live or says what needs a restart. See config.toml. Its status notes also name the providers native compaction is off for, with why and since when.

docs.title: cookie config edit
docs.text: cookie config edit [PATH] opens a document in $VISUAL, else $EDITOR, else vi, or on Windows code --wait when VS Code is on PATH, else Notepad: config.toml by default, or agents/<id>.md or agents/<preset>/<id>.md. A path that does not exist yet is created, an agent document from a template. It needs an interactive terminal. Saving it unchanged does nothing; a change the daemon refuses as invalid offers to edit again.

docs.title: cookie config set
docs.text: cookie config set <KEY> <VALUE> sets one dotted key of config.toml, such as cookie config set loop_warning.enabled false. The value is TOML; text that does not parse as TOML is a string.

docs.title: cookie config unset
docs.text: cookie config unset <KEY> removes one key of config.toml.

docs.title: cookie config remove
docs.text: cookie config remove <PATH> removes an agent document; a preset's last one removes the preset.

docs.title: cookie config reload
docs.text: cookie config reload re-reads the configuration files and applies them, after editing them by hand.

docs.title: cookie config status
docs.text: cookie config status shows whether the applied configuration matches the files, why the last reload failed, and what needs a restart.

docs.title: cookie machine
docs.text:
cookie machine <COMMAND> [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Manages the machines the daemon's runtimes run on. See Machines.

docs.title: cookie machine list
docs.text: Lists each machine with its machine IDs, pinned and connected runtimes, the offline runtimes it remembers with when each was last seen, platform, and memories.

docs.title: cookie machine rename
docs.text: cookie machine rename <MACHINE> <NAME> renames a machine; its memory folder moves with it.

docs.title: cookie machine assign
docs.text: cookie machine assign <RUNTIME> <MACHINE> pins a runtime ID to a machine, created when the name is new.

docs.title: cookie machine unassign
docs.text: cookie machine unassign <RUNTIME> removes a runtime's pin, so that it follows the machine ID it reports.

docs.title: cookie machine merge
docs.text: cookie machine merge <FROM> <INTO> moves one machine's IDs, pins, and memories into another and removes it.

docs.title: cookie machine forget
docs.text: cookie machine forget <MACHINE> removes a machine that has no connected runtimes and no memories.

docs.title: cookie machine forget-runtime
docs.text: cookie machine forget-runtime <RUNTIME> forgets where an offline runtime ran, so it is no longer listed on its machine. A pin stays.

docs.title: cookie memory
docs.text:
cookie memory <COMMAND> [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Manages the daemon's memories. See Memory.

docs.title: cookie memory list
docs.text: cookie memory list [LAYER] lists the memories of every layer, or of one: user, agent, machine, or project. Invalid files and entries that are not memories are listed with the reason. Under each memory, a line gives when it was created, modified, and last read by a model, and its size against its limit.

docs.title: cookie memory show
docs.text: cookie memory show <URL> prints a memory, such as project://web/build: when it was created, modified, and last read, its size against its limit (and whether it is over it), then its text without the created and modified lines the daemon keeps.

docs.title: cookie memory edit
docs.text: cookie memory edit <URL> opens a memory, frontmatter included but without the created and modified lines the daemon keeps, in the editor cookie config edit uses, such as project://web/build; a memory that does not exist yet is created. Text that is not a valid memory, or a memory that changed since it was opened, offers to edit again.

docs.title: cookie memory rm
docs.text: cookie memory rm <URL> [-y | --yes] deletes a memory, asking first unless --yes.

docs.title: cookie project
docs.text:
cookie project <COMMAND> [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Manages the daemon's projects by name.

docs.title: cookie project list
docs.text: cookie project list prints one line per project: its emoji and name, its sessions and memories, whether it has an AGENTS.md, and its defaults.

docs.title: cookie project create
docs.text: cookie project create <NAME> [--emoji <EMOJI>] creates a project with an empty project://<name>/overview memory. The name is a lowercase letter or digit, then up to 63 lowercase letters, digits, or -; the emoji is exactly one emoji.

docs.title: cookie project rename
docs.text: cookie project rename <OLD> <NEW> renames a project; its memory folder moves with it, so its memories become project://<new>/….

docs.title: cookie project delete
