docs.text: cookie project delete <NAME> [-y | --yes] deletes a project with its sessions, its memories, its AGENTS.md, and its defaults, asking first unless --yes, with the counts of sessions and memories that go. The daemon refuses while a session of the project runs.

docs.title: cookie project edit
docs.text: cookie project edit <NAME> opens the project's AGENTS.md in the editor cookie config edit uses; saving it empty removes the file. A project that changed since it was opened offers to reload it and edit again.

docs.title: cookie project defaults
docs.text: cookie project defaults <NAME> --from-session <SESSION_ID> sets the project's defaults from a session: its runtime attachments, whether it has global, and its agent and agent preset.

docs.title: cookie cron
docs.text:
cookie cron <COMMAND> [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Manages the daemon's cron jobs: prompts it fires on a schedule into a session, or into a new session per fire. See Scheduling prompts. The daemon needs client protocol 1.15 or later; an older one is refused with a message saying so. Times are printed in this machine's time zone; cron expressions are the daemon host's local time.

docs.title: cookie cron list
docs.text: cookie cron list prints two lines per job: its ID, its name (or the start of its prompt), and why it is disabled; then its schedule read plainly (such as every day at 03:00), its next fire, its target, and the outcome of its last fire. When [cron] enabled = false holds on the daemon, a first line says jobs do not fire.

docs.title: cookie cron show
docs.text: cookie cron show <ID> prints a job: its schedule and its plain reading, target, state, next fire, runs against its limit, delivery or agent, model pin, and permission mode, failures in a row, who created it and when, and the session an agent created it in; the target and that session are named by title with their session IDs; then its prompt and its history, newest first, with each fire's outcome and the session it went to.

docs.title: cookie cron create
docs.text:
cookie cron create --prompt <TEXT> --schedule <SCHEDULE>
                   (--session <SESSION_ID> [--delivery steer|queue]
                    | --agent <AGENT> [--model <MODEL>] [--permission-mode <MODE>] [--project <NAME>])
                   [--name <NAME>] [--max-runs <RUNS>] [--disabled]

Creates a job and prints its ID and next fire.

Option Meaning --prompt <TEXT> What each fire sends. --schedule <SCHEDULE> Five cron fields in the daemon host's local time, such as "0 3 * * *", or a delay, such as "in 20m" (s, m, h, or d, from 1s to 365d), which fires once. --name <NAME> What lists show instead of the prompt's start. --max-runs <RUNS> Cron schedules only: the fires the job delivers, a whole number, 0 or less for no limit; 1 when omitted. --session <SESSION_ID> Fire into this session, a root or a delegated one. --delivery <MODE> With --session: queue (after the running turn, the default) or steer (into it). --agent <AGENT> Start a new session with this agent per fire instead. --model <MODEL> With --agent: pin provider/model or provider/model[variant]; the agent's own models otherwise. --permission-mode <MODE> With --agent: the run sessions' mode, spelled as for cookie run; auto-approve-n when omitted. --project <NAME> With --agent: the project the run sessions belong to. --disabled Create the job disabled.

docs.title: cookie cron edit
docs.text: cookie cron edit <ID> [OPTIONS] changes a job; only what the options give changes, and an edit that changes nothing says so. It takes --prompt, --schedule, --name (empty removes the name), --max-runs, --session (fire into that session instead), --delivery, --agent (start a new session with that agent per fire, or change a new-session job's agent), --model (empty removes the pin), and --permission-mode. A new schedule computes the next fire from now.

docs.title: cookie cron rm
docs.text: cookie cron rm <ID> [-y | --yes] deletes a job, asking first unless --yes. Its run sessions stay.

docs.title: cookie cron enable
docs.text: cookie cron enable <ID> enables a job: its next fire is computed from now, its failure count resets, and a finished job's run count starts again. A one-shot whose time has passed needs a new --schedule first.

docs.title: cookie cron disable
docs.text: cookie cron disable <ID> disables a job; it keeps its history.

docs.title: cookie cron run
docs.text: cookie cron run <ID> fires a job now, as its schedule would, and prints the fire's outcome and the session it went to. A run now counts toward neither the job's run limit nor its failures, and fires even with [cron] enabled = false.

docs.title: cookie skills
docs.text:
cookie skills <COMMAND> [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

Lists the daemon's skills and refreshes its official skills, the ones it keeps up to date in official_skills/ of its data root; see Official skills.

docs.title: cookie skills list
docs.text: cookie skills list prints the daemon's own skills, its user and official ones (project skills belong to a session's workspaces): each skill's name, where it comes from (user, or official with its version), marked (shadowed) when another skill of the same name wins, and its file.

docs.title: cookie skills update
docs.text: cookie skills update refreshes the official skills now, as the daemon does at start and daily, and prints what changed and the skills it keeps. A refresh that fails keeps the skills it had and fails with the reason; with [skills] official = false it does nothing.

docs.title: cookie skills check
docs.text:
cookie skills check <DIR> [--docs <DIR>]

Checks skills before they are published, with no daemon: each <DIR>/<name>/SKILL.md (or <DIR>/SKILL.md alone) must parse, every backticked cookie … command it names must exist in this build, and every link to https://cookie-agent.github.io/doc/dev/… must name a page. Links are fetched from the published site, or checked against a docs/site checkout with --docs. An index.json in <DIR> must list every skill there, with a version, a requires_cookie range, and each file's SHA-256. Each problem is printed with its file, and any problem fails the command. The official skills repository runs it on every push.

docs.title: cookie sessions upgrade
docs.text:
cookie sessions upgrade [--all]

Converts the sessions of the current directory, or with --all of every directory, in ~/.cookie-agent to this build's history format, as opening each one would. The originals stay beside them as events.jsonl.v<N>.bak, and a session tree another cookie process holds is skipped. It works on the files directly, without a daemon. It prints a line per tree it converted or could not convert and a summary, and exits 1 when any session could not be converted. See Sessions.

docs.title: cookie mcp
docs.text: cookie mcp <COMMAND> [--url <URL>] [--token <TOKEN>]

docs.title: cookie mcp list
docs.text: Lists every runtime's MCP servers, one per line: the name, its tool count, its state, and the runtime (with its workspace) that hosts it.

docs.title: cookie mcp auth
docs.text: cookie mcp auth <SERVER> authorizes a remote MCP server of the global runtime that needs OAuth. It prints the authorization URL and waits for the browser to return to a callback on this machine's loopback; when the browser runs on another machine, paste the URL it was redirected to. A stop signal cancels the authorization. See MCP.

docs.title: Headless runs
docs.text: cookie run executes one prompt through the local engine without starting the TUI, daemon, or an in-process protocol server. It is intended for CI and scripts.

docs.title: Prompt input
docs.text:
Provide exactly one prompt source:

cookie run "Review this workspace"
cookie run -p "Review this workspace"
cookie run -f request.txt
printf '%s\n' 'Review this workspace' | cookie run -
printf '%s\n' 'Review this workspace' | cookie run -p -

The positional prompt, -p/--prompt, and -f/--prompt-file conflict with each other. - reads standard input for any of them.

docs.title: Selection and limits
docs.text:
The default agent is the root-runnable primary agent, or the first root-runnable agent. The default model is its first live fallback, including a valid variant; if none is live, the first available model and its default variant are used. Select an agent preset with --preset; override the effective selection with -a/--agent, -m/--model, and --variant. Use --variant base to select no named variant. Every override is validated against the current coherent runtime before a session starts.

--resume-session <id> continues an existing session and defaults to its creation preset. Supplying --preset selects a different preset for that run without rewriting the session's creation selection. See Agent presets for resolution and persistence details. --data-dir <path> selects the session and artifact store. --max-turns and --timeout are positive guards and default to 100 root model turns and 600 seconds. Reaching either guard cancels the run and waits for its terminal event. A stop signal (SIGINT, SIGTERM, or SIGHUP; on Windows Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Break, a closed console, logoff, or shutdown) follows the same cancellation path.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
--permission-mode accepts auto-approve (auto_approve), auto-approve-n (auto_approve_n), auto-approve-y (auto_approve_y), ask, or yolo. The selected mode applies to the whole runtime session tree, including delegated descendants. Headless runs never wait for approval input. In auto-approve-n, a reviewer escalation is rejected and cancels the root run with exit code 3. In auto-approve-y, an escalation is approved once and the run continues automatically, except a call whose review failed, which escalates. Other escalations anywhere in the session tree are rejected; the runner cancels the root run and waits for the matching terminal event. A question an ACP agent asks anywhere in the tree is declined, with the reason "a headless cookie run has no one to answer", and the run goes on.

--allowed-tools may be repeated or comma-delimited and accepts any permission action, such as read, write, bash, webfetch, delegate, or mcp (a lowercase letter, then lowercase letters, digits, or _, at most 32 bytes), and skill:<name> — each entry adds an allow overlay rule (resource *, or the given skill name). It does not deny omitted actions. The rule replaces only the agent's rule with the same pattern: --allowed-tools bash turns the agent's bash: ask into allow, but a narrower agent rule such as delegate: {reviewer: ask} still decides the calls it matches (see How the levels combine).

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: --skill <name> loads a user-invocable skill before the prompt run. --skill-args <text> supplies its raw arguments and requires --skill. Skill permission is evaluated before injection; use --allowed-tools skill:<name> to grant it explicitly in unattended runs. The load appends the same durable event used by interactive and model invocation.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Select text, json, or none with -o/--output. --json is an alias for --output json and conflicts with an explicit --output. --output-file redirects text or JSON output to a file and cannot be combined with --output none.

Text mode writes only the terminal final_text to standard output. It does not stream model deltas. With --verbose, ANSI-free progress lines are written to standard error, including one for each finished tool call: cookie run: tool and the call's title (with (failed), (cancelled), or (interrupted) when it did not complete), then the first eight lines of its display as plain text, indented, and a count of the rest. --output none prints the same lines. Failures and model fallback diagnostics are written to standard error regardless of verbosity, including recovered failures in a successful run.

JSON mode writes JSON Lines. Records use these stable type tags:

  • event: one accepted, ordered event for the active run.
  • tool_output: a retained or live tool-output delta, emitted with --verbose.
  • tool_output_gap: a tool-output retention or delivery gap, emitted with --verbose.
  • summary: the final record, containing terminal status and exit code, IDs, turn/rejection/recovery counts, cancellation cause, final text, error detail, and the session usage and estimated-cost rollup.

--output none suppresses command output. Diagnostics and verbose progress still use standard error.

docs.title: Failure diagnostics
docs.text: cookie run writes failure diagnostics to stderr even with --output none and without --verbose. JSON output retains diagnostic event fields and adds an error field to the final summary (null for success). A failed tool or fallback can produce stderr diagnostics even if the overall run subsequently succeeds. This includes internal-agent fallback failures and session-scoped plugin notices for the selected session. Events from unrelated sessions/runs remain excluded. Exit codes retain their existing meanings.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
The active run's terminal event determines the runtime exit code. Command-line syntax errors use Clap's exit code 2 before the runtime starts.

Exit code Meaning 0 RunCompleted, or user_before_input intentionally handled the input without starting a run 1 RunFailed, blocked model selection, or an unrecoverable active-driver failure 3 RunCancelled after the engine accepted a permission-triggered cancellation 4 Other RunCancelled outcomes and every RunInterrupted, including a stop signal, timeout, and turn-limit cancellation 5 Environment or setup failure before the run becomes active

docs.title: Terminal UI
docs.text: This page covers the terminal UI: starting it, the composer and its attachments, the command palette, steering and queueing, the transcript, error details, background calls, approvals, the runtimes panel, and the usage dashboard. The web client works with the same daemon from a browser, the command line runs a prompt without a UI, and Persistent daemon covers running the daemon apart from the TUI and how plain cookie finds one already running.

docs.title: Starting the TUI
docs.text:
Start in the workspace where the agent should operate:

cookie

When a daemon already runs on this machine, cookie opens the terminal client on it (see A daemon already running); otherwise it starts the engine and the terminal client together in one process. The bottom bar starts with where the engine runs: the daemon's address, or standalone (after the session's project, while no run is active). Configure the theme and diagnostic filter in the independent client configuration. When at least one model is available, select an agent and model if needed, type a request in the composer, and press Enter. If no authored root agent is runnable, the engine supplies the built-in default coding agent. Every clickable element highlights under the mouse pointer; text fields, such as the composer and picker searches, show their caret instead.

Useful first commands, from the command palette, are /sessions, /new, /model, /compact, and /cancel. Agent covers authored prompts and permissions.

Model fallback progress is local to the session. For a chain [A, B, C], once B commits a successful model turn after fallback, later turns and runs continue from [B, C]. A later successful fallback to C leaves [C]. This survives replay and restart, and the TUI updates its next-run model accordingly. A failed attempt alone does not advance the durable selection; if every candidate fails, the last accepted/successful starting point remains available.

Choose an earlier model in the picker, or use cookie run --model ... when resuming, to explicitly restore its suffix. Explicit agent/preset choices take precedence. New sessions use the configured starting selection; configuration files and previous runs' frozen chains are never rewritten.

docs.title: Composer
docs.text:
Enter submits the composer, and Alt-Enter queues it (see Steering, queueing, and the pending strip). Use Shift-Enter, Ctrl-Enter, or Ctrl-J to insert a newline. Arrow keys move by character or visual line; Ctrl-Left and Ctrl-Right move by word. Ctrl-Backspace and Ctrl-Delete remove a word. Home and End move within a line, while Ctrl-Home and Ctrl-End move to the start or end of the whole draft. Tab and Shift-Tab cycle the draft agent; Ctrl-T cycles the draft model's variants, like clicking the bracketed variant in the composer title. In an existing session the agent, model, and variant are the session's: once a pick settles it is shared with every client attached to the daemon, whose drafts follow it and say another client picked it. The latest pick wins. Ctrl-A selects the whole draft; typing or pasting over a selection replaces it. The composer keeps keyboard focus while you click around the conversation; only a panel, the command palette, or an approval on top of it takes focus away. Each session keeps its own draft, text and attached files: switching to another session shows that session's, and switching back brings yours back. A new session's draft (/new) is kept the same way until its first message creates the session. Drafts stay in the TUI's memory and end when it exits.

The agent and model panels include search fields. Agent search matches agent IDs and descriptions; model search matches display names and provider/model_id. Both are case-insensitive. Use Down, Tab, or Enter to move from the search field into the matching rows.

On Unix, Ctrl+Z suspends the TUI to the shell as it would any terminal program, and fg brings it back with its screen redrawn. A TUI stopped some other way, such as kill -STOP or an editor opened from /config or /memory being suspended along with it, takes its terminal back and redraws when it is continued.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text: When the selected model accepts files (images, PDFs, audio, or video; see Attaching media), /attach asks for the path of a file and attaches it to the next message. Pasting text that is exactly the path of one existing file, as a terminal pastes a file dropped on it, asks whether to attach that file; Cancel pastes the path as text instead. The TUI uploads the file to the daemon, which may run on another machine, so the path only needs to exist where the TUI runs. Before uploading, it refuses a kind of file the model does not accept (and says which kinds it does), a file larger than the model's limit, and an image with more pixels than the model takes, naming the limit; it does not shrink images. Each attachment shows on the composer's bottom border as 📎 name · type · size; Backspace at the start of the draft removes the newest one. A message may be attachments alone. A message taken back from the pending strip, or handed back after it failed to send, returns its attachments with its text.

docs.title: Command palette
docs.text:
Press / in an empty composer, or Ctrl-P at any time, to open the command palette. The palette has its own search field: what you type there filters the commands and never touches the composer, so a half-written message survives opening, searching, and closing the palette. Up and Down move, Enter chooses, and Esc closes. Matches rank exact names first, then prefixes, then substrings. Some commands have aliases, listed below, that match the search the same way but are never shown in the list.

Commands that need input ask for it in a follow-up step instead of taking typed arguments; /rename alone takes its title after it in the search. Esc in a step returns to the command list with the search intact.

Command Action /new Choose the next root-run agent /preset Select the preset for the next root run and future new sessions; see Agent presets /agent Choose the agent for the next run /model Choose the model for the next run, then its variant; nothing applies until the variant is chosen, and Esc in the variant list returns to the models; each row shows, dimmed after its name, the ID an agent document's models writes for it (the model's provider/model key, the variant's ID, an ACP agent's option value), once when the name is the ID; for an ACP agent, which chooses its own model, it lists the values of the agent's model option, and the title's bracketed variant (or ctrl+t) cycles its effort option; a new session's draft offers what the agent last started a session with /options Change the options of the session's ACP agent, such as its model, mode, and effort: pick an option, then a value; listed while the agent offers options /connect Connect or update a managed provider; Enter on a connected one opens its details, titled by its name with its ID dimmed and listing its available models (each name with its model ID dimmed beside it; ↑↓, PgUp/PgDn, Home/End, and the wheel scroll), where R reconnects (signs in again) and D disconnects /mcp Manage MCP servers; see MCP servers /runtime (also runtimes) Attach and detach the selected session's runtimes, or choose a new session's before its first prompt; see Runtimes panel /background (also bg) List and stop the selected session's background calls; see Background calls /config Edit the daemon's config.toml and agent documents in your editor, create and delete agents, reload hand edits (r or Reload from disk), and restart the daemon (R or Restart daemon, highlighted while a part waits for a restart); see config.toml /restart Restart the daemon, when idle or now; see Restarting the daemon /onboard Set up Cookie: connect a provider, choose the default and small models, and install the starter kit; see Setting up /memory (also memories) Browse the daemon's memories by layer, edit one in your editor, create and delete memories, and see invalid files with the reason; see Memory /cron (also crons) List, create, edit, enable and disable, run now, and delete the daemon's cron jobs; see Scheduled prompts /cron new Schedule a prompt in the session on screen: opens a new job's form for it; listed only while a session is open; see Scheduled prompts /plugins (also plugin) Show each plugin's status, tools, hooks, and last failure, and restart one with r; see Plugins /permissions (also perms) Edit session permission overrides; see Permissions /sessions (also resume, load, continue) Choose a session, rename or delete one, or list every directory's; see Session picker /project (also projects) Choose the project of the selected session, or of a new session before its first prompt; see Projects /rename (also title) Rename the selected session: /rename <title> sets the title, /rename --auto goes back to the generated title, and /rename alone asks for the title in a field holding the current one; see Renaming /skills Search user-invocable skills, pick one, then enter optional arguments; see Skills /attach (also file, image) Ask for a file's path and attach it to the next message; listed only when the selected model accepts files; see Attachments /usage Show selected-session and session-tree usage /cancel Cancel the active run /goal Prompt for an objective and set the root session's goal; see Goal mode /compact Prompt for an optional focus, then compact the selected idle session /events Pick the diagnostic event filter from a list /transcript reduced, /transcript full Fold each reply's thinking and tool calls into one row, or show all of them; saved as transcript in tui.toml; see Transcript details /agent-panel show, /agent-panel hide, /agent-panel auto Pin the agent panel shown or hidden for the current root session, or return it to following delegated agents (the default) /quit (also q, exit) Exit the TUI

In a read-only session owned by another cookie process, commands that write to the session (/permissions, /runtime, /skills, /attach, /cancel, /goal, /compact, /rename, /cron new, /options) are hidden.

In a session of an ACP agent, the palette also lists the slash commands the agent offers, after cookie's own and marked (agent). Choosing one that takes input asks for it; choosing one sends /<name> <input> to the agent. The agent picker lists the agents runtimes offer with where the session would run them (claude [on local]); one that cannot run there is dimmed with why ([needs lab attached], [offered by lab, local: attach one], [on lab · unavailable]) and cannot be picked. The agent's plan shows in the transcript as a checklist ([x] done, [~] in progress, [ ] pending), its own tool calls name it after their title and fill in their arguments as the agent sends them, and its notices show as Notice blocks. A message steered into the agent's running turn stays in the pending strip until the agent takes it, then shows as any user message; every ACP v2 agent can be steered; only a session last run by an ACP v1 agent of an earlier build says queued: this agent can't be steered in the pending strip, the message waiting for the agent's next turn.

The composer only ever sends messages: text beginning with / is sent as a prompt like any other. To start a message with /, open the palette and type / in its empty search; the palette closes and a literal / lands in the composer. A / typed after other text, as in a path, is always literal.

docs.title: Restarting the daemon
docs.text:
While the daemon's configuration lists parts that apply only after a restart, a banner above the conversation says so, such as ⟳ Restart needed to apply: plugins, runtimes, with a Restart daemon button. The button, /restart, and R or Restart daemon in /config open the same confirmation:

  • Restart when idle (Enter or i, the default) waits until no turn is running in any session and every background call has reported; new turns are refused meanwhile.
  • Restart now (n) interrupts the running turns and ends the background calls; the confirmation says how many turns there are.
  • Cancel (Esc) keeps the daemon running and returns to the panel it opened over.

Once the daemon announces the restart, the banner shows Restarting when idle… (2 running turns, 1 background call) until the connection closes, then the TUI reconnects as after any dropped connection. A daemon not started by cookie daemon, including the engine of cookie --standalone, cannot restart itself and says so. See Restarting the daemon.

docs.title: Setting up
docs.text:
When the TUI connects to a daemon that is not set up (no provider connected, or default_model or small_model not naming an available model), a notice takes the bar above the composer: what is left, then Set up and Not now. Set up opens the onboarding panel; Not now hides the notice on this machine (in ~/.cookie-agent/tui-state.json) until what the daemon misses changes. /onboard opens the panel any time, also on a daemon that is set up. Every client sees the same state: finishing in the web client or with cookie onboard hides the notice here too.

The panel shows the four steps as tabs, each done one with a check; ← and → (or Tab) move between them, and a tab can be clicked:

  1. Provider: the connected providers with their count of available models. Enter opens the connect panel (/connect); it returns to the panel when it closes.
  2. Default model: Enter opens the model list, searchable and grouped by provider; choosing a model with variants opens its variants, the model's default variant highlighted.
  3. Small model: the same list with nothing suggested; the variant list highlights the model's first listed variant, its cheapest. It may be the same model as the default.
  4. Starter kit: what installing the kit does to each file (new, same as yours and skipped, or differs and written beside yours as .new); Up and Down select a file and d shows its diff. i turns installing on or off, and o takes the path of a downloaded cookie-agent-defaults.tar.gz instead of the release's kit.

f (or the finish button) sets everything up with onboarding.run; while something is missing the panel says what instead. The summary lists the settings and files written and offers a first session on primary. n is Not now, and Esc closes the panel.

docs.title: Steering, queueing, and the pending strip
docs.text:
While a run is active, a message can reach it two ways:

  • Enter steers. The message enters a durable pending lane the model has not seen yet. At the next tool or completion boundary, pending messages join the running conversation in submission order as separate user messages.
  • Alt-Enter queues. The message waits for the run to finish, then starts a new run of its own with the selection current when it was queued. Queued messages run one at a time, oldest first.

On an idle session both keys simply start a run. The daemon decides between starting, steering, and queueing atomically, so a run that another client starts or that ends while you type only changes which of those happens.

The Pending strip shows both lanes: ⏳ rows are steered messages and ⏭ rows are queued ones. It shows up to three rows and folds additional entries into +N more. Several clients can share one daemon (see Architecture); a message another client sent is labelled with that client, such as · tui-0192f3. Click a row to take that message back into your composer for editing, another client's too (a daemon before client protocol 1.31.0 lets only the client that sent it), or press Up in an empty composer to take back your newest one.

Queued messages run only after the current run completes normally. If the run fails or is cancelled, or the daemon restarts mid-run, the queue is cleared, and each client gets its own unsent messages, steered or queued, back in its composer, as it does with steered messages a run never reached. This happens only for a run that ends while the TUI is connected; replayed history never restores text, so opening or reattaching to an old session leaves the composer alone.

docs.title: Selection and clipboard
docs.text:
Drag in the conversation or composer to select text. Ctrl-C copies the selected text and clears the selection; Ctrl-X cuts only a composer selection. With no selection, Ctrl-C cancels the active run, stopping the tool calls it is running at once (see Cancelling a run); when there is nothing to interrupt, pressing it twice within two seconds quits. Esc clears a selection before it can count toward the double-Esc run-cancel gesture.

Conversation copy removes role gutters, borders, and code-fence chrome, so code is copied as raw source. Clipboard writes use OSC 52 and work over SSH when the terminal emulator supports OSC 52.

docs.title: Session picker
docs.text:
/sessions lists the root sessions of the directory the TUI started in, newest first under day headings, by your last message or delegation in each (its own output does not move it; one with none goes by its last event); type to filter them by title, and press Enter or click a row to open one.

  • Ctrl+A, or the All directories button, lists every directory's sessions instead, each row naming its directory; press it again (the button now reads This directory) to go back. In the search field, Home still moves to the start of the text.
  • Ctrl+P, or the project button beside it, filters by project: all projects, then each project oldest first, then the sessions in no project, then all again. The picker's title names the project shown. Each row names its project, with its emoji, before its agent.
  • A session a cron job started leads with a clock, 🕒, before its title, and an unread one with ●: it finished, or waits on an approval or a question, while nobody was there to see it (unread sessions). Viewing it in a focused terminal you used in the last 2 minutes reads it, in every client.
  • Ctrl+K, or the Mark read / Mark unread button, marks the highlighted session read, or unread when it is read (with a daemon of client protocol 1.51 or later).
  • Ctrl+R, or the Rename button, renames the highlighted session: a field holding its title opens over the search. See Renaming.
  • Ctrl+D, Delete while the list has focus, or the Delete button asks to delete the highlighted session. The confirmation names the session and says how many subagent sessions go with it; y or Enter (or Confirm) deletes it, and n or Esc (or Cancel) keeps it. While it is open, the rows behind it do not respond to clicks.

Deleting removes the whole tree from disk: the session, its subagents, and their messages, tool output, and attachments. It cannot be undone. The daemon refuses while the session or one of its subagents is running, while another cookie process owns it, and when it changed since the picker showed it; the status line then says why. A daemon older than client protocol 1.5 cannot delete sessions, and the TUI says so instead of asking. When the session you are viewing is deleted, from this TUI or another client, the TUI leaves it for a new session, as it does when it starts without one. See Delete.

docs.title: Renaming
docs.text:
A session's title is generated from its first messages (see Session Title); a title you set replaces it.

  • /rename Fix the parser sets the selected session's title.
  • /rename --auto drops your title for the generated one again.
  • /rename alone, and Ctrl+R in the session picker, open a field holding the current title. Enter saves it; Enter on an emptied field goes back to the generated title, and Esc keeps the title as it was.

The title can be up to 512 bytes, without line breaks; a longer one stays in the field with the reason in the status line. Every client sees the new title at once. A session you have not sent a first message to yet has nothing to rename.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
While no run is active, the bottom bar starts with the session's project: its emoji and name, or no project. That covers a session you have open and a new session before its first prompt. An emoji counts as two columns. Click the name, or choose /project, for the project picker: the projects, No project, and New project…, which asks for a name and creates the project.

  • An open session moves to the project you pick with session.project.set, even while it runs; its runtimes and agent stay. A subagent belongs to its root session's project, so select the root to move it.
  • A new session is created in the project you pick. A project whose defaults name runtimes gives them to the draft, and the bottom bar shows their workspaces before you send anything; otherwise the draft keeps the usual runtimes. Its default agent and preset become the draft's, with the agent's own model; an agent that is gone, or cannot start a session, leaves the usual one, and the status line says so.

A new session belongs to no project unless you pick one; cookie --project <name> starts in one, and nothing is ever picked from the directory the TUI started in. A daemon older than client protocol 1.8 keeps no projects, so the bar names none and /project is not offered.

docs.title: User-message menu
docs.text:
Click a past You message to open its action menu. Use Up/Down and Enter, Esc to close, or the c, r, and f accelerators.

  • Copy writes the original message text to the clipboard.
  • Revert asks for confirmation, removes that message and everything after it from the session (including subagents it started), and restores the message text to the composer. If the session gained events since this view last showed it, for example a turn another client started, the revert is refused so nothing unseen is deleted; review the new turns and revert again.
  • Fork creates and selects an independent session whose copied prefix includes that message.

Assistant and tool rows keep their normal expand/collapse behavior and do not open the message menu.

docs.title: Transcript details
docs.text:
By default the transcript is reduced: each reply's thinking, tool calls, and the text written between calls fold into one row above the reply, ▸ Working… 42s · 3 tool calls with what the agent is doing now on the line under it while it works, then ▸ Worked for 1m 23s · 7 tool calls. Click the row to open the work, and again to fold it. A call waiting for your approval stays outside the fold. Ctrl-O, /transcript full, and /transcript reduced switch between the reduced and the full transcript, which shows every thinking block and tool call, and save the choice; see Transcript.

The conversation follows new output while it rests at the bottom. Scrolling up (the wheel, Page Up, the scrollbar) stops following at once, and the title says ↑ scrolled · PgDn: bottom until you scroll back to the bottom or send a message (steered or queued too): output that streams in, or a block that folds below, never moves a scrolled-up view.

System prompts, AGENTS.md context, loaded skills, context compaction checkpoints, plugin-injected messages, and committed media parts appear collapsed by default. An AGENTS.md row appears at a run whose loaded context differs from the previous run's: the first load, a change, or loading again after a run without AGENTS.md. A run that reloads identical files adds no row. A run's loads make one row, as they make one turn for the model: its header names the files, and expanded, it shows the turn as the model reads it, the instructions around the files and each file's <contents from=…> tag included. A compaction row opens to the summary in the frame the model reads it in. A skill row shows the skill's source path, arguments, and rendered body. An AGENTS.md file skipped for size appears as a warning row. A reply an interrupt cut off with content left says model interrupted and quotes the marker later requests follow it with, [Response interrupted — it was cut off before it finished].

Everything else the engine adds to the model's input has a collapsed row too, whose body is the exact text the model reads: the memory snapshot (🧠 memory · 42 lines, again whenever the snapshot changes, and a row saying so when memory leaves the model's context), each deferred tools announcement (deferred tools · 3 added), the parent's conversation a subagent starts from (context from the parent · 4 turns), and the context an ACP agent's first prompt carries (context sent to claude · 120 lines). Under a tool call's output, its row shows what the result sent the model beyond the tool's own output: a loop warning, each message the tool emitted, and, once the output left the model's context, the marker the model reads in its place. These bodies are bounded like system prompts. A session's system-prompt row remains hidden until its first run starts, then identifies the agent from the latest run snapshot. If the next-run draft uses another agent, the row also shows next: <agent>. Click one of these rows to show or hide its text or metadata. Expansion state is kept separately for each session. Expanded system prompts, skill bodies, and each AGENTS.md file are display-bounded to 256 lines or 32 KiB of sanitized text; compaction, plugin-message, and media bodies are bounded to 64 lines or 8 KiB. Oversized content ends with a truncated-lines indicator while the complete data remains in session state.

Expanding a tool row opens its title block: the header, followed by the rest of the call's title and primary argument when the collapsed header had to shorten them. The whole title block is one click target. A row's icon comes from the tool's hint (shell, file read, file edit, fetch, search, delegation, and so on; any other tool gets the hammer), never from its name, so a plugin or MCP tool shows the same way a built-in one does when it describes itself the same way. The header shows the call's title, and its primary argument after it unless the title already names it. While a call runs, its latest progress message follows the title.

Expanded tools use ordinary text colours and end with a blank row: a grey title block over a lighter grey panel. The panel shows the call's argument blocks (a command, a URL) under a muted arguments label, leaving out what the header already says: a block whose text is the header's primary argument or the text its title quotes, and a key/value row that only repeats the primary argument. A block that says more, such as a long command the header shortened, stays. Then comes what the call shows, drawn by the kind of each block rather than by which tool sent it:

  • Diffs name how the file changed (created, modified, deleted, or renamed), its path, and the lines added and removed, then each hunk with real file line numbers and +/- markers in a gutter, added and removed rows on the theme's diff tints, highlighted by language. A diff too large to carry its lines shows the counts alone.
  • Terminal output draws the program's SGR colours (fitted to the terminal's colour depth, and none under NO_COLOR), stderr in the warning tone unless the program coloured it, and the exit code below, red when it is not zero. It grows while the command runs.
  • File excerpts and code show file line numbers and are highlighted by language; JSON is pretty-printed; markdown renders like the assistant's text; tables and key/value lists align their columns.
  • Media shows a chip, 📎 name · type · size; a link its label and address; a session reference a row you can click to open that session.

A call without argument blocks shows its raw arguments instead, and only when the diagnostic filter is info or debug (see /events). Output beyond the row budget ends with … N more lines (click to expand). A block the tool had to cut says how much is missing, and when it names its complete content (a long command's stdout, a large diff), click to load the full output reads up to 1 MiB of it from the daemon and shows it in place of the cut rows; click the row under it to put it away again.

OpenAI Responses turns can retain opaque continuation witnesses for provider metadata such as message phase, annotations, and logprobs. Keep these parts alongside native replay data when preserving or restoring history. Internal agents validate the transport parts while using the text for summaries, approval decisions, and titles. Older saved turns may lack witnesses that were not captured at the time; historical events are not rewritten to invent them.

docs.title: Error details
docs.text:
When the daemon refuses a request, the TUI's status line and the CLI show its message, a sentence a person can act on, and then its hint, what to do next. Every refusal also has a stable code (see Errors). Technical detail, such as the upstream cause or a path, is shown on request: the TUI adds an error row to the session you are viewing whose first line is the error and whose collapsed rest, behind ▸, is the detail; the CLI prints it with --error-details, an option of every command.

Run failures show a concise headline followed by available model/provider identity, HTTP status, provider code, request ID, and response body. The same diagnostics are retained in session events and shown on replay. Model fallback and internal agent failures also include the available response diagnostics. Warning and error rows lead with 🚨 or ❌ instead of a badge row. A multiline diagnostic row shows only its first line, behind a ▸; click it to show the rest, such as a response body. A warning or error identical to the row before it counts on that row (repeated 6×) instead of adding a copy, so a retry loop hitting the same provider error stays one row; this includes subagent rows shown in an ancestor's transcript. For a failed tool, expand the tool row for its display output. Failed tools show their failure reason before their bounded inline output, even when they supplied separate display text. Tools with usable output do not add a separate TUI error row; output-less failures still do. A bash command's non-zero exit code is normal result data, not a tool failure. Genuine execution failures such as timeouts remain failures. Bounded diagnostics prioritize exit status, source context, and diagnostic streams such as stderr. Each stream gets space for its beginning and end so loud stdout cannot hide a later failure cause. MCP connection failures appear in /mcp; plugin initialization and RPC failures preserve operation context and selected cause fields. Configuration errors identify invalid settings and, for file/parse failures, available paths and locations without printing configuration source lines. Transport failures retain send/receive context for pending calls and appear as connection diagnostics in the TUI. Rejected WebSocket handshakes show a bounded, response body with its content preserved when supplied, without printing response headers.

Response bodies are capped at 4,096 UTF-8 bytes with a truncation marker. JSON is formatted for reading; plaintext and HTML gateway errors remain plain text. Terminal controls and Unicode format controls are stripped or replaced with spaces; newlines and tabs are preserved. The application does not redact credential-like text, sensitive field names, header records within a response body, or echoed secret values. It does not add request headers or credential-store dumps to diagnostics. MCP OAuth failures likewise preserve bounded response bodies and authorization error descriptions. Retained diagnostics have the same access and persistence rules as other session events.

The pinned model SDK preserves sanitized HTTP error-body text for OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Google, Google Vertex, Bedrock, Azure, and Cohere. SDK body retention is bounded to 64 KiB; the application further sanitizes and bounds displayed and persisted body diagnostics to 4 KiB. The pinned SDK still redacts some provider response fields before the application receives them; the application preserves the text it receives and cannot recover replaced values. A body is available only when the provider returned one: validation, connection, or cancellation errors may have no HTTP response body. Missing detail is not reconstructed or fetched with another API request.

cookie run reports failures on its own streams; see Failure diagnostics.

Internal tracing logs are off by default. Setting RUST_LOG (for example RUST_LOG=debug, using tracing-subscriber filter syntax) writes them to stderr, never stdout, so they cannot mix into cookie run output or the daemon ready line. The TUI draws on the same terminal, so redirect stderr to a file when logging a TUI session: RUST_LOG=debug cookie 2>cookie.log.

docs.title: Live tool output
docs.text: Expanded command rows show sanitized stdout and stderr while the command runs, with the call's latest progress message above them. The live display is capped at 64 KiB. On completion, failure, cancellation, or interruption, the same row swaps to the call's result display; a call that ended without one keeps what it showed while running. Reopening a session renders only that committed content. Assistant text follows the same rule: streamed partials are replaced by the committed turn.

docs.title: Scheduled prompts
docs.text:
/cron opens the daemon's cron jobs: prompts it fires on a schedule, into a session or into a new session per fire. Each row shows the job's name (or the start of its prompt), its schedule read plainly (every day at 03:00, every Monday to Friday at 09:30, once, once at 2026-10-23 03:00), how long until its next fire, its target (the session's title, subagent <title>, or new session · <agent>), whether it is enabled or why not (finished, failed 3 times in a row, disabled by you), and what its last fire did. Under the list, Details gives the selected job's target and, for a job an agent made, the session it was created in, both by title; a click on either, or o and c, shows that session's transcript. Then come its schedule, run count, delivery, template, and prompt. History lists its fires, newest first, each with its outcome and how its run ended. The title says when the daemon's firing is off ([cron] enabled = false).

Up and Down select a job, or click its row. Each action is a key and a button below the panel:

Key Action e or Enter Edit the selected job n Create a job: into the session on screen, or, with none open, into a new session per fire t Enable or disable the selected job r Run it now; the status line says what the fire did d Delete it, after y confirms; its run sessions stay o Show the transcript of the session it fires into c Show the transcript of the session an agent created it in Esc Cancel a confirmation or a refused form, else close the panel

/cron new in the command palette opens a new job's form for the session on screen directly: a root session is targeted as a session, a subagent's as a subagent.

A job is created and edited as a short form in $VISUAL or $EDITOR, as /memory and /config edit theirs: key: value lines, then the prompt after a --- line. Lines starting with # explain the fields and are ignored.

name: Nightly dependency check
schedule: 0 3 * * *
max_runs: 0
target: new
delivery: queue
agent: builder
model: deepseek/deepseek-flash[high]
permission_mode: ask
---
Check for outdated dependencies and open a summary.
  • schedule is five cron fields in the daemon host's local time, a delay (in 20m), or a time (at 2026-10-23T03:00:00Z).
  • max_runs applies to cron schedules: a whole number, 0 or less for no limit; left empty, the job fires once.
  • target: session fires into the session the form was opened for (or the job's own session when editing); target: new starts a session per fire.
  • delivery (queue or steer) applies to a session target; agent, model, and permission_mode to a new-session target. model pins provider/model or provider/model[variant]; empty, the agent's own chain runs. permission_mode empty means auto_approve_n.

A new-session job's template starts from the session on screen: its agent and preset (the agent you picked for its next run), its project, and the directory the TUI started in; with no session open, from the agent a new session would get. Saving unchanged text creates or changes nothing, and an edit sends only the fields it changed. A form the TUI cannot read, or that the daemon refuses, stays open with the reason: e edits it again as you left it, Esc drops it. The panel refreshes when any client or agent changes a job. A daemon older than client protocol 1.15 keeps no jobs: /cron says so, and /cron new is not offered. See Scheduling prompts for how jobs fire.

docs.title: Background calls
docs.text:
A running call of a tool that supports the background (such as bash or delegate_subagent) shows a [background] button at the right end of its title row. Clicking it moves the call to the background once the tool can be detached: the call's row ends with the result the model got (User manually moved this call to the background …) and · background, and the run goes on while the call keeps running. The model can also start a call in the background itself.

While the selected session has background calls, a bar above the composer lists them; clicking it, or /background, opens a panel with one row per call (job, tool, its argument, how long it has run, and who moved it). Up/Down select a row, s or a row's [stop] stops that call, and Esc closes the panel. A stopped call still reports to the model, as stopped by you. A subagent working on its own, outside a call that waits for it, is listed under its handle; stopping it cancels the turn it is running, and the subagent reports that turn as cancelled. Cancelling the session's run (Esc) never stops its subagents. See Background calls for what the model sees.

An ACP agent's own command that keeps running after its call ended (such as Claude Code's background shell) is listed in the bar too, without a stop. When it ends, the transcript shows a row where the end arrived, ◇ ▸ Background: <command> ended; opening it shows the agent's tool, how long the command ran in the background, its exit code when the agent says it, and the whole command. When the end wakes the agent, the row comes before the agent's own run, which still says only that the agent woke on its own.

docs.title: Approvals
docs.text:
An approval docks above the status bar in place of the composer, leaving the conversation visible above it. It shows the call it gates the way you need to judge it: its icon and title, its argument blocks (such as a command), and its preview (such as an edit's or write's diff as of preparing the call), drawn as the transcript draws them; a call that describes neither shows the request's resources. Below that, why says what asked (your permission rule and its source, or the model's own reason), reviewer gives the approval reviewer's reason for passing the call to you ("The reviewer asks: …", or that its review failed), and a last row says what the focused decision does. A call the reviewer allowed or denied without you names its reason in its info row. A countdown appears in the top border when the request expires (the window opens when the call reaches you), and d (or clicking details) expands the full prepared-operation identity: ids, fingerprints, and the policy trace.

The decisions follow the request's constraints: allow once, allow for the session tree, reject, or cancel. Left/Right or Tab move focus between them and Enter answers with the focused one; each button also names its own key: y allows once, a allows for the session tree, n rejects, and Esc cancels when the request is cancellable. Letter keys are case-insensitive and do nothing for a decision the request does not offer. Clicking a button answers with it.

e opens a note for a rejection: type why, or what the agent should do instead, and press Enter to reject with it; the agent receives the note with the refusal. Esc closes the note without answering, and an empty note sends a plain rejection. Long panels scroll with arrows, Page Up/Page Down, Home, and End, or the mouse wheel.

While an approval is on top it owns the keyboard: other typing and pastes are dropped rather than landing in the hidden composer (a paste goes into an open note), and Ctrl-C still cancels the run. Enter, the letter keys, and e ignore presses for 400 ms after a request appears, so keystrokes already on their way to the composer cannot answer it; the panel says so beside its buttons, and a second press once it has settled goes through.

The permission mode appears in the bottom bar. Click it to cycle auto-approve -> auto-n -> auto-y -> ask -> yolo; the mode applies to subsequent approvals throughout the selected session tree, including delegated descendants. While a new-session draft is open, the mode shown and cycled is the draft's own, applied when its first prompt creates the session. Hard policy denies and doom-loop rejection still win in every mode. See Permissions.

When pricing is available, the bottom bar also shows the selected session's estimated cost between the permission mode and context usage. Click the cost to open the /usage dashboard. Unpriced sessions omit the segment.

The left of the bottom bar shows the session's project while no run is active (see Projects), then the runtimes the selected session, or a new session before its first prompt, attaches besides global. With one, it shows the runtime and its workspace, for example labpc · ~/api; with several, their attachment names, for example local_web, labpc_api. It shows global when that is all the session attaches, and no runtimes for a session with none.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: An ACP agent's question docks in the same place, titled <agent> asks · waiting on you, while no approval is on top. A form lists its fields: radios for a choice, boxes for a multiple choice and for yes or no, and a line for text and numbers, each with its title, what it takes (required, bounds, a format), and its description. Tab and Shift-Tab move between the fields and the buttons, the arrows between a field's choices (past the last, on to the next field), Space picks a choice or flips a box, and Enter picks and moves on, or presses the focused button. Submit checks the form and, when a field does not fit, names it under the field and moves there; Decline and Cancel (Esc) answer at once. A page to open shows its host, the whole URL, and any warning; focus starts on Copy link (c), and Done answers once you have finished there. The panel owns the keyboard and pastes (a paste goes into the focused text field), the wheel scrolls it when it is long, Ctrl-C cancels the run, and the answers wait out the same 400 ms as an approval's.

docs.title: Notifications on other devices
docs.text: The daemon can push a notification to a phone or a browser when a session finishes its turn or an approval waits (turn them on in the web client; see Notifications). It pushes nothing for the session the TUI shows while its terminal has focus and you used it in the last two minutes. The TUI asks the terminal to report focus; in a terminal that does not (or inside a multiplexer that does not pass it on), the TUI never says you are there, so the push still comes.

docs.title: Runtimes panel
docs.text:
/runtime (titled Attached runtimes) lists the selected session's runtime attachments: each attachment's name, runtime and capability (labpc/coding), workspace, and instance status (starting, ready, reconnecting, failed, stopped, or not running), and the MCP servers its instance hosts counted by state (MCP 1 connected, 1 failed). The details pane shows the selected attachment's kind, what its capability offers (the runtime's description of it), platform, for a failed instance the reason, and each MCP server the instance hosts with its state, tool count, and why it failed or what it waits for (from mcp.server.list), its runtime's runtime-scoped servers among them marked runtime-wide. The machines view counts each runtime's MCP servers the same way and lists them in the selected runtime's details, including, before any workspace of it is open, its runtime-scoped servers and its workspace-scoped ones as starts with a workspace. Under each server the details list its tools by the server's own names (tools:) and those its filters left out (left out:), then the ACP agents the runtime offers, each available or not, with the templates over it. The details grow with them, up to half the panel. On a runtime, s opens /mcp with that runtime's servers only, where n adds one to it, and a opens its ACP agents: n declares one (its ID, command as a JSON array, environment, description, and whether it is enabled), e edits the selected one (a new ID renames it, and its document when no other runtime declares the old ID), space enables or disables it, d removes it (its documents stay), o opens its document in the editor (a new one from a template when it has none), t writes a template over it (acp.agent), and Esc returns to the machines. Every change is written to the runtime's [runtimes.<id>] table in the daemon's config.toml, and a connected runtime takes it at once. The panel refreshes on every runtime change and while it is open.

Press a to attach: the panel lists every capability of every runtime (labpc/coding, devbox/computer_use), with its description and whether the runtime is connected; the details below the list repeat the selected capability's description. Type to filter by runtime, capability, kind, or description, choose with the arrow keys, and press Enter. A capability that takes no workspace attaches at once; one that takes a workspace asks for its path next (Enter attaches, Esc returns to the list). A runtime that has not connected yet is one entry: attaching it connects it and takes its only capability, its workspace is optional, and the details show why its last connection failed. The path is passed to the runtime as typed and resolved on its machine (see Runtimes). Press d to detach the selected attachment, and r to retry its instance now, for example after fixing why it failed (runtimes.reconnect). The daemon refuses both while the session has an active run, and refuses attaching an instance the session already has; the refusal appears in the status line. Attaching starts the instance first and records nothing when it fails to start.

Before a new session's first prompt (at startup, or after /new), the panel edits the runtimes that session will attach, starting from the defaults: global, and the coding capability at the TUI's directory (local's, or this machine's when the daemon is remote). Each instance opens as soon as it joins the list, so its status and any failure show before the session exists, and an instance the list already holds is refused. a, d, and r edit the list and contact no session; the first prompt creates the session with exactly the listed runtimes, and fails without a session when one of them cannot start.

When an MCP server or runtime instance a session uses fails to connect, or drops and does not reconnect, the TUI adds an error row to each affected session naming the server or runtime and the reason (see MCP connection lifecycle).

docs.title: Usage dashboard
docs.text:
/usage opens a read-only view with the selected session first and its complete delegation tree second. The tree count includes the selected session. Each section shows request count, input, output, and reasoning tokens, cache reads and writes, cache hit percentage, estimated cost when configured, and a per-model breakdown. Models are sorted by descending estimated cost, with unpriced models last; ties use input tokens and then model name. Token counts use thousands separators, hit rates use one decimal place, and costs use the same formatting as the bottom bar. unpriced means the active configuration does not provide all rates needed for the observed token categories, while n/a means a hit rate cannot be computed.

Use Up/Down, Page Up/Page Down, or the mouse wheel to scroll when needed, and Esc to close. Clicking the selected session cost in the bottom bar still opens this panel.

See Usage and cost for recording and pricing semantics.

docs.title: Web
docs.text: cookie daemon serves a web client on the same port as its client endpoint. Open it in a browser on the daemon's machine, or on a laptop or phone that reaches that port (see Remote access). It does what the TUI does with the daemon's sessions and the daemon itself: chat, approvals, subagents, history edits, goals, attachments, skills, permissions, runtimes and machines, MCP servers, providers, the configuration, memory, scheduled prompts, and plugins. Two things stay in the TUI and the CLI; see What the page does not do.

docs.title: Opening the page
docs.text:
The daemon takes the page's connection from any origin, and the token is the guard (see Web clients). Print the page's address with the token:

cookie web          # prints http://127.0.0.1:7419/#token=<token>
cookie web --open   # also opens it in the system browser

cookie web finds the daemon like cookie attach:

  • --url and --token (or COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN) first;
  • then [server] url and [server] token in this machine's config.toml.

The page is the client URL with ws turned into http (wss into https) and the final /ws dropped. The daemon also prints the page's address, without the token, after its ready line.

The token travels in the address's fragment (#token=), which a browser never sends to a server. The page keeps the token in the browser's localStorage under the daemon's URL and removes the fragment from the address bar.

docs.title: The connect screen
docs.text:
• Daemon URL. The page fills it in from its own address:
  • http becomes ws, and https becomes wss;
  • the host and port stay the same;
  • ws is added to the page's directory.

You can edit it; the page remembers the last URL it connected to. - Token. It comes from a cookie web link, or you paste it from the daemon's ready line. - Connecting. With both a URL and a token, the page connects without a click. - Forget this daemon deletes the stored token and stops the daemon's notifications in this browser. Once connected, the same button is in the connection panel (below), behind a confirmation. - A refused connection. A browser shows a page no reason when the daemon refuses or closes its connection before the handshake, or nothing answers. The page says so and asks you to check the daemon URL and that the daemon is running. - Once connected, the foot of the rail (see Layout) shows the connection's state: connected, connecting, reconnecting, or offline. Hover over it for the daemon's address and version, or click it for a panel with them, Restart daemon (see Restarting the daemon), and Forget this daemon. Settings › This browser has Forget this daemon too. - Dropped connection. The page redials with the TUI's backoff, 500 ms rising to 10 s, under the same client identity. - Background tab. When it becomes visible again, the page checks the connection. - Separate clients. Each browser tab is its own client. - Theme. The theme button at the foot of the rail (in the header of the connect screen) cycles through system (a half circle), light (a sun), and dark (a moon). The choice stays in the browser.

docs.title: Setting up a daemon
docs.text:
A daemon that is not set up yet, with no provider connected or without a default_model and a small_model its providers offer (see onboarding), offers a first-run sheet when the page connects. It walks four steps, each starting from what is already configured, with Back and Next and a check on each step done:

  1. Provider: the connected providers with their count of available models, then the same provider list and connect forms as Settings › Providers; errors show in the form, which can be sent again. Several may be connected.
  2. Default model: a searchable list of the connected providers' models, grouped by provider, with their context size. Choosing one shows its variants as chips, the model's own default variant chosen.
  3. Small model: the same list, with nothing suggested; its chips start on the model's first listed variant, the cheapest. It may be the default model.
  4. Starter kit: what installing the release's kit does to each file, new, same as yours (skipped), or differs → written as .new, with Show the diff on a changed file; Install the kit or Skip it, and Use a downloaded kit… for a cookie-agent-defaults.tar.gz saved earlier.

Finish (onboarding.run) is disabled, with what is still needed beside it, until the daemon would be set up. It ends on a summary of the settings and files written and Start your first session, a new session drafted on the kit's primary agent. Not now closes the sheet; the browser remembers it for this daemon, and Settings › Set up Cookie opens the sheet again at any time, also on a daemon that is set up. Every page connected to the daemon follows onboarding.changed: finishing in one tab closes the sheet in the others. On a phone the sheet fills the screen.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
• The rail. An icon strip on the far left switches between six views; each icon names itself in a tooltip, and the view shown is marked by a bar at the rail's edge:
  • Chat (the default): the sessions sidebar and the transcript;
  • Agents: the agent documents and their presets, in a sidebar beside the one open;
  • Settings: Set up Cookie (see Setting up a daemon), config.toml, providers, MCP servers, plugins, and this browser's preferences;
  • Machines & runtimes: the daemon's machines and its runtime registry;
  • Memory;
  • Scheduled prompts (the clock): the daemon's cron jobs, shown only by a daemon of client protocol 1.15 or later (see Scheduled prompts).

The connection and the theme button are at its foot. - Chat. The title bar has the sidebar button, the session's title, and the ⋮ menu of the session's commands. Click the title to rename the session (see Renaming). Below the transcript are the composer and the bottom bar. While a subagent's session is open, the title is a path from its root, such as Fix the greeting › reviewer: check tests: click a parent to go up to it. The ⋮ menu acts on the session shown. - Widths. - 1024 px and wider: the sessions sidebar is pinned beside the transcript, and the agents beside the open agent. The sidebar button hides and shows it, and the browser remembers the choice (one for both views). - 640 to 1023 px: the rail stays; the sidebar button shows the sessions as the page in place of the transcript (the agents in place of the open agent), and hides them again. Choosing one, or browser Back, hides them too. - Narrower, a phone: see Phones. - Sheets. The session's panels open as a sheet on the right (from the bottom on a phone): approvals, the agent, model, permission mode, and preset pickers, usage, the diagnostics filter, compacting, the goal, background calls, skills, permission rules, a message's actions, the session's runtimes, and the ⋮ menu. - Long lines in code, diffs, and terminal output scroll inside their block.

docs.title: Sessions and chat
docs.text:
• Paths show under the home directory of the runtime they belong to, as ~/web, and absolute when that runtime reported no home (a daemon older than client protocol 1.7 reports none).
  • Sessions. The page has no directory of its own, so the list shows every session, grouped by project (below). A daemon older than client protocol 1.8 keeps no projects: its list has a filter by the session's directory (its first workspace) instead, named by its runtime, such as labpc · ~/api.
  • Rows. Each session shows its title, how long ago it was last active beside it, and where it runs as badges on the line below. In each project, active sessions come first (those that run, are held, or wait on something that will start their next run: an active goal, a background call, a subagent, or a plugin or runtime), then the others, each newest first by your last message or delegation in it (its own output does not move it, so a busy session keeps its place; a session with none goes by its last event). A session that runs has a turning circle before its title, a held one has a pause (red when its runs kept failing; its tooltip says why, such as held: stopped by you), one that waits has a clock (its tooltip says what it waits on, such as waiting on: goal, background call), and one whose last run failed or was interrupted has a mark; the others have none. A daemon older than client protocol 1.9 does not say what a session waits on. A session a scheduled prompt started has a filled clock before its title, which names the job; click it to open the job in Scheduled prompts. The open session's row has a chevron before its badges, which turns with its subagent tree. Hover over a row for its status and every workspace with its machine, runtime, and path, and over its title for the whole title when the row cuts it.
  • Unread. A session that finished, or that waits on an approval or a question, while you were away has a dot before its title, and the rail's Chat button a dot while any session has one (unread sessions). "Away" is what suppresses a push: no client shows the session (or one of its subagents) in a visible, focused window used in the last 2 minutes. Showing it that way clears the dot in every client; a row's ⋮ has Mark read and Mark unread too. A daemon older than client protocol 1.51 keeps no unread sessions.

  • Badges show machines, not runtimes. The global attachment never counts:

    • nothing else: no badge;
    • one runtime: its machine's badge, then its workspace, as ~/web;
    • several, all on one machine: the machine's badge, then the workspaces, separated by commas;
    • more than one machine: a badge for each machine, in the order the session attached them.

    A root session's badges also count where its subagents work: the runtimes and workspaces they were given, after the root's own (see Delegating to runtimes). A root with only global whose subagents work on labpc shows labpc and their workspace. A subagent's row shows its own attachments.

    A machine's badge has its operating system's icon, as on the Machines view. A runtime whose machine the daemon does not know counts as a machine of its own, under its runtime ID. Each machine keeps one of eight colours, chosen from its name, so it looks the same in every row and every browser; the dots marking runtimes in the bottom bar and on the runtime cards take their machine's colour. The badges have the row's second line to themselves. A machine's name is never cut: when the line is too narrow, the workspaces shrink first, down to …, then give way, and then the last machines give way to a +N badge whose tooltip names them. The row's tooltip lists every workspace with its machine, runtime, and path. A daemon older than client protocol 1.7 lists no attachments: the row shows the session's directory instead. - New session opens its runtime cards with only global selected, and the composer under them (below); the first message creates the session with the selected cards and the agent, model, and permission mode in the bottom bar. - Owned elsewhere. A session another cookie process owns opens as a read-only snapshot. - Renaming. Click the title in the title bar, or choose ⋮ › Rename, and the title becomes a field holding it: Enter saves and Escape (or clicking elsewhere) keeps the old title. In the list, hover over a row for its pencil, beside the trash, which does the same with the row's title. Empty the field for Use the automatic title, which goes back to the title the daemon generates (as does Enter on an empty field). Every client sees the new title at once. - Deleting. Hover over a session's row for its trash button (on a touch screen, press the row for about half a second and let go; the press never opens the session, scrolling cancels it, and it offers the row's ⋮ and Rename too). A confirmation in the row names the session; Delete removes it and its subagents from the daemon's disk, for good. The daemon refuses while the session tree runs, while another cookie process holds it, or when it changed since the list showed it; the row then shows the daemon's reason. A deleted session leaves every client's list, and a page showing it starts a new session. A daemon older than client protocol 1.5 cannot delete, and the page offers no trash. - Selecting several. The list's select button (beside New session) turns its header into a selection bar: a click on a root session's row selects it or lets it go, Shift+click selects the rows from the last one clicked, and Select all selects every root row the list shows. Mark read and Mark unread mark the selection and keep it; Delete asks once, naming up to five, then deletes each tree as its row showed it. A tree that cannot go (it runs, changed since you selected it, or another cookie process holds it) is skipped and stays selected, the rest are deleted, and the status says what was skipped and why. Done leaves select mode. - Projects. The sessions sidebar has a section for each project, oldest project first, so a new one goes last and the others keep their places, then No project last. - Headers. A project's header shows its emoji (a folder when it has none) and its name; when its defaults attach runtimes, a second line shows them as badges, by the session rows' rules. Click a header to fold or unfold its section; the browser remembers it. A folded section still shows its sessions at work: running, or waiting on a producer (a goal, a background call, a subagent) to start their next run, but not held ones. +, always there, starts a new session in the project. Hover over a header (on a touch screen, press it for about half a second) for its pencil, which opens the project editor, and its trash. No project has only its +. The folder button beside New session makes a new project. - Moving a session. Drag its row onto a project's header, or onto No project: a mouse drags at once, a finger after pressing the row for half a second (the list scrolls when the row nears its edge). Or hover over the row for its ⋮, left of its pencil, and choose Move to project…, which lists the projects and No project. The ⋮ menu holds a row's less frequent actions: it opens under the button (a sheet from the bottom on a phone), the arrow keys move through it, and Escape or a click outside closes it. The session keeps its runtimes and agent; its next message sees the project's memory and AGENTS.md. - Deleting a project asks first, saying how many sessions and memories go with it; the daemon refuses while one of its sessions runs, and the header names the running sessions. - The project editor opens on the right (filling a phone's screen): the name; the emoji; the runtime cards a new session in the project starts with, as on New session, with Use this session's attachments; the default agent, with its preset, or None; the project's AGENTS.md; and a way to its memory folder. Save sends the whole change at once; if the project changed meanwhile, in another client or on disk, the editor says so and offers Reload, which drops your edit. Closing with unsaved edits asks first. - Emoji. The picker lists a few hundred common emoji by category, with a search by name; the field below it takes any one emoji, from your system's emoji keyboard too, and says at once when what you typed is not one. No emoji clears it. On a phone the picker rises from the bottom. - New session. The new session's runtime cards fill the page where its transcript will be, with the composer under them, so you draft the first message right away: text, files, and the agent, model, preset, permission mode, and permission rules, as in any session. There is no Start button: sending the first message creates the session with the selected cards, starting every runtime that is not running (a template, such as an ssh runtime, is started then), and the message goes to it. Only global is selected to start with: such a session has no workspace, and hands work that needs files or commands to subagents on the runtimes it names (see Delegating to runtimes). The browser remembers no selection: each new session starts with global alone, or with its project's defaults. On a phone the cards scroll above the composer, which stays at the foot. - Project. The Project picker comes first: the section whose + you used, else No project, and New project…, which opens the editor and picks the project it makes. A project whose defaults attach runtimes prefills the cards with them; left as they are, the session is created with the project's defaults. Picking a project also gives the bottom bar its default agent and preset, with the agent's own model; an agent that is gone, or cannot start a session, leaves the usual one, and the status line says so. Everything stays editable, and choosing a project never changes a running session.

The runtimes a session can use show as cards, grouped by the machine each runs on, this daemon's machine first. - Groups. A group's header says its machine, how many runtimes it has, how many are ready, and how many cards are selected; click it to fold or unfold the group. This daemon's machine, and a machine with a selected card, start unfolded; the browser remembers what you fold. - Cards. One for global (the daemon's own tools, MCP servers, and memory; selected to start with, and you can deselect it), and one for each runtime capability that takes a workspace. Each says whether its runtime is ready, starts on use (the daemon starts it when the session is created), or offline (a runtime that dials in and is not connected), which cannot be selected. Click anywhere on a card to select or deselect it. - Workspaces. A selected card asks for its workspace, suggesting the directories this browser opened on that runtime and the ones sessions use there, as ~/…; any path works. another workspace adds a field for the same runtime at a second directory. While a field is empty, the cards say so and the first message waits, staying in the composer. With no coding card selected, the session works in no workspace. With two workspaces or more, a note says their tools get prefixes, with an example name. Under the cards, a line shows where the session will work. - Colours.
