Each card has a dot in its machine's colour, the colour of that machine's badge in the session rows. - When the session cannot be created. A runtime that fails to start, refuses its workspace, or is offline stops the whole creation: no session is made, the cards stay as they were, and the message, with its files, goes back into the composer. The daemon's reason shows on the card of the runtime it names, which scrolls into view, and a line above the composer says so; an error that names no runtime shows in that line whole. Change the cards and send again. If the session is created but the message is not taken, the session stays and the message comes back to its composer, as any refused message does. The page never falls back to the daemon's own directory. - Runtimes in the ⋮ menu points at the cards while a new session is composed. - Subagents. Only the open session's row has its subagents nested under it, each with its status (a turning circle while it runs, a check, failed, or cancelled), its agent, its short handle, and its task. Click one to open it. Under each session its subagents come in the session list's order: those that run, are held, or wait first, then the others, each group newest by the last message or delegation in it. Subagents have no trash: they go with their root. The tree has two states; click the open session's own row, whose chevron turns with it, to switch between them (clicking another session still opens it), and the browser remembers the choice for each session. A subagent's handle gives way before its agent's name when the row is narrow: - Collapsed (the default): only the subagents that run, at any depth, and the one you have open. A running subagent whose parent has finished shows under its parent, dimmed, so it sits in its place. When nothing runs, nothing shows under the session. - Expanded: the whole hierarchy, finished subagents included; the chevron beside a subagent folds its own. - Transcript. Markdown is rendered with any HTML in it shown as text. Links open in a new tab, but only http, https, and mailto links; images show as links. - Following the end. While a reply streams, the transcript stays at its end, and moves only when what it shows grows (a delta inside a folded block moves nothing). Scrolling up in any way (the wheel, the keys, a finger, the scrollbar) stops that at once: the view stays where you left it until you scroll back to the end, press Latest, which shows at the bottom meanwhile, or send a message (steered or queued too). A session opens at its end. - Pinned at the top, folded side by side on one line, as in the TUI: the system prompt of the session's last run (system prompt · primary (last run) (42 lines); before its first run, the one it was created with), with · next: <agent> when the bottom bar's agent differs, and the tools the last model request offered (tools · 12 available (last request), or tools · 12 provided, 40 searchable (last request) when it deferred some). Click one to open it: the prompt in monospace with its line breaks and indentation, up to 256 lines or 32 KiB, and the tool names as chips, up to 8 KiB of names, the provided and searchable ones under their own headings. - What the model reads beyond the conversation has a collapsed row wherever it enters, as in the TUI: AGENTS.md (a run's files as one turn, with the instructions around them), a loaded skill, the memory snapshot (again whenever it changes), a compaction summary (in its frame), a deferred tools announcement, the parent's conversation a subagent starts from, and an ACP agent's first-prompt context, each opening to the exact text the model reads. A reply an interrupt cut off quotes the marker later requests follow it with. A tool call's output is followed by what its result sent the model beyond the tool's own output: a loop warning, the messages the tool emitted, and the marker that stands for the output once it left the model's context. - Agent work folds by default, as in the TUI: each reply's thinking, tool calls, and the text written between calls are one row above the reply, Working… 42s · 3 tool calls with what the agent does now under it while it works (the newest step or line of its thinking, or its newest call's title), then Worked for 1m 23s · 7 tool calls (· 1 failed when calls failed, Stopped after … when the run was stopped). Click the row to open the work. A call waiting for your approval stays outside the fold. Settings › Display switches to the full transcript, which shows every thinking block and tool call; the choice stays in the browser and applies to its other tabs at once. - Replies end with the TUI's footer line, ⚡ 42.1 tps · 12.5K ctx · $0.0040: generation speed, the context the reply left, and its estimated cost when every request was priced, then interrupted when its run was. A thinking block's line reads thinking… while it streams, then how long the model thought, as thought for 12s. - Tool calls are one line each until you open them, as in the TUI: an icon for the kind of tool (from its presentation hint, never its name), the title, the primary argument unless the title names it, and the status: a turning circle while running, a check when done, and a word with its icon when it failed, was cancelled, or was interrupted. While a call runs, its latest progress follows the title. A call waiting for your approval says approve? on its line, which opens the approvals. A running call that can move to the background offers background. - An open call. Click a call's line (or press Enter on it) to open it, and again to close it. Open, its line wraps to show the whole title and argument a closed line cuts short. It shows its arguments under a muted arguments label, leaving out what the line already says (a block or key/value row that only repeats the primary argument or the text the title quotes), then its output. Output past 64 lines ends with "… N more lines (click to expand)", which shows up to 1024. The page remembers which calls you opened in each session until you reload it. - A delegate call names the subagent it started with its handle and an open link; while the subagent runs, the row says whether it is thinking, running a tool, or waiting for an approval. - Output blocks each have their own view: code highlighted by the bundled highlight.js, diffs with the file's line numbers, terminal output with its colours, tables, JSON, links, session links, and media shown inline. - Images and videos in messages, replies, and tool output open in the media viewer when clicked. It shows the file's size in pixels and zooms with the wheel, a pinch, its buttons, or +, -, and 0 (fit). A drag moves the zoomed file, and a double click zooms in or back to fit. Zoomed pixels show crisp rather than blurred. A video plays in the viewer, with play and pause (Space), a frame back or forward (, and .), five seconds back or forward (Left and Right), a seek bar, its speed, and its sound. Escape, ✕, or a click beside the file closes it. - Cut output offers its complete content. - Your messages show the files they attached. Their ⋯ shows while the mouse is over the message's row (or the keyboard is in it); on a touch screen a long press on the message (about half a second; moving or scrolling cancels it) opens the same menu. The menu copies the message, reverts to before it (it and every later turn are removed, and its text comes back into the composer), or forks a new session with the conversation up to it. A revert is refused when another client added to the session since the menu opened. - An ACP agent's commands. In a session of an ACP agent, typing / in the composer lists the slash commands the agent offers above it, marked agent, narrowed as you type the name. Choosing one that takes input puts /<name> in the composer for it; one that takes none is sent. The agent's plan shows in the transcript as a checklist, its own tool calls name it and fill in their arguments as the agent sends them, and its notices show where they arrive. A command of the agent's that ran in the background (such as Claude Code's background shell) shows a Background: … ended row when it ends, before the run the end may wake; opening it shows how long the command ran, its exit code when the agent says it, and the whole command. A message steered into the agent's running turn stays in the strip above the composer until the agent takes it, then shows as any message. Every ACP v2 agent can be steered; only a session last run by an ACP v1 agent of an earlier build shows the Steer button as "Queue (this agent can't be steered)", the message waiting for the agent's next turn. - Composer. One line to start; it grows with what you write up to five lines, then scrolls, and shrinks back when you send. The paperclip (and on a phone the camera) is inside it at the bottom left, and round buttons at the bottom right:

The session The box The buttons idle empty Send, disabled idle has text or files Send starts a run running or compacting empty Stop cancels it, as Escape does running has text or files Queue and Steer

Text that starts with / is sent like any other message: the page has no slash commands (the ⋮ menu has them). Each button's tooltip names its key. The keys work like the TUI's: - Enter sends, steering a running run. - Alt+Enter queues the message behind the run. - Shift+Enter or Ctrl+J inserts a newline. - Escape cancels the run, or a compaction in progress. Cancelling stops the run's tool calls at once (see Cancelling a run). - Up in an empty composer takes back your newest pending or queued message.

Each session keeps its own draft, text and attached files: opening another session shows its draft, and coming back brings yours back. A new session's draft is kept the same way, its files held in the page, until its first message creates the session. A message a session did not take goes back to that session's draft, even when another is open. Drafts stay in the page and end with it.

A status message, such as "reconnected to the daemon", shows for a few seconds as a tip over the composer's top left corner, on every width; one of work in progress, ending in "…", stays until the next replaces it.

The strip above the composer lists pending and queued messages; tap one to take it back into your composer, another client's too (a daemon before client protocol 1.31.0 lets only the client that sent it). - Commands. The ⋮ menu in the title bar has the session's commands, each by name with an icon and a line saying what it does, and each opens a sheet with labelled fields and a main button: Compact context, Goal, Schedule a prompt (which opens the job form in Scheduled prompts instead), Skills, Background calls, Runtimes, Permission rules, Usage, Diagnostics, and Agent preset. The others have their place in the page: the bottom bar picks the agent, model, and permission mode and answers approvals; the composer attaches, sends, and stops; the sidebar starts and opens sessions; and the rail has the daemon's views. - Approvals. When a tool call needs an answer, the bottom bar says so. Open it to approve once, approve for the session tree, or reject. - Questions. An ACP agent's question shows as a card above the composer, naming who asks (with 1 of N when several wait), and the transcript's last line says waiting for your answer; a subagent's delegate row says the same. A form lists its fields in order: radios for a choice (No choice for an optional one), checkboxes for a multiple choice and for yes or no, and text, email, URL, date, or number boxes, each with its hint and a * when required. Submit names the first field that does not fit under it and sends nothing until it does; Decline and Cancel answer at once. A page to open shows the whole URL with its host in bold and any warning, an Open link that only your click follows (in a new tab), then Done, Decline, and Cancel. - Compacting. Compact context opens a sheet with an optional Focus (what the summary should keep) and Compact. While it compacts, the sheet offers Cancel compaction, as the composer's Stop and Escape do, and then says how it went. - Goal. Goal shows the root session's goal, its checklist, and the controls its state allows (Pause, Resume, Cancel), and sets a New objective with the agent and model shown. The goal bar above the composer shows the objective with the same controls. Goals belong to root sessions; a child session or a read-only snapshot offers none. - Background calls. While the session has calls running in the background, a bar above the composer lists them. Click it, or use Background calls, to see how long each has run and stop one; a stopped call still reports to the model. - Files. Attach files with the paperclip (the file picker), by dropping them on the page, or by pasting them; on a phone, the camera button takes a photo. They upload at once and wait on the draft as chips; the × on a chip removes it. A new session's files wait in the page and upload once the first message has created the session. - Only the kinds of file the selected model takes are offered: the picker lists their types, and a model that takes none offers no attaching. - The page reads each file's type from its content, as the daemon does, and says why it cannot attach one the model does not take. - An image too large for the model or the daemon is offered as Downscale and attach: the page redraws it smaller and attaches that. Video is never downscaled. - Skills. Skills lists the skills you can run, searched as you type. Pick one, give its arguments, and run it. - Permissions. Permission rules shows the session's rules by action, and where each comes from: the agent, the default, or a session override. A rule limited to one runtime shows its key as agent documents write it, such as bash@labpc. Click an effect to override it, the pencil on an override to edit it in the form, or the × to remove it. The form takes a rule as action @ runtime, a pattern, and an effect. The action is any name a tool declares ([a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}), suggested from the actions the session's tools and rules use. The runtime is optional: empty applies the rule on every runtime, and suggestions come from the daemon's runtimes. message and skill take no runtime, so the field turns off for them. A name the daemon would refuse is flagged before it is sent. While a new session is composed, the same table edits the rules it will be created with, previewed against its agent. - Working. While the session runs, the transcript's last line says working… (or waiting for your answer); a view following the end keeps it in sight. Latest shows only when the transcript scrolls and you scrolled up from its end. - Bottom bar. Below the composer (above it on a phone); each part has an icon and says more on hover: - the agent, the model, and the permission mode, as three chips of one shape, each opening its picker. The mode chip has a shield of its own for each mode; its picker lists every mode with its shield and what it does, checks the current one, and sets the one you click: - auto-approve (the default): the approval agent decides; what it won't approve comes to you; - auto-approve-n: the approval agent decides; what it would pass to you is rejected; - auto-approve-y: the approval agent decides; what it would pass to you is approved once; - ask: every ask comes to you; - yolo: every ask is approved at once.

Deny rules and the loop guard hold in every mode.

The agent picker lists the [ACP agents](../extend/acp-agents.md)
runtimes offer with the runtime the draft (or the viewed session)
would run them on; one that cannot run there (no attached runtime
offers it, two do, or its runtime is away) is dimmed with why and
cannot be picked. For an ACP agent the model chip shows the agent's
own model and effort (`Opus • High`) and opens their values, each
with its value ID muted beside its name (as for cookie's models, whose
rows show the `provider/model` key and whose variant chips the variant
ID: what an agent document's `models` writes), a click
changing them on the agent (on a new session's draft, the values its
session starts with; a draft offers what the agent last started a
session with); **All agent options** there lists every option the
agent offers (model, mode, effort) with its values, the current one
pressed;
  • the approvals waiting, when there are any (click to answer them); each card shows the call and, when the approval reviewer passed it to you, its reason ("The reviewer asks: …", or that its review failed);
  • where the session works, its workspaces under their runtimes' homes, after a dot in each runtime's machine's colour (click for Runtimes; not on a phone);
  • the context size, in tokens, of the last request (also in Usage);
  • the session's cost (click for Usage).
  • Diagnostics. Diagnostics picks which diagnostic rows the transcript shows; the choice stays in the browser.
  • Messages from producers (goal control and reminders, background-call reports, delegation reports, plugins) show as one folded line with their summary; click one to read it whole.

docs.title: Managing the daemon
docs.text:
• Runtimes. Runtimes (in the ⋮ menu) lists the session's attached runtimes with their status: Attach a runtime searches every runtime's capabilities and asks for a workspace when one is needed, Detach removes one (the daemon refuses while the session runs), and Retry restarts a failed instance.
  • Under each runtime are the MCP servers its instance uses (from mcp.server.list, by runtime and workspace): each one's name, state (connected, connecting, needs_auth, failed, …), tool count, and why it failed or what it waits for; a server its runtime shares across workspaces (scope = "runtime") is marked runtime-wide.
  • The open panel reads the runtimes again every second, and links to the Machines & runtimes view.
  • Machines. The Machines & runtimes view shows each machine as a card: an icon for its operating system (Linux, macOS, Windows, or a generic computer), its name, its runtimes and memories, and buttons to rename it, merge it into another (its memories move too), or forget it. Under it are its runtimes, each with an icon for how it came to the daemon (built in, started from a template, or dialled in), whether it is connected (a green dot), pinned (a pin), its platform, its capabilities, its MCP servers counted by state (MCP 1 connected, 1 failed) and listed with their state, tool count, and workspace, its runtime-scoped ones (runtime-wide) and its workspace-scoped ones that no workspace has started yet (starts with a workspace) included, each server's tools by the server's own names under Tools (those its include_tools or exclude_tools left out dimmed and struck through), the ACP agents it offers, and why it last failed to connect. Each runtime is managed there too, its changes written to its [runtimes.<id>] table in the daemon's config.toml and taken by a connected runtime at once:
  • MCP servers. MCP server adds one to the runtime; each server has Edit (a new name renames it; a runtime's server says whether it runs once for the runtime or once per workspace), Enable or Disable, and Remove. Selecting a tool under Tools leaves it out or takes it back: its exact name goes into or out of exclude_tools, or into include_tools when that is what leaves it out; a tool an exclude_tools pattern leaves out says so instead.
  • ACP agents. ACP agent declares one on the runtime (its ID, its command as a JSON array, its environment, description, and whether it is enabled); each declaration shows whether a session that attaches the runtime can run it now, its command, and its documents, with Edit (a new ID renames it, and its document when no other runtime declares the old ID), Enable or Disable, New template (a document over it with acp.agent), and Remove, which keeps its documents. A document opens in the Agents view; Create document starts one when it has none. A runtime that connected before and is offline now stays on its machine, under the connected ones, dimmed, with when it was last seen and Forget, which drops the daemon's record of where it ran (see Offline runtimes). Runtimes that have never connected, such as a template no session has used, sit under On no machine yet.
  • Moving a runtime. Drag it onto another machine's card: with a mouse, press anywhere on its row and drag; on a touch screen, hold the row for about half a second until it lifts, then drag (moving sooner scrolls the page). The card under it is outlined, and dropping it there pins the runtime to that machine. A row held and let go without moving opens Move to…, which each row also has as a button (the keyboard reaches it): pick another machine, or type a new name to create one. Unpin (the crossed-out pin) lets a pinned runtime follow the machine it reports again.
  • Add a runtime opens three ways to add one:
    • Start one over ssh: a runtime ID, the ssh host, and optionally the one directory its workspaces must be under. The page shows the [runtimes.<id>] template, as in the ssh example, and Add to config.toml writes it with config.apply. The daemon starts the runtime only after a restart, and says so. The page refuses an ID the daemon has, and a host or directory that ssh would split or take as an option.
    • Let one dial in: the cookie runtime serve --daemon command to run on the other machine (see Runtimes that dial in), with an optional runtime ID and Copy. The daemon's address is the page's own unless the page reached it on a loopback address, when it is a placeholder. The command carries the token this page connected with: it shows as dots until Show token, and Copy takes the real one. A page that keeps no token shows a placeholder.
    • Guides: links to the runtimes, ssh, dial-in, remote access, and service guides of the released documentation.
  • MCP servers. Settings › MCP servers lists every runtime's servers with their state, tools (with how many its include_tools and exclude_tools left out), and last error. The global runtime's servers can be added, edited, enabled or disabled, removed, and kept in your config.toml; a coding runtime's come from its template. The form takes the tool filters as comma-separated patterns (see choosing a server's tools). Reconnect works for any server.
  • A server that needs authorization offers Sign in (see Signing in to MCP servers).
  • Providers. Settings › Providers lists the catalog's providers, each name with its provider ID in small type. Pick one to connect it, or to update or disconnect its stored connection; a connected one lists its available models, each name with its model ID beside it. Credentials are typed into password fields, read once when you connect, and never kept by the page; closing the form clears them.
  • Configuration. Settings › Configuration has config.toml. Open it to edit it in the page and Apply it. A change the daemon refuses stays open with the reason, to be fixed and applied again; a document that changed meanwhile is reloaded instead. Notes about what the configuration names that does not exist yet, such as a delegation target no runtime has reported, are listed above it. Reload from disk applies edits made by hand, and Restart daemon beside it applies what only a restart does (see Restarting the daemon); it is highlighted while a change waits for a restart.
  • Restarting the daemon. While the daemon's configuration lists parts that only a restart applies, a banner across the top says so, such as Restart needed to apply: plugins, runtimes, with Restart daemon. That button, the one in the connection panel, and the one in Settings › Configuration ask first: Restart when idle (the default) waits until no turn runs and every background call has reported, refusing new turns meanwhile, and Restart now (interrupts 2 running turns) stops the running turns and the background calls, counting the sessions the page sees running. Cancel or Escape closes the question; on a phone it is a sheet at the bottom. Once the daemon accepts, the banner says Restarting when idle… (1 running turn, 2 background calls) until the connection closes, then the page shows its reconnecting bar (the daemon is restarting) and reconnects on its own. A daemon older than client protocol 1.19 shows neither the banner nor the button. See Restarting the daemon.
  • Agents. The Agents view lists the agent documents in a sidebar, like the sessions in Chat: the shared agents, then each preset with its agents. Each row has an icon for the agent's mode (a robot for a primary agent, a person with a gear for a subagent), its ID, its description, and off when it is disabled or not applied when an edit was refused. Click one to edit it beside the list; Apply and Close are at the editor's foot, with Delete behind a confirmation. New agent asks for the document's path (agents/<id>.md, or agents/<preset>/<id>.md), and the ↻ button reloads the documents from disk after editing them by hand.
  • Memory. The Memory view lists the memories by layer, grouped by machine and project, with the files that are not valid memories. Open one to edit it, create one at a URL (clicking a layer or group, or a project's +, fills in its prefix), or delete one. A memory that changed since you opened it is never overwritten silently: you choose to reload it, overwrite it, or drop your edit. After a save, the status line says what the daemon kept in place of your text, when it kept anything.
  • Projects are folders, folded until you open one; the browser remembers which you opened. A project's trash deletes the project, with its sessions, memories, and AGENTS.md, after a confirmation that counts them, as its header's trash in the sessions sidebar does. A daemon older than client protocol 1.8 has no projects, only memory folders: there the trash deletes the folder's memories, one memory.delete each; the files in it that are not memories stay, and so does the folder when there are any.
  • An agent's memory (agent://<agent>) opens as its parts: the description and the first keywords (the agent's ID and its mode) belong to the daemon and show locked; the other keywords (separated by commas) and the memory itself are yours to edit.
  • Scheduled prompts. See Scheduled prompts.
  • Plugins. Settings › Plugins lists each plugin with its state, tools, hooks, and why it last failed, and restarts one. A plugin's events show in the bottom bar.
  • Notifications. Settings › Notifications turns push notifications on in this browser and lists every device the daemon pushes to; see Notifications.
  • Display. Settings › Display picks how the transcript shows agent work (Reduced or Full, see Sessions and chat) and which diagnostics it shows (as Diagnostics does); both stay in this browser.
  • This browser. Settings › This browser installs the page as an app and forgets the daemon.
  • About. Settings › About shows this page's version and client protocol, the daemon's version, client protocol, and address, links to cookie's website, documentation, and GitHub repository, and the credits.

docs.title: Scheduled prompts
docs.text:
The clock in the rail opens Scheduled prompts, the daemon's cron jobs; a daemon older than client protocol 1.15 keeps none, and the page hides the icon and the ⋮ menu's Schedule a prompt. The view reads crons.list again whenever a job changes (crons.changed), from any client or agent.

  • The list. Each job shows its name (or the start of its prompt), its state (enabled, finished, failed 3 times in a row, disabled by you, …), its schedule with a plain reading (0 9 * * 1-5 · every Monday to Friday at 09:00, once at 2026-10-23 03:00), the next fire in this browser's time with how long until it, the target (the session's title, subagent <title>, or new session · <agent>), and how its last fire went. A banner says when the daemon's firing is off ([cron] enabled = false).
  • A job. Click a job for its details (schedule, runs counted against its limit, delivery, a new-session job's agent, model, project, and mode, failures in a row, who made it, and the session an agent made it in; the target and that session are links to their transcripts), its prompt, its history (newest first: when, what the fire did, and Open session for the session it went to), and its actions: Edit, Disable or Enable, Run now (a fire now, recorded as run now, which counts toward neither the run limit nor the failures), and Delete, behind a confirmation; the sessions a job started stay.
  • The form. New in the view, or Schedule a prompt in the ⋮ menu (for the open session), opens it:
  • Name (optional) and Prompt;
  • Schedule: five cron fields in the daemon host's local time, or a delay such as in 20m; Runs: a whole number, 0 or less for no limit, 1 when empty, for cron schedules. The line under them reads what you typed as you type, or says why it is not a schedule;
  • Target, when creating: the open session (or subagent), or A new session each run. A job for a session has a Delivery: queue (after the current turn) or steer (into the running turn);
  • a new-session job's Agent, Model (the agent's own models, or a pin), and Permission mode (auto-n unless you choose another). Only you set the model and the mode; an agent's jobs always start in auto-n. The template takes the open session's agent, the preset in use, and the open session's project (the new session's, with none open); the daemon attaches what session.create would.

The daemon checks the job when it is saved and says what it refused under the form.

docs.title: Phones
docs.text:
• Size. The page works from 360 px wide, in portrait and landscape. Buttons are at least 44 px, and long lines in code, diffs, and terminal output scroll inside their block rather than the page.
  • Chat.
  • Title bar: the sidebar button, the session's title on one line, and ⋮, which opens the session's commands as a sheet from the bottom. A subagent's session has ‹ before its title, which goes to its parent.
  • Bottom bar: one row, above the composer and on its background. The model chip takes the room left and shortens its name first; the agent chip shows only its icon below about 380 px; the permission mode chip shows only its shield; the cost shows to the cent ("$0.02") and opens Usage, which also has the context size. Every picker, and every sheet of the ⋮ menu, opens from the bottom.
  • Status line: a thin line above the bottom bar, only while approvals wait (tap the badge to answer).
  • Two levels. Each view has a first level, its list, and a second level, the item open in it. The first level fills the screen beside the rail, which stays an icon strip with the theme button at its foot; the second level fills the whole screen, without the rail, and the sidebar button at the left of its title bar goes back up to the list.
  • The sessions. The page opens on them, over a new session (a notification's session opens instead). In a session, the sidebar button shows them again with the rail, the open session's subagents nested under its row; browser Back, the sidebar button in their title bar, choosing a session, or choosing another view hides them. Choosing Chat on the rail shows the sessions, and a tap on the open session's row switches its tree and leaves them shown. A swipe from the edge is the browser's Back. A long press on a session's row, let go in place, reveals its ⋮, a sheet with Move to project…, which lists the projects, its Rename, which makes its title a field, and its Delete, then the confirmation; held and moved, it drags the row onto a project's header. A long press on a project's header shows its pencil and trash.
  • List first. A view with a list shows the list when you choose it on the rail, and opens an item only when you choose it there: Chat's sessions, the agents, the Settings sections, the memories, and the scheduled prompts. Machines & runtimes has no list: it opens at once, beside the rail.
  • Agents: the agent open fills the screen; the sidebar button shows the agents with the rail, and browser Back returns to the agent.
  • Other views fill the screen under the same title bar. A Settings section, a memory, or a scheduled prompt open is the second level: the sidebar button, or browser Back, returns to the list. A document open in a Settings section is a third level, with a back arrow in the title bar up to the section. An editor fills the screen with Apply or Save and Cancel at its foot. Only Chat has the composer and the bottom bar.
  • On its side (about 844×390), a phone gets the 640 px layout: the rail stays, the sessions show as the page, and the bottom bar sits beside the composer.
  • The on-screen keyboard. The page sizes itself to what the keyboard leaves visible, so the composer and an open sheet stay above it. While the composer has focus, the bottom bar steps aside, so only the composer (and the status line, when it shows) sits above the keyboard.
  • Home screen. The page installs as an app; see Installing as an app.
  • Background tabs. A phone suspends a tab it does not show. When the tab shows again, the page checks its connection, reconnects if the daemon stopped answering, and catches up on what happened meanwhile.
  • Reaching the daemon from a phone takes one of the ways in Forwarding and tunnels. Without TLS the token crosses the network in the clear.

docs.title: Installing as an app
docs.text:
The page installs to a phone's home screen, or as a desktop app, and then opens in its own window without the browser's address bar, with the cookie icon. It still works only while it reaches the daemon: it stores nothing for offline use, so it always matches the daemon's own build.

It needs HTTPS. A browser installs only a page from a secure origin: HTTPS, or localhost and 127.0.0.1 on the daemon's own machine. A page opened over plain HTTP on a LAN or Tailscale address cannot be installed, and Settings › This browser says so. The easy way to HTTPS is Tailscale Serve on the daemon's machine, with the daemon on its default loopback address:

tailscale serve --bg 7419   # https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net/ → 127.0.0.1:7419

Open the page on the phone with cookie web --url wss://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net/ws's link.

Tailscale Serve needs HTTPS certificates turned on for the tailnet (MagicDNS and HTTPS in its admin console). tailscale serve reset turns it off again (see Remote access).

Where the browser can install the page, the page offers it:

  • Android (Chrome and other Chromium browsers) and desktop Chrome or Edge. Install app opens the browser's install prompt. It is in Settings › This browser and under the connect screen, and on a phone a banner over the page offers it once (× dismisses it for good). Chrome offers the prompt once the page has been used for a moment; before that, or in a browser without one (Firefox), Settings › This browser points to the browser's own menu (Install app, Add to Home screen).
  • iPhone and iPad. iOS has no install prompt, so the same places say how: tap Share in the browser's toolbar, then Add to Home Screen and Add. The app iOS adds keeps its own storage, apart from the browser's, so the first time it opens it asks for the token: paste the link cookie web prints into its Token field (the page takes the token out of it).
  • Already installed. Running as an app, the page offers nothing, and Settings › This browser says it runs as an installed app.

The app opens at the page's own address without a token and connects with the token the browser stored when a cookie web link was opened. Its title bar follows the page's theme, the user's choice included.

To uninstall the app, use the platform's own way; cookie keeps nothing outside the browser's storage for it:

  • Android. Long-press the app icon, then Uninstall (or App info › Uninstall).
  • iPhone and iPad. Long-press the icon, then Remove App › Delete App.
  • Desktop Chrome or Edge. Open the app, open its window menu (the three dots), and choose Uninstall; or open chrome://apps (edge://apps in Edge), right-click the app, and choose Remove.

The browser keeps the daemon's token and the page's settings in site storage even after the app is gone. Forget this daemon (Settings › This browser, or the connect screen) deletes the token; to clear everything else, clear the site data for the daemon's address in the browser's settings.

The page has a service worker, sw.js, which installing needs on some browsers, and which shows notifications. It caches nothing and passes every request to the daemon, so a daemon that is not running shows the browser's own error, and a restarted daemon of a new build serves its own page at once. It never touches the /ws and /runtime WebSockets.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
The daemon can notify your phone, or any browser, when a session needs you, even while the page is closed:

  • A session finished. A root session's run ended (completed or failed) and nothing will start another one without you: no subagent, background call, plugin, or one-time scheduled prompt is still due to wake it, and no queued message is waiting. A recurring scheduled prompt does not hold it back. The notification shows the session's title and the start of its reply, or the error.
  • An approval or a question waits. An approval the reviewer handed to you, or a question an ACP agent asks, anywhere in a session's tree.
  • The daemon restarts. Restarting… when it goes down for a restart a client asked for (every device but the one whose page asked), then Restarted once it is back, to every device. A daemon started another way, by its service manager or a boot, says Started. A daemon a TUI runs in-process says nothing.

Nothing is pushed for a session a client shows you at that moment: an open, focused page or app that you used in the last two minutes, or a TUI whose terminal reports focus. [notifications] in config.toml turns pushes off, shows less on the lock screen, and more (see Push Notifications).

Turning them on. Open Settings › Notifications and choose Turn on notifications; the browser asks whether to allow them.

  • It needs HTTPS, as installing does (see Installing as an app).
  • iPhone and iPad (iOS and iPadOS 16.4 or later) notify only the installed app: add the page to the Home Screen first, open it from there, and turn notifications on in the app.
  • Android notifies Chrome and other browsers through Google's push service, so a phone without Google Play services may not receive them.
  • Blocked. If you blocked notifications for the page, allow them again in the browser's site settings.

Once on, Send test sends one at once, the field names this device in the list, and Turn off stops them. Devices, below, lists every browser the daemon pushes to, with when it last sent one and why the last one failed; Remove stops another device's. Turn off and Forget this daemon both remove this browser from Devices (when the page is connected) and drop the browser's subscription.

Uninstalling the app, or clearing the site's data, ends the browser's subscription where the platform ties it to the app (an iPhone's Home Screen app, for one). The push service then refuses the next push, and the daemon removes the device from Devices. Until a push is attempted it stays listed. On a desktop or Android, removing the app may leave the browser's own permission and subscription for the site in place, so notifications keep arriving in the browser: turn them off before uninstalling, or Remove the device from another client. A browser takes notifications from one daemon at a time: on a page that connected to another daemon since, Settings offers Switch to this daemon.

Clicking one opens its session, in the open page or a new one, on the daemon the notification came from; an approval or a question opens in its session, ready to answer. Opening a session closes its notifications. A daemon the device cannot reach shows the usual connection error.

What leaves the machine. The daemon sends each notification to the browser's push service (Google, Apple, or Mozilla), which delivers it to the device. It is encrypted for the browser, so the push service sees only its size and time. The daemon needs outbound HTTPS to reach it; nothing has to reach the daemon from the internet. No account or registration is needed: the daemon makes its own key, kept in push/ in its data directory.

docs.title: Signing in to MCP servers
docs.text:
A remote MCP server that wants OAuth shows needs_auth in Settings › MCP servers, with Sign in. The page is its own redirect: the authorization server sends the browser back to the page's address with ?oauth=callback, for example https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net/?oauth=callback. The daemon keeps the PKCE verifier and exchanges the code; the tokens never reach the page. Only the daemon's own (global) servers can sign in, and only with a daemon of client protocol 1.11 or later; an older daemon's servers say to run cookie mcp auth <server> instead.

  • Sign in opens the authorization page in a new tab. If the browser blocks the tab, the page goes there itself.
  • Coming back. The tab the authorization server sends back takes the code and state out of its address bar at once, then hands the address to the tab that started the sign-in and closes. That tab finishes the sign-in and says "Signed in to <server>" or what went wrong. With no such tab open, the tab that came back finishes the sign-in itself and opens Settings › MCP servers.
  • Paste the address you landed on. While a sign-in waits, the MCP servers show it with a field for the address the browser ended on. Use it when the sign-in ends somewhere the page cannot continue from: on an iPhone, the app added to the home screen keeps its storage apart from Safari, so the page Safari opens cannot finish a sign-in the app started. It says so and shows the address with Copy the address; paste it into the app. Cancel gives the sign-in up.
  • Refused callbacks. A sign-in waits 10 minutes in the page (the daemon gives up after 5). A callback for one that waited longer, or whose state this browser does not know, is not finished.
  • HTTPS. Most authorization servers send the browser back only to an https address or to this machine's loopback. On a page served over plain http at another address, the MCP servers warn and point to remote access; Tailscale Serve (see Installing as an app) is the easy way to HTTPS. Sign in stays, for servers that allow it.
  • A configured client_id. The daemon registers a client for the page's address by itself when the server offers dynamic client registration. A server configured with oauth = { client_id = "…" } needs the page's address with ?oauth=callback among the redirect URIs allowed for that client, on the server's side (see MCP).

docs.title: What the page does not do
docs.text: • Offer this machine as a runtime. A browser has no workspace to share. The TUI's machine can attach as a runtime that dials in; the page uses the runtimes the daemon already has.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text:
Settings › About credits what the page is built from, each with its licence:

  • the icons, Font Awesome Free by Fonticons, Inc., under the CC BY 4.0 licence: inline SVG in the page's code (from the icondata crate, shown through leptos_icons), not a web font;
  • the code font, JetBrains Mono, under the SIL Open Font License 1.1;
  • code highlighting, highlight.js, under the BSD 3-Clause licence.

docs.title: Hosting the page elsewhere
docs.text: Every release attaches the page as cookie-agent-web.tar.gz. Its files use relative paths, so any static host can serve them from any path. The page then fills in a URL on that host, which you edit to name the daemon.

docs.title: Building the page
docs.text:
A cookie built from a fresh checkout serves a placeholder page. scripts/build-web.sh builds the real one:

  • it needs trunk 0.21.14 and the wasm32-unknown-unknown target;
  • it writes the page to crates/web_assets/bundle/, which the next build of cookie embeds;
  • it fails when the page, gzipped, is over its budget of 10 MB, a backstop against runaway growth.

The daemon sends the page gzip-compressed to browsers that accept it, under a Content-Security-Policy that allows only the page's own scripts and WebSocket connections to daemons.

docs.title: Agents and presets
docs.text:
An agent is a role a model plays: a system prompt, the models it runs on with their fallbacks, the permissions its tools get, and whether it runs as a root, as a subagent, or both. Agents are Markdown documents with YAML frontmatter in ~/.cookie-agent/agents/, <id>.md:

---
description: Reviews a change for correctness
mode: subagent
enabled: true
models: [{ model: "openai/gpt-5" }]
permissions:
  read: allow
  bash: ask
---
You review diffs. Report bugs with file and line.

Replace the model with one your providers offer. See Agent document structure for every key.

docs.title: Roots, subagents, and internal agents
docs.text:
An agent's mode says where it may run: primary as a root that you talk to, subagent only when another agent delegates to it, all for both, or internal for the daemon's own helpers. A root agent's permissions say which subagents it may delegate to, so a set of agents forms a team: a primary that plans and delegates, and specialists for exploring, testing, or review.

The daemon also runs three internal agents of its own: approval, the classifier that answers permission asks in the auto-approve mode; compaction, which summarizes context; and title, which names sessions. Each can be replaced by an authored internal document. See Internal agents.

When no authored agent can run as a root, the daemon supplies a built-in default coding agent on the first available model, so a fresh install works without any documents. See Layering and replacement.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text: A preset is a named team. Documents directly in agents/ are shared; a directory one level down, such as agents/python/, is a preset whose documents replace shared ones of the same ID and add their own. Choosing a preset (/preset, or cookie run --preset) switches the whole team for new runs at once; no preset is selected by default. See Agent presets.

docs.title: Choosing what runs
docs.text: A session's selection, its agent, model, variant, and preset, is shared by every client and changes with /agent, /model, /preset, or the CLI's --agent, --model, and --preset. When a model fails, the run falls back along the agent's model chain, and later runs keep starting from the model that worked. See Selecting an agent and Providers for models and variants.

docs.title: Context an agent gets
docs.text:
Besides its own prompt, a run's context carries the repository's AGENTS.md files, the skills it may load, sections the tools contribute, and a memory snapshot; all of it is fixed when the run starts and visible in the transcript. See System prompt, Skills, and Memory.

Agents are changed live: edit them with /config or cookie config, and the next run uses the new documents. See config.toml.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text:
A client shows the daemon's sessions and acts on them. cookie ships three:

  • the terminal UI, cookie or cookie attach;
  • the web page the daemon serves on its own port, opened with cookie web;
  • the command line: cookie config, memory, machine, mcp, connect, and the other commands that call a running daemon. cookie run is the exception: it runs its own engine.

docs.title: One protocol
docs.text: All of them speak the same client protocol: JSON-RPC 2.0 over a WebSocket, versioned with semver and frozen at its major (see Compatibility). A connection starts with a handshake naming the protocol version and the client: a free-form kind such as tui, cli, or web, and an instance_id the client keeps across reconnects. The daemon never treats one kind differently from another, so a client of your own is a peer of the shipped ones; see Write a client.

docs.title: Many clients at once
docs.text:
Any number of clients can attach to one daemon. Each sees every session live, can work in any of them, and is told about changes another client makes:

  • Selections are shared. A session has one agent, model, variant, and permission mode. When one client picks them, every client's draft follows, and the latest pick wins.
  • Steer or queue. While a run is active, a message either steers, joining the running conversation at the next tool or completion boundary, or queues, starting a run of its own when this one completes. The daemon decides atomically, so a run that another client starts or that ends while you type only changes which happens. See Steering and queueing.
  • Only the sender takes a message back. A pending message shows which client sent it; only that client can recall it into its composer.
  • Edits check what you saw. Reverting a session is refused when it gained events the client has not shown yet, so nothing unseen is deleted.

docs.title: Browsers
docs.text: A browser page connects like any client, with the token in its handshake. The daemon takes it from any origin; the token is the guard. See Web clients.

docs.title: A client's machine
docs.text: A TUI attached to a daemon on another machine offers its own machine to it as a runtime that dials in, client_<host name>, so its sessions still work in the directory it was started in. See Runtimes.

docs.title: The daemon
docs.text: The daemon is the gateway at the center of cookie. It owns everything that outlives one terminal: the provider connections and the model catalog, the sessions and their history, the agents and presets, the permission rules and approvals, and memory. It runs the models, and it reaches the tools a session uses through runtimes. Clients only show and steer what the daemon holds.

docs.title: In process or on its own
docs.text:
The same daemon runs in two ways:

  • Inside a client's process. Plain cookie with no daemon around starts one inside the TUI's process; the bottom bar then says standalone. cookie --standalone always does this, and cookie run always runs an engine of its own for its one prompt. When the process ends, so does the daemon.
  • On its own. cookie daemon serves the client protocol on a WebSocket, by default ws://127.0.0.1:7419/ws, until it is stopped. Every client that reaches it shares its sessions, and it can run as a service. See Persistent daemon.

Either way it is one engine with one store: sessions, artifacts, memory, and the machines registry live under ~/.cookie-agent.

docs.title: Finding a running daemon
docs.text:
Plain cookie looks for a daemon on this machine before starting its own, but only when config.toml has [server] token, which cookie daemon writes at its first start. It dials ws://<host>:<port>/ws from the [server] table, never [server] url:

  • nothing listening within half a second: it starts its own engine, silently;
  • a daemon that accepts the handshake within two seconds: the TUI opens on it;
  • something that answers but cannot be used, such as a refused token or another protocol major: it starts its own engine and says why.

Reaching a daemon on another machine takes cookie attach --url, and listening for other machines takes cookie daemon --listen; see A daemon already running and Remote access.

docs.title: The token
docs.text: Every connection presents the daemon's bearer token, [server] token. Clients and runtimes on the daemon's machine read it from the same config.toml; elsewhere it is passed with --token or COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN. Anyone holding the token is a fully trusted client. See Security.

docs.title: One store, one owner
docs.text: A session tree is written by one process at a time, which holds its owner.lock. An engine started beside a running daemon still lists the daemon's sessions, but opens them as read-only snapshots. See Sessions.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Persistent daemon and Remote access for running it.
  • Server [server] for its keys.
  • Architecture for how the engine, the server, and the clients are built.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text: A machine is the daemon's name for a computer its runtimes run on. Several runtimes can share one: the daemon's local runtime, a cookie runtime serve started over ssh, and a TUI's client_<host> runtime on the same laptop. The daemon groups them so that you, and the agents' memory, can talk about the computer rather than each connection to it.

docs.title: How a runtime finds its machine
docs.text:
A runtime reports a machine ID when it connects. cookie's own runtimes report a hash of the operating system's machine ID (/etc/machine-id or /var/lib/dbus/machine-id), or of a random ID kept in ~/.cookie-agent/machine-id where there is none, together with the host name. The daemon then places the runtime, first match first:

  1. on the machine the runtime ID is pinned to;
  2. on the machine that already lists the reported machine ID;
  3. on a new machine named after the host name;
  4. without a reported ID, on a new machine named after the runtime ID, which pins it there.

A runtime's machine is worked out each time from the machines, which are stored in ~/.cookie-agent/machines.json; only the daemon writes it.

docs.title: Offline runtimes
docs.text:
The registry also remembers where each runtime ran: when a template or dial-in runtime connects, the daemon records the machine ID, platform, and home directory it reported, and when it last saw the runtime connect or disconnect. A runtime that is not connected stays on its pin's machine, else on the machine its record names, shown as offline with when it was last seen, across daemon restarts too. Only a runtime that has never connected is on no machine. So an ssh template's sessions keep their machine badges and ~/… paths while it is down, and list_runtimes still places it.

A record goes away with forget on the offline runtime (cookie machine forget-runtime <runtime>, or Forget in the web client's Machines view), with its machine when the machine is forgotten, and, for a template, when config.toml no longer has its [runtimes.<id>] table at the next reload or restart. A dial-in runtime's record stays until it is forgotten.

docs.title: Regrouping
docs.text:
Two IDs can be one computer (a container and its host), or one ID can be the wrong place for a runtime. cookie machine, the Machines tab of the TUI's /runtime, and the web client's Machines & runtimes view (where a runtime moves by dragging it onto another machine) change the registry:

  • rename a machine, which moves its memory folder;
  • assign a runtime ID to a machine, pinning it, or unassign it so it follows the ID it reports;
  • merge one machine into another, moving its IDs, pins, and memories;
  • forget a machine that has no connected runtime and no memories (its offline runtimes' records go with it);
  • forget an offline runtime, so the machine no longer lists it.

See cookie machine and Machines.

docs.title: Memory per machine
docs.text: The machine memory layer keeps notes per machine: machine://<machine>/<name>, such as where a toolchain lives or which ports are free on it. Renaming or merging a machine carries its memories along. See Memory.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Memory is what agents keep between sessions: notes about you, about each agent's work, about each machine, and about each project. The daemon stores memories as Markdown files with a short frontmatter, and agents read and write them with tools, so what one session learns the next can use.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Layer URL For user user://<category> you: preferences, conventions, how you like to work agent agent://<agent> one agent's own notes about doing its job machine machine://<machine>/<name> one machine: toolchains, paths, services project project://<project>/<name> one project, wherever its checkouts live

Every agent has its agent:// memory from the start: the daemon makes one file per agent, names the agent in its description and keywords, and keeps those in line with the agent's document; the agent writes the body. An empty one is not shown to the model. See Agent memory.

Project memories belong to a project: a project memory can be written only to a project that exists, and every project has an project://<name>/overview whose description the daemon owns. A project memory names what identifies the project across machines, such as repository names, remote URLs, and <machine>:<path> places, so an agent can search for it from any checkout. See Layers and files.

docs.title: How agents use it
docs.text:
Memory comes with the global runtime, which new sessions attach. A run starts with a snapshot of it after the AGENTS.md context: every user memory, the run's agent's own, and an index of the memories of the machines the session works on. A session in a project also sees the project's overview in full and an index of its other memories; other projects' memories the agent searches for. The memory tools, memory_search, memory_read, memory_write, memory_edit, and memory_delete, read and change memories by URL. A whole-memory write needs the memory as the session last saw it, so one that changed meanwhile is never silently overwritten. The memory related to the session is what the agent is told to maintain: the system prompt asks it to keep memory small, accurate, and current, a write that looks like an existing memory is refused unless the agent says it is new, each kind of memory has a size limit, and every change is a line in the transcript. See What the model sees and Tools.

The memory and memory_write permission actions govern the tools, with the memory URL as the resource. A root run whose agent names no memory rules reads every memory and writes the memory related to its session (the user's, its own agent file, and its session's machines and project); a delegated run without them reads and writes only its own agent memory, and internal agents get none. A declared rule replaces the default for its action, so memory: deny turns memory off. The snapshot shows each memory only as far as the memory rules allow. See Memory permissions.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text: Memories are files under ~/.cookie-agent/memory/ on the daemon's machine, one folder per layer, so you can read, edit, or version them like any other files. /memory in the TUI and the web page, and cookie memory, list, edit, create, and delete them through the daemon, and show files that are not valid memories with the reason. See Managing memory and the [memory] settings.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Every tool call a model makes passes a permission check before it runs. The check asks one question: may this action touch this resource? The answer comes from rules, and an ask answer comes from you, or from a classifier on your behalf, depending on the session's mode.

docs.title: Actions and resources
docs.text:
Each tool declares a permission action and names the resource of each call:

  • read and write (write also covers edit): the file path;
  • bash: the whole command string;
  • webfetch: the URL;
  • delegate: the subagent's agent ID; message: the recipient's relation, parent, child, or sibling;
  • mcp: the MCP tool's name; skill: the skill name;
  • memory and memory_write: the memory URL;
  • cron: the target kind of the cron job a call touches, session, subagent, or new;
  • list_runtimes: nothing to name; any rule pattern matches.

Actions are free-form labels, a lowercase letter then up to 31 lowercase letters, digits, or underscores, so a runtime's or a plugin's tools can declare actions of their own. A few tools declare none and are always allowed, such as read_artifact, which reads only the tree's own retained output. See Resource labels.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
An agent document maps each action to an effect, allow, ask, or deny, either outright or per resource pattern:

permissions:
  read: allow
  bash:
    "git status": allow
    "*": ask
  write:
    ".env*": deny
    "*": ask

The most specific pattern wins, and a resource no rule matches is denied. A tool whose action has no allow or ask rule is not even offered to the model. See Permissions.

Two actions have a default by the agent's mode, which applies only while the document names no key for that action (a key with a runtime selector counts):

Mode list_runtimes mcp primary, all allow "*": ask subagent none "*": ask internal none none

So every agent that is not internal is offered the connected MCP servers' tools and asks before each call. A declared key replaces its action's default entirely: mcp: {"my_chrome_*": ask} offers only that server's tools, and mcp: deny hides them all. /permissions shows a default with the source default. See MCP default.

The memory actions have a default by whether the run is delegated, with the same rule that a declared key replaces it (patterns may use ${agent_id}, ${session_machine}, and ${session_project}):

Run memory memory_write root, agent not internal allow user://*, agent://${agent_id}, machine://${session_machine}/*, project://${session_project}/*: allow delegated, agent not internal "agent://${agent_id}": allow "agent://${agent_id}": allow internal agent none none

So a root agent reads every memory and writes the memory related to its session, and memory: deny turns memory off. See Memory permissions.

The cron action, which the cron tools use, has a default the same way: cron: allow for a root run of any agent but an internal one, and none for a delegated run or an internal agent, so a subagent sees the cron tools only when its document grants cron. Whatever the rules say, an agent can target only its own session or one below it, and only you, from a client, can set a new-session job's permission mode or pin its model. See Cron permissions.

docs.title: How the levels combine
docs.text:
A run's rules come from three levels: the daemon's defaults, the agent document, and the session's own rules, which you add in /permissions, the web client's permissions panel, or with cookie run --allowed-tools without touching the agent. They merge into one rule list:

  1. the defaults, for each action the document names no key for;
  2. the document's rules;
  3. the session's rules. A session rule with the same action, runtime selector, and pattern as a rule above replaces it; any other session rule is added.

That one list decides everything: a tool is offered when some rule for its action allows or asks, and a call follows the most specific matching rule, with a session rule winning a tie. /permissions shows the same list, each rule with its source (session, agent, or default).

Session rule Document and defaults A call cron: deny default cron: allow none: the cron tools are hidden memory: {"user://*": deny} default memory: allow user:// denied, every other memory readable bash: {"cargo test *": allow} bash: {"*": ask} cargo test runs, the rest asks bash: {"*": allow} bash: {"*": ask, "git push *": deny} git push denied, the rest runs bash: {"git push *": allow} bash: {"*": ask, "git push *": deny} git push runs, the rest asks mcp: deny default mcp: {"*": ask} none: the MCP tools are hidden

So a session can turn off a tool a default gives (memory, cron, MCP, list_runtimes), and a broad session rule does not override a narrower rule of the document: to change that rule for one session, override that exact pattern, which is what editing a row in /permissions does. See Session permission overlays.

docs.title: Rules for one runtime
docs.text:
A rule keyed action@runtime_id applies only to that runtime's tools, whatever workspace they work in, so bash: ask with bash@labpc: {"git *": allow} lets git run freely on labpc and asks for everything else. Of the daemon's own tools' actions, message and skill take no selector; delegate@labpc checks a root's delegation that gives its subagent the labpc runtime (see Delegating to runtimes). See Runtime selectors.

A path pattern starting with ~/ means the home directory of the runtime the tool runs on, so read: {"~/notes/*": allow} allows the notes under each runtime's own home. On a runtime that does not report its home the pattern matches nothing. See Paths under the home directory.

docs.title: Modes and approvals
docs.text:
A rule that says ask is resolved by the session tree's permission mode, shown in the TUI's bottom bar and shared by every client:

Mode An ask is auto-approve (the default) decided by the approval reviewer agent, which passes to you what it will not approve auto-approve-n decided by the reviewer; what it would pass to you is rejected auto-approve-y decided by the reviewer; what it would pass to you is approved once, unless its review failed ask always yours yolo approved at once

The reviewer judges each call against the whole session: your messages, in order, with what the agent has done so far (its tool calls and their outcomes, never their output) and the project's AGENTS.md. Only your own messages, your scheduled prompts, and AGENTS.md authorise a call; a later aside adds to the task rather than replacing it. Each decision comes with a one-sentence reason, shown to you and, on a denial, to the agent. A review that fails is passed to you in auto-approve and auto-approve-y and rejected in auto-approve-n. The mode is kept in the tree's log, so it survives a daemon restart. See The approval reviewer.

A deny rule and the doom-loop guard hold in every mode. An approval shows the call as it will run, such as the command or the diff of an edit, and you allow it once, allow it for the whole session tree, reject it, or reject it with a note for the agent. See Live permission modes and Approvals.

docs.title: What permissions do not do
docs.text: Rules decide which calls run; they are not a sandbox. An allowed bash command runs with your user's rights, and cat .env is a bash call, not a read. See Security.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
A project is a named body of work the daemon keeps, such as a repository you come back to across machines. A session may belong to one project, and moves in or out of one at any time. A project carries:

  • a name and an optional emoji clients show before it;
  • defaults for a new session: the runtimes it attaches and the agent it starts with;
  • its own AGENTS.md, instructions every session of the project gets;
  • its memories, project://<name>/…, with an overview shown in full to its sessions.

docs.title: Sessions in a project
docs.text:
session.create takes a project; a session belongs to no project unless one is chosen. When the creation names a project and no runtimes, the daemon attaches the project's default runtimes, so every client gets them. The default agent and preset are applied by the client to the new session's selection, since a session is always created with one; cookie --project <name> does so.

A session moves to another project, or out of any, with session.project.set, also while it runs: the move takes effect at its next run. Moving never changes the session's attachments or agent. A subagent belongs to its root session's project and moves with it.

docs.title: What sessions of a project see
docs.text:
At every run of a root session in a project:

  • the project's AGENTS.md comes first in the AGENTS.md context, before every workspace's files, so a workspace's own AGENTS.md has the last word;
  • the memory snapshot gains a ## Project <name> section: the overview in full, then an index of the project's other memories. Other projects' memories stay searchable.

Subagents see neither: like the machine index, the project section is for root runs.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: A project's memories live in ~/.cookie-agent/memory/projects/<name>/; the folder's name is the project's name. The daemon creates project://<name>/overview empty with the project, and owns its description. A memory can be written only to a project that exists, by an agent or by you: projects are created from a client, never by writing memory. Every memory folder that existed before projects did became a project, with no defaults, the first time the daemon started.

docs.title: In the clients
docs.text:
• The web client groups its sessions sidebar by project, No project last; each header shows the project's emoji, its name, and its default runtimes as badges. Drag a session onto a header, or use its row's ⋮ › Move to project…, to move it. The project editor sets the name, emoji, defaults, and AGENTS.md, and New session starts from a project's defaults. See Projects in the web guide.
  • The TUI starts its bottom bar with the session's project while no run is active; click it, or choose /project, to move the session or pick the new session's project. The session picker filters by project with Ctrl+P. See Projects in the TUI guide.
  • The CLI has cookie project and cookie --project <name>.

docs.title: Managing projects
docs.text:
projects.list, project.create, project.update, and project.delete manage projects from any client; cookie project does from the command line. Every change sends the revision it read, so two clients never overwrite each other.

  • Rename moves the memory folder with the project. Old project://<old>/… URLs in transcripts no longer resolve; sessions keep the project, and their next run shows the new name.
  • Delete removes the project's sessions, its whole memory folder, its AGENTS.md, and its defaults. It is refused while a session of the project runs.

The project itself lives in ~/.cookie-agent/projects/<id>/: project.toml (name, emoji, defaults) and the optional AGENTS.md. See cookie project, Projects in the protocol reference, and the projects spec.

docs.title: Runtimes and capabilities
docs.text: A runtime is where a session's tools run. It offers one or more capabilities, each a named set of tools with a self-declared kind, and says whether the capability works in a workspace directory. A session attaches the capabilities it uses; each attachment brings its tools into the session.

docs.title: The runtimes there are
docs.text:
Runtime Where it runs Capability Offers global inside the daemon, always global, no workspace top-level MCP servers, plugins, the memory tools, a fallback webfetch local inside the daemon coding, any directory on the daemon's machine read, write, edit, bash, webfetch, project skills, AGENTS.md [runtimes.<id>] a process the daemon starts from a template, typically ssh host cookie runtime serve --stdio whatever it declares; cookie runtime serve offers coding the same as local, on that machine dial-in a process that connects to the daemon's /runtime route, such as cookie runtime serve --daemon the same the same

A new TUI session attaches global and local's coding at the client's directory; a new web session starts with global alone, and its runtime cards, above the composer, pick others for the first message to create it with. The runtimes panel (/runtime) attaches and detaches others between runs, and in the TUI before the first prompt too. See Runtimes for templates, dial-in, and lifecycles.

Every runtime other than the built-in ones speaks the runtime protocol, so a runtime of your own can offer any tools; see Write a runtime.

docs.title: Attachments and tool names
docs.text:
Each attachment has a session-unique name: global for the global runtime, and for a workspace the runtime ID and the directory's name, such as local_web or labpc_api (with _2, _3, … when taken). The model sees a tool by its bare name while one attachment offers it. When several do, each copy is published as <attachment>_<tool>, such as local_web_bash and labpc_api_bash, and the bare name disappears. A tool can instead declare that it overrides others of its name, or that it is only a fallback, like the global runtime's webfetch, which hides whenever local offers one. A runtime tool never takes the name of a built-in tool such as delegate_subagent.

Names change only at a compaction, so the model's cached conversation stays valid. Attach labpc_api while the model works with local_web's bash, and bash stays local_web's while labpc_api's arrives as labpc_api_bash; from the next compaction both are prefixed. A tool that leaves stays declared until then, and a call to it is refused. See Example: a repository on another machine.

Permission rules can target one runtime's tools with action@runtime; see Permissions.

docs.title: Workspaces and homes
docs.text: A workspace is stored as the runtime reports it: canonical and absolute on the runtime's machine. A runtime may also report its home directory. Clients then show its paths as ~/… under that home, the runtime's and not their own, so a remote /home/lab/api reads ~/api only on the runtime whose home is /home/lab; a runtime that reports none shows its paths absolute. Permission rules written ~/… expand against the same home (see Paths under the home directory). A session's directory is its first workspace (see Where sessions live).

docs.title: Instances
docs.text: Attaching a capability at a workspace opens an instance of it. One runtime process serves every instance of every session that uses it, and an instance reports its status: starting, ready, reconnecting, failed, or stopped. A dropped runtime is reconnected; a session whose instance stays down shows an error row. The daemon notices a connection that died without closing within 45 s, and never creates a session, attaches a runtime, or delegates to one that is offline: a dial-in runtime that is not connected is refused at once, and one the daemon starts must come up first. See Lifecycle and failures.

docs.title: A client's machine
docs.text: When a TUI attaches to a daemon that runs on another machine, its sessions still need tools in the TUI's directory. Plain cookie and cookie attach pick, in order: the daemon's own local runtime when the daemon is on this machine; else a connected runtime on this machine that takes a workspace; else the TUI dials in as client_<host name>, serving only its directory, for as long as it runs. See Persistent daemon.

docs.title: Delegating to runtimes
docs.text: A root session decides where its subagents work. With global attached it has list_runtimes, which lists every machine and runtime, and its delegate_subagent takes capabilities: the runtime capabilities the child works through, such as labpc/coding at ~/src/api. The daemon starts those runtimes before it creates the child. Without capabilities a child inherits its parent's attachments, and only the root can choose. A root with only global has no workspace at all and must name one for each subagent, which lets it orchestrate work across machines. delegate@<runtime> rules limit where it may delegate. See Delegating to runtimes.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text: Each runtime reports the machine it runs on, and the daemon groups runtimes by machine, remembering where a runtime ran while it is offline; see Machines.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text: A session is one conversation: its messages, the runs that answered them, every tool call with its result, and the settings it ran with. The daemon keeps each session as an append-only event log, and every client renders the session from those events.

docs.title: Trees and delegation
docs.text:
A session you start is a root. When its agent delegates a task with delegate_subagent, the daemon creates a child session for the subagent, under the root; the subagent may delegate in turn, up to the configured depth. Together they form a session tree. Each subagent has a short handle, such as explore_1a2b3c4d, by which the agents address it: to read its result, send it a message, or stop its turn. A subagent reports every turn it finishes to its parent, and runs on whether or not the parent waits. See Delegation, Agent messaging, and the delegation tools.

Usage, permission modes, and approvals granted "for the session tree" all apply to the whole tree; /usage shows the selected session and its tree.

docs.title: Where sessions live
docs.text:
Sessions are stored per directory under ~/.cookie-agent/sessions/, each tree in its own folder with its subagents below it and the artifacts its tools retained. A session exists on disk from its first message. Its directory decides where it is listed: the TUI shows the sessions of the directory it was started in, and Ctrl+A in its session picker switches to every directory's; the web page lists every directory's. See Lifecycle and persistence.

A session's directory is decided once, when it is created, after its runtimes have attached: it is the workspace of its first attachment that has one, as that runtime reported it, canonical and absolute on the runtime's machine. What a client typed never decides it, so ~/web typed in the browser and /home/ada/web sent by the TUI are one directory, listed together. A session without a workspace keeps the client's directory as the daemon resolves it, or as typed when it cannot. Subagents share their parent's directory, and sessions created before this rule keep the directory they recorded.

Paths are stored canonical and absolute and shown short: a path of a runtime that reports its home directory reads ~ and ~/… under that home, the runtime's own and not the client's, and a path of a runtime that reports none stays absolute. See Home.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text: One process writes a tree at a time. The daemon that opens a tree takes its owner.lock; another cookie process, such as a standalone TUI beside a running daemon, can read the tree but shows it as a read-only snapshot until the owner exits. Clients of one daemon share its ownership, so they all write. See Tree-scoped session ownership lock.

docs.title: History that lasts
docs.text: The log is a compatibility surface. Each session records the history format it was written in (currently 1); a later build reads it tolerantly, skipping what it does not know, and a build that changes the format converts older logs when it opens them, keeping the originals as events.jsonl.v<N>.bak. cookie sessions upgrade converts a directory's sessions at once. See History formats and Compatibility.

docs.title: Changing history
docs.text:
• Revert removes a message and everything after it, subagents it started included, and puts the message back into the composer. It needs an idle session and is refused when the session gained events the client has not shown. See Revert.
  • Fork copies a session up to a message into a new, independent session. See Fork.
  • Compaction replaces older context with a summary when the context fills, or on /compact. See Compaction.
  • Delete removes a whole tree from disk: the root, its subagents, their events, and their artifacts. Only a root is deleted, after you confirm; it is refused while a session of the tree runs, while another process owns the tree, and when the root gained events since you looked. It cannot be undone. See Delete.

docs.title: What a session is bound to
docs.text: A session has one selection (agent, model, variant, preset) shared by every client, one permission mode for its tree, and the runtimes it attaches. A run freezes its model binding and system prompt when it starts, so changes to the configuration apply from the next run. See Agents and presets and Runtimes.

docs.title: Persistent daemon
docs.text: This page covers running the daemon as a process of its own: starting it and attaching clients to it, how plain cookie finds a daemon already running on the machine, and running the daemon as a service on Linux, macOS, and Windows. Its clients are the terminal UI, the web client, and the command line; Remote access covers reaching it from other machines, Runtimes the runtimes it uses, Running a runtime as a service keeping a runtime on another machine connected, and Security its trust boundaries.

docs.title: Separate server and client
docs.text:
The daemon binds to 127.0.0.1:7419 by default:

cookie daemon
