                            "output": {"kind": "single", "text": now}},
                "media": []}
    if method in ("runtime/ping", "runtime/shutdown"):
        return {}
    return None

for line in sys.stdin:
    if not line.strip():
        continue
    message = json.loads(line)
    if "id" not in message or "method" not in message:
        continue  # a notification such as tool/release, or a reply
    result = handle(message["method"], message.get("params") or {})
    if result is None:
        send({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": message["id"],
              "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "unknown method"}})
    else:
        send({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": message["id"], "result": result})
    if message["method"] == "runtime/shutdown":
        break

Run it from a template in the daemon's config.toml:

[runtimes.buildbox]
command = ["ssh", "-o", "BatchMode=yes", "buildbox", "python3", "clock_runtime.py"]

Then attach buildbox/clock from /runtime. The tool declares no permission, so every agent may call it; declare one to put it under permission rules. A version that dials in instead connects with a WebSocket library and exchanges the same messages as text frames.

docs.title: Check your messages
docs.text: The runtime protocol's schemas are published with these pages: methods.json and one JSON Schema per params and result root under schemas/runtime/schemas/, as crates/protocol/compat/runtime/ commits them. Validate what you send against them in your tests. See Published schemas. In Rust, cookie_agent_coding_runtime's server is the reference implementation, and cookie_agent_runtime_api has the tool provider types it builds on; see the Rust API.

docs.title: ACP Agents [acp]
docs.text:
Control how the daemon runs ACP agents, the external coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI that runtimes host and that take a session's turns over the Agent Client Protocol (see the ACP agents guide). The agents themselves are declared on their runtime, under [runtimes.<id>.acp.agents.<agent>], or once for every runtime under [acp.agents.<agent>]. Complete config.toml:

[acp]
idle_shutdown_ms = 300000

[acp.agents.claude]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp"]
description = "Claude Code"

An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml.

Key Type Default Description idle_shutdown_ms integer 300000 How long an agent's process stays up with no turn in progress before the daemon stops it. Each agent runs one process per runtime, shared by its sessions; the next turn starts it again and resumes the session's ACP session. Must be at least 1. agents.<agent> table none An ACP agent every runtime offers (all but global), run on each runtime's own machine. Its fields are those of a runtime's declaration: command, env, description, enabled. A runtime's own [runtimes.<id>.acp.agents.<agent>] of the same key replaces it on that runtime, with another command or enabled = false to leave it off there.

The table applies at once when the configuration changes: the next idle period reads it.

docs.title: AGENTS.md Context [agent_md]
docs.text:
Complete config.toml to disable automatic repository context:

[agent_md]
enabled = false

An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail. See config.toml.

Repository-authored context is untrusted input. Review it before running in an unfamiliar workspace; admission is independent of tool read permissions. See security boundaries.

Controls root-run AGENTS.md discovery documented in Agents. This is the global default; an agent document may set agent_md: true or agent_md: false to override it for that agent, for example to keep a lean agent's context free of repository instructions:

---
description: Minimal-context agent
mode: primary
enabled: true
models:
  - { model: "openai/gpt-5", variant: null }
agent_md: false
---
Answer using only what the user provides.
Key Type Default Description enabled boolean true Load AGENTS.md context files at each root run start: the session's project's, then each workspace's. Delegated and internal agents remain excluded. An agent document's agent_md field, when present, overrides this for that agent's root runs.

Files larger than 2 MiB (2097152 bytes) are skipped entirely and surfaced as an AgentMdSkipped warning event; they are never partially loaded or truncated. Loaded entries are rendered into a single user context turn wrapped in a <system-reminder> block, with each file delimited as <contents from="/abs/path/AGENTS.md">…</contents>; a project's file comes first, as <contents from="project:<name>/AGENTS.md">…</contents>.

docs.title: Approval [approval]
docs.text:
Set the expiry for pending user approvals and how long the approval reviewer's conversation stays in its provider's prompt cache. By default a pending approval waits until you answer it. Complete config.toml:

[approval]
timeout_ms = 600000
cache_ttl = "1h"

This does not select a permission mode or grant tools; those decisions belong to Agent permissions. Expiry leaves an unattended request unapproved. The window opens when a call reaches you, after the approval reviewer passed it on, so the reviewer's own model-call budget (its limits.timeout_ms) never comes out of it. An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml.

Key Type Default Description timeout_ms integer none How long a user approval stays pending before it expires unattended, counted from when the call reaches you. Absent, 0, or negative: it never expires, and waits until it is answered, the run is cancelled, or the daemon stops. cache_ttl string "1h" The reviewer's prompt-cache lifetime: "1h", "30m", "12h", "5m", "provider" (the reviewer model's provider's own cache configuration), or "off" (no cache writes). See The reviewer's cache.

docs.title: The reviewer's cache
docs.text:
The reviewer keeps one conversation per session and adds a turn per review, so each request ends with a rolling cache marker that the next review reads back. cache_ttl maps onto the provider of the model the reviewer runs on, whatever the session's provider is. A lifetime the provider does not offer becomes the nearest one it does, by ratio with ties going longer, and cookie config status says so:

Reviewer's provider 1h 30m 12h 5m provider off Anthropic rolling 1h; system and tools raised to 1h 1h 1h rolling 5m the provider's cache table and the session layer's defaults no markers Bedrock 1h on models that take it, else 5m as 1h as 1h rolling 5m the provider's cache table no cache points OpenAI Responses with the GPT-5.6 controls rolling breakpoint at 30m 30m 12h 30m the provider's cache table explicit mode with no breakpoint OpenAI Chat Completions, Azure, with the controls rolling breakpoint at 30m 30m 30m 30m the provider's cache table explicit mode with no breakpoint OpenAI and Azure without the controls, OpenAI-compatible, Gemini, Cohere no effect: the provider caches on its own

The value is read at each review, so a configuration change reaches the next one. The title agent never sends a rolling marker.

docs.title: Why did the reviewer decide this?
docs.text:
Each decision of the approval reviewer carries a one-sentence reason:

  • A call it passed to you shows "The reviewer asks: " in the TUI's approval panel and on the web client's approval card.
  • A call it allowed or denied names the reason in its info row, which the TUI shows at the info event level; a denied call's tool result gives the agent the same reason.
  • The session log records it as the rationale of the approval's approval_step evaluated decision (events).

    • When a decision looks wrong, check what the reviewer could see:

    • "The reviewer failed, so the call is yours to decide." The review itself failed: no model, a timeout, an error, or a reply that was not the verdict JSON. The evaluated step's reason is internal_agent_failed and the approval's internal_agent_finished says why. Set small_model, or check its provider.
    • It judged against a message without your authority. Only [user] messages, your scheduled prompts, and the project's AGENTS.md authorise a call; another agent's message or a parent agent's instructions only describe the situation. Say in the session what you want done, and the next review sees it.
    • It never saw what made the call routine. The reviewer sees the agent's tool calls and their outcomes, never their output or the agent's own text. Put standing permissions in the project's AGENTS.md, or turn a call you always approve into an allow rule.
    • It weighed the call too strictly or too loosely. Add rules of your own to the reviewer's prompt with an approval.md that wraps {{default_prompt}} (internal agents), or choose another variant for small_model.

    cookie config status also notes when cache_ttl maps to another TTL on the reviewer's provider, or has no effect there.

docs.title: config.toml
docs.text:
The engine reads ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml over built-in defaults. The file is not required; an empty file is valid. This complete example changes one setting:

[model_retry]
standard_retries = 1

docs.title: Locations and inheritance
docs.text:
Configuration is the built-in defaults plus one optional authored layer, the user layer in ~/.cookie-agent/. Within it, config.toml and the agents/ directory are optional. There is no workspace layer: a <cwd>/.cookie-agent/config.toml or <cwd>/.cookie-agent/agents/ directory is never opened, so a leftover file there is ignored without a warning. The working directory still supplies AGENTS.md context and project skills, which are context, not configuration.

An authored settings table replaces the built-in table as a whole. Omitted fields in it use defaults. For example, the snippet above leaves overload_retries and backoff_ceiling_ms at their defaults. An omitted table keeps the defaults unchanged. Global headers are the exception: names merge with the built-in headers and empty values delete them. Model and variant sparse inheritance happens within one provider definition.

Agents are separate Markdown documents; skills have their own discovery rules. The client loads tui.toml independently.

docs.title: Accepted top-level keys
docs.text:
Every key is optional. Unknown keys, including removed top-level pricing, fail.

Key Canonical settings page default_model Default models: the model agents reach as ${default_model} small_model Default models: the model agents reach as ${small_model} server Server: where the daemon listens, its token, and the daemon clients on this machine use tool_output Tool Output subagent_output Subagent Output agent_md AGENTS.md Context loop_warning Loop Warning approval Approval model_retry Model Retry context_compaction Context Compaction session_title Session Title delegation Delegation messaging Agent Messaging producers External Producers memory Memory cron Cron Jobs deferred_tools Deferred Tools: built-in tool groups sent up front instead of deferred notifications Push Notifications shell_environment Shell Environment: the environment runtimes start processes in acp ACP Agents skills Official skills: official, whether the daemon keeps the official skills up to date and offers them headers Request Header providers Providers mcp MCP plugins Plugins runtimes Runtimes

Every key above except default_model and small_model, which are values, is a top-level table: write [messaging], [delegation], and so on, never [runtime.messaging] or another nested spelling. Older docs used the [runtime.messaging] form; a nested table such as that is an unknown top-level field and fails strict validation.

docs.title: Default models
docs.text:
default_model and small_model name the models agent documents reach as ${default_model} and ${small_model}, so one edit retargets every agent that uses them. Each is a model key, which means the model's default variant, or a table { model, variant }; both are optional, and unknown keys in the table fail. Being top-level values, they go before the first table:

default_model = { model = "anthropic/claude-opus-5-5", variant = "high" }
small_model   = "deepseek/deepseek-flash"

[model_retry]
standard_retries = 1

In the starter kit small_model serves the internal approval and title agents, and the variant chosen for it, during onboarding or here, is the approval reviewer's effort. Reasoning output dominates what each review costs, and the reviewer's prompt cache reduces only the input side, so a low variant keeps reviews cheap (the reviewer's cache).

Only the key's grammar is checked when the file loads. Whether the model is available is a runtime matter: a model whose provider is disconnected loads fine, and the agent entries naming it are skipped until it is available again. See agents for how documents use them and onboarding for setting both from a client.

docs.title: Changes while the daemon runs
docs.text:
The daemon reads config.toml and the agent documents when it starts. Clients read them with config.get and change them with config.apply: a set of whole-document puts and deletes and single-key set edits of config.toml, checked against the revision and fingerprints the client read, validated whole, written, and applied together (see the protocol reference). After editing the files by hand, reload them with config.reload. A configuration that fails validation is not applied: the daemon keeps running on the one it has and reports the error. Applying a configuration does this:

Part When it takes effect default_model, small_model At once for new runs: the agents are recompiled, and every entry naming them follows skills official = false stops refreshing at once; whether the official skills are offered follows at the next start tool_output, subagent_output, agent_md, loop_warning, approval, model_retry, context_compaction, session_title, delegation, messaging, producers, memory, cron, notifications At once, from each setting's next use; a run keeps the result limits, retry policy, and delegation depth it started with Agent documents and presets At once for new runs; a run in progress keeps its agent, and its delegated children resolve against the agents it started with providers, headers At once: models are recompiled mcp At once: changed servers restart, removed ones stop; servers added or changed at runtime (/mcp) stay on top tool_output for runtime instances When an instance next starts or reconnects server.session_idle_eviction_after At once, from the next check of idle sessions runtimes.<id>.mcp, runtimes.<id>.acp At once, for a connected runtime: added servers and agents start, removed ones stop, changed ones restart (see Runtime templates) shell_environment, runtimes.<id>.shell_environment At once: each connected runtime captures again, and processes it starts afterwards get the new environment; a reload captures again even when nothing changed (see Shell Environment) server (its other keys), plugins, a template's command, env, and timeouts Only after the daemon restarts; the reload reports them as needing a restart, and a client can restart the daemon (see Restarting the daemon)

Skills are not reloaded.

docs.title: Editing from a client
docs.text:
In the TUI, /config lists config.toml, the shared agents, and each preset with its agents. Enter opens the selected document in $VISUAL (else $EDITOR, else vi, or on Windows code --wait when VS Code is on PATH, else Notepad); saving and quitting applies it. A document the daemon refuses, because the result does not validate, is not applied: the panel shows why and marks the document not applied, and Enter reopens your text to fix it. n creates an agent document (agents/<id>.md, or agents/<preset>/<id>.md with a preset selected) from a template, d deletes the selected agent after a y, and r reloads hand edits. The status pane shows when the files differ from the applied configuration, why the last reload failed, and what needs a restart. The text travels over the protocol, so this works against a daemon on another machine.

From a terminal, cookie config does the same against the daemon that --url and --token (or [server] in this machine's config.toml) name:

cookie config edit                      # config.toml in $VISUAL or $EDITOR
cookie config edit agents/reviewer.md   # a new document starts from a template
cookie config set loop_warning.enabled false
cookie config set 'providers."custom.x".base_url' https://llm.example/v1
cookie config unset model_retry
cookie config remove agents/reviewer.md
cookie config reload                    # after editing the files by hand
cookie config status

set takes a dotted key with TOML quoting and a TOML value; a value that is not TOML, such as a bare URL, is a string. It edits only that key, keeping the rest of the file and its comments. edit asks to edit again when the daemon refuses the result.

docs.title: State kept beside the configuration
docs.text:
Some files in the data folder are what the daemon learned, not configuration: they are not validated as authored files, and an unreadable one counts as empty and is written again. native-compaction.json is the record of providers the daemon stopped attempting native compaction for, one entry per provider ID:

{
  "providers": {
    "my-gateway": {
      "state": "unsupported",
      "since": "2026-10-24T12:00:00Z",
      "reason": "the compact endpoint answered HTTP 404",
      "config_digest": "sha256:…"
    }
  }
}

state is unsupported or rejects_windows. An entry expires 7 days after since, and is dropped when the provider's configuration no longer matches config_digest. Delete the file, or an entry, to try native compaction again. The daemon writes the file through a temporary file and a rename.

deferred-tools.json is the record of models that refused deferred tools, one entry per provider/model, each with since, reason, and config_digest:

{
  "models": {
    "my-gateway/claude-opus-4-6": {
      "since": "2026-10-27T12:00:00Z",
      "reason": "a request with deferred tools was refused (HTTP 400)",
      "config_digest": "sha256:…"
    }
  }
}

A recorded model is sent every tool up front. An entry expires 7 days after since, and is dropped when the model's provider configuration, or the deferral support it is compiled with, no longer matches config_digest. Delete the file, or an entry, to try deferral again. cookie config, the TUI's /config, and the web client's settings list both records' entries as notes.

docs.title: Strictness and limits
docs.text:
Every authored file is parsed strictly. Unknown keys, leftover schema or schema_version keys, wrong types, and malformed content are hard errors with an actionable path, key, and line where available. No authored-file migrations or unknown-field ignores exist. Decoded values that hold secrets are zeroized when the load completes.

TOML-level limits (enforced before deserialization):

  • Configuration file at most 1 MiB; agent document at most 256 KiB.
  • Maximum TOML nesting depth 32; at most 4096 entries per table or array.
  • String values at most 256 KiB; TOML datetimes rejected; floats must be finite.

docs.title: Environment interpolation
docs.text:
${env:NAME} is single-pass interpolation. ${env:NAME:-fallback} uses the fallback when the variable is unset; the fallback may be empty and is split on the first :-. $$ emits a literal $. Interpolation is allowed only in these paths:

  • providers.<id>.endpoint
  • providers.<id>.base_url
  • providers.<id>.setup.<field>
  • providers.<id>.api_key
  • providers.<id>.auth_override.values.<field>
  • providers.<id>.auth.values.<field>
  • headers.<name>
  • providers.<id>.headers.<name>
  • providers.<id>.models.<model>.headers.<name>
  • model and model-override variants.<variant>.headers.<name>

NAME must be [A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]* (uppercase letters, digits, underscore, starting with a letter or underscore). A missing variable, a non-UTF-8 value, or an interpolation used anywhere else is a load error. A missing variable without a default remains an error. Header templates are validated at load time but kept unresolved for request-time expansion and stable manifests. Interpolation is not available in permission patterns or agent documents.

docs.title: Context Compaction [context_compaction]
docs.text:
Complete config.toml using the defaults:

[context_compaction]
auto = true
trigger = { percent = 70 }
max_summary_bytes = 262144
keep_recent_tokens = 16384

For fixed headroom, replace trigger with { buffer_tokens = 33000 }. An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table completely and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml.

Controls the automatic context-limit behavior documented in Compaction. Native compaction has no setting here: it runs beside the summary on every Responses model unless the model sets compaction = "unsupported" (see native compaction).

The built-in compaction agent has a flat 3-minute timeout. An authored compaction.md can override limits.timeout_ms, which is honored exactly; zero or omission uses the 30-second internal-agent default. The timeout does not scale with serialized history size.

The internal summarizer receives only the span the checkpoint replaces: the active, unpruned history up to the recent messages retained unchanged after the summary, which are never sent to it. This is the currently assembled history, not a reload of events replaced by earlier checkpoints. The request keeps the session's own system prompt and tool definitions so it stays a cache-friendly prefix of the latest conversation request; the compaction agent's prompt is folded into the trailing instruction message instead of replacing the session system prompt. A tool-call answer is rejected as non-text output and counts as a compaction failure. Internal agents have no local byte-based admission gate. A provider context-length failure permits at most one pruned retry; other failures do not trigger pruning. Bindings are tried in order. Automatic compaction stops after three consecutive failures in a run and emits one diagnostic; a successful checkpoint resets the counter. The retry changes only an in-memory copy of the summarizer input, using ArtifactStore::retain and artifact-ID reference markers for tool results and replacing output from read_artifact calls with [artifact read output omitted for compaction], detected by the tool name. Ordinary filesystem reads are pruned normally. The pruned retry also drops the session tool definitions: cache affinity is already lost once tool outputs are rewritten, so fewer tools means less to send. Markers include a read_artifact hint with artifact="<digest>"; internal stored references retain their URI format. The session tree reads that artifact back with read_artifact. Text content is retained as it was, so it pages line by line. Non-text tool content is retained line-structured, a [tool content: <kind>] header and each part under a [part N: kind] line with its text's own line breaks and JSON pretty-printed, and the marker describes this layout; artifacts earlier builds stored keep their one line of serialized JSON. It emits no durable tool_output_elided events and preserves the original saved log and recent retained message contents even if the retry fails. After compaction, model context contains the summary and retained recent messages alongside pinned context.

Key Type Default Description auto boolean true Enable automatic compaction signals (post-check usage and predictive pre-send estimation). Manual /compact and context-overflow recovery compaction remain available when false. trigger inline table { percent = 70 } Trigger threshold selection. { percent = N } uses N% of the model's input budget, where N must be from 1 through 99. { buffer_tokens = N } subtracts positive N from the input budget, saturating at zero. The input budget is the model's input limit when it declares one, otherwise its context limit less min(output cap, 32000, context / 2) (see compaction). buffer_tokens integer unset Legacy alias for trigger = { buffer_tokens = N }. Must be greater than zero and cannot be set together with trigger. max_summary_bytes integer 262144 (256 * 1024) Hard byte limit for a compaction summary produced by the internal compaction agent. Must be greater than zero and at most 2 * 1024 * 1024 (2 MiB). keep_recent_tokens integer (u64) 16384 Nonnegative token budget for recent original messages retained unchanged after an internal summary. The summarizer receives only the messages before them. 0 disables retention, so the summary covers the whole active history. The effective target is at most min(keep_recent_tokens, input_budget / 4), further limited by actual post-checkpoint available space. Complete tool-call/result groups are never split; an oversized newest indivisible group leaves no recent messages retained. Configuration does not clamp the requested value. Native windows receive no independent recent messages.

docs.title: Cron Jobs [cron]
docs.text:
Control how the daemon fires cron jobs, the prompts you and agents schedule into sessions (see Scheduling prompts and the cron spec). Complete config.toml:

[cron]
enabled = true
max_consecutive_failures = 3
history = 20

The jobs themselves live in crons.json in the data directory, not in the configuration. An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml.

Key Type Default Description enabled boolean true Whether the daemon fires jobs. With false, each due fire is recorded as skipped (firing_disabled) and the job moves to its next fire; jobs, the crons.* requests, and the cron tools keep working. max_consecutive_failures integer 3 Failures in a row that disable a job, unless the job sets its own max_consecutive_failures. A failure is a fire that cannot start or a run it started that ends failed; skips and cancelled runs do not count, and a completed run resets the count. Must be at least 1. history integer 20 Fires each job's history keeps, oldest dropped first. Must be 1..=1000.

The table applies at once when the configuration changes: the next fire reads it.

docs.title: Deferred Tools [deferred_tools]
docs.text:
On a model that loads deferred tools, the tools of these built-in groups are deferred: agents, cron, goal, memory, and runtimes. The model sees their names in announcements and loads them with tool_search when it needs them. A deferred group's instructions, such as memory's, arrive with its first load instead of in the system prompt. Complete config.toml to send a group up front instead:

[deferred_tools]
always_load = ["memory"]

An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail. See config.toml.

Key Type Default Description always_load array of strings [] Built-in groups sent up front: any of agents, cron, goal, memory, and runtimes, each at most once. Any other name fails.

MCP servers and plugins have their own always_load keys: see MCP and plugins.

docs.title: Delegation [delegation]
docs.text:
Bound delegated work and idle residency. Complete config.toml:

[delegation]
max_depth = 3
max_concurrency = 4
max_resident_subagents = 20
idle_eviction_after = "1h"

These limits do not authorize delegation. Configure eligible targets and tool access in Agent permissions. An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml.

max_resident_subagents accepts zero. Duration values are a nonnegative integer followed by one supported unit, without spaces or compound units; "0s" is valid. Overflow is rejected. Residency is a soft threshold, not an admission cap.

Each root and delegated session is assigned a short, tree-unique handle (<agent_type>_<8 hex>, e.g. explore_1a2b3c4d) when its creation event is written. The handle is carried on session_created.short_id and surfaces through the delegation tools as an alternative to the full session UUID; it is a presentation-and-resolution layer, not a storage identity. See the delegation tool reference.

Key Type Default Description max_depth integer 3 Maximum delegation depth below a root session. Must be greater than zero. max_concurrency integer 4 Maximum concurrently running root-level background delegations. Excess calls queue FIFO, up to 4 × max_concurrency; a full queue rejects admission. Foreground and nested delegations bypass this queue. A value of 0 is rejected. max_resident_subagents integer 20 Soft trigger for resident delegated sessions, counted per root session tree. When one tree's count is above it, the janitor evicts that tree's eligible idle children oldest-first until the tree's count reaches the trigger or no eligible child remains; other trees are unaffected. Recently active children may keep residency above the trigger. idle_eviction_after duration string "1h" Minimum time since a delegated session's last run ended before it can be evicted. Compact ms, s, m, h, and d suffixes are accepted.

docs.title: Request Header [headers]
docs.text:
Complete config.toml to add a public header and delete a shipped one:

[headers]
x-client-name = "workspace-agent"
x-session-affinity = ""

This key accepts a map of header names to string values, with no fixed nested field names. Invalid names, values, forbidden ownership, or limits fail loading. Unlike settings tables, the user header map merges with the shipped one by normalized name; an omitted name inherits and an empty value deletes it. See config.toml for templates.

Global request headers are merged with provider, model, and variant headers tables. Names are case-insensitive and later values win:

shipped defaults -> global -> provider -> model or variant

An empty value deletes an inherited header. Each authored table and each merged result is limited to 64 entries, 128 bytes per name, 8192 bytes per value, and 64 KiB in aggregate. The shipped lowest-priority layer is:

Header Value user-agent cookie-agent/<build version> x-session-id ${session_id} x-session-affinity ${session_id} x-opencode-session ${session_id}; OpenCode Zen/Go pins a session to one upstream with it x-session-parent-id ${parent_session_id}; omitted for root sessions session-id ${session_id}; the ChatGPT sign-in route keys prompt-cache affinity on it thread-id ${session_id}; sent beside session-id, as Codex sends it

${session_id} and ${parent_session_id} are expanded for each request. Templates, rather than resolved session IDs or environment values, are stored in model manifests and fingerprints. Header values are public behavior metadata: environment interpolation is supported, but the configured template and its resolved plaintext value may be exposed in process memory and on the wire.

Transport-owned headers (host, content-length, transfer-encoding, connection, proxy-authorization) and protocol-owned headers (content-type, accept, anthropic-version, anthropic-beta, and every x-amz-* name) are forbidden at every level. Auth-owned headers (authorization, x-api-key, api-key, cookie, set-cookie, x-goog-api-key) and user-agent are allowed. If any auth-owned header is configured, caller headers take precedence and the adapter does not inject its typed authentication header.

docs.title: Loop Warning [loop_warning]
docs.text:
Complete config.toml to turn off repeated-tool-call warnings:

[loop_warning]
enabled = false

An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail. See config.toml.

Key Type Default Description enabled boolean true Warn the model when it keeps repeating the same tool calls with identical results. Applies to root and delegated agent runs.

A run counts as looping when its latest tool calls are at least three consecutive copies of the same block of one to eight calls: same operations, same outputs or errors. Changing output counts as progress, and user input starts the count over. The engine then appends a <system-reminder> to the latest successful result, telling the model how many times it has repeated itself and to work from the results it already has. The warning repeats, with a rising count, for as long as the loop continues. It never blocks a call or stops the run. The TUI and the web client show the warning under the call's output, as the model reads it.

docs.title: Memory [memory]
docs.text:
Size limits of memory documents and of the memory snapshot a session's model sees. Complete config.toml:

[memory]
user_max_bytes = 16384
agent_max_bytes = 16384
machine_max_bytes = 16384
project_max_bytes = 16384
overview_max_bytes = 16384
snapshot_user_bytes = 12288
snapshot_index_bytes = 4096

Memory is a folder of Markdown notes, ~/.cookie-agent/memory; see the memory spec. An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail, max_file_bytes included, which the five document limits replaced; see config.toml.

Key Type Default Description user_max_bytes integer 16384 Largest user:// category, frontmatter included, in bytes. Must be positive and at most 57344. agent_max_bytes integer 16384 Largest agent:// file, frontmatter included, in bytes. Must be positive and at most 57344. machine_max_bytes integer 16384 Largest machine:// memory, frontmatter included, in bytes. Must be positive and at most 57344. project_max_bytes integer 16384 Largest project:// memory other than an overview, frontmatter included, in bytes. Must be positive and at most 57344. overview_max_bytes integer 16384 Largest project overview, project://<project>/overview, frontmatter included, in bytes. Must be positive and at most 57344. snapshot_user_bytes integer 12288 Room for the user categories in a snapshot, in bytes of rendered text. Categories that do not fit are listed by name only. Must be positive. snapshot_index_bytes integer 4096 Room for the index of the session's machine memories in a snapshot, in bytes of rendered text, summed over all machines. Memories that do not fit are only counted. Must be positive.

A write or edit that would leave a memory over its kind's limit is refused, and the model is told to read it with memory_read and condense it. A memory already over its limit, as after the limit is lowered, stays valid and is still shown, marked over its limit; only changes that make it smaller are accepted until it fits. A file larger than 57344 bytes is invalid: search and the snapshot skip it.

The snapshot limits are measured on the snapshot's rendered text (see System Prompt Composition): a category or machine memory is shown only while its whole section still fits. The run's agent's own file is measured on its escaped description and body against the room the two snapshot limits leave in the event; a file that does not fit is named instead of shown. A snapshot is recorded as one session event, bounded at 64 KiB. agent_max_bytes, snapshot_user_bytes, and snapshot_index_bytes together must not exceed 57344 bytes, which leaves 8 KiB for the snapshot's fixed text, headings, and escaping; a configuration whose limits sum to more fails to load.

The limits apply at once when the configuration is applied or reloaded: a lowered document limit applies from the next write, and the next snapshot marks the memories over it.

docs.title: Agent Messaging [messaging]
docs.text:
Bound agent-to-agent mail (send_message) inside a delegation tree. Complete config.toml:

[messaging]
enabled = true
max_hops = 0
max_body_bytes = 32768
max_pending_per_session = 32
max_inflight_per_pair = 4

Authority to send at all comes from message permission rules in agent documents, not from this table; messaging is deny-by-default even when this feature is enabled. See Agent Messaging. An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml.

All delivery is producer-backed: running recipients receive mail at their next safe model-request boundary, and idle or finished recipients wake through the producer reconcile path rather than user-steering machinery.

Key Type Default Description enabled boolean true Master switch. When false, send_message fails with the send_message:disabled tool error even if permission rules allow the send. max_hops integer 0 Chain-length guard for message hops. Hop counting is internal producer metadata and never appears in the delivered envelope. Mail between a parent and its direct child adds no hop, so the pair can exchange as much as it needs; subagent reports are not mail and never count. A send that would exceed the limit fails with send_message:max_hops_exceeded. Values <= 0 disable the guard. max_body_bytes integer 32768 Maximum UTF-8 size of a message body. Tighter than the 256 KiB plugin body cap because agent mail should be terse. A 0 value is accepted at parse time and rejects every send at runtime with send_message:invalid_body. max_pending_per_session integer 32 Pending agent mail per recipient session. Beyond the cap, new sends fail with send_message:inbox_full and nothing is admitted or discarded. Only Agent-owner producer messages count; plugin, subagent-report, background-result, and goal mail never consume the budget. max_inflight_per_pair integer 4 Per-directed-pair window of unacknowledged messages, to stop ping-pong storms. A pair message is unacknowledged while accepted, admitted, claimed, or released, and acknowledged once it is consumed or discarded. A full window fails the send with send_message:inflight_full. A value of 0 disables the guard.

max_hops and max_inflight_per_pair are enforced at send time and disabled by non-positive and zero values respectively, so operators can opt out of each guard independently. max_body_bytes and max_pending_per_session boundaries are enforced at send time; no value here is validated at load time beyond its type.

docs.title: Model Retry [model_retry]
docs.text:
Complete config.toml using the defaults:

[model_retry]
standard_retries = 3
overload_retries = 5
backoff_ceiling_ms = 60000

An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces it completely, with defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail. See config.toml for layer precedence.

Controls retries on the current model before the engine advances through its fallback chain. Values count retries after the initial attempt. Zero disables retries for that class, while any negative value retries indefinitely until the request succeeds or the run is cancelled.

Key Type Default Description standard_retries signed 64-bit integer 3 Retry budget for ordinary retryable model errors: one initial attempt plus three retries gives up to four total attempts by default. overload_retries signed 64-bit integer 5 Separate retry budget for overload errors and retryable HTTP 429/503 responses. backoff_ceiling_ms integer 60000 Positive local ceiling, in milliseconds, for exponential backoff after jitter.

Retries use exponential backoff from one second with 25% jitter, clamped to backoff_ceiling_ms and a positive minimum of one millisecond. A provider Retry-After is authoritative when longer and may exceed that local ceiling without a cap. Cancellation still interrupts the wait.

The retry budget applies no matter how far an attempt got: an ordinary retryable failure that arrives mid-stream, after partial output was already produced, still consumes standard_retries on the same model before the loop falls back. The abandoned attempt's partial deltas are discarded (the request is rebuilt from committed history), so provider prompt caches remain warm for the retry.

docs.title: Push Notifications [notifications]
docs.text:
Control the Web Push notifications the daemon sends to the phones and browsers you turned notifications on in (see the push notifications spec). Complete config.toml:

[notifications]
enabled = true
preview = "reply"
approvals = true
cron_sessions = true
contact = "mailto:you@example.com"

The daemon pushes when a root session settles (its run ended completed or failed, and nothing but a recurring cron job can start another run), and, with approvals, when an approval or an ACP agent's question waits for you anywhere in a session's tree. The persistent daemon also pushes when it goes down for a restart a client asked for (not to the device that asked) and when it is up again. Nothing is pushed for a session a client shows you at that moment. The subscriptions themselves live in push/ in the data directory, not in the configuration. An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml.

Key Type Default Description enabled boolean true Whether the daemon sends pushes. With false, nothing is pushed; turning notifications on, the device list, and test pushes keep working. preview string "reply" What a notification shows on the lock screen: "reply", the start of the final reply, the error, the tool call, or the question; or "status", only Finished., Failed., Approval waiting, or Question waiting. approvals boolean true Push approvals and ACP agents' questions that wait for you. cron_sessions boolean true Push when a root session a new-session cron job created settles. Its approvals and questions are pushed either way. contact string the repository URL the daemon was built from The contact push services see for this daemon (the VAPID sub claim): an https: URL or a mailto: address. Nothing checks it but its form; set it when you want to be the one a push service writes to.

The table applies at once when the configuration changes: the next push reads it.

docs.title: External Producers [producers]
docs.text:
Bound what plugins and runtimes may send into sessions as producers. Complete config.toml:

[producers]
max_body_bytes = 65536

A plugin or a runtime produces under an external { source, name } owner: the daemon derives source from the connection (plugin:<name> or runtime:<runtime ID>), and the sender picks a name for each producer it registers. See the external producers spec. An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml.

Key Type Default Description max_body_bytes integer 65536 Largest body an external producer may send, in UTF-8 bytes. A larger or empty body fails the send; the body otherwise reaches the model as sent. Must be 1..=4194304.

The limit covers external producers only. The engine's own producers (background results, subagent reports, goal reminders) have their own bounds, and agent mail is bounded by [messaging] max_body_bytes.

docs.title: Server [server]
docs.text:
Configure the separate server/client mode. Complete config.toml:

[server]
host = "127.0.0.1"
port = 7419
token = "<43-char base64url>"
url = "ws://127.0.0.1:7419/ws"
session_idle_eviction_after = "30m"

Omission keeps the defaults. An authored table replaces them completely; omitted fields use the defaults below. See config.toml. Unknown fields fail. The port accepts 0 through 65535; 0 asks the OS for an available port, so clients must use the actual bound port. cookie daemon --port <N> overrides the configured port for that run (including --port 0).

By default the daemon binds IPv4 loopback at the configured port. Its bearer token is [server] token: when the configuration has none, the daemon generates one at its first start and writes it there, so it stays the same across restarts. It also prints it in its first stdout line (daemon-ready {"url":...,"token":...}). Clients and dial-in runtimes on this machine read it from the same config.toml; elsewhere, pass --token, set COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN, or copy it into that machine's [server] token. See the security contract.

Plain cookie on this machine uses a daemon listening at ws://<host>:<port>/ws of this table, when token is set, instead of starting an engine of its own; it never reads url for that. See A daemon already running.

For clients and runtimes on other machines, cookie daemon takes --listen and TLS options; see Remote access.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text: Key Type Default Description host string "127.0.0.1" Interface the daemon listens on. Must be non-empty and at most 255 characters. The cookie binary additionally requires exactly "127.0.0.1" at startup; use --listen to bind another address. port integer 7419 TCP port for the WebSocket daemon. token string (none) The daemon's bearer token, exactly 43 base64url characters. The daemon writes a fresh one here when there is none; clients and dial-in runtimes on this machine use it when given no --token. url string ws://<host>:<port>/ws The daemon clients and dial-in runtimes on this machine connect to when given no --url (or URL after --daemon): a ws:// or wss:// URL whose path is /ws. Set it on a machine whose daemon runs elsewhere. The daemon itself ignores it. session_idle_eviction_after duration string "30m" How long a root session's tree sits unused (no new event, nobody watching it, no pending work) before it is paged out of memory. Using the session again reloads it from disk. Compact ms, s, m, h, and d suffixes are accepted; "0s" pages a tree out at the next check, made every minute, once nobody watches it. Unlike the rest of the table, a change applies at once, from the next check.

docs.title: The web page
docs.text:
The daemon serves the web client on its listener, over TLS when it serves wss. The page needs no token: it holds no secret, and the connection it opens authenticates in its handshake. /ws takes a connection from any web origin, or none; the token is the guard.

Path Answer / index.html, Cache-Control: no-cache a file of the page the file, with its content type; Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable when its name carries a hash of its content, no-cache otherwise /ws, /runtime the client and runtime endpoints; see Listening on other addresses anything else 404

Every file carries an ETag, so a revalidated file costs no body. A file that compresses is sent gzip-compressed to a browser whose Accept-Encoding takes gzip (Vary: Accept-Encoding, with its own ETag). Every response carries the page's Content-Security-Policy:

  • scripts only from the daemon, including WebAssembly and the page's inline scripts by hash;
  • WebSocket connections to any daemon (ws:, wss:), since the page may name one on another host;
  • its service worker and manifest only from the daemon;
  • blob: media;
  • no framing.

The page includes a web app manifest, its icons and screenshots, and a service worker (sw.js, sent with no-cache like index.html), so a browser can install it as an app (see Installing as an app). The service worker caches nothing, so the page always matches the daemon's build. A cookie built without the page (see Building the page) serves a placeholder index.html that says how to build it. After its ready line, the daemon prints the page's address.

docs.title: Session Title [session_title]
docs.text:
Complete config.toml to keep titles manual:

[session_title]
generate_on_first_turn = false

An omitted table inherits. An authored table replaces the lower table, with defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml. Title workflows belong to Sessions, and the model prompt belongs to the internal title agent.

Controls automatic session titles generated from the first user message.

Key Type Default Description max_chars integer 80 Maximum title length in characters. Must be greater than zero. max_input_messages integer 4 Maximum number of opening user messages included in the title-agent prompt. The engine uses the first N messages so the title remains anchored to the session's original topic. Must be greater than zero. generate_on_first_turn boolean true Generate a title automatically after the first user message. When false, no automatic title is produced (user-set titles still work). fallback_to_input_excerpt boolean true When the internal title agent fails or returns an unusable title, fall back to an excerpt of the first user message instead of leaving the session untitled.

docs.title: Shell Environment [shell_environment]
docs.text:
Give the processes a runtime starts the environment you have in a new terminal on that machine (see the shell environment spec). Complete config.toml:

[shell_environment]
capture = "interactive"
timeout_ms = 10000
shell = ""

A daemon run as a service starts with the service manager's environment, and a runtime started over ssh with sshd's, not your shell's. Your setup usually lives in your shell's rc files instead: PATH entries, conda or micromamba, nvm, API keys. So each runtime runs your shell once, on its own machine, captures its environment, and starts every process of its work in it:

  • the bash tool's commands, background calls included;
  • stdio MCP servers;
  • ACP agents;
  • on the daemon's machine, plugins and the commands of runtime templates, such as ssh.

The daemon's and the runtime's own processes keep the environment they started with. A process's configured env still applies over the captured variables.

Key Type Default Description capture string "interactive" "interactive" runs $SHELL -l -i, which reads what a new terminal reads, including a .bashrc that returns early unless interactive, as Debian's and Ubuntu's do. "login" runs $SHELL -l, which misses such an rc file. "off" keeps the runtime's own environment. timeout_ms integer 10000 How long a capture may take before the runtime gives up and keeps its own environment. 0 or less waits indefinitely. shell string "" The shell to capture with. Empty: the runtime's $SHELL, else /bin/sh.

A runtime's own [runtimes.<id>.shell_environment] table, local and runtimes that dial in included, replaces the keys it sets for that runtime and keeps the others:

[runtimes.labpc.shell_environment]
capture = "login"

An omitted table inherits; an authored top-level table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml.

docs.title: Functions and aliases
docs.text:
When the shell is bash, the capture also writes a snapshot of its options, aliases, and functions, and the bash tool sources it before each command. So micromamba activate, conda, nvm use, and your aliases work in a command as they do at your prompt. Each command is still a fresh shell: an environment activated in one command is gone in the next, so activate it in the same command (micromamba activate ucma && python train.py). Shells other than bash give the bash tool their variables only.

What was active where the daemon or runtime was started carries over: a daemon started from a terminal with a conda environment active runs every command in it.

docs.title: When it is captured
docs.text: A runtime captures when it starts, which for the daemon's local runtime is every daemon start, and again when its settings change and when the configuration is reloaded (cookie config reload, or Reload in a client), since you may have edited your rc files. A new capture applies to processes started afterwards; running MCP servers, ACP agents, and plugins keep their environment until they restart.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
A capture that times out, or a shell that exits before printing its environment, leaves the runtime's own environment, and the configuration status (cookie config status, /config in the TUI, the web client's settings) names the runtime and the reason until a capture succeeds. A runtime older than cookie with runtime protocol 1.12.0 does not capture, and the status says so too. Common causes:

  • An rc file that execs another shell or attaches to tmux. The capture sets COOKIE_SHELL_CAPTURE=1, so guard such a line:
[ -z "$COOKIE_SHELL_CAPTURE" ] && exec tmux new -A -s main
  • An rc file slower than timeout_ms: raise the timeout or use capture = "login".

The capture runs your rc files with no terminal and nothing on standard input, in a session of its own; what they leave running in it is ended when the capture finishes.

Agents can read every exported variable, API keys included, as an agent in your terminal can. Use capture = "off" to keep a runtime's processes on its own environment.

docs.title: Subagent Output [subagent_output]
docs.text:
Complete config.toml using the defaults:

[subagent_output]
max_lines = 100
max_bytes = 10240
head_lines = 20
tail_lines = 20

An omitted table inherits. An authored table replaces the lower table, with defaults for omitted fields; unknown fields fail. See config.toml.

Controls the preview of a subagent's final message in the delegate_subagent result and in the <subagent_report> each finished turn sends its parent. It truncates the way [tool_output] does: a report within both max_lines and max_bytes is shown whole and ends in full output shown; a longer one shows its first head_lines and last tail_lines lines, splitting max_bytes between them in the same ratio, around a marker such as [… 200 lines omitted. Read more: get_subagent_result(session_id="explore_1a2b3c4d", offset=21)]. The marker's offset is the 1-based line of the first line it left out. get_subagent_result pages the full report, as read pages a file, and is never truncated.

The preview is stored when the turn reports, on the parent's delegation_finished event or report message, so changing these limits affects later reports only.

Key Type Default Description max_lines integer 100 Longest report, in lines, shown whole. Must be greater than zero. max_bytes integer 10240 (10 * 1024) Longest report, in bytes, shown whole. Must be 1..=61440 so the stored preview fits its 64 KiB event bound. head_lines integer 20 Lines kept from the start of a truncated report. When omitted it is 20, capped at the rest of max_lines after tail_lines, or at half of max_lines (rounded up) when both are omitted. tail_lines integer 20 Lines kept from the end of a truncated report. When omitted it is 20, capped at the rest of max_lines after head_lines, or at half of max_lines (rounded down) when both are omitted. head_lines + tail_lines must be 1..=max_lines.

docs.title: Tool Output [tool_output]
docs.text:
Complete config.toml using the defaults:

[tool_output]
max_lines = 500
max_bytes = 12800
head_lines = 100
tail_lines = 100

An omitted table inherits. An authored table replaces the lower table, with defaults for omitted fields; unknown fields fail. See config.toml and the retained-output contract.

Controls each output stream's inline preview. A stream within both max_lines and max_bytes is shown whole. A longer one shows its first head_lines and last tail_lines lines, splitting max_bytes between the two ends in the same ratio, around a marker such as [… 1340 lines omitted. Read more: read_artifact(artifact="<digest>", stream="stdout", offset=100)]. The marker counts bytes instead when no line break falls in the omitted part, and its offset is the 1-based number of the first line not fully shown, as read_artifact takes it. Full single output and every named stream are retained by the runtime, with generic manifests for named streams. Declaration order determines rendering order; only truncated streams get read hints. Aggregate event bounds may further reduce previews with truthful hints. The limits apply only to tools using the normal bounded policy. The self-paginating read, read_artifact, and get_subagent_result tools opt out absolutely; configuration cannot re-enable truncation for them. The delegate_subagent terminal result also opts out because its teaser preview follows [subagent_output] instead.

Key Type Default Description max_lines integer 500 Longest stream, in lines, shown whole. Must be greater than zero. max_bytes integer 12800 Longest stream, in bytes, shown whole. Must be greater than zero. head_lines integer 100 Lines kept from the start of a truncated stream. When omitted it is 100, capped at the rest of max_lines after tail_lines, or at half of max_lines (rounded up) when both are omitted. tail_lines integer 100 Lines kept from the end of a truncated stream. When omitted it is 100, capped at the rest of max_lines after head_lines, or at half of max_lines (rounded down) when both are omitted. head_lines + tail_lines must be 1..=max_lines.

docs.title: ACP agents
docs.text:
External coding agents, such as Claude Code and Codex, can take a session's turns, or a subagent's, as cookie agents. Cookie drives them over the Agent Client Protocol (ACP): cookie is the ACP client, the external agent the ACP agent. Cookie speaks ACP version 2 only. The agent keeps its own conversation, model, file tools, and shell; cookie renders its turns, decides its permission requests with your rules, offers it cookie's own tools (memory, cron, delegation, MCP servers), and keeps the session's history as for any other agent.

A runtime hosts each agent: the daemon's own local runtime, a runtime the daemon starts over ssh, or a runtime that dials in, such as one on a lab machine or the one a TUI or web client offers. The runtime starts the agent on its own machine, with that machine's credentials, and relays its messages to the daemon over the runtime connection; the agent's host needs no route to the daemon. The ACP agents spec has the design, and ACP v2 the port to version 2.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
On the machine that runs the agent:

  • Install the agent and log in to it there, as you would to use it in a terminal: claude and its /login, or codex login. Cookie runs no login flow; it uses the credentials already on that machine.
  • Install its ACP adapter, or let npx fetch it: Claude Code speaks ACP through @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp, and Codex through @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp. Both speak ACP v2. npx needs Node.js on that machine's PATH, as the runtime sees it.
  • ACP v2 only. An agent that answers initialize with version 1 is refused, and its runs fail with <agent> speaks ACP v1; cookie needs ACP v2. Update its adapter, or start it in v2 mode. Gemini CLI's gemini --acp may speak only v1; Claude Code's adapter serves both and can be pinned to v2 with CLAUDE_AGENT_ACP_PROTOCOL=v2 in the declaration's env.
  • cookie must be on that machine: the MCP bridge that offers cookie's tools to the agent is cookie runtime mcp-bridge. A runtime always has it, since it is cookie runtime.

docs.title: On the daemon's machine
docs.text:
Declare agents under [runtimes.local.acp.agents.<agent>] in ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml:

[runtimes.local.acp.agents.claude]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp"]
description = "Claude Code"

[runtimes.local.acp.agents.codex]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp"]
description = "Codex"

The daemon lists them as claude and codex, the keys of their declarations, as soon as the configuration is applied: a changed acp table reaches its runtime at once. Pick one in the agent picker of the TUI (/agent) or the web client (the agent chip) for a new session, and send a message: the daemon starts the agent's process on the first turn, opens an ACP session in the session's workspace, and shows the agent's reply, thoughts, tool calls, and plan as they stream.

Key Type Default Meaning command array of strings required The program and its arguments, run without a shell on the runtime's machine, in its home directory. On Windows, a bare program name also finds a .cmd or .bat launcher on PATH, such as npx's. env table of strings {} Variables merged over the runtime's environment. description string "" Shown where the agent is listed when its daemon document gives none. enabled boolean true A disabled agent is listed as unavailable.

Runtimes: ACP agents has the rules for IDs, availability, and processes.

docs.title: On a machine the daemon reaches over ssh
docs.text:
A runtime template declares its agents in the daemon's config.toml, next to its command. They run on the remote machine, with its credentials:

[runtimes.labpc]
command = ["ssh", "-o", "BatchMode=yes", "labpc", "cookie", "runtime", "serve", "--stdio"]
startup_timeout_ms = 20000

[runtimes.labpc.acp.agents.codex]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp"]
env = { CODEX_HOME = "/home/ada/.codex" }
description = "Codex on labpc"

The agent is codex, run on labpc by a session that attaches labpc (a labpc workspace); the daemon starts the runtime when the session first uses it. See Which runtime runs it.

docs.title: On a machine that dials in
docs.text:
A runtime that dials in hosts the agents of its table in the daemon's config.toml: a [runtimes.<id>] without command, named after the ID it dials in with, exactly where its MCP servers go. The command runs on the lab machine:

# ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml on the daemon's machine
[runtimes.lab.acp.agents.claude]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp"]
description = "Claude Code on the lab machine"

# On the lab machine: dial in as `lab`.
cookie runtime serve --daemon ws://laptop:7419/ws --id lab --token <token>

The agent is claude, which a session that attaches lab runs on the lab machine while the runtime is connected. A change to the table reaches the connected runtime at once, so adding an agent needs no restart. To keep it connected, run it as a service.

docs.title: On every runtime
docs.text:
To offer an agent on every runtime without declaring it on each, declare it once under [acp.agents.<agent>]:

[acp.agents.claude]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp"]
description = "Claude Code"

Every runtime but global offers it, and runs it on its own machine, so the command must work there. A runtime's own declaration of the same key replaces it on that runtime: give it another command there, or leave it off with enabled = false:

[runtimes.labpc.acp.agents.claude]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp"]
enabled = false

In the web client, the Machines view lists these under On every runtime, where ACP agent adds one; each runtime's card shows the ones it offers with an every runtime badge, and Turn off here writes that runtime's own declaration with enabled = false.

docs.title: Which runtime runs it
docs.text:
An agent's ID is the key of its declaration, whichever runtime declares it: [runtimes.local.acp.agents.claude] and [runtimes.lab.acp.agents.claude] both offer the one agent claude. A session runs it on the runtime it attaches that offers it:

  • A session that attaches local (the default for a new session) runs claude on the daemon's machine; one that attaches only the lab machine's runtime runs it there.
  • A session with no attached runtime that offers it cannot run it: creating the session, starting a run, or delegating to it is refused with, for example, \`claude\` needs a runtime that offers it attached: lab, local, and the agent pickers show it dimmed with what it needs.
  • A session that runs it may not attach two runtimes that offer it: attaching the second is refused, naming both. Sessions of other agents attach any runtimes.
  • Moved to another runtime (detach one, attach the other), the agent starts a new ACP session there, and the transcript says so: the old one stays on the machine that ran it.
  • A subagent runs it on the runtimes it has: its parent's, or the capabilities its delegation names, by the same rule.
  • The agent works in the session's first workspace on that runtime (the runtime's home without one). The session's other workspaces on the same runtime reach an agent that supports it (additionalDirectories) as extra workspace roots, when its session starts or resumes: attach local at two folders and the agent may work in both. Workspaces on other runtimes are on other machines, and the agent does not get them.

list_agents shows an agent's runtimes and whether it runs in the calling session, and list_runtimes names the ACP agents each runtime offers.

docs.title: Cookie settings: the daemon-side document
docs.text:
Cookie settings come from an agent document of the agent's ID in the daemon's agents directory, never from the runtime, so a runtime cannot grant itself permissions. Every runtime that offers the agent shares it:

# ~/.cookie-agent/agents/codex.md
---
description: Codex on labpc, for refactors
mode: all
models: [{ model: "gpt-5", variant: "high" }]
acp:
  mode: auto
  hide_tools: [read, write, edit, bash, webfetch]
permissions:
  read: allow
  write: { "${workspace_dir}/*": allow, "*": ask }
  bash: { "git *": allow, "*": ask }
  webfetch: allow
  mcp: { "exa_*": allow }
  memory: allow
---
You review changes for this project before they are committed.
  • Optional. Without it, the agent has mode all, the first offering runtime's description, the rules every agent gets for actions it names no key for, and the default hide_tools.
  • acp marks the document as the agent's; acp: {} is enough. mode picks the mode its sessions start in (else the agent's auto mode, else its default), and config sets its other config options by ID, such as Claude Code's fast; an unknown option or value is reported in the session and skipped.
  • models picks the agent's model and effort, as a fallback chain over the agent's own values (not cookie's model keys): each entry's model is a value of the agent's model option and its variant one of its effort option, or null for the agent's default effort. For Claude Code, models: [{ model: "opus", variant: "high" }, "sonnet"]. The first entry whose model the agent offers applies when its session starts; when none does, the session says so and the agent keeps its own. The model and variant pickers show each value's ID, dimmed beside its name: the ID to write here. models beats acp.config for the model and effort (the configuration status says so when both set one), and a draft's or session's own choice beats models. ${default_model} and the other variables name cookie's models, so an entry naming one is skipped with a configuration diagnostic.
  • A document without an acp block of the same ID is the daemon's own agent: it keeps the ID, the runtimes' declarations are ignored, and the configuration status (cookie config status, the TUI's /config, the web's configuration page) says so.
  • The body goes with the first prompt of each of the agent's ACP sessions (see What the first prompt carries); an empty body sends nothing. Cookie adds no preamble of its own: tell the agent what it is and how to work with cookie here, as the reference document for Claude Code does.

ACP agent documents lists every key.

docs.title: Several documents over one agent
docs.text:
One declaration can serve several documents, each its own agent with its own permissions, mode, hide_tools, and body. acp.agent names the declaration a document runs; without it, a document runs the declaration of its own ID:

# ~/.cookie-agent/agents/claude-review.md
---
description: Claude Code, read-only reviewer
mode: subagent
acp:
  agent: claude          # a [runtimes.*.acp.agents.claude] declaration
  mode: plan
permissions:
  read: allow
  write: deny
  bash: { "git diff *": allow, "*": ask }
---
You review the change you are given and report findings; you do not edit.
  • The document's ID is the agent's. claude-review is listed, picked, delegated to, and scheduled by that ID, on the runtimes that declare claude; the pickers say claude on local, and list_agents adds acp agent: claude.
  • The declaration stays an agent of its own ID while no document has that ID; a claude.md with enabled: false hides it and leaves the documents over claude running. A claude.md whose acp.agent names another declaration takes the ID, and the configuration status says the claude declaration is ignored.
  • One process. The documents over a declaration share its agent process on each runtime, each cookie session with its own ACP session, and share what the agent offered there (its models and options in the pickers). Switching a session to another document starts a new ACP session, and so does changing a document's acp.agent.
  • command and env stay with the declaration, so documents cannot change them; a different environment (another CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR) is a second declaration.
  • A document whose acp.agent no runtime declares yet is no agent until one does; the configuration status says so.

docs.title: A reference document for Claude Code
docs.text:
The agent learns from the document's body that it runs inside cookie and which of cookie's tools to prefer over its harness's own. Adapt this one to your setup; it names Claude Code as the harness, so change that line for another agent:

---
description: Claude Code
mode: all
models: [{ model: "opus", variant: "high" }]
acp: {}
permissions:
  read: allow
  write: { "${workspace_dir}/*": allow, "*": ask }
  bash: { "git status*": allow, "git diff*": allow, "*": ask }
  memory: allow
---
You are an agent in cookie agent, running in ACP mode: cookie drives you
over the Agent Client Protocol, and your actual harness is Claude Code. The
user talks to you through cookie (its terminal UI, web client, or CLI,
possibly from another machine), and cookie records this conversation.

Guidelines:

- Cookie's tools come from the MCP server named `cookie`. Your harness's
  own tools stay available, but when a cookie tool covers the same job, use
  the cookie tool: cookie applies the user's permission rules, shows the
  call in its transcript, and other cookie agents can see the result.
- Keep durable notes in cookie memory (memory_search, memory_read,
  memory_write), not in your harness's own memory or notes files.
- Delegate with cookie's delegate_subagent (list_agents shows who), not
  with your harness's own subagents; schedule follow-ups with cookie's cron
  tools.
- Your built-in file and shell tools work in this session's workspace;
  with several attachments, the first prompt says which one, and on which
  machine.
- Some calls need the user's approval through cookie; if one is refused,
  do not retry the same call.
- Messages wrapped in <scheduled_job> or <subagent_report> come from
  cookie, not from the user typing.
- When you finish a delegated task, make your last message a
  self-contained summary: cookie returns it as your report.
- Change cookie's own configuration only when the user asks (the
  customize-cookie-agent skill explains how).

Save it as ~/.cookie-agent/agents/claude.md: every runtime that offers claude shares it.

docs.title: What the first prompt carries
docs.text:
The first prompt of each of the agent's ACP sessions carries, before your message and in this order, each part left out when it is empty:

  1. the tool instructions cookie would give a model for the tools the agent is offered over the bridge, after hide_tools and the rules (<tool_instructions provider=...> sections, such as memory's: how memory is included, and the rubric for writing it when a write tool is offered);
  2. the skills a model would see (<available_skills>: each skill's name, description, and file), when the agent is offered cookie's skill tool over the bridge, with the same rules a model's listing follows (a denied skill, or one that opts out of model invocation, is left out);
  3. where the session's attachments work, as a model's system prompt says it, even for an attachment whose tools hide_tools hides: with one attachment, its working directory and machine; with several, a <machines> listing of every attachment by machine and runtime, which explains tool names such as labpc_read, with the attachment your harness's built-in tools run on marked builtin_tools="true" and a sentence naming that attachment, its runtime and machine, and the working directory: the built-in tools act on that machine and workspace only, while cookie's tools act on the attachment their description or <attachment>_ prefix names. A session in a project also names the project here;
  4. the session's memory as a model would see it at the start of a session (the # Memory reminder);
  5. the agent document's body.

AGENTS.md is not sent: the agents read it themselves. The prompt carries these again when cookie has to start a new ACP session because the agent lost the one it had (or a fork or revert before its first reply starts over), and not when it resumes, loads, or forks one, since the agent remembers them there. Later prompts carry only the input.

docs.title: Forking, reverting, and deleting a session
docs.text:
The agent keeps its own conversation, so cookie keeps it in step when you change the session's:

  • Fork. A fork of the session gets its own agent conversation: at its first turn cookie asks the agent to fork the source's (session/fork), and the source keeps its own. An agent without session/fork cannot be forked after its first reply; the fork is refused with `<agent>` on `local` can't fork its own conversation. A fork at an earlier point than the end of the agent's conversation also needs its fork to start at a given message (below). An agent whose fork cannot start at a given message is asked to fork as you fork the session, so the fork holds the conversation as it was then; if the agent cannot, the fork is refused.
  • Revert. After a revert the agent's next turn forks its conversation at its last reply the session keeps, then deletes the old conversation, and the transcript says the agent continues from the revert point. The agent must fork at a given message: cookie names it with JetBrains AIR's fork point, which Claude Code's and Codex's adapters read. Cookie checks whether the agent does once per agent process, after its first reply in a run; until then, and for an agent that does not (one without session/fork, or whose fork ignores the fork point), a revert past the agent's first reply is refused with `claude` on `local` can't rewind its own conversation (or that cookie has not checked yet). A revert to before the agent's first reply always works: the next turn starts a new agent conversation.
  • Delete. Deleting a session also deletes the agent's own transcripts of it (session/delete, when the agent offers it), but never those of the session it was forked from.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The agent runs its own file and shell tools, and asks cookie before the calls its own policy asks about. Cookie decides each request with the document's rules, by the request's ACP tool kind:

The agent asks to Decided as read or search a file read, by the file's path edit, delete, or move a file write, by the file's path run a command bash, by the command fetch a URL webfetch, by the URL call a tool of an MCP server it connects itself (mcp__exa__search) mcp, by exa_search, the name cookie gives the same tool call one of cookie's own tools (mcp__cookie__memory_search) allowed: the call reaches cookie, whose rules decide it there think allowed switch its mode, or anything else asks you

So bash: {"git *": allow} allows the agent's own git commands as it allows cookie's bash tool, and mcp: {"exa_*": allow} covers an exa server whether cookie or the agent connects it. A request that touches several files needs each allowed. An ask goes through the approval flow like any other, and cookie answers the agent with its allow-once or reject-once option, never an "always" one, so a repeat comes back to your rules. In the agent's auto mode, which cookie picks when it offers one, the agent asks about few calls.

docs.title: Questions from the agent
docs.text:
An agent can ask you something mid-turn (ACP elicitation): Claude Code's AskUserQuestion arrives as a form, and an MCP server that needs you to sign in as a page to open. Cookie advertises both kinds, so the agent asks instead of guessing or failing. The run waits on you meanwhile, and the clients show the question in the viewed session:

  • A form lists its fields in order, each with its title, description, and what it takes: a choice (pick one), a multiple choice (pick any), yes or no, text, or a number, and whether it is required. Submit sends your answers; cookie checks them against the form first and names a field that does not fit. Decline says no, and Cancel dismisses the question without an answer. With Claude Code, each question comes with an Other field for an answer of your own; leaving everything empty skips the question.
  • A page to open shows the whole URL and its host, and warns when it is not HTTPS, has a punycode host, or carries a user name. Open it yourself (cookie never opens or fetches it), finish there, then choose Done; or Decline or Cancel. When the agent reports that you finished there before you choose, cookie answers Done for you.

No permission rule or mode answers a question: it is the agent asking you, not an action. Where no one is there to answer, cookie declines it at once with the reason, so the turn goes on: a session in auto_approve_n (a cron run's default mode), and a headless cookie run. Interrupting the turn cancels a question still waiting. The transcript keeps a line for each answered question (an info event).

docs.title: Cookie's tools for the agent: the MCP bridge
docs.text:
Each ACP session gets one stdio MCP server, cookie, whose command is cookie runtime mcp-bridge on the agent's machine. The bridge reaches the runtime over a local socket, and the runtime relays its messages to the daemon over the connection it already has. Through it, the agent sees the tools cookie would offer a model in that session: memory, cron, list_agents, delegate_subagent and the subagent tools, MCP servers' tools, and runtime tools, each listed only when the rules offer it, and each call decided by the rules as a model's would be.

acp.hide_tools lists cookie's tools the agent does not get, with * and ?. By default it hides the coding runtime's read, write, edit, bash, and webfetch, since the agent has its own; [] offers them too. hide_tools only hides: the rules still decide every call.

The transcript's tools row, pinned under the system prompt in the TUI and the web client, lists the tools the bridge offers the agent in its latest turn (cookie tools · 12 offered to the agent); the agent's own tools are not in it.

docs.title: In the clients
docs.text:
• Agent pickers. The TUI's /agent and the web client's agent chip list the agents runtimes offer with where the new session (or the viewed one) would run them (claude [on local]). One that cannot run there is shown dimmed with why and cannot be picked: no attached runtime offers it (needs lab attached), two do (offered by lab, local: attach one), or its runtime is away or has it disabled (on lab · unavailable). No model picker lists an ACP agent's synthetic model acp/<agent>: the agent chooses its own, and the model picker lists the agent's models instead (below).
  • Agent commands. Once the agent has announced its slash commands, the TUI's command palette (/ on an empty composer, or ctrl+p) lists them after cookie's own, marked (agent); a command that takes input asks for it. In the web client, typing / in the composer lists them above it. Choosing one sends /<name> <input> to the agent.
  • Model and effort. The agent's model option (category model) and its reasoning effort (category thought_level), when it offers them, read as the session's model and variant: claude • Opus[High] in the TUI's title, Opus • High on the web client's model chip.
