Tightening a rule durably invalidates existing tree grants for that action under the session root before the overlay event is committed. A change counts as tightening when it makes the rule stricter for the base layer or any runtime the session is attached to, each evaluated against that runtime's workspace. Invalidation is action-wide because tree-grant records retain opaque prepared identities rather than normalized resource labels; a qualified rule only invalidates grants of its runtime ID.

Tree grants record the runtime ID of the tool they were approved for and only apply to calls on that runtime ID; base-layer grants record none. Grants and approval requests written before runtimes existed carry no runtime ID and are read as local.

docs.title: Giving agents a browser
docs.text:
Playwright MCP is an MCP server that drives a web browser: it opens pages, reads them as accessibility snapshots, clicks, types, and takes screenshots. Configured in cookie, its tools become agent tools like any other MCP server's, gated by the agent's mcp permissions. This page shows how to set it up, where to run it, and how to decide which agents may use it.

Playwright MCP is Microsoft's project, not part of cookie. The flags and tool names below are those of @playwright/mcp 0.0.83 and the Playwright Extension 0.4.0 (October 2026); check its README when a newer version behaves differently.

docs.title: Two ways to give agents a browser
docs.text:
A browser Playwright launches Your own running Chrome Flag none (or --headless, --isolated, --user-data-dir) --extension Needs Node.js and a browser Playwright can start Node.js, Chrome or Edge with the Playwright Extension, your login session Logins none, unless you sign in once in its persistent profile every site you are signed in to Privacy sees only what the agent opens sees the tabs you hand it, with your cookies and sessions Interference its own window, or none when headless works in your browser while you use it Runs on any machine, headless on a server only the machine whose Chrome it attaches to

A browser Playwright launches is the safe default. Playwright starts Chrome (or Chromium, Edge, Firefox, WebKit) for the agent, headed or headless, with one of three profiles:

  • persistent (the default): a profile directory Playwright keeps under the user's cache directory, named after the browser and a hash of the server's working directory, so a login the agent (or you) makes there survives restarts. --user-data-dir <dir> puts it somewhere you choose. One browser at a time can use a profile.
  • isolated (--isolated): the profile lives in memory and is gone when the browser closes. --storage-state <file> seeds it with cookies and local storage saved earlier.
  • --isolated and --user-data-dir exclude each other; Playwright refuses the combination.

Your own Chrome (--extension) attaches to the browser you are already using, through the Playwright Extension (earlier listed as Playwright MCP Bridge; same extension). The agent can then work on sites where you are signed in, without handing it passwords. On the agent's first browser call the extension opens a connect page in Chrome, and keeps the tabs each MCP client may use in a tab group of its own, so the agent sees only the tabs in its group. Without a token you approve every connection in that page; with the token from the extension's status page (PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_EXTENSION_TOKEN) it connects without asking.

What the agent sees in your browser

In extension mode the agent acts as you on every site you are signed in to. Tools such as browser_network_request return request headers and bodies, which can include cookies and tokens, and every page the agent reads is untrusted text that may try to instruct it. Keep ask on the tools that act (see Permissions), drag only the tabs the task needs into the agent's tab group, and prefer a launched browser for anything that does not need your logins.

Playwright MCP starts or attaches to the browser at the first browser tool call, not when cookie connects to the server: a server shows connected in /mcp even while Chrome is closed or missing, and browser problems surface as a failed tool call.

docs.title: Where to run it
docs.text:
An MCP server runs on the machine of the runtime that hosts it (see where servers run), and the browser runs where the server runs. Put it where the browser belongs:

Configured as Runs Use it for [mcp.servers.<name>] on the daemon's machine, in the global runtime; every session that attaches global (the default) gets it a headless browser next to a daemon on a server or your own desktop [runtimes.<id>.mcp.servers.<name>] on the machine of the runtime template <id>, which the daemon starts a browser on a host the daemon reaches over ssh [runtimes.<id>.mcp.servers.<name>] without a command for the runtime on the machine that dials in as <id>, in that runtime your desktop's Chrome, while the daemon runs elsewhere

In the two runtime forms, give the server scope = "runtime". A browser belongs to the machine, not to a workspace: the runtime starts one copy when it connects, in its user's home directory, and every workspace of that runtime shares it (see scope). With the default scope = "workspace", every workspace a session opens on that runtime would start another server and another browser, each with its own profile. Top-level [mcp.servers] entries take no scope; they already run once.

The browser must run where its display and Chrome are. A headless browser can run anywhere. A headed browser needs a desktop session, and extension mode needs the very Chrome you use: the server starts Chrome from its local install, opens the extension's connect page in it, and talks to the extension over a loopback connection. So when the daemon runs on a Linux server and you work on a Windows desktop, a server under the daemon's [mcp.servers] would look for Chrome on the server. Run it on the desktop instead, in a runtime that dials in from there:

Windows desktop                                  Linux server
  Chrome + Playwright Extension                    cookie daemon
    ^ loopback                                       sessions, agents, permissions
  npx @playwright/mcp --extension                    ^
    ^ stdio                                          |
  cookie runtime serve --daemon ... --id winbox -----+  (WebSocket to /runtime)

The runtime has to run as you, inside your login session, or it cannot reach your Chrome: on Windows a Task Scheduler task at logon, not a Windows service (see Running a runtime as a service).

One browser per runtime, shared by its sessions. A runtime-scoped server is one MCP client of Playwright, so every session using that runtime drives the same browser. Two sessions browsing at the same time can switch each other's tabs; run them one after the other, or configure a second server with its own name and profile.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
A Playwright tool is published as <server>_<tool>: with the server named my_chrome, browser_navigate becomes my_chrome_browser_navigate (see tool names). Name the server for what it is (my_chrome, playwright), not browser, or the tools read browser_browser_click. Give each browser server a name no other runtime's server uses: when two attached runtimes publish the same tool name, both are prefixed with their attachment, and rules written for the bare names stop matching.

Each tool is offered by its own rules: an agent sees a browser tool only when its merged rules (agent document, defaults, session overlay) do not deny mcp for that tool's name. An agent document with no mcp key gets the default mcp: {"*": ask}, so the browser tools are offered and every call asks (see MCP default). A declared mcp key replaces that default entirely, so keep a "*" rule if the agent should still see other servers' tools:

permissions:
  mcp:
    "*": ask                                # other servers: offered, each call asks
    "my_chrome_*": allow                    # browse without asking...
    my_chrome_browser_evaluate: ask         # ...but ask before page JavaScript,
    my_chrome_browser_file_upload: ask      # handing local files to a page,
    my_chrome_browser_fill_form: ask        # submitting forms,
    my_chrome_browser_handle_dialog: ask    # and answering dialogs

The most specific rule wins, so the exact names override "my_chrome_*". An agent that should only read pages gets just those tools; nothing else of the server is offered to it:

permissions:
  mcp:
    my_chrome_browser_navigate: allow
    my_chrome_browser_snapshot: allow
    my_chrome_browser_find: allow
    my_chrome_browser_take_screenshot: allow

mcp@winbox keys limit rules to one runtime's tools (see runtime selectors), and mcp: deny in /permissions hides every MCP tool for one session.

docs.title: Trimming the server's tools
docs.text:
Permissions choose among the published tools per agent; include_tools and exclude_tools decide what is published at all, for every agent. They match the server's own tool names (browser_click), not the published ones (see choosing a server's tools).

Exclude browser_run_code_unsafe unless you need it. It is one of Playwright MCP's default tools, and in its own words it "executes arbitrary JavaScript in the Playwright server process and is RCE-equivalent": a call runs code with the runtime user's rights, outside the page.

[mcp.servers.playwright]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@playwright/mcp@latest", "--headless"]
exclude_tools = ["browser_run_code_unsafe"]
# or publish a fixed set:
# include_tools = ["browser_navigate", "browser_navigate_back", "browser_snapshot", "browser_find", "browser_click", "browser_type", "browser_tabs"]

The default tools of @playwright/mcp 0.0.83 are browser_click, browser_close, browser_console_messages, browser_drag, browser_drop, browser_emulate_media, browser_evaluate, browser_file_upload, browser_fill_form, browser_find, browser_handle_dialog, browser_hover, browser_navigate, browser_navigate_back, browser_network_request, browser_network_requests, browser_press_key, browser_resize, browser_run_code_unsafe, browser_select_option, browser_snapshot, browser_tabs, browser_take_screenshot, browser_type, and browser_wait_for. --caps adds groups: vision (coordinate mouse tools such as browser_mouse_click_xy), pdf (browser_pdf_save), devtools (tracing, video, highlighting), and, listed in the README's tool sections, network, storage, testing, and config.

docs.title: Windows: your own Chrome, daemon elsewhere
docs.text:
The daemon runs on another machine (a Linux server, say, reachable at wss://host.example.ts.net/ws; see Remote access). The Windows desktop dials in as the runtime winbox and hosts the browser server.

  1. Install Node.js 18 or newer (the current LTS is fine), for example with winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS, then open a new PowerShell and check node --version.
  2. Install cookie on the desktop (see Install).
  3. Install the extension. In Chrome (or Edge), add the Playwright Extension, open its status page from the toolbar icon, and copy the PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_EXTENSION_TOKEN value. The token belongs to that Chrome profile.

  4. Configure the server in the daemon's config.toml, for the runtime the desktop dials in as. The table has no command, since the daemon does not start the runtime; the server runs on the desktop:

    [runtimes.winbox.mcp.servers.my_chrome]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@playwright/mcp@latest", "--extension"]
env = { PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_EXTENSION_TOKEN = "<extension-token>" }
scope = "runtime"
exclude_tools = ["browser_run_code_unsafe"]
timeout_ms = 90000
    • If the extension is installed in several Chrome profiles, it connects to the one used last; add "--profile-dir-name", "Profile 2" (the last part of Profile Path in chrome://version) to pick one, with that profile's token.
    • timeout_ms bounds the connection and each call. The first start downloads the package; pre-fetch it with npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest --version so the first connection does not run out of time.
    • The token sits in the daemon's config.toml, which reaches the desktop in the runtime's settings; keep that file to yourself.

  5. Try it in a terminal first, with the daemon's token from [server] token in the daemon's config.toml:

    cookie runtime serve --daemon wss://host.example.ts.net/ws --id winbox --token <token>

    In a second terminal, list the servers:

    cookie mcp list --url wss://host.example.ts.net/ws --token <token>

    my_chrome   24 tools    Connected   winbox

    The tool count depends on the Playwright MCP version and your filters. A Failed state means the server did not start; /mcp in the TUI shows why (see Troubleshooting).

  6. Keep it running. Stop the terminal runtime (Ctrl-C) and register the logon task from Running a runtime as a service, with --id winbox. It runs in your session, so it reaches your Chrome. A change to the server's table reaches the connected runtime at once.

  7. Use it in a session. The browser tools come with the runtime: attach winbox/coding in /runtime (a, then a workspace such as ~), or let a root session delegate to winbox (see Delegating to runtimes). Attaching the coding capability also gives the session read, write, and bash on the desktop; cookie runtime serve --root <dir> limits its workspaces, and bash@winbox and write@winbox rules limit the rest.

When you only need the browser while you are at the desktop, the TUI does the same without a task: cookie attach --url wss://host.example.ts.net/ws --token <token> on the desktop dials in as client_<host name> for as long as it runs, hosting the [runtimes.client_<host name>.mcp.servers] of the daemon's configuration (see A client's machine).

docs.title: Linux and macOS: a headless browser next to the daemon
docs.text:
A browser for research and testing that never touches your own profile, on the daemon's machine.

  1. Check Node.js 18 or newer (node --version); install it from your package manager or nodejs.org if needed.

  2. Install a browser for Playwright. By default Playwright MCP uses Google Chrome (--browser chrome). On a server, Playwright's own Chromium build is simpler:

    npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest install-browser chromium

    install-browser runs Playwright's installer for the version the package ships with. install-browser chrome installs Google Chrome instead, and on Linux asks for administrator rights. A Linux machine missing the browser's system libraries fails at the first browser call with Missing system dependencies ... Install them with: sudo npx playwright install-deps chromium; run what it says.

  3. Configure the server in ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml:

    [mcp.servers.playwright]
command = "npx"
args = [
  "-y", "@playwright/mcp@latest",
  "--headless",
  "--browser", "chromium",
  "--isolated",
]
exclude_tools = ["browser_run_code_unsafe"]
timeout_ms = 90000
    • --headless: on Linux, Playwright already runs headless when DISPLAY is unset, as under a systemd user service; elsewhere it is headed by default. To watch the browser on a Linux desktop from a service, drop --headless and add env = { DISPLAY = ":0" }.
    • --isolated: a fresh, in-memory profile each time the browser starts. For a profile that keeps logins, replace it with "--user-data-dir", "/home/ada/.cache/cookie-browser", sign in once, and keep --headless off for that first sign-in.
    • --output-dir <dir> sets where screenshots without an explicit file name go; without it, .playwright-mcp in the server's working directory (the daemon user's home here).
    • @latest checks for a newer release when the server starts; pin a version (@playwright/mcp@0.0.83) to upgrade on your own schedule.
    • On Linux, Playwright already starts its own Chromium build without Chrome's sandbox. Google Chrome (--browser chrome) under root, as in many containers, needs --no-sandbox.

  4. Apply and check. cookie config reload applies [mcp] changes at once (see changes while the daemon runs), then:

    cookie mcp list

    playwright  24 tools    Connected   global

Every session that attaches global now gets playwright_browser_* tools, subject to its agent's mcp rules. To run the browser on another machine the daemon starts over ssh, put the same table under [runtimes.<id>.mcp.servers.playwright] with scope = "runtime".

docs.title: ACP agents
docs.text:
ACP agents such as Claude Code get cookie's tools through cookie's MCP bridge: one MCP server named cookie carrying the session's tools as cookie composes them for a model, the browser tools of every attached runtime included. Claude Code lists them as mcp__cookie__my_chrome_browser_navigate and so on.

  • acp.hide_tools in the agent's document removes tools from the bridge. Its default hides only cookie's coding tools (read, write, edit, bash, webfetch), so the browser tools pass through; add "my_chrome_*" to keep them from an agent that has a browser of its own.
  • Permissions work as for a model: a tool the merged rules hide is not listed, and each call is decided by the agent document's mcp rules.
  • When an agent asks permission for one of cookie's own tools (Claude Code's mcp__cookie__<tool>), cookie allows the request at once: the call itself reaches cookie's MCP server, where the mcp rules decide it, so you are asked at most once. See ACP agents.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
/mcp in the TUI shows each server's state and, for a failed one, the error; cookie mcp list shows the state alone.

The server fails to start.

  • Node.js missing or not on PATH: the error names the command that could not be started. Services start with a smaller environment than your shell: a systemd user unit needs Environment=PATH=... with Node's directory, and a version manager such as nvm installs Node where services do not look. An absolute command (/usr/bin/npx) avoids the question.
  • connect timed out on the first start: npx was still downloading the package. Pre-fetch it (npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest --version, as the user the daemon or runtime runs as) or raise timeout_ms.

The server connects, but browser calls fail. The browser starts at the first call, so its errors come back as tool errors:

  • Browser "chrome" is not installed ... Run npx @playwright/mcp install-browser chrome: install it, or switch to --browser chromium and install that.
  • Missing system dependencies required to run browser ...: run the install-deps command it prints.
  • Browser is already in use for <dir>, use --isolated: two servers (or a server and a browser you opened) share one profile. Give each its own --user-data-dir, or use --isolated.
  • Screenshots need a model that accepts images; for others a browser_take_screenshot call fails like any gated media. browser_snapshot is text and works with every model; --image-responses omit stops Playwright attaching images at all.

Protocol versions. cookie first offers the newest MCP version and falls back to the 2025-11-25 initialize handshake for a server that does not know it: one that answers "method not found", or, over Streamable HTTP, refuses the version with HTTP 400, as servers built on the MCP TypeScript SDK (Playwright MCP among them) can. That covers Playwright MCP over stdio and also run by hand as an HTTP server (npx @playwright/mcp@latest --port 8931, with url = "http://localhost:8931/mcp" in cookie). Nothing needs configuring. If /mcp still shows a protocol error, update Playwright MCP (or drop a pinned version) and cookie.

Extension mode does not connect.

  • Playwright extension did not connect within 30s after opening the connect page. Make sure the extension is installed in the Chrome profile and PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_EXTENSION_TOKEN matches its token.: the token is wrong, or belongs to another Chrome profile. Copy it again from the status page of the profile you mean, and add --profile-dir-name when you have several.
  • Without a token, the first call waits for you to approve the connection in Chrome, and cookie ends it after timeout_ms. Set the token.
  • Nothing opens at all: the runtime is not in your login session (a Windows service, an ssh session), or the daemon's own [mcp.servers] entry is looking for Chrome on the daemon's machine. Run the server in a runtime on the desktop, as above.

Files land in odd places. Playwright MCP takes its working directory as its workspace root: the default profile's hash, .playwright-mcp for output files, and the directories browser_file_upload may read from all follow it. cookie starts it in the directory its working directory table gives: the daemon user's home for [mcp.servers], the runtime user's home for scope = "runtime", the workspace for scope = "workspace" (so a .playwright-mcp folder appears in your repository). Set cwd to a dedicated directory, or --output-dir, to keep both elsewhere, and a narrow cwd also narrows what uploads can read.

The tools do not show up for an agent.

  • cookie mcp list or /mcp shows the server Connected with fewer tools than you expect: include_tools and exclude_tools filtered them (/mcp says how many, as 12 tools, 13 filtered).
  • The agent document declares an mcp key without a rule offering my_chrome_*, or only a mcp@<other runtime> key: a declared key replaces the default "*": ask. /permissions shows the merged rules.
  • The session does not attach the runtime that hosts the server: runtime servers reach a session only through an attachment of their runtime (/runtime), and top-level servers only with global attached.
  • The runtime is offline: a dial-in runtime's tools leave the session while it is away, and come back when it reconnects.
  • The tool names are prefixed (winbox_my_chrome_browser_click) because another attached runtime has a server of the same name; rename one.

docs.title: MCP [mcp]
docs.text:
Cookie Agent supports MCP tools through tools/list and tools/call. It does not expose MCP resources or prompts. Server requests for sampling, elicitation, roots, or other interactive input are rejected.

To give agents a web browser, see Giving agents a browser, a guide to Playwright MCP that builds on this page.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
mcp accepts one optional servers map, empty by default. Define entries in ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml; this is a complete illustrative file:

[mcp.servers.github]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"]
cwd = "/workspace"
timeout_ms = 30000

[mcp.servers.remote]
url = "https://mcp.example.com/mcp"
oauth = true

Servers are configured only in the user file. A <cwd>/.cookie-agent/config.toml is never read, so a repository cannot add MCP servers.

docs.title: Where servers run
docs.text:
An MCP server belongs to the runtime that hosts it, and runs on that runtime's machine:

  • Top-level [mcp.servers.<name>] servers belong to the daemon's global runtime and run where the daemon runs. Every session that attaches global (the default) can use them. Only these servers can use OAuth. /mcp and the web client edit them, and a runtime's servers too (see below).
  • [runtimes.<id>.mcp.servers.<name>] servers belong to a coding runtime template and run on the runtime's machine, for example a language server next to a repository on another host over ssh. Their scope says how many copies run (see scope). [runtimes.local.mcp.servers.<name>] servers run in the daemon's built-in local coding runtime. A table without command, such as [runtimes.desk.mcp.servers.<name>], gives its servers to the runtime that dials in as desk (cookie runtime serve --daemon, or the TUI attached to a daemon on another machine), which runs them on its own machine; see runtimes that dial in.
[runtimes.labpc]
command = ["ssh", "labpc", "cookie", "runtime", "serve", "--stdio"]

[runtimes.labpc.mcp.servers.rust_analyzer]
command = "rust-analyzer-mcp"          # scope = "workspace", the default

[runtimes.labpc.mcp.servers.browser]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
scope = "runtime"

[runtimes.local.mcp.servers.docs]
command = "docs-mcp"

docs.title: Scope: one per workspace or one per runtime
docs.text:
A runtime template's server takes scope = "workspace" (the default) or scope = "runtime":

  • workspace: every workspace instance of the runtime starts its own copy when it opens, and its tools belong to that instance. Two workspaces of one runtime in a session run two copies, and their tools are published under each attachment's prefix (labpc_api_rust_analyzer_hover). Use it for servers about a project: a language server, a repository index, a test runner.
  • runtime: the runtime starts one copy when it starts (when it answers the daemon's runtime/initialize), before any workspace is open, and every workspace of that runtime shares it until the runtime stops. Its tools are the runtime's own: a session gets them once per runtime however many of the runtime's workspaces it attaches, published bare, or under the runtime's ID (labpc_browser_navigate) when another tool takes the name, and they run without a workspace. Use it for servers about the machine: a browser and its profile, a desktop, a device, anything that should not start twice.

A runtime does not hold up its handshake for its runtime-scoped servers: it answers runtime/initialize while they connect, and the first workspace to open waits for their first attempt, which each server's timeout_ms bounds. They reconnect like any server (see connection lifecycle). Top-level [mcp.servers.<name>] servers take no scope: they already run once, in the daemon's global runtime, and a scope key on one fails validation.

A connected runtime reports every server it is configured with, so /mcp and the runtime panels list them even when no session has a workspace of it open: a runtime-scoped server with its live state, listed without a workspace, and a workspace-scoped one as "starts with a workspace" until an instance hosts it.

docs.title: Working directory
docs.text:
A stdio server starts in a directory chosen by where it runs, never in whatever directory the daemon or the runtime process happened to start in (a Windows runtime started by Task Scheduler runs in C:\Windows\System32):

Server Without cwd A relative cwd resolves against Top-level [mcp.servers.*] the daemon user's home directory that home Runtime template, scope = "workspace" the instance's workspace the workspace Runtime template, scope = "runtime" the runtime user's home directory that home

An absolute cwd is used as written, on the machine that runs the server.

A runtime's servers use the same table schema and are parsed as strictly, except that a template server that enables OAuth (oauth = true or an oauth table) fails validation: OAuth credentials live in the daemon's mcp-oauth.json and only the global runtime uses them. A runtime's remote servers connect with their static headers only. A command, its cwd, and its environment are resolved on the runtime's machine, and the process inherits the runtime's environment plus env. Template servers change only when the daemon restarts.

docs.title: Choosing a server's tools
docs.text:
A server publishes every tool it lists unless its table narrows them with include_tools and exclude_tools, lists of patterns over the tool names as the server lists them (browser_click, not the published my_chrome_browser_click), so a filter keeps working when the server is renamed. * matches any characters and ? one character, as in permission patterns; a pattern without either is an exact name.

[mcp.servers.my_chrome]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
include_tools = ["browser_*", "tab_?"]   # default: every tool
exclude_tools = ["browser_install"]      # applied after include_tools

A tool is published when it matches an include_tools pattern (every tool when the key is absent) and no exclude_tools pattern, so an exclusion wins. The runtime that hosts the server applies them to its first tools/list and to every refresh after notifications/tools/list_changed, so a tool the server adds later is filtered too; a filtered tool is never published, to any agent. Both keys work wherever a server is configured: [mcp.servers], and [runtimes.<id>.mcp.servers]. An empty pattern, or an include_tools = [] that would publish nothing, is a configuration error. /mcp, the runtime panels, and the web client's MCP servers show how many tools the filters left out, as 12 tools, 30 filtered. The machines views list each tool by the server's own name and leave one out or take it back: t on a server in /mcp lists its tools, where space toggles one, and in the web client's Machines view a tool is a button. Toggling edits the filters by the tool's exact name and never rewrites a pattern.

docs.title: Deferred tools: sent up front, and the server's summary
docs.text:
On a model that loads deferred tools, an MCP server's tools are sent deferred: the model sees their names, under the server's name, and loads one with tool_search before calling it. Two keys send tools up front instead, wherever a server is configured:

[mcp.servers.my_chrome]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
always_load_tools = ["browser_snapshot", "tab_*"]   # just these up front
# always_load = true                                 # every tool up front
# instructions = false                               # no summary

always_load = true sends every tool of the server up front; always_load_tools takes patterns over the server's own tool names, as include_tools does, and sends the matching tools up front. An empty pattern is a configuration error. A tool joins the up-front tools at the session's next compaction, as any tool that arrives mid-round does.

The instructions a server sends when it connects are its summary: the model sees them, marked as the server author's text rather than the user's, with the server's tools when they are first announced. They are cut to 2,048 characters. instructions = false leaves them out.

When a session has loaded a tool of a server that has since failed, the daemon reconnects that server before the session's next request, and waits for the attempt, so the tool stays callable when the server comes back.

Each server must set exactly one of command or url. args, env, and cwd apply only to stdio commands; headers applies only to Streamable HTTP. Servers are enabled by default. timeout_ms bounds connection, listing, and calls and defaults to 30000. A call that reaches it, or whose run is cancelled, ends at once and sends the server notifications/cancelled for its request.

docs.title: Connection lifecycle
docs.text:
Every enabled server connects eagerly, in every runtime: there is no deferred connection, and an authored lazy key is an unknown field.

  • At startup every enabled server connects, in parallel: the global runtime's when the daemon starts, a coding runtime's runtime-scoped ones when the runtime starts, and its workspace-scoped ones when an instance opens, before the instance answers the daemon (so the template's startup_timeout_ms must cover them, and the runtime-scoped ones' first attempt, which every open waits for). The first run waits for every server's initial connection and tools/list attempt to finish, so its tool context is not built from a partial startup snapshot. Each wait is bounded by that server's timeout_ms; one server's failure does not block the others.
  • A failed server publishes no tools. It is retried when a session that uses its runtime instance is created or opened (and when the instance is attached to a session or retried from /runtime), and the session's next run waits for that attempt too. r in /mcp (or mcp.server.reconnect) retries it on demand.
  • A dropped server (a stdio process that exits, a closed pipe, or an HTTP session the transport gives up on) is restarted by the runtime that hosts it up to 3 times, after 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s. While it reconnects it shows as reconnecting, its tools stay published so the model's tool list does not change, and calls fail fast with the runtime_unavailable failure code; calls are never retried for the model. A successful attempt restores the server with its current tool list. When every attempt fails, its tools are dropped and it becomes failed.

A failure at connect time and a drop that exhausts its reconnects reach every client viewing a session that uses the server, that is, a session attached to the instance that hosts it, or to any instance of the runtime for a runtime-scoped server: the TUI shows an error row in each such session naming the server, its runtime (and the instance's workspace), and the reason (see connection failures).

docs.title: OAuth for remote servers
docs.text:
OAuth is available only to top-level [mcp] servers, which the daemon's global runtime hosts; see where servers run. Streamable HTTP servers use OAuth automatically when an unauthenticated request returns an authorization challenge. OAuth can be selected explicitly or disabled:

[mcp.servers.remote]
url = "https://mcp.example.com/mcp"
oauth = true

[mcp.servers.pre_registered]
url = "https://other.example.com/mcp"
oauth = { client_id = "cookie-agent", scopes = ["mcp"] }

[mcp.servers.no_oauth]
url = "https://static.example.com/mcp"
oauth = false
headers = { Authorization = "Bearer REPLACE_WITH_LOCAL_TOKEN" }

Omitting oauth is the default auto mode. true and {} enable the same reactive flow. The settings object may contain client_id, client_secret, client_metadata_url, and scopes. Cookie Agent follows protected-resource and authorization-server discovery, uses S256 PKCE, and selects a pre-registered client, a server-supported Client ID Metadata Document, or Dynamic Client Registration in that order. A static Authorization header takes precedence over OAuth when both are configured; other static headers are sent alongside OAuth requests. OAuth is not used for stdio servers.

MCP environment values and headers do not support engine ${env:NAME} interpolation. Configure credentials locally, never in a committed example. Names must be nonempty, at most 128 bytes, and contain no control characters. command and an authored cwd must be nonempty. OAuth client IDs, secrets, and scopes must be nonempty; a secret requires a client ID. Metadata URLs must use HTTPS with a non-root path. Unknown fields and mixed transport fields fail, including on disabled entries.

An authorization challenge changes the server state to needs_auth, with the message "OAuth authorization required; authenticate to connect" (plus the authorization server's own error response when it sent one). Run cookie mcp --token <TOKEN> auth <server> (or set COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN), or select the server in /mcp and press a, then open the displayed URL. The client, not the daemon, listens on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 callback port and hands the browser's redirect to the daemon, so a daemon reached through an SSH tunnel or on another machine authorizes the same way. When the browser runs on a different machine from the client, its redirect cannot connect; copy the URL from the browser's address bar and paste it into /mcp or the cookie mcp auth prompt instead. The daemon keeps the flow for five minutes. The TUI can copy the URL with c and cancel the wait with Escape. Successful authorization stores the token and reconnects the server. Expired tokens refresh automatically. A rejected refresh or revoked token returns the server to needs_auth instead of repeatedly opening a browser flow. A transient refresh failure also returns to needs_auth immediately; Cookie Agent does not silently retry token requests or open a browser flow.

docs.title: Signing in from the web client
docs.text:
The web client signs in with Sign in in Settings › MCP servers. A page cannot listen on a loopback port, so its redirect is the page's own address with ?oauth=callback, such as https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net/?oauth=callback. The page catches the browser there and hands the address to the daemon as the TUI does with its loopback callback. The daemon accepts as a redirect the client's loopback callback (plain http to 127.0.0.1, [::1], or localhost) or any https address without user info or a fragment (client protocol 1.11).

  • Which redirect a server takes. With Dynamic Client Registration the daemon registers a client for the redirect of each sign-in: as a native client for a loopback redirect, a web client for an https one. A configured client_id is used as is, so its authorization server must already allow the redirect: add the page's address with ?oauth=callback to that client's redirect URIs on the server's side. If the server refuses it, its error reaches the page unchanged.
  • HTTPS. Most authorization servers refuse a redirect to plain http anywhere but loopback. Serve the page over https (see remote access); a page on plain http at another address warns, and still lets you try.

OAuth failures show the available response body or authorization error description in the MCP diagnostic, capped at 4,096 UTF-8 bytes. Content is preserved, including credential-like text returned by the server; terminal and Unicode format controls are stripped or replaced. This does not change credential storage or Debug formatting.

Only the authorization code crosses the client connection: the daemon keeps the PKCE verifier, performs the token exchange, and stores and refreshes the tokens. The code is single-use and useless without that verifier.

Authorization codes are held only by a one-shot in-memory relay. Cookie Agent passes a fixed redacted surrogate through rmcp's traced exchange path and restores the real code only in the outbound token request, preventing debug logs from containing the browser callback code.

OAuth credentials are user-level and stored in the single ~/.cookie-agent/mcp-oauth.json file. On Unix the file is owner-only (0600) when Cookie Agent creates it. The unversioned file is parsed strictly, but an existing file is used regardless of permissions, ownership, links, or symlinks. Stop the daemon and delete this file to revoke all locally stored MCP OAuth credentials. Removing a server through MCP management removes its credential. Writers serialize through mcp-oauth.lock, reread the current file, and merge one credential key before each atomic replacement.

Each credential is keyed by the server name and a SHA-256 hash of its canonical resource URL, and is also bound to that URL and the configured OAuth client identity. Canonicalization lowercases the scheme and host, removes default HTTP and HTTPS ports, and resolves dot-segments. Path bytes after dot-segment resolution, including trailing slashes, remain significant. It does not combine query strings or different subpaths. Editing the endpoint or client identity invalidates the record before the replacement server can connect, even when both resources advertise the same authorization-server issuer. The same server name and canonical URL can reuse authorization across projects.

OAuth credentials establish identity with the remote server. They do not alter which agents can see or call that server's tools; agent permissions control that separately.

docs.title: TUI management
docs.text:
Run /mcp to open the live MCP panel. It lists the servers of every runtime, grouped and labelled by the runtime instance that hosts them: global for top-level [mcp] servers first, then each coding runtime instance as <runtime> at <workspace>, with their source. The list reports connected with its tool count, connecting, reconnecting, failed with the connection error, needs_auth, and disabled. The panel refreshes on every MCP change and polls the daemon while it is open. Select a server to inspect its complete command, arguments, environment, and working directory, or URL and headers. Press a on a needs_auth remote server to begin OAuth.

The panel can reconnect any runtime's server (r, which the daemon passes to the runtime that hosts it), and toggle enablement and add, edit, or remove definitions of global-runtime servers only; a coding runtime's servers come from its runtime template. Add/edit forms accept either a command, JSON string array of arguments, JSON string object of environment variables, and optional working directory, or a URL plus a JSON string object of headers, and for both the include_tools, exclude_tools, and always_load_tools patterns, comma-separated (an empty include field publishes every tool), with always_load and instructions toggles. The list shows a server's tool count with how many its filters left out. Choose runtime only or user config.toml before submitting. Edits do not rename a server; remove the old name and add the new one instead.

Stdio servers negotiate MCP 2025-11-25 when needed. Servers that implement the 2026-07-28 discovery lifecycle use that version. Remote servers use Streamable HTTP, including SSE responses on that endpoint; the retired two-endpoint legacy SSE transport is not supported.

docs.title: Repository security
docs.text:
There is no separate MCP trust store or approval prompt. Every configured, enabled server connects eagerly. MCP tools are permission-gated like normal tools: an agent with no mcp permission entry cannot see them, and scoped rules decide each call.

MCP servers and agent documents come only from your user configuration; a repository's .cookie-agent/config.toml and .cookie-agent/agents/ are never read, so opening a repository cannot add a server or an agent that permits its tools. Repository AGENTS.md files and project skills still enter model context; review them in repositories you do not trust.

Connection failures are isolated per server. A failed server publishes no tools and does not prevent other servers from connecting (see Connection lifecycle).

Definitions created or changed through the TUI are runtime-layer entries and live only for the current daemon unless explicitly written to a file. After a write-back the file holds the entry, and it is no longer a runtime entry.

docs.title: Tool names and permissions
docs.text:
An MCP tool is exposed as <server>_<tool>. Both components replace characters outside [a-zA-Z0-9_-] with _; there is no mcp_ prefix. For example, github plus search/repos becomes github_search_repos. Inside the global runtime, a server whose generated name collides with another MCP or plugin tool, or with the global webfetch, is rejected; inside a coding runtime, one that collides with another of its MCP servers' tools or its built-in tools is rejected the same way, and the built-in tools keep their names. A name that collides with a tool of another runtime or of the base layer is published with the runtime's attachment prefix instead, for example global_github_search_repos or labpc_api_rust_analyzer_hover; see tool composition.

permissions:
  mcp:
    "github_*": allow
    github_delete_repo: deny

MCP availability is permission-driven. An agent document with no mcp key (in any form, mcp@<runtime> included) gets the daemon's default mcp: {"*": ask} when its mode is primary, all, or subagent, so every connected MCP tool is offered and each call asks; an internal agent gets none. A declared mcp key replaces the default entirely (see MCP default).

An MCP tool's permission resource is its complete published name, known before any call, so each tool is offered by its own rules: a tool is offered when the run's merged rules (agent document, defaults, and session overlay) do not deny mcp for its name on its runtime. The most specific matching rule decides, as it does for a call: allow and ask offer the tool, deny or no matching rule hides it. With only "my_chrome_*": allow, the agent sees only that server's tools, and the YAML above hides github_delete_repo while offering the rest of github's tools. Narrow mcp rules therefore narrow the tool list, not only the calls, and a session override in /permissions changes the list at the next model request. An "allow for this session" grant never offers a tool the merged rules deny. Calls use the same name as their resource: more-specific patterns override broader ones, and unmatched calls are denied. Each delegated agent is evaluated against its own permission map.

include_tools and exclude_tools drop a server's tools for every agent; permissions choose among the published ones per agent.

Each MCP description and result is treated as untrusted server output.

Media blocks in tool results (images, audio, and embedded resource blobs) are sniffed by content, gated on the model's capabilities and the provider's delivery channel exactly like media reads, and retained as content-addressed attachments. Gated media fails the tool call with an actionable error; malformed blocks degrade to inline notes. Blob resources without a declared MIME type are retained under the sniffed type. Results that would exceed the combined attachment budget keep what fits and degrade the remainder to inline notes.

docs.title: Accepted fields
docs.text:
These are the complete fields under [mcp.servers.<name>]. File precedence is described in config.toml.

Key Type Default Description command string (none) Stdio server executable, started without a shell. On Windows, a bare program name also finds a .cmd or .bat launcher on PATH, such as npx's. Exactly one of command or url is required. args array of strings empty Command arguments; valid only with command. env map of strings empty Command environment additions; valid only with command. cwd string (none) Child working directory; valid only with command. Without one, and for a relative one, see working directory. scope "workspace" or "runtime" "workspace" Only in [runtimes.<id>.mcp.servers.<name>]: one copy per workspace instance, or one per runtime that its workspaces share (see scope). A top-level server with scope fails validation. url string (none) Absolute HTTP or HTTPS Streamable HTTP endpoint. Exactly one of url or command is required. headers map of strings empty Static request headers; valid only with url. oauth boolean or table auto Streamable HTTP OAuth. Omit, set true, or use {} for reactive OAuth; set false to disable it. A table accepts optional client_id, client_secret, client_metadata_url, and scopes. A static Authorization header takes precedence. enabled boolean true Whether the server may connect. timeout_ms integer 30000 Positive timeout for connect, list, and call operations. include_tools array of strings every tool Patterns (*, ?) over the server's own tool names; only matching tools are published. Present, it may not be empty. See choosing a server's tools. exclude_tools array of strings empty Patterns over the server's own tool names, applied after include_tools: matching tools are not published. always_load boolean false On a model that loads deferred tools, send every tool of the server up front. See deferred tools. always_load_tools array of strings empty Patterns over the server's own tool names: matching tools are sent up front on a model that loads deferred tools. No pattern may be empty. instructions boolean true Whether the instructions the server sends when it connects are its summary in deferred tool announcements.

docs.title: Runtime layers and persistence
docs.text:
The running engine adds a mutable Runtime layer for MCP server entries. It wins over the user file and lasts for the daemon lifetime. Runtime removals are tombstones: the named server is absent even when the user file defines it. Runtime and user-file entries use the same connection lifecycle. Nothing is written automatically.

Explicit MCP write-back (mcp.server.persist) replaces only [mcp.servers.<name>] in the user config.toml, or removes it for a runtime removal, using a format-preserving TOML document edit, as a configuration change. Unrelated keys, tables, and comments are retained. The complete candidate, with the agent documents beside it, is passed through the strict configuration loader before an atomic replacement; an existing unknown field, type conflict, or malformed table fails without changing the file. The replacement syncs the candidate before rename and syncs the containing directory afterward. The newly staged replacement is owner-only; the existing source path is not validated before replacement. The source file is re-read and compared immediately before replacement, and a mismatch fails with a conflict instead of overwriting the external edit. A modification landing between that comparison and the rename itself cannot be detected — a narrow residual race that only matters if another writer edits the file in the same instant; avoid concurrent external edits while applying changes. A successful write applies the configuration, and the server's entry comes from the file from then on.

docs.title: Plugins [plugins]
docs.text:
Plugins are local programs that extend Cookie Agent from their own process. A plugin can declare tools, intercept engine hooks, watch session events, publish to a bus other plugins hear, and send messages to sessions. Install a plugin by getting its executable from its author and adding it to your configuration.

To write a plugin, see Plugin development.

docs.title: Configure a plugin
docs.text:
Configure each plugin under [plugins.<name>] in the user config.toml (~/.cookie-agent/config.toml). Names must be nonempty, at most 128 bytes, and contain no control characters.

[plugins.issues]
command = ["/opt/cookie-plugins/issues", "--stdio"]
env = { ISSUES_URL = "https://issues.example.com" }
cwd = "/workspace"
enabled = true
producer_messaging = false
interception_timeout_ms = 2000
startup_timeout_ms = 10000
shutdown_grace_ms = 3000

command is the program and its arguments, as for a runtime. The plugin's process inherits the daemon's environment, like an MCP stdio server, and env adds to it, overriding inherited variables of the same name. A plugin therefore also sees provider API keys and other secrets the daemon reads from its environment.

Each enabled plugin starts with the daemon. Set enabled = false to keep a plugin configured without starting it. Configuration changes take effect when the daemon next starts. Plugins run their hooks in the order the file lists them.

Key Type Default Description command array of strings (required) The program and its arguments. On Windows, a bare program name also finds a .cmd or .bat launcher on PATH, such as npx's. env map of strings empty Additions to the inherited environment; a listed variable overrides the inherited value. cwd string (none) The process's working directory. enabled boolean true Whether the plugin starts with the daemon. producer_messaging boolean false Lets the plugin register producers and send messages to sessions. interception_timeout_ms integer 2000 How long one hook may take. startup_timeout_ms integer 10000 How long the plugin may take to start and answer plugin/initialize. shutdown_grace_ms integer 3000 How long the plugin may take to exit before it is killed. always_load boolean false On a model that loads deferred tools, send the plugin's tools up front rather than deferred.

Plugin entries reject unknown fields. command must name a program, cwd must be nonempty when set, and every timeout must be greater than zero. These rules apply to disabled entries too.

Plugins are defined only in the user config.toml; a <cwd>/.cookie-agent/config.toml is never read.

docs.title: Plugin tools
docs.text:
A plugin's tools join the daemon's global runtime, next to its MCP servers' tools, and reach every session that keeps global attached. A tool keeps the name the plugin gives it unless another tool has that name; then each is published under its source's prefix, such as issues_search for the issues plugin's search. A plugin may declare a tool an override instead: it keeps the bare name and the other tool is prefixed. The daemon's base tools, such as skill, are never overridden.

A plugin tool is approved like any other tool. Its plugin names the permission action it needs, such as issue_read, and the resource a call works on; a tool may need no permission. Allow the action in an agent's policy or a session overlay:

permissions:
  issue_read: allow
  issue_close:
    "*": ask

The plugin's author should document its actions. See Permissions for policy precedence and session overrides.

docs.title: Status and restarts
docs.text:
Open /plugins in the TUI to see every configured plugin: its state, the tools and hooks it declares, why it last failed, and what it last wrote to standard error. Press r to restart the selected plugin.

State Meaning disabled Configured with enabled = false. starting The process is starting or answering plugin/initialize. connected Running. reconnecting It exited or its connection dropped; the daemon restarts it after 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s. failed Every attempt failed. It stays failed until you restart it. stopped Stopped with the daemon.

A failing plugin never stops the daemon or other plugins. While a plugin is not connected, its tools are not published and its hooks are skipped, unless the plugin declared that a hook blocks when it fails: a policy plugin may, so that what it guards (a tool call, an input, a fork) is refused while it is down instead of going on unchecked. A refusal names the plugin; restart it from /plugins. A plugin's standard error is kept as a short tail (the last 32 lines, at most 4 KiB) rather than shown on the terminal.

At shutdown, the daemon asks each plugin to stop, waits shutdown_grace_ms, and then kills its process group.

docs.title: Producer messages
docs.text:
A plugin with producer_messaging = true can send messages to any session: steer messages reach the next safe model request, and queue messages start or join a later run. Enable it only for plugins you trust to talk to your models. Sending to an idle session can start a run. A send is acknowledged once the message is durably accepted, not once a model has read it or an external action has finished.

A plugin can discard a message it sent while the message is still waiting. Once a model request claims the message, discard is rejected until the claim is released; consumed messages cannot be discarded.

When it starts, and after every restart, a producing plugin restores its pending work from its own storage and then reports itself ready or failed. session.producers shows each plugin's readiness as starting, ready, failed, or disabled. A goal waits while a plugin it hears from is starting, and work a failed or disabled plugin owned is unknown, never complete. The daemon cannot tell a plugin with no pending work from one that lost its state, so recovery is only as complete as the plugin's own records. See Producers.

docs.title: Trust
docs.text: Plugin commands are trusted local code, not a sandbox. A plugin runs with your user's rights, sees the daemon's environment, and its hooks see and may change prompts, tool calls, and model requests. Tool permissions govern its tools, not its hooks. See security boundaries.

docs.title: Providers [providers]
docs.text: Use /connect for a catalog-backed provider, or define a custom endpoint and model below. Provider configuration lives under [providers.<id>] in config.toml. The authored map defaults to empty; managed providers can still be available through the catalog and user provider store.

docs.title: Managed providers
docs.text:
/connect in the TUI, or cookie connect --token <TOKEN> against the daemon (or set COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN), walks through provider setup and authentication: choose the auth method, fill in its setup values (a region, project, or resource name, shown and pre-filled from the stored connection), then type the credentials, which are masked. Connections are stored in the daemon's provider store (~/.cookie-agent/providers/ on the daemon's machine), not in config.toml. Setup is validated locally; the first model request tests the credentials. A failed connect keeps what you typed in the TUI's form, so it can be corrected and resent; a connect that raced a catalog refresh is retried once when the provider's form did not change. Errors name the cause, such as missing_setup_field, missing_credential, or custom_provider_not_store_backed for a [providers.*] provider. Never commit credential-bearing files.

At startup, the engine serves the validated catalog cache (or the bundled catalog on first run) and refreshes https://models.dev/catalog.json in the background right away, then hourly. Supported, non-deprecated text-output models are included automatically. Catalog declarations are not probes of your endpoint: account access, deployed model features, and billing may differ. Models the catalog lists without tool calling are unsupported: they are listed as unavailable with the reason no tool calling and are never selectable, by any agent. Claude on Vertex AI (the google-vertex-anthropic provider and any model routed to @ai-sdk/google-vertex/anthropic) is unsupported: it needs the Anthropic Messages rawPredict wire, which cookie-agent does not implement.

This is a complete config.toml alternative to /connect, with credentials supplied by the environment:

[providers.openai]
source = "models_dev"
api_key = "${env:OPENAI_API_KEY}"

Authored api_key or auth_override takes precedence over an eligible saved connection, then no-auth access, otherwise the provider is unavailable. In /connect (TUI and web client), a provider whose effective credentials are an authored api_key or auth_override, with no required setup missing, reads configured in config.toml. Its details say where the credentials are; a stored connection can still be added for when they are removed, but it is not used while they are there. No-auth access applies to a catalog provider that declares no credential variable, and to a local server: an authored provider whose endpoint (base_url, else the catalog API URL) is on localhost, 127.0.0.1, or ::1. Local catalog providers such as LM Studio stay unavailable until authored, so [providers.lmstudio] with source = "models_dev" is enough to use a running LM Studio. An authored base_url cannot inherit store credentials or setup. Endpoint selection uses authored base_url, catalog API URL, then family default; setup-derived families retain their own routing.

Some catalog providers mix wires: zenmux, ofox, and opencode serve Anthropic, Gemini, or Responses models next to OpenAI-compatible Chat ones, and a model may pin its own catalog API URL. An authored base_url replaces the provider-level API URL, and each model's endpoint follows these rules:

  • A model without its own API URL, or with the provider's, uses base_url.
  • A model API URL on the provider API's origin is rebased by path. With zenmux's https://zenmux.ai/api/v1 and an Anthropic model at https://zenmux.ai/api/anthropic/v1, base_url = "https://gw.example/api/v1" sends that model to https://gw.example/api/anthropic/v1.
  • When base_url does not end with the provider's differing path suffix (v1 above), it is a gateway with its own layout and every model uses base_url itself, whatever its wire (/chat/completions, /messages, /responses, ...).
  • A model API URL on another origin is a separate upstream and is kept.

To send a single model somewhere else, define it in a custom provider.

docs.title: Unavailable models
docs.text:
A catalog model that cookie cannot run stays visible with its reason instead of disappearing. A model is unavailable when it is:

  • quarantined: its models.dev record failed validation (for example invalid_catalog_model_record);
  • unsupported: the record is valid but cookie has no way to drive it (for example an unknown protocol family or capabilities the endpoint cannot honor);
  • needs setup: provider setup values such as a region or resource name are missing;
  • needs credentials: no authored or stored credentials are available.

Where it shows:

  • Provider rows in /connect explain a connected or configured provider that yields no usable models, for example connected · no usable models: 4 quarantined (invalid_catalog_model_record). An unconfigured provider is flagged only when connecting could not help because every model is quarantined or unsupported.
  • Provider details (Enter on a row) count every kind, list each unavailable model of a configured provider with its reason, and show the models.dev documentation URL and environment variable names.
  • The model picker lists configured providers' unavailable models as a dimmed Unavailable (N) — not selectable group below the selectable models.
  • The connect form shows Docs: <url> and, for single-API-key providers, a config line such as [providers.kimi] source = "models_dev", api_key = "${env:KIMI_API_KEY}". cookie never reads those environment variables on its own; only the authored ${env:NAME} interpolation does.
  • The catalog line at the top of the /connect panel names the catalog source (network, cache, or bundled bootstrap), an age warning after 7 or 30 days, quarantine counts, and the last refresh error.
  • The CLI: cookie connect lists model counts per provider and prints the unavailable models, docs URL, and config alternative in the provider details. cookie run --model <provider/model> names the reason when that model is unavailable.

Per-model reasons are listed only for providers you configured (authored or stored); unconfigured providers report counts alone.

docs.title: Provider fields
docs.text:
Key Type Default Description source string (required) Must be "models_dev", or "chatgpt" for the built-in ChatGPT provider, which takes only headers and models. base_url string (none) Override of the provider-level API URL; per-model catalog endpoints follow the rules above. Must be https, or http to localhost, 127.0.0.1, or ::1. Requires same-definition auth (api_key or auth_override) unless it is such a loopback URL, and never inherits provider-store setup or credentials. Forbidden for families that compute their endpoint from setup (Vertex, Bedrock, Azure). setup map of string values empty Setup fields the provider recipe requires (for example project, location, region, resource_name). Azure Responses compacts natively only with model, version, and deployment_type. Interpolates ${env:NAME}. api_key string (none) Single-secret default auth. Allowed only for providers whose default method is an unambiguous single API key. Interpolates ${env:NAME}. auth_override table (none) Explicit auth method override. Mutually exclusive with api_key. cache table family default Prompt-cache policy matching the resolved adaptor family. headers map of strings empty Provider request-header overrides. models map empty Sparse per-model overrides: enabled, display_name, model_id, generation_options, adaptor_options, variants, default_variant, compaction, deferred_tools, headers, pricing. Unmentioned catalog models remain available. Cannot invent models or directly change catalog capabilities.

Every model on a Responses adaptor compacts natively by default (see native compaction): OpenAI Responses, official, compatible, or credential-less, and Azure OpenAI Responses when setup has model, version, and deployment_type. Within a model override, compaction = "unsupported" turns native compaction off for that model. "openai-responses-compact" and "azure-responses-compact" are still accepted and redundant: they mean the default, on any recipe. A variant that switches request_endpoint compacts natively when its own adaptor does. Frozen manifests store the compiled native/unsupported capability, not this setting string. The removed "v1" fails with an error.

compaction = "in-stream" asks an OpenAI Responses model for server-side compaction inside its own requests instead of the standalone compact call (see in-stream compaction). It is the default of the ChatGPT provider, where "unsupported" turns it off. On a model that is not OpenAI Responses it is an error, and a variant that leaves Responses through request_endpoint drops it.

Whether a model loads deferred tools is decided per model, in this order:

  1. deferred_tools in a model override: "native" declares that the model loads deferred tools, "unsupported" that it does not. Any other value is an error. "native" on an adaptor that cannot load deferred tools (Gemini, Vertex, Bedrock, Cohere, OpenAI or Azure Chat Completions) is an error.
  2. models.dev's dynamically_loaded_tools: true declares native. On an adaptor that cannot load, it is ignored.
  3. Automatic rules:
  4. A Claude model that Anthropic lists for tool search (Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 4.5 and later, Fable, Mythos), on api.anthropic.com, is native.
  5. OpenAI's own Responses and Azure OpenAI Responses are native.
  6. Any other model on an Anthropic or Anthropic-compatible adaptor, a Claude model through a gateway included, is attempted: deferral is tried, and a rejected request falls back to sending every tool up front.

A request with deferred tools that an attempted model refuses (any HTTP 400 or 422), or that a native model refuses naming deferral, is tried once more with every tool up front. When that retry succeeds, the daemon records the model in deferred-tools.json (see state kept beside the configuration) and sends it every tool up front until the entry expires. - Everything else, an OpenAI-compatible gateway included, is unsupported.

A model on an OpenAI-compatible Chat adaptor that is native loads tools the way Kimi K3 does, with a system message carrying them. A variant that switches request_endpoint decides again for its own adaptor.

auth_override:

Key Type Description method string One of the current auth method IDs (see below). values map of strings Credential values keyed by credential field name (for example api_key, access_token, access_key_id, secret_access_key, session_token). Interpolates ${env:NAME}.

docs.title: Managed model overrides
docs.text:
Use models.<model-id> for a sparse override, not an allowlist. Unmentioned models and omitted or empty variant maps retain catalog availability and variants. An unknown catalog model ID is an error; use a custom provider to define new models. Omitted enabled retains catalog behavior; false disables the model. Capabilities cannot be authored on a managed override.

This complete file illustrates an override for the bundled catalog's gpt-5 model. Confirm availability in your runtime before making requests:

[providers.openai]
source = "models_dev"
api_key = "${env:OPENAI_API_KEY}"

[providers.openai.models.gpt-5]
generation_options = { max_output_tokens = 8192 }
default_variant = "base"

[providers.openai.models.gpt-5.variants.high]
generation_options = { max_output_tokens = 4096 }

Model overrides accept enabled, display_name, model_id, generation_options, adaptor_options, pricing, variants, default_variant, compaction, and headers. Omitted fields retain catalog/base values. Display names and generation settings have the same constraints as custom definitions. Variant and pricing rules are below.

docs.title: Catalog reasoning variants
docs.text:
Managed models get variants from the catalog's reasoning_options:

  • Each effort level becomes a variant of the same name (low, high, max, ...).
  • A toggle becomes off and on; on is dropped when a supported effort or budget variant already turns reasoning on.
  • A token budget becomes budget-min (the catalog minimum), budget-high (half the usable maximum), and budget-max. The usable maximum is the catalog maximum capped at 31,999 tokens and at the output limit less 4,096 tokens kept for visible output (a 32K-output model's budget-max is 27,904). A dynamic minimum (-1) becomes budget-auto.

Variants the selected wire cannot express are dropped. Wire mapping by family:

Family Effort off on Budget Anthropic and Anthropic-compatible thinking = {type = "adaptive", display = "summarized"} plus output_config.effort thinking = {type = "disabled"} adaptive, summarized thinking = {type = "enabled", budget_tokens = N, display = "summarized"} Claude on Bedrock Converse additionalModelRequestFields thinking = {type = "adaptive", display = "summarized"} plus output_config.effort thinking = {type = "disabled"} adaptive, summarized thinking = {type = "enabled", budget_tokens = N} Other Bedrock Converse models reasoningConfig.maxReasoningEffort reasoningConfig.type = "disabled" reasoningConfig.type = "enabled" reasoningConfig.budgetTokens OpenAI-compatible Chat reasoning_effort provider switch below provider switch below not sent

Claude models before 4.6 accept only manual budgets, so their effort and on variants send an enabled budget of half the output room above those 4,096 visible tokens (1,024 to 16,000 tokens) instead of adaptive thinking. Claude on Bedrock follows the same rules and requires its signed thinking to be replayed, so its native replay is required.

The Anthropic wire sends max_tokens as visible output plus the thinking budget, and the total may not exceed the model's output limit. Requests send the full output limit (or a smaller agent cap) as visible output, so with a manual budget the visible output is lowered to output limit - budget when it would not otherwise fit; a smaller agent cap that fits is kept.

OpenAI-compatible providers get off/on only where the provider documents a thinking switch: thinking = {type = "disabled" | "enabled"} for DeepSeek, Z.ai/Zhipu GLM, and Volcengine Ark; enable_thinking = false | true for Alibaba Cloud Model Studio (alibaba, alibaba-cn); and reasoning_effort = "none" for Kimi Code, which has no on variant. Kimi Code serves thinking-off K3 requests with its K2.8 Preview model. Other providers, including Moonshot, get no toggle variants.

docs.title: ChatGPT
docs.text:
The built-in chatgpt provider, shown as Codex / ChatGPT, runs models on a ChatGPT plan (Go, Plus, Pro, Business, and others) through OpenAI's Sign in with ChatGPT token sharing, with no API key and no per-token billing. It is not in models.dev: its models are the ones the signed-in plan lists.

Sign in from /connect in the TUI, the web client's provider list, or cookie connect chatgpt, and choose Continue with ChatGPT. The first sign-in registers cookie with OpenAI as Cookie Agent, which then appears in ChatGPT's connected apps.

  • The browser returns to http://127.0.0.1:<port>/auth/callback. The TUI and cookie connect listen for it on the machine they run on, so a daemon on another machine works the same way.
  • When the browser runs somewhere else, the page it returns to fails to load: paste that page's address into the sign-in.
  • A web page the daemon serves from 127.0.0.1 or localhost shares the daemon's machine, so the daemon catches the redirect itself.

What is stored. The tokens live beside the provider store, in ~/.cookie-agent/providers/chatgpt-sign-in.json, and the plan's model list in chatgpt-models.json there. The provider store keeps only the account. Access tokens last an hour and refresh on their own; a daemon refreshes at least daily, so the 30-day refresh token stays valid while it is idle. When a sign-in can no longer refresh, the provider says sign-in expired: sign in again, its models fail with that reason, and signing in again restores them. Disconnecting signs out and revokes the sign-in.

Compaction. The route refuses the standalone /responses/compact, so ChatGPT models compact in the stream: each request asks the server to compact once its input reaches the configured trigger (see in-stream compaction).

Models. The list comes from the account's GET /v1/models: at sign-in and hourly after. Codex's ultra reasoning (its multi-agent mode) is left out. Requests never send max_output_tokens, temperature, top_p, truncation, user, service_tier, or prompt-cache retention, which the route refuses; a setting that names one is dropped with a warning.

Usage limits. A plan that has reached its limit answers with subscription_sharing_usage_limit_exceeded, which is not retried. OpenAI gives no reset time; ChatGPT's settings show the plan's usage.

[providers.chatgpt] is optional, and only source = "chatgpt" with headers and models (managed model overrides) is accepted:

[providers.chatgpt]
source = "chatgpt"
models = { "gpt-6-luna" = { display_name = "Luna" } }

source = "chatgpt" names this provider and no other, and the chatgpt ID accepts no other source. api_key, auth_override, base_url, setup, and cache are refused: ChatGPT is signed in, not configured.

docs.title: Custom providers
docs.text: Custom providers are config-only, never appear in /connect, and never use the provider store. Any valid provider ID is allowed; on collision with a catalog provider ID the custom definition takes precedence.

docs.title: Custom model example
docs.text:
Complete config.toml for an illustrative endpoint. Replace the URL, model ID, limits, and capability declarations with those of your actual service. The reasoning-only variants inherit sampling and endpoint settings from the base:

[providers."custom.example"]
source = "custom"
endpoint = "https://api.example.invalid/v1"
adaptor = "openai-compatible"
auth = { method = "bearer-api-key-v1", values = { api_key = "${env:CUSTOM_API_KEY}" } }

[providers."custom.example".models."example-model"]
display_name = "Example Model"
model_id = "backend-model-v1"
generation_options = { temperature = 1.0, top_p = 0.95, max_output_tokens = 4096 }
adaptor_options = { request_endpoint = "completions" }

[providers."custom.example".models."example-model".capabilities]
input = ["text"]
output = ["text"]
context_tokens = 32768
output_tokens = 4096
reasoning = true
temperature = true
top_p = true
seed = false
media = {}

[providers."custom.example".models."example-model".variants.low]
reasoning = { type = "effort", value = "low" }

[providers."custom.example".models."example-model".variants.medium]
reasoning = { type = "effort", value = "medium" }

[providers."custom.example".models."example-model".variants.xhigh]
model_id = "backend-model-high-v1"
reasoning = { type = "effort", value = "xhigh" }

The local selection key is custom.example/example-model. The base, low, and medium variants send backend-model-v1; xhigh sends backend-model-high-v1. All variants still inherit the base sampling and endpoint settings unless overridden. No default variant is selected by this example. Setting an effort requests that behavior; parsing or HTTP acceptance does not prove that the backend implements distinct effort levels.

For a local service, change endpoint to its loopback base URL, such as http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1, and use auth = { method = "no-auth-v1", values = {} }. Compatible Responses supports tools and native replay with no auth when explicitly declared and supported by the server; it is not restricted to a tool-less text-only legacy path.

docs.title: Provider fields
docs.text: Key Type Default Description source string (required) Must be "custom". endpoint string (required) Absolute, query-free URL. Must be https, or http to localhost/a loopback address. Interpolates ${env:NAME}. adaptor string (required) Protocol adaptor ID (see below). setup map of string values empty Adaptor-required setup fields (Vertex location/project/resource, Bedrock region, Azure api_version/deployment). Interpolates ${env:NAME}. auth table (required) Typed auth definition (see below). headers map of strings empty Public provider request-header overrides. Supports environment and session templates. cache table adaptor default Prompt-cache policy matching adaptor. models map (required) At least one custom model definition.

docs.title: Authentication and adaptors
docs.text:
Custom auth accepts required method and values, plus optional parameters (empty by default). Each method requires exactly the listed credential fields; only api-key-header-v1 accepts parameters.

Method Credential fields in values Additional requirement no-auth-v1 Empty map No parameters bearer-api-key-v1 api_key Bearer header api-key-header-v1 api_key parameters = { header_name = "x-api-key" } or "api-key" anthropic-api-key-v1 api_key Anthropic key header google-api-key-header-v1 api_key Google key header oauth-access-token-v1 access_token Caller-supplied access token aws-sigv4-credentials-v1 access_key_id, secret_access_key, optional session_token SigV4 signing azure-api-key-v1 api_key Azure key header Custom adaptor Allowed auth methods Required setup openai-compatible Bearer, API-key-header, no-auth None openai-chat, openai-responses Bearer, no-auth None anthropic, anthropic-compatible Anthropic API key None google-gemini Google API key None google-vertex-gemini OAuth access token project, location; resource defaults to publishers/google aws-bedrock-converse AWS SigV4 region azure-openai-chat, azure-openai-responses Azure API key deployment, api_version cohere-v2-chat Bearer None

The short auth labels above refer to the full method IDs in the preceding table. Managed providers instead use their catalog family recipes, including their setup fields and allowed methods; /connect presents that exact form. Vertex, Bedrock, and Azure compute routes from setup and reject arbitrary managed base_url overrides. Custom endpoints must satisfy the selected adaptor's route constraints too.

The anthropic adaptor and the managed anthropic provider send anthropic-version: 2026-10-21. That version rejects temperature, top_p, and top_k, so their models have no sampling capabilities: declaring temperature or top_p as true, or setting either in generation_options, is a load error. The anthropic-compatible adaptor and the other managed Anthropic-protocol providers send 2023-06-01 and keep sampling; a custom provider that needs sampling on Anthropic's own API uses anthropic-compatible.

docs.title: Model fields
docs.text:
Custom model definition under [providers."custom.x".models."<model-id>"]:

Key Type Default Description enabled boolean true Whether the model is compiled into the runtime. display_name string (required) Nonblank, at most 512 bytes, no control characters. model_id string inherited Provider request identifier, independent of the local selection key; see Request model identity. capabilities table (required) Explicit capability declarations (see below). generation_options table empty Generation settings (see below). adaptor_options table empty Typed adaptor-specific settings (see below). pricing table absent Whole-model rate override, including an explicitly empty rate set. headers map of strings empty Model request-header overrides. Variants accept the same header map. variants map empty Implicit variant creation or sparse overrides. default_variant string (none) "base" or a named variant that must exist in variants.

docs.title: Request model identity
docs.text:
Optional model_id is accepted on custom models, managed-model overrides, and variants. Later supplied values win:

  1. Provider-supplied identifier, normally the catalog/model key; custom Azure uses its configured setup.deployment as the fallback.
  2. Model-level model_id.
  3. Variant-level model_id.

Omission inherits. Values must be nonempty, at most 2,048 bytes, without control characters or surrounding whitespace, and valid for the selected adaptor's request route. Wire identifiers are not restricted to local alias syntax. OpenAI-style and Messages requests use the resolved model field; Gemini and Vertex use it in their model resource, Bedrock in its model path, and Azure in its deployment/model mapping. Resource restrictions still apply: for example, Gemini requires a bare model ID rather than a models/ prefix, slash, colon, query, fragment, or whitespace. Unsupported route/identifier combinations fail when constructing the executable model, rather than ignoring the override.

Changing model_id does not rename the local model, change its pricing lookup, modify catalog membership, or infer new capabilities. A managed alias must still name an existing catalog entry.
