The selected effective wire ID and endpoint are frozen with the executable settings, so reconstruction preserves them even when the current configuration or catalog changes.

docs.title: Capabilities and media
docs.text:
Custom fields are required unless a default or omission rule is stated below.

Key Type Description input array of strings Nonempty modalities: text, image, audio, pdf, video; subject to adaptor support. output array of strings Currently only ["text"] is supported. Structured JSON is text, not a separate modality. context_tokens integer Context window in tokens; must be greater than zero. input_tokens integer Optional input-token limit for providers that document one below the context window; must be greater than zero and at most context_tokens. Omitted, the input budget is the context window less min(output cap, 32000, context_tokens / 2). Compaction triggers against this budget. output_tokens integer Maximum output tokens; must be greater than zero and at most context_tokens. tool_calling boolean Defaults to true when not declared or inherited. A model with tool_calling = false is unsupported and never selectable. parallel_tool_calls boolean Defaults to true; requires tool_calling = true. structured_output boolean Defaults to true; declares JSON-structured output support. reasoning boolean Reasoning support. temperature boolean Temperature parameter support. top_p boolean Top-p parameter support. seed boolean Seed parameter support. compaction string Optional; "unsupported" is the only accepted value and turns native compaction off. Omitted, a model on a Responses adaptor (or an openai-compatible adaptor with request_endpoint = "responses") compacts natively, and Azure Responses does so with model, version, and deployment_type in setup. deferred_tools string Optional "native" or "unsupported"; whether the model loads deferred tools. Omitted, the automatic rules under provider fields decide: on an anthropic or anthropic-compatible adaptor a model is attempted (or native for a Claude model on api.anthropic.com), and every other custom model is unsupported. "native" on an adaptor that cannot load deferred tools is an error. native_replay string Optional "unsupported", "optional", or "required"; omission derives supported replay from the resolved adaptor and endpoint. media map Per-kind (image, audio, pdf, video) input limits: nonempty mime_types string array, positive max_bytes and max_count. max_count is per request: when the history holds more parts of a kind, the oldest are replaced by a text placeholder in the outgoing request (see media reads). Exactly the non-text input modalities need entries; text-only models use {}.

The three optimistic true defaults are declarations, not endpoint detection. Set unsupported features to false. Invalid effective declarations are errors. For an endpoint without parallel tool calls or structured output, add this fragment to its capabilities table:

parallel_tool_calls = false
structured_output = false

cookie-agent requires tool calling. tool_calling = false (which also requires parallel_tool_calls = false) is accepted, but the model compiles as unsupported with the reason no tool calling and is never offered for selection; a fallback chain skips it like any other unavailable model.

These flags neither request JSON for ordinary turns nor guarantee parallel execution or backend support. Managed models retain explicit catalog false declarations; only missing metadata falls back to true.

Input support also depends on the delivery channel. A modality accepted in a user turn is not necessarily accepted in a tool result. Counts are enforced per request; a tool result and its emitted messages share a combined budget. See media reads for supported channels, MIME types, retention, and operational limits. Unsupported combinations produce tool errors, not generated media output.

docs.title: Replay and cancellation
docs.text:
Cancellation is derived as local-only; it does not guarantee server generation or billing stops, and capabilities.cancellation is rejected.

All integrated SDK codecs support replay. Automatic replay is optional except Anthropic reasoning, which requires native state. Azure ordinary replay does not require deployment revision metadata; model, version, and deployment_type remain required for native compaction, which Azure Responses skips without them. Azure Chat supports native text/tool replay, not provider-authoritative reasoning replay. Explicit replay declarations remain authoritative and fail when incompatible; native_replay = "unsupported" disables replay. Automatic replay is recomputed for the effective variant endpoint.

Replay preserves assistant response history, not a prior HTTP request. With replay enabled, the target prefers valid native blocks it supports:

Content Eligibility Standard supported text, tools, and non-encrypted reasoning blocks Portable across local models, variants, providers, endpoints, headers, and deployment fingerprints when the target supports their format and semantics Encrypted/opaque reasoning: Responses encrypted_content, redacted Messages/Converse state, Gemini/Vertex thoughtSignature Target format support and equal, known source/target effective wire model IDs are both required Custom-adaptor-specific or unknown blocks/codecs Only explicit target support authorizes replay; unknown formats are not guessed or translated

Signed visible thinking is not encrypted reasoning. A supported Messages signed thinking block can remain eligible across wire-model changes, but is not automatically convertible to Responses reasoning. Native payload integrity and agreement with normalized history are still validated; provider/header/model fingerprints are not additional eligibility restrictions for standard blocks. When a validated bundle can be separated safely, portable siblings survive exclusion of an ineligible encrypted block.

Ordinary tool history can reconstruct from normalized text and calls if native data is unavailable. Required continuation state cannot silently disappear: missing, corrupt, or ineligible required reasoning/signatures fail closed, even when ordinary siblings are portable. Saved evidence that opaque state was required is distinct from an ordinary integrity marker; a tool call alone does not imply encrypted state. Legacy history without that evidence is read best-effort, not repaired by inventing missing native data. Missing source wire identity never establishes equality for encrypted replay.

Switching providers can send eligible prior native state to the new endpoint. Equal wire model IDs are necessary for encrypted replay, but a different service can still reject ciphertext or signatures, even for that ID. A provider HTTP 400 is not automatically recovered by stripping reasoning and resending. Errors follow the normal retry and fallback policy. Replay neither enables prompt caching nor guarantees cache hits or live backend acceptance. Cache policy and native compaction retain their separate scope and validation rules: a compacted window serves only its own provider and model, and other requests use the summary.

docs.title: Generation options
docs.text:
Model and variant generation_options supply shared generation settings. On a custom base model, omission leaves optional values unset and stop empty; on managed models and variants, supplied fields override individually. Agent limits and explicit request settings can further constrain the effective request.

Key Type Description temperature float Finite value; requires capabilities.temperature. top_p float Finite value; requires capabilities.top_p. max_output_tokens integer Must be greater than zero and at most capabilities.output_tokens. Sent when the agent sets no output cap of its own; without it, requests send the full output_tokens. Catalog models have no default. stop array of strings Stop sequences. seed integer Requires capabilities.seed. tool_choice string or table "auto", "none", "required", or { named = "tool-name" }; requires capabilities.tool_calling.

Current integration limitation: authored stop, seed, and tool_choice are accepted, validated, inherited, and recorded in run bindings, but the shared request-default application does not forward them to SDK requests. Do not rely on those authored fields to control a live request. Temperature, top-p, maximum output tokens, and supported reasoning settings do reach request construction; final behavior still depends on the selected adaptor and backend.

docs.title: Adaptor options
docs.text:
These are typed model/variant settings, not arbitrary JSON body fields. All are optional; omission inherits before adaptor defaults apply. Explicit false and empty lists remain overrides. Nonempty wrong-adaptor settings fail.

Key Type Description request_endpoint string "completions" (Chat Completions) or "responses"; selects the complete codec and route. beta array of strings Anthropic beta header values; rejected for non-Anthropic adaptors. organization string OpenAI-Organization header for OpenAI Chat (with or without auth) and authenticated OpenAI Responses; rejected for compatible and unauthenticated Responses. project string OpenAI-Project header for OpenAI Chat (with or without auth) and authenticated OpenAI Responses; rejected for compatible and unauthenticated Responses. store boolean OpenAI/compatible Responses only, not Azure. The stateless encoder supports false; true is rejected.

docs.title: Request endpoint
docs.text:
Adaptor Omitted completions responses openai-chat Chat Completions Supported Supported openai-responses Responses Supported Supported openai-compatible Chat Completions Supported Compatible Responses azure-openai-chat Azure Chat Supported Supported azure-openai-responses Azure Responses Supported Supported Anthropic, Gemini, Vertex Gemini, Bedrock Converse, Cohere Native API Rejected Rejected

Managed omission preserves catalog routing. Selection chooses the encoder, decoder, streaming protocol, and route, not just a URL suffix. completions means /chat/completions, not the legacy /completions API. Azure retains its deployment-specific routing. Backend compatibility must be verified separately; selecting Responses cannot add it to a server that only implements Chat.

Changing a variant endpoint validates all inherited settings against that endpoint. For example, an inherited store = false conflicts with a Chat variant; omit it on the base and put it only on the Responses variant instead.

docs.title: Variants and inheritance
docs.text:
Variant entries create absent IDs and sparsely update existing catalog variants. Generation and adaptor fields inherit in order: catalog base, model overrides, catalog variant, user variant. Omitted fields inherit, explicit false survives, and lists replace ([] clears). Reasoning omission preserves the prior value; a supplied tagged reasoning object replaces it as a whole. Headers merge by normalized name, preserving empty-string deletion markers through composition.

Variants accept display_name, model_id, generation_options, adaptor_options, reasoning, headers, and optional enabled. enabled = false removes an existing variant or is a no-op for an absent ID; other fields alongside it are errors. Existing positions are preserved, and new IDs append in sorted order. An omitted or empty map preserves catalog variants. Named defaults must exist and be enabled after composition. A new unnamed display label is derived from its ID. Custom variants have no catalog layer, so editing shared base settings changes every variant that does not override those fields.

default_variant selects a variant; it is not a generation setting. Omission does not select the first authored variant. "base" explicitly selects the base; named defaults are resolved after creation, overrides, and disabling.

Reasoning is optional and requires the model's reasoning capability. The tagged object accepts exactly one of:

Type Fields Constraints effort value none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max, default; not Cohere toggle enabled boolean Anthropic, Gemini, Vertex Gemini, Bedrock Converse, Cohere budget_tokens value signed integer Same families as toggle; final adaptor validation determines supported budgets

A concrete off toggle or none effort is not removal of the reasoning object. There is no null/clear operation. Example fragment disabling a managed variant:

[providers.openai.models.gpt-5.variants.low]
enabled = false

docs.title: Provider definitions and headers
docs.text: Providers are defined only in the user config.toml. The sparse rules above apply inside one provider definition. Headers use the separate Request Header composition and ownership rules; their values are public metadata, not secret-typed storage.

docs.title: Breaking configuration migration
docs.text: Removed keys fail without aliases: model_overrides becomes models, model and variant defaults becomes generation_options, and options becomes adaptor_options. Replace shape and the ineffective api_path with adaptor_options.request_endpoint. Remove authored capabilities.cancellation. Replace variant operation directives with sparse entries or enabled = false. Move top-level pricing to the model's pricing table.

docs.title: Prompt caching
docs.text:
Prompt-cache policy belongs to the provider definition. Omit cache, or a field of it, to use the family defaults. A cache table is validated against the provider's resolved adaptor; wrong-family fields and unknown keys are load errors.

The following are fragments for already-defined providers, not a complete file:

[providers.anthropic.cache]
system = "1h"
tools = "1h"
rolling = "1h"

[providers."custom.bedrock".cache]
system = "5m"
tools = "5m"
rolling = "5m"

[providers.openai.cache]
mode = "auto"
ttl = "30m"
system = true
rolling = true

[providers."custom.compatible".cache]
prompt_cache_key = "tenant-${session_id}"

Here custom.bedrock is an existing custom aws-bedrock-converse provider. A managed provider can contain models routed through different adaptor families; a shared cache table must validate for its resolved models. In particular, do not apply a Converse-only cache policy to a mixed Bedrock catalog provider that also routes models through Responses. Use a custom provider for explicit family-specific policy when the managed definition cannot share it.

Anthropic and Bedrock share three fields, system, tools, and rolling, each "1h", "5m", or "off". Their defaults depend on the layer of the session the run belongs to:

Session system tools rolling Root (no delegation parent) "1h" "1h" "1h" Subagent (a delegated child) "1h" "1h" "5m"

An authored value applies to both layers: only the defaults differ. An agent's entry-level cache fills its unset fields from the same layer defaults, and a subagent that inherits its parent's models inherits the parent's entry-level cache with them. Internal agents (compaction, titles, the approval reviewer) use the defaults of the layer of the run they serve; compaction reuses that run's markers so it reads the cached prefix.

Marker order is tools, system, then rolling history, and a one-hour marker cannot follow a five-minute marker. Authored values that break the order are a load error. A default never does: an unset field after a five-minute marker defaults to five minutes, so tools = "5m" alone gives five-minute system and rolling markers too.

The one-hour TTL is generally available on the Anthropic API and needs no anthropic-beta header, so "1h" placement, authored or default, sends only the marker's ttl. Cookie agent never inserts an anthropic-beta value on the user's behalf.

On Bedrock, only some models take a one-hour TTL: Claude Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5, Opus 4.5, and later Claude models; older Claude models and other families take five minutes only and may reject a ttl. Bedrock publishes no capability for it, so Cookie agent reads it from the model ID: an anthropic.claude-<family>-<major>-<minor> ID of version 4.5 or later, in any region or profile prefix. On any other model, an application inference profile ARN included, every default is "5m". An authored "1h" is sent as written, and an authored "1h" that would follow those five-minute defaults fails the run's policy freeze with a cache-strategy error; author the earlier markers too, or leave the field unset.

Setting all three Bedrock fields to "off" emits no cache points. Rolling always marks the last non-system message. There is no enabled switch and no indexed messages list. System and tool points are omitted from requests without eligible system text or tools. The three structural placements stay below Bedrock's four-point request limit.

Anthropic and Bedrock use structural markers. The selected policy is frozen for the run, prior markers are cleared, and ordinary and compaction requests resolve the same system, tools, and last-non-system placements. Compaction shares the parent's cached prefix instead of creating an isolated cache namespace.

OpenAI and Azure OpenAI always send the session's bare UUIDv7 as prompt_cache_key; this has no configuration field or opt-out. Their cache table accepts prompt_cache_retention, mode, ttl, system, and rolling. prompt_cache_retention is "in_memory" or "24h", for models before GPT-5.6. Setting mode or ttl, or setting system or rolling to true, enables GPT-5.6 controls, which cannot be combined with prompt_cache_retention. Both placements default to false; omitted mode and ttl then default to "auto" and "30m". ttl is "30m" or "12h"; "12h" requires the OpenAI Responses API, and Chat Completions and Azure OpenAI reject it. mode = "explicit" disables the provider-managed breakpoint, so system = false and rolling = false produce zero cache writes. There is no tools placement.

Custom openai-compatible providers accept only prompt_cache_key. Omission defaults to ${session_id}, an empty string disables the key, and another value is sent verbatim after ${session_id} expansion. The expanded value must be at most 64 characters. Other template variables are rejected.

Gemini caching is always implicit and has no configuration surface. A cache table on Google Gemini or Vertex Gemini providers is an error. Cohere caching is server-side automatic and likewise has no authored cache table.

Provider behavior changes independently of Cookie agent. See the official OpenAI prompt-caching guide, Gemini context-caching guide, Amazon Bedrock prompt-caching guide, Cohere API reference, and Anthropic prompt-caching guide for current model support, thresholds, retention, and billing.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
1. The global [prompt_caching] table and all [prompt_caching.<family>] subtables are removed; use [providers.<id>.cache].
  2. Anthropic and Bedrock TTLs accept only "1h", "5m", and "off". The former "one_hour" and "five_minutes" values are removed. Configuration is strict: any other TTL string (for example "automatic", "short", "long", "standard", "none", or "ephemeral") was never a cookie-agent literal and is a hard error, not an alias.
  3. Google cache configuration is removed, including mode ("implicit", "explicit", or "off") and cached_content; Gemini caching is always implicit.
  4. Bedrock now uses only system, tools, and rolling. The enabled field, messages list, and each message entry's history_index and ttl fields are removed.
  5. First-party OpenAI and Azure cache tables no longer accept prompt_cache_key; the bare session UUIDv7 is always sent. OpenAI-compatible providers own that field, default to ${session_id}, and use prompt_cache_key = "" to disable it.
  6. OpenAI cache mode = "implicit" is removed; use mode = "auto". mode = "explicit" remains supported.

docs.title: Model pricing
docs.text:
Pricing overrides are empty by default. Managed models use prices from the selected models.dev catalog. Add an entry for a custom model absent from the catalog, or to override catalog prices with the provider terms that apply to your account. Catalog context tiers are selected independently for each request from its reported input-token count. Both managed and custom models use this model-local table. Rates are validated even for disabled or unavailable models; managed model IDs must still exist in the catalog.

[providers."custom.example".models."model-name".pricing]
input_per_million_usd = "1.25"
output_per_million_usd = "5.0"

All fields are optional quoted, finite, nonnegative decimal USD rates per million tokens. Quoting preserves the authored decimal exactly.

Rates use fixed-point precision of 12 decimal places in USD per million tokens, stored as an unsigned 128-bit scaled integer. Scientific notation is accepted when exactly representable. Negative values, non-finite values, overflow, and nonzero precision below that scale are rejected, not rounded. Pricing has no variant override. The example above is a fragment for an existing model.

Key Applies to input_per_million_usd Input tokens not attributed to cache reads or writes output_per_million_usd Plain, non-reasoning output tokens reasoning_per_million_usd Reasoning output tokens; falls back to the output rate when omitted cache_read_per_million_usd Provider-reported cache-read input tokens cache_write_per_million_usd Provider-reported cache-write input tokens

Precedence is config override, then catalog price, then no estimate. A config entry replaces the catalog rate set for that model. When a selected rate set does not distinguish cache reads or writes, those tokens use its plain input rate; reasoning tokens similarly use its output rate when no reasoning rate is present. An estimate is returned only when the selected source prices every nonzero observed category and the provider reports every split needed by a distinct rate. A session, agent, or global total is unpriced if any model within it is unpriced. These are estimates from provider-reported token counts, not invoices.

docs.title: Skill
docs.text: Skills are reusable instruction bundles loaded once when the runtime that contributes them starts. A skill is a directory whose name contains lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens, with an exact-case SKILL.md file inside it. Other files under the directory are available as scripts, references, or assets.

docs.title: Discovery and precedence
docs.text:
A session's skills come from the runtimes it is attached to. The global runtime contributes the user skills:

  • ~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (cross-client convention, shared with other agents)
  • ~/.cookie-agent/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (cookie-agent-native user skills, which win over the shared location)

Each coding runtime contributes the project skills it finds for its own workspace: .agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, then .cookie-agent/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, in every directory from the repository root (the nearest ancestor with .git) down to the workspace, deeper directories winning. The built-in local runtime does this for the daemon's working directory when the daemon starts; another coding runtime does it when its instance starts.

The user locations resolve from the standard home directory and are the normal place for reusable personal skills; ~/.agents/skills is the right home for skills shared with other agents that follow the cross-client convention.

Same-named skills are replaced whole, never merged: a project skill shadows a user skill of the same name, and within one directory scope the cookie-agent-native root wins over .agents/skills. When project skills of two attachments share a name, each is offered as <attachment>_<name>, for example local_web_deploy and labpc_api_deploy, like colliding tools. Shadowed skills remain visible in skills.list, but cannot be invoked and are not offered by the TUI. A session without the global runtime has no user skills, and one without a coding runtime has no project skills. Skill files are not hot-reloaded; restart the engine after changing them.

docs.title: Official skills
docs.text:
Cookie keeps a set of official skills about itself up to date on every daemon: customize-cookie-agent, pointers for an agent asked to change cookie (its configuration, providers, runtimes, MCP servers, agents, skills, and cron jobs), and add-cookie-runtime, for bringing another machine in as a runtime over ssh or by dialing in. They come from the cookie-agent/skills repository, served at https://cookie-agent.github.io/skills/, a source whose URL carries no version.

  • Where. official_skills/<name>/ in the daemon's data root (~/.cookie-agent/official_skills/), which only the daemon writes. It is the lowest skill root: a user or project skill of the same name wins, and the official one shows as shadowed.
  • Refresh. At start and then every 24 hours the daemon reads the source's index.json, downloads the files whose SHA-256 changed, and checks each against the index before it replaces the cached copy. Skills the index no longer lists, or whose requires_cookie range this version does not satisfy, are removed. A failed refresh keeps the cached skills and shows as a configuration diagnostic (cookie config status, /config) until a refresh succeeds; an offline daemon keeps working. A refresh that changes them reloads the daemon's skills, user skills included, for new sessions.
  • Off. [skills] official = false in config.toml stops refreshing at once and leaves the folder unused from the next start.
  • Commands. cookie skills list shows each skill with where it comes from and an official skill's version, cookie skills update refreshes now, and cookie skills check <dir> validates skills you write; see cookie skills. The TUI's skill picker and the web page's skill list mark official skills.

Skills grant no tools; the skill permission and every tool's own rules still decide each call.

[skills]
official = true   # the default

official is the table's only key; an unknown key fails.

docs.title: Authoring
docs.text:
Complete release-check/SKILL.md:

---
name: release-check
description: Check a release candidate for packaging and changelog problems.
when_to_use: Use before publishing a tagged build.
allowed-tools: Bash(git:*) Bash(jq:*) Read
argument-hint: <tag>
---
Review release $1 from $ARGUMENTS.
Read supporting files from ${COOKIE_SKILL_DIR}.

name and description are required; descriptions are limited to 1024 bytes. Optional fields are when_to_use, allowed-tools, disable-model-invocation, user-invocable, model, context, argument-hint, license, compatibility, and metadata. Unknown fields are errors. model must be a valid provider/model key and is rejected during discovery otherwise. context accepts only fork.

disable-model-invocation defaults to false and user-invocable defaults to true. allowed-tools is omitted by default (no extra grants); an authored empty string is invalid. Optional text fields are strings; model and context are unset by default, and metadata is an empty map of YAML values. Files are limited to 256 KiB and must have a nonempty body. The declared name must match the directory name.

Arguments replace $ARGUMENTS and positional $1, $2, and later forms. ${COOKIE_SKILL_DIR} expands to the skill directory. Expansion is textual and does not execute a shell.

docs.title: Invocation and permissions
docs.text:
The model uses skill({"name":"release-check","args":"v1.2.0"}). The tool is absent when policy leaves no skill effectively usable, and skills with disable-model-invocation: true are omitted from the model listing. In the TUI, users choose /skills in the command palette, search for a user-invocable skill, press Enter, and type optional arguments such as v1.2.0 into the prompt that follows. The highlighted skill's source, permission effect, and location show under the list. Headless runs use cookie run --skill release-check --skill-args v1.2.0 "Check the release".

Skill access uses the skill permission action and the skill name as its resource. A denied skill is hidden from the model listing. Headless runs can grant one skill with --allowed-tools skill:release-check.

allowed-tools uses the agentskills.io/Claude Code syntax: a space-separated string of bare Tool names or Tool(pattern) entries. Patterns may contain spaces and parentheses; a bare tool means *. Tool names are case-insensitive, and Edit maps to the write permission just like the builtin edit tool. Every other name is the permission action itself, lowercased: Read, Bash, Webfetch, and so on for the built-in tools, or a runtime's own action such as Browse(https://docs.rs/*). A name that lowercases to no valid action (see permissions) is an error. The older Cookie Agent action:pattern list form is not accepted.

A plugin's tools are granted by the actions their plugin declares, like a runtime's: Issue_read grants every issue_read call, and Issue_read(42) only the calls on resource 42.

Claude's prefix:* convention is translated to Cookie Agent's full-resource glob semantics. For example, Bash(git:*) creates grants for both git and git *, matching git, git status, and longer git commands. Other inner patterns pass through unchanged: Write(src/**) grants the src/** glob.

On load, these entries create turn-scoped allow grants labeled for that skill. A project skill's grants apply only to the tools of the attachment that contributed it (and, for Skill and Delegate grants, to the base layer's skill and delegate_subagent tools); a user skill's grants apply to every runtime. Grants from every skill loaded during the same turn are merged; loading a grantless skill does not remove grants from an earlier skill. The complete collection disappears on the next committed user input. Grants can only upgrade an ask decision to allow: they never override a deny, including the unmatched default deny, and they do not make a tool visible on their own. The agent still needs an explicit allow or ask rule for each granted action — for example bash: ask before relying on a skill's Bash grants. A model override applies to the next model turn only.

Every first rendered load appends skill_loaded, including the rendered body, source and base paths, arguments, and up to ten supporting-file paths. Loading the identical rendered body again appends skill_invocation_noted. Loaded skill bodies remain in model context across compaction. With context: fork, the exact staged skill payload is persisted in delegation admission. The child gets the rendered instructions once through its skill_loaded event and a synthetic user prompt starts the run. Forks use the normal delegation approval, queue, paging, cancellation, recovery, and permission behavior.

docs.title: Rust API Documentation
docs.text:
The workspace rustdoc output is published with each documentation version.

Open workspace API documentation

The API index includes all eleven workspace crates and documents public items only. Build it locally together with this site by running:

./scripts/build-docs.sh

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: The client protocol, the plugin protocol, the runtime protocol, and session history carry a compatibility promise: a client, plugin, or runtime written against 1.x keeps working with every daemon that speaks 1.x, and a session log keeps opening in every later build. These are the rules every change to them follows. The compatibility specification gives the reasons; this page states the rules.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
• Each protocol has a semver version MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH in crates/protocol/src/semver.rs: CLIENT_PROTOCOL_VERSION, PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_VERSION, and RUNTIME_PROTOCOL_VERSION. All three froze at 1.0.0.
  • Bump the major for a breaking change: something removed or renamed, a meaning changed, a new required member in a message the peer receives, a closed enum grown. Peers of different majors never connect, and a daemon does not keep serving the previous major.
  • Bump the minor for any addition: a method, a notification, a hook, an event type, a display-block kind, an optional member, a value of an open enum.
  • Bump the patch for a change that leaves every wire shape alone: a documented behaviour clarified, a validation bug fixed.
  • Know which surfaces a message belongs to. Session events belong to the client and the plugin protocols, so adding an event type bumps both minors. The tool/* messages belong to the plugin and the runtime protocols. Display blocks belong to all three.
  • Update the human-readable references in the same commit as a bump: AGENTS.md lists them.

docs.title: Handshakes
docs.text:
• Read the peer's protocol_version from the raw JSON before decoding anything else (negotiate_version), and answer another major with unsupported_protocol naming both versions.
  • Two peers of one major share the lower of their minors. Send a command (a method, a member of a command's params, a hook) only when the receiver's minor includes it. Information an older receiver ignores may stay in place; a value an older receiver would misread may not.
  • Features carry only what depends on configuration, never what a version implies. A receiver ignores a feature it does not know.

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
What arrives Unknown member Unknown enum value or tag Information (results, notifications, events, hook params, initialize results, stored events) Ignored The documented fallback Command (client params, producer/*, tool/progress, tool/detachable, plugin/emit) Refused: -32602 unknown_field with its JSON path Refused: -32602 unknown_variant with its JSON path
  • Never put #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] on a type that crosses a surface as information. The checker rejects an information type whose schema has additionalProperties: false. Command params stay strict, and so does configuration.
  • Writers stay strict. Validate every value before it is sent or written: bounds, required members, grammar. Strictness lives in constructors and in the writer's validation step, not in the decoder.
  • Make every enum a reader may meet open, and document what its unknown value means where it is read: Open<T> (open_enum!) for tagged enums with data, an Unknown variant or a #[serde(other)] fallback for unit enums, validated label strings for label-like values. Mark open enums x-open: true in the schema. Close an enum only when growing it is a breaking change by design, and say so.
  • A known tag with a malformed body is an error, not Unknown: Unknown means "from a newer peer".
  • Do not add #[non_exhaustive] to protocol types; only the plugin SDK's own types use it.

docs.title: Wire types
docs.text:
• No surface embeds a type owned by oven-sdk or by engine policy, stored events included. Where the engine needs data it does not model, store an opaque value and decode it best-effort when it is used, never when loading.
  • Every error is a registry error (cookie_agent_protocol::errors): a stable data.code, a message a user understands, an optional hint, and detail for technical detail. Add a code to the registry rather than building error data by hand; clients branch only on data.code.

docs.title: Making a wire change
docs.text:
1. Change the type or the method registry (surface_methods in crates/protocol/src/bindings.rs).
  2. Bump each affected surface's version by what the change needs (above).
  3. Run crates/protocol/scripts/update-compat-baseline.sh. It regenerates crates/protocol/compat/<surface>/ and refuses when a version lacks the bump its changes require.
  4. Run crates/protocol/scripts/check-schema-additive.sh, which CI runs: it compares the generated schemas with the baselines under the rules of the specification's section 7.1 and runs the checker's mutation test.
  5. Commit the baselines with the change and the reference updates.

A change the checker calls breaking needs a major bump; there is no way to mark a breaking change as compatible.

docs.title: Test sets
docs.text:
• Frozen corpora are never regenerated. crates/protocol/compat/corpus/ holds, per surface and version, recorded conversations that the current build must keep accepting, and future fixtures that inject what a newer build could send. crates/engine/tests/fixtures/history/<format>/ holds recorded session trees with snapshots of their projection and model history. No COOKIE_UPDATE_* switch applies to them, and the baseline update leaves them alone.
  • When a test over frozen data fails, fix the code, not the data. A failure means the change breaks data an earlier build wrote or sent.
  • A minor release that adds wire shapes records its own corpus directory next to the earlier ones. A history format bump records history/<format>/ with its own recorder run, beside the older formats, which keep testing their converters.

docs.title: Session history
docs.text:
• Class every event as state (anything the projection, model history, delegation recovery, goals, producers, approvals, or usage read) or audit (everything else), and list its class in Events. Audit events carry "skippable": true; a reader skips an unknown skippable event and opens a log with an unknown state event render-only.
  • Additive rules for writers: a new optional member must be safe to ignore, its absence meaning the old behaviour; a member whose absence would be misread needs a new event type; a new open-enum value needs a fallback that is safe for old readers.
  • The loader never recomputes what it can read. Trust stored fingerprints, quarantine a record that fails a cross-event check instead of failing the open, keep size caps writer-only, and keep every record's raw line so that a fork, a publish, or a conversion copies what this build did not understand.
  • Storage encodings stay on disk. An encoding only the log holds, such as a tool result's display ranges of its output, is expanded when the log is read; nothing outside the engine meets it.
  • The history format bumps only for a change that cannot follow the additive rules, and every bump ships a converter: crates/engine/src/events/convert/v<N>_to_v<N+1>.rs, a pure function over the old log's JSON lines that never uses old Rust types, registered in CONVERTERS and kept forever, so converters chain. Converters are the only migrations allowed; nothing else upconverts, aliases, or migrates stored or authored data. See History formats.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Configuration is not a compatibility surface. It stays strict: unknown keys, removed fields, wrong types, and malformed values are hard errors, and authored files are never migrated or upconverted. A configuration key change is a configuration change, not a protocol change, even where config.get and config.apply carry the document.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every error the client, plugin, and runtime protocols send has a stable data.code and a message a user can understand; data.hint says what to do next where that helps, and data.detail carries technical detail for a details view. Clients branch only on data.code, show message and then hint, and show detail on request. A code a client does not know is still readable: its message and hint are written for people. See the compatibility spec section 6.

The JSON-RPC code is -32000 for every application error; the protocol codes are the standard -32700, -32600, -32601, -32602, and -32603, and -32001 (handshake required), -32002 (unsupported_protocol), and -32003 (unauthenticated).

data.code JSON-RPC Meaning Message Hint Fields parse_error -32700 A frame that is not JSON; the daemon answers it and reads on, while the shared client closes its connection. A message could not be read because it is not valid JSON. – – invalid_request -32600 A frame that is not a JSON-RPC request, notification, or reply. A message is not a valid request. – – request_id_required -32600 A method that only works as a request arrived as a notification. {method} must be sent as a request with an ID. – method: The method that was sent as a notification. method_not_found -32601 A method the receiver does not know. The other side does not know the method {method}. Update the older of the two programs. method: The method name. invalid_params -32602 Params that do not match the method. The request's parameters are not valid. – field (optional): The JSON path of the first bad member. unknown_field -32602 A command carried a member its receiver does not know. The request has a member the receiver does not know: {field}. Update the older of the two programs. field: The JSON path of the member. unknown_variant -32602 A command carried an enum value or tag its receiver does not know. The request uses a value the receiver does not know at {field}. Update the older of the two programs. field: The JSON path of the value.value (optional): The value that is not known. internal_error -32603 A failure the receiver cannot describe further. Something went wrong while handling the request. Try again; if it keeps failing, check the daemon log. – handshake_required -32001 A request before the handshake. The connection must complete its handshake first. – – unsupported_protocol -32002 The peer speaks another major version of the protocol. The two sides speak incompatible protocol versions: {supported_version} here and {peer_version} on the other side. Update cookie or the program connecting to it so that their versions match. supported_version: The version the receiver speaks.peer_version: The version the peer sent. unauthenticated -32003 A request before authentication, or a wrong token. The connection is not authenticated. Connect with the daemon's token. – engine_error -32000 A failure with no more specific code; detail says what failed. The daemon could not complete the request. See the details for the cause. – no_runnable_model -32000 No configured model can run: no provider is connected or none offers the model. No model is ready to run. Connect a provider with /connect, or choose another model. – provider_store_reload_failed -32000 Reloading the provider store after a change failed. The saved provider connections could not be reloaded. Check the details, then reconnect the provider. – session_owned_elsewhere -32000 Another process holds the session's lock. This session is open in another cookie process. Close it there, or open it read-only. session_id (optional): The session. session_not_found -32000 A request named a session the daemon does not have. The session does not exist. – session_id (optional): The session. session_running -32000 run.start on a session that is running. Another run is already active in this session. This daemon can't restart itself. Stop it and start it again the way it was started. – idempotency_conflict -32000 An idempotency key was reused with different params. Attach a smaller file, or downscale it first. kind: The media kind.byte_length: The file's size.max_bytes: The largest accepted size.width (optional): The image's width.height (optional): The image's height.max_dimension (optional): The longest accepted side.max_pixels (optional): The most accepted pixels. media_type_unsupported -32000 An upload whose content is not an accepted media type. docs.title: Event Reference
docs.text: A session's history is events.jsonl: one JSON record per line, appended in order. Subscriptions deliver the same records. The format follows the compatibility specification: events and fields are added without a version bump, and only a change that cannot be made additively bumps the history format.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
{ "engine_version": "0.5.0", "origin": "user", "session_id": "…",
  "run_id": null, "seq": 1, "timestamp": "…", "skippable": true,
  "payload": { "type": "…" } }
Member Meaning engine_version The writing engine's binary semver: diagnostic metadata, not a compatibility gate origin Who authored this record (below) session_id The session run_id Required and nullable: the run a run-scoped event belongs to, null for a runless one seq A positive physical sequence, strictly increasing down the file timestamp When the record was written skippable Present and true exactly on audit events payload The event, tagged by type

origin is either user or <class>:<slug>, where class is engine, plugin, or client and slug matches [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}. It identifies the author of that individual event, not the component described by its payload. For example, a diagnostic about a plugin can have origin engine:plugin-host. Events caused by a client request carry that connection's handshake origin, client:<kind>-<instance id> (see the handshake); the headless CLI's in-process runs use client:headless. A run cancelled through run.cancel records the caller's origin on its run_finished, and the engine's origin when it cancels on its own. When tool-emitted additional messages are materialized as persisted turns, their origin is engine:tool-result: the engine authors the durable turn from a validated tool result, and the tool name remains payload context.

The first record is always session_created. It carries history_format (currently 1, the HISTORY_FORMAT constant of cookie_agent_protocol), and the optional short_id, the tree-unique model-facing handle.

docs.title: Reading a log
docs.text:
Writers are strict: every appended record passes validation (bounds, required fields, grammar, and the cross-event checks below), including a skippable that agrees with its payload's class. Readers are tolerant, since a newer build may have written the log. Each line is read on its own:

  • A fully readable record loads normally. Members this build does not know are ignored, in the envelope (on the first line too) and at any depth of the payload: they are what a newer build added.
  • A known event with an absent or type-mismatched optional field loads with that field defaulted and an in-memory degradation diagnostic.
  • A record with a broken required field, corrupt JSON, or a failed record check is skipped with a diagnostic.
  • An event type this build does not know is skipped silently when its record says skippable. Without skippable it is a state event from a newer build: the record is skipped with a diagnostic naming its type, and the session is render-only. It opens and can be viewed and subscribed, but nothing appends to it: run.start, run.steer, session.submit_input, revert, fork, compaction (manual or automatic), title generation, and every other change fail with error code session_requires_newer_engine, and adopting it repairs nothing.
  • Sequence numbers must increase strictly. Gaps are retained and reported, one bounded diagnostic per contiguous missing range. A sequence that does not increase ends the readable log at that line: what follows is not read, a diagnostic names the line, and the session is render-only as above, except that changes fail as a broken sequence. Nothing is cut from the file.

Records that decode are then checked against each other: runs, attempts, turns, tool calls, approvals, internal agents, delegations, and admitted input must agree with the records they name. A record that fails such a check is quarantined instead of failing the open: it is left out like a skipped record, with a quarantined: … diagnostic (the first 64, then one that counts the rest), and every record that depends on it is excused the same way a dependent of a skipped record is. Appends stay strict: a new record must pass every check against what the log holds. A delegation whose stored records the delegation store cannot verify becomes unrecoverable on its own, and the tree still loads.

Nothing derived is recomputed on read. Stored approval operation fingerprints and delegation request fingerprints are trusted, and the size caps writers keep to that no schema states (a tool result's output, metadata, and display budget, a model turn's serialized size, native replay payloads, a diagnostic's detail, a delegation's seeded-context total) bound only what is written. Bounds a schema states stay part of the type.

A metadata cache that does not decode is rebuilt from events.jsonl, so the session stays listed; subagents/index.json likewise rebuilds from the tree.

docs.title: What survives a newer build
docs.text: A loaded log keeps the bytes it was read from. Rewriting a log whole — a fork, or a conversion — copies every line it read as it was written: a record this build reads in full keeps the members it does not know, and a skipped event, a quarantined record, or a degraded one survives as well. A fork sets only each copy's session_id to the new session's; records appended since the log was read are written as this build serializes them. The exception is a fork's source's delegation records, which it leaves behind with its subagents (see Delegation): each becomes a record_omitted written by this build, so what a newer build added to one goes with it. Artifact liveness (what a revert may delete, and what a fork links into its own tree) scans the lines as they were read, so a reference inside an unknown event or an unknown member keeps its artifact: both an artifact://sha256/<digest> anywhere in a string and an ArtifactRef object (sha256, byte_length, media_type) count.

docs.title: History formats
docs.text:
The first record decides whether the log opens at all. Without a readable session_created the session cannot open: the engine reports an unsupported-era or corrupt-log error. A session_created without history_format was written before history formats and is not read. A higher history_format than this build's fails with session_requires_newer_engine. A lower one is converted to this build's format by the chain of converters it ships, one per format step, each a function from the old log's JSON lines to the new one's:

  • A read-only open converts in memory and leaves the files alone.
  • Taking a tree for writing converts the whole tree under its lock first: the root's log, every child's, and their metadata caches. Each new file is written beside its original and synced; only once every log converted does each original become events.jsonl.v<N>.bak (N its old format) and the new file take its place, and subagents/index.json is rebuilt by the next tree load. A failure leaves every original untouched.
  • cookie sessions upgrade converts the trees on disk up front.

Backups are kept until you delete them. The format bumps only for a change that cannot follow the additive rules below.

crates/engine/tests/fixtures/history/<format>/ holds session trees recorded from scripted runs against fake model providers, with snapshots of what the recording build read from them: every session's metadata, usage, events as clients receive them, and model history. Every later build must open them, read-only and owned, and read the same; they are never regenerated, and a build that bumps the format records its own directory beside them.

CI compares the generated EventPayload schema with the committed baseline in crates/protocol/compat/events/ (see Schemas). A new optional field must be safe to ignore, since its absence means the old behaviour; a field whose absence would be misread needs a new event type; and a new value of an open enum needs a fallback that is safe for older readers.

Terminal tool-result truncation and tool_output_elided references use the retained-output readback lifecycle.

docs.title: State and audit events
docs.text:
Every event type is a state event or an audit event. A state event is read by the projection, model history, delegation recovery, goals, producers, approvals, or usage; an audit event changes none of them, so an older reader may skip it. Writers stamp skippable on audit events. Live-only events are never stored.

Event Class Run scope Records session_created state runless The session's creation: origin, handle, workspace, selection, agent, revisions, history_format session_permission_overlay_set state runless The session's permission overlay runtime_attached, runtime_detached state runless The session's runtime attachments skill_loaded state either A loaded skill body skill_invocation_noted audit either A repeat of an identical skill load session_title_committed state either A title change session_project_set state runless The root session's project permission_mode_set state runless The root session tree's permission mode, restored when the tree loads acp_session_started state either The ACP session the session's ACP agent talks in: new, resumed, or loaded acp_session_updated state either What the ACP agent reported of its session: its commands, options, or plan; a notice; input steered into its turn; a tool call's new presentation; or the starting options the session was created with elicitation_requested state run An agent of the run asks the user a question, a form or a URL (see Questions) elicitation_resolved state run How the question was answered: accept, decline, or cancel, by whom, and an accepted form's values delegated_attachments_added state runless The attachments a root's subagent brought that the root did not record yet (delegated attachments) agent_md_loaded state run The AGENTS.md context of one attachment, or of the session's project memory_loaded state run The memory snapshot the model sees from this run on memory_changed audit run A model's memory tool saved, edited, or deleted a memory. Only daemons before 2026-10-24 record it: the memory tool's own row now shows the change, and a client folds this event into the call it follows (a line of its own only when it follows none). Queued for removal at the next major diagnostic audit either A notice about the engine, a plugin, or a runtime record_omitted audit either A record its writer deliberately did not carry over goal_activated, goal_checklist_revised, goal_lifecycle_changed state runless or run The session goal producer_message_accepted, producer_message_discarded state runless or run A producer message's body; its withdrawal producer_message_admitted, producer_messages_claimed, producer_messages_released, producer_message_consumed state run A producer message's delivery message_injected state run A message agent_before_start injected user_input_admitted state run or runless A steer waiting for the next turn user_input_submitted state run Input that became model history user_input_transformed audit run A user_before_input rewrite of direct input user_input_recalled state run or runless A withdrawn admission user_input_applied state run Where an admitted input took effect user_input_queued, user_input_queue_recalled, user_input_queue_voided state runless The queued-input lane session_model_selected state runless The session's model selection delegated_context_seeded state runless A child's inherited context run_started, run_finished state run A run's start and end model_attempt_started, attempt_abandoned, model_fallback state run A model attempt's lifecycle model_request_prepared, model_tools_published, model_output_started, model_replay_evaluated audit run Request and streaming bookkeeping tool_round_started, deferred_tools_announced audit run Deferred tools: a tool round's eager tools, and what the model was told it can load prompt_blocks_recorded, prompt_blocks_announced audit run Prompt blocks: where a run's prompt carries its blocks, and what changed since model_turn_committed, model_usage_recorded state run A committed turn and its usage native_replay_cut state run Reasoning at or before through_seq is no longer replayed, after a thinking-binding mismatch automatic_runs_held, automatic_runs_resumed state runless A held session: its automatic runs stopped, and the resume that cleared it tool_call_started, tool_call_terminated, tool_output_elided, tool_call_linked state run A tool call's lifecycle delegation_reserved, delegation_progressed, delegation_finished state run A delegation on the parent delegate_child_terminated state runless A delegation ended the child before it ran approval_requested, approval_finalized, tree_approval_grant_committed state run An approval approval_step state; audit for doom_loop run An approval step internal_agent_started, internal_agent_usage_recorded, internal_agent_finished, internal_agent_fallback state run An internal agent invocation context_checkpoint_committed state run A compaction checkpoint text_delta, reasoning_delta, internal_agent_text_delta, native_compaction_started, native_compaction_finished, tool_call_progress live-only run Stream output

docs.title: Live-only stream output
docs.text:
text_delta, reasoning_delta, internal_agent_text_delta, native_compaction_started, native_compaction_finished, and tool_call_progress are live-only. The engine delivers them to event subscribers and plugins as they stream but never appends them to events.jsonl or to a session's in-memory log, and a stored record carrying one fails validation. Their durable record is the committed turn (model_turn_committed), the tool termination (tool_call_terminated, with its retained output), and the internal agent's terminal event. A replay or a reload therefore sees finished turns only.

A view that attaches while output streams does not start from a fragment: the daemon keeps each session's output still in flight in memory, and a tail registered by a subscription without a cursor (one that replayed the whole log) first receives it as live-only messages positioned after the durable tip it replayed to. A subscription that resumes from a cursor does not, since its reader may already hold part of that output; its later deltas continue it. Each open attempt's text and reasoning arrive as one text_delta or reasoning_delta per uninterrupted run of a kind, in order; each running tool as one tool_call_progress carrying its latest message and its live display so far as one replace delta (within the 64 KiB budget); a running provider-native compaction as its native_compaction_started; and a streaming compaction summary as one internal_agent_text_delta. Later deltas append as usual, and the durable record replaces it all as before. Output a daemon restart cut off is not kept.

internal_agent_text_delta (invocation_id, text) streams the compaction agent's summary text. Other internal agents do not stream. native_compaction_started and native_compaction_finished (resolved_model) bracket a provider-native compaction call, whether or not it succeeds; a committed context_checkpoint_committed is the durable record of a success.

model_output_started (attempt_id, kind: text or reasoning) is the durable trace of streaming. The engine appends it before the first delta of each streamed part: an attempt's first output and every switch between text and reasoning. Views use it to keep an attempt that is already streaming ahead of inputs admitted meanwhile, and to time thinking identically live and on replay (each reasoning part runs from its mark to the next mark or the commit).

A stored record of a live-only payload fails validation, so the reader skips it with a diagnostic like any other invalid record.

docs.title: Goal and producer contracts
docs.text:
Goal and producer state is projected independently from model summaries. The engine serializes mutations, message acceptance, and admission through the session actor. Goal activation and producer acceptance persist an otherwise buffered session, even before its first model request.

Event Payload fields Run scope goal_activated goal_id, objective, revision Runless allowed goal_checklist_revised goal_id, items, revision Runless allowed goal_lifecycle_changed goal_id, status, revision Runless allowed producer_message_accepted message_id, producer_owner, mode, idempotency_key, description, body (user content, text parts only); optional reminder, retained_output Runless allowed, including during an active run producer_message_admitted message_id Requires the destination run producer_messages_claimed Nonempty message_ids Requires the admission run; envelope seq identifies the claim producer_messages_released Positive claim_seq Requires the claimed run producer_message_consumed message_id, run_id Requires matching envelope run_id producer_message_discarded message_id; optional producer_owner, optional reminder Runless allowed

GoalId and ProducerMessageId are durable UUID identities. GoalItem contains only description and finished, with no item ID. Writer validation rejects blank objectives/descriptions. Revision is an engine-owned u64, including zero; strictly increasing revisions, overflow rejection, matching goal identity, and lifecycle transitions are enforced by the engine projection. Model updates replace the entire ordered checklist through the session actor: the last accepted update wins for the current/latest session goal at actor acceptance, without a model-supplied goal_id, expected_revision, or lost-update protection. An older run's update can intentionally affect a newly activated active or paused goal; updates reject if the current goal is absent or terminal. The engine records the selected goal's ID and revision in durable events. User lifecycle RPC controls retain SessionGoalLifecycleParams.goal_id and expected_revision, including stale-identity and stale-revision rejection. Empty checklist revisions preserve the active/paused lifecycle. Completion requires nonempty all-finished items, including while paused.

The session projection folds the goal events too: while the goal is active, SessionMeta.waiting_on lists goal (client protocol 1.9.0), so a rebuilt metadata cache keeps it. An event the goal projection rejects changes nothing there either.

A stored checklist item carrying an id does not decode.

ProducerOwner is tagged by type: external { source, name } (a plugin's or a runtime's named producer), delegation { invocation_id }, goal { goal_id }, goal_control { goal_id }, agent { session_id }, tool { tool_call_id }, or subagent { session_id } (a child's <subagent_report>, keyed by its run ID), or acp_agent { agent } (the session's ACP agent starting work on its own, a message recorded to start the run that shows it and never sent to the agent; client protocol 1.38.0). It identifies a specific stable owner, not a volatile registration or merely an owner kind. Accepted events are the sole authoritative message body/mode storage, including deferred queue sends while a run is active. Registration records are never session events. GoalControl { goal_id } owns engine-authored pause/cancel steering, not goal continuation reminders. These accepted messages survive goal-controller teardown and reminder invalidation. Accepted agent-owned messages carry agent_hop metadata for the messaging loop guard. It is present exactly on agent-owned messages, is not rendered in the agent-visible envelope, and does not participate in idempotency comparison. Tool { tool_call_id } owns the single <background_result> of that tool call once it ran in the background. Its accepted message carries the call's captured output as retained_output, the same shape a tool result uses, and the body previews it the way a tool result does. Recording the reference on the event is what keeps those artifacts alive; plugins cannot supply retained_output.

The optional accepted-event reminder: GoalReminderIdentity { goal_id, revision, kind } identifies a goal reminder; if present, its goal must match the goal owner. kind is the required started or continuation. Its body must contain the full objective and checklist, including finished items and revision. Each continuation attempt has a fresh message ID/idempotency key even at an unchanged revision. A consumed reminder cannot suppress later continuation. New goals use started until a same-goal reminder is covered by committed model input; acceptance, claims, discarded startup messages, and lifecycle-control notifications alone do not switch subsequent reminders to continuation.

Producer descriptions are compact, human-facing text; the full body remains model-facing. An absent description is empty, and clients then fall back to a truncated body.

producer_message_admitted links the accepted body to a run without duplicating user-input storage or changing existing input events. Its physical sequence is covered by model_turn_committed.input_through_seq. Admission is not consumption: append producer_message_consumed only after a committed turn covers the admission in that same run. Recovery repairs missing consumption markers from committed coverage; an uncommitted API attempt remains retryable. Queue acceptance does not create a forbidden runless pending user input during an active run.

producer_messages_claimed durably reserves admitted messages at the actor boundary before request preparation/dispatch. The claim's envelope sequence is its token, not evidence that the provider received input. Projection requires unique accepted, admitted, unconsumed, undiscarded message IDs belonging to the claim's run. Claims cover compaction, hooks, streaming, and model commit. producer_messages_released references the claim sequence in the same run and removes that claim. Failed or cancelled attempts release their reservation; recovery also releases surviving claims. Once all claims are released, an unconsumed, undiscarded message returns to waiting and the queue strip. Consumed messages remain consumed after release. Claim/release is not consumption and does not establish exactly-once model execution.

Discard is separate from consumption and is a generic durable producer-message event, not restricted to goal reminders. discard(session, message_id) checks the caller's ownership against the accepted message, including after its producer unregisters. Owned already-discarded retries are idempotent; cross-owner discard is rejected. Only unclaimed waiting messages qualify, including admitted messages not yet claimed. Consumed or claimed messages reject discard, even before actual provider dispatch; absence of a consumption marker is not proof that a message is retractable. The actor serializes discard against claim acquisition. Durable discard removes the message from pending delivery/readiness and the queue strip, and replay must not restore it as pending. Goal reminder invalidation still checks its identity; it does not authorize discarding another owner's real message.

Projection requires the discard's producer_owner to exactly match the accepted owner; a supplied reminder must also match. A discard of a consumed or claimed message is rejected. Claimed messages are hidden from the waiting strip until release makes them eligible again; in-flight input cannot be retracted.

Missing/corrupt optional reminder metadata follows the existing best-effort reader, with degradation diagnostics. Engine projection must quarantine invalid goal-owned reminder records rather than reclassifying them as real sends. Cross-event ownership, at-most-once consumption, and commit coverage are engine invariants, not properties a single-event decoder can verify.

Goal state and unconsumed messages must survive compaction. Fork copies durable branch data, never registrations; revert reconciles only the visible branch. Failed/disabled recovery notices are runless diagnostic events whose source is the producer source and whose kind is recovery_failed or recovery_disabled, not persisted readiness/registration records.

docs.title: Event details
docs.text:
model_replay_evaluated records, for one model attempt, the replay decision for each history entry of its request. Every attempt re-evaluates the whole history, so a long run would otherwise write a list that grows with every turn. When base_attempt_id is present, the event names an earlier attempt of the same run, with the same resolved_model, whose full list is an exact prefix of this attempt's list; ordered_decisions then holds only the decisions after that prefix. The full list is the base's full list followed by ordered_decisions. Without base_attempt_id, ordered_decisions is the full list, which is what a run's first evaluation writes, as does any attempt whose model changed or whose earlier decisions changed (compaction, a pinned turn, a late tool result). Readers that ignore the field see only new decisions for such an attempt.

agent_md_loaded is a run-scoped root-session event stamped engine:agent-md. It contains one or two AGENTS.md entries a coding runtime discovered in its workspace, each with a bounded display source, retained content, truncation flag, and original byte size, and the attachment naming that runtime's attachment. A run writes one event per attachment that returned a file. A session in a project with an AGENTS.md gets one more, written first, whose optional project ({ id, name }, since client protocol 1.8.0) names the project; its attachment is global, where the file lives, and its entry's source is project:<name>/AGENTS.md. Missing or disabled context produces no event. History uses only the latest run's events, the latest per attachment and the project's, and replays their entries as one provenance-delimited user turn, the project's first. Compaction pins that turn alongside loaded skill bodies. See System Prompt Composition.

docs.title: Memory snapshots
docs.text:
memory_loaded is a run-scoped event stamped engine:memory, appended at a run's admission (root or delegated, each in its own session's log) when the run's memory changed: the memory spec lists when. Its members, each left out when empty or false:

Member Meaning delegated The snapshot was taken for a delegated run and holds only agent writable The run could see the memory write tools user [{ category, description, keywords?, body }]: user categories, whole, in name order user_omitted Names of the categories that did not fit user_listed [{ url, description, keywords? }]: categories the run's memory rules ask before reading, listed only (since client protocol 1.12.0) agent { agent, memory?: { description, keywords?, body }, omitted?, listed?: { url, description, keywords? } }: the run's agent and its file; omitted when the file did not fit; listed (since 1.12.0) when the rules ask before reading it machines [{ machine, attachments?, memories?: [{ url, description, keywords? }], omitted? }]: the session's machines, each with an index of its memories, newest first, and how many more it has project { project, overview?: { description, keywords?, body }, memories?: [{ url, description, keywords? }], omitted? }: the session's project (since client protocol 1.8.0), root runs only: its name, its overview whole when it has a body and fits, and an index of its other memories, newest first, and how many more it has rules A fingerprint of the run's memory rules reaching global (since 1.12.0); a run whose rules differ takes a new snapshot

Each memory is in the event only as far as the run's memory rules allow for its URL: whole when they allow it, listed when they ask, and left out, uncounted, when they deny or do not match. An event without agent is empty: memory is no longer available, and the model sees no memory turn from then on. One with agent but no memory to show renders no turn either. History renders only the latest memory_loaded of the log, as one user turn right after the AGENTS.md turn, and compaction pins it like that turn; the text depends on the event alone, so a replay shows exactly what the model saw. The stored event is at most 128 KiB of JSON; its rendered text stays within 64 KiB. See System Prompt Composition.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text: session_project_set { project? } is a runless state event a root session records when it moves into project, or out of any project when project is absent, and with its creation when it is created in one (client protocol 1.8.0). SessionMeta.project is its fold, so a rebuilt metadata cache keeps it; a log without one reads as being in no project. Delegated sessions never record it: they belong to their root's project. See Projects.

docs.title: Delegated attachments
docs.text:
delegated_attachments_added { child_session_id, attachments } is a runless state event a root session records when a subagent of its tree is created with attachments the root records neither as its own nor as delegated before, global aside (client protocol 1.10.0). attachments are the new ones, as the child named them, at least one. SessionMeta.delegated_attachments is its fold, which keeps one entry per runtime, capability, and workspace and only grows, so a rebuilt metadata cache keeps it; a log without one reads as having none. A child that only inherits records nothing new. A fork leaves it behind with its source's subagents, as record_omitted. See Where a root's subagents work.

diagnostic { source, kind, message, count?, detail? } is a notice about the engine, a plugin, or a runtime: something it turned off, could not do, or dropped. source is engine:<area>, plugin:<name>, or runtime:<id>; kind is a snake-case label (at most 64 bytes) that readers show whatever it is; message is the nonempty text to show; count (at least 2 when present) says how many occurrences the record coalesces; and detail is display-only JSON of at most 16 KiB. Nothing but a view reads it. A diagnostic about a run belongs to that run; any other is runless. The kinds written today:

Source Kind Meaning plugin:<name> interception_timeout, interception_crash (the plugin was not connected or exited during the hook), interception_rejected (it answered with an error or a malformed result), hook_blocked, invalid_modification, oversized_event, event_drop, context_mismatch, rate_limited A plugin's operational notice, coalesced by count plugin:<name>, runtime:<id> recovery_failed, recovery_disabled A producer source cannot restore the external work it tracks; goal continuation is held engine:auto-compact auto_compaction_disabled Automatic context compaction failed three times in a row and stays off for the rest of the run engine:agent-md agent_md_too_large An AGENTS.md file is over the size limit and contributes no context; run-scoped, with detail { path, byte_length, attachment }

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
delegated_context_seeded is a runless creation event containing the bounded, text-only user/assistant turns copied by inherit_context; it must precede the child's first run and deterministically rebuilds the same initial model history after restart.

The delegation_* records are durable control events on the parent session, in the parent run. delegation_reserved contains the complete current delegate request, the child agent snapshot (whose selected suffix is the child's models), one cache strategy per entry of that suffix, its runtime revisions when they changed (see Runs and internal agents), the request fingerprint, and optional typed staged-skill provenance. The child records its attachments, the root session's, with runtime_attached events at creation. delegation_progressed { invocation_id, stage } records how far the delegation got; stage is started { child_session_id } (the child session was published), run_started { child_run_id } or run_attached { child_run_id } (a new child run, or attachment to an already-running resumed child), or queued { position? } (the child waits for a background slot). A stage this build does not know changes nothing.

delegation_finished { invocation_id, child_session_id, child_run_id?, status, reason?, short_id?, preview, total_lines } records the terminal status, the optional recovery reason, and the child references, together with the teaser transcripts render: short_id is the child's handle and preview the report as [subagent_output] previews it, whole or its first and last lines around an omission marker (at most 64 KiB; empty when no child run started). One record per invocation lets repeated resumes of one child each finish once. It is not model history: a foreground delegation's result reaches the parent's model as its tool result, and a background one's as the steer producer message the engine durably accepts for it (see Goal and producer contracts), so the result is in history exactly once. Full output remains available through get_subagent_result.

delegate_child_terminated is written runless to the child session when a delegation ends it before it ran (cancelled or failed); it sets the child's own status.

A fork does not take its source's subagents: they stay the source's. The fork keeps the conversation as it was (the delegate calls and their results, tool_call_linked, and the producer messages that brought the children's reports, which read as any other message), but none of the delegation_* records. Each is replaced, at its sequence and with its run, time, and origin, by record_omitted { omitted_type } naming its type, so the sequence stays contiguous. The fork has no children until it delegates itself, and get_subagent_result refuses the source's children. Runtime revisions that only a dropped delegation_reserved recorded go with it.

Engine startup projects delegation state while opening session logs. A reserved or started delegation without a terminal event resumes or rolls back according to its child and parent state. Recovery trusts the stored request fingerprint and never computes it again; it is compared only when the same invocation is reserved again. If best-effort reading skips a corrupt delegation event, that delegation is not recovered, the parent session records the diagnostic, and unrelated delegations remain recoverable.

docs.title: Runs and internal agents
docs.text:
run_started freezes the run's agent snapshot. The snapshot's fallback_chain lists the agent's models in fallback order, and selected_suffix_start is where the run starts in it: the run's model is that entry (its exact selection, variant included, equals the run selection's), and its fallbacks are the entries after it. session_created and delegation_reserved carry snapshots of the same shape, and the snapshot has no schema version.

session_created records the seven revisions of the runtime the session was created against as revisions (runtime_revision, catalog_revision, provider_state_revision, model_revision, agent_revision, recipe_registry_revision, and manifest_revision). run_started and delegation_reserved carry revisions only when the run or the delegated child was frozen against different ones than the latest the log recorded before it; without the field, an event was frozen against those latest revisions. Readers fold them in log order.

Each chain entry, like a model fallback of a frozen internal agent, is a stored model binding { selection, provider_id, provider_model_id, adapter, resolved, selection_fingerprint, blueprint_fingerprint, frozen }. adapter is the protocol adapter the binding speaks (such as oven.openai.responses), and resolved is the model reference the run's attempts record: model_attempt_started and model_fallback must name the resolved of the entry at their fallback index, counted from selected_suffix_start. frozen holds the complete binding (descriptor, request defaults, provider options, credential and setup bindings, static headers) as an opaque value. Loading a log never decodes it. The engine decodes it only to run the binding again: manual compaction, title generation, and the history view of the latest run, and the model fallbacks of that run's internal agents. When this build cannot read it, that operation fails with unreadable_model_binding; the session still opens, and a new run resolves its models afresh as always.

run_finished { outcome } ends a run. outcome is completed { final_text? }, failed { error, model_error?, resolved_model? }, cancelled { reason? }, or interrupted { reason? }; an outcome this build does not know reads as interrupted. internal_agent_finished { invocation_id, internal_run_id, kind, outcome } ends an internal agent invocation the same way, with completed { result }, failed { failure }, cancelled { reason? }, or interrupted { reason? }. run_started.internal_agents freezes the run's internal agent definitions, one per kind, and an internal_agent_usage_recorded of the run names the agent frozen for its kind.
