docs.title: Approvals
docs.text:
approval_requested stores the request's tool_call_id, the call it gates, whose tool_call_started carries the call's presentation, and its operation_fingerprint, which the writer computes from the prepared operation and readers trust as written. An approval's lifecycle after its approval_requested is a series of approval_step { approval_id, step } records and one approval_finalized { approval_id, outcome }. step is evaluated { decision } (the internal decision pipeline decided; a decision of the approval reviewer carries its one-sentence rationale when it gave one, and a failed review the reason internal_agent_failed), escalated { reason_code, expires_at? } (it waits for the user until expires_at, the window opening at this step; an earlier writer's request carries the window instead), user_decision { client_response_id, decision, feedback? } (a client answered; feedback only with reject), or doom_loop { operation_fingerprint, repetitions } (the same operation was requested at least four times in a row); a step this build does not know changes nothing. outcome is decided { decision }, the final decision of policy, a grant, the reviewer, or the user, or cancelled { reason_code }, the engine withdrawing the approval (request_cancelled, approval_expired, operation_changed, or prepared_capability_lost), which reads as a system decision that expired or cancelled the request. An outcome this build does not know reads as cancelled, so the operation is not approved.

The approval reviewer's conversation is rendered from these records and the session's messages and tool calls, never stored separately (The approval reviewer).

permission_mode_set { mode } is a runless state event of a root session: its tree's permission mode changed to mode. Loading the tree restores the newest one; a session without one is in auto_approve.

docs.title: Runtime attachments
docs.text: The runless runtime_attached and runtime_detached events record the session's runtime attachments. runtime_attached carries the session-unique attachment name, the runtime_id, the capability attached, the kind label the capability declared (such as global or coding), and, when the instance has one, the canonical workspace it reported. runtime_detached carries the name it removes. The attachment set is the fold of these events in log order; a session's creation writes one runtime_attached per initial attachment together with session_created, so both reach disk with the session's first persistence. A session created with no attachment records no attachment event. Delegated children record their own attachments.

docs.title: Other events
docs.text:
record_omitted { omitted_type } stands in for a record its writer deliberately did not carry over, at that record's sequence, run (if any), time, and origin; omitted_type is the left-out record's type. Its run, when it has one, is a run the log started. Nothing reads it but a view; today only a fork writes it, for its source's delegation records.

The runless session_permission_overlay_set event's overlay contains the complete, validated set of unique (action, resource) rules for the session. The latest visible event wins. Because it is an ordinary branch event, restart replay, revert, and fork recover the same overlay without a sidecar file.

model_usage_recorded follows a committed provider turn and contains the positive model_turn_seq, agent ID, resolved model identity, and Oven's normalized usage fields: inclusive input/output totals plus optional uncached input, cache-read input, cache-write input, text output, and reasoning output counts. A reported reasoning count of zero on a turn that streamed reasoning text is recorded as unknown, together with the text output count derived from it. The required estimated_cost_pico_usd stamps the engine-selected price for that request: a number is priced, and null is unpriced. internal_agent_usage_recorded stamps its price the same way. Usage rollups preserve stamped prices exactly and never price a record again. Event-log validation requires its run, agent, model, and turn to match and rejects duplicate records for one turn. Session, agent, and global usage projections rebuild from these events after restart, revert, and fork.

model_request_prepared follows request assembly and all accepted model/provider request hooks. Its prompt_fingerprint hashes the authoritative normalized request sent to the provider, while model_attempt_started remains the earlier cancellation and lifecycle boundary.

model_tools_published comes just before model_request_prepared for the same attempt and lists the tool_names sent with the request, after request hooks. It is recorded only when the names differ from the session's latest visible record, so an unchanged tool set adds nothing to later attempts. Validation allows at most 1,024 names, each nonempty, at most 256 bytes, and free of control characters; a request whose names do not fit is still sent, without a record. deferred_tool_names (since 1.48.0, absent when empty) lists the ones of tool_names the request sent deferred and not yet loaded, each also in tool_names; the record is skipped only when both lists match. The TUI and the web client show the latest record as a collapsible tools block under the system prompt, split into provided and searchable tools when the request deferred any.

docs.title: Deferred tools
docs.text:
Two records come before a request, after its run's input (deferred tools in cookie, and the stable prompt prefix for models that do not defer):

  • tool_round_started lists the eager tools the session declares until its next compaction, each as name, description, parameters (its JSON Schema), and optional provider_options, exactly as a request sends it. A runtime's tool also has source (label, its attachment or the label its provider composes under, and tool, its own name): until the next compaction it keeps its published name, and a tool that arrives with the same name takes its <label>_<tool> form instead. prompt_groups names the tool groups whose prompt sections the system prompt carries. A later record before the next checkpoint replaces the round, when the loader tools join it. Every session records rounds, on any model: a round tool that leaves the session stays declared until the next compaction, and a call to it is refused. On a model that does not defer, a tool that joins mid-round is sent up front at once.
  • deferred_tools_announced, on a model that loads deferred tools, carries added and removed, lists of groups: name, source (mcp, plugin, or builtin, an open set), tools, and an optional summary, with untrusted when the summary is the source's author's text. Model history renders it in place as a user turn.

A checkpoint starts the round, the announcements, and the loads over. The first request after it records a new round, which declares the tools the checkpoint folded (folded_tools), and announces every tool still deferred afresh. In the messages the checkpoint keeps raw, announcements, loader calls (tool_search, and tool_load in older history), and calls to tools the new round does not declare are left out with their results.

Both are audit events: an engine that does not know them defers nothing. At most 1,024 tools a record, and 2 MiB for a round's tools. A tool result's loaded_tools names the deferred tools it loaded (only the loader sets it); its output reaches the model as text where the model cannot load natively.

tool_call_started records the call's presentation: its title, an optional hint label (for icons and grouping), an optional primary_argument, arguments and preview display blocks (absent when empty; clients then show the raw model arguments), and tool, which the daemon fills: name (the name the tool's source knows it by), published_name (the name the model called), and source, tagged by type: base, runtime { runtime_id, attachment, capability }, plugin { plugin }, or mcp { server, runtime_id? }. source is absent for a call that names no tool the session offers. Today's runtimes report only the title and display argument. It also records the single/named output declaration, including arbitrary named streams, and background: true when the call's tool supports the background, so a client may offer to move the running call there (run.tool_background); the field is absent otherwise. tool_call_progress is live-only. It contains a control-free status message and an optional UI-only display delta, tagged by type:

  • append { index, text, stream? } appends text to block index of the live display, a text block, or a terminal block when the append names a stream (stdout or stderr), which extends that block's last segment of the stream or starts one. An append to the index just past the list creates the block. Today's tools send append to block 0.
  • replace { blocks } replaces the live display.

The terminal result.display replaces the live display. A live message and an append's text are each bounded at 1 KiB. A call's deltas share a cumulative 64 KiB budget (an append costs its text, a replacement its serialized size), and its messages another. TUI state is bounded and never reconstructs display by merging authoritative streams.

A result's display is a list of display blocks (see the compatibility spec), sanitized by the daemon and fit to 64 KiB serialized; blocks of a kind the daemon does not know are dropped. An empty list shows nothing.

events.jsonl stores display text that repeats the result's output as [start, end) byte ranges of output instead of a second copy, and the daemon expands them when it reads the log, so clients and plugins always receive whole blocks:

  • a display that is a single whole text block found in output (a single-output tool's whole output) is stored as the result's display_span in place of display;
  • otherwise a text, markdown, or code block's text, and a terminal segment's text (a shell's streams), may be stored as text_span, and a file_excerpt's lines as lines_span: a range of output holding the lines one per line, each after its file line number and :, as read numbers them.

The writer uses a range only when expanding it gives back the same text, and never inside a block of a kind it does not know.

The result a call commits when it moves to the background carries background { state, by, job? }: state is job (the call runs as background job job) or self_reporting (the work, such as a subagent, reports itself); an unknown state still means the call is backgrounded. by is model or user. Only the daemon sets it; it drops one a tool returns.

Authoritative output chunks go to runtime capture before completion, not into unbounded event records. Terminal retained_output contains ordered per-stream byte/line counts, truncation offsets, and an incomplete flag. Only a stream that outgrew its preview has an artifact (reference and sha256); a stream the result output holds whole has neither, and retained_output.reference (the single stream's artifact or the generic manifest) is absent when no stream needed one. Failed/cancelled calls retain accepted output with their terminal status and error. Self-paginating tools omit output retention and fail instead when a requested page exceeds the 2 MiB result bound. tool_output_elided records which retained output compaction elided.

During cancellation cleanup, a progress record is considered retained once its append command enters the session actor mailbox; actor FIFO then orders it before the later terminal command even if persistence has not completed yet. Cleanup deadline diagnostics count only display progress records that never entered that mailbox; authoritative chunks already accepted into capture remain retained.

For a batch of tool calls from one model turn, tool_call_started events are written in model content order before execution begins. Calls may then execute in parallel, so progress and tool_call_terminated events from different calls may interleave, and terminations commit in completion order. The ordering guarantee is per call: its start precedes all of its progress events, which precede its single termination. Consumers must correlate calls by tool_call_id rather than cross-call event position. A failed termination carries one of the tool failure codes.

internal_agent_usage_recorded attributes each completed internal model request to its internal run, internal agent ID, kind, and resolved model. It carries the same optional estimated_cost_pico_usd stamp. The same session, agent, and global projections include these records.

skill_loaded and skill_invocation_noted persist skill use. skill_loaded stores the rendered body, skill name, source path, arguments, base directory, and at most ten supporting-file paths. It is pinned across context checkpoints. An identical repeat uses the shorter skill_invocation_noted payload.

user_input_admitted normally belongs to an active run. A steer accepted for a queued delegated child is runless and requires that the session have no active run. It is persisted immediately and enters the next run's pending-input FIFO, including when a terminal child is queued for resume. A queued cancellation appends a runless user_input_recalled naming each such admission so those inputs cannot leak into a later resume. Promotion appends the ordinary run-owned user_input_submitted event, so transcript rendering and model history use the same path as interactive run steering.

Every input-lane event stores its input as content: UserContent, a nonempty list of parts tagged by type: text { text } or file { artifact: { sha256, byte_length, media_type, filename? } }. That covers user_input_admitted, user_input_submitted, user_input_recalled, and user_input_queued. Model history sends text parts as they are and file parts as files read from the session tree's artifact store, the way tool-emitted user messages carry theirs; a missing or damaged artifact becomes a short note. A part of a kind this build does not know is kept and never sent to a model. The content is what the client submitted (run.start, run.steer, session.submit_input), after any user_before_input transform. A writer rejects a file part whose artifact reference is malformed. The artifact a file part names stays in the tree's store for as long as an event references it, like a tool attachment: revert sweeps and fork linking count it.

message_injected is a run-owned role and content message accepted from agent_before_start. It is written during run setup and projected into model history, so reopen, fork, revert, and compaction use the injected message without consulting the plugin again. Its content, like a producer_message_accepted body, has text parts only. user_input_transformed is the run-owned audit record written immediately before user_input_submitted when user_before_input changes direct input; it contains both original_content and the non-blank committed content.

Running-resume rollback and session.recall_input append user_input_recalled with the exact user_input_seq of its admission (in the same run, or runless for a runless admission). Replay removes that specific pending input and preserves the others.

session_model_selected (selection) is the session-level model pick a client made with session.select_model; it is runless and its origin names the client. Later runs that name no selection of their own use it.

docs.title: Prompt blocks
docs.text:
Frozen blocks:

  • prompt_blocks_recorded comes before a run's first request, unless the run is an ACP agent's or a plugin replaced its prompt. blocks lists key (runtimes, tool_instructions, or skills), start, and len, in bytes of the run's composed_prompt; composed_live says whether the run composed them rather than copying the previous run's.
  • prompt_blocks_announced carries blocks, each a key and its new text, or no text when the block no longer applies. Model history renders it in place as a user turn; a checkpoint leaves earlier ones out of the messages it keeps, and the next request announces afresh.

Both are audit events: an engine that does not know them composes every prompt afresh.

docs.title: The queued-input lane
docs.text: The queued-input lane is session-level, so its events are runless. user_input_queued holds an input waiting for the running run to complete, with the selection and client_run_id of the run it will start; its origin is the client that queued it. The entry leaves the queue when a run_started carries its client_run_id, when user_input_queue_recalled names its queued_seq, or when every entry is voided by a run_finished that did not complete, or by user_input_queue_voided (written when a queued input cannot start). A voided entry goes back to the client that queued it.

docs.title: Compaction checkpoints
docs.text:
context_checkpoint_committed carries a commit containing the text summary or opaque native checkpoint, boundaries, and budgets. Internal summaries cover the active pre-compaction history before the recent messages retained unchanged after the summary; the two do not overlap. Active history is the currently assembled context, not a reload of events replaced by earlier checkpoints. The original saved log is preserved; retained recent messages are replayed from it. System and tool context comes first, followed by pinned AGENTS.md, the latest memory snapshot, loaded skills, the summary, and the recent messages. See Compaction for selection and fit rules.

The retention fields:

Field within commit Type Meaning boundaries.recent_from_seq u64 or null Inclusive starting sequence of the retained original-message suffix. null means no retained suffix. budgets.keep_recent_tokens u64 Effective recent-history token budget for this checkpoint, not the raw configured request or a count of retained tokens. checkpoint.native object, optional On an internal_summary checkpoint, the provider window compacted from the same events (window) and the last event it covers (source_through_seq). Absent when native compaction was not attempted or failed. checkpoint.folded_tools string array, optional On an internal_summary checkpoint, the deferred tools loaded before it, and the previous checkpoint's: the next tool round declares them up front. Absent when empty; at most 1,024 names.

The effective budget is at most min(configured keep_recent_tokens, input_budget / 4) and is further limited by actual post-checkpoint available space. Complete tool-call/result groups can leave the retained suffix smaller than that budget; an oversized newest indivisible group yields no tail rather than exceeding the budget. A reader never infers a suffix from current configuration.

A request on the window's provider and model uses the window, with no independently appended recent-message suffix; every other request uses the summary and its recent messages. The native_window checkpoint, a window without a summary, is read but no longer written. Neither checkpoint path rereads files.

docs.title: Subscriptions
docs.text:
events.subscribe returns retained events after the optional cursor and starts events.subscription notifications. With limit, it returns at most that many events; when more remain it sets has_more: true and starts no notifications, and the client asks again with the last returned seq as the cursor. Only the final page (no has_more) subscribes, atomically with its snapshot, so events appended between pages arrive in a later page and none are missed. Without limit the first response is the final page. Paging a session this process does not own parses its log once and serves later pages from memory while the file is unchanged.

events.unsubscribe ends the connection's live tail for a session: no further events.subscription or events.plugin notification for it is sent, and the shared client drops messages already in flight and stops recovering it until it subscribes again. A session no connection has a tail on can be evicted from the daemon's memory, so a long-lived client releases sessions it no longer shows. The TUI keeps the sessions of its eight most recently viewed trees subscribed, so switching back is instant, and releases the others once they have no run and no pending or queued input; it keeps their last state and catches up from it when one is reopened.

A connection holds at most one live tail per session. Subscribing a session the connection already follows (reopening it, or a recovery replay) replaces its tail in the same step as the new snapshot: notifications the old tail had already queued are written first, then the new tail's, and nothing reaches both. Durable events carry a seq a client can drop a copy by, but transient output does not, so two tails would show every streamed delta twice.

A notification is tagged as a stored event:

{ "type": "event", "event": { "engine_version": "0.1.0", "seq": 43 } }

live-only stream output, which has no sequence of its own:

{
  "type": "transient",
  "event": {
    "session_id": "...",
    "run_id": "...",
    "after_seq": 43,
    "timestamp": "...",
    "payload": { "type": "text_delta", "attempt_id": "...", "text": "..." }
  }
}

or a gap indicating that the subscriber must rebuild its disposable projection:

{
  "type": "gap",
  "session_id": "...",
  "last_delivered_seq": 42
}

Stored sequences stay gap-free across a streamed turn, so replay cursors only ever point at durable events. A transient event belongs right after the durable event after_seq: it never advances the cursor, is never stored, and is never a reason to recover. A subscriber that starts from the beginning (no cursor, or 0) first receives the output streaming at that moment, coalesced into transient messages after the durable tip; one resuming from a cursor does not, since it may already hold part of it. The shared client delivers one only when its after_seq equals the subscription cursor, including output buffered while a replay is in flight; anything else is stale or outruns a durable event the view has not seen, and is dropped. The engine drops transient output for a subscriber whose queue is nearly full rather than spending the slot reserved for a gap.

A revert cuts the log and the next appends reuse the removed sequence numbers, so live subscribers receive a rewind:

{ "type": "rewound", "session_id": "...", "through_seq": 41 }

A subscriber drops everything it holds past through_seq; later events follow on from it. The shared client also replays the session in full. A reader that was not subscribed when the cut happened cannot tell a reused sequence from the event it replaced, so a replay request may carry cursor_timestamp, the timestamp of the event at cursor as the reader saw it. When the session's event at cursor has a different timestamp (or no longer exists), the response is { "events": [], "stale_cursor": true }, no tail is registered, and the reader must replay from the start. The shared client sends it on every recovery replay.

Tool stdout and stderr use separate snapshot, delta, and gap notifications. Offsets are byte offsets, and clients use a snapshot after a gap before applying later deltas. The ordinary event subscription also includes live-only tool_call_progress output chunks and the durable terminal events without a separate filter.

docs.title: Client Protocol Changelog
docs.text: The client protocol's version is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (cookie_agent_protocol::CLIENT_PROTOCOL_VERSION). From 1.0.0 a minor only adds and a major breaks; before it, every minor could break the wire (see the compatibility spec section 3).

• Two audit events (stable prompt prefix section 6): prompt_blocks_recorded (blocks, each a key, start, and len in bytes of the run's composed_prompt, and composed_live) before a run's first request, and prompt_blocks_announced (blocks, each a key and an optional text), the instructions that changed since the system prompt carried them, rendered in place as a user turn (model_text::prompt_blocks_announcement). Plugin protocol 1.30.0 carries them in events the same way.

• A tool_round_started tool has an optional source (label, tool): the attachment, or the label its provider composes under, and the tool's own name, for a runtime's tool. A round's tools keep their published names until it ends (stable prompt prefix section 5). Plugin protocol 1.29.0 carries it in events the same way.

• acp_session_updated has an optional prompt_context: the text blocks an ACP session's first prompt carried ahead of the input, as sent, so clients show what the agent reads beyond the conversation. Plugin protocol 1.28.0 carries it in events the same way.

• SessionMeta has an optional unread (left out when false): a root session with a finished turn, an approval, or a question the user has not seen (unread sessions). The daemon marks it when a settle or a needs-you push signal comes while nobody is present on the tree, and client.presence on the tree marks it read; sessions.changed upserted announces each change.
  • session.unread.set (session_ids, unread) marks root sessions unread or read, answering the changed ones and the skipped ones with a reason (session_not_found, not_a_root_session with its root_session_id).

• acp_session_updated has an optional background_ended (AcpBackgroundEnded: tool_call_id, tool, display, started_at, exit_code, signal): a command of an ACP agent's that ran in the background ended. Clients show it as a background call's report, so a wake the end causes no longer arrives unexplained (ACP v2 section 9).

• Providers can be connected by a browser sign-in instead of typed credentials (Sign in with ChatGPT). ProviderDescriptor has an optional sign_in_methods (SignInMethodDescriptor: id, display_name, redirect_path) and sign_in_account (SignInAccountDescriptor: email, sign_in_required). A sign-in method is never listed in auth_methods.
  • provider.auth.begin (provider_id, method, redirect_uri, null for the daemon to catch the redirect itself), provider.auth.complete (provider_id, callback_url), and provider.auth.cancel run it; the daemon holds the PKCE verifier and the tokens. provider.auth.completed announces a sign-in whose redirect the daemon caught.
  • provider.connect refuses a sign-in method with provider_sign_in_rejected, the error of every failed provider.auth.* request.

• model_tools_published has an optional deferred_tool_names: the tools of tool_names the request sent deferred and not yet loaded, which clients show as searchable apart from the provided ones (deferred tools in cookie section 12). Each must also be in tool_names. Plugin protocol 1.26.0 carries it in events the same way.

• MCP server definitions (mcp.server.*) take always_load, always_load_tools (patterns over the server's own tool names, none empty), and instructions (absent reads as true), for deferred tools section 10: tools sent up front, and whether the server's initialize instructions are its summary. A server_tools entry has always_load: true for a tool sent up front. Runtime protocol 1.11.0 carries the instructions and the flag in MCP reports.
  • Plugin protocol 1.25.0: the initialize result's optional summary, what the plugin's tools are for, shown with them in deferred tool announcements.

• ConfigStatus has an optional deferred_tools, a list of DeferredToolsMark (provider_id, model_id, reason, age_seconds): the models the daemon sends every tool up front after they refused deferred tools (deferred tools in cookie section 9).

• A summary checkpoint's folded_tools (context_checkpoint_committed, internal_summary only, left out when empty): the deferred tools loaded before it, and the previous checkpoint's. The next tool round declares them up front (deferred tools in cookie section 8.3). Plugin protocol 1.24.0 carries it in events the same way.

• Deferred tools (deferred tools in cookie): a model that loads tools natively is sent MCP and plugin tools deferred, with tool_search and tool_load to find and load them.
  • tool_round_started (tools, prompt_groups): the eager tools a session declares until its next compaction.
  • deferred_tools_announced (added, removed, each a list of groups with name, source (mcp, plugin, builtin, open), an optional summary and untrusted, and tools): what became loadable, and what left, as the model was told.
  • A tool result's loaded_tools: the deferred tools it loaded.

Both events are skippable audit events. Plugin protocol 1.23.0 carries them, and the result field, in events the same way.

• runtimes.agents.* take runtime_id global for the top-level [acp.agents] table: ACP agents every runtime offers, which a runtime's own declaration of the same key replaces there. A global declaration is available while some runtime runs it. Older daemons refuse global.
• crons.create and crons.update take max_runs as a whole number of 0 or less for no limit, besides "unlimited". Jobs still report no limit as "unlimited".

• acp_session_updated has compaction (compaction_id, state, summary), a compaction of the ACP agent's own, recorded as it starts and as it ends, and session_message (direction, peer, text), a message between the agent's sessions. Both were notices before; clients show them as the session's own compaction and as producer messages. A compaction's end the agent repeats is recorded once. Plugin protocol 1.22.0 carries them in events the same way.

• A background call may be an ACP agent's own command still running after its call ended (ACP v2 spec section 9), such as Claude Code's backgrounded commands: agent_task: true, its terminal as job. session.background.stop refuses it; it leaves the list when the command's terminal exits. An idle daemon.restart waits for it, and it counts in background_calls.

• The ACP agent's own subagents (ACP v2 spec section 8) are child sessions of its session: delegated in origin, listed by session.children and session.tree, whose log starts with acp_session_started how: subagent. Their runs are the subagent's own work, started by an acp_agent message ("Started with a task", the task as its body); they report nothing to the parent and take no prompts. An older client reads how: subagent as new. Plugin protocol 1.21.0 carries it in events the same way.

• Work an ACP agent starts on its own (ACP v2 spec sections 6 and 7), such as Claude Code's follow-up after a background command, is a run started by a producer message of the new owner acp_agent { agent } (description "Woke on its own"). An older client reads the producer_message_accepted event as an unknown payload. Plugin protocol 1.20.0 carries the owner in events the same way.

• Clients change a runtime's [runtimes.<id>] table (runtime management spec phase 2), all additions an older peer ignores (see Runtime tables):
  • mcp.server.add, edit, remove, and set_enabled take an optional runtime_id; without it, or with global, they act on the top-level [mcp] servers as before.
  • mcp.server.rename { runtime_id?, name, new_name }.
  • McpServerDefinition.scope: a runtime server's runtime or workspace.
  • runtimes.agents.list, set, remove, and rename, and their types RuntimeAgentDeclaration, AcpAgentDefinition, RuntimesAgentsResult, and RuntimesAgentsRenameResult.

• McpServerInfo.server_tools (runtime management spec phase 1): every tool the server lists, by its own name and in its order, as McpServerTool { name, filtered }; absent while it has listed nothing. An older peer ignores it. Runtime protocol 1.9.0 adds the same list to McpServerReport.

• An idle daemon.restart waits for background calls too: a call still running in the background, or one whose result is not yet committed, holds the restart, since the shutdown ends it without a report. Both additions an older peer ignores:
  • DaemonRestartResult.background_calls and DaemonRestartingNotification.background_calls: the pending background calls, omitted when zero.
  • daemon.restarting is sent again whenever the count changes.

• Held sessions (held sessions spec): a session whose run the user stopped, or whose runs failed past [model_retry] standard_retries, is held until it is resumed. All additions an older peer ignores:
  • automatic_runs_held { reason } and automatic_runs_resumed {}, new runless state events. reason (HeldReason) is open: stopped, or failing with failures and an optional error.
  • SessionMeta.held: the reason while the session is held.
  • session.held.resume { session_id } → { resumed }: clears the hold and lets what waits run; resumed: false for a session that is not held. A message the user sends clears it too.
  • The cron skip reason session_held.
  • While held, producer.send from a plugin or runtime answers producer_rejected with the hold in its detail, and send_message from an agent other than the session's parent fails with send_message:recipient_held. Plugin protocol 1.19.0: plugins receive the new events.

• native_replay_cut { through_seq }, a new state event (thinking-replay recovery spec): the provider refused a replayed reasoning block bound to a conversation prefix that changed since, and the reasoning of every turn committed at or before through_seq is no longer replayed. A diagnostic of kind native_replay_cut beside it says so in the transcript. A reader that does not know the event opens the log render-only, as for any unknown state event. Plugin protocol 1.18.0: plugins receive the event.

• An ACP agent's document may run another declaration (acp.agent), so several agents can run one declaration, each with its own permissions, mode, and body. AgentRuntime.agent then differs from the agent's ID: it names the declaration, and clients show it beside the runtime (claude on local). No wire change.

• session.recall_input takes back any client's pending or queued input, not only the caller's: the recall is recorded under the caller's origin and the content goes back to the caller. not_owner is no longer answered; clients offer recalling another client's input only to a daemon of 1.31.0 or later. No wire change.

• Push notifications (push notifications spec), all additions an older peer ignores:
  • notifications.get, notifications.subscribe, notifications.unsubscribe, and notifications.test: the daemon's VAPID public key and the browsers it pushes to (PushSubscription: id, label, push_service, created_at, last_sent_at, last_error). NotificationsTestStatus is open; an unknown value reads as unknown.
  • notifications.changed, sent to every connection when a subscription is added, changed, or removed.
  • client.presence: the session a connection shows the user, or null, so the daemon does not push what is on screen.
  • The errors push_subscription_not_found, push_subscription_invalid, and push_unavailable.

• Native compaction beside the summary (native compaction spec), all additions an older peer ignores:
  • The internal_summary checkpoint of context_checkpoint_committed has an optional native (CheckpointNativeWindow: window, source_through_seq), the provider window compacted from the same events. An older reader uses the summary. Plugin protocol 1.17.0 carries it too.
  • The native_window checkpoint is no longer written; earlier logs keep reading.
  • ConfigStatus has an optional native_compaction, a list of NativeCompactionMark (provider_id, state, reason, age_seconds): the providers the daemon stopped attempting native compaction for (unsupported) or whose windows it ignores (rejects_windows). NativeCompactionState is open; an unknown value reads as unknown.

• The approval reviewer (approval reviewer spec sections 7, 10, and 11), all additions an older peer ignores:
  • ApprovalInternalDecision has an optional rationale, the reviewer's one-sentence reason for its verdict, at most 300 characters.
  • ApprovalReasonCode has the value internal_agent_failed: the reviewer failed (an error, a timeout, an unparseable reply, or no model), so the evaluated step escalates and no permission mode approves it for the user. An older reader reads it as system_error; a reader before 1.28.0 also checked an evaluated step's decision with that fallback and refuses the step as contradictory, which 1.28.0 readers no longer do. The escalated step that follows keeps the reason escalated.
  • The escalated approval step has an optional expires_at, when the user's window to answer ends: it now starts at the escalation, so the request a 1.28.0 daemon writes carries no expires_at of its own, and the approval's record (approval.list) carries the step's.
  • New event permission_mode_set (mode), which a root session records outside its runs when its tree's permission mode changes. Plugin protocol 1.16.0 carries these too; an older reader skips the event.

• FrozenOpenAiPromptCacheTtl (the ttl of an openai frozen cache strategy, in run_started and delegation events) gains 12h, OpenAI's 12-hour lifetime for the Responses API, and is now an open enum: a value a reader does not know reads as 30m. Plugin protocol 1.15.0 carries it too.

• ACP agents (ACP agents spec section 15, input and pickers), all optional members an older peer ignores:
  • AgentRuntime (an entry of AgentDescriptor.runtimes, and runtime) has options, the config options a new ACP session of the agent starts with on that runtime as the daemon last saw them, with the agent document's acp.mode and acp.config applied, and input_media, the files the agent takes in a prompt (image, audio, text).
  • session.create takes agent_options ([{ option_id, value }]): the values the session's new ACP sessions start with, on top of the agent document's acp.config. Send it only to a daemon of 1.26.0 or later.
  • acp_session_updated has starting_options, those values, recorded as the session is created. Plugin protocol 1.14.0 carries it too.

• Questions an agent asks the user (ACP agents spec section 15, elicitation; Questions):
  • New events elicitation_requested (elicitation_id, agent, optional tool_call_id, message, and a form of typed fields or a url) and elicitation_resolved (action accept/decline/cancel, an accepted form's content, answered_by, and the daemon's reason). Plugin protocol 1.13.0 carries them too; an older reader skips them.
  • New method elicitation.respond (session_id, elicitation_id, action, and content for an accepted form), with the new errors elicitation_not_pending and elicitation_answer_invalid.

• ACP agents (ACP agents spec section 15, session lifecycle): acp_session_started has the how value forked (the agent's session/fork of a session a fork or a revert left behind; an older client reads it as new) and the optional forked_from, the agent's session it was forked from. acp_session_updated has the optional detached (acp_session_id, reason forked or reverted, and the optional message_id of the agent's last message the session keeps): a fork or a revert left that ACP session behind, so the agent's next turn branches off it instead of resuming it. acp_session_started also has the optional fork (the agent offers session/fork) and fork_point (its fork takes a fork point), and acp_session_updated the optional fork_point, found once the daemon has asked the agent. Plugin protocol 1.12.0 carries them; an older reader ignores them.
  • New error acp_agent_unsupported (reason): session.revert or session.fork would cut into the conversation of an ACP agent that cannot fork it there.

• ACP agents (ACP agents spec section 15, display round): acp_session_updated has the optional context (used, optional size), the agent's context use from its latest usage_update, which clients show as the session's context; an older client shows no context for an ACP session, as before.
  • AcpConfigOption has the optional kind (select, left out, or boolean). A boolean option's current_value is true or false, and its values are true (On) and false (Off), so an older client shows it as a two-value select that still sets it; session.agent_option.set takes "true" or "false" for it.
  • Plugin protocol 1.11.0 carries both in the events plugins receive; an older plugin ignores them.

• Onboarding (default models and onboarding spec):
  • New methods onboarding.get (whether the daemon is set up: ready, missing, providers_connected, default_model, small_model), onboarding.preview (what installing the starter kit from a release or a sent archive would do, per file), and onboarding.run (sets the models and installs the kit as one change, or refuses with the new error onboarding_incomplete and writes nothing). A kit that cannot be fetched or used is the new error onboarding_kit_unavailable.
  • New notification onboarding.changed, the new onboarding.get answer, to every connection. An older client ignores it.
  • AgentDescriptor has the optional unset_models: the configuration fields (default_model, small_model) its models entries name that are not set. An older client does not show them.
  • The frozen ${parent_model} fallback of an internal agent definition in run_started has the optional variant that replaces the parent model's variant. Plugin protocol 1.10.0 carries it too; an older reader runs the parent's own variant.
  • Official skills: the skill source official (an older client reads it as user; runtime protocol 1.8.0 carries it too), the optional version of an official skill's SkillDescriptor, skills.list without a session_id for the daemon's own skills, and the new method skills.update, which refreshes the official skills now.

• ACP agents (ACP agents spec section 15, naming) are named by the key of their runtimes' declarations (claude), not <runtime>-<agent>, and every runtime that declares an ID offers the one agent: AgentDescriptor has runtimes, every runtime that offers it (runtime_id, agent, available); runtime stays for an agent exactly one runtime offers, so a client older than 1.21.0 lists one several runtimes offer as a daemon agent. A session runs the agent on the one runtime it attaches that offers it; with none or two, creating the session, starting a run, or delegating is refused, and so is attaching a second runtime that offers a session's ACP agent.

• ACP agents (ACP agents spec section 15, 2026-10-23 addendum), all optional members an older client ignores:
  • acp_session_started has steering: the agent takes messages into its running turn (its steering extension). Clients label the Steer button as queueing for a session whose agent does not.
  • acp_session_updated has notice (severity info, warning, or error, title, optional description): a notice of the agent's, or a compaction it reported; steered (user_inputs, the user_input_submitted sequence numbers, and producer_messages): input delivered into the running turn; and tool_presentation (tool_call_id, presentation): a new title, hint, primary argument, arguments, and preview for one of the agent's tool calls whose raw input arrived after it started.
  • The plugin protocol is 1.9.0 for the same event members.

• Clients restart the daemon (engine configuration spec section 11):
  • New method daemon.restart (when: idle, the default, or now), answering scheduled and active_runs, and the notification daemon.restarting (when, active_runs, optional reason).
  • New errors restart_unsupported, for a daemon that cannot relaunch itself, and daemon_restarting, for a run asked for while an idle restart waits.
  • The cron skip reason daemon_restarting; an older client shows it as an unknown skip.
  • A restarting daemon closes client connections with WebSocket close code 1012 and the reason restarting. Behaviour, with no message change: a daemon that shuts down now sends the replies and notifications it has queued and a close frame before it closes a connection.

• ConfigStatus (in the results of config.get, config.apply, and config.reload) has the optional diagnostics: what the applied configuration names that does not exist yet, such as a delegation target no agent has (an ACP agent whose runtime has not reported it, or a typo). The configuration applies anyway; a diagnostic clears once the agent appears. An older client does not show them.

• ACP agents (ACP agents spec, phases 1 to 3): external coding agents a runtime hosts take a session's or a subagent's turns over the Agent Client Protocol.
  • AgentDescriptor has the optional runtime (runtime_id, agent, available) for an agent a runtime hosts, listed as <runtime>-<agent> with the synthetic model acp/<agent ID>. An older client lists it as any agent.
  • New events acp_session_started (the agent's ACP session: agent, runtime, ACP session ID, cwd, protocol version, agent info, and whether it was new, resumed, or loaded) and acp_session_updated (the agent's commands, options, and plan). The plugin protocol, 1.8.0, carries them too; an older reader skips them.
  • The display block plan (entries of content, status, and an optional priority), which an older client receives as text; it is also part of runtime protocol 1.7.0 and plugin protocol 1.8.0.
  • The tool source acp (agent, runtime_id) of the calls an ACP agent reports. An older reader shows it as an unknown source.
  • New method session.agent_option.set (session_id, option_id, value), answering the session's agent options.
  • Runtime protocol 1.7.0 adds the agents' declarations, relay, and MCP bridge (see the runtime protocol).

• MCP tool filters (MCP tool filters spec):
  • McpServerDefinition (in mcp.server.list, mcp.server.add, mcp.server.edit, and their results) has the optional include_tools and exclude_tools, pattern lists over the server's own tool names. An older client that edits a server sends a definition without them, which clears them, as it would any member it does not know of a command.
  • McpServerInfo has the optional filtered_tools: how many of the tools the server lists its filters left out, absent when none were. Runtime protocol 1.6.0 adds the same member to an MCP server report, so a runtime's servers say it too. The plugin protocol and history format 1 are unchanged.
  • Behaviour, with no message or field change: an MCP tool is offered only when the run's merged rules do not deny mcp for its published name on its runtime, where any mcp allow or ask rule used to offer every MCP tool. Agents with narrow mcp rules see fewer tools, and a session override changes the list at the next model request. Other actions stay offered by action.

• Cron jobs (cron spec, phase 1): the daemon keeps scheduled prompts in crons.json and fires them into a session or into a new session per fire.
  • New methods crons.list, crons.create, crons.update, crons.delete, and crons.run, and the notification crons.changed; new errors cron_not_found, cron_invalid, and cron_store_failed.
  • SessionMeta.cron ({ job_id, fired_at }), also the optional cron member of session_created, names the job whose fire created a run session. A reader that does not know it shows an ordinary session.
  • WaitingOn::ScheduledJob (scheduled_job): an enabled job with a next fire targets the session. A 1.14 client reads it as an unknown producer (Unknown), still something the session waits on.
  • A fire's prompt is a producer message whose producer_owner is external with source cron:<job id> and name scheduled: the closed ProducerOwner keeps its shape, and the source kind cron is the daemon's own, which no plugin or runtime connection has.
  • The built-in permission action cron joins PermissionAction::BUILT_IN, so the effective permissions list it.
  • Plugin protocol 1.7.0 too, since plugins receive events and SessionMeta. History format 1 and the runtime protocol are unchanged.
  • Behaviour, with no message or field change and no version bump (2026-10-23, permission consolidation): a session's permission overlay merges with the agent's frozen rules into one list. An overlay rule replaces the agent rule with the same action, runtime selector, and pattern, and the most specific matching rule decides a call, so a broad overlay rule no longer beats a narrower agent rule. An overlay deny that replaces every allowing rule now hides the action's tools. session.permission.get (and the results of session.permission.set, session.permission.clear, and session.permission.preview) keeps listing the agent's patterns under an overlay * rule, each with its source, where it used to drop them. Recorded approvals and decisions replay as they were written.

• Memory that stays worth keeping (memory spec section 16.9):
  • A new audit event, memory_changed { change, url }, records each write, edit, or delete a model's memory tool makes; change is the open enum MemoryChangeKind (saved, edited, deleted; an unknown value reads as a change). A transcript shows it as one line, such as Saved project://cookie-agent/release. Plugin protocol 1.6.0 too, since plugins receive events.
  • memory_loaded records when the snapshot was taken (taken_at), and each memory it shows, whole or as an index line, carries the optional modified, size, and max_size (MemoryDocumentStatus, flattened into MemorySnapshotCategory, MemorySnapshotMemory, and MemorySnapshotIndexEntry); a size above max_size marks a memory over its limit. A snapshot without taken_at was taken by an earlier daemon, and a run takes a new one.
  • memory.list entries (MemoryInfo) carry the optional created, modified, last_read, and max_size; memory.read (MemoryReadResult) carries created, modified, size, and max_size. memory.write and memory.delete keep their revisions. A memory.write that would leave a memory over its limit is memory_refused.
  • A 1.13 client ignores the new members and skips memory_changed, which is marked skippable; a 1.14 client reading a 1.13 daemon sees no stamps or limits. History format 1 is unchanged.

• Runtime-scoped MCP servers (scope = "runtime" on a runtime template's server; runtime protocol 1.5.0): McpServerInfo has the optional scope, runtime or workspace (an open enum; an unknown value reads as workspace), for a server a runtime other than global hosts. mcp.server.list lists a runtime-scoped server once, without a workspace, with its live state, and, while no instance of a connected runtime hosts it, a workspace-scoped server without a workspace, disconnected with the message "starts when a workspace opens", so a client shows a runtime's servers before any session opens a workspace of it. mcp.server.reconnect without a workspace reconnects a runtime-scoped server; for a waiting workspace-scoped one it fails. A runtime-scoped server's failure names no workspace and reaches the sessions attached to any instance of its runtime.
  • A 1.12 client ignores scope and shows a runtime-scoped server as one its runtime hosts without a workspace, and a waiting one as disconnected with its message; a 1.13 client reading a 1.12 daemon sees no scope.

• mcp.server.list lists the MCP servers a dial-in runtime hosts from [runtimes.local.mcp] on its own machine, which earlier daemons left out because they do not see those definitions. Such a server has the new McpConfigSource value machine (an open enum value) and an empty definition (no command or url); its state, tool_count, and message are live as for any server. A failure of one is now also among the failures a client hears when it subscribes to a session.
  • A memory_loaded snapshot holds only what the run's memory rules let it read (memory spec section 7.5): a memory they allow is shown as before, one they ask for is listed by URL and description only, in the new MemorySnapshot.user_listed (user categories) and MemorySnapshotAgent.listed (the agent's file; a project overview they ask for joins the project's memories), and one they deny or do not match is left out and not counted. MemorySnapshot.rules, a fingerprint of the rules it was taken under, makes a run whose rules changed take a new snapshot. All three are optional; plugin protocol 1.5.0 too, since plugins receive events. History format 1 is unchanged; older logs read as having none.
  • A 1.11 client reads machine as runtime (a server mcp.server.* cannot edit); a 1.12 client reading a 1.11 daemon sees no dial-in servers, as before; a 1.11 client ignores the snapshot's new members.

• MCP OAuth from the web client (spec): mcp.auth.begin accepts an https redirect_uri (a host, no user info, no fragment, any path and query) and plain http to localhost as well as to a loopback IP literal, with or without a port, path, or query. The web client uses its own page with ?oauth=callback. A dynamic registration is made for each flow's redirect (application_type web for an https one, native for loopback); a configured client_id is used as is.
  • mcp.auth.complete also requires the redirect's own query parameters (such as oauth=callback) in the callback_url.
  • No wire type changes. A 1.10 daemon refuses the new redirects, so a client offers them only to a 1.11 daemon; a 1.10 client sees nothing new.

• The machine registry remembers where runtimes ran (memory spec section 16.8): a runtime that is not connected keeps the machine it was last seen on, by a new assigned_by reason, last_seen (an open enum value). MachineInfo in machines.list gains remembered, the offline runtimes it remembers (RememberedRuntime: runtime_id, assigned_by, platform, home, last_seen). runtimes.list gives such a runtime its remembered machine, platform, and home.
  • machines.forget_runtime { runtime } drops an offline runtime's record and answers with the machines afterwards, with the error codes runtime_not_remembered and runtime_still_connected. machines.forget no longer counts remembered offline runtimes, and drops their records.
  • Delegating to runtimes (spec): SessionMeta gains delegated_attachments, a root session's record of the attachments its subagents brought, folded from the new runless state event delegated_attachments_added { child_session_id, attachments } (plugin protocol 1.4.0 too). sessions.changed upserted announces it. History format 1 is unchanged; older logs read as having none.
  • list_runtimes joins the built-in permission actions that session.permission.get lists. The delegate_subagent and list_runtimes tool changes are model-facing and need no wire change.
  • A 1.9 client ignores the new members and event, and sees offline runtimes as before; a 1.10 client reading a 1.9 daemon sees no remembered runtimes and no delegated attachments, and calling machines.forget_runtime gets method_not_found.

• SessionMeta gains waiting_on: what will start the session's next run without the user, each kind once, omitted when nothing will. Kinds (an open enum WaitingOn): goal (the root's goal is active; folded from the goal events, so the metadata cache keeps it), background_call (a background call is running), subagent (a direct child runs a turn on its own, or a background delegation is queued or running), and external_producer (a plugin or runtime holds a live producer registration for the session). The last three are the daemon's live state, never cached, and end with it. It is reported whatever status says; clients show a running session as running first (see What a session waits on).
  • sessions.changed upserted announces every change of waiting_on: a goal activated, paused, resumed, completed, or cancelled, a background call detached or reported, a child's turn started or ended, a registration made or dropped.
  • A 1.8 client ignores the member; a 1.9 client reading a 1.8 daemon sees no session waiting on anything.

• Projects: projects.list, project.get, project.create, project.update, and project.delete manage named bodies of work, each with an ID, a name, an optional emoji, default attachments and agent, an AGENTS.md, and a memory folder; projects.changed announces every change (see Projects). They come with the error codes project_not_found, project_name_taken, project_changed, project_invalid, project_sessions_running, project_root_session_only, and project_store_failed.
  • Sessions in projects: session.create takes an optional project, whose default runtimes the session attaches when the creation omits runtimes; session.project.set moves a root session into a project or out of one; session.list takes an optional project filter (an ID, or "none"); SessionMeta gains project.
  • Events (plugin protocol 1.3.0 too): the state event session_project_set, memory_loaded's optional project (the overview and an index of the project's memories), and agent_md_loaded's optional project, which names a project's AGENTS.md. History format 1 is unchanged; older logs read as having no project.
  • A project:// memory write, from memory.write as from a model, is memory_refused unless the project exists; the first write no longer creates the project. A project's overview memory keeps the daemon's description, reported in memory.write's notice.
  • A 1.7 client ignores the new members and notification, and sees sessions without projects; a project's AGENTS.md and memory still reach its sessions' prompts, which the daemon renders. A 1.8 client calling a project method on a 1.7 daemon gets method_not_found.

• Paths and runtimes: SessionMeta gains attachments, the session's runtime attachments now (RuntimeAttachment: name, runtime_id, capability, kind, workspace), kept current on attach and detach, which also announce the session with sessions.changed upserted; session lists can show and filter sessions by runtime and workspace without a session.get each. RuntimeListing in runtimes.list gains home, the home directory the runtime reported (runtime protocol 1.3.0), which clients show the runtime's paths under as ~/… (see Runtimes). A 1.6 client ignores both; a 1.7 client reading a 1.6 daemon sees no attachments and no homes, and shows paths absolute.
  • A new root session's cwd_identity is decided at creation, once its attachments have opened: the canonical workspace its first attachment with a workspace reported, else cwd canonicalized on the daemon's machine (as given when that fails). A client's ~/x and another's /home/ada/x attaching one workspace now give one identity. Sessions created before keep the identity they stored.

• memory.write results carry an optional notice: what the daemon kept in place of the text it was given. The daemon now keeps a memory file for every agent and owns its description and two keywords, so a write of an agent:// file that changes them keeps the daemon's and says so (see Memory). A 1.5 client ignores the member.

• Session deletion: session.delete { session_id, expected_last_seq } deletes a root session's whole tree from disk and returns the deleted session IDs, the root first; every connection gets sessions.changed removed for each (see Delete). It comes with the error codes not_a_root_session, session_tree_running, and session_changed, besides the existing session_not_found and session_owned_elsewhere. A 1.4 client sees only the removed changes; a 1.5 client calling session.delete on a 1.4 daemon gets method_not_found.

• Memory for clients: memory.list, memory.read, memory.write, and memory.delete list, read, and change the daemon's memory files for the user, with no session (see Memory). They come with the error codes memory_url_invalid, memory_not_found, memory_exists, memory_revision_mismatch, memory_invalid, memory_refused, memory_busy, and memory_store_failed. The memory.changed notification reaches every connection when a memory file changes through the daemon. A 1.3 client sees none of it; a 1.4 client calling a memory.* method on a 1.3 daemon gets method_not_found.

• A new state event, memory_loaded, records the memory snapshot a session's model sees from a run on: user categories, the run's agent's memory, and an index of the session's machines' memories (see Events). An event without agent records that memory is no longer available. A 1.2 client reads it as an unknown state event. The plugin protocol is 1.2.0 for the same event.
  • memory and memory_write join the built-in permission actions that session.permissions.get lists.

• Machines: the computers runtimes run on. machines.list, machines.rename, machines.assign, machines.unassign, machines.merge, and machines.forget read and change the daemon's machine registry (see Machines), with the error codes machine_not_found, machine_name_taken, machine_in_use, machine_memory_conflict, machine_merge_self, runtime_not_pinned, and machine_store_failed. The machines.changed notification reaches every connection when the registry changes, and each runtimes.list entry gains machine. A 1.1 client sees none of it; a 1.2 client calling a machines.* method on a 1.1 daemon gets method_not_found.

• A new audit event, record_omitted { omitted_type }, stands in for a record its writer deliberately did not carry over, at that record's sequence, run, and time. A fork writes one for each of its source's delegation_reserved, delegation_progressed, and delegation_finished records: the fork keeps the conversation but not the subagents, which stay the source's (see Events). It is skippable and changes nothing a reader projects; a 1.0 client reads it as an unknown event. The plugin protocol is 1.1.0 for the same event.

The client protocol is frozen: every later 1.x version reads and is read by this one. A 0.x build never interoperates with a 1.x one: the handshake refuses another major with -32002 unsupported_protocol, so a client and a daemon from before the freeze must be upgraded together. The plugin and runtime protocols froze at 1.0.0 too, and session history is history format 1.

What 1.x keeps:

  • Versions. The handshake carries "MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH" strings and connects equal majors; each side sends a method, a member, or a display block kind only when the other's minor includes it, and the patch never matters.
  • Information is tolerant, commands are strict. Results, notifications, events, and the JSON-RPC envelope ignore members a reader does not know, and their enums are open, read as a documented fallback or as unknown; an event a client cannot read arrives as an unknown event, and a notification that does not decode fails no call. Params refuse an unknown member (unknown_field) or value (unknown_variant) with its JSON path.
  • Errors. Every application error is -32000 with a registry data.code, a readable message, an optional hint, and detail on request (see Errors); clients branch only on data.code.
  • User content and media. Inputs are content: text and file parts naming artifacts uploaded with artifact.upload.*, admitted against the input_media each model of the catalog view advertises, and read back with artifact.read.
  • Tool display. Tool calls carry presentation v2 (title, hint, tool identity, argument and preview blocks), progress display deltas, and result display blocks of twelve kinds with a canonical text rendering; a connection receives only the kinds its version includes. A result always carries its whole display.
  • The catalog view. runtime.snapshot.get and runtime.changed carry a ModelCatalogView with one opaque revision.

Changed since 0.52.0: a tool result's display is always whole and required; display_span belonged to the session log's storage encoding and no longer reaches clients.

• Every model of the catalog view states input_media: the kinds it accepts in user input, with their media types and effective byte, dimension, pixel, and count limits.
  • run.start, run.steer, and session.submit_input take content (text and file parts) in place of input, and a recalled outcome of session.recall_input returns content.
  • artifact.upload.begin, artifact.upload.chunk, artifact.upload.finish, artifact.upload.cancel, and artifact.read upload media into a session tree's store and read any of its artifacts back; new error codes upload_offset_mismatch, upload_size_mismatch, and too_many_uploads.
  • Input file parts are admitted against the model the input reaches: media_unsupported, media_type_unsupported, media_too_large, media_limit_exceeded, and artifact_not_found.

• The handshake's protocol_version is a semver string. A client of another major or, before 1.0, another minor is refused with -32002 unsupported_protocol, as is a build that sends the old integer.
  • The handshake takes an optional token and features, and its reply carries engine_version and features. The WebSocket upgrade no longer requires Authorization: a connection without it authenticates with the handshake's token, and gets -32003 for anything else until it does.
  • [server] allowed_origins lets web pages of listed origins connect.
  • Results, notifications, and the JSON-RPC envelope are information: a reader ignores members it does not know, and every enum in them is open, read as a documented fallback or as unknown (see Decoding). Params stay strict.

  • Every application error is -32000 with a registry data.code, a message and hint from the registry, and the cause as data.detail (see Errors). The old codes -32011, -32012, -32020 to -32022, -32030, -32031, and -32040, the several meanings of -32602 for refusals, the typed error data (RunStartConflict, SessionRenameError, SessionRevertConflict, ApprovalRespondError, ProviderConnectError, ProviderDisconnectError, ConfigApplyError), and debug_code are gone.

  • runtime.snapshot.get and runtime.changed carry a ModelCatalogView (revision, catalog, providers, models, agents) in place of the runtime snapshot: one opaque revision replaces the snapshot schema version and the eleven revisions and counters, and descriptors lose their fingerprints. provider.connect and provider.disconnect take that revision as expected_revision; the disconnect receipt keeps its ID and time only. runtime.changed takes any number of reasons.

  • SessionMeta.short_id is required (nullable).
  • The daemon sends a connection only the display-block kinds its version includes, downgrading newer kinds to text and leaving out kinds it does not know.

docs.title: Before semver versions
docs.text: Builds before 0.51.0 sent the protocol version as an integer, from 34 to 50; the last of them was 50. They cannot connect to this build.

docs.title: Protocol Reference
docs.text: The daemon exposes JSON-RPC 2.0 over a WebSocket at /ws. This build speaks client protocol 1.34.0; the changelog lists what each version changed. A client and a daemon connect when their majors are equal: a minor only adds, so the two use what the lower minor includes, and the patch never matters. Compatibility states the rules every change to the protocol follows.

docs.title: Handshake and authentication
docs.text:
A client must call handshake before any other method:

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "handshake", "params": {
    "protocol_version": "1.54.0",
    "client": { "kind": "web", "instance_id": "<uuid>" },
    "token": "<the daemon's token>",
    "features": [] } }

The reply:

{ "protocol_version": "1.54.0", "engine_version": "0.3.0",
  "origin": "client:web-<id>", "machine_id": "<opaque>", "features": [] }
  • protocol_version is the sender's semver version, a "MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH" string. The daemon reads it from the raw params before anything else: a client of another major (a 0.x build from before the freeze included), or a build from before semver versions that sends an integer, is answered with -32002 unsupported_protocol, whose data names both supported_version and peer_version. A client only sends a method or a member the daemon's version includes.
  • client.kind names the client program: a lowercase letter followed by up to 15 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens (the shipped clients use tui, cli, and web). client.instance_id is a UUID identifying one running client; a client keeps it across reconnects so it can recognize events it caused. Any number of clients may connect to one daemon at once.
  • origin is client:<kind>-<id>, where <id> is the instance id as 32 lowercase hex digits. The daemon stamps that origin on every event the connection's requests cause, so each client can tell its own actions from another client's. A repeated handshake on the same connection keeps the first identity.
  • engine_version is the daemon's own version, for display and logs; machine_id an opaque identity of the daemon's machine when it has one, so a client can tell whether it runs on the same machine.
  • features list what each side's configuration enables. None are defined yet; an unknown feature is ignored.

Authentication. A client authenticates with the daemon's bearer token ([server] token) in one of two places:

  • the Authorization: Bearer <token> header of the WebSocket upgrade, which the native clients send; a wrong header is refused with HTTP 401;
  • or token in the handshake, which a browser must use, since it cannot set headers on a WebSocket.

Until a connection without the header has sent the right token, the daemon answers only handshake; any other request gets -32003 unauthenticated. A handshake with a wrong or missing token gets -32003, and the connection closes. A connection that has not authenticated within 10 seconds is closed. A connection that authenticated with the header but has not handshaken gets -32001 handshake_required for anything but handshake.

Web origins. /ws accepts an upgrade request from any web origin, or with no Origin header (every native client); the token is the guard. Dial-in runtimes on /runtime always authenticate with the header, and a request there with an Origin header is refused with HTTP 403. Refusals there name their reason in the response body or the close frame (see Dial-in refusals).

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
The daemon and its clients read what they receive by its role (see the compatibility spec section 4):

  • Results, notifications, and the JSON-RPC envelope are information. A reader ignores members it does not know, and request IDs may be integers or strings. Every enum in them is open: a value a newer daemon added reads as the fallback its type documents (for example an unknown permission effect as ask, an unknown approval status as cancelled), or as unknown for states a client only shows (session status, plugin state, MCP server state, runtime instance status, producer source status, runtime change reasons). An unknown sessions.changed change reads as resync, an unknown events.subscription message type is ignored, and an unknown session.submit_input or session.recall_input outcome fails that call with a readable error.
  • A notification a client cannot read is dropped. The shared client reports it as ClientDelivery::Diagnostic, and no call in flight fails. A response it cannot read fails only its own call. A frame that is not JSON, or not a request, notification, or reply, ends the shared client's connection; the daemon instead answers such a frame with parse_error or invalid_request and reads on.
  • Events. A client reads stored events with an open payload: an event of a type this build does not know, or one it cannot read, is delivered in its place as ClientDelivery::UnknownEvent, which advances the session's sequence and changes nothing else (the TUI shows a dim row in its debug view). A replay page does not fail for it.
  • Display blocks. The daemon sends each connection only the display-block kinds its client protocol version includes: a block of a newer kind arrives as a text block of its canonical text rendering, and a block of a kind the daemon itself does not know (from a log a newer build wrote) is left out of what it sends, while the log keeps it. Every kind of this build exists from the first minor, so today no block is downgraded.
  • Params are commands. An unknown or mistyped member fails with -32602 and data.code unknown_field (or unknown_variant for a value or tag), with data.field naming the JSON path. A client sends a method or member only if the daemon's version includes it; -32601 for a method the client expected reads as "the daemon is too old for" that method.

docs.title: Error diagnostics
docs.text: ModelErrorSummary.response_body is an optional DiagnosticText that preserves the supplied content, with terminal/Unicode format controls removed or replaced and a maximum of 4,096 UTF-8 bytes, including any truncation marker. Newlines and tabs are permitted. It is used for terminal, fallback, and internal-agent model failures. A failed run_finished keeps its short error and optionally includes model_error and resolved_model. Missing fields in old events default to null and are omitted when serialized; this is an additive event change without a protocol version bump.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Every application error is -32000 with a registry data.code, a message a user can understand, and optional data.hint and data.detail; the error reference lists every code with its fields. The daemon builds message and hint from the registry, so a code always reads the same way, and keeps its own description of the cause (bounded and terminal-safe, without secret-pattern redaction) as detail. Clients branch only on data.code, show message and then hint, and show detail on request; a code a client does not know reads as a generic error, whose message and hint are already readable. JsonRpcError Debug formatting redacts data. No request headers or credential dumps are added. See Error details for display and upstream limits.

docs.title: Tool-emitted messages
docs.text:
PersistedToolResult carries optional additional_messages, alongside its independent display and output references. The field is an ordered array of at most four messages. Each message has role system or user and one or more ordered text or file content parts. Empty arrays are omitted on the wire; event validation bounds text and attachment counts and validates every referenced artifact.

The engine materializes these messages from the persisted terminal result, so replay and restart are deterministic. The paired tool result is placed first, then messages are inserted in array order before the next assistant turn. User-role messages retain their role. System-role messages are represented as user turns whose first text part is the deterministic marker [tool-emitted system message; materialized as user history]; their original text and file parts follow in order. This translation keeps the initial system prefix and its cache breakpoint stable because provider families disagree on mid-history system semantics. Terminal result events use origin engine:tool-result.

Elision treats a tool result and its additional_messages as one unit. If the parent result is elided, none of its emitted messages enter model history and the marker reports how many were lost. Retried or replayed termination events replace the call record rather than applying first-attempt messages twice. Attachments in compacted history are not recoverable from the checkpoint.

docs.title: Session mechanics
docs.text:
The JSON-RPC session layer lives in the protocol crate so the server, the TUI, and the CLI share one implementation of the protocol mechanics.

  • Transport. protocol::Transport is a frame-level channel: send(MessageFrame) / recv() -> Option<MessageFrame>, with MessageFrame either a Text string or a Value. It carries no JSON-RPC semantics. The protocol crate provides the InProcessStream pair and, behind its websocket feature, the client WebSocketTransport; the daemon's axum accept path in the server crate implements the same trait server-side.
  • ServerProtocol. The server contract is one async method per RPC plus connected. The server crate implements it over Engine. protocol::serve drives one complete session over a transport: it authenticates the connection (by the transport, or by the handshake's token), rejects every method before the handshake with -32003 or -32001, correlates requests by id, dispatches to the implementation, and delivers notifications through a ServerContext. After the handshake, requests on one connection run concurrently (at most 64 in flight) and each response is written when it is ready, so responses can arrive out of request order. Notifications from work a request started, such as the live tail of events.subscribe, are written only after that request's response. A connection holds one live tail per session: subscribing again replaces it, and the replaced tail's queued notifications are written before the new tail's.
  • Client. The client side is the concrete protocol::Client. Its connection task correlates requests by id, demuxes notifications into an ordered ClientDelivery stream, injects cursor replays and gap recovery before buffered live notifications, fetches replays in pages of 2,000 events and delivers each replay whole once its final page arrives, wipes secret-bearing serialized frames, and fails outstanding calls on shutdown.
  • TUI and CLI. The TUI client is a thin adapter re-exporting the server's Client wrapper; the CLI uses the same client. Both still work without the tui feature.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Params are commands: a member a method's params schema does not list is refused with -32602 and data.code unknown_field, whose field is the member's JSON path (selection.model.extra). That holds inside types session history also stores, such as a run selection or a permission rule, which ignore unknown members when they are read as history.

run.start accepts optional reset_fallback (default false). The server normally trims a requested earlier model's suffix to the latest successfully committed fallback in this session, matching exact model/variant identity and agent/preset scope. Set reset_fallback: true for an explicit picker/model reset. The accepted effective selection and suffix are recorded in run_started; existing committed-turn events preserve progress without a new event type. Idempotent redelivery resolves against the state preceding the original run.

docs.title: User content
docs.text:
run.start, run.steer, and session.submit_input take the user's input as content, a nonempty list of parts, and session.recall_input hands the recalled input back the same way:

"content": [
  { "type": "text", "text": "What is wrong with this layout?" },
  { "type": "file", "artifact": { "sha256": "…", "byte_length": 482113,
      "media_type": "image/png", "filename": "screenshot.png" } }
]

A text part carries text; a file part names an artifact of the session tree's store by its ArtifactRef, as an upload returned it. The input-lane events store the same content (see Events).

docs.title: Media
docs.text:
A client attaches a file by uploading it into the session tree's artifact store and naming the result in a file part. A client that attaches before its first prompt creates the session first; the upload publishes a session that was still only in memory.

  1. artifact.upload.begin { session_id, byte_length, filename? } returns { upload_id, chunk_bytes }. chunk_bytes is 1 MiB. A byte_length above the largest attachment cap (25 MiB) is refused with media_too_large whose kind is file. The upload belongs to this connection: another connection cannot see it, it is dropped when the connection closes, and a connection may have at most 8 in progress (too_many_uploads). Its bytes stream into a temporary file of the store, never into memory.
  2. artifact.upload.chunk { upload_id, offset, data } appends data (standard base64, at most chunk_bytes decoded bytes) at offset, which must be exactly the bytes received so far (upload_offset_mismatch names expected_offset otherwise; the upload waits for the right chunk). A chunk past byte_length is upload_size_mismatch. Requests run concurrently, so send a chunk once the previous one is answered.
  3. artifact.upload.finish { upload_id, sha256 } checks the digest (digest_mismatch), recognizes the media type from the content alone (a filename never decides it), validates the content as tool attachments are validated (structure, the 20 MiB cap or 25 MiB for video, and for images at most 16384 pixels a side and 16 Mi pixels), and stores the blob under its digest.
