Since 1.26.0 content that is no media file but UTF-8 without NUL bytes is a text file, text/plain of kind text, up to 1 MiB: an ACP agent may take it, a model never does. It returns { artifact: ArtifactRef, image? }; put artifact in a file part as it is. An upload whose digest or content is refused (digest_mismatch, media_type_unsupported, media_too_large) is dropped; one finished before all of its bytes arrived (upload_size_mismatch) stays in progress.
  4. artifact.upload.cancel { upload_id } drops an upload in progress.

An unknown or another connection's upload_id is upload_not_found.

Leases. A finished upload is kept for an hour while no event references it, then removed. Once an input that names it is submitted, its event keeps it, as tool attachments are kept: a revert that removes every reference removes it after its lease, and a fork takes it into the fork's tree. A daemon restart forgets leases; an upload no event referenced then stays in the store.

Admission. run.start, run.steer, and session.submit_input check every file part against the model the input reaches: the run's selected model (for a steer, the running run's; for a queued input, the model of the selection it will start with). The part must name an artifact of the tree's store whose content is what the reference says (artifact_not_found, or media_type_unsupported when the content is not that type), of a kind the model accepts (media_unsupported with kind and model), of a media type it lists (media_type_unsupported), within its byte and image limits (media_too_large, with the image's width and height and the model's limits), and the parts of one kind must not outnumber max_count (media_limit_exceeded). These are the model's input_media; a client that checks them first never meets these errors. A refused input records nothing. A model the input does not reach this way, such as a fallback or a model the session moves to later, sees a placeholder for each file it does not accept (Media reads describes the wording). A run of an ACP agent checks none of this: the agent gets each file it takes (its AgentRuntime.input_media) and a note naming the others.

artifact.read { session_id, sha256, offset, length } returns { data, total_bytes, media_type }: up to length (at most 1 MiB) bytes from offset of any artifact of the session's tree (user uploads, tool attachments, and the full content of truncated display blocks), base64 encoded, fewer at the end, and none at offset = total_bytes. media_type is recognized from the content: a media type, text/plain for UTF-8 text, or application/octet-stream. A blob is verified against its digest when it is first read. An artifact the store does not have is artifact_not_found.

Model, agent, and catalog discovery uses runtime.snapshot.get. Skills use the session-aware skills.list and skills.get methods because visibility depends on the governing run policy and session overlay. session.list returns root sessions only: a delegated child is selected as part of its root's tree, not as a top-level entry, and stays reachable via session.tree, session.children, session.get, and session.resume.

docs.title: Runtimes
docs.text:
A session uses the tools and workspace context of the runtime capabilities it is attached to. A RuntimeAttachment is { name, runtime_id, capability, kind, workspace? }: the session-unique attachment name (also the tool prefix on name collisions), the runtime_id, the runtime's capability the session uses, the capability's kind (a label the runtime declares, such as global or coding; the daemon never branches on it), and the canonical workspace the runtime reported, if any. The session create, get, and resume results carry the session's attachments in attach order; clients follow later changes through the runtime_attached and runtime_detached events of the session. Since 1.7.0 every SessionMeta also carries them as attachments, kept current on attach and detach, so session.list and sessions.changed show each session's runtimes and workspaces without a session.get. Metadata an older build wrote has none until the session records an event; a 1.6 daemon sends none.

session.create attaches global unless global is false, then each entry of runtimes (runtime_id, optional capability, optional workspace) in order; without runtimes it attaches local's coding capability at cwd, or at the daemon's working directory without one. cwd is the client's directory as it names it. One daemon serves sessions of many directories, and session.list with a cwd_identity shows one directory's. A session's cwd_identity is decided once, when it is created, after its attachments have opened: it is the canonical workspace that the first attachment with a workspace reported, on its runtime's machine, never the client's text. So a web client's ~/x and a TUI's /home/ada/x attaching one workspace give one identity. A session with no workspace attachment records cwd canonicalized on the daemon's machine, or as given when that fails (the daemon's working directory without cwd). Delegated sessions copy their parent's, and sessions created before 1.7.0 keep the identity they stored. An empty runtimes list creates a session with no coding runtime. Instances that are not running are started first, and a failure creates no session and records no instance. No session is created over a runtime that is not online: a dial-in runtime that is not connected, the one a project's defaults name included, is refused at once with runtime `<id>` is not connected (last seen <time>), and an instance that is already open is used only over a connection that answers (see Liveness). session.runtime.attach follows the same rules.

session.runtime.attach and session.runtime.detach are rejected while the session has an active run (session running). Attach connects the runtime and opens the capability's instance when needed, and records nothing when that fails: neither an attachment nor, for an instance that never opened, a failed instance in runtimes.list. The error says which step failed: runtime `<id>` failed to start: <reason> when the runtime could not be reached, and runtime `<id>` could not open `<capability>` for workspace `<workspace>`: <reason> with the runtime's own reason when it refused the workspace, such as one outside the directories it serves. Without capability it attaches the runtime's only capability; a runtime that offers several asks for one, naming them. The attachment's name is the name the instance reports (global, or <runtime ID>_<workspace basename> for a coding instance), suffixed _2, _3, ... when the session already has an attachment of that name; attaching an instance a session already has is an error. A capability that takes a workspace requires workspace, except local's coding, which opens at the daemon's working directory without one; a capability that takes none refuses one. Besides global and local, the runtimes are the configured [runtimes.<id>] tables and the dial-in runtimes that have connected since the daemon started; attaching any other runtime ID is an unknown runtime error, and attaching a dial-in runtime that is not connected now fails. The daemon passes workspace to the runtime exactly as given; the attachment records the canonical path the runtime reported, and two spellings of one workspace share an instance.

runtimes.list returns each runtime as a RuntimeListing: its runtime_id; its lifetime (builtin for global and local, spawned for a template, dial_in for a runtime that connected on its own); whether the daemon is connected to it now; its capabilities (name, kind, takes_workspace, description), empty until it has connected once; its platform; its machine (see Machines); since 1.7.0 its home, the home directory it reported (runtime protocol 1.3.0, absent when it reported none), which global and local report as the daemon's; and a message saying why its last attempt to connect failed, or, for a dial-in runtime that went away, runtime `<id>` disconnected: <reason>, where a runtime that stopped cleanly gives the other end closed the connection. Clients store and compare paths canonical and absolute and only show them shorter: a path of a runtime with a home reads ~ for the home itself and ~/rest under it, and a path of a runtime without one stays absolute (cookie_agent_client_state::paths::display_path). Each instance has its runtime_id, capability, reported attachment_name, kind, workspace, and platform once started, its status (starting, ready, reconnecting, failed, or stopped), and a failure message.

runtimes.reconnect retries an instance now: a failed instance is started again, under a new generation, and keeps its identity; an instance that is not running is started; a ready or reconnecting one is left as it is. capability and workspace follow the attach rule, and for a failed instance it is the workspace that runtimes.list reports. A start that fails is an error with the reason, worded as for attach. An instance runtimes.list already showed stays failed with the new reason, which runtimes.changed reports; one it did not show stays unrecorded. Retrying global also retries its failed MCP servers.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text:
Every runtime belongs to one machine, the computer it runs on (see the memory spec). The daemon keeps its machines in a registry, machines.json in its data folder, which only the machines.* methods change. A runtime is assigned when it connects, in this order: the machine that pins its runtime ID; the machine that stands for the machine ID it reported in the runtime protocol; a new machine for that ID, named after the runtime's sanitized host name with -2, -3, … added on a clash; and, for a runtime that reported no ID, a new machine pinning it, named after its runtime ID. global and local belong to the daemon's own machine. Machine names are a lowercase ASCII letter followed by up to 31 lowercase letters, digits, _, or -. runtimes.list gives each runtime's machine: the one it is assigned to while connected, else the one it is pinned to or the daemon last saw it on.

Since 1.10.0 the registry remembers where each spawned or dial-in runtime ran: when it connects, machines.json records the machine ID, platform, and home it reported, and when the daemon last saw it connect or disconnect. A runtime that is not connected is placed by its pin, else by that record, so it keeps its machine while it is offline and across restarts; only a runtime that never connected has no machine. runtimes.list gives such a runtime its remembered machine, platform, and home, with connected: false. A record goes with machines.forget_runtime, with machines.forget of its machine, and, for a configured runtime, when a configuration reload or a restart no longer has its [runtimes.<id>] table; a dial-in runtime's stays until it is forgotten.

machines.list returns each machine as a MachineInfo: its name; the machine ids it stands for; the runtime IDs pinned to it; the connected runtimes assigned to it, each with its runtime_id, assigned_by (pinned or machine_id), and platform; since 1.10.0 the remembered runtimes that are not connected, each with its runtime_id, assigned_by (pinned or last_seen), platform, home, and last_seen time; the platform its connected runtimes agree on; and its number of memories, the memory files in its memory folder.

Each change answers with the machines afterwards, moves the connected runtimes it affects at once, and sends machines.changed; a session's system prompt names the new machine from its next run. A change holds the memory lock while it rewrites the registry and moves memory folders, and fails, changing nothing, when it cannot:

  • machines.rename fails with machine_name_taken when another machine, or a memory folder that belongs to none, has the name.
  • machines.assign removes the runtime's pin from any other machine.
  • machines.unassign of a runtime no machine pins is runtime_not_pinned.
  • machines.merge fails with machine_memory_conflict when both memory folders hold a file of one name, and with machine_merge_self for one machine.
  • machines.forget fails with machine_in_use while a connected runtime belongs to the machine or its memory folder holds anything. Remembered runtimes do not keep it; their records go with it.
  • machines.forget_runtime fails with runtime_still_connected while the runtime is connected, and with runtime_not_remembered when the registry keeps no record of it. A pin stays.

An unknown machine is machine_not_found; a registry or folder that cannot be read or written is machine_store_failed.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
The daemon's memory is Markdown files with description and keywords frontmatter, in four layers, each file addressed by a memory URL: user://<category>, agent://<agent>, machine://<machine>/<name>, and project://<project>/<name> (see the memory guide and the memory spec). The memory.* methods act on the files for the user, with no session; a change never refreshes the memory snapshot of an open session, which a later run takes when it would anyway.

memory.list returns each file as a MemoryInfo: its url, layer (user, agent, machine, or project), group (the machine or project of a machine:// or project:// memory), revision, size in bytes, and either its description and keywords or the reason it is invalid. An agent:// file whose agent the agent registry no longer has is orphaned. ignored lists, by path in the memory folder, what is not a memory file of the layout (a file without .md, a name that breaks the naming rules, something nested too deep) with the reason. layer keeps one layer; agent, machine, or project keeps one agent's file, one machine's memories, or one project's, and only one of the three may be given. A filter that contradicts layer or another filter is -32602.

A revision is the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the file's bytes. memory.write takes the whole file text, frontmatter included, and checks it like the model's memory_write: it must parse, follow the file format, and fit its kind's [memory] limit (a memory already over it may only shrink; otherwise memory_refused). Without revision it creates the memory, and fails with memory_exists when it exists; with revision it replaces the memory at that revision, and fails with memory_revision_mismatch when the file changed since, or memory_not_found when it is gone. Both errors carry the file's current revision. memory.delete needs the revision as well. Unlike the model, the user may create and delete user:// categories and delete agent:// files; an agent:// file is created only for an agent the agent registry has (memory_refused).

The daemon keeps an agent:// file for every agent that is not internal and owns its description and two keywords, the agent ID and its mode (see the memory guide). A memory.write of such a file keeps them: when the text gives another description or leaves a daemon keyword out, the daemon puts its own frontmatter in place, keeps the body and any other keywords, and says what it kept in the result's notice (since 1.6.0). A file whose agent the registry no longer has keeps the description it has.

A URL that is not a memory URL is memory_url_invalid; text that is not a valid memory is memory_invalid with the reason; a malformed revision is -32602. Another process holding the memory lock is memory_busy, and a file that cannot be read or written is memory_store_failed. Each change sends memory.changed to every connection; changes another daemon sharing the data folder makes are not announced.

A project:// URL must name a project that exists: a write to another is memory_refused, naming the projects there are (since 1.8.0). Every project has project://<name>/overview, whose description the daemon owns, kept by a write and reported in its notice like an agent file's.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
Since 1.8.0 the daemon keeps projects: named bodies of work a session may belong to (see Projects and the projects spec). projects.list returns each project as a ProjectInfo: its opaque id, which sessions refer to it by; its name, which follows the memory name rule and is the name of its memory folder; an optional emoji; its revision; its defaults; whether it has_agents_md; and the counts of its root sessions and its memories.

defaults is { preset?, agent?, global, runtimes }: global and runtimes ([{ runtime_id, capability?, workspace? }]) have the shape of session.create's members of the same names; agent and preset name an agent and its preset as a RunSelection does. project.create and project.update check them like session.create's runtimes, except that the runtimes need not be connected, and refuse an agent the daemon does not list in that preset, or one that cannot run as root (project_invalid). An emoji is exactly one emoji: one extended grapheme cluster of at most 32 bytes that Unicode marks as an emoji, not ASCII, whitespace, or a control character.

A project's revision is the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its project.toml and its AGENTS.md; project.update and project.delete send the revision last read, and a project changed since is project_changed with its current revision. project.get returns the AGENTS.md text with the revision of the file alone. A name another project has is project_name_taken; an unknown ID is project_not_found.

  • Sessions. session.create with project records it with the creation (session_project_set); an unknown ID is project_not_found, checked before anything is attached. When the creation omits runtimes and the project's defaults name runtimes or leave out global, the session attaches the defaults' global and runtimes; an explicit runtimes, even an empty one, wins. The daemon never applies the default agent and preset: the creation's selection is the client's to set.
  • Membership. SessionMeta.project is the project a session belongs to: a root's own, a delegated session's root's. A session whose project no longer exists has none. session.project.set moves a root session, also while it runs, which takes effect at its next run; a delegated session is project_root_session_only. Moving announces sessions.changed upserted, and never changes the session's attachments or agent.
  • Rename. project.update with name moves the memory folder under the memory lock before it rewrites the project; when the move fails nothing changes. Old project://<old>/… URLs no longer resolve.
  • Delete. project.delete is project_sessions_running, naming the root sessions in session_ids, while any session tree of the project is busy. Otherwise it deletes every session tree of the project as session.delete does (each announced as removed), then the project's whole memory folder, non-memory files included, then the project, and returns the counts.

Each change sends projects.changed to every connection. A failure to read or write a project is project_store_failed.

docs.title: Cron jobs
docs.text:
Since 1.15.0 the daemon keeps cron jobs: prompts it fires on a schedule, into an existing session or into a new session per fire (see the cron spec). A CronJob is its daemon-assigned id (eight lowercase letters and digits), an optional name, the prompt, the schedule, max_runs, the target, delivery for an in-session job, permission_mode for a new-session job, an optional max_consecutive_failures, enabled with a disabled_reason (finished, failed with failures, or disabled by the user or an agent), created_by ("user" or { agent: { agent, session } }), created_at, and its state: next_fire, runs, consecutive_failures, last_fire, and the history of its latest fires.

  • Schedule. { cron: "<minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week>" } in the daemon host's local time, day of month and day of week combining with OR when both are restricted; { in: "<n>s|m|h|d" } (1s to 365d) on create and update, which the daemon stores as { at: <time> }; or { at: <time> } in the future. max_runs is a whole number from 1 or "unlimited", 1 when omitted, for cron schedules only; crons.create and crons.update also take a whole number of 0 or less for "unlimited" (1.42.0), which jobs report as "unlimited". A job that reaches it is kept disabled as finished when you created it, and deleted when an agent did.
  • Target. { session: <root session ID> }, { subagent: <delegated session ID> }, or { new: <template> }. A template is { agent, preset?, model?, permission_rules?, runtimes?, global?, cwd?, project? }, checked as session.create would check it; its agent must be able to run as a root. delivery is queue (default) or steer; permission_mode defaults to auto_approve_n.
  • Fires. Each history entry is a CronFire: scheduled_at (absent for a run now), fired_at, run_now, the outcome (pending, delivered, skipped with a reason, or failed with an error), missed for a fire skipped because the daemon was down, the session_id it went to, and the run_id and run_end ({ status, at }) of the run its prompt landed in. A skip reason is previous_fire_not_delivered, previous_run_still_running, daemon_was_down, interrupted, firing_disabled, daemon_restarting (since 1.19.0), or session_held (since 1.34.0), an open set.
  • Run sessions. A new-session fire's session records the job in SessionMeta.cron ({ job_id, fired_at }, also on its session_created event) and is otherwise ordinary.
  • Waiting. A session targeted by an enabled job with a next fire lists scheduled_job in SessionMeta.waiting_on.

crons.run fires a job now, as a scheduled fire would; it is recorded as a run now and counts toward neither max_runs nor the failure count. Each change and fire sends crons.changed to every connection. An unknown job is cron_not_found, a refused value cron_invalid, and a failure to read or write crons.json cron_store_failed.

docs.title: Push notifications
docs.text:
Since 1.30.0 the daemon sends Web Push notifications to the browsers clients registered (push notifications spec): when a root session settles (its run ended and nothing but a recurring cron job can start another), when an approval or an ACP agent's question waits for the user, and when the persistent daemon goes down for a daemon.restart (to every device but the one whose connection asked: the one whose last notifications.subscribe came over it) and comes back up. [notifications] configures them.

  • Subscribing. A client subscribes the browser with the daemon's public_key (applicationServerKey), then sends the subscription's endpoint (an https:// URL), p256dh and auth keys (base64url), and a label of 1 to 80 characters to notifications.subscribe. A PushSubscription as clients see it is { id, label, push_service, created_at, last_sent_at?, last_error? }; the endpoint and keys are never sent back. A subscription the push service reports gone is removed.
  • Presence. client.presence names the session a connection shows the user; the daemon pushes nothing for that session's tree while any connection shows it, and since 1.51.0 it marks the tree's root read. It lasts until the next call or the connection's end.
  • Errors. An unknown subscription is push_subscription_not_found, a refused value push_subscription_invalid, and a push folder the daemon cannot read or write push_unavailable. Each subscription change sends notifications.changed to every connection.

docs.title: Restarting the daemon
docs.text:
Since 1.19.0, daemon.restart restarts the daemon: it relaunches its own executable with the same arguments and environment, so a restart applies the restart_required parts of the configuration status and runs a binary upgraded on disk. Any client holding the token may call it.

  • when: "idle" (the default) waits until no run is active in any session and no background call is pending: since 1.35.0 a call still running in the background, or one whose result is not yet committed, holds the restart too, since the shutdown would end it without a report. Meanwhile a new run (run.start, session.submit_input on an idle session, a producer's wake) is refused with daemon_restarting, queued input and producers' messages wait, and a cron fire is recorded as skipped with the reason daemon_restarting. A run's delegated children still start, as part of the turn being waited for.
  • when: "now" interrupts the running turns as a stop does; they end as cancelled and the restarted daemon closes out anything left. Background calls end without a report.
  • A second call while a restart is scheduled changes its when; now wins. Its scheduled is false.
  • daemon.restarting (when, active_runs, background_calls since 1.35.0, optional reason) reaches every connection when the restart is scheduled and whenever either count changes while it waits.
  • The restart stops the daemon as a shutdown does (runs, plugins, runtimes, and MCP servers stop and the session logs and stores are flushed), sends the replies already queued, and closes every client connection with WebSocket close code 1012 and the reason restarting. Clients reconnect as after any dropped connection; the handshake's engine_version tells them when the build changed.
  • restart_unsupported answers a daemon that cannot relaunch itself: only cookie daemon can, and an engine embedded in a test harness or another program cannot.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
plugins.list returns every configured plugin in the order its hooks run. A PluginInfo is { name, state, reason?, tools, hooks, subscribe_events, subscribe_bus, publish_bus, producer_messaging, dropped_events, stderr? }: its state (disabled, starting, connected, reconnecting, failed, or stopped), why it failed or last disconnected, the tools it declares and the names of the hooks it intercepts, what it streams and publishes, whether its producer messaging is open, how many notifications it dropped for falling behind, and the tail of its standard error.

plugins.restart starts a plugin again now: a failed or reconnecting plugin is started at once, and a connected one is stopped and started. An unknown or disabled plugin is an error (plugin request rejected). Status changes arrive as plugins.changed.

docs.title: ACP agents
docs.text:
Since 1.17.0 the daemon lists the external coding agents its runtimes host over the Agent Client Protocol (see the ACP agents spec) with its own agents:

  • An AgentDescriptor of the catalog view's agents has the optional runtime (runtime_id, agent, the agent's own ID on the runtime, and available) for an ACP agent exactly one runtime offers, and, since 1.21.0, runtimes, every runtime that offers it. Its ID is the key of the runtimes' declarations (claude); a session runs it on the one runtime it attaches that offers it, so clients show it as runnable for a draft or session with exactly one of those attached. Its resolved_fallback is the synthetic model acp/<agent ID>: a run selects it like any agent, and the agent chooses its own model. An offering runtime that is away, or has the agent disabled, is listed with available: false; an agent no runtime can run is runnable_as_root: false. Creating a session, starting a run, or delegating with it is refused at once when the session's runtimes cannot run it (none of them offers it, two do, or the one that does is away), and attaching a second runtime that offers a session's ACP agent is refused.
  • The event acp_session_started records the ACP session the agent talks to the session in (agent, runtime_id, runtime_agent, acp_session_id, cwd, protocol_version, agent_info, and how: new, resumed, or loaded). acp_session_updated carries what changed of the agent's commands (its slash commands: name, description, input_hint), options (its config options: id, name, category, current_value, values), and plan (a plan display block); each member is the whole new value, and clients keep the latest of each. Choosing a command sends /<name> <input> as the prompt's text.
  • Since 1.20.0, acp_session_started has steering when the agent takes messages into its running turn; without it, a message sent to steer waits for the agent's next turn, and clients label the Steer action as queueing. acp_session_updated may carry, each shown once where it arrives, a notice (severity info/warning/error, title, optional description), which was also how a compaction the agent reports reached clients before 1.41.0; steered (user_inputs, the sequence numbers of the user_input_submitted events, and producer_messages): input delivered into the running turn, which clients mark on the message; and tool_presentation (tool_call_id, presentation): a new title, hint, primary argument, arguments, and preview for one of the agent's tool calls, which replace the call's own (its tool identity stays).
  • Since 1.41.0, acp_session_updated may carry compaction (compaction_id, state in_progress/completed/failed/cancelled, and summary when it completed with one): a compaction of the agent's own conversation, recorded once as it starts and once as it ends. Clients show it as they show the session's own compaction; a failure also carries a warning notice saying why. It may also carry session_message (direction received/sent, peer, the other session as the daemon named it then, and text): a message between the agent's sessions, such as a subagent's task or its report, which clients show as they show a producer message. Before 1.41.0 both were notices.
  • Since 1.50.0, acp_session_updated may carry background_ended (tool_call_id, tool, display, started_at, and exit_code and signal when the agent reports them): a command of the agent's that ran in the background after its tool call ended, such as Claude Code's background shell, has ended. It is recorded where the end arrives, between runs too, before the run the end may wake, and clients show it as they show a background call's report.
  • Since 1.52.0, acp_session_updated may carry prompt_context: the text blocks the session's first prompt to the agent carried ahead of the input (the tool instructions, the skill listing, the attachments, the memory snapshot turn, and the agent document's body), recorded as the prompt is sent. Clients show it as a collapsed row.
  • Since 1.23.0, acp_session_updated may carry context (used, and size when the agent reports its window): the agent's context use from its latest usage_update, recorded as it changes. The agent's turns report no usage, so clients show used as the session's context, of a window of size tokens, until a model's turn reports its own.
  • Since 1.23.0, an option of options may have kind: boolean (left out for a select): an on/off option whose current_value is true or false and whose values are true (On) and false (Off), so a client that reads every option as a select can still set it. session.agent_option.set takes "true" or "false" for it, and the daemon sends the agent a boolean.
  • The agent's turns are model turns of acp/<agent ID>; the calls it reports are tool calls whose tool.source is acp (agent, runtime_id), and the calls it makes of cookie's tools through the MCP bridge are ordinary tool calls of its turn.
  • session.agent_option.set changes one of the session's options and answers the options after the change.
  • Since 1.26.0 each entry of an agent's runtimes (and runtime) has options, the config options a new ACP session of the agent starts with on that runtime, as the daemon last saw them with the agent document's acp.mode, acp.config, and models applied, and input_media, the files the agent takes in a prompt (image, audio, and text entries, as input_media on a model); both are empty until the agent has started there. A draft offers those options, the model-category one as its model and the thought_level one as its variant, and sends its choices as session.create's agent_options ([{ option_id, value }], at most 64, each option once; refused for an agent that is not an ACP agent). The session records them as acp_session_updated.starting_options, and each new ACP session of the session applies them after acp.config and the document's models; one the agent does not offer then is skipped with a diagnostic.
  • The display block plan (entries, each content, status pending/in_progress/completed, optional priority high/medium/low) reaches a client older than 1.17.0 as its text.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Since 1.25.0 an agent of a run can ask the user a question: an ACP agent's elicitation/create (see the ACP agents spec). The run waits on it, and clients show it as waiting on the user.

  • elicitation_requested (run-bound) carries elicitation_id, agent (who asks), the optional tool_call_id it belongs to, message, and exactly one of form and url. A form has an optional title and description and fields, each with name (its member in the answer), optional title and description, required, and input, tagged by type: text (min_length, max_length, pattern, which is shown but not checked, format email/uri/date/date-time, default), choice (choices, each value, title, optional description; default), multi_choice (choices, min_items, max_items, default), number and integer (minimum, maximum, default), and boolean (default). An input of a type a client does not know cannot be filled in; a question with neither form nor url can only be declined or cancelled. A url question asks the user to open the page (show the whole URL and its host first); accepting means the user agreed to open it.
  • elicitation.respond answers it: accept with content, the form's values by field name (text and choices as strings, multi-choices as arrays of strings, numbers, booleans), decline, or cancel. The daemon checks an accepted form against its fields and refuses a value that does not fit with elicitation_answer_invalid, leaving the question waiting.
  • elicitation_resolved records the answer: elicitation_id, action, content for an accepted form, answered_by (user; unattended, a decline for a session whose permission mode is auto_approve_n or a headless run; run_ended, a cancel as the run was cancelled or ended; completed, an accept when the agent reported that the URL's interaction finished; unsupported, a decline of a form with a required input this daemon cannot show), and the daemon's reason when it answered. Clients stop showing a question when it is resolved or its run finishes.

docs.title: Provider sign-in
docs.text:
A provider whose descriptor lists sign_in_methods is connected by a browser sign-in instead of typed credentials (since 1.49.0); a sign-in method is never in auth_methods, so older clients do not offer it, and provider.connect refuses one with provider_sign_in_rejected. The daemon holds the PKCE verifier, does the code exchange, and keeps the tokens; only the single-use authorization code crosses the connection.

  1. The client binds a loopback listener on redirect_path and calls provider.auth.begin with its http://127.0.0.1:<port><redirect_path>. A client that cannot listen (a web page) names any port and asks the user to paste the address the browser fails to load; a page served from loopback, on the daemon's machine, passes null and lets the daemon listen.
  2. The user signs in at authorization_url.
  3. The client hands the address the browser landed on to provider.auth.complete. When the daemon listened itself, provider.auth.completed reports the outcome instead.

The connected provider's sign_in_account names the account, and sign_in_required turns true when the sign-in can no longer refresh; the user signs in again with the same flow. provider.disconnect signs out and revokes the sign-in. Every failure is provider_sign_in_rejected, whose reason starts with the sign-in's own code: sign_in_denied, sign_in_not_eligible, sign_in_scope_missing, sign_in_state_mismatch, sign_in_expired, sign_in_not_pending, sign_in_client_rejected, invalid_redirect_uri, invalid_callback, sign_in_required, sign_in_failed, sign_in_unsupported, sign_in_method_unknown, or sign_in_method_not_connectable.

docs.title: The catalog view
docs.text:
runtime.snapshot.get returns, and runtime.changed carries, a ModelCatalogView:

{ "revision": "<opaque>",
  "catalog": { "source": "network", "stale": false, "age": "current",
               "provider_quarantine_count": 0, "model_quarantine_count": 0,
               "last_error": null },
  "providers": [ … ], "models": [ … ], "agents": [ … ] }
  • revision is one opaque string: it changes whenever anything the view shows changes. Clients compare it and send it back, never parse it. provider.connect and provider.disconnect take the revision of the view their form was filled from as expected_revision; a view whose catalog (for a connect) or provider state (for a disconnect) has changed since is refused with catalog_revision_conflict or runtime_revision_conflict, and the client reads the view again.
  • catalog says where the model catalog stands: its source (network, cache, or bootstrap), whether it is stale, its age (current, older_than_seven_days, or older_than_thirty_days), the records it quarantined, and its nullable last_error.
  • providers, models, and agents are client-facing descriptors only: no frozen model bindings, recipe identities, fingerprints, compiler versions, or the internal revisions and counters the view's revision stands for. models lists only selectable models; an agent's resolved_fallback names model selections. Since 1.22.0 an agent also has unset_models, the configuration fields (default_model, small_model) its models entries name that are not set, omitted when empty; those entries are skipped.
  • input_media on every model says what it accepts in user input, one entry per kind (an open label: image, pdf, audio, or video; and text, which only an ACP agent's AgentRuntime.input_media lists):
{ "kind": "image", "mime_types": ["image/jpeg", "image/png"],
  "max_bytes": 7864320, "max_dimension": 16384, "max_pixels": 16777216,
  "max_count": 20 }

The limits are effective: the lowest of the model's catalog capability, the delivery limits of its adapter family for a user turn, and the attachment caps (20 MiB, or 25 MiB for video). mime_types lists the model's types an upload can be recognized as from its content; max_dimension and max_pixels are present for images. A kind absent from the list is not accepted: clients offer attachments only for the kinds of the session's selected model and check sizes before uploading.

docs.title: Model availability
docs.text:
Unusable models are visible instead of silently dropped. Each ProviderDescriptor carries:

  • model_counts: available, quarantined, unsupported, needs_setup, and needs_credentials counts over the provider's catalog rows (deprecated, disabled, and non-text models are not counted).
  • unavailable_models: one entry per unusable model with id, display_name, kind (the four unavailable kinds above), and a nullable reason (the quarantine code or compiler reason). The list is strictly sorted by id and is populated only for configured (authored or stored) providers; unconfigured providers report counts alone.
  • documentation_url and environment: the models.dev doc URL and env variable names. They are display hints; cookie never reads those variables.

docs.title: Goal/producer integration handoff
docs.text:
The engine implements these methods through its per-session actor. Goal mutations are root-only; producer inspection is available for any owned session. Tool calls declare their output channels, and results carry terminal output references and a display independent of their output.

Surface Public contract Implementation owner Goal projection GoalState, GoalItem, GoalStatus, GoalId Engine; TUI renders durable events Goal read SessionGoalGetParams/Result, get_session_goal Engine; TUI/clients call async API Activation SessionGoalSetParams/Result, set_session_goal User-only root command, rejects active/paused goal Lifecycle SessionGoalLifecycleParams/Result, change_session_goal_lifecycle, GoalLifecycleAction User-only root pause/resume/cancel; reject stale/terminal goal Model tools GoalGetParams/Result, GoalSetParams, GoalUpdateParams/Result Root-only goal_get/goal_set/goal_update, frozen at run admission Runtime inspection SessionProducersParams/Result, session_producers, ProducerRegistration, ProducerSourceState Session runtime snapshot, not global catalog snapshot or persistence Producer messaging Producer{Register,Send,Discard,Unregister}Params/Result producer/* requests of plugins and runtimes; SDK mirrors register/send/discard/unregister Recovery handshake RecoveryStartParams, RecoveryCompleteParams/Result, RecoveryOutcome producer/recovery/start daemon notification (no deadline/response); completion request

Goal activation accepts an optional selection: RunSelection, including agent, model, variant, and preset. The engine validates and persists this selection before scheduling a wake, so it survives waiting for producers and restarting. Lifecycle requests accept selection only with action: "resume"; pause and cancel reject a supplied selection. Resuming without it preserves the goal's previous selection. If activation omitted it and no later resume supplied one, automatic runs use the latest persisted run selection, falling back to the session's creation selection. None of these changes mutate an already-running turn's frozen selection or attribution.

GoalItem { description, finished } has no item ID. GoalUpdateParams { items } replaces the entire ordered checklist through the session actor: the last accepted update wins for the current/latest session goal at actor acceptance. Model updates have no goal_id, expected_revision, or lost-update protection. An older run's update can intentionally affect a newly activated active or paused goal; updates reject if the current goal is absent or terminal. Internal GoalId and engine-owned GoalState.revision remain for durable state and reminder identity. User lifecycle RPC controls retain SessionGoalLifecycleParams.goal_id and expected_revision and reject stale identities and revisions. GoalSetParams { objective, items? } lets the model start a goal when none is active or paused, as session.goal.set does; no model tool can change an objective or issue lifecycle commands. Empty lists preserve the active/paused lifecycle and can bootstrap an active goal without completion. The goal tools declare no permission: they are published to every root run (an ACP agent's only while the goal is active or paused), and every call is allowed. There is no permission action or goal configuration for them.

To preserve strictly increasing event revisions, an all-finished update appends checklist revision r+1, then completion revision r+2, and returns the final state. Recovery repairs a missing completion event after a committed all-finished checklist. Empty checklists never complete through this rule.

See Events for admission/commit coverage and owned-message discard, and Plugin development for method names, idempotency, recovery, and the no-implicit-registration requirement.

docs.title: What a session waits on
docs.text:
Since 1.9.0 every SessionMeta carries waiting_on: what will start the session's next run without the user, each kind once and in this order, and omitted when nothing will. It is an open enum; a client reads a kind it does not know as something the session waits on.

Kind The session waits on Source goal Its goal, which is active: goal mode keeps scheduling runs. A paused, completed, or cancelled goal schedules none. Root sessions only. The fold of the goal events, so the metadata cache and a rebuild of it keep it background_call One of its background calls, whose <background_result> starts a run The daemon's live background calls subagent A direct child running a turn on its own (one session.background.list lists), a background delegation still queued or running, or a direct child that itself waits on a background call, an external producer, or a subagent (recursively), so it can still wake and report; its <subagent_report> starts a run The daemon's live runs, delegations, and its children's live waits external_producer A plugin or runtime that holds a live producer registration for the session and may send to it The daemon's live registrations

The last three end with the daemon: a restart kills background calls and drops registrations, so they are never written to the metadata cache and a client never shows one a restart ended. A delegated session reports its own background calls, subagents, and producers; its parent reports its turns as subagent. Accepted producer messages that have not started a run yet are not listed: a message to an idle session starts its run at once, and one queued behind a running run starts the next.

waiting_on is reported whatever status says. A session list shows a session that is running as running, else one that waits on something as waiting, else a failed, cancelled, or interrupted last run as a problem, and nothing for an idle or completed one; cookie_agent_client_state::activity implements that order. sessions.changed upserted announces every change: a goal activated, paused, resumed, completed, or cancelled; a background call detached or reported; a child's turn started or ended; a delegation or external registration made or dropped; a child started or stopped waiting on something live. A session the daemon evicted from memory keeps reporting what it waits on. A 1.8 daemon sends no waiting_on.

docs.title: Unread sessions
docs.text: Since 1.51.0 a root session's SessionMeta carries unread: true (left out when false) while it has a finished turn, an approval, or a question the user has not seen (spec). The daemon marks a root unread when it settles (the case that sends a settle push), or when an approval in its tree escalates to the user or an ACP agent there asks a question, while no connection reports presence (client.presence) on a session of its tree; [notifications] decides only whether a push goes out. A client.presence naming any session of the tree marks the root read, and session.unread.set marks roots either way. The state lives in <data_root>/unread.json and survives restarts; it is not in the session log, so it moves neither last_event_seq nor the activity times. Delegated sessions are never unread. Each change sends sessions.changed upserted. A 1.50 daemon sends no unread and answers session.unread.set with -32601.

docs.title: Held sessions
docs.text:
Since 1.34.0 a session whose run the user stopped (run.cancel) while something could start the next one on its own, or whose runs failed more than [model_retry] standard_retries times in a row, is held (spec). Nothing starts a run of it on its own: its pending producer messages wait, goal reminders stop, a plugin's or runtime's producer.send is refused with producer_rejected, a cron fire into it is skipped as session_held, and mail from any agent but its parent fails with send_message:recipient_held. The engine's own reports (subagent turns, delegations, background calls) are accepted and wait.

SessionMeta.held carries the reason while it lasts, from the latest automatic_runs_held event. It ends with automatic_runs_resumed, written by session.held.resume or by the parent's mail to its subagent, or with any input the user submits; the failure count starts over then. A run that a daemon restart interrupted is neither a stop nor a failure: it resumes as before. Clients show the hold and offer Resume in place of Send; a session held for failures sends a push notification, one the user stopped does not.

docs.title: Where a root's subagents work
docs.text: Since 1.10.0 a root session's SessionMeta carries delegated_attachments: the attachments its subagents were created with that it records neither as its own attachments nor as delegated before, in the order they brought them, global aside, and the same runtime, capability, and workspace once. It is the fold of the root's delegated_attachments_added events (see Events), so the metadata cache keeps it. It only grows: a child that finishes or is evicted, and a detach on the root, leave it as it is. A client builds a root's badges from attachments followed by delegated_attachments (cookie_agent_client_state::badges), and a child's from its own attachments only. A delegated session's list is empty, and a 1.9 daemon sends none.

docs.title: User steering
docs.text:
run.steer requires an active target run. It immediately appends user_input_admitted and returns { "accepted": true }; admission does not change model history. At each completed tool batch and no-tool completion boundary, all pending inputs are promoted FIFO as separate user_input_submitted events before the next request. A no-tool boundary with no pending input completes the run.

run.steer also returns the admission's user_input_seq. Terminal run events void anything still pending.

docs.title: The session's model selection
docs.text: A session has one model selection (agent, model, variant, preset) that every client shares. session.select_model validates a selection as a run start would and appends a runless session_model_selected event under the caller's origin; selecting what the session already has records nothing and returns { "changed": false }. cookie_agent_protocol::SessionModelState folds the session's selection from its events: the creation selection, then each run's selection and successful fallback, with an explicit pick replacing it and dropping any fallback the session had settled on. A run started without a selection (session.submit_input with selection omitted, or a queued input queued that way) uses it, and clients keep their drafts at it, so the latest pick from any client is what the next message runs on. A request that names its own selection still runs on that one.

docs.title: Submitting from several clients
docs.text:
session.submit_input is how clients send a message without first finding out whether the session is running. On the session's actor it either starts a run ({ "outcome": "started", "run_id" }), or, while a run is active, follows delivery:

  • steer admits the input as run.steer does: { "outcome": "steered", "run_id", "user_input_seq" }.
  • queue appends a runless user_input_queued event holding the input, its selection, and client_run_id: { "outcome": "queued", "queued_seq" }.

A run that starts or ends while the request is in flight only changes which outcome happens; the daemon retries a few times before answering with a session_running conflict. An omitted selection means the session's current selection. A plugin that handles the input yields { "outcome": "handled", "reason" }. Retrying the same client_run_id with the same input returns the original run or queue entry; different input is an idempotency_conflict.

When a run completes normally, the daemon starts a run with the oldest queued input under the origin of the client that queued it; that run's run_started carries the entry's client_run_id, which removes it from the queue. A failed, cancelled, or interrupted run voids every queued input, and the daemon appends user_input_queue_voided when a queued input cannot start at all. Clients reduce the queue with cookie_agent_protocol::QueuedInputs, as the daemon does.

session.recall_input takes back one pending steered input or one queued input by its seq. Since 1.31.0 any client may, another client's input too: the recall is recorded under the origin of the client that asked, and the content goes back to it. A daemon before 1.31.0 lets only the client whose origin admitted it, and answers another client { "outcome": "not_owner" }. A pending input is withdrawn with user_input_recalled and a queued one with user_input_queue_recalled; both return { "outcome": "recalled", "content" }, the input's content for editing. An input that was already promoted, started, or voided returns { "outcome": "gone" }.

run.start on a session whose run is active fails with code -32602 and RunStartConflict data whose code is session_running, so a client can fall back to session.submit_input.

docs.title: Revert and fork
docs.text:
session.revert is idle-only. The target must be a positive existing sequence, and expected_last_seq must be the session's current last event sequence: a session that has moved on since the client looked (another client's turn, say) is refused with the error stale_revert, whose data carries current_last_seq, so a revert never deletes what the requester has not seen. The engine removes every event after it from the log (a run left with nothing but its run_started goes too), closes any run, tool call, internal agent, or approval the cut left open, and deletes the subagent sessions created by removed delegations; a running one refuses the revert. Later appends reuse the freed sequence numbers. Subscribers receive a rewound notification (see Subscriptions).

session.fork takes a client_fork_id: while the daemon runs, a retry with the same key and target returns the first fork instead of making another, and the same key with a different target is an idempotency_conflict. session.fork may read an active source but requires a persisted prefix that contains a submitted user message. The fork copies that prefix exactly under a new session ID, closes any copied in-flight run locally, appends (fork) to the title, and continues with new physical sequences.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
session.delete { session_id, expected_last_seq } deletes a root session's whole tree from disk: the root, every delegated session under it, their events and metadata, and the tree's artifacts. Nothing is kept for undo, so clients ask the user first. It is new in 1.5.0: a client sends it only to a daemon of minor 5 or later, and reads -32601 as "the daemon is too old to delete sessions".

expected_last_seq is the root's last_event_seq from the metadata the user confirmed. The delete is refused, changing nothing, when:

  • the session does not exist (session_not_found);
  • it is a delegated session (not_a_root_session, with its root_session_id): a tree is deleted through its root;
  • a session of the tree has an active run, a compaction, or a subagent waiting for a slot (session_tree_running, with the busy running_session_id);
  • another cookie process holds the tree's owner.lock (session_owned_elsewhere);
  • the root's last event is no longer expected_last_seq (session_changed, with current_last_seq).

The checks run in this order, so a running tree is session_tree_running even when its guard is stale too, as it is while a run streams past the listed last_event_seq; session_changed means the tree is idle and moved.

A tree this daemon does not hold is deleted under its lock without being opened, so nothing is appended to it first. The tree's background calls are stopped without a report and its uploads in progress are dropped. The daemon moves the tree's directory aside to a .deleted-<root>-<id> tombstone in the work directory, which commits the delete, forgets the tree, sends sessions.changed removed for each deleted session (the root first) to every connection, and removes the tombstone; a daemon that stopped in between removes the tombstone when it next opens the directory. Each connection's subscriptions to the deleted sessions end with them: no further events.subscription arrives for them and events.unsubscribe answers false. The result is { "deleted": [<root>, <descendants>…] }.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
Notification Payload runtime.changed The previous view's revision, the complete new catalog view, and the change reasons, sorted and without repeats events.subscription One stored event, live-only stream output, a session sequence gap, or a rewind events.plugin Session-scoped non-durable plugin event sessions.changed One session index change: upserted, removed, approvals_changed, permission_mode_changed, or resync mcp.changed MCP server configuration or status changed; optional failures runtimes.changed A runtime template was registered or an instance's status changed; optional failures background.changed A subscribed session's background calls changed: session_id and its current calls plugins.changed A plugin's status changed; an empty object machines.changed The machine registry changed, or a runtime joined a new machine; an empty object memory.changed A memory file changed through the daemon; an empty object projects.changed A project was created, changed, or deleted; an empty object crons.changed A cron job was created, changed, fired, or deleted; an empty object notifications.changed A push subscription was added, changed, or removed (since 1.30.0); an empty object daemon.restarting A restart is scheduled: when (idle or now), the active_runs and background_calls (since 1.35.0, omitted when zero) it still waits for, and an optional reason to show (since 1.19.0; see Restarting the daemon) onboarding.changed onboarding.get's answer changed (since 1.22.0): the new answer, after a configuration apply or reload, a provider connected or disconnected, or a model becoming available or not provider.auth.completed A sign-in whose redirect the daemon caught itself ended (since 1.49.0): provider_id, and the account or the error

A background call in session.background.list and background.changed is { job, tool, tool_call_id, display?, started_at, detached_at, by, agent_task? }: the job ID, the tool's name as the model called it, the call it came from, its display argument, when the call started and when it moved to the background, and who moved it (model or user). agent_task: true (since 1.40.0) marks an ACP agent's own command still running after its call ended: job is its terminal, and session.background.stop refuses it, since only the agent can stop it. The list lives in the daemon, so it never shows a call a daemon restart killed. background.changed reaches only connections subscribed to the session; one that falls behind gets every subscribed session's list again.

docs.title: Daemon-wide changes
docs.text:
runtime.changed, sessions.changed, mcp.changed, runtimes.changed, plugins.changed, machines.changed, memory.changed, projects.changed, crons.changed, notifications.changed, daemon.restarting, and onboarding.changed reach every connection from its handshake on, whether or not it subscribed to any session, so each client sharing a daemon stays current with what the others do. Clients ignore notification methods they do not know.

sessions.changed carries one change, tagged by change:

change Fields Sent when upserted session (SessionMeta) A session, root or delegated, is created, first persisted, or reverted, or its status, title, attachments, delegated attachments, project, what it waits on (waiting_on), or whether it is unread (unread, since 1.51.0) change removed session_id A revert deleted a delegated session, or session.delete deleted a session of a tree; the connection's subscription to it has ended approvals_changed root_session_id, session_id An approval in any session of the tree was requested, escalated, decided, or cancelled; approval.list for the root shows the result permission_mode_changed root_session_id, mode, changed_by session.set_permission_mode changed the tree's mode; changed_by is the caller's origin resync none This connection fell more than 256 changes behind and missed some; refetch session.list, approvals, and permission modes

The permission mode is runtime-only and has no event, so permission_mode_changed is the only way other clients learn of a change.

runtime.changed notifications form a chain through previous_revision. A connection that falls more than 64 notifications behind receives one with a null previous_revision, the current snapshot, and the reason resync; a client that holds a different revision refetches runtime.snapshot.get rather than trusting either. A status mcp.changed is an empty object; bursts coalesce into one notification, and a client refetches mcp.server.list. runtimes.changed and plugins.changed work the same way for runtimes.list and plugins.list, machines.changed for machines.list and runtimes.list, memory.changed for memory.list, projects.changed for projects.list, crons.changed for crons.list, and notifications.changed for notifications.get.

docs.title: Connection failures
docs.text:
When an MCP server fails to connect, or drops and does not reconnect, and when a runtime instance fails to start, the daemon sends one notification for it with a failures list to each connection subscribed (events.subscribe) to a session that uses it. Each entry names the affected session_ids among that connection's subscriptions:

Notification failures entry mcp.changed runtime_id hosting the server (global for top-level [mcp]), workspace of the hosting instance when its runtime has one, server, reason, session_ids runtimes.changed runtime_id, capability, workspace when the capability takes one, reason, session_ids

Subscribing to a session also sends the failures that already affect it, so a client that opens a session after its servers failed still learns why their tools are missing. Failures are live notifications, not session events; the TUI shows each as an error row in every named session it displays. failures is omitted when empty.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text: mcp.server.list returns the servers of every runtime: the global runtime's top-level [mcp] servers first, then those each running coding runtime instance hosts, from its [runtimes.<id>] table in the daemon's configuration, a dial-in runtime's included (since runtime protocol 1.10.0; an older dial-in runtime hosts [runtimes.local.mcp] of its own machine). Each entry has the hosting runtime_id, the hosting instance's workspace (absent for global), name, source, definition, state, tool_count, message, and auth_in_progress. Since 1.36.0 it also has server_tools: every tool the server lists, by the server's own name (what include_tools and exclude_tools match) and in its order, as { name, filtered }, with filtered: true (omitted when false) for a tool its filters left out; absent while the server has listed nothing and from a runtime older than runtime protocol 1.9.0. source is user_file (the daemon's config.toml), runtime (a global server changed in the running daemon only), or, since 1.12.0, machine: defined on the hosting runtime's machine (an older dial-in runtime's own servers), which the daemon does not read, so its definition is empty (no command or url). source is an open enum; a 1.11 client reads machine as runtime. Before 1.12.0 a dial-in runtime's own servers were left out of the list. Since 1.13.0 an entry of a runtime other than global may carry scope, runtime or workspace (an open enum; an unknown value reads as workspace; see scope): a runtime server is one process its runtime shares across its workspaces, listed once without a workspace; a workspace server is listed for each instance that hosts it, with the instance's workspace, and, while no instance of a connected runtime hosts it, once without one, disconnected with the message "starts when a workspace opens". state is connected, connecting, reconnecting, failed, needs_auth, disabled, or disconnected. A reconnecting server dropped and is being restarted: its tools stay published and calls fail with the runtime_unavailable failure code until it reconnects or, after every attempt failed, becomes failed and its tools are dropped (see MCP). The mcp.server.* mutations act on the global runtime's servers, or, since 1.37.0, with runtime_id, on another runtime's (see Runtime tables); mcp.auth.* act on the global runtime's. mcp.server.reconnect { name, runtime_id?, workspace? } reconnects a server of any runtime and waits for the attempt: without runtime_id (or with global) a top-level server, otherwise the one the instance of runtime_id at workspace hosts, as mcp.server.list names them; without workspace, a runtime-scoped server of runtime_id (a waiting workspace-scoped one fails: it starts with a workspace).

docs.title: Runtime tables
docs.text:
Since 1.37.0 clients change a runtime's [runtimes.<id>] table in the daemon's config.toml: its MCP servers with the mcp.server.* mutations and a runtime_id other than global, and its ACP agent declarations with runtimes.agents.*. Each change is one configuration edit, written and applied as config.apply writes (it fails config_conflict when the file changed meanwhile), and a connected runtime gets it at once (runtime protocol 1.10.0, runtime/settings_changed). A runtime server's definition carries scope (runtime or workspace), which a global server refuses. A server another dial-in runtime of an older cookie defines on its own machine (source: machine) is not in the file and cannot be changed.

  • mcp.server.rename moves the server's table in one edit. A global server changed in the running daemon only, without mcp.server.persist, is refused, and a global server's OAuth sign-in does not follow its new name.
  • Agents every runtime offers. Since 1.43.0, runtimes.agents.* with runtime_id global change the top-level [acp.agents] table: the ACP agents every runtime but global offers, each run on the runtime's machine. A runtime's own declaration of the same key replaces it there, with another command or enabled = false to leave it off; removing that one offers every runtime's again. A global declaration is available while some runtime runs it. Before 1.43.0 a daemon refuses global.
  • runtimes.agents.list returns each declaration's agent (its key and the ID of the agent it offers), definition, available (the runtime reported it and a session that attaches the runtime can run it now), and documents: the agent documents that run it, the one of its own ID and the templates whose acp.agent names it, as config.get paths.
  • runtimes.agents.rename moves the declaration. When no other runtime declares the old key, the same edit moves agents/<agent>.md to agents/<new_agent>.md (moved); templates whose acp.agent names the old key are not rewritten, and stale_templates lists them. Sessions keep the agent ID they recorded.
  • runtimes.agents.remove leaves the agent's documents in place.

The shared client maps these to ClientDelivery variants (Live, replay deliveries, PluginEvent, RuntimeChanged, RecoveryFailed), so a UI consumes one ordered stream and never parses raw JSON-RPC frames.

Tool display comes from tool_call_progress and tool_call_terminated events; retained output is read through its artifact references. Raw tool output is not streamed to clients.

text_delta, reasoning_delta, and tool_call_progress are live-only: events.subscription delivers them as transient messages carrying the durable after_seq they follow instead of a sequence of their own, and they are never stored or replayed. model_output_started durably marks where each streamed part began. See live-only stream output.

The MCP OAuth callback runs on the client, so a daemon reached through a tunnel or on another machine can still be authorized from the client's browser. mcp.auth.begin requires redirect_uri, where the browser lands: the client's own loopback callback, plain http to a loopback IP literal or localhost (http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path>), or, since 1.11.0, an https address such as the web client's own page with ?oauth=callback. Any path and query are allowed; user info and fragments are refused. Before 1.11.0 the daemon accepts only loopback IP literals with a port and no query, so a client offers an https redirect only to a 1.11 daemon. With dynamic client registration the daemon registers a client for the redirect of each flow (as native for a loopback redirect, web for an https one); a configured client_id is used as is, and its authorization server must allow the redirect. The client then sends the browser's redirect to mcp.auth.complete { server, callback_url }; the daemon keeps the PKCE verifier, exchanges the code, and stores the tokens, which never cross the connection. A callback_url that is not a redirect to the pending redirect_uri (its scheme, host, port, path, and every query parameter of its own) with a code or error parameter is rejected and leaves the flow waiting. Any other completion, including a state mismatch, ends it. A begin with the pending redirect_uri returns the same authorization URL; one with a different redirect_uri replaces the pending flow.

A client can configure permissions before a session exists. session.create accepts an optional permission_mode for the new tree and optional permission_rules, which are validated like any overlay (no duplicate action, runtime selector, and pattern, at most 256, and no runtime selector on message or skill) before the session is created and committed as its first session_permission_overlay_set event, so the first run already sees them. session.permission.preview { selection, rules } returns the effective permissions such a session would have, computed from the selection's frozen agent policy exactly as session.permission.get computes them for a live session.

Background jobs report through the tool { tool_call_id } producer owner (the completion report of a job a tool call started, such as a bash call with background: true), and producer_message_accepted may carry retained_output naming the job's captured output artifacts.

Tool output that fits its preview is stored only in the result's output: RetainedToolStream.reference and sha256 are absent for such a stream, and RetainedToolOutput.reference is absent when no stream needed an artifact. RetainedToolStream.dropped_bytes is present when output past the 128 MiB capture limit was not retained. A result always carries its whole display: the ranges of output a session log stores display text as (Events) never reach clients.

Session metadata includes additive skipped_events entries with the physical sequence (or source line number when no sequence was readable) and a safe reason. An empty array means the event log loaded without skipped records. Optional-field degradations remain available to the engine as load diagnostics but are not reported as skipped events.

See Events for event payloads and durability semantics.

docs.title: Runtime Protocol
docs.text:
The runtime protocol connects the daemon to a runtime: a source of tools and workspace context that runs outside the engine (see the runtimes specification). The daemon's built-in local coding runtime speaks it on a task of the daemon's own process over an in-memory frame pair; a configured [runtimes.<id>] template runs a command, typically ssh host cookie runtime serve --stdio, and speaks it over the child's stdin and stdout. The local and remote paths are one code path. The global runtime does not speak it; the engine calls it in-process.

The wire types live in the Apache-2.0 protocol crate's cookie_agent_protocol::runtime_protocol and the JSON-RPC peer both ends run in cookie_agent_protocol::peer, so the plugin SDK shares them; cookie_agent_runtime_api::protocol and ::rpc re-export them. The coding runtime's server is in cookie_agent_coding_runtime::server and the daemon's client in the engine's runtimes::remote module. Plugins declare and run their tools with this protocol's tool messages over their own connection (see Plugin development).

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
The daemon reaches a runtime in one of two ways, and speaks the same protocol over either:

  • Spawned: it runs a template's command and frames the child's stdio, one message per line, as above.
  • Dial-in: the runtime opens a WebSocket to the daemon's /runtime?id=<runtime ID> endpoint with the daemon's bearer token in an Authorization: Bearer header, one message per text frame. The daemon then sends runtime/initialize exactly as for a spawned runtime, with no MCP servers: a dial-in runtime hosts its own. A dial-in runtime gets 30 seconds to answer runtime/initialize and each capability/open, and 3 seconds to answer runtime/shutdown. See Dial-in refusals for how the daemon refuses one. Either end that ends the connection sends a close frame, normal closure (1000), and waits up to 2 seconds for the other's answer; a runtime that stops does so before it exits. The daemon reads a normal closure, going away (1001), or a close frame without a code as the runtime disconnecting, and another code, or a connection that ended without a close frame, as a failure with that code or error.

docs.title: Dial-in refusals
docs.text:
Since 1.2.0 the daemon says why it refuses a runtime that dials in, and whether dialing in again can succeed (runtime_protocol::dial_in). A request it can refuse from the request alone is answered before the WebSocket upgrade with an HTTP status and the reason as the plain-text body:

Status Reason Permanent 400 The runtime ID does not match [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}. yes 401 The bearer token is missing or wrong. yes 403 The ID is reserved (global, local) or names a [runtimes.<id>] template the daemon configures, or the request carries an Origin header. yes 409 A runtime is connected under the ID, or being accepted under it, now. The daemon may not have noticed yet that an earlier connection of the same runtime ended. no

A runtime that fails runtime/initialize after the upgrade, such as one of another major version or one that does not answer in time, sees the daemon close the connection with code 1011 and the reason as the close frame's reason, cut to the frame's 123 bytes. That refusal is not permanent.

A runtime stops dialing in after a permanent refusal and dials in again, after a wait, after any other, including a status this table does not list, such as one a proxy answers with. cookie runtime serve --daemon prints the reason either way, exits with an error on a permanent refusal, and checks its own ID first, so a malformed or reserved one never reaches the daemon. A daemon before 1.2.0 closes the connection after the upgrade without a reason for an ID it refuses, which a runtime can only treat as transient.

docs.title: Framing
docs.text:
• JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per frame: a frame of an in-memory transport, or one line of newline-delimited JSON over a byte stream such as a child's stdio (peer::LineTransport).
  • Both ends send requests. The daemon drives tools; a runtime reports progress back while a call runs. Request IDs are chosen by the sender and may be integers or strings, as JSON-RPC 2.0 allows; a reply echoes its request's ID. Both ends of this repository send integers.
  • The envelope is information. Members JSON-RPC does not define are ignored.
  • Bounded. No frame exceeds 48 MiB (runtime_protocol::MAX_FRAME_BYTES), which fits an execute reply carrying the largest attachment as base64 next to a full tool result. A sender refuses to send a larger message; a receiver that gets one closes the connection.
  • Information and commands. Every message is information except the ones a runtime sends that ask the daemon to act: tool/progress, tool/detachable, and the producer/* requests. Information ignores members its reader does not know, at any depth, and reads an enum value it does not know as that enum's fallback (see Open enums), so either end may be newer. A command is checked against its schema before it is decoded: a member, or an enum value or tag, the schema does not list is refused with -32602, data.code unknown_field or unknown_variant, and data.field set to its JSON path, such as progress.display.type. A sender gates new fields of a command on the receiver's version. The one exception is a display block of a kind the daemon does not know in a tool/progress replacement: it is only shown, so the daemon drops it with a diagnostic instead (see Display blocks).
  • Unreadable messages. A frame that is not JSON, or not a request, notification, or reply, closes the connection. A request whose params do not match its method is answered with -32602 (invalid_params, with serde's message as detail), and the connection stays up. A notification that cannot be read cannot be answered: the receiver reports it (the daemon in its log, a runtime on its standard error) and ignores it. The daemon also reports and ignores runtime/tools_changed from a runtime: only a plugin sends it.

docs.title: Open enums
docs.text:
An enum value a reader does not know reads as the fallback below. The fallbacks are chosen so that an older reader stays safe:

Value Where An unknown value reads as collision tool declarations prefix concurrency tool declarations exclusive, the most conservative result_truncation tool declarations bounded: the daemon still bounds the result tool error kind prepare, revalidate, and execute results; mcp/reconnect failed, a generic tool failure MCP server state capability/open and runtime/initialize results, mcp/changed, runtime/mcp_changed disconnected: no tools, and no retry as a failure MCP server scope the same workspace: hosted by an instance media delivery tool/prepare and tool/execute turns unknown: the tool does not attach that kind display block type prepare presentations, execute results, tool/progress replacements dropped, with a diagnostic (see Display blocks) media kind tool/prepare and tool/execute turns a label: a tool does not attach a kind it does not know

These are closed by design, since every reader must understand each value: a prepare result's and an execute outcome's status, an output's and an output declaration's kind, and a skill's source. The commands producer/send's mode and producer/recovery/complete's outcome are closed as every command is. The plugin protocol adds its own (see Plugin development).

docs.title: Version
docs.text:
The protocol version is a semver string, currently 1.12.0 (cookie_agent_protocol::RUNTIME_PROTOCOL_VERSION). The daemon sends its version in runtime/initialize and the runtime answers with its own. Each end reads the other's protocol_version from the raw JSON before it decodes anything else, so a peer of another version is answered with unsupported_protocol, naming both versions, rather than with a decoding error of a shape the two do not share; a hello without a readable version fails as invalid_params. Two versions are compatible when their majors are equal: a minor only adds, so the two ends use what the lower minor includes, and the patch never matters (see Compatibility). A 0.x build from before the freeze, and a build from before semver versions, which sends an integer, are refused the same way.

Both ends also send features: what their configuration enables, never what a version already implies. None are defined yet for runtimes; an end ignores a feature it does not know, and the daemon says so in its log.

Versions before 0.7.0 were integers. 3 removed tool/stdin and the stdin flag of tool/execute: tools no longer take input while they run.
