Code Meaning execution_failed The tool ran, or tried to, and failed. operation_changed What the call was prepared and approved against changed before it ran, such as an MCP tool list or a restarted runtime. prepared_capability_lost The prepared call was lost, for example in a daemon restart between preparation and execution. permission_denied A permission rule denied the call. runtime_unavailable The runtime or MCP server that owns the tool is reconnecting or dropped during the call. The call is not retried for the model; the tool stays published while its owner reconnects. unsupported_platform The tool cannot run on this platform. invalid_url, redirect_error, timeout, transport_error, unsupported_content_type webfetch failures (see Webfetch).

docs.title: Cancelling a run
docs.text:
Interrupting a run (run.cancel: the TUI's Ctrl-C or double Esc, the web client's Stop or Escape, a stop signal to cookie run) cancels every call it has in the foreground at once, and each call ends as cancelled:

  • bash kills the command's whole process group (a job object on Windows) with no grace period. Output still in flight drains for at most 250 ms, so a process that left the group and holds the pipes open does not hold the call.
  • A runtime's or plugin's tool gets tool/cancel. The coding runtime and the plugin SDK drop a call that has not stopped 2 s later.
  • An MCP tool stops waiting and sends the server notifications/cancelled for the request, as a call that reaches timeout_ms does.
  • webfetch drops its request.
  • A foreground delegate_subagent stops waiting; its subagent keeps running and reports its turn (see Background calls). Its result says so: The user interrupted this run. Subagent `<handle>` keeps running; its <subagent_report> arrives when its turn ends., followed by the handle's note.

Every other interrupted call ends with a result that names who stopped it: Interrupted by the user before it finished. for run.cancel, and for other cancellations a wording that names their cause, such as Interrupted by engine shutdown before it finished. (background tools spec, section 14). The engine waits at most 2 s for a call to stop on its own. A call still running then ends as cancelled with ; cleanup deadline elapsed added to that result, its late result is dropped, and the run records RunCancelled without waiting further. Calls in the background belong to the session, not the run, and keep running; stop_background stops them.

docs.title: Tool display
docs.text:
Every built-in tool describes its calls to clients as typed display blocks (the structured tool display spec). Display never enters model history: the output, title, and metadata the model reads are the same with or without it.

  • Presentation. tool_call_started.presentation carries a human title (such as Edit src/main.rs or Run `cargo test`), a hint for icons and grouping, the primary_argument shown beside the title, arguments (the call's arguments as blocks), and, for edit and write, a preview of what the call will do.
  • Results. A result's display replaces the live progress display when the call ends.
  • Diffs. edit and write show a diff with 1-based file line numbers and five lines of context on each side of each change. Changes whose context overlaps or touches share a hunk. A preview is as_of: prepare and a result as_of: execute; the two differ when the file changed between preparation and execution. A side with no lines in a hunk starts at the line before it (0 at the top of the file), as a unified diff numbers it.
  • Budget. A result's blocks share 64 KiB serialized. A block that had to be cut counts what it left out (omitted, omitted_lines, or omitted_rows) and, where its complete content exists, names it in full: an executed edit or write retains its complete diff (as unified-diff text, text/plain, named <file>.diff) and bash names its retained output. Previews and read excerpts have no full: nothing is retained when a call is prepared, and a read page is the file itself.

The per-tool Display sections below list each tool's hint, arguments, preview, and result blocks.

docs.title: Filesystem tools
docs.text:
read numbers lines from 1, and its offset is the 1-based line (or directory entry) to start at: offset=1, the default, is the first line, and an offset of 0 is refused. limit, 2000 lines or entries when left out, must be positive. An offset past the last line or entry is an error, except that line 1 of an empty file is an empty page. The path is resolved when the call is prepared; the content is read when it executes. A text line longer than 4 KiB is cut and ends with a ... [line truncated: N more bytes] marker. A page that leaves lines or entries out ends with a continuation marker that names the 1-based offset to read next: [N more lines; continue with offset=M] (or entries for a directory) when the limit stopped it, and [page cut at the result size limit; continue with offset=M] when it would have exceeded the result size limit. The metadata reports the same offset as next_offset. Media files are checked against the size limits before they are read in full.

memory_read and read_artifact page the same way: the same 1-based offset, the same limit and its default, the same numbering, line cut, page cap, and continuation marker (Memory tools, read_artifact).

write takes the file's complete content and says whether it Created <path> (N bytes). or Replaced <path> (N bytes).. edit requires oldString to occur exactly once, or at least once with replaceAll, and reports Edited <path>: N replacement(s).. When it occurs some other number of times, the call fails with `<oldString>` occurs N times in <path>; include more context so it occurs once or set replaceAll, the echoed text cut to 200 characters. A path that is not there fails read and edit with <path> does not exist. All three refuse arguments they do not define. Preparation checks the replacement against the current content so a mismatch fails before approval, but the edit itself is applied to the file's content at execution: changes made while an approval was pending are kept, and an oldString that no longer matches fails the call. Both tools publish through a staged file renamed over the target. Writes and edits that resolve to the same file share a serialization key and run one at a time, in call order, so same-file edits in one turn apply on top of each other.

Tool results may include image, PDF, audio, or video attachments. Attachments are validated, content-addressed, and supplied to models as file parts rather than embedded in text output.

docs.title: read
docs.text:
read(filePath: string, limit?: integer, offset?: integer)

Description sent to the model:

Read a file or a directory. A text file comes back as numbered lines, `N: text`, counting from 1. `offset` is the 1-based line to start at (default 1) and `limit` the most lines to return (default 2000). A line longer than 4 KiB is cut and ends with `... [line truncated: N more bytes]`, and a page stops before it passes the result size limit (about 2 MiB). A page that leaves lines out ends with a note such as `[120 more lines; continue with offset=2001]`: read again from that offset. An offset past the last line is an error. A directory lists its entries, one per line with `/` after a folder's name, paged by the same 1-based `offset` and `limit`. An image, video, or other media file the model accepts is attached instead.
Parameter Type Required Description filePath string yes Path to the file or directory. Relative paths resolve against the session working directory. limit integer no The most lines, or directory entries, to return. Defaults to 2000. offset integer no The 1-based line, or directory entry, to start at. Defaults to 1. Parameters JSON Schema 
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "filePath": {
      "description": "Path to the file or directory. Relative paths resolve against the session working directory.",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "limit": {
      "description": "The most lines, or directory entries, to return. Defaults to 2000.",
      "format": "uint",
      "minimum": 0,
      "type": [
        "integer",
        "null"
      ]
    },
    "offset": {
      "description": "The 1-based line, or directory entry, to start at. Defaults to 1.",
      "format": "uint",
      "minimum": 0,
      "type": [
        "integer",
        "null"
      ]
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "filePath"
  ],
  "title": "ReadArgs",
  "type": "object"

docs.title: Display
docs.text:
Paths are shown as the call's display argument shows them: relative to the workspace, or under ~. A path relative to the workspace (a display argument, an AGENTS.md file's name) separates its components with / on every platform. An absolute path (the workspace root a runtime reports, the path in a read page, a write's or an edit's result) is spelled the platform's way; on Windows it is the canonical long form without the \\?\ verbatim prefix, which is kept only where the path needs it (longer than MAX_PATH, or naming a device such as CON). The title and display argument already name the file, so no argument block repeats the path, and an edit's or a write's new text shows in its preview diff rather than again as an argument. A diff's and an excerpt's language comes from the path's extension (rs is rust, py is python, and so on; an extension the table does not know is passed on lowercased).

read write edit Hint file_read file_write file_edit Title Read <path> Write <path> Edit <path> Arguments key_value of offset and limit when the call gives them – key_value replace all: yes when set; newString as code in the path's language only when there is no preview (a call that failed to prepare) Preview – diff against the file preparation finds (created when there is none) diff of the edit applied to the content preparation read Result file_excerpt of the page (start_line is the 1-based offset, total_lines the file's), table (name, type) of a directory page, or media of the retained attachment diff against the text the write replaced diff built from the ranges the edit replaced
  • edit's diff comes from the replaced byte ranges, not a diff algorithm. Each replacement covers the whole lines it touches; replacements whose lines overlap (several on one line, for example) are one change, and lines oldString and newString share at either end are context. With replaceAll, each replacement is its own change, and the changes share hunks where their context overlaps.
  • write's diff is a line diff of the old and new text when both are UTF-8 of at most 1 MiB. Otherwise the diff has no hunks and counts the lines each side has (a side that is not text counts its newline-separated lines; a file that cannot be read counts none).
  • A read excerpt holds the page's lines as the output shows them, without line numbers (a cut long line keeps its [line truncated: N more bytes] marker), up to 64 KiB; the budget cuts the rest.

docs.title: Media reads
docs.text:
When read targets an image (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP), PDF, audio file (MP3, WAV, Ogg, FLAC), or video container (MP4/MOV/WebM/MKV/AVI/FLV/MPEG/WMV/3GPP), the file is sniffed by content (never by extension alone), strictly validated, and retained as an attachment. Whether the attachment reaches the model depends on two checks, in order:

  1. Model capability. The selected model must declare the matching input modality in the catalog (for example image for image/png). If it does not, the call fails with a tool error naming the model and the missing capability.
  2. Family deliverability. The provider's wire API must accept the media kind either inside a tool result or in a following user turn (see the delivery matrix). If it does not, the call fails with a tool error naming the family.

Both rejections are ordinary tool errors: the model sees the reason and can recover (for example by asking the user, or by sampling the file through bash). Size is clamped to the smaller of the model's advertised limit and the provider's inline limit (Anthropic: 7.5 MiB raw images, 10 MiB once base64-encoded; Bedrock: 3.75 MiB images, 4.5 MiB documents, ≈18.7 MiB raw video; Vertex: 7 MiB images; Gemini API: 14 MiB for any media, keeping the base64 request under its 20 MiB cap; other families: 20 MiB images, PDFs, and audio, or 25 MiB video). Media goes in the tool result when the family's wire API accepts it there; otherwise, when the API accepts that kind in user messages, it is sent as a file in one emitted user turn immediately after the tool result. Each model also advertises per-kind count limits, enforced per request (catalog models: 20 images, 5 PDFs, 5 audio files, and 2 videos, 1 on Bedrock). When the history holds more parts of a kind than the limit, the oldest are replaced in the outgoing request by a placeholder such as [image omitted: over the model's per-request image limit]; the saved history keeps them. The elided count grows in steps of half the limit, so later media appends to an unchanged prompt prefix (and prompt cache) until the limit is reached again, at the cost of sending as few as half the limit's parts right after a step. The latest user message is never elided: a request fails only when that message alone attaches more parts than the limit. Media parts do not contribute to context fit estimates, except video, which carries a flat conservative cost.

Before the count applies, every file part in the outgoing request that the attempt's model cannot take is replaced by a placeholder: user attachments, tool results' attachments, and emitted user messages alike. That covers a session that moved to another model, and a fallback to a model without the kind. A part fits when the model accepts its kind and media type within its byte limit, in a user turn for user and emitted messages and in a tool result for a tool result's attachment (the delivery matrix). The placeholder says why, for example [image omitted: acme/text-model does not accept images (screenshot.png, 471 KB)], [image omitted: acme/model does not accept image/webp (…)], [image omitted: larger than the 3.8 MB acme/model accepts (…)], or [image omitted: acme/model does not accept images in tool results (…)]. It depends only on the history and the model, so the prompt prefix stays cacheable; the saved history keeps the files.

MCP media blocks (images, audio, embedded resource blobs) follow the same gate and delivery selection. Blob resources without a declared MIME type are retained under the sniffed type. Results that would exceed the combined attachment budget keep what fits and degrade the rest to inline notes. The MCP wire format cannot author arbitrary additional messages.

Media does not survive context pressure. Tool-output elision removes the parent result and all of its emitted messages as one unit, and compaction checkpoints drop attachments. The model can re-read the source file to recover it.

docs.title: bash
docs.text:
bash(command: string, timeout?: integer)

Description sent to the model on Linux and macOS:

Execute one prepared shell command. The timeout applies in the background too: pass timeout 0 for commands that keep running, such as dev servers.

Description sent to the model on Windows, where commands run in Git Bash:

Execute one prepared Git Bash command. Single-quote native Windows paths (for example, 'C:\Users\name\file') or use C:/ paths. The timeout applies in the background too: pass timeout 0 for commands that keep running, such as dev servers.
Parameter Type Required Description command string yes timeout integer no Milliseconds before the command is killed; 0 or less never times out. Default: 120000. Parameters JSON Schema 
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "properties": {
    "command": {
      "type": "string"
    },
    "timeout": {
      "default": 120000,
      "description": "Milliseconds before the command is killed; 0 or less never times out.",
      "format": "int64",
      "type": "integer"
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "command"
  ],
  "title": "BashArgs",
  "type": "object"
}

bash takes one complete command. It is background-capable: the host adds background (default false), and the timeout applies in the background too, so a command that keeps running, such as a dev server, needs timeout: 0. The command's standard input is empty: tools take no input while they run. Standard output and standard error are streamed separately during execution and retained as separate artifacts for the terminal result.

On Linux and macOS the command runs in the runtime's shell environment, the environment of a new terminal of the user's, once one was captured; with a bash shell it is run as source '<snapshot>' 2>/dev/null followed by the command on its own line, so the user's options, aliases, and functions apply. The approval, permission rules, and transcript see the command as the model wrote it. Each command is a fresh shell: variables it exports, environments it activates, and directories it changes into do not carry over to the next.

The command runs in its own session and process group (a job object on Windows). When the shell exits, whatever it left in that group is killed, so cmd & and nohup cmd & do not outlive the call; only a process that leaves the group, such as one started with setsid, does.

A bash call reaches its detach point as soon as its command runs; its detach note is Process <pid>. In the background it keeps its timeout and process-group cleanup.

docs.title: Display
docs.text:
bash Hint shell Title Run `<command>`, the whole command on one line; clients cut it to the width they have Arguments the command as code in sh Preview – Result one terminal block: stdout and stderr segments in the order they were read, with exit_code

Terminal text keeps SGR colour sequences (ESC [ … m); every other escape sequence and control character but newline and tab is removed. An escape sequence split across two reads of a pipe is held until it is whole. Live progress appends each chunk to block 0 with its stream, so the live display is the same terminal block as it grows. The block holds at most 64 KiB of output: the rest, and whatever the display budget cuts, is counted in omitted_lines, and a cut block's full names the call's retained output: the first declared stream (stdout, then stderr) that outgrew its preview and was kept as an artifact. When neither stream was kept (both fit their previews), the model's output holds everything and full is absent.

docs.title: webfetch
docs.text:
webfetch(raw?: boolean, url: string)

Description sent to the model:

Fetch an HTTP or HTTPS URL. Output has final_url, status_code, content_type, and truncated header lines, a blank line, then the text body. Returns HTML as plaintext unless raw is true; other text passes through. Use read_artifact with the artifact a truncation hint names to page retained output, including the body.
Parameter Type Required Description raw boolean no Default: false. url string yes Parameters JSON Schema 
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "raw": {
      "default": false,
      "type": "boolean"
    },
    "url": {
      "type": "string"
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "url"
  ],
  "title": "WebfetchArgs",
  "type": "object"
}

A call looks like {"url":"https://docs.quantumcookie.xyz/", "raw":false}. The URL must start with a lowercase http:// or https:// prefix; any other scheme is rejected with invalid_url before a request is sent. One permission check uses the initial URL including its query string. Without a matching rule the call is denied. Explicit ask rules still use the normal approval flow.

Output starts with four header lines (final_url, status_code, content_type, and truncated), followed by a blank line and the text body verbatim. Body newlines are physical newlines, not JSON escapes. Structured url, final_url, status_code, content_type, and truncated fields remain in result metadata. HTML (text/html or application/xhtml+xml) is rendered by html2text at width 80 unless raw is true. Text types, JSON, XML, JavaScript, form data, and +json/+xml types pass through as text; raw and non-HTML text use UTF-8 lossy decoding. Binary types are rejected, including in raw mode. Missing or invalid Content-Type is treated as application/octet-stream and rejected.

The request has a 30-second overall timeout, inherits environment proxies, and uses reqwest's default redirect policy (10 hops). Redirect hops are not permission-checked. HTTP error statuses are returned with their text bodies. There are no additional SSRF, host/IP, DNS, or userinfo checks.

Downloads are streamed to a fixed 16 MiB cap, or 4 MiB for HTML that is converted to text. Over-cap responses return the fetched prefix with truncated: true, not an error. The caps have no input or configuration parameter. Full results use the standard event log and result store. The standard Bounded policy retains oversized output and sends a preview to the model. read_artifact pages the retained header and body by physical line, numbered from 1; its 1-based offset 6 starts at the body. Follow the continuation marker, or next_offset, for successive pages. Metadata is separate and is not paged.

Errors distinguish invalid_url, redirect_error, timeout, transport_error, and unsupported_content_type (which names the content type). permission_denied uses the standard policy-denial path and its structured tool_denied reason.

docs.text: webfetch Hint fetch Title Fetch <url> Arguments link of the URL, plus key_value raw: yes when raw is set Preview – Result key_value of status, content type, and final URL (and truncated: yes for an over-cap body), then the body's first lines within 24 KiB as markdown for text/markdown and text otherwise, counting the rest in omitted_lines

docs.title: Background calls
docs.text:
A tool that declares background support (bash, delegate_subagent, and a runtime's own tools that declare it) can run in the background, as the background tool calls spec describes:

  • The host owns the argument. It adds background (a boolean, defaulting to the tool's background_default) to the tool's schema and removes it before the tool prepares the call, so the tool never sees it and an approval covers the call either way.
  • Detaching. A call the model starts with background: true, or one the user moves to the background (run.tool_background; the TUI's background button), detaches once the tool reaches its detach point. A call that finishes first returns as an ordinary result. Detaching commits an immediate result for the call, Started in the background as job job_1a2b3c4d. … or User manually moved this call to the background; it is still running as job job_1a2b3c4d. …, ending with Stop it with stop_background(job_1a2b3c4d). and followed by the tool's note, and the run goes on. Cancelling the run no longer reaches the call.
  • Reporting. When the call ends, the engine accepts one producer message owned by tool { tool_call_id } that steers into the active run or wakes the idle session: <background_result job="…" tool="…" status="…"> wrapping exactly what the foreground result would have said, its output previewed with a read_artifact hint into the retained output for anything omitted. status is completed, failed, or stopped. The call reports only after its immediate result is committed; a revert past the call, deleting its session, or the daemon stopping kills it without a report.
  • Stopping. stop_background (job) stops a background call of the session tree and returns once it has ended; it needs no permission and is published only while a background-capable tool is. A user stops one with session.background.stop. Either way the call still reports, with status="stopped" and a first line saying who stopped it.
  • Subagents report themselves. A delegate_subagent call in the background, or moved there, gets no job: its immediate result names the subagent's handle, and every turn the subagent finishes reports to the parent as a <subagent_report handle="…" status="…"> producer message owned by subagent { session_id }, keyed by the turn's run ID so it reports once. A foreground call's first turn is its tool result instead. The subagent's running turn lists among the parent's background calls under its handle, and stop_background with the handle cancels that turn (status="cancelled"; an idle subagent is an error). Cancelling the parent's run does not reach its subagents: a foreground call it was waiting on ends cancelled with the detach note, and the subagent reports its turn as if the call had been moved to the background.

docs.title: Retained tool output
docs.text:
Tools declare ToolOutputDeclaration::Single or an ordered list of 1 to 8 named streams. Names are unique, case-sensitive ASCII path segments, 1 to 64 bytes, using letters, digits, _, -, and .; . and .. alone are forbidden. The same validator governs declarations and the stream argument of read_artifact.

The runtime keeps bounded previews and counts of accepted text chunks in memory. A stream that fits its preview is stored nowhere else: the result output holds all of it and it has no artifact. Once a stream outgrows its preview, its bytes are buffered and written in batches to a temporary file, hashed as they are written, and published as a full artifact at completion. An artifact keeps at most the first 128 MiB of a stream; past that only the last mebibyte is kept, after a marker line counting the dropped bytes, and the stream's dropped_bytes and the result's read hint report the loss. A single output has at most one artifact; named output gets a generic manifest when any stream has an artifact, and the manifest lists every declared stream. Declaration order determines model rendering. Bash uses the same named-output interface as other tools; it does not build its own retained-output manifest.

Each stream receives its own configured [tool_output] line/byte preview limits. Only truncated streams receive a read_artifact(artifact="<digest>", stream="<stream>", offset=...) hint, where the digest identifies the manifest and offset is the 1-based line of the first line the preview left out, as read_artifact takes it. (The stream's next_offset in retained_output stays the zero-based index of that line.) Single-output hints omit stream and the heading. A partial-line byte cut points back to that line, so readback does not skip unseen text. Aggregate preview construction also reserves 16 KiB for headings/hints inside the existing 2 MiB output bound; when necessary, previews are reduced with truthful read hints.

ToolProgress.output carries at most 8 typed chunks and 64 KiB of authoritative text per delta. Its optional display is a delta of the live display, independent of the output: append { index, text, stream? } appends to a text (or, with a stream, a terminal) block, creating it when index is just past the list, and replace { blocks } replaces the list. The message and an append's text are each limited to 1 KiB; the runtime caps the cumulative live-display budget at 64 KiB per call, and the messages' at another 64 KiB, without stopping authoritative output. bash appends to block 0 with each chunk's stream.

A result's display is a list of display blocks; empty means nothing to show, and a result a tool completes with ToolCompletion::single and no display shows its output as one text block. Each built-in tool's blocks are listed in its Display section, and Tool display describes the shared rules. Final display replaces live display; the daemon sanitizes its blocks, drops kinds it does not know (with a diagnostic naming the plugin or runtime that sent them), and fits the list to its own 64 KiB serialized budget, cutting a block to whole lines and counting the rest in its omitted_lines. A prepared call's presentation (its title, hint, primary argument, and display blocks of its arguments and preview) is fitted the same way. Control characters are sanitized while newlines and tabs remain usable in display text. Display is never included in model history.

Executors return ToolCompletion: Single/Named supplies terminal output once, whereas Streamed finalizes accepted deltas without resending them. Resupplying terminal output after streaming is an error. Failures and cancellation preserve accepted output as incomplete, retain the correct terminal status, and expose the error alongside output previews to the model. Terminal events carry retained_output references and final display; replay does not recapture chunks.

The self-paginating read, read_artifact, and get_subagent_result tools declare an absolute truncation opt-out. Their requested page is returned in full without artifact retention or truncation metadata, regardless of [tool_output]. Callers bound these results with each tool's offset/limit arguments. read and read_artifact cut each line after 4 KiB and stop a page before it passes the 2 MiB output limit, ending it with the offset to read next; a get_subagent_result page above that limit fails with a resource-limit tool error. No page is silently truncated. The delegate_subagent terminal result also opts out, because its teaser preview is bounded by [subagent_output] instead; the owner of the delegation flow is the only place it is bounded. MCP and plugin tools remain subject to normal truncation. External opt-out would require a future extension-protocol capability and is not currently authorable.

Artifacts are content-addressed by SHA-256, deduplicated, and newly created with mode 0600 on Unix. Their digest is verified when content is first read. A missing or corrupt artifact produces a normal tool error and does not prevent the engine or session from opening. Artifacts are written without fsync and without a store-wide lock (each publish is one atomic rename), so a crash or power loss can lose an artifact a durable event already references. Reads then report the output as unavailable, and model history replaces a lost attachment with a short note instead of failing.

Artifacts are collected only when a session is reverted. The revert deletes the digests that the cut-away events (and any delegated children the revert deletes) referenced, directly or through a generic manifest, unless an event still in the tree's logs references them too. The sweep is skipped while any session of the tree runs or a capture is still publishing its terminal references. Artifacts orphaned any other way, such as by a crash or a cancelled capture, stay in the tree's artifacts/ directory until the tree is deleted.

docs.title: read_artifact
docs.text:
read_artifact(artifact: string, limit?: integer, offset?: integer, stream?: string)

Description sent to the model:

Read retained tool output by line, as `read` reads a file. A truncated result or elided history names the artifact (and stream) to read in a read_artifact hint, with the 1-based `offset` of the first line it left out: read from there. Lines come back numbered, `N: text`, counting from 1. `offset` is the 1-based line to start at (default 1) and `limit` the most lines to return (default 2000). A line longer than 4 KiB is cut and ends with `... [line truncated: N more bytes]`, and a page stops before it passes the result size limit (about 2 MiB). A page that leaves lines out ends with a note such as `[120 more lines; continue with offset=2001]`: read again from that offset. An offset past the last line is an error.

Always, whatever the agent's permission rules: it reads only output retained by the session's own tree.

Parameter Type Required Description artifact string yes The artifact's 64-character lowercase SHA-256 digest, as a truncation hint names it. limit integer no The most lines to return. Defaults to 2000. offset integer no The 1-based line to start at. Defaults to 1. stream string no Named stream of a multi-stream output, such as stdout, as a truncation hint names it. Parameters JSON Schema 
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "artifact": {
      "description": "The artifact's 64-character lowercase SHA-256 digest, as a truncation hint names it.",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "limit": {
      "description": "The most lines to return. Defaults to 2000.",
      "format": "uint",
      "minimum": 0,
      "type": [
        "integer",
        "null"
      ]
    },
    "offset": {
      "description": "The 1-based line to start at. Defaults to 1.",
      "format": "uint",
      "minimum": 0,
      "type": [
        "integer",
        "null"
      ]
    },
    "stream": {
      "description": "Named stream of a multi-stream output, such as `stdout`, as a truncation hint names it.",
      "type": [
        "string",
        "null"
      ]
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "artifact"
  ],
  "title": "ReadArtifactArgs",
  "type": "object"
}

read_artifact is a base-layer tool. A digest that names content another tree stored does not resolve. Digests are content-addressed SHA-256 references, not random secrets. Malformed digests (bare artifact:// URIs, the internal sha256/ form, uppercase or short digests) and invalid stream names are rejected. read reads only the filesystem.

Artifact reads return the stored content without unwrapping JSON. Normal single-output artifacts contain the original full text. Named-stream artifacts contain their complete individual text. A compaction retry artifact holds the elided result's text as it was, or, for content that is not plain text, a line-structured form: a [tool content: <kind>] header line, then each part under its own [part N: text|json|file ...] line, text keeping its own line breaks, JSON pretty-printed over several lines, and a file named by its media type and filename without its bytes. Its marker says so and exposes a usable ID without requiring durable elision events. Artifacts earlier builds stored are read as they are: their non-text content is one line of serialized tool-content JSON, of which a page shows the first 4 KiB.

Without stream, read_artifact reads stored text as-is, including manifest JSON; it does not merge streams. stream selects a declared name from the generic manifest. This is content-based and works for results, diagnostics, or any other valid declared name, not just Bash streams. Unknown names and selection on non-manifests are errors. Stored ArtifactReference values keep the internal artifact://sha256/<digest> form, which is not a read_artifact argument.

A page reads as a read page of a file does, without the <path> wrapper: lines numbered from 1 (N: text), a 1-based offset (default 1, and 0 is refused), a positive limit (default 2000, with no maximum), each line cut after 4 KiB with a ... [line truncated: N more bytes] marker, the page stopped before it passes the result size limit, and a continuation marker ([N more lines; continue with offset=M], or [page cut at the result size limit; continue with offset=M]) when lines follow it, reported again as the 1-based next_offset in the metadata. An offset past the last line is an error. Bytes that are not UTF-8 show as replacement characters. Missing and corrupt artifacts produce tool errors.

{"artifact":"aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa","stream":"results","offset":1,"limit":200}

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text: MCP tools are shown with the hint generic, the published tool name as the title, and their arguments as one json block (none for an empty object). A result shows its text content as text (consecutive text parts as one block, joined as the output joins them), each retained image, audio, or embedded resource blob as media in place of its placeholder, and structured_content that the text does not already hold as json. structured_content also stays in the result's metadata, which the model reads.

docs.title: Deferred tools
docs.text:
On a model that loads deferred tools natively, or one deferral is attempted on (see providers for which models are), MCP and plugin tools, and the built-in groups marked deferred below, are sent deferred ([deferred_tools] sends a group up front): the model sees their names in announcements, not their definitions, until it loads them with tool_search: select:<name> loads tools by exact name, and keywords load the best matches. A loaded tool stays callable. The deferred tools spec has the details: tool rounds, announcements, and compaction.

Every tool belongs to a group: its MCP server, its plugin, or one of the built-in providers below. Announcements list deferred tools under their group, with the group's summary the first time a round announces it; an MCP server's summary is the instructions it sends when it connects, and is marked untrusted. A provider whose tools are all deferred sends its prompt sections (its <tool_instructions>, see the system prompt) with the first load of one of its tools instead of in the system prompt.

Group Tools Deferred Summary sent to the model agents list_agents yes The agents this session can delegate to or schedule, and what each is for. artifacts read_artifact no Tool output too large for the conversation, kept aside and read back by range. background stop_background no Calls running in the background, and stopping them. coding read, write, edit, bash, webfetch no The workspace: reading, writing, and editing files, running shell commands, and fetching web pages. cron cron_create, cron_list, cron_update, cron_delete, cron_run yes Scheduled prompts: run a prompt once after a delay or on a cron schedule, in this session, a subagent's, or a new session. delegation delegate_subagent, get_subagent_result no Subagents: hand a focused task to another agent, and collect its result. goal goal_get, goal_set, goal_update yes The session's goal and the checklist that tracks it. memory memory_search, memory_read, memory_write, memory_edit, memory_delete yes Durable notes across sessions: what the user prefers, project decisions, and facts about machines. messaging send_message no Messages between the agents of a session tree. runtimes list_runtimes yes The runtimes this session can work through: the machines and capabilities a subagent can be started on. skills skill no Skills: packaged instructions for a kind of task, loaded by name.

tool_search(limit?: integer, query: string)

Description sent to the model:

Load deferred tools so you can call them. Use "select:<name>,<name>" to load tools by the exact names a <tools_added> announcement lists, or keywords to find and load the best matches by name, group, description, and parameters. Loaded tools stay callable.

Only when the request defers a tool: on a model that loads deferred tools, when an MCP or plugin tool, or a tool of a deferred built-in group, is offered. It stays until the session's next compaction.

Parameter Type Required Description limit integer no At most how many keyword matches to load; 5 when absent, and every match when 0 or less. A select: query loads every name it lists. query string yes "select:," loads those tools by exact name; any other text is keywords, such as "browser click", and loads the best matches. docs.title: Goal checklist tools
docs.text:
goal_get returns the current root goal's objective, status, revision, and entire checklist. goal_update { items } replaces the entire ordered checklist; each item contains only description and finished, with no item ID. The session actor serializes replacements, and the last accepted update wins. The tool has no goal_id or expected_revision parameter or lost-update protection. Its target is the current/latest session goal when the engine actor accepts the update, so an older run's update can intentionally affect a newly activated active or paused goal. Lifecycle changes do not change an already-admitted run's tool set. Updates reject if the current goal is absent or terminal, even when the tool remains in an admitted run. Engine-owned goal IDs and revisions remain; SessionGoalLifecycleParams.goal_id and expected_revision apply to user lifecycle RPC controls, not model checklist updates.

The model cannot set an objective, pause, resume, or cancel. Empty checklists preserve the active or paused lifecycle; nonempty all-finished checklists complete it even while paused. The root must verify evidence before marking items finished. Both tools return the full state without display truncation. Neither declares a permission: setting the goal is what publishes them, and they act on that goal alone, so permission rules do not govern them and every call is allowed.

Verify evidence directly or through subagents before marking items finished; the root checklist is authoritative over subagent self-reports.

Only in a root session. An ACP agent's root session has them only while the user's goal is active or paused when the run starts.

docs.title: Delegation and skills
docs.text:
Delegation tools start, inspect, and cancel owned subagent sessions. Skill tools load configured skill instructions for the current turn. Their availability and targets are derived from the frozen agent policy.

When delegation is available, its provider also freezes the currently eligible target IDs and agent descriptions into the run's system prompt under <tool_instructions provider="builtin.delegate">. The list uses the same depth ceiling and enabled-target filtering as delegate_subagent; no section is added when no target is available.

delegate_subagent, get_subagent_result, stop_background, and send_message address subagents by a short tree-unique handle (<agent_type>_<8 hex>, e.g. explore_1a2b3c4d) or a full session UUID. A handle is generated when the session is created and resolves only within the caller's tree; a partial handle, another tree's handle, or a fabricated value is rejected with a self-repairing error that lists the live candidates as handle — description — status plus their UUIDs. Detach notes and reports pre-wrap the handle, for example [subagent session explore_1a2b3c4d] Each time its turn ends you get a <subagent_report handle="explore_1a2b3c4d">. … and [subagent session explore_1a2b3c4d; completed; 79 lines; use get_subagent_result with session_id "explore_1a2b3c4d" for the full output]. The report previews the turn's final message per [subagent_output], with its line breaks and tabs kept and other control characters folded to spaces. A report over the limit shows its first and last lines around a marker such as [… 200 lines omitted. Read more: get_subagent_result(session_id="explore_1a2b3c4d", offset=21)]; a complete one ends in full output shown. Terminal and lifecycle results keep the UUID under the unified session_id metadata key and add handle. resume_session_id accepts the same two forms, and a terminal child woken by send_message reports as running until its new turn ends.

In a root session with the global runtime attached, delegate_subagent also takes capabilities: the runtime capabilities the child works through, each written <runtime_id>/<capability_id> with a workspace when the capability takes one (see Delegating to runtimes). It is required when the root has nothing but global attached, optional when it has other attachments too, and absent everywhere else, where a child inherits its parent's attachments. Each runtime it names is checked as delegate@<runtime>, and every runtime starts before the child is created: one that cannot start fails the call and creates nothing. A root with only global also gets a paragraph in its delegation instructions saying it has no workspace.

docs.title: delegate_subagent
docs.text:
delegate_subagent(agent_type: "<subagent id>", capabilities?: object[], description: string, inherit_context?: boolean, prompt: string, resume_session_id?: string)

Description sent to the model:

Delegate a self-contained task to a specialist agent. In the foreground (default) the call waits for the subagent's first turn and returns its result. In the background it returns at once with the subagent's handle. Every later turn of the subagent, and the first one when it runs in the background, arrives as a <subagent_report> that wakes this session, so to wait for one, tell the user and end your turn. To continue an existing subagent, pass its resume_session_id or send it a message.

Only when the agent can delegate to at least one subagent at this depth. The agent_type enum lists those subagents; this page shows a placeholder. capabilities exists only in a root session with the global runtime attached: optional, as shown, when the root has other attachments too, and required when it has only global. Each runtime it names is checked as delegate@<runtime>.

Parameter Type Required Description agent_type "<subagent id>" yes capabilities object[] no Optional. Leave it out and the subagent inherits this session's attachments. Each item gives the subagent one runtime capability to work through, at workspace when the capability takes one. These are runtime capabilities, where the subagent works, not its tools or permissions. Write each as the full <runtime_id>/<capability_id>, from a <runtime id=…> and one of its <capability name=…> in list_runtimes, e.g. labpc/coding. The same runtime may be listed twice with different workspaces. The subagent also has global whenever this session does. Cannot be combined with resume_session_id. description string yes Short (3-5 words) summary of the task inherit_context boolean no Default: false. prompt string yes Full task brief with objective, context, and deliverable resume_session_id string no Optional. Handle or UUID of an existing subagent of yours to resume, e.g. "explore_1a2b3c4d". Only subagents you delegated are valid. Parameters JSON Schema 
{
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "agent_type": {
      "enum": [
        "<subagent id>"
      ],
      "type": "string"
    },
    "capabilities": {
      "description": "Optional. Leave it out and the subagent inherits this session's attachments. Each item gives the subagent one runtime capability to work through, at `workspace` when the capability takes one. These are runtime capabilities, where the subagent works, not its tools or permissions. Write each as the full `<runtime_id>/<capability_id>`, from a `<runtime id=…>` and one of its `<capability name=…>` in list_runtimes, e.g. `labpc/coding`. The same runtime may be listed twice with different workspaces. The subagent also has `global` whenever this session does. Cannot be combined with resume_session_id.",
      "items": {
        "additionalProperties": false,
        "properties": {
          "capability": {
            "description": "`<runtime_id>/<capability_id>`, from list_runtimes, e.g. `labpc/coding`",
            "type": "string"
          },
          "workspace": {
            "description": "Directory on that runtime's machine; required when the capability takes a workspace",
            "type": "string"
          }
        },
        "required": [
          "capability"
        ],
        "type": "object"
      },
      "minItems": 1,
      "type": "array"
    },
    "description": {
      "description": "Short (3-5 words) summary of the task",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "inherit_context": {
      "default": false,
      "type": "boolean"
    },
    "prompt": {
      "description": "Full task brief with objective, context, and deliverable",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "resume_session_id": {
      "description": "Optional. Handle or UUID of an existing subagent of yours to resume, e.g. \"explore_1a2b3c4d\". Only subagents you delegated are valid.",
      "type": "string"
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "description",
    "prompt",
    "agent_type"
  ],
  "type": "object"
}

docs.title: get_subagent_result
docs.text:
get_subagent_result(limit?: integer, offset?: integer, session_id: string)

Description sent to the model:

Read the current status and latest result of a subagent you delegated, such as the full output a <subagent_report> cut short. This call returns immediately; it never waits. Use the subagent's handle, e.g. "explore_1a2b3c4d". Only your own subagents are visible. The result comes back as numbered lines, `N: text`, counting from 1, as `read` returns a file: `offset` is the 1-based line to start at (default 1) and `limit` the most lines to return (default 2000); a line longer than 4 KiB is cut, and a page that leaves lines out ends with a note such as `[120 more lines; continue with offset=2001]`. A <subagent_report> cut short names the offset to continue from.

Only when the agent can delegate to at least one subagent at this depth.

docs.text:
delegate_subagent get_subagent_result skill Hint delegate delegate skill Title Delegate to <agent> Read subagent <session> Load skill <name> Arguments key_value of agent, description, resume and inherit context when set, and prompt key_value of session, and offset (when not 1) and limit when given key_value of name, and arguments when not empty Preview – – – Result session_ref of the subagent (handle as short_id, <agent> · <status> as label), then its whole final message as markdown session_ref (its status as label), then the page's lines as markdown the loaded skill as markdown

A delegation that moves to the background commits the immediate result the background section describes, which shows its output.

docs.title: Agent messaging
docs.text: send_message delivers a durable message to another session in the same delegation tree. It replaces the removed steer_subagent tool; see the migration notes. Its argument object is strict, and body is the markdown message text. The earlier recipient_session_id spelling of to is not an alias and fails with send_message:invalid_arguments. A non-UUID recipient is resolved as a handle in the sender's tree; if it matches no live peer the send fails with the self-repairing unknown subagent reference error rather than a send_message: code.

docs.title: send_message
docs.text:
send_message(body: string, mode?: "steer" | "queue", to: string)

Description sent to the model:

Send a message to another agent in your session tree. Recipient accepts a subagent handle or a full UUID.
Parameter Type Required Description body string yes mode "steer" \| "queue" no Default: "steer". to string yes Handle or full UUID of the recipient agent. Parameters JSON Schema 
{
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "body": {
      "minLength": 1,
      "type": "string"
    },
    "mode": {
      "default": "steer",
      "enum": [
        "steer",
        "queue"
      ],
      "type": "string"
    },
    "to": {
      "description": "Handle or full UUID of the recipient agent.",
      "type": "string"
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "to",
    "body"
  ],
  "type": "object"
}

Calls use the message permission action. The resource label is the recipient's relationship to the sender — parent, child, sibling, or * for any other same-tree peer — derived from stored session-origin metadata. Messaging is deny-by-default and the tool is hidden until an agent document or session overlay declares a message allow or ask rule. Denied calls use the standard policy-denial path and ask rules use the normal approval flow; there is no messaging-specific permission error.

A successful result means durably accepted: the message is persisted in the recipient's event log and survives a daemon restart. It does not mean the recipient has seen or consumed the message. The result carries message_id, the effective mode, and recipient_state (running, queued, or waking_finished). A steer send joins a running recipient's next safe model-request boundary; a queue send is claimed into the recipient's prompt at the next safe boundary. Idle and finished recipients are woken through the producer reconcile path, resuming the session with the message as input. There is no inbox tool.

Failures are explicit tool errors with stable codes:

Code Meaning send_message:disabled [messaging] enabled = false send_message:invalid_arguments Missing, unknown, or wrongly typed arguments, including the removed recipient_session_id spelling send_message:invalid_body Empty body or body over max_body_bytes send_message:unknown_session Well-formed recipient UUID that names no session send_message:not_tree_peer Well-formed recipient UUID in a different delegation tree send_message:self_send Sender targeted its own session send_message:inbox_full Recipient has max_pending_per_session pending agent messages; nothing was admitted send_message:max_hops_exceeded The message chain exceeded max_hops send_message:inflight_full The directed pair already has max_inflight_per_pair unacknowledged messages send_message:engine_shutdown The send raced daemon shutdown

Retries are safe: the idempotency key derives from the sender session, run, and tool call, so a retried call returns the original message_id and delivers once. Two loop-safety guards reject sends, and each can be disabled: max_hops <= 0 turns off hop counting (hop metadata is internal and never appears in the delivered envelope; mail between a parent and its direct child adds no hop, and subagent reports are not messages), and max_inflight_per_pair = 0 turns off the per-pair window. A pair message counts as unacknowledged while accepted, admitted, claimed, or released, and is acknowledged once consumed or discarded. See Agent Messaging for the settings and the agent messaging spec for the full contract.

docs.title: Memory tools
docs.text:
The memory tools search, read, and change the memories the global runtime keeps; see Memory.

They follow the filesystem tools where they can. memory_read pages a memory's body as read pages a file: under the metadata header, the body's lines numbered from 1, a 1-based offset (default 1), a limit (default 2000), the same 4 KiB line cut, page cap, continuation marker, and error for an offset past the last body line. memory_write reports Created <url> (N bytes). or Replaced <url> (N bytes)., memory_edit Edited <url>: 1 replacement., and a memory that is not there is <url> does not exist. memory_edit takes oldString and newString, as edit does, and preparation checks that oldString occurs exactly once in the body, so an edit that cannot apply fails before anyone is asked to approve it, with `<oldString>` occurs N times in the body of <url>; include more context so it occurs once (the echoed text cut to 200 characters). What stays different on purpose: an edit matches the body only and has no replaceAll; a replacing write needs the session to have read the memory as it is now, and is refused otherwise with an operation_changed error; a bad memory URL is an invalid_url error; a delete is final; the permission actions are memory and memory_write by URL; and the write tools run one at a time.

docs.title: memory_search
docs.text:
memory_search(layer?: "user" | "agent" | "machine" | "project", limit?: integer, query: string)

Description sent to the model:

Search memory: notes saved in earlier sessions about the user, agents, machines, and projects. Terms are matched case-insensitively against each memory's keywords, description, and URL segments (user, agent, machine, or project, then the names after it), never its body; results are ranked by keyword hits first. Each result shows a memory's URL and description, whether it is related to this session, whether you may change it, and its age, then its keywords; a result you need approval to read shows only its first two lines. `layer` narrows the search to `user`, `agent`, `machine`, or `project` memories.

Only when the session has the global runtime attached and the agent or the session overlay has an allow or ask rule for memory. memory_search needs no rule of its own: each result is checked against the memory rules for its URL instead.

docs.title: memory_read
docs.text:
memory_read(limit?: integer, offset?: integer, url: string)

Description sent to the model:

Read one memory by its URL (user://<category>, agent://<agent>, machine://<machine>/<name>, or project://<project>/<name>). Returns whether it is related to this session and whether you may change it, when it was created and modified, its size and its size limit, its description and keywords, and then its body as numbered lines, `N: text`, counting from 1. `offset` is the 1-based body line to start at (default 1) and `limit` the most lines to return (default 2000). A line longer than 4 KiB is cut and ends with `... [line truncated: N more bytes]`, and a page that leaves lines out ends with a note such as `[120 more lines; continue with offset=2001]`: read again from that offset. An offset past the last body line is an error. The line numbers are not part of the memory.

Only when the session has the global runtime attached and the agent or the session overlay has an allow or ask rule for memory. memory_search needs no rule of its own: each result is checked against the memory rules for its URL instead.

Parameter Type Required Description limit integer no The most body lines to return. Defaults to 2000. offset integer no The 1-based body line to start at. Defaults to 1. url string yes The memory URL. Parameters JSON Schema

docs.title: Display
docs.text:
Each memory tool call is one row. Its title names the memory's URL, which the TUI and the web client draw as a link that opens the memory in the Memory panel or view, a click target of its own; the rest of the row expands and collapses it. A write's, an edit's, and a delete's diff is built as write's and edit's are (five lines of context, real line numbers), labelled with the memory's URL, in markdown, over the memory file without the created and modified stamp lines the daemon rewrites on every save, as the memory editors show it.

memory_search memory_read memory_write memory_edit memory_delete Hint search file_read file_write file_edit file_write Title Search memory Read memory <url> Write memory <url> Edit memory <url> Delete memory <url> Arguments key_value of query, layer, and limit key_value of offset and limit when the call gives them key_value of reason when given; without a preview, also description, keywords, and body – ; without a preview, key_value of oldString and newString – Preview – – diff against the memory preparation finds (created when there is none) diff of the replacement applied to the memory preparation read diff of the memory's removed text (deleted), when it exists Result a link per memory found, its URL with its description as the label, or No memories match. file_excerpt of the body's page, as read shows a file's: path the URL, language markdown, start_line the 1-based offset, total_lines the body's diff against the memory the write replaced (created for a new one) diff built from the range the edit replaced, or a line diff of the whole file when the daemon also rewrote its frontmatter (an agent:// file, a project's overview) diff of the text the memory held (deleted)

A link block whose url is a memory URL (user://, agent://, machine://, or project://) opens that memory in the clients.

docs.title: list_runtimes
docs.text:
list_runtimes()

Description sent to the model:

List the daemon's machines and runtimes, as they are now: each runtime's capabilities, whether it is connected or starts when used, its home directory, the ACP agents it offers (external coding agents such as Claude Code; a session runs one on the attached runtime that offers it), and this session's own attachments on it. Name a runtime capability from here in delegate_subagent's `capabilities`, as `<runtime id>/<capability name>`. A runtime that connects later shows up on the next call.

Only when the session has the global runtime attached and the agent or the session overlay has an allow or ask rule for list_runtimes, which primary and all agents have by default.

Parameters JSON Schema 
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "description": "`list_runtimes` takes no arguments.",
  "title": "ListRuntimesArgs",
  "type": "object"
}

list_runtimes reads the daemon's state at each call. Its output is grouped by machine, the daemon's own first and the rest by name, and within a machine by runtime ID; a runtime the daemon cannot place on a machine goes under <unplaced>. global is never listed as a runtime: a <global/> element, with a comment, says when the root of the caller's tree has it. Only the calling session's own attachments are shown. A runtime that is not connected keeps the machine, platform, and home the daemon last saw it with. The output is never truncated.

<runtimes>
  <!-- global is attached to this session's root, so every subagent in this tree has it, whether or not its capabilities list it. -->
  <global/>
  <machine name="laptop" platform="linux">
    <runtime id="local" connected="true" home="/home/u">
      <capability name="coding" takes_workspace="true" description="Read, write, edit, and run commands in a workspace"/>
      <attachment name="local_web" capability="coding" workspace="/home/u/web" status="ready"/>
    </runtime>
  </machine>
  <machine name="labpc" platform="linux">
    <runtime id="labpc" connected="false" starts_on_use="true" home="/home/u">
      <capability name="coding" takes_workspace="true" description="Read, write, edit, and run commands in a workspace"/>
    </runtime>
  </machine>
</runtimes>

docs.text:
list_agents(for?: "delegate" | "cron")

Description sent to the model:

List the agents you can pick: for `delegate` the subagents delegate_subagent can start from here, for `cron` the agents a new-session cron job can run. Each shows its mode, description, presets, models, and the permission rules its document declares, with the actions left to the daemon's defaults on one `defaults:` line; the defaults themselves are listed once at the end. An ACP agent (an external coding agent such as Claude Code, marked `acp`) shows the runtimes that offer it and whether it runs here: it runs on the one attached runtime that offers it, and not with none or several. Leave `for` out to list both.

Only when the session has the global runtime attached and the run is offered delegate_subagent or a cron tool. It has no permission of its own.

Parameter Type Required Description for "delegate" \| "cron" no List only the agents usable for this Parameters JSON Schema 
{
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "for": {
      "description": "List only the agents usable for this",
      "enum": [
        "delegate",
        "cron"
      ],
      "type": "string"
    }
  },
  "type": "object"
}

list_agents reads the agent registry of the calling run's preset. For delegate it lists the run's delegation targets; for cron every enabled primary or all agent, the ones a new-session job can run. Each agent shows its mode, description, presets, models, what it is usable for, and the permission keys its document declares, each in full with ${agent_id} written as the agent's ID; the actions it names no key for, which get the daemon's defaults, share one defaults: line. An agent usable both as a delegation target and for a new-session job shows its rules as a root run and as a subagent when they differ, each block with its own defaults: line. After the agents comes the defaults section, once: what the defaults are for a root run and for a subagent (as the listed agents need them), which ones only some modes get, and what ${session_machine}, ${session_project}, and ${workspace_dir} stand for. The result ends with Actions not listed are denied. (cron spec section 8.1).

docs.title: Cron tools
docs.text: The cron tools manage the daemon's scheduled prompts (cron spec). Every one but cron_list is checked under cron, with the target kind of each job it touches as a resource: session, subagent, or new; cron_update that changes a job's kind is checked for both. cron_list shows only the jobs whose kind the rules allow or ask for. A target an agent names is "self", a session below its own, or a new-session template; anything else is refused whatever the rules say. Agents never set a job's permission mode or pin its model.

docs.text:
cron_create(delivery?: "queue" | "steer", max_runs?: integer, name?: string, prompt: string, schedule: object | object, target?: string | object)

Description sent to the model:

Schedule a prompt: once after a delay ({"in": "20m"}) or on a five-field cron schedule ({"cron": "0 3 * * *"}). `target`: "self" (the default) fires into this session; a subagent's handle (e.g. "explore_1a2b3c4d") fires into that subagent's session, which must be below this one; {"new": {...}} starts a new root session per fire, whose agent, runtimes, and project default to this session's. A new session's agent must be able to run as a root (call list_agents with for="cron"). `delivery` (in-session jobs): "queue" (default) waits for the current turn, "steer" joins it. Schedules are in the daemon host's local time. Each fire arrives marked as a <scheduled_job>, never as the user, and is not user consent. docs.title: Runtimes
docs.text:
A runtime is where a session's tools run. It offers one or more capabilities, and a session attaches each one it uses separately. The daemon's built-in local runtime offers coding (read, write, edit, bash, webfetch) for any directory on the daemon's machine, and the global runtime offers global: top-level MCP servers and plugins. Other runtimes run elsewhere, typically on another machine, so a session on your laptop can read, edit, and run commands in a repository on that machine. The runtimes specification and the runtime capabilities specification describe the model; Runtimes and capabilities introduces it.

This page covers what every runtime shares: capabilities, instances and workspaces, lifecycle and failures, and machines. The rest of this section covers the two ways to add a runtime, keeping one connected, and what a runtime hosts:

  • Runtime templates: [runtimes.<id>] tables, whose runtimes the daemon starts itself, such as over ssh, and cookie runtime serve --stdio.
  • Runtimes that dial in: runtimes that run on their own and connect to the daemon.
  • Running a runtime as a service: keeping a runtime that dials in connected, on Linux, macOS, and Windows.
  • MCP servers and ACP agents: the servers and agents a runtime hosts on its machine.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
A runtime reports its capabilities when it connects. Each has a name, a self-declared kind, and whether it takes a workspace. runtimes.list and the /runtime panel show them once the runtime has connected. When a runtime offers one capability, attaching it needs no capability name; when it offers several, choose one (/runtime lists each capability of each runtime as its own entry). Each attached capability is its own attachment, with its own name and tools.

Runtime Capability Workspace Offers global global none top-level MCP servers, plugins, the memory tools, the fallback webfetch local coding any directory on the daemon's machine; the daemon's own directory when none is named read, write, edit, bash, webfetch, project skills, AGENTS.md cookie runtime serve coding any directory on its machine, or under its --root directories the same

docs.title: Instances and workspaces
docs.text:
A capability instance is one capability of a runtime opened for one workspace (or none), shared by every session attached to it. The daemon passes the workspace path exactly as it was typed and never resolves it on its own machine; the runtime reports the canonical path on its machine, and that path identifies the instance. Two requests that resolve to the same directory, such as ~/cookie-agent and /home/me/cookie-agent, share one instance. A session records the reported path, and reopening the session asks for that path. A new session's directory is the reported path of its first workspace too, so both spellings list the session under one directory (see Where sessions live).

A runtime may report its home directory when it connects; cookie runtime serve and the built-in global and local report their user's, canonical. runtimes.list gives it as home. Clients show the runtime's paths under it as ~/… and absolute without one, and permission rules starting with ~/ expand against it (see Paths under the home directory).

docs.title: Lifecycle and failures
docs.text:
• Start. A runtime's process starts when a session first needs one of its capabilities, and stays up until the daemon exits; its instances open as sessions attach them. Creating a session, attaching a runtime, and delegating with capabilities wait until the runtime is actually online, runtime/initialize and capability/open answered, before anything is created. A start that fails or exceeds startup_timeout_ms publishes no tools and creates nothing: the session, attachment, or subagent is refused with the reason, and clients viewing an affected session get an error naming the runtime and the reason. runtimes.list shows why the runtime last failed to connect.
  • Liveness. A connection can die without closing, as a hung ssh leaves it. The daemon pings a runtime it has heard nothing from for 15 s (runtime/ping) and ends the connection once nothing has arrived for 45 s, which counts as a drop (below). Every request has a deadline: preparing and revalidating a call and fetching AGENTS.md context get 30 s, and a runtime that misses one fails the call as runtime_unavailable and has its connection checked at once (10 s to answer). See Liveness.
  • Reuse. An instance that is already open is handed to a new session, attachment, or subagent only over a live connection: one heard from in the last 15 s, or that answers a ping within 10 s. When it does not, the daemon ends the connection and waits, up to 2 minutes, for the runtime to be started again (see Drop) before it gives the instance out, or refuses with the reason.
  • Refused workspaces. A runtime that is up can still refuse to open a capability, for example for a workspace outside its --root directories. The error then reads runtime `labpc` could not open `coding` for workspace `/tmp`: workspace /tmp is outside the directories this runtime serves rather than saying the runtime failed to start. Attaching, creating a session, and retrying (runtimes.reconnect) record nothing when the instance never opened: no attachment, and no failed instance in runtimes.list.
  • Diagnostics. The process's standard error is captured into a bounded buffer (its last 32 lines, at most 4 KiB). Failure reasons end with that tail, so an ssh or cookie runtime error shows up in the TUI. The daemon does not copy the process's standard error to its own as it arrives, but when a session is created, opened, or starts a run while one of its attachments is unavailable, the daemon writes cookie-agent: session <id>: runtime `<attachment>` is unavailable: <reason> to its standard error, and that reason ends with the tail.
  • Drop. When the process exits, its pipe closes, or it stops answering, calls in flight fail with runtime_unavailable (a backgrounded call reports the failure as its background result), and the daemon starts the process again up to 3 times after 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s, reopening every instance over the new connection. Meanwhile the instances show as reconnecting, their tools stay published, and new calls fail fast with runtime_unavailable. A successful restart re-lists their tools under a new instance generation (a call the model planned before the restart fails as operation_changed). When every attempt fails, their tools are dropped, they become failed, and clients get an error.
  • Retry. A failed instance is retried when a session that uses it is created or opened, and on demand with r in /runtime (or runtimes.reconnect).
  • Shutdown. When the daemon exits it sends runtime/shutdown, waits up to shutdown_grace_ms, and then kills the process group (a job object on Windows).

docs.title: Machines
docs.text:
Every runtime belongs to a machine, the computer it runs on. The model is told which machine each attachment's runtime runs on, so it knows which tools share files (see the system prompt). The daemon groups runtimes into machines on its own: runtimes that report the same machine ID, such as global, local, and a cookie runtime serve on the daemon's own computer, share a machine, and a computer it has not seen gets a machine named after its host name. A runtime that reports no machine ID gets a machine of its own, named after its runtime ID. Machines are kept in ~/.cookie-agent/machines.json, which only the daemon writes; there is no configuration for them.

Regroup them by hand when the automatic grouping is wrong, for example when a container reports its own machine ID. In the TUI, the Machines view of the /runtime panel (press m, or click its tab) lists each machine with its runtimes; select a machine to rename (n), merge (g), or forget (f) it, or a runtime to move it to another machine (v) or unpin it (u). In the web client's Machines & runtimes view, drag a runtime onto another machine's card, or use its Move to… (see Web); the view also adds an ssh template or shows the dial-in command. From a terminal, cookie machine does the same and works against a remote daemon like cookie config:

cookie machine list                  # machines, their runtimes, and memories
cookie machine rename labpc lab      # a machine's memory folder moves with it
cookie machine assign box labpc      # pin runtime `box` to machine `labpc`
cookie machine unassign box          # follow the machine ID it reports again
cookie machine merge box labpc       # move `box`'s IDs, pins, and memories
cookie machine forget old-laptop     # only with no connected runtimes or memories
cookie machine forget-runtime roamer # forget where an offline runtime ran

A runtime that has connected once stays on its machine while it is offline, across restarts too: the registry records where it ran, and cookie machine list shows it under offline with when it was last seen. Removing a template from config.toml drops its record at the next reload; a dial-in runtime's record stays until forget-runtime. See Offline runtimes.

A change applies to connected runtimes at once; sessions see the new machine names from their next run.

Each machine has its own memories, machine://<machine>/<name>, in the folder ~/.cookie-agent/memory/machines/<machine> (see Memory): renaming a machine moves its folder, merging moves its memories into the other machine's and fails when both have a memory of one name, and a machine can be forgotten only once its folder is empty. A session's model sees an index of the memories of the machines its attachments run on.

docs.title: Runtimes that dial in
docs.text:
A runtime can also run on its own and connect to the daemon, instead of the daemon starting it from a template. It needs no template: it names itself, and sessions attach it like any other runtime while it is connected.

# On the daemon's machine: a listener the runtime reaches.
cookie daemon --listen 0.0.0.0:7419

# On labpc: dial in, named after the host, and stay connected.
cookie runtime serve --daemon ws://laptop:7419/ws --token <token>
  • Daemon. --daemon takes the daemon's client URL, or, without one, [server] url of this machine's config.toml, else the local daemon that table describes. --token is the daemon's token, [server] token in its config.toml, where the daemon keeps it so it survives restarts. COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN and [server] token on labpc work too; flags override the configuration. The runtime does not pass the token on to the processes it starts.
  • Identity. --id is the runtime ID, [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}; without it, the host name, sanitized (host_ in front when it does not start with a letter). It must not be global, local, or a [runtimes.<id>] template with a command, and only one runtime may be connected under an ID at a time.
  • Refusals. The daemon says why it refuses a runtime, and the runtime prints it. A refusal that retrying cannot fix, a configured or reserved ID or a wrong token, ends cookie runtime serve --daemon with an error:
cookie: cannot dial in to ws://laptop:7419/ws as `labpc`: the daemon refused the runtime (HTTP 403): runtime `labpc` is configured on the daemon ([runtimes.labpc]) and cannot dial in

Any other, such as an ID a runtime is still connected under (the daemon may not have noticed yet that an earlier connection dropped), is printed and retried with the same backoff as a drop:

cookie runtime: cannot dial in to ws://laptop:7419/ws as `labpc`: the daemon refused the runtime (HTTP 409): runtime `labpc` is already connected; retrying in 1 s

A dropped connection prints the reason too, such as disconnected from ws://laptop:7419/ws: the daemon closed the connection with code 1011: runtime `labpc` failed to start: … for a runtime of an incompatible version. See Dial-in refusals. - Reconnecting. The runtime reconnects after every drop, waiting 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, and so on up to 30 s. While it is away, its instances go reconnecting and then failed, and their tools leave the sessions' tool lists; when it dials in again, the daemon reopens them over the new connection. runtimes.list shows it with lifetime dial_in, and, while it is away, why it disconnected. - Connections that die without closing. A machine that sleeps, or loses or changes its network, can leave the WebSocket half-open: neither end hears a close. Both ends watch for that. The daemon pings a runtime it has heard nothing from for 15 s and drops it once nothing has arrived for 45 s (runtime `labpc` disconnected: nothing arrived from it for 45 s); calls in flight then fail with runtime_unavailable, and a request the runtime does not answer in time (30 s for preparing a call) fails the call and has the connection checked at once. The runtime sends WebSocket pings once its connection has been quiet for 15 s and dials in again once nothing, a pong included, has arrived for 45 s (disconnected from ws://laptop:7419/ws: … nothing arrived from the daemon for 45 s). A runtime that dials in while the daemon still counts its old connection as connected is refused (HTTP 409) and the daemon checks the old connection at once, so the next attempt gets in. - Offline means refused. While the runtime is not connected, creating a session with it, attaching it, delegating to it with capabilities, and creating a session in a project whose defaults name it are refused at once, naming the runtime and when the daemon last heard from it: runtime `labpc` is not connected (last seen 2026-10-22T18:12:51Z). The daemon never waits for a dial-in runtime to come back, and never hands out an instance of a connection that does not answer: it is checked first (see Reuse under Lifecycle and failures). A runtime the daemon remembers from before it restarted, but that has not dialed in since, is refused the same way. It stops on a stop signal (SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP), so it runs as a service; see Running a runtime as a service. - Stopping. A stopping runtime closes its WebSocket with a close handshake (normal closure). The daemon records that as runtime `labpc` disconnected: the other end closed the connection, in runtimes.list and in its instances' reasons as they go reconnecting and then failed; a runtime that vanished without one, such as one that was killed or lost its network, shows the transport's error instead, for example Connection reset without closing handshake. - MCP servers and ACP agents. It hosts the ones the daemon's configuration gives it: a [runtimes.<id>] table with no command, named after the ID it dials in with, holds its MCP servers and ACP agents, a scope = "runtime" server from the moment it connects.
