Changes to the table reach the connected runtime at once: added servers and agents start, removed ones stop, changed ones restart, and the rest keep running. The machine itself keeps only how to reach the daemon, [server] url and token; its own [runtimes.local] is its own daemon's, and a runtime that dials in warns at startup that it does not host it:

# ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml on the daemon's machine
[runtimes.labpc]
[runtimes.labpc.mcp.servers.my_chrome]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
scope = "runtime"
[runtimes.labpc.acp.agents.claude]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp"]
- Roots. --root limits its workspaces, as for --stdio. - Clients on its machine. Plain cookie and cookie attach on the runtime's machine use it for their directory when the daemon runs elsewhere, such as in a container; see A daemon already running.

Running a runtime as a service keeps such a runtime connected; Remote access covers the daemon's listener and tunnels, and Runtimes what every runtime shares, such as its capabilities and machine.

docs.title: Running a runtime as a service
docs.text:
This page covers keeping a runtime that dials in connected to its daemon: a service on Linux, macOS, or Windows that starts cookie runtime serve --daemon and restarts it. To keep the daemon itself running, see Persistent daemon.

Not next to the daemon

A daemon already carries a runtime on its own machine: the built-in local runtime with the coding capability, and global. Sessions work on the daemon's machine without anything else running. A runtime service is for other machines, such as a lab computer, a server, or the laptop whose browser or files a session should reach.

docs.title: What the service runs
docs.text:
cookie runtime serve --daemon <daemon-url> --id <id> --token <token>
  • <daemon-url> is the daemon's client URL, wss://host.example.ts.net/ws or ws://192.168.1.10:7419/ws: ws:// or wss:// and the exact /ws path. Without it, --daemon takes [server] url from this machine's config.toml, else the local daemon.
  • --id <id> names the runtime; without it, it is the host name. Only one runtime may be connected under an ID. See Runtimes that dial in.
  • --token <token> is the daemon's token: copy it from [server] token in the daemon's config.toml. The examples below put it in the service definition. An inline token is visible in that definition and in the process's command line on that machine; the runtime does not pass it on to the processes it starts, such as its bash calls and MCP servers. COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN and [server] token in this machine's config.toml work too; see Reaching a daemon.
  • --root <dir>, repeated, limits the workspaces the runtime serves.

Four things decide how a service has to be set up:

  • It retries. The runtime does not exit when the daemon is unreachable, at its start or later: it prints the reason and retries after 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, and so on up to 30 s, and reconnects after every drop. Start order does not matter, and a daemon restart, a network change, or a sleeping laptop waking up needs no help from the service manager. Its instances go reconnecting and failed meanwhile, and are reopened when it is back; see Reconnecting.
  • It exits on a refusal that retrying cannot fix, a wrong token or an ID that is reserved or configured on the daemon, with an error. A service manager that restarts it will repeat that error; read the log rather than raising the restart count.
  • It stops cleanly on a stop signal (SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP; on Windows Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Break, a closed console, logoff, or shutdown), cancelling its calls and stopping its MCP servers, so a service manager's ordinary stop is right. A clean stop exits successfully, so restart-on-failure leaves it stopped.
  • It runs as the user it serves. The runtime runs the MCP servers and ACP agents of its [runtimes.<id>] table in the daemon's configuration (see MCP servers and ACP agents) as that user, and its tools see that user's files and profile. Run the service as the account whose files and browser profile it needs, and, for browser MCP servers, inside that user's login session. A browser belongs to the machine, not to a workspace, so give it scope = "runtime": the runtime starts it once when it connects, in that user's home directory, and every workspace shares it:
# The daemon's config.toml, for the runtime that dials in as `labpc`
[runtimes.labpc.mcp.servers.my_chrome]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
scope = "runtime"

The installers put the binary in Cargo's home: ~/.cargo/bin/cookie on Linux and macOS, %USERPROFILE%\.cargo\bin\cookie.exe on Windows. Adjust the paths if you installed elsewhere. A sleeping machine runs nothing: the runtime is away until the machine wakes, and then reconnects by itself.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
A systemd user service, ~/.config/systemd/user/cookie-runtime.service:

[Unit]
Description=Cookie Agent runtime
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
ExecStart=%h/.cargo/bin/cookie runtime serve --daemon wss://host.example.ts.net/ws --id <id> --token <token>
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

The unit holds the token, so make it readable only by you, then start it:

chmod 600 ~/.config/systemd/user/cookie-runtime.service
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now cookie-runtime
loginctl enable-linger "$USER"

enable-linger starts the user's services at boot without a login session. Without it the runtime runs only while you are logged in. Follow the output with journalctl --user -u cookie-runtime -f.

A user service starts with a minimal environment, not your shell's. The runtime captures your shell's environment when it connects, so the commands, MCP servers, and ACP agents it starts find what your rc files set (see Shell Environment); the daemon's [runtimes.<id>.shell_environment] controls it. Environment= lines in the unit are only needed for what your shell does not set.

To remove the service, stop it, delete the unit, which holds the token, and tell systemd:

systemctl --user disable --now cookie-runtime
rm ~/.config/systemd/user/cookie-runtime.service
systemctl --user daemon-reload

A unit set up under earlier versions of this page read the token from ~/.config/cookie-agent/runtime.env; delete that file too (rm -f ~/.config/cookie-agent/runtime.env).

Lingering is per user, not per service: run loginctl disable-linger "$USER" only when no other user service of yours, such as the daemon's, needs it.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
A LaunchAgent runs in your login session, which a runtime that reaches your browser or profile needs. ~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.cookie-agent.runtime.plist, with absolute paths because launchd expands neither ~ nor $HOME:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key>
  <string>dev.cookie-agent.runtime</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>/Users/<you>/.cargo/bin/cookie</string>
    <string>runtime</string>
    <string>serve</string>
    <string>--daemon</string>
    <string>wss://host.example.ts.net/ws</string>
    <string>--id</string>
    <string><id></string>
    <string>--token</string>
    <string><token></string>
  </array>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key>
  <true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key>
  <dict>
    <key>SuccessfulExit</key>
    <false/>
  </dict>
  <key>ThrottleInterval</key>
  <integer>10</integer>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key>
  <string>/Users/<you>/Library/Logs/cookie-runtime.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key>
  <string>/Users/<you>/Library/Logs/cookie-runtime.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>

The plist holds the token, so make it readable only by you, then load it:

chmod 600 ~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.cookie-agent.runtime.plist
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.cookie-agent.runtime.plist
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/dev.cookie-agent.runtime

launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/dev.cookie-agent.runtime restarts it, and tail -f ~/Library/Logs/cookie-runtime.log shows what it prints. A LaunchAgent starts when you log in, not at boot.

To remove the agent, unload it and delete the plist, which holds the token, and the log:

launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/dev.cookie-agent.runtime
rm ~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.cookie-agent.runtime.plist
rm -f ~/Library/Logs/cookie-runtime.log

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
A Task Scheduler task at your logon is the recommended path: it runs in your session, with your profile, and so reaches your Chrome for browser MCP servers. Register it, with the token in its action:

$cookie = "$env:USERPROFILE\.cargo\bin\cookie.exe"
$logs = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\cookie-agent"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $logs | Out-Null
$action = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute "conhost.exe" -Argument "--headless cmd.exe /c `"`"$cookie`" runtime serve --daemon <daemon-url> --id <id> --token <token> >> `"$logs\runtime.log`" 2>&1`""
$trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogOn -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"
$settings = New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet `
  -ExecutionTimeLimit (New-TimeSpan) `
  -RestartCount 999 -RestartInterval (New-TimeSpan -Minutes 1) `
  -AllowStartIfOnBatteries -DontStopIfGoingOnBatteries
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Cookie Agent runtime" -Action $action `
  -Trigger $trigger -Settings $settings -RunLevel Limited
Start-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Cookie Agent runtime"

The empty New-TimeSpan removes the task's default three-day execution limit. The task's output goes to %LOCALAPPDATA%\cookie-agent\runtime.log. Stop-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Cookie Agent runtime" stops it.

  • No console window. conhost.exe --headless runs the command without a window on Windows 10 and 11. It is a switch of the console host that Microsoft does not document: if a Windows update changes it, drop it, and the task shows a console window while the runtime runs; closing that window stops the runtime.
  • A Windows service (NSSM, or sc.exe with a wrapper) can start before anyone logs in, but it runs outside your session, as another account or LocalSystem. It then reads that account's config.toml, and cannot reach your Chrome, so browser MCP servers do not work through it. Use it only for a runtime that needs files and shell commands, not your session.

To remove the task, which holds the token, unregister it and delete its log:

Stop-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Cookie Agent runtime" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Unregister-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Cookie Agent runtime" -Confirm:$false
Remove-Item "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\cookie-agent\runtime.log" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

A task set up under earlier versions of this page read the token from a COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN user variable that setx stored. Delete it from the registry (HKCU\Environment) for processes started afterwards:

[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN', $null, 'User')

A shell that is already open keeps its copy until you close it. Do not use setx COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN "": that stores an empty value instead of deleting the variable. %LOCALAPPDATA%\cookie-agent also holds the daemon task's log; delete the folder when neither task remains.

docs.title: Runtime templates [runtimes]
docs.text: A [runtimes.<id>] table in ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml is a runtime template: the daemon starts the runtime's process itself when a session first needs it, typically cookie runtime serve --stdio on another machine over ssh. Runtimes covers what every runtime shares, such as its lifecycle and failures; Runtimes that dial in start on their own instead, and MCP servers and ACP agents covers what a template's mcp and acp tables host.

docs.title: Example: a repository on another machine over ssh
docs.text:
Install the same Cookie Agent version on the remote machine (the runtime protocol versions must be compatible: their majors must match) and make sure ssh labpc cookie --version works without a password prompt. Then add a template to ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml on the machine that runs the daemon:

[runtimes.labpc]
command = ["ssh", "-o", "BatchMode=yes", "labpc", "cookie", "runtime", "serve", "--stdio"]
startup_timeout_ms = 20000

Start cookie, open /runtime, press a, type labpc and press Enter, then type a path on the remote machine such as ~/cookie-agent and press Enter. Before the first prompt this chooses the runtimes the new session starts with; in an existing session it attaches labpc to it. The daemon runs the command once, the remote cookie runtime serve resolves the path on its own machine and opens its coding capability there, and the session gains an attachment named after the runtime ID and the workspace's directory name, here labpc_cookie_agent. Tools that two attachments offer are prefixed with the attachment name, so the model sees local_web_bash and labpc_cookie_agent_bash; detach local (d on its row) to keep the bare names for the remote runtime only.

Attaching another workspace on labpc opens it over the same connection: one cookie runtime serve process serves every workspace and every session that uses labpc.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
runtimes maps a runtime ID to a template; it is empty by default.

Key Type Default Meaning command array of strings none The program and its arguments. Without it, the table holds the settings of the runtime that dials in with its ID (see below). env table of strings {} Variables added to the daemon's environment for the process: its shell environment when one was captured. startup_timeout_ms positive integer 10000 Bound on starting the process and its answer to runtime/initialize, and on each capability opening, which follows its MCP servers' first connection attempts. shutdown_grace_ms positive integer 3000 How long a stopping runtime gets before its process group is killed. mcp.servers.<name> MCP server table none MCP servers the runtime hosts on its machine, one per workspace instance or, with scope = "runtime", one for the runtime; see MCP servers. Their include_tools and exclude_tools filter tools on the runtime's machine (choosing a server's tools). acp.agents.<agent> ACP agent table none ACP agents the runtime starts on its machine; see ACP agents. shell_environment table none The [shell_environment] keys this runtime replaces: how it captures the user's shell environment on its machine.
  • Runtime IDs match [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31} because they become tool name prefixes. global is reserved. [runtimes.local] configures the built-in local runtime and accepts only mcp, acp, and shell_environment tables.
  • A table without command is no template: the daemon starts nothing for it, and it holds the MCP servers and ACP agents of the runtime that dials in with its ID. Like [runtimes.local], it accepts only mcp, acp, and shell_environment; env or a timeout without command is rejected.
  • Live changes. A runtime's mcp, acp, and shell_environment tables reach it at once when the configuration is applied, whether the daemon started it or it dialed in: added servers and agents start, removed ones stop, changed ones restart, and the others keep running. command, env, and the timeouts take effect when the runtime next starts, which the configuration status reports as a restart needing to apply runtimes.
  • command must be nonempty and its first element must name a program. One process serves every workspace, so the command names none. An element containing {workspace}, which older templates used, is rejected.
  • No shell is involved. cookie starts the program directly; on Windows, a bare program name such as npx also finds its .cmd or .bat launcher on PATH. ssh itself, however, joins its arguments into one string that the remote login shell interprets, so arguments with spaces or shell metacharacters need quoting that survives that shell. A workspace path travels in the runtime protocol, not on the command line, and cookie runtime serve expands a leading ~ in it.
  • Environment. The process inherits the daemon's environment, which ssh needs for SSH_AUTH_SOCK and similar variables, plus env. Names must be nonempty without = or NUL. ssh finds its configuration, keys, and known_hosts through that environment's HOME, so a daemon run with another HOME (a scratch or service home) needs env = { HOME = "/home/me" } in the template, or the files named on its command line as absolute paths, since no shell expands ~ there: -F /home/me/.ssh/config, -i /home/me/.ssh/id_ed25519, and -o UserKnownHostsFile=/home/me/.ssh/known_hosts.
  • MCP servers are parsed with the MCP server schema, and a server that enables OAuth (oauth = true or an oauth table) is rejected: OAuth credentials live on the daemon and are available to top-level [mcp] servers only. Static-header HTTP servers are allowed. See MCP servers.
  • Templates declare no capabilities and accept no plugins table: the runtime reports its capabilities when it connects, and plugins run only in the global runtime.

Unknown keys and invalid values fail the configuration load, as everywhere in config.toml. Changes take effect when the daemon next starts.

docs.title: cookie runtime serve
docs.text:
cookie runtime serve --stdio [--root <dir>]...
cookie runtime serve --daemon [<url>] [--id <runtime ID>] [--token <token>] [--root <dir>]...

With --daemon it dials in instead (see Runtimes that dial in); the rest of this section describes --stdio.

Serves this machine's runtime over standard input and output with the runtime protocol: the coding capability for every workspace the daemon opens. --root (repeatable) limits coding to workspaces under those directories; a root that does not exist fails at start. It needs no provider configuration and reads no config.toml; a leading ~ in a workspace or root is expanded, and paths are resolved on the machine it runs on. It reports its user's home directory, canonicalized, and expands a tool's ~/… path argument against the same home. Standard output carries only protocol messages and diagnostics go to standard error. It exits on runtime/shutdown, when standard input closes, or on a stop signal (SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP). A template normally runs it; running it by hand is only useful for debugging.

docs.title: MCP servers and ACP agents on runtimes
docs.text: A runtime hosts MCP servers and ACP agents on its own machine. Declare them in the runtime's mcp.servers and acp.agents tables, all in the daemon's config.toml: under [runtimes.<id>] for a template and for a runtime that dials in as <id> (a table without command), and under [runtimes.local] for the daemon's machine. MCP servers and ACP agents cover the servers and agents themselves; this page covers hosting them on a runtime.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text:
The runtime process (cookie runtime serve on the remote machine, or the daemon's process for [runtimes.local]) hosts the template's mcp.servers itself, so commands, working directories, and URLs are resolved on the runtime's machine. A server's scope says how many copies run:

  • scope = "workspace" (the default): each coding instance starts its own copy for its workspace, in that workspace unless the server sets a cwd. Right for servers about a repository, such as a language server.
  • scope = "runtime": the runtime starts one copy when it starts, in its user's home directory unless the server sets a cwd, and every workspace of the runtime shares it until the runtime stops. Right for servers about the machine, such as a browser.
[runtimes.labpc]
command = ["ssh", "-o", "BatchMode=yes", "labpc", "cookie", "runtime", "serve", "--stdio"]
startup_timeout_ms = 30000

[runtimes.labpc.mcp.servers.rust_analyzer]
command = "rust-analyzer-mcp"

[runtimes.labpc.mcp.servers.browser]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
scope = "runtime"

[runtimes.local.mcp.servers.docs]
command = "docs-mcp"
  • Connecting. An instance connects every enabled workspace-scoped server before it answers the daemon, and waits for the runtime-scoped ones' first attempt, which the runtime started when it initialized without holding up its answer; so a session's first use of the instance lists their tools. startup_timeout_ms covers these first attempts; raise it for servers that start slowly. A server that fails publishes no tools, and clients viewing a session attached to the instance (any instance of the runtime, for a runtime-scoped server) get an error naming it.
  • Tools. A workspace-scoped server's tools are the instance's tools, named <server>_<tool> like any MCP tool and gated by the mcp permission. When another attachment offers the same name, they are prefixed with the attachment name like the built-in tools. A runtime-scoped server's tools are the runtime's own: a session gets them once however many of the runtime's workspaces it attaches, prefixed with the runtime ID when another tool takes the name, and they run without a workspace.
  • Drops and retries. The runtime restarts a dropped server (1 s, 2 s, 4 s) with its tools still published, and drops them when every attempt fails. A failed server is retried when a session that uses the instance is created or opened, when the instance is attached or retried (r in /runtime), and with r on the server in /mcp.
  • Status. /mcp lists the servers of every instance as <runtime> at <workspace>, a runtime-scoped server once as <runtime>, runtime-wide, and, while no instance of a connected runtime hosts it, a workspace-scoped one as <runtime>, in each workspace, which "starts with a workspace" (client protocol 1.13.0). The /runtime panels list each attachment's servers, the runtime's shared ones included, with their state, tool count, and failure, and the machines view lists every server of each connected runtime, so a runtime's servers show before any session opens a workspace of it. Each lists its tools by the server's own names, those its filters left out apart (client protocol 1.36.0). Edits to a runtime's table reach it at once (see Live changes).

docs.title: ACP agents
docs.text:
A runtime hosts ACP agents, external coding agents that take a session's or a subagent's turns over the Agent Client Protocol (see the ACP agents spec, and the ACP agents guide for setting up Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI). Declare them exactly where MCP servers go: [runtimes.local.acp.agents.<agent>] for the daemon's machine, and [runtimes.<id>.acp.agents.<agent>] for a template or a runtime that dials in.

[runtimes.local.acp.agents.claude]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp"]
description = "Claude Code"

[runtimes.labpc.acp.agents.codex]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp"]
env = { CODEX_HOME = "/home/ada/.codex" }
Key Type Default Meaning command array of strings required The program and its arguments, run without a shell on the runtime's machine, in its home directory. On Windows, a bare program name also finds a .cmd or .bat launcher on PATH, such as npx's. env table of strings {} Variables merged over the runtime's environment. description string "" Shown where the agent is listed when its daemon document gives none; at most 512 bytes without control characters. enabled boolean true A disabled agent is listed as unavailable.
  • IDs. The table key is an agent ID (lowercase letters, digits, and single inner hyphens) and the agent's ID: [runtimes.local.acp.agents.claude] is the agent claude. Runtimes that declare the same key offer the same agent. A daemon agent document of that ID without an acp block keeps the ID; the declarations are ignored and the configuration status says so.
  • Which runtime runs it. A session runs the agent on the one runtime it attaches that offers it. With none, or with two, the agent cannot run in that session: creating the session, starting a run, or delegating is refused, saying which runtimes offer it, and a session that runs an ACP agent cannot attach a second runtime that offers it. See Which runtime runs it.
  • Availability. An agent of local or of a template is available whenever the daemon runs, since the daemon starts its runtime on demand; an agent of a runtime that dials in is available while that runtime is connected, and listed as unavailable while it is away.
  • The daemon-side document. Cookie settings come from the agent document of its ID, ~/.cookie-agent/agents/<agent>.md, shared by every runtime that offers it, whose acp block marks it as the agent's (see ACP agent documents). Without one the agent has mode all, the first offering runtime's description, and the default rules.
  • Changes. A changed acp table reaches a connected runtime at once: it starts the new agents, stops the removed ones, and reports the change.
  • Processes. Each agent runs one process per runtime, shared by its sessions, started on its first turn and stopped after [acp] idle_shutdown_ms with no turn in progress, with its runtime, and with the daemon.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
Use /sessions to search and open saved sessions, or /new for a fresh root. Selecting a saved session restores its visible transcript; submitting another message continues it. A headless continuation uses:

cookie run --resume-session <session-id> "Continue the investigation"

See Command line for selection overrides. For shortening model context without removing the saved log, see Compaction.

docs.title: Lifecycle and persistence
docs.text:
A new empty session exists only in memory. Its directory, metadata cache, and event JSONL are created atomically when the first user message is submitted. Closing an empty session leaves no persisted session.

Persisted sessions use an append-only JSONL history. New events are stamped with the writing engine version for diagnostics, but opening a session does not require an exact version match. The engine reads what a newer build wrote tolerantly: it ignores members it does not know, skips unknown audit events, quarantines records that do not agree with the rest of the log, reports what it skipped in session metadata, and tolerates the resulting sequence gaps (Event Reference). The derived metadata file is only a cache: missing, stale, mismatched, or unreadable cache content is rebuilt from the event history. Streamed text, reasoning, and tool progress are live-only: they reach attached views but are never written to events.jsonl, whose history holds finished turns and tool results. Reattaching to a session while a reply streams shows its finished turns, then the reply from the next live output on; a daemon that dies mid-reply leaves no partial reply on disk, and the run reopens as interrupted. Every stored event is written before it is published, and every event recovery depends on is also synced first. Per-attempt bookkeeping (model_attempt_started, model_tools_published, model_request_prepared, model_replay_evaluated, model_output_started, model_usage_recorded) is synced by the next event that is, so a system crash can drop only such records at the end of the log. While a run is in flight, fold-ignored records do not rewrite the metadata tip (last_event_seq, last_activity); it catches up at the run's next projection change or terminal event, on eviction, and on shutdown.

Shutting the daemon down cleanly cancels whatever runs are in flight and waits, under a short bound, for them to record RunCancelled; a run only comes back as interrupted by daemon restart when the process died without that chance.

Reopening a session adopts it: the engine reconciles that session's interrupted work and then waits, under a short bound, for the delegation recovery the adoption scheduled. Background subagents whose runs died with the previous process are therefore already settled — marked interrupted, reported to their parent, and their concurrency slots released — by the time the session is usable again.

Use /new to create a fresh root session and /sessions to search and switch between sessions. Delegated sessions form a tree beneath the root that created them. The Agents panel lists each session's subagents by their latest user-initiated activity, newest first: a user input submitted or admitted, or a delegate_subagent call started. Output and tool results never reorder it. Session metadata carries this time as last_agent_activity, so a reopened session orders its subagents the same way before any of them is replayed. Accepted runs retain their frozen model binding even if catalog, configuration, or provider-store state changes later.

Several cookie processes may share one project directory, but a root session and every delegated session beneath it are written by one process at a time: ownership is taken for the whole tree, not for a single session. Reopening any session of a tree another process still has open reports session is owned by another cookie process, for the root and its subagents alike. Such a session is still readable — the TUI shows it as a read-only snapshot with input disabled — and becomes writable once the process holding the tree exits. Adopting one session of a free tree claims the tree, while each session in it still reconciles its own interrupted work the first time it is written.

docs.title: History formats
docs.text:
A session log records its history format. A build that reads a newer format cannot open the session and asks for a newer cookie. A build that reads an older one converts it the first time it takes the session's tree for writing, keeping each original log beside the new one as events.jsonl.v<N>.bak; a read-only view converts in memory only. To convert every session up front instead:

cookie sessions upgrade        # the sessions of this directory
cookie sessions upgrade --all  # the sessions of every directory

It reports each tree it converted, each it skipped because another cookie process holds it (that process converts it itself), and each session it cannot convert, such as one written before history formats, and exits nonzero when there was one. The backups stay until you delete them.

docs.title: Titles
docs.text: Root sessions may generate a title from their opening user messages according to the Session Title configuration. A delegated session is titled immediately from the delegate_subagent description instead. The description is bounded by session_title.max_chars, and the delegated child does not run the title internal agent.

docs.title: Revert
docs.text:
Revert is available only while the session is idle. It removes every event after the selected positive sequence from events.jsonl; new events reuse the freed sequence numbers. A run left holding nothing but its start goes with it, and a run the cut falls inside is closed as interrupted, along with its open tool calls, internal agents, and approvals. Subagent sessions created by the removed delegations are deleted, together with their own subagents; a revert that would delete a running subagent is refused. A revert cannot be undone: fork first to keep the current branch.

In the TUI, click a past user message, choose Revert, and confirm. The TUI targets the sequence immediately before that user message and restores the message text to the composer for editing.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
Deleting a session removes its whole tree from disk: the root session, every subagent session under it, their events.jsonl and metadata, and the tree's artifacts (uploads and retained tool output). Only a root can be deleted; a subagent goes with its root. Its background calls are stopped without reporting. A delete cannot be undone: fork first to keep a copy, since a fork holds its own copy of the artifacts.

The daemon refuses while any session of the tree is running or compacting, while another cookie process owns the tree, and when the root gained events since the client showed it, such as another client's new turn. It moves the tree's directory aside first and then removes it, so a crash in between leaves only a .deleted-… directory, which the next start removes. Every client is told the sessions are gone.

In the TUI, open /sessions, highlight the session, press Ctrl+D (or Delete while the list has focus), and confirm with y. In the web client, use the trash icon on the session's row. See session.delete.

docs.title: Fork
docs.text:
Fork copies a persisted prefix containing at least one submitted user message into a new independent session. It may read an active source session. Copied events retain their sequence numbers, timestamps, run IDs, and payloads, while their envelope is rebound to the new session ID. Shared content-addressed artifacts remain resolvable without copying their bytes.

A fork does not take its source's subagents. The conversation comes along, including what the subagents reported, but the subagents stay the source's: the fork starts with no children, get_subagent_result refuses the source's, and the fork creates its own when it delegates. Each delegation record the fork leaves behind is replaced by a record_omitted event (see Events).

A fork of a root session is a new root, with a tree of its own, and may be taken from a session another process owns. A fork of a delegated session stays inside its source's tree, so it is published into that root's directory and needs that tree's ownership: forking a subagent of a tree another process holds fails with session_owned_elsewhere ("This session is open in another cookie process.").

In the TUI, choose Fork from a user message. That message is included in the copied prefix, the new title receives (fork), and the new session is selected.

docs.title: Compaction
docs.text:
Compaction reduces a long session history to a checkpoint. Internal compaction keeps a budgeted tail of recent messages unchanged and summarizes everything before it; the summary replaces those older messages in model context, and the original saved log is preserved. On a Responses provider, provider-native compaction runs beside it and the checkpoint also stores the opaque window the provider returned.

Active history means the currently assembled context before compaction, including any existing summary and the messages after it. It does not reload historical events already replaced by earlier checkpoints.

docs.title: Native provider compaction
docs.text:
Every model on a Responses adaptor compacts natively by default: OpenAI Responses, whether the managed openai provider, an OpenAI-compatible gateway, or a credential-less endpoint, and Azure OpenAI Responses when the provider's setup table has model, version, and deployment_type, which scope the window to an explicit deployment. Azure without them, and every other adaptor, compacts with the summary alone. Set compaction = "unsupported" on a model override, or on a custom model's capabilities, to turn native compaction off for that model.

Native compaction runs beside the summary. When a checkpoint is due, the engine calls the provider's compact endpoint and the internal compaction agent at the same time:

  • both succeed: the checkpoint holds the summary and the window;
  • native fails: the checkpoint holds the summary alone, and the failure may mark the provider (below);
  • the summary fails: nothing is committed, even when native succeeded. Every checkpoint carries a summary.

A failed native call costs only its own time, which overlaps the summary. Cancelling compaction cancels both calls, and compaction hooks see one compaction.

The window serves only its own model. A request whose model has the same provider ID and model ID as the window, on the same adaptor, sends the window with the messages after it. A variant change keeps the window. Every other request, on another model, another provider, or a provider marked as rejecting windows, uses the summary and its recent messages instead. Switching models in the picker, or a fallback chain moving to its next model, therefore continues on the summary. The window also keeps its exact scope (its endpoint and account): a window whose scope the adaptor no longer accepts, after an endpoint change for example, is passed over for the summary too.

A window has a 32 MiB cap; max_summary_bytes applies only to the summary. A window keeps no independent recent-message tail. The next native compaction is seeded with the window when the model can use it. Neither native nor internal compaction rereads files.

Older sessions. Builds before client protocol 1.29.0 stored a window without a summary. Such a checkpoint still serves its own model. On any other model the engine first summarizes the events it covers from the saved log, once, and commits that as a new checkpoint; the request then proceeds on it.

docs.title: In-stream compaction
docs.text:
A model with compaction = "in-stream", and every ChatGPT model, compacts inside its own requests instead of with the standalone call:

  • The server compacts at the trigger. Each request carries context_management with compact_threshold set to the trigger threshold. When the rendered input reaches it, the server compacts before it answers and streams compaction items beside the answer.
  • The items travel with their turn. They are kept in the turn's native replay and sent back to the same model, which continues from them. Another model replays the turn without them, from the turns themselves.
  • The engine's own checkpoint is a backstop. It waits until the latest turn's usage reaches halfway from the trigger to the input budget (85% of the budget with the default 70% trigger), so it fires only when the server did not compact. The context-length retry is unchanged.
  • No standalone call. Such a model declares compaction unsupported, so a checkpoint holds the summary alone.

docs.title: The provider record
docs.text:
The daemon remembers, per provider ID, what native compaction answered, in native-compaction.json in its data folder (~/.cookie-agent by default):

  • unsupported: the compact endpoint answered definitively that the provider has no native compaction: HTTP 404, 405, or 501, or a refusal naming the compaction item (an adaptor that cannot build the compact request counts too). Native compaction is not attempted; stored windows still serve.
  • rejects_windows: the provider refused a request that carried a window (below). Native compaction is not attempted, and requests use the summary instead of stored windows.

Transient failures (timeouts, rate limits, 5xx other than 501, network errors) and authentication errors mark nothing. An entry expires after 7 days, and is dropped when the provider's configuration (its source, endpoint, recipe, setup, or authentication method) changes. There is no option to force native compaction past an entry: delete the file, or change the provider's configuration. The configuration status (/config in the TUI, cookie config, and the web client's configuration view) lists each entry with its reason and age.

A window refused at request time. When the provider answers a request that carried a window with a 400 or 422 naming the compaction item or its encrypted content (OpenAI answers an unusable compaction item with invalid_encrypted_content; a gateway without compaction support typically names the compaction item type or the encrypted_content field), that request fails with the provider's error, as any refusal does, and the provider is marked rejects_windows. The next request, in that session or any other, uses the summary. A refusal that names neither marks nothing.

docs.title: The trigger threshold
docs.text:
Triggers are measured against the model's input budget, the number of tokens a request may occupy:

input_budget = model_input_limit                     when the model declares one
input_budget = model_context_limit - output_reserve  otherwise
output_reserve = min(max_output_tokens, 32000, model_context_limit / 2)

Catalog models take the input limit from models.dev limit.input when it is narrower than the context window (for example gpt-5: 400,000 context, 272,000 input); custom models declare it as capabilities.input_tokens. max_output_tokens is the output cap the run sends (see agent limits), by default the model's full output limit. The reserve is capped at 32,000 tokens so a large output limit does not claim a big share of the window, and at half the context so a model whose output limit equals its context window keeps a usable budget.

By default, compaction uses a proportional trigger:

trigger_tokens = input_budget * percent / 100

percent defaults to 70, so a model with a 200,000-token context window and a 64,000-token output limit triggers at 117,600 tokens, and gpt-5 at 190,400. Valid percentages are 1 through 99; 100 is rejected because compaction at the model limit does not preserve useful request headroom.

The fixed-buffer form preserves the earlier behavior:

trigger_tokens = input_budget - buffer_tokens

This subtraction saturates at zero. If the buffer equals or exceeds the input budget, the trigger becomes 0 and automatic compaction is disabled for that model.

Before each model request, the engine compares the input + output tokens the provider reported for the latest model turn against the threshold, and compacts when they reach it. Usage recorded before the latest checkpoint is ignored, so a fresh checkpoint waits for the next reported turn. Messages added since the latest turn, such as a new prompt or steering input, are not counted until the provider reports them, and they are kept verbatim only when they fit the recent history budget (see step 4 below). If a request still exceeds the provider's context length, the engine compacts once regardless of the threshold and retries.

docs.title: What happens when it triggers
docs.text:
1. Native call. On a model that compacts natively and a provider the record does not mark, the native call starts beside the summary below and compacts the whole active history, without selecting recent messages. Native compaction uses the bound model's context limit minus the effective compaction output allowance; when the history exceeds it, bulky tool outputs are elided in the saved log first (tool_output_elided). If that allowance is unknown, the engine reserves 20,000 tokens as conservative summary-output headroom.
  2. Recent-history selection. For internal summarization, the engine first selects a contiguous suffix of original messages to keep unchanged. Its effective token target is at most min(keep_recent_tokens, input_budget / 4), using integer division, and is further limited by actual available space in the post-checkpoint request. System and tool context, pinned context, the summary, and the output reserve must still fit. Tool calls and their results are retained as complete groups, never split at the suffix boundary. If the newest indivisible group exceeds the target, no tail is retained; the engine does not exceed the target or substitute an older, noncontiguous group. keep_recent_tokens = 0 disables the tail.
  3. Replaced-span trial. The summarizer receives only the span the checkpoint replaces: the active, unpruned history up to the selected suffix, including any earlier summary. The suffix itself is never sent. The request keeps the session's own system prompt, pinned context, and tool definitions, so it is a cache-friendly prefix of the latest conversation request; the compaction agent's prompt rides along in a trailing instruction message instead of replacing the session system prompt. A tool-call answer is rejected as non-text output and counts as a compaction failure. The provider is authoritative for internal-agent input size; there is no byte-based pre-flight admission gate. The session's calibrated estimator still sizes the retained recent history and the post-checkpoint budget.
  4. Context-fit retry. A provider context-length failure permits one pruned retry. Other failures do not trigger pruning. Internal model bindings are tried in order, advancing after provider failures. The retry uses an in-memory copy of the same replaced span and drops the session tool definitions (cache affinity is already lost once tool outputs are rewritten): tool results are retained with ArtifactStore::retain and replaced by reference markers with a structured read_artifact hint carrying artifact="<digest>". Saved ArtifactReference URIs remain unchanged. The session tree can read the retained artifact back with read_artifact. Structured tool content is retained as serialized JSON, not flattened into original output; the marker labels this format. All outputs of read_artifact calls are replaced with [artifact read output omitted for compaction] in the private retry input, including named-stream reads. Detection uses the tool name; ordinary filesystem read results follow normal tool-output pruning. This does not emit durable tool_output_elided (ToolOutputElided) events or change the original saved log or the retained recent messages, even if the retry fails.
  5. Summary. The internal compaction agent (see Internal agents) writes a structured checkpoint with fixed sections (objective, requirements, decisions, work state, files, commands and errors, next step, important context). When the replaced span starts with an earlier internal summary, the prompt asks it to merge that summary into one updated checkpoint instead of starting fresh. An authored compaction.md can extend or replace this prompt with placeholders, and the user's focus text is added to it. It must return summary text only, at most max_summary_bytes (256 KiB by default); non-text output is rejected. The built-in compaction document sets no output cap of its own, so it inherits the owner run's max_output_tokens, bounded by the model's own output limit; the same inheritance applies to any authored internal-agent document that omits the limit. A nonzero limits.max_output_tokens in compaction.md overrides the inherited value. The suffix-selection output reserve equals that same effective cap. The built-in compaction document uses a flat 3-minute timeout. An authored compaction.md can override limits.timeout_ms; the configured value is honored exactly, while zero or omission uses the 30-second internal-agent default.
  6. Checkpoint commit. A context_checkpoint_committed event records the text summary, the native window beside it when the native call succeeded, source and recent-suffix boundaries, and the budget math, including the effective recent-history token budget. Retained messages come from saved history, not new file reads.

docs.title: Context after an internal checkpoint
docs.text:
The next request assembles context in this order:

  1. System prompt and tool definitions.
  2. Pinned AGENTS.md context.
  3. Pinned loaded skill bodies.
  4. Summary of everything before the retained suffix.
  5. Recent original messages retained unchanged, followed by any new messages.

Pinned context is preserved separately from the suffix. With retention disabled, or when the newest complete group cannot fit, the recent suffix is absent and only the summary remains alongside pinned context. The summary and the retained suffix do not overlap. A request on the window's own model uses the window and the messages after it instead of this summary-and-tail layout.

With deferred tools, a checkpoint folds the tools loaded before it: from the next request on they are declared up front, and the model is told afresh what it can still load. The retained messages keep calls to the folded tools, and lose the loader calls that loaded them, the earlier announcements, and calls to tools the session no longer offers.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: See Context Compaction for settings, defaults, trigger forms, and inheritance.

docs.title: Manual compaction
docs.text:
Choosing /compact in the command palette forces a checkpoint for the selected idle session. The palette then asks for an optional focus, for example:

preserve the parser decisions and failing test evidence

Press Enter with the prompt empty to compact without a focus. The focus text is added to the compaction prompt (appended, or placed where an authored compaction.md puts {{focus}}) so the summary emphasizes the areas you care about. Steering remains available while compaction runs; admitted pending inputs are promoted only after the checkpoint, honoring any recalls made during compaction. A message sent to an idle session that is compacting, from this or another client, waits for the compaction to finish and then starts its run.

To stop a manual compaction, press Ctrl-C (or Esc twice) while the session shows compacting, as you would to cancel a run; session.compact.cancel does the same over the protocol. A cancelled compaction commits no checkpoint.

session.compact returns whether a checkpoint was actually committed. Manual compaction follows the same recent-history selection, replaced-span trial, and context-fit retry rules.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Native compaction stopped being used for a provider. The provider record marked it. The configuration status (/config in the TUI, cookie config, or the web client's configuration view) names the provider, its state, the answer that marked it, and when. unsupported means the compact endpoint answered that it has none (for example HTTP 404 from a gateway that does not implement /responses/compact); rejects_windows means the provider refused a request that carried a compacted window, and requests now use the summary. The mark lifts after 7 days, when the provider's configuration changes, or when you delete native-compaction.json from the data folder (or its entry); compaction keeps working on the summary meanwhile.
  • A request failed with an encrypted-content error. That request carried a window its provider refused; the provider is now marked rejects_windows, so send the message again and it goes out on the summary.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Compaction produces these event payloads:

  • internal_agent_started / internal_agent_finished / internal_agent_fallback — the compaction agent invocation
  • internal_agent_text_delta (live-only) — the summary as it streams
  • native_compaction_started / native_compaction_finished (live-only) — a provider-native compaction call

While compaction runs, the TUI shows a 🧹 compacting context… row and the bottom bar reads compacting. Expanded, the row streams the summary, or reads calling native compaction endpoint (model) while the native call runs beside it. When compaction finishes, the row is replaced by the context compacted checkpoint row, or removed if compaction failed. - context_checkpoint_committed — the checkpoint with boundaries and budgets

The internal summarizer's in-memory pruning retry does not produce tool_output_elided events.

See the event reference for checkpoint retention fields.

docs.title: Delegating to runtimes
docs.text: A session can hand work to a subagent with delegate_subagent (see Subagents and the tools reference). A root session can also say where that subagent works: on which runtime, and in which workspace. A root with only the global runtime attached has no workspace of its own, so it can orchestrate work across machines and leave the files and commands to its subagents.

docs.title: A session with only global
docs.text:
The web client's New session starts with only global attached (see Web); the TUI's plain cookie attaches global and local at the current directory, and its /runtime panel can detach local before the first message. Such a session:

  • has memory, MCP servers, plugins, and the other global tools, but no read, write, edit, or bash;
  • gets list_runtimes, which lists the daemon's machines and runtimes;
  • gets a paragraph in its delegation instructions saying that it has no workspace and that work needing files or commands goes to a subagent;
  • must name where each subagent works: delegate_subagent's capabilities is required.

Its row in the session list still shows where it works: its badges add the machines and workspaces its subagents were given (see Badges).

docs.title: list_runtimes
docs.text:
list_runtimes takes no arguments and reads the daemon's state at every call, so a runtime that dials in mid-session shows up on the next call. It prints every machine and its runtimes, each runtime's capabilities with their descriptions, whether the runtime is connected or starts_on_use (a template the daemon starts when a session needs it), its home directory, and the calling session's own attachments. Other sessions' instances are never shown. A runtime that is offline keeps the machine, platform, and home it was last seen with (Machines). See the tools reference for the format.

The list_runtimes permission controls it. An agent document without a list_runtimes key gets allow when its mode is primary or all, and no rule when it is subagent or internal, so subagents do not see the list unless their document grants it:

permissions:
  list_runtimes: allow   # or deny, to hide it from a primary agent

docs.title: Naming where a subagent works
docs.text:
In a root session that has global attached, delegate_subagent takes capabilities, a list of the runtime capabilities the child works through. Each item is the full <runtime_id>/<capability_id>, as list_runtimes prints a <runtime id=…> and one of its <capability name=…>, with a workspace when the capability takes one:

{
  "agent_type": "coder",
  "description": "Fix the API tests",
  "prompt": "Run the API test suite and fix what fails.",
  "capabilities": [
    {"capability": "labpc/coding", "workspace": "~/src/api"}
  ]
}
  • When it is there. Required when the root has only global; optional when the root has global and other attachments, where leaving it out lets the child inherit the root's attachments; absent when the root has no global, and in every subagent: only the root chooses runtimes.
  • What the child gets. global, because the root has it (whether children have global follows the root, never the model, so global/global cannot be listed), then each listed capability, in order, under the usual attachment names (labpc_api, with _2 for a duplicate). The same runtime may be listed twice with different workspaces; two workspaces or more give the child's tools prefixes, as in any session.
  • Starting the runtimes. The daemon starts every listed runtime before it creates the child, as session.create does: a template runtime starts, and a dial-in runtime must be connected. If one cannot start, the call fails naming the runtime and the reason, and nothing is created.
  • Refusals. A runtime the daemon does not have, or a capability the runtime does not offer (the error lists the ones it does), refuses the call. So does a missing workspace for a capability that takes one, and capabilities together with resume_session_id: a resumed subagent keeps its own attachments.
  • Deeper children inherit their parent's attachments, with global exactly when the root has it. A runtime attached to or detached from the root later reaches only the children created afterwards.

docs.title: Limiting where the root delegates
docs.text:
The delegate permission accepts a runtime selector, as other actions do (see Runtime selectors). Each runtime a call names in capabilities is checked as delegate@<runtime>: a runtime that denies refuses the whole call, and one that asks puts the call through the usual approval, which lists the runtimes and workspaces. A call without capabilities is checked as plain delegate.

permissions:
  delegate: allow
  delegate@labpc: ask     # confirm before a subagent works on labpc
  delegate@prod: deny     # never on prod

The resource of delegate rules is the subagent's agent ID, and the most specific rule wins: delegate: {coder: allow} outranks delegate@labpc: deny, which is "*": deny. Write delegate@labpc: {coder: deny} to deny that one. The child's own rules still decide what it can do on the runtime, including any bash@labpc-style selectors.

docs.title: Badges
docs.text: A root session's badges in the session lists count its own attachments followed by the ones its subagents were given, each runtime, capability, and workspace once, by the usual badge rules: one machine shows its badge and workspaces, several machines show their badges. The daemon records them on the root as each child is created (SessionMeta.delegated_attachments), so the list needs no extra reads, and they only grow: a child that finishes, or a detach on the root, leaves them. A subagent's own row shows its own attachments. The TUI's session picker shows the same places for a root with no workspace of its own.

docs.title: Bringing a machine in from a subagent
docs.text:
No tool starts runtimes on other machines, but a coding subagent on the daemon's machine can bring one in for a while with the tools it has:

  1. The root delegates to a coding subagent on local.

  2. That subagent runs a background bash call that dials the remote runtime in:

    ssh labpc cookie runtime serve --daemon ws://daemon-host:7419/ws --id labpc --token <token>

  3. The root calls list_runtimes, sees labpc, and delegates to it with capabilities.

  4. Stopping the background call (stop_background) ends the dial-in connection, and the runtime shows as disconnected (and stays on its machine as an offline runtime until forgotten).

See Runtimes that dial in for the listener and IDs.

The subagent needs the daemon's token

Dialing in takes the daemon's token, [server] token in ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml. Any agent that may read or bash on the daemon's machine can already read that file; this pattern gives it no new access, but it does put the token in the agent's hands. To prevent that, deny reads of the file in that agent's rules, for example read: {"~/.cookie-agent/config.toml": deny, "*": allow}, and keep bash from reaching it. Adding a [runtimes.<id>] template to config.toml instead takes effect only after config.reload or a daemon restart, which a subagent cannot trigger through a tool, so the dial-in path is the one to use.

docs.title: Goal Mode
docs.text:
Goal mode lets you give a root session a durable objective and a checklist the agent maintains while it works. You set one with /goal, or the agent sets one with goal_set, for example when you ask it in your own words to set a goal. Only root sessions can have one.

The goal mode design spec describes the runtime, plugin, and persistence contracts behind this workflow.

docs.title: Activation and goal bar
docs.text:
Activate goal mode in the root session by choosing /goal in the command palette and entering the objective in the prompt that follows. An empty objective is refused in place, and Esc returns to the command list. Outside a root session, or in a read-only one, the palette explains why instead of prompting.

A persistent one-line goal bar appears above the message composer whenever the selected session has a goal. Click its objective description to open a detail modal with the full objective, checklist, and lifecycle status. The checklist view is read-only; the root agent maintains it through its items-only update tool.

Use the bar's Pause or Resume button and Cancel button to control an active or paused goal. From the keyboard, F6 focuses the bar, Left/Right or Tab move between its controls, Enter activates one, and Esc returns to the composer. Completed and cancelled goals keep a read-only bar and detail view; the bar is hidden when no goal exists. The producer queue strip is separate and appears above the goal bar and composer.

Setting a new objective errors if a goal is already active or paused; cancel or complete the current goal first. The same holds for the agent's goal_set.

A goal moves through four lifecycle states: active, paused, completed, and cancelled. Completed and cancelled are terminal. The agent can start a goal when none is active or paused, and read and revise its checklist, but only you can pause, resume, or cancel one.

docs.title: Checklist and tools
docs.text:
Every root run has three goal tools: goal_get, goal_set, and goal_update. They are root-only: delegated child sessions never see them, and there is no goal inheritance into subagents. They are also not a configurable capability; they cannot be granted to anything else. On a model that loads deferred tools they are deferred: the model sees their names and loads them when it needs them. An ACP agent's root session has them only while your goal is active or paused when the run starts.

goal_set { objective, items? } starts a goal, with its first checklist when it gives one, as /goal does. A goal the agent started is continued and completed like yours.

The goal tools declare no permission. They act on the session's own goal alone, so permission rules do not govern them and every call is allowed.

Each checklist item contains only a description and a finished flag, with no item ID. goal_update { items } replaces the entire ordered checklist of the current/latest session goal when the engine actor accepts the update. The engine serializes updates: the last accepted replacement wins, with no model-supplied goal ID, revision check, or lost-update protection. An older run's update can intentionally affect a newly activated active or paused goal. Updates reject if the current goal is absent, completed, or cancelled. The engine still numbers durable state revisions for reminders and user lifecycle controls; those controls retain their goal-ID and expected-revision checks. The root checklist is the authoritative record of progress: the agent is instructed to verify work directly or through subagents before marking an item finished, and to trust its own checklist over any subagent's self-report.

Completion has one automatic rule. When a checklist update leaves the checklist non-empty and every item finished, the goal is recorded as completed. An empty checklist preserves the current active or paused state and never completes a goal: activating a goal with no checklist yet still starts work, and the initial goal message asks the agent to establish the checklist.

Checklist updates are also preserved while a goal is paused, including an all-finished update, which records completion without scheduling any further work.

docs.title: Continuations
docs.text:
While a goal is active, the engine can wake an idle session with a message carrying the full objective and the entire checklist. The first delivery says Goal started and asks the agent to establish the checklist if it is empty. Later reminders say Continue the root goal.

The distinction comes from committed model input, not from merely accepting or claiming a queued reminder. If the startup message is discarded before delivery, the next eligible message still says Goal started. A consumed introduction survives restart and pause/resume, while activating a new goal starts fresh.

A goal message is scheduled only when all of the following hold:

  • the goal is active, and the checklist is empty or has unfinished items;
  • the session is idle (no active run);
  • no pending user, steer, or queued messages exist;
  • no other live producer registration (background delegation or plugin) exists;
  • no goal reminder is already pending.

The condition is rechecked when the run actually starts, so real work that arrives in between always wins. Because the reminder re-injects the objective and checklist, compaction cannot strand the goal.

docs.title: Pause, cancel, and interruption
docs.text:
Pausing or cancelling a goal stops future goal continuations. The engine also durably queues a steering notification before closing the producer registration if the root has an active run, other live producers (excluding the goal's own registration), or queued real messages. This includes an idle root waiting for subagent results or plugin work. At the next safe model API request, the model is told that the goal was paused or cancelled, to stop autonomous pursuit of that old goal, and to follow your directions. These are durable lifecycle-control messages, separate from continuation reminders, so closing the goal controller does not remove them.

Because the notification uses steer delivery, it can wake a normal root run when the root is idle but has other producers or queued real messages. That wake does not resume goal reminders: the goal remains paused or cancelled. A fully idle root with no other live producers and no queued real messages saves the lifecycle change without starting an announcement run. The goal's own registration or pending reminder alone does not trigger one.

This does not cancel an in-flight request, abort active delegations, or undo actions already emitted. The existing explicit interrupt (/cancel) remains unchanged and separate from goal lifecycle controls. Checklist updates still target the current session goal at actor acceptance; the notification does not bind an older run's updates to its former goal.

docs.title: Producers: plugins and background work
docs.text:
Background delegation results and plugin-originated messages reach the session through runtime producer registrations. Registrations are runtime-only: they vanish on restart. Messages that were accepted before a restart are durable, and accepted-but-unconsumed messages that have not been discarded are delivered after recovery even if their producer never re-registers.

Each message is sent in one of two modes, chosen per send:

  • Steer — inserted into the next model API request, including mid-run at a tool boundary. It never cancels an in-flight request. Background subagent results always steer; a steer to an idle session starts a normal run.
  • Queue — starts a subsequent normal run. While a run is active it is persisted and deferred, then delivered when the session is idle.

Pending and admitted producer messages in either mode appear in the existing queue strip above the goal bar and composer, which automatically shows and hides with its contents. Messages reserved for a model request are hidden while claimed; release after a failed/cancelled attempt returns them to the strip unless already consumed or discarded. Discarded messages are removed from the strip. Producer messages cannot be recalled into the user composer; displaying them does not make them user-authored input.

The producer's owner can discard its own waiting message through the producer discard API, even after unregistering, because accepted messages are independent of runtime registrations. Discard is durable and retrying an owned already-discarded message is idempotent; another owner cannot discard it. Only unclaimed waiting messages qualify, including admitted messages not yet reserved by the engine. Reservation happens before provider dispatch, so a claimed message cannot be discarded even if the provider has not received it yet. Releasing all claims makes an unconsumed, undiscarded message waiting again. In-flight or consumed input cannot be retracted, and discard cannot undo actions already taken.

After a restart, producer-capable plugins reconstruct their own pending work from their own storage or the external services they front; the engine does not replay plugin state for them. A goal's automatic continuation waits until all tracked producer-capable plugins report ready, so recovered external work can register before the agent resumes. A failed or disabled producer is surfaced as a notification and holds goal continuation; it is not silently treated as work done. Already accepted real messages can still be delivered.

There are no watchdogs or deadlines for producers. A producer that registers and then stalls stays visible in the runtime inspection API (a read-only snapshot of registrations) and blocks automatic goal continuations, but no TUI command manufactures a wake around it. A plugin that never finishes startup recovery can likewise keep the readiness barrier waiting indefinitely. The engine also makes no exactly-once claim: a producer that does not see an acknowledgment retries with the same sender-chosen idempotency key, and the engine deduplicates the retry, but external side effects of a repeated attempt are the producer's own concern.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Sessions — session persistence, revert, and fork
  • Compaction — how history checkpoints interact with durable goal state
  • Goal mode design spec — the governing technical specification

docs.title: Held sessions
docs.text: A session can start runs on its own: a subagent reports, another agent sends mail, a plugin or a cron job delivers a prompt, or a goal reminds the agent to go on. When that goes wrong, the session is held instead of trying again and again.

docs.title: When a session is held
docs.text:
• You stop its run while something could start the next one: a message waiting for it, an active goal, or a background call, subagent, or plugin that will report. Stop (Esc in the TUI, the Stop button on the web) ends the run, and none of these starts the next one. With nothing such, a stop holds nothing.
  • You revert it to a point where messages were still waiting: they wait for you.
  • Its runs keep failing. A run that fails is tried again after a short backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, ... up to [model_retry] backoff_ceiling_ms), as long as the failures in a row stay within [model_retry] standard_retries (3 by default; negative never holds). Past that, the session is held, and a push notification says so.

A run that a daemon restart interrupted is neither: it resumes as before.

docs.title: While it is held
docs.text:
• Nothing starts a run of the session on its own, and goal reminders stop.
  • What was waiting stays waiting: nothing is lost.
  • Reports from its own subagents, delegations, and background calls are taken and wait too.
  • Plugins and runtimes are refused with producer_rejected, a cron job's fire into it is skipped (session held), and mail from any agent other than its parent is refused.

The transcript records why (Automatic runs held: stopped by you or failed 4 times in a row: ...), and the session's line says what waits. In the session list a held session sorts with the active ones and shows a pause: before its title on the web (red when its runs kept failing, its tooltip saying why), and ⏸ after its title in the TUI.

docs.title: Resuming
docs.text:
• Resume clears the hold and sends what waits in one run. On the web it takes the place of Send and Queue, and sends the composer's text too, if any. In the TUI, click resume on the banner above the composer, or press Enter in an empty composer.
  • Any message you send resumes the session as well, and takes what waits with it.
  • A subagent's parent resumes it by continuing it (delegate_subagent with its resume_session_id) or by sending it a message.

Clients use session.held.resume (client protocol 1.34.0); see Held sessions in the protocol reference.

docs.title: Attaching Media
docs.text: A message can carry images, PDFs, audio, and video alongside its text, when the session's model accepts them. The daemon stores each attachment in the session's artifact store and sends it to the model as a file.

docs.title: What a model accepts
docs.text:
Every model in the catalog view states its input_media: the kinds it accepts in a message, the media types of each, and the limits that apply (see The catalog view). The limits are the lowest of the model's own, its provider's for a message, and the daemon's caps: 20 MiB per file, 25 MiB for video, and at most 16384 pixels a side and 16 Mi pixels for an image. A client offers attachments only for the kinds the selected model accepts and checks a file before sending it.

For example, an Anthropic model that accepts PNG and JPEG images and PDFs takes images of up to 7.5 MiB and PDFs of up to 20 MiB, and no video; a Gemini model takes each kind it accepts up to 14 MiB, which keeps the whole request within the Gemini API's limit.

docs.title: Attaching a file
docs.text:
A client uploads the file into the session first, then names it in the message:

  1. artifact.upload.begin with the session, the file's size, and its name.
  2. artifact.upload.chunk for each piece of at most 1 MiB, in order.
  3. artifact.upload.finish with the file's SHA-256. The daemon recognizes the file by its content (the name never decides its type), checks it, and returns the reference to send.
  4. run.start, run.steer, or session.submit_input with content holding the text and a file part with that reference.

The protocol reference lists every rule and error. An upload the connection leaves unfinished is dropped when it closes.

The daemon checks every attachment again when the message arrives, against the model the message goes to. An attachment the model does not accept, one over its limits, or more of a kind than it takes refuses the message, and nothing of it is recorded; the error says which limit, so a client can offer to downscale an image that is too large.

docs.title: In the terminal UI
docs.text: /attach asks for a file's path and attaches the file to the next message, and pasting the path of one existing file (what a terminal pastes when a file is dropped on it) offers to attach it. Both appear only while the selected model accepts some kind of file. The TUI checks the file's kind, size, and an image's pixels against the model's limits before it uploads, and shows the limit when a file is refused, by the TUI or the daemon; it does not downscale. Attachments show on the composer's border as 📎 name · type · size, and Backspace at the start of the draft removes the newest. See Terminal UI.

docs.title: When the model changes
docs.text:
A session can move to another model, or a run can fall back to one. A model that does not accept a file in the history is sent a short note in its place, such as:

[image omitted: acme/text-model does not accept images (screenshot.png, 471 KB)]

The saved history keeps the file, so a later model that accepts it sees it again. Compaction summaries never see media: the summarizer reads notes in place of every file.

docs.title: How long a file is kept
docs.text:
An uploaded file no message references is kept for an hour, then removed. Once a message names it, it lives as long as the session history references it: a revert that removes every message naming it removes the file once its hour is up, and a fork takes it into the forked session. A daemon restart forgets the hour; a file no message referenced then stays in the store.

Any artifact of a session, an uploaded file, a tool's attachment, or the full output behind a truncated tool display, can be read back with artifact.read.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Memory is what Cookie Agent keeps between sessions: Markdown notes that the agent and you write, which later sessions see or find again. It belongs to the global runtime, so a session has memory while global is attached; detaching global turns it off for that session. Memory is gathered context: reading or writing it never changes a session's attachments, runtimes, or workspaces. The memory spec has the full design.

docs.title: Layers and files
docs.text:
Each memory is one Markdown file with a short frontmatter, in ~/.cookie-agent/memory (the memory folder of the data root):

memory/
  user/<category>.md            user://<category>
  agents/<agent>.md             agent://<agent>
  machines/<machine>/<name>.md  machine://<machine>/<name>
  projects/<project>/<name>.md  project://<project>/<name>
Layer About Created by Deleted by user You, in every task: profile, preferences, feedback, references You, or an agent whose memory_write rules allow it You, or an agent whose rules allow it agent One agent's way of doing its job, such as what you want from reviews The daemon, one for every agent (Agent memory) You, or an agent whose rules allow it; the daemon removes an empty one it made when its agent goes machine One machine: OS quirks, toolchains, paths, rules such as "read-only unless asked" The agent or you The agent or you project One body of work: conventions, decisions, gotchas The agent or you, in a project that exists; the daemon creates the project's overview The agent or you; the folder goes with its project

A project's memory folder is the project's: a project:// write to a name that is no project is refused, from an agent and from you alike, and the refusal names the projects there are. Projects are created from a client (cookie project create, the web client), which also creates project://<name>/overview with an empty body. Like an agent file's, the overview's description is the daemon's: Overview of the `<name>` project, loaded in full into its sessions; a write keeps it and says so. Renaming a project moves its folder, and deleting it deletes the folder whole. Every folder under projects/ from before projects existed became a project the first time the daemon started. See Projects.

The first time the daemon starts without a memory folder, it creates the four layer folders and the categories profile, preferences, feedback, and references with empty bodies. Add a category by creating a file in user/.

---
description: Build and test conventions for cookie-agent
keywords: [cargo, clippy, msrv, no-fail-fast, cookie-agent]
---
- Run `cargo test --no-fail-fast`; plain `cargo test` stops at the first
  failing crate.

description is required (one line, 1 to 200 characters); keywords is an optional list of up to 32 search terms. Names are a lowercase letter or digit followed by up to 63 lowercase letters, digits, or -; machine folders use machine names. A file that breaks these rules, or is larger than 57344 bytes, is invalid: search and the snapshot skip it. You may edit the files with any editor. A session that replaces a whole memory it has not seen as it is now, because you changed it since, is refused and told to read it first, so your edit is never overwritten.

docs.title: Stamps and size limits
docs.text:
The daemon adds two lines to each memory's frontmatter, created and modified (RFC 3339 UTC timestamps), and keeps them current on every write, edit, and save from a client; whatever a write sends for them is ignored, and a file without them gets them from its modification time the first time the daemon starts. The daemon also keeps when each memory was last read, outside the file (memory/.reads.json). Ages built from the stamps show in the snapshot, in search results, and in reads.

Each kind of memory has its own size limit, the whole file counted: user_max_bytes, agent_max_bytes, machine_max_bytes, project_max_bytes, and overview_max_bytes under [memory] (16384 bytes each by default; see Memory [memory]). A write or edit by a model, or by you from a client, that would leave a memory over its limit is refused, and the model is told to read it with memory_read and condense it first. The refusal leaves the content out: after a write, the model could take it for what the write left. A memory already over its limit, as after you lowered the limit, stays valid and is still shown, marked over its limit; only changes that make it smaller are accepted until it fits.

docs.title: Agent memory
docs.text:
The daemon keeps one agents/<agent>.md for every agent of the shared agent set and of every preset, internal agents (approval, compaction, title) aside. It makes the missing ones at start and after every configuration reload or config.apply, with an empty body, and writes nothing when there is nothing to do.

The daemon owns two things in each file:

  • The description: Memory of the `<agent>` agent: <description>, with the agent document's description on one line and the whole cut to 200 characters. When an ID is in the shared set and in presets, the shared document is used; otherwise the preset that comes first alphabetically. Changing the agent document's description rewrites it.
