  • Two keywords: the agent ID and the agent's mode (primary, subagent, or all; one keyword when the ID is the mode's name). You and the agent may add more; the daemon keeps them and puts its two back first when they are removed.

So a write of an agent's file, by the agent or by you, keeps the daemon's description and keywords: memory_write and memory_edit say what they kept, and /memory and cookie memory edit show the daemon's notice after saving. The body is the agent's: it starts empty, and an empty one is left out of the model's memory turn entirely.

When an agent leaves every agent set, its file is removed only if the daemon made it and nobody touched it: the body is empty, and the description and keywords are exactly the daemon's. A file with notes stays, and /memory and memory.list mark it as belonging to no current agent.

docs.title: Managing memory
docs.text:
In the TUI, /memory lists every layer: the user categories, each agent's file, and the machine and project memories grouped by machine and project, with invalid files marked and, at the end, anything in the memory folder that is not a memory, each with the reason. The details show when the selected memory was created, modified, and last read by a model, with exact times, and its size against its limit; a memory over its limit says so. Enter opens it in $VISUAL or $EDITOR, frontmatter included but without the created and modified stamps, which the daemon keeps; saving writes it at the revision it read. n creates a memory, starting from the URL of the selected layer, machine, or project, and d deletes the selected one after you confirm. Every action is also a button under the details. When the text you saved is not a valid memory, e reopens it as you left it; when the memory changed since you opened it, nothing is overwritten: r reloads the current version into the editor, and o overwrites it with your edit. The panel refreshes when a memory changes through the daemon, by you, another client, or the agent. The transcript shows the memory snapshot the model reads as a collapsed memory row, at the run that loads it and again whenever it changes. An agent's memory tool call is one row in the transcript, such as Edit memory project://web/build: expanding it shows the change as a diff, like an edit's, and clicking its URL opens /memory at that memory; a search's results open theirs the same way. The web client's Memory view shows the same ages and sizes, and its rows the same diffs and links. Its editor shows a memory's description, keywords, and body as fields, with an agent's description and first keywords fixed, and the whole text only for a file the fields cannot hold, such as an invalid one.

From a terminal, cookie memory lists, edits, and deletes memories through the daemon, so it works against a remote daemon as well (--url and --token, or [server] in config.toml, as for cookie config):

cookie memory list                      # every layer, invalid files with the reason
cookie memory list project              # one layer: user, agent, machine, or project
cookie memory show project://web/build  # stamps, size, and text
cookie memory edit project://web/build  # in $VISUAL or $EDITOR; created when absent
cookie memory rm machine://labpc/gpu    # asks first; --yes does not

list gives each memory's ages and size under it. edit opens the file, frontmatter included but without the daemon's stamps, and saves it at the revision it read. Text that is not a valid memory is offered again as you left it; a memory that changed since you opened it is not overwritten, and you can reload it and edit the current version. You may add and remove user:// categories and agent:// files, as an agent may when its rules allow. An agent:// file can be created only for an agent that exists; a file whose agent was removed or renamed stays and is listed as belonging to no current agent. Your edits never change the snapshot of an open session; it sees them when it next takes one.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text: The machine layer is keyed by machine names, the computers runtimes run on, which the daemon assigns on its own and you can rename, merge, and forget from the Machines view of /runtime or with cookie machine (see Machines). A machine's memories live in memory/machines/<machine>/ and move with it when it is renamed or merged into another; machines.list and cookie machine list count them.

docs.title: Related memory
docs.text:
The memory a session's snapshot includes on its own is related to the session; the prompt, the results of memory_search and memory_read, and the permission rules all use the word.

  • A root run: every user:// memory, the run's own agent://<agent> file, the memories of the machines the session's attachments run on, and those of the session's project.
  • A delegated run: its own agent file, and nothing else.

Related memory is the memory an agent is told to maintain; the rest it leaves alone unless what it says is stale or wrong, or you ask. This is guidance, not a limit: the permission rules alone decide what a run may read, write, edit, or delete.

docs.title: What the model sees
docs.text:
At the start of a run that has memory, the model gets a snapshot as one user turn after the AGENTS.md turn: every user category, the run's agent's own file, and an index of the memories of the machines the session's attachments run on, each as far as the agent's memory rules (and the session overlay's) allow for its URL: a memory they allow is shown, one they ask for is listed by URL and description only, and one they deny or do not match is left out and not counted. When nothing is left to show, there is no memory turn at all; the tools stay offered. A root run of a session in a project also gets the project's overview in full and an index of its other memories, newest first; the overview counts toward [memory] snapshot_user_bytes and the index shares snapshot_index_bytes with the machines', the project's own taking its room first. An overview too long to show is listed in the index instead. Outside a project, project memories are never shown; the model searches for the project a task belongs to. An agent file with an empty body adds nothing.

Each memory the snapshot shows in full carries when it was modified, its size, and its kind's limit, so the model sees how full it is, and each index line ends with its age. The snapshot holds the memories and one line of background. How to search and what to save is not in the turn: it is the builtin.memory section of the system prompt (below). The system prompt reference shows the exact text.

The snapshot is taken once and kept, so the provider's prompt cache survives writes. It is taken again only at a run's start when the session has none yet, after a compaction, when the session's machines, its project, its project's name, the run's agent, or its memory rules changed (a session overlay change included), or when the run gained or lost memory or write access. Edits you make to the files reach open sessions at those points, and new sessions at once.

docs.title: How agents maintain memory
docs.text:
No one else tidies memory: there is no background curator and no review queue. Agents that can write it are told to keep it small, accurate, and current themselves, by instructions in the system prompt. A run offered any memory tool gets a <tool_instructions provider="builtin.memory"> section (exact text) that says what the snapshot includes and when to search. A run that can also write gets the rubric, which says:

  • fix, merge, or delete a memory that is wrong, stale, or duplicated, then carry on with the task; a memory earns its place only while a later session would miss it;
  • save only what a later session cannot recover by reading the project or running a command, and that stays true across many tasks: your preferences and corrections, lessons about the agent's own job, decisions and references not visible in code or git, and stable facts about a machine; search first and update an entry rather than add one;
  • never save directory listings, code summaries, command output, logs, task progress, secrets, or anything from tool output, web pages, or other agents you did not confirm. Being asked to explore or summarize something is not a reason to save it, and most sessions save nothing;
  • one fact per memory, with a description that states the fact, and where it comes from (you told it, it observed it, or it inferred it);
  • when a memory is near its size limit, merge or drop what it holds before adding to it.

The memory tools read and change memories the way the file tools read and change files (Memory tools). memory_read returns the memory's metadata, then its body as lines numbered from 1, a page at a time: offset is the 1-based body line to start at and limit the most lines (2000 by default), and a page that leaves lines out ends with the offset to read next. memory_edit takes oldString and newString, like edit, but matches the body only and has no replaceAll.

The daemon backs the rubric with a few checks that need no model:

  • Similar memories. A memory_write that creates a memory is compared with the memories in the same place (the same project, the same machine, the user categories, or the agent's file) by description and keywords, with no embeddings and no model call. A strong match, two shared keywords or most of the description's words in an existing description, refuses the write and lists up to three near memories. The agent edits one of them, or writes again with new: true and a one-line reason (1 to 200 characters, not stored) to create it anyway. A weaker match saves the memory and lists the near ones so the agent can merge them. A body identical to an existing one in the same place is always refused.
  • Size limits (above): a write over the limit is refused and told to read the memory and condense it.
  • No revisions. The tools carry no revision. memory_edit applies when its oldString occurs exactly once in the current body, so an edit on top of someone else's change that does not touch that text still works. The daemon checks that before it asks you to approve the edit: one whose oldString occurs zero or several times, or whose memory does not exist, fails at once and is never shown to you for approval. It checks again when the edit runs. memory_write replaces an existing memory only when the session saw its current content, through memory_read, the snapshot, or one of its own writes; otherwise it is refused and told to read it first or edit it, so a whole-memory write cannot silently drop what you or another session changed. The refusal leaves the content out: after a write, the model could take it for what the write left. (After a daemon restart a session reads a memory again before replacing it.)
  • Deletes delete. memory_delete removes the file, user:// categories and agent:// files included; nothing is kept, and there is no undo.
  • Every change is visible. The tool row of each write, edit, and delete a model makes is the record of its change: its header links to the memory, and expanding it shows the change as a diff, as an edit row does. No separate transcript line is added. A change you make from a client records none.

When an agent's memory_write rule is ask, the approval reviewer is given the same rubric and the write's content; in auto-approve mode it rejects writes that fail it.

An agent whose document turns memory off with memory: deny has no memory tools, no snapshot, and no section.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
The global runtime offers five tools (Tools):

Tool Does memory_search Searches every memory by keywords, descriptions, and the segments of its URL, never bodies. Each result shows its URL and description, whether it is related to the session, whether the run may change it, its age, and its keywords, as far as the memory rules for its URL allow memory_read Reads one memory whole: whether it is related and editable, when it was created and modified, its size and limit, its description and keywords, and its body memory_write Creates a memory, or replaces one the session has seen; keywords may be left out, and description too for the agent's file, whose description the daemon sets; new with reason creates a memory a similar one exists for memory_edit Replaces one occurrence of a text in a memory's body memory_delete Deletes a memory; nothing is kept

The three write tools are offered only to a run that can both read and write some memory: at least one URL must match an allow or ask rule for memory and one for memory_write (the check compares the patterns, so no file has to exist). memory: {"user://*": allow} with memory_write: {"project://*": allow} offers none. deny rules do not count in this check.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: The tools use two permission actions with the memory URL as resource: memory for searching and reading, memory_write for writing, editing, and deleting. A root run of an agent document that names neither, the built-in default agent included, gets a default: it reads every memory and writes the memory related to its session, user://, its own agent:// file, and its session's machines and project. A key replaces the default for its action: memory_write: deny leaves an agent that only reads, and memory: deny turns memory off. memory: allow lets an agent read every memory, and memory_write rules let it write. A session rule in /permissions grants or denies them for one session tree, replacing the agent's rule with the same pattern, so memory: deny there turns memory off for that session without touching the agent document. Rules may name the agent, machine, and project of the run with variables such as ${agent_id}. See Memory permissions for the variables, the delegated default, and an example agent document.

docs.title: Subagents
docs.text: A delegated run's snapshot holds only its own agent's file, and its prompt says so. For each of memory and memory_write its agent document has no key for, it gets agent://${agent_id} allowed: it sees and maintains its own agent file, and nothing else (no user://, machine, or project memory). A document that declares either key gets exactly the rules it declares, user:// included if it grants it; there is no hard limit behind the default. Only the root agent keeps what it learns about you, machines, and projects unless you give a subagent that access.

docs.title: Scheduling Prompts
docs.text:
A cron job is a prompt the daemon sends on a schedule: once after a delay, or on a cron schedule. Each fire goes into a session that already exists or starts a new session. You create jobs from the TUI, the web client, or cookie cron; agents create them with the cron tools. The daemon keeps the jobs in crons.json in its data directory, fires them while it runs, and records what each fire did. The cron spec has the full design.

Jobs need a daemon of client protocol 1.15 or later. The clients hide their cron views from an older one, and cookie cron refuses it with a message.

docs.title: A job
docs.text: A job has an ID (eight lowercase letters and digits, which the daemon assigns), an optional name of at most 80 characters, a prompt of up to 32 KiB, a schedule, and a target. Lists show the name, or the start of the prompt when the job has none.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
A schedule is one of:

  • A cron expression: five fields, minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week, with *, lists (1,15), ranges (1-5), and steps (*/15); months and days may be named (jan, mon), and both 0 and 7 mean Sunday. When both day of month and day of week are restricted, either one matching fires, as in Vixie cron (0 8 13 * 5 fires on the 13th and on every Friday). An expression that can never match, such as 0 0 30 2 *, is refused.
  • A delay: in and a whole number with s, m, h, or d, from 1s to 365d, such as in 20m. The daemon turns it into the time it fires at once, and the job fires once.

Cron times are the daemon host's local time. Daylight saving time is handled as it comes: a time skipped by the spring change fires at the moment the clock jumps to, and a time that occurs twice in autumn fires the first time only.

The clients read a schedule plainly beside the expression: every day at 03:00, every Monday to Friday at 09:00, every 15 minutes, on the 1st of every month at 08:00, once at 2026-10-23 03:00.

docs.title: How many times it runs
docs.text:
max_runs limits a cron schedule's fires: a whole number, where 0 or less means no limit. It defaults to 1, so a job fires once unless it says otherwise. A delay always fires once.

A job that has delivered max_runs fires, or a one-shot that has fired, is finished:

  • a job you created stays, disabled with the reason finished, until you delete it or enable it again (which starts its count over; a one-shot whose time has passed needs a new schedule first);
  • a job an agent created is deleted.

A job without a limit runs until it is disabled or deleted. There is no other expiry.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
A job's target is chosen when it is created:

Target Each fire A session Sends the prompt into that root session A subagent's session Sends the prompt into that delegated session, which reports its turn to its parent as every subagent turn does A new session Creates a new root session from the job's template and sends the prompt as its first input

You can target any session. An agent can target only its own session or a session below it (one of its subagents'); anything else is refused whatever its rules say.

docs.title: Steer or queue
docs.text:
A job that fires into a session has a delivery:

  • queue (the default): the prompt starts the session's next run when it is idle, or waits for the running turn to end;
  • steer: the prompt joins the running turn; on an idle session it starts a run.

Either way the prompt runs with the session's current agent, model, and permission mode. A session that has paged out is loaded again by the fire. While an enabled job has a next fire, the session it targets counts as waiting (waiting on: scheduled job in the session list), and a subagent with such a job keeps its parent waiting. A disabled or finished job counts for nothing, and a job never keeps a session in memory.

The model sees a fire marked as a scheduled job, never as you:

<scheduled_job id="k3v9q2xa" name="Nightly dependency check" fired_at="2026-10-23T03:00:00+02:00">
Check for outdated dependencies and open a summary.
</scheduled_job>

A fire is not user input: it never answers an approval and never counts as consent.

docs.title: New sessions
docs.text:
A new-session job carries a template: the agent each run session starts with (and its preset), the permission rules added to it as a session overlay, its runtime attachments and working directory, and its project. When you create the job from the TUI or the web, the agent, its preset, and the project start as the current session's, and the attachments are what a new session gets (global and the daemon's default runtimes); a model pin and a permission mode are yours to add. An agent's job takes the creating run's agent and the creating session's attachments and project. The template is checked when the job is saved, as session.create would check it, and again at each fire.

Each run session:

  • runs an agent that can run as a root (primary or all mode);
  • starts in the permission mode auto-approve-n unless you chose another: the approval reviewer decides each ask, and what it would pass to you is rejected, so an unattended run never waits on you. Only you can set a job's mode, from a client; agents cannot, and the tools have no mode parameter;
  • runs the agent's own models unless you pinned a model; only you can pin one;
  • is titled <name or the prompt's start> · <local time of the fire>, which you can rename as usual;
  • appears in the session list with a clock mark, and records the job and the fire that started it (SessionMeta::cron). It is an ordinary session otherwise, and stays when the job is deleted.

Because the creator adds the template's rules, a job can do more than the session that created it: an agent allowed to create new-session jobs can start sessions of any agent with any rules. Grant cron on new to a subagent with that in mind (Permissions).

docs.title: Skips and no catch-up
docs.text:
A fire is skipped, and recorded with the reason, when:

  • the job's previous prompt into its session has not been delivered yet (previous fire not delivered);
  • a new-session job's previous run session is still running (previous run still running);
  • [cron] enabled = false holds (firing turned off);
  • the daemon stopped between recording a fire and delivering it (interrupted);
  • the target session is held (session held).

There is no catch-up. A fire missed while the daemon was down is not run: when the daemon starts, each job whose time passed gets one history entry, skipped: daemon was down, with the number of fires missed, and moves to its next future time. Each fire happens exactly once, even across a restart or two daemons sharing a data directory.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text:
A fire fails when it cannot start (the agent is missing or disabled, no model is available, a runtime is offline, or the session cannot be created) or when the run it led to ends failed. A fire's outcome is the run its prompt lands in: a steered prompt succeeds or fails with the turn it joined, a queued one with the run that takes it.

After [cron] max_consecutive_failures failures in a row (see Cron jobs), which a job can override, the job is disabled with the reason failed <n> times in a row. A completed run resets the count; a cancelled run and a skip change nothing. Enabling the job again resets the count. A failed fire does not count toward max_runs.

docs.title: History
docs.text: Each job keeps its last [cron] history fires. An entry has the scheduled time and the time it fired, the session it went to and the run it started or joined, its outcome (delivered, skipped with the reason, or failed with the error), and how that run ended. The clients show it newest first.

docs.title: Running a job now
docs.text:
You can fire a job at once from any client (crons.run): it is delivered as its schedule would deliver it, a new root session for a new-session job, and recorded as run now. A run now counts toward neither max_runs nor the failure count, moves nothing else, and fires even with [cron] enabled = false. It still obeys the skips: a run now of a job whose previous prompt is still waiting is recorded as skipped.

An agent runs a job now with cron_run, the way it delegates: a new-session job runs as a subagent of the caller with the job's agent, rules, and attachments, in the foreground (waiting for the result) or in the background (reporting when done), and counts against the caller's delegation depth. The job's agent need not be one the caller may delegate to. An in-session job fires into its session as scheduled.

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text: Deleting a session deletes the jobs that target it or any session in its tree. Deleting a project deletes its sessions with their jobs, and the new-session jobs whose template names the project. Deleting a job keeps its run sessions.

docs.title: Terminal UI
docs.text: /cron opens the cron panel: each job with its name, schedule and its plain reading, next fire, target, state, and the outcome of its last fire; under it, the selected job's details and history. Its actions, create, edit, enable or disable, run now, and delete, are keys and buttons. /cron new from the command panel creates a job that fires into the session on screen. A job is written as a short form in your editor. Run sessions have a 🕒 mark in the session picker. See Terminal UI.

docs.title: Web
docs.text: The clock icon in the left rail opens Scheduled prompts, with the same list, details, history, and actions. In a session, Schedule a prompt in the ⋮ menu creates a job that fires into it. A run session's clock mark in the session list opens its job. See Web.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
cookie cron create --name "Nightly dependency check" \
  --prompt "Check for outdated dependencies and open a summary." \
  --schedule "0 3 * * *" --max-runs 0 --agent builder
cookie cron list
cookie cron run k3v9q2xa

cookie cron talks to the daemon like cookie memory; for a remote one pass --url wss://host/ws --token <token>. See cookie cron.

docs.title: Agents and the cron tools
docs.text: The global runtime offers five tools: cron_create, cron_list, cron_update, cron_delete, and cron_run, and list_agents, which lists the agents a new-session job may run with their models and starting rules. Their arguments and descriptions are in the tools reference. An agent's target is "self", a subagent's handle, or {"new": {…}}.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The tools are checked under the cron action, whose resource is the target kind of the job a call touches: session, subagent, or new. One action covers listing, creating, editing, enabling and disabling, deleting, and running:

Run Default without a cron key Root, any agent but an internal one cron: allow Delegated none: the tools are hidden Internal agent none

An agent manages every job its rules allow, its own or not; cron_list shows only the jobs whose kind its rules allow or ask for. To let a subagent schedule prompts into its own session and the sessions below it, but not start new sessions:

permissions:
  cron:
    subagent: allow

A session rule in /permissions works the same way for one session tree: cron: deny there hides the cron tools for that session, and cron: {"new": deny} keeps the others. See Cron permissions.

docs.title: Usage and Cost
docs.text:
Cookie agent records normalized provider usage after every committed model turn and completed internal-agent model request. Records include inclusive input and output token totals and cache read or write counts when the provider reports them. Anthropic cache creation maps to cache writes and cache reads map directly; OpenAI cached_tokens maps to cache reads. GPT-5.6+ can additionally report cache_write_tokens, which maps to cache writes when supplied by the provider adapter. Cohere cached_tokens similarly records server-side automatic cache reads. Providers that omit a field leave it unknown rather than estimating it.

The event log is the source of truth. Session rollups and their per-model rows are rebuilt from the session's log when it is loaded and obey revert/fork visibility. Session-tree rollups combine the selected session with all of its delegated descendants, including descendants that have been evicted from memory. There are no rollups across sessions: usage is always read for one session or one session tree.

Open /usage in the TUI to compare the selected session with its session-tree totals; the web client's Usage sheet shows both too. Programmatic clients can call session.usage and session.tree_usage. Cache hit rate is cache-read tokens divided by inclusive input tokens (uncached input plus cache reads and cache writes), counted over the requests whose provider reported cache reads: a request that says nothing about the cache is left out rather than counted as a miss. The rate is unavailable (n/a in the TUI, a dash on the web) when no request reported cache reads or there was no input; an explicitly reported zero remains a 0% hit rate. The web sheet gives the token counts behind the rate under it.

Each TUI section shows formatted totals and a per-model table. Models are sorted by descending estimated cost, with unpriced models last, then by input tokens and model name. Token counts use thousands separators, cache hit rates use one decimal place, and costs use two decimal places at or above one cent and four below it. Use the arrow keys, Page Up, Page Down, or the mouse wheel when the panel content exceeds its viewport.

When a request is priced, the assistant block's closing footer includes its estimated cost after generation speed and context usage. The bottom bar shows the selected session total; clicking it opens /usage. Unpriced costs are omitted from both locations.

Cost is always optional. Managed models use the selected models.dev catalog price tier for each request's reported input-token context size. Model-specific entries under [providers.<provider>.models.<model>.pricing] supply prices for custom models or override catalog prices, as described in the model pricing reference. The precedence is config override, catalog, then no cost. An aggregate remains unpriced when any used model lacks a required rate or when a provider omits a usage split needed to apply a distinct cache or reasoning price.

Cache economics are model-specific. In particular, current GPT-5.6+ pricing charges reads and writes differently, while earlier OpenAI models use model-tier-dependent cached-input discounts. The selected catalog model's cache_read and cache_write rates, or explicit pricing overrides, are the authoritative inputs to Cookie agent's estimate; do not assume a fixed cached discount.

Usage events stamp the request price selected when the request completes. Footers and rollups preserve those stamps, so later pricing changes do not rewrite already stamped costs. An unpriced stamp also remains unpriced after configuration or catalog changes, and a rollup containing such a record has no complete estimated-cost total.

To evaluate prompt caching, compare equivalent workloads before and after changing [providers.<id>.cache]. Track cache_hit_rate after the first turn and estimated_cost_usd over the whole session. Providers that expose writes may report them when a prefix is first cached and reads on later matching requests; compare totals only after enough repeated-prefix turns to amortize any write and storage charges. Use the provider's off configuration as the baseline: set all Anthropic or Bedrock system, tools, and rolling values to "off"; for OpenAI GPT-5.6+, use mode = "explicit" with both placements false. Gemini caching is always implicit and has no off control. Disabling authored cache placements is not a guarantee that provider-managed cache activity or billing stops; use the reported usage rather than assuming zero reads or writes.

docs.text: User-facing configuration pages describe the current source tree. Specifications also preserve proposals and design decisions; a draft is not an installed-binary configuration reference.

docs.title: ACP agents
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-23); see Implementation notes. The user guide is ACP agents.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
Run external coding agents, such as Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI, as cookie agents: a session or a subagent whose turns an external agent takes, driven over the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). Cookie is the ACP client; the external agent is the ACP agent.

Naming: the docs call these ACP agents, never "the client protocol", which stays the name of cookie's own protocol.

Decided 2026-10-23:

  • Runtimes host ACP agents. A runtime (the daemon's own local, a template runtime the daemon starts, or a dial-in runtime, including one a TUI or web client offers) declares agents in its configuration, next to its MCP servers. The daemon registers each as <runtime_id>-<agent_id>, the runtime ID's _ spelled - (local-claude, labpc-codex, client-myhost-codex), available while that runtime is connected. The runtime travels next to the ID wherever agents are described; it is never parsed from the ID. (Decided 2026-10-23, replacing the dotted form, which the agent ID grammar does not allow and could not gain within a minor. Superseded the same day: the ID is the declaration's key, and the session's attachments decide which runtime runs it; section 15, naming.)
  • The runtime spawns the agent on its own machine and relays its ACP messages to the daemon over the runtime protocol. The daemon speaks ACP: sessions, rendering, permissions, cancel, resume.
  • Cookie's tools reach the agent as an MCP server over stdio, through a bridge the runtime spawns: the agent's MCP traffic reaches the daemon over the runtime's existing connection, so the agent's host needs no route to the daemon. (MCP-over-ACP, which would carry MCP on the ACP connection itself, is a draft RFD; not used.)
  • Cookie settings come from a daemon-side agent document with the same id (~/.cookie-agent/agents/labpc-codex.md; since the naming of section 15, agents/codex.md, shared by every runtime that offers codex): mode, permissions, body, hide_tools, starting mode and config options. Without one, the agent gets the defaults (section 4).
  • cwd: the session's workspace on that runtime, else the runtime's home.
  • The agent runs its own file and shell tools. Cookie does not advertise ACP fs or terminal. hide_tools lists the cookie tools it does not get; by default cookie's coding runtime tools.
  • Its permission requests are decided by permissions, its ACP tool kinds mapped onto cookie's actions (section 8).
  • Mode: the agent's "auto" mode when it offers one, else its default.
  • Login: credentials already on the runtime's machine; authentication errors reach the session with what the agent said. No login flow in cookie.
  • The agent document's body is sent with the session's first prompt; an empty body sends nothing. (Extended 2026-10-23: the first prompt also carries the tool instructions and the memory snapshot; section 15, round 3.) (Extended 2026-10-25: and the session's attachments, with where the harness's built-in tools run; section 15, Attachments in the first prompt.)
  • Slash commands the agent offers appear in the TUI and web composers.
  • deny stays the spelling for turning a permission off.

Out of scope for v1: ACP fs and terminal, logins run from cookie, ACP v2, MCP-over-ACP, the agents' vendor extensions (_meta, AIR, goal). (Revised 2026-10-23: the steering extension is used when advertised, and _meta enriches tool calls where it helps; section 15, round 3.)

docs.title: 2. ACP in brief
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0 over the agent's stdin and stdout, one message per line; the agent's stderr is diagnostics. Version 1 (schema 1.26, Oct 2026).

  • Client to agent: initialize, authenticate, session/new (cwd, mcpServers), session/prompt (content blocks, returns a stop reason), session/cancel, and when the agent supports them session/load, session/resume, session/close, session/set_config_option.
  • Agent to client: session/update notifications (message and thought chunks, tool calls and their updates, plans, available commands, config options, usage, session info) and session/request_permission.
  • Every agent MUST accept stdio MCP servers in session/new; HTTP is optional.
  • Adapters: Claude Code @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp, Codex @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp, Gemini CLI gemini --acp.

docs.title: 3. Declaring agents on a runtime
docs.text:
# The daemon's own machine, and any machine that dials in: its `local` table
[runtimes.local.acp.agents.claude]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp"]
env = {}
description = "Claude Code"

# A runtime template the daemon starts (for example over ssh)
[runtimes.labpc.acp.agents.codex]
command = ["npx", "-y", "@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp"]
env = { CODEX_HOME = "/home/ada/.codex" }
description = "Codex"
  • Where: exactly where MCP servers can be declared: [runtimes.local] on the daemon's machine and on a dial-in runtime's machine, and [runtimes.<id>] templates in the daemon's config.
  • Fields: command (argument vector, run without a shell, on the runtime's machine), env (merged over the runtime's environment), description, enabled.
  • Agent ids: the table key, following the agent id grammar (lowercase letters, digits, and single inner hyphens, at most 64 bytes). The daemon's id is <runtime_id>-<agent_id>, the runtime ID's _ spelled -; the agent's runtime is carried explicitly where agents are described (AgentDescriptor.runtime) and kept in the engine's registry entry, never parsed from the id. Refused, with a message naming both sides: a combination that is not an agent id (a runtime ID with __ or a trailing _), one longer than 64 bytes, and one that names a daemon agent or another runtime's agent (lab_pc + codex and lab + pc-codex).
  • Reporting: the runtime reports its agents when it connects and when its configuration changes; the daemon adds or removes them and announces the change like any agent registry change.
  • Offline: an agent whose runtime is not connected is listed as unavailable; starting a session or a delegation with it is refused at once, as for offline runtimes.

docs.title: 4. The daemon-side agent document
docs.text:
# ~/.cookie-agent/agents/labpc-codex.md
---
description: Codex on labpc, for refactors        # overrides the runtime's
mode: all
acp:
  mode: auto                         # optional; section 5
  config: { model: "gpt-5" }         # the agent's config options, by id; labels
  hide_tools: [read, write, edit, bash, webfetch]
permissions:
  read: allow
  write: { "${workspace_dir}/*": allow, "*": ask }
  bash: { "git *": allow, "*": ask }
  webfetch: allow
---
You review changes for this project before they are committed.
  • Optional. Without it, <runtime_id>-<agent_id> is an agent of mode all with the runtime's description, the defaults every agent gets for actions it names no key for, and the default hide_tools.
  • No acp.command: the runtime launches the agent. (Revised 2026-10-24: models names the agent's own model and effort values; see Document models in section 15.)
  • acp.hide_tools: patterns with * and ? over the tool names cookie publishes (read, bash, memory_*, exa_*). Default: cookie's coding runtime tools (read, write, edit, bash, webfetch), since the agent has its own; [] offers them too. Independent of permissions, which keep deciding calls.
  • acp.config: initial values for the agent's config options, matched by option id; unknown ids or values are reported in the session and skipped.
  • The document lives with the daemon's other agents, so a runtime cannot grant itself permissions. The agent appears in the agent pickers, presets, list_agents, and delegate_subagent like any other.

docs.title: 5. Modes and config options
docs.text:
• Cookie reads the agent's configOptions from session/new, and its modes when it offers no mode option.
  • Starting mode: acp.mode when set; otherwise the mode option or mode whose id is auto; otherwise the agent's default. Mode ids are labels.
  • Then acp.config is applied.
  • Clients show the session's agent options (model, mode, effort) in the session's details; changing one calls session/set_config_option.

docs.title: 6. Running a turn
docs.text:
• The runner. start_run_direct keeps everything it does today (run start, idempotency, RunStarted, the end of the run) and, for an ACP agent, calls the ACP runner instead of the model loop.
  • The prompt. The user's message (or a producer's: a cron fire, a subagent report) becomes session/prompt content: text, images when the agent accepts them, and the document's body before the session's first prompt.
  • Rendering, from session/update:
  • agent_message_chunk → assistant text, streamed as text deltas;
  • agent_thought_chunk → thinking;
  • tool_call / tool_call_update → a cookie tool call from a new tool source, acp:<agent>, upserted by its ACP id: title and kind, status as the call's state, diff content as a diff block, content as text or media blocks, locations as file links, raw input and output in metadata;
  • plan → a checklist block, replaced on each update;
  • usage_update → recorded usage, without a cost when cookie cannot price the agent's model;
  • session_info_update → the session title, unless the user set one;
  • available_commands_update → the session's agent commands (section 10);
  • config_option_update → the session's agent options (section 5);
  • unknown kinds are ignored.
  • Durability. Each turn is recorded as model turns and tool calls with a synthetic model reference (acp:<agent>), so history, reports, and clients work unchanged. The agent keeps its own conversation; cookie never replays history to it.
  • The end. end_turn completes the run with the last message as its final text; cancelled cancels it; max_tokens, max_turn_requests, and refusal fail it with that reason.
  • Steering falls back to queueing: ACP has no standard steer. (Revised 2026-10-23: through the agent's steering extension when it advertises one; section 15, round 3.)
  • Interrupt sends session/cancel, answers every pending permission request cancelled, and waits for the cancelled stop reason within the existing cleanup grace.

docs.title: 7. Sessions, processes, and the runtime relay
docs.text:
• One ACP session per cookie session, created on its first turn; its ACP session id and cwd are recorded in the session log.
  • cwd: the session's workspace attachment on the agent's runtime; without one, the runtime's home directory.
  • After a daemon or runtime restart, or a process exit, the next turn reconnects with session/resume when the agent offers it, else session/load (its replay is ignored), else a new ACP session, which the session is told about.
  • Processes: one per agent per runtime, shared by its sessions, started on first use, stopped after an idle period with no live session ([acp] idle_shutdown_ms), with the runtime, and with the daemon. session/close when the agent offers it, as a cookie session is deleted or unloaded. A process exit fails the runs it served, with its stderr tail.
  • Errors, including auth_required, end the run as failed with the agent's message.
  • The relay (runtime protocol, additive):
  • the runtime's hello and runtime/agents_changed carry its agents (id, description, enabled);
  • agent/start and agent/stop (daemon → runtime) start and stop an agent's process;
  • agent/message carries one ACP JSON-RPC line in either direction, unchanged; agent/exited reports an exit with its status and stderr tail;
  • the daemon's local runtime does the same in process.

docs.title: 8. The agent's own permission requests
docs.text:
Each session/request_permission is decided by its ACP tool kind, mapped onto cookie's actions and the agent's merged rules (revised 2026-10-23: no acp action):

ACP request Decided as Resource read, search read the location's path edit, delete, move write the location's path execute bash the command (from the call's raw input, else its title) fetch webfetch the URL a tool of cookie's own MCP server (mcp__cookie__<tool>) allowed at once none: the call reaches cookie's MCP server, where the rules decide it a tool of an MCP server the agent connects itself (mcp__<server>__<tool>) mcp <server>_<tool>, cookie's own name for the tool think allowed none switch_mode, other, unknown the approval flow the title
  • bash: {"git *": allow} allows the agent's own git commands exactly as it allows cookie's bash tool, and mcp: {"exa_*": allow} covers cookie's and the agent's exa tools alike. A request with several locations needs every one allowed.
  • Cookie's own tools are asked about at most once: the agent's request is allowed, and the call that reaches the bridge meets the rules (section 9).
  • An MCP tool is recognized only by a title or raw input of one of the adapters' whole forms (mcp__<server>__<tool>, Tool: <server>/<tool> with {server, tool}, <tool> (<server> MCP Server)), and only for kind other or a kind ACP does not know, so a command or a path that merely contains such a name is still decided as a command or a path.
  • Answers: allow picks the agent's allow-once option; deny its reject-once option; ask goes through the approval flow (the reviewer in auto modes), and the answer picks allow-once or reject-once. Cookie never picks an "always" option: repeats come back to cookie's rules and grants.
  • In the agent's auto mode most calls never ask; those that do still meet the rules.

docs.title: 9. Cookie's tools for the agent (MCP over the runtime)
docs.text:
• On session/new cookie passes one stdio MCP server, cookie, whose command is a bridge on the runtime's machine: cookie runtime mcp-bridge --socket <path>.
  • The bridge connects to the runtime process over a local socket (a Unix socket, a named pipe on Windows) created for that ACP session, readable only by the runtime's user, removed with the session. The runtime relays its MCP messages to the daemon (agent/mcp frames), and the daemon serves them.
  • The tools: the session's tools as cookie composes them for a model request (memory, cron, list_agents, delegate_subagent and the subagent tools, MCP servers' tools, runtime tools), minus acp.hide_tools.
  • Permissions apply as for a model: a tool the merged rules hide is not listed; a call is decided by the rules, ask goes through the approval flow.
  • Calls through the bridge appear in the session as calls of the ACP agent, linked to its turn.
  • The bridge needs cookie on the runtime's machine, which a runtime always has: it is cookie runtime.

docs.title: 10. Agent commands
docs.text:
• available_commands_update gives the session's agent commands (name, description, input hint). The clients list them in the session's commands (the TUI command palette, the web ⋮ menu) after cookie's own, each with an agent badge.
  • Choosing one always asks for its input, which may be left empty, and sends /<name> <input> as the prompt text, as ACP specifies.
  • The agent's compact and goal replace cookie's commands of those names when the agent offers them (decision of 2026-10-27). The agent's compact runs as cookie's compaction (session.compact, which waits for it, section 15). With the agent's goal, the session has no cookie goal mode: no goal bar, goal tools, or reminders; /goal is the agent's command like any other, and the agent keeps its goal itself.

docs.title: 11. Protocols and storage
docs.text:
• Session log: a new event records the ACP session (agent, runtime, ACP session id, cwd, protocol version, agent info). Tool calls from acp:<agent> use the existing events with a new tool source.
  • Client protocol minor: runtime-hosted agents in the agent list (with their runtime and availability), the session's agent commands and options, an RPC to set an option, the plan block, the acp:<agent> tool source.
  • Runtime protocol minor: agent declarations and the relay (section 7), the MCP bridge frames (section 9).
  • Plugin protocol minor: the new events.
  • Config: [runtimes.*.acp.agents.*], [acp] idle_shutdown_ms (since 2026-10-27 also [acp.agents.*], declared once for every runtime but global, which a runtime's own declaration of the same key replaces there; runtimes.agents.* reach it as global's), and the agent document's acp block.

docs.title: 12. Tests
docs.text: A scripted ACP agent fixture (like the MCP fixture) that speaks ACP v1: declarations on local, a template runtime, and a dial-in runtime, with dotted ids and collisions; offline refusal; handshake and capabilities; auto-mode selection and acp.config; a turn with chunks, thoughts, tool calls with diffs, a plan and usage; every stop reason; cancel with a pending permission request; permission requests decided by the mapped rules and by approvals; resume, load with an ignored replay, and a new session after a lost one; process exit; the MCP bridge listing and gating cookie's tools with hide_tools; the body sent once; agent commands; delegation to an ACP subagent; a cron fire into an ACP session; cwd with and without a workspace on the runtime.

docs.title: 13. Phases
docs.text:
1. Runtime relay: declarations, agent ids, agent/* frames, the local in-process runtime, dial-in and template runtimes.
  2. Engine: the ACP client and runner, rendering, sessions and processes, permission mapping, the daemon-side document, protocol additions.
  3. MCP bridge: cookie runtime mcp-bridge, the runtime's socket, the daemon's MCP service with hide_tools.
  4. Clients: runtime agents in pickers, agent commands and options, the plan block, ACP tool calls.
  5. Docs: an ACP agents guide with Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI examples on local, a template runtime, and a dial-in runtime.

docs.title: 14. Open questions
docs.text: None.

docs.title: 15. Implementation notes
docs.text:
Phases 1 to 3 (2026-10-23): client protocol 1.17.0, plugin protocol 1.8.0, runtime protocol 1.7.0; history format unchanged (two new event types).

Where the spec left a detail open, or where the code differs:

  • Ids. <runtime>-<agent> with the runtime's _ spelled - (user decision of 2026-10-23); cookie_agent_protocol::runtime_agent_id makes it, and AgentDescriptor.runtime (runtime_id, agent, available) carries the runtime. Collisions among the daemon's own templates and with daemon documents fail the configuration load; a dial-in runtime's refused declaration is skipped and reported in the daemon's log.
  • Availability. Agents of local and of templates are available whenever the daemon runs (it starts their runtime on demand); a dial-in runtime's are available while it is connected and listed unavailable, as it last reported them, while it is away. A disabled agent is listed unavailable. A best-effort selection (an engine wake-up, a client continuing) never swaps an ACP agent for another: the run is refused.
  • Declarations. Template and [runtimes.local] agents change with the rest of runtimes, at the next start. A dial-in runtime reads its machine's configuration again every 5 seconds and sends runtime/agents_changed. The relay messages are information; no agent/configure was needed.
  • The agent document. Its acp block marks it as an ACP agent's (acp: {} is enough); such a document is an agent only while a runtime declares the id. It names no agent_md, limits, or mode internal (nor models, until Document models and picker IDs below), and its body may be empty. models and enabled became optional for every document (enabled defaults to true). A delegation target needs no document (user decision of 2026-10-23): a named target no agent has, and a pattern that matches none, load as configuration diagnostics (ConfigStatus.diagnostics, client protocol 1.18.0, recomputed from the published agents, so a diagnostic clears once a runtime reports the agent), the name is not a target meanwhile, and delegating to it is refused with "no agent <id> (its runtime is not connected)". A target whose document exists but is disabled or primary still fails the load.
  • Synthetic model. Runs record the model acp/<agent id> (a model key needs a /, so not acp:<agent>), adapter acp, through a persisted binding no build can run as a model; the frozen policy has no model suffix. Each prompt round's steps are attempts of that model.
  • Rendering. Text and thoughts stream as deltas. A new ACP tool call commits the turn so far as a model turn holding the call (finish tool_calls), then starts a cookie tool call of source acp; updates are its progress (a display replacement), and completed/failed end it, with diffs as diff blocks, content as text blocks, locations as links, and raw input and output in metadata.acp. Calls left open when the round ends end as failed (cancelled when the turn was). The ACP tool call id is the model call id, made unique within the run.
  • Events. acp_session_started records the ACP session (agent, runtime, the agent's own id, session id, cwd, protocol version, agent info, and how: new, resumed, or loaded). acp_session_updated carries the agent's commands, options, and plan, each the whole new value. The plan is a plan display block there, not inside a tool call. An agent that offers modes but no mode option shows them as an option mode of category mode, set with session/set_mode.
  • Sessions. Updates that arrive before a session is routed (the commands an agent announces right after session/new) are kept for it; turn output that arrives before a prompt (a load's replay) is dropped. A replaced session is announced with a runless diagnostic (kind acp_agent). The body goes with the first prompt of every new ACP session, so a replaced session gets it again. A round's prompt is the input the session took since its last committed model turn.
  • Processes. Started in the runtime's home directory; idle means no run in progress for [acp] idle_shutdown_ms. session/close is sent when a session is deleted or unloads; a deleted session's ACP sessions are also deleted (session/delete) since the lifecycle round below. The engine stops every process as it shuts down.
  • Permissions. Requests go through the tool permission pipeline (grants included) with the agent's runtime as the scope and the session's cwd as ${workspace_dir}. The acp action of phase 2 is gone (user decision of 2026-10-23): a request for one of cookie's own tools is allowed at once (the bridge decides the call), the agent's own MCP tools are mcp rules, think is allowed, and switch_mode and the rest go to the approval flow as an approval of the kind's label (switch_mode or other) with no tree grant offered. PermissionAction is an open label and acp was never in BUILT_IN, so dropping the constant changes no wire. A request whose resources cannot be read is rejected; an agent that offers no allow-once or reject-once option is answered cancelled. Approvals name the cookie tool call the agent's call is shown as. The approval reviewer of the auto modes runs on ${small_model}; an ACP run has no model of its own to fall back to, so without small_model its requests escalate to the user.
  • Usage. The prompt answer's usage when the agent sends one, else the last usage_update's used as input tokens; a cost only from a usage_update cost in USD. Recorded once per round, on its last turn, whether the round completed, failed, or was cancelled (since the lifecycle round of 2026-10-24; before, only a completed round's).
  • Titles. session_info_update sets a fallback title while the user has set none. (Revised 2026-10-24: each new agent title applies until the user names the session, and an untitled session gets cookie's generated title after a round; see the lifecycle round below.)
  • Not run for ACP agents: AGENTS.md loading, the skill listing, tool prompt sections, and attachments block in a system prompt (round 3, Input and pickers, and Attachments in the first prompt put them in the first prompt), the agent_before_start hook, and input media admission (files go to the agent as its prompt capabilities allow, others become a note; see Input and pickers below).
  • The bridge. The daemon's MCP server is hand-written (initialize, ping, tools/list, tools/call); rmcp's server features are not used. A bridged call runs inside the agent's turn as a cookie tool call of the run (the runner commits the turn so far with the call in it), through preparation, the rules, approvals, and execution; outside a turn it is refused. The agent usually reports the same call as its own tool call too. On Windows the pipe has a random name and refuses remote clients but keeps the default security descriptor, not one limited to the user.
  • ACP client. Hand-written JSON-RPC types over the protocol crate's peer (the agent-client-protocol crate was not needed); initialize advertises no fs and no terminal (it asks for terminal output, see the display round below, and declares elicitation {form, url}, see elicitation below). A runtime that cannot start an agent answers the new error agent_failed.

Revisions of 2026-10-23 (user decisions; client protocol 1.18.0): the acp permission action is gone (section 8), and a delegation target no agent has yet is a configuration diagnostic rather than a load error (see The agent document above). ConfigStatus.diagnostics carries the diagnostics in config.get, config.apply, and config.reload; cookie config status, the TUI's /config, and the web's configuration page show them.

Phase 4, the clients (2026-10-23; no wire change beyond 1.17.0):

  • Pickers. The agent pickers list the root-runnable agents and the ACP agents that would be but are unavailable (runtime away, or disabled), with their runtime ([on lab · unavailable]), dimmed and refused with the reason. A draft of an ACP agent runs its acp/<agent> model, which the clients treat as live though no catalog lists it; the model pickers list only the catalog's models, and choosing the model of an ACP draft opens its options instead (/options in the TUI, Agent options from the web's model chip, which shows the agent's model option).
  • Commands. The reducer folds acp_session_updated into the session's acp view (commands and options, each the latest whole value). The TUI lists the agent's commands in the command palette after cookie's own, each behind an agent badge; choosing one asks for its optional input in a text step. The web client lists them in the ⋮ menu (Session commands) after cookie's own, badged, under one filter for both; one opens a sheet with a box for its optional input. The web composer offers no commands. Both send /<name> <input> as an ordinary prompt; the agent's compact opens cookie's compaction instead (section 10), and cookie's own compact and goal give way to the agent's.
  • Options are set with session.agent_option.set, and its answer replaces the session's options at once (the daemon's acp_session_updated follows).
  • Plan. A plan in acp_session_updated is a transcript row per run, replaced in place by the run's later plans, after the run's reply: a checklist with [x], [~], and [ ] (an icon and a screen-reader label in the web) and a high or low priority. A plan block inside a tool's display renders the same way.
  • Tool source. A call of source acp named <agent> on <runtime> after its title. Since 2026-10-27 its block's header names the agent and the call reads as cookie's own: neither client names its source, and the web shows the call's paths under its runtime's home, as for a runtime's calls. A running call's progress shows only when its header does not already say it: an ACP agent's progress is its title, which for a command repeats the command.
  • No new pointer target: the TUI's /options is a picker modal on the existing PickerRow targets, and palette rows are PaletteRows.

Phase 5, the docs (2026-10-23): the ACP agents guide (Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI on local, an ssh template, and a dial-in runtime; the daemon-side document; permissions; hide_tools; the bridge; the clients; delegation; troubleshooting), with the TUI, web, agents, runtimes, and [acp] pages pointing to it.

What the adapter does that the spec did not anticipate:

  • It connects its MCP servers while it answers session/new, so the bridge is bound to the session before the request goes out (a test covers it).
  • It offers resume and options mode, model, effort, and fast; it announces its commands twice right after a session opens, and a title (session_info_update) between turns.

Round 3 (2026-10-23; user decisions of the same day; client protocol 1.20.0, plugin protocol 1.9.0; history format unchanged):

  • First-prompt context. The first session/prompt of an ACP session carries, as separate text blocks before the input and each left out when empty: the <tool_instructions provider=...> sections cookie would compose for a model run, for exactly the tools the agent is offered over the bridge (after hide_tools and the merged rules: a provider gives its sections only when one of its tools is offered, and memory's section has part A when a memory tool is offered and part B when a write tool is); the session's memory snapshot as a model run sees it (the latest memory_loaded, which ACP runs record at admission like model runs, so it is there even when no memory tool is offered); and the agent document's body. No cookie-written preamble or guidelines: those belong in the agent document, and the guide has a reference document for Claude Code. AGENTS.md is not sent. The context goes with the first prompt of every new ACP session, so a lost session's replacement gets it again; a resumed or loaded one does not. (Extended 2026-10-25: the session's attachments come after the skills listing and before the memory snapshot; Attachments in the first prompt below.)
  • Prompt boundary. A round's prompt is now the input after the input_through_seq of the session's last committed turn (was: after that turn's own sequence number). The two agree for every round so far; the new one also covers input taken to steer that the agent did not take.
  • Steering. An agent advertises the steering extension with _meta.steering.supported: true in its initialize answer (top-level _meta, not agentCapabilities; Claude Code's adapter 0.95.0 and Codex's do). The client declares nothing to enable it. While a round runs, input admitted to steer (a user's steer, a producer message of mode steer: a cron steer fire, a subagent report) wakes the runner, which commits the turn so far, promotes and claims the input as a round does, and sends _session/steering {sessionId, prompt, _meta: {steering: {idleBehavior: "promptRequired"}}}. injected (and startedNewTurn, an agent that does not know idleBehavior) means the agent took it: the turns after cover the input, and acp_session_updated.steered records which (user_inputs, the user_input_submitted sequence numbers, and producer_messages). promptRequired (no turn running), failed, or an error leave the input for the next round, which the run then takes even when nothing else is pending; an error is reported in the session as a diagnostic. A steer still waiting when the round ends is awaited for up to 10 s. Claude Code's adapter also advertises agentCapabilities._meta.claudeCode.promptQueueing (a second session/prompt while one runs is queued by the agent); cookie does not use it, since it queues input itself. acp_session_started.steering records whether the agent steers; clients derive the Steer button from it (the web client's reads "Queue (this agent can't be steered)", the TUI's pending strip says so) when the session's running agent is that ACP agent.
  • Tool calls. A call's presentation is rebuilt from what the agent reported so far (title, the kind's hint, a primary argument from the raw input's command, file_path, path, url, pattern, or query, and the raw input as arguments; since 2026-10-27 shaped as cookie's own tools' presentations, below) and recorded as acp_session_updated.tool_presentation whenever it changes, since Claude Code's adapter sends the raw input in a later tool_call_update (and then once more per streamed field). Clients replace the call's title, hint, primary argument, arguments, and preview with it. Content renders as Markdown (text), media (images, stored as artifacts), links (resource links), code (embedded text resources), and diff blocks; locations as file links; raw output as code or JSON when the call has no content. _meta is optional enrichment only: Claude Code's claudeCode.toolName becomes the call's published name and metadata.acp.tool_name; its claudeCode.toolResponse (the whole tool response, including written files) is not kept.
  • Looking like cookie's own calls (2026-10-27). An ACP agent's turns and calls render as a model's do:
  • an execute call with a command is Run `<command>` with the command as an sh code argument, as cookie's bash;
  • arguments are the raw input's fields as keys and values, without the primary argument, a field the title repeats, an option left false, or an edit's strings its diff shows; nested values keep JSON;
  • a read whose content is a fenced excerpt the agent numbered (360\t…) is code from that line in the file's language, and a read shown so, or an edit with a diff, gets no location link;
  • a diff names a file under the session's cwd relative to it, and Claude Code's patch header (diff --git <path> <path>, no a//b/) is one file;
  • clients leave out a primary argument the title names by its trailing path (Read src/main.rs for /work/src/main.rs);
  • every session cookie opens sends _meta.claudeCode.options.extraArgs {"thinking-display": "summarized"}, so Claude Code streams its thinking (recent models omit the text by default), which shows as a model's thinking;
  • the reply's footer (⚡ tps · ctx · $cost) folds the round's recorded usage: its output over the block's time, the agent's latest context use, and the round costs.
  • Notices and compaction. initialize declares clientCapabilities.session: {notices: {}, compaction: {}}. A notice update (severity, title, description) and a completed or failed compaction_update (its summary, else the streamed compaction_summary_chunks; its error) are recorded as acp_session_updated.notice; clients show it where it arrived, with no level filter. In progress and cancelled compactions show nothing. Since client protocol 1.41.0 a compaction is acp_session_updated.compaction instead, recorded once as it starts and once as it ends (the agent may repeat its end); clients show a compacting row, then a compaction row with the summary, as for the session's own compaction. A failure still adds a warning notice.
  • Usage and session info were already handled (usage_update, session_info_update); Claude Code's PromptResponse._meta.quota is not read.
  • Checked by hand against Claude Code (claude 2.1.309, adapter 0.95.0, scratch daemon): the first prompt's context; a Read (its raw input arrived after the call started and the header updated; content as Markdown and a file link); an Edit (presentation updated three times as old_string, new_string, and replace_all streamed in; a diff); a Bash call; a steer during a running sleep (injected, and Claude moved the foreground command to the background so the message could reach it); and a cancel. The adapter sent no notice or compaction_update in these short turns; it did send current_mode_update, three session_info_updates, and a background task's follow-up text after a turn ended, which cookie drops as output between rounds.

Tests (round 3): the first prompt's parts and their order, with and without memory write tools and with every memory tool hidden; a steer through the fixture's extension (one round, the steered record, the request's idleBehavior) and without it (the next round); a cancel after a steered turn; a call whose raw input arrives later (the recorded presentation, Markdown, media, and link content, the tool name); notices and a compaction; the client reducer, the TUI, and the web rendering of notices, steered messages, and presentations.

Naming (2026-10-23, user decision; client protocol 1.21.0, no runtime or plugin protocol change):

  • IDs come straight from the declaration. [runtimes.local.acp.agents.claude] is the agent claude; the <runtime>-<agent> ID, the _-to-- spelling, and the refusals of combined IDs that are malformed, too long, or shared are gone (cookie_agent_protocol::runtime_agent_id is removed). Every runtime that declares an ID offers the one agent of that ID (the engine's AcpOffers), sorted by runtime ID.
  • The session's attachments decide where it runs. A turn of claude runs on the attached runtime that offers it. With none attached, or with two or more, it cannot run in that session: session.create, a run's admission (before run_started), and a delegation (against the child's attachments: the parent's inherited ones, or the delegated capabilities; a resumed child is checked when its run starts) are refused with `claude` needs a runtime that offers it attached: labpc, local or `claude` is offered by more than one attached runtime (labpc, local); a session runs it on one, so detach the others; an offering runtime that is away or has the agent disabled refuses with that reason. A session whose current agent is an ACP agent cannot attach a second runtime that offers it (runtime.attach is refused, naming both); sessions of other agents attach any runtimes.
  • One document per ID. ~/.cookie-agent/agents/claude.md serves every runtime that offers claude. Without one, the default document takes the first offering runtime's description (in runtime ID order).
  • Assumptions (recorded for the user to adjust):
  • A daemon document without an acp block whose ID a runtime declares wins as the daemon's own agent; the declaration is ignored and ConfigStatus.diagnostics says so (ACP agent \claude` of runtime `local` is ignored: ...`). This used to fail the configuration load.
  • When the hosting runtime is detached and another attached runtime offers the agent, the next turn starts a new ACP session there, with a diagnostic in the transcript: the old ACP session lives on the old machine.
  • A delegated child resolves its ACP agent against its own attachments with the same one-provider rule.
  • The ACP session record keeps the hosting runtime (runtime_id), and resume and load require it: the latest record for the agent is resumed only when its runtime is the one that runs the agent now.
  • Synthetic binding. acp/<agent>'s binding no longer names a runtime (cookie-agent/acp-binding/v2, frozen: {"acp": {"agent"}}); a run's policy names the agent, and the runner places it on a runtime.
  • Protocol. AgentDescriptor.runtimes lists every offering runtime (runtime_id, agent, available); runtime stays populated when exactly one runtime offers the agent, so a client older than 1.21.0 lists an agent several runtimes offer as a daemon agent. runnable_as_root is true while some offering runtime could run it; the clients compute where it runs from the draft's or session's attachments (cookie_agent_client_state::acp::placement): the TUI's and web's agent pickers show [on local], [needs labpc, local attached], [offered by labpc, local: attach one], or [on lab · unavailable], and refuse the ones that cannot run with the reason.
  • Model-facing tools. list_agents marks an ACP agent (<mode>, acp), drops its synthetic model line, and adds offered by runtimes: labpc, local and runs here: yes, on runtime local (or no — needs one of: labpc, local attached, no — two attached runtimes offer it: labpc, local, no — runtime lab is not connected, no — disabled on runtime local), judged against the calling session's attachments (a child inherits them). list_runtimes gives each runtime an acp_agents attribute (acp_agents="claude, codex"). Both tool descriptions say so.
  • cwd. With the agent's runtime always attached, the runtime's home is the working directory only when that attachment has no workspace.
  • Delegation diagnostics resolve unknown names against the plain IDs: a target clears once any runtime declares it. A refused delegation to a name no runtime offers yet says no agent \codex` (no connected runtime offers it)`.

Tests (naming): two runtimes offering one ID (the descriptor's runtimes, a turn placed on local, list_agents and list_runtimes, attaching the second refused, a move to labpc starting a new ACP session with the notice, none or both attached refused at creation); a session and a run without the agent's runtime refused before the run starts; a daemon document without an acp block shadowing a declaration (the configuration diagnostic); the client placement and picker notes; the list_agents placement lines.

Input and pickers (2026-10-24; client protocol 1.26.0, plugin protocol 1.14.0; history format unchanged):

  • Model and effort as cookie's model and variant. ACP dropped session/set_model: an agent's model is a config option of category model, its reasoning effort one of category thought_level (Claude Code's adapter: model and effort; Codex's: model and reasoning_effort). The clients show them as the model and variant (cookie_agent_client_state::acp::model_label, Opus • High; the TUI's title claude • Opus[High]), the model picker lists the model option's values and the variant (the TUI's bracketed variant and ctrl+t, the web sheet's effort buttons) the effort option's, and choosing one is session.agent_option.set. The other options stay in /options and the web client's All agent options. An option is the model by its ID model when none has the category. Gemini CLI's older models API is not read.
  • Drafts. The daemon remembers, per agent and runtime, the options a new ACP session answered session/new with (the agent's own starting values, before cookie sets any), and keeps them in acp-agents.json in its data folder, a cache it rewrites when they change and ignores when unreadable. A resumed or loaded session's options are taken only while nothing is known (their values are that session's). They reach clients as AgentRuntime.options, with the document's acp.mode (or auto) and acp.config applied, so a draft shows what its session would start with; a change republishes the agents. A draft's choices are kept per agent (DraftAgentOptions) and sent as session.create's agent_options; they need an ACP agent, at most 64, each option once. The session records them as acp_session_updated.starting_options, and every new ACP session of that cookie session applies them after acp.config (a session created but not started yet shows them over the remembered options); one the agent does not offer, or a value it does not take, is skipped with a diagnostic as acp.config is. Assumption: they apply to every new ACP session of the cookie session, a lost session's replacement included, not only the first.
  • Files as prompt input. An agent's promptCapabilities decide how a file the user attached reaches it (acp/prompt.rs): an image as an image block (as before), audio as an audio block when it advertises audio (Gemini CLI does), and a text file as a resource block (uri attachment:///<file name>, mimeType, text) when it advertises embeddedContext (Claude Code's and Codex's adapters do). Anything else, PDFs and video included, stays the note [attached file <name> (<type>), which this agent cannot read]: ACP's blob resources would carry them, but Claude Code's adapter drops blob resources, so a note says more. Uploads take text files: content that is no media file but UTF-8 without NUL bytes is text/plain of the new media kind text (an open label), up to 1 MiB (MAX_TEXT_ATTACHMENT_BYTES); models list no text, so a model run still refuses one at admission. Audio was already admitted (audio/flac, mpeg, ogg, wav, 20 MiB). The clients check attachments against AgentRuntime.input_media, which the daemon records from the agent's initialize answer each time it starts (image, audio, and text entries with the upload types and caps, 20 files of a kind), since the synthetic model is in no catalog; the web client's file picker offers every file when the agent takes text.
  • Additional directories. When the agent offers sessionCapabilities.additionalDirectories, session/new, session/resume, session/load, and the session/fork a fork or a revert branches off with carry additionalDirectories: the workspaces of the session's attachments on the agent's runtime other than cwd (the first of them), each once, in attachment order, as the runtime reported them (canonical paths on its machine). Workspaces on other runtimes are left out. An agent without the capability gets none, and the member is left out when there are none. They are the attachments when the ACP session starts or resumes: attaching a workspace to a live ACP session reaches the agent with its next new, resumed, or loaded session. (ACP has no request that changes a live session's roots.)
  • Skills. When the agent is offered cookie's skill tool over the bridge (after hide_tools and the merged rules), the first prompt's context carries the <available_skills> listing a model run's system prompt would, right after the tool instruction sections: the session's skills with the native visibility rules (Engine::skill_listing, which compose_skill_listing now uses too), sized for a 200k-token context since the agent's own is unknown. Without the tool the agent could not load a skill, so nothing is listed. acp_first_prompt_context keeps its signature.
  • Protocol shape. session.create rather than the first run.start: the draft becomes a session there in both clients (attachments are uploaded into it first), the choices are the session's like its permission overlay, and recording them at creation keeps run.start free of a member that would mean something only once.

Fixes (2026-10-23):

  • Processes stop with the daemon. agent/stop and a runtime that stops (the end of its connection, runtime/shutdown) kill each agent's process group and answer only once it has been reaped; before, the kill ran after the answer, so a daemon that exited right after stopping its agents (its shutdown, SIGTERM, or daemon.restart) could leave an agent and its children running.
  • A cancel always reaches the agent. The round's loop polls the run's cancellation first (a biased select), so an agent that streams without a pause cannot hold session/cancel back; a steer being taken when the run is cancelled is dropped instead of sent; and a turn the agent ends after the cancel was accepted ends the run as cancelled, as a model run's does. The manual check of round 3 saw an accepted run.cancel that never sent session/cancel while Claude Code streamed updates; this was the window.

Display round (2026-10-24; client protocol 1.23.0, plugin protocol 1.11.0; history format unchanged):

  • Context. Each usage_update whose used or size changed is recorded as acp_session_updated.context (used, and size when it is not 0). ACP turns still commit with empty usage, since the turns' usage feeds the session's usage totals and the round's usage is recorded once (above); the reducer keeps an ACP agent's context across its turns (a turn of the acp provider leaves it standing) and takes the window from size, which no catalog lists for acp/<agent>. The TUI's status line shows ctx with the percentage of that window, the web's the tokens (the window in its title). All three adapters send usage_update.
  • Mode updates. current_mode_update moves the current value of the option that shows the agent's modes (id mode or category mode) when it lists the new mode, whether cookie made the option of the agent's modes or the agent offers its own mode option beside them, as Claude Code's adapter does; before, only the made-up option followed, and Claude Code leaving plan mode by itself left the chip on plan.
  • Terminal output. initialize declares clientCapabilities._meta.terminal_output: true (and still terminal: false: cookie runs no terminal/*). Claude Code's and Codex's adapters then report an execute call's output in _meta: terminal_info (terminal_id) names the call's terminal, terminal_output or terminal_output_delta (terminal_id, data) carry output, which cookie appends in both cases (Codex sends chunks under either key, Claude Code the whole output once), and terminal_exit (exit_code, signal) the end. The runner (acp/terminal.rs) treats them as cookie's bash tool treats a command: the output goes to an output capture (retained, an artifact past the preview, retained_output on the result) and the call's output hub, and the live display gets a terminal block, replaced once with the display and then grown by appends to it, up to the display budget. A terminal content item renders that block, with the exit code, where it stands (first when no item names it), plus a line for a signal; the old [terminal <id>] placeholder is gone. The result's output is the capture's preview. A failed call keeps its output as the termination's partial result, marked incomplete like every failed call's, and says the command exited with code <n> when its content says nothing; calls left open when the round ends keep theirs the same way.
  • Boolean options. initialize declares clientCapabilities.session.configOptions.boolean: {}, so an agent sends its on/off options as type: boolean (Claude Code's fast, category model_config) rather than an on/off select.
