AcpConfigOption.kind (select, left out, or boolean) says which; a boolean's current_value is true or false and its values list both (true named On, false Off), so a client older than 1.23.0 still shows a two-value select that sets it. session.agent_option.set keeps its string value ("true" or "false"), and the daemon sends session/set_config_option with type: boolean and a JSON boolean; a select's request is unchanged (no type). acp.config takes "true" or "false" for a boolean. An option of a type cookie does not know is left out, as ACP asks. The TUI's /options toggles a boolean from its row and stays open; the web's Agent options sheet shows a switch (role="switch").
  • Images in replies. An agent_message_chunk whose content is an image becomes a file part of the turn (an artifact of the session, like a model's generated image) in place of the [image] note, so the clients show it as media in the reply (AssistantChild::MediaFile); text after it starts a new text part. An image that cannot be decoded or stored still becomes the note. Images in thoughts stay notes.
  • Subagents stay flat. Claude Code's Task subagents arrive as flat tool calls whose _meta.claudeCode.parentToolUseId names the Task call, and ACP's subagent_update and child sessions (for a client that declares clientCapabilities.subagents) are unstable. Cookie deliberately shows them as the turn's own calls and declares no subagents capability: neither nesting by parentToolUseId nor child sessions is implemented until the subagent API is stable.
  • Checked by hand against Claude Code (claude 2.1.309, adapter 0.95.0, scratch daemon): a Bash call of printf 'one\ntwo\n'; exit 3 showed its output in a terminal block (replaced into the live display once the adapter sent it, with the result) and ended failed with exit code 3, the command exited with code 3, and the output retained; the context was recorded twice (used 21205, then 21285, of a 1000000-token window); the options came as mode, model, effort, and fast as a boolean, which session.agent_option.set turned on.

Tests (display round): the context use recorded once for a repeated usage_update, and the client reducer keeping it across ACP turns and clearing it at a model's; the TUI status line's ctx with the agent's window; the agent's own mode switch on its own mode option and on one made of its modes, and an unknown mode ignored; terminal output streamed as Codex and Claude Code send it (the capabilities, the live replacement and append, the exit codes, the retained output, a failed call's partial result); a boolean option recorded with its values and set with a JSON boolean, and the TUI toggling it; an image in a reply as a file part whose artifact holds its bytes; the acp_agents browser scenario (context chip, command output, the reply's image, the boolean switch).

Session lifecycle (2026-10-24; user decisions of the same day; client protocol 1.24.0, plugin protocol 1.12.0; history format unchanged):

  • Fork points. Each committed ACP turn records the ACP messageIds of the agent messages it holds (response_metadata.acp_message_ids), so a fork or a revert can name the agent's last message it keeps.
  • Detached sessions. A fork of a cookie session, and a revert that cuts turns of the agent's conversation, record the ACP session the cookie session talked in as left behind: acp_session_updated.detached (acp_session_id, reason forked or reverted, and the agent's last kept message_id). The fork's log keeps the source's acp_session_started (so the fork knows what to fork); a record followed by detached is never resumed. A revert keeps no marker of its own, so this event is how the log says the agent's session no longer matches.
  • Branching. The agent's next turn in such a session calls session/fork on the detached session with the fork point as _meta.jetbrains.air.fork = {version: 1, messageId} and records the new session (how: forked, forked_from). After a revert the old session is then closed when live and deleted (session/delete), and the session is told the agent continues from the revert point; after a fork the source keeps its session. With no agent message kept (a fork or a revert before the agent's first reply) the turn starts a new session instead, and a revert's old session is deleted. A session whose every record a revert cuts is deleted at once. A fork the agent refuses at that turn fails the run with what it said.
  • The AIR extension is a vendor extension. Standard ACP session/fork (unstable, gated by sessionCapabilities.fork) forks a whole session; the fork point is JetBrains AIR's _meta, which Claude Code's adapter (src/fork-session.ts) and Codex's (src/SessionFork.ts) read and nothing advertises. An agent that does not know it ignores it and forks the whole session. The engine therefore asks once per agent process, after the agent's first completed round (Claude Code's adapter cannot fork a session it has not written to disk yet, and answers -32603 "Session ... not found" before), off the turn's path: session/fork of that session at a messageId that cannot exist (cookie-fork-probe-<uuid>), without messageFingerprint (Codex validates its format). Invalid params (-32602, "Fork point message ... was not found") means the fork takes a fork point; a fork that succeeds means it does not, and that fork is deleted (closed when the agent offers no session/delete); any other answer counts as no. The answer stays with the process and is recorded on every session it serves (acp_session_updated.fork_point) and on later records (acp_session_started.fork_point, next to fork, whether the agent offers session/fork), so a revert can be judged while the process is down. A record without them is unknown until the next probe.
  • Refusals (error acp_agent_unsupported, its reason the message, checked before anything changes and before plugin hooks):
  • a revert past the agent's first reply when its fork takes no fork point (`claude` on `local` can't rewind its own conversation, so the session can't be reverted past the agent's first reply) or nothing was learned yet (cookie has not yet checked whether ... (it checks after the agent's next reply) ...);
  • a fork after the agent's first reply when it offers no session/fork (... can't fork its own conversation, so the session can't be forked after the agent's first reply), and a fork whose point cuts into the agent's conversation when its fork takes no fork point (... can't fork its own conversation at an earlier point, ...). A fork at the end of the conversation is a plain whole-session fork, taken as the cookie fork is made (see below). Revert or fork before the agent's first reply always works. Gemini CLI (no session/fork) therefore refuses both past its first reply.
  • Superseded the same day: a first version started a new session given a condensed cookie transcript when the agent could not fork; dropped for the refusals above.
  • Eager whole forks (2026-10-24, closing a gap the first version left): a fork of a cookie session at the end of the agent's conversation, when the agent's fork takes no fork point or the engine has not asked yet, calls session/fork while session.fork runs (starting the agent's process when needed) and records the fork's own session then, so turns the source runs before the fork's first turn stay out of it. When the agent cannot fork there, or the session is on a runtime that does not run the agent for the fork, the cookie fork is deleted and refused with acp_agent_unsupported (`claude` on `local` could not fork its own conversation for the new session: ...). A fork that takes a fork point still forks at the fork's first turn, at the recorded message.
  • Deleting a session closes its live ACP session and deletes every ACP session it owns with session/delete when the agent offers it, starting the agent's process for it when needed (one a fork left behind stays its source's). Paging a session out only closes.
  • Usage is recorded for failed and cancelled rounds too, from the answer's usage, else the last usage_update.
  • Stop reasons. refusal, max_tokens, and max_turn_requests fail the run with "the agent refused", "the agent hit its output token limit", and "the agent hit its turn request limit" (each naming the stop reason), and the turn so far commits as finished refused, length, or max_turn_requests. RunOutcome has no kind that fits; the failure stays failed.
  • Compaction. session.compact on an ACP session used to fail reading the synthetic acp/<agent> binding as a model ("the stored binding of model acp/<agent> cannot be read by this build"). It now runs the agent's compact command, when its available_commands_update lists one, as a run of /compact <focus> and waits for it; otherwise it is refused with acp_agent_unsupported (`claude` does not offer compaction). Automatic compaction belongs to the model loop and never runs for an ACP run.
  • Titles. After a completed round, an ACP session with no title runs cookie's title generation on the title agent's models minus the synthetic acp/<agent> it would inherit as ${parent_model}; with small_model unset none remain and nothing runs. A later session_info_update title still replaces it, and each new agent title applies, until the user names the session.
  • Checked by hand against Claude Code (adapter 0.95, outside the daemon, over the adapter's stdio): its initialize advertises fork, delete, close, resume, list; the probe on a fresh session answers -32603, and after one turn -32602; a fork at the first of two replies' messageId (msg_...) remembered only the first turn's word; session/delete of the fork succeeded.

Tests (lifecycle; crates/engine/src/runtime/tests/acp/ against the scripted agent in its three fork modes: at a fork point, whole sessions only (ACP_FIXTURE_FORK_WHOLE), and no fork): the probe's answer in each mode, recorded once per process and on later records, and the deleted probe fork; a fork at its fork point remembering only the turns before it, the source keeping its own; a whole fork allowed at the end and refused earlier; a fork refused without session/fork and a fork before the first reply starting fresh; a whole fork taken as the cookie fork is made, so a turn the source runs before the fork's first turn stays out of it, and a cookie fork the agent fails to take refused and deleted; a revert forking at the revert point and deleting the old session, refused for whole and no-fork agents and while not asked yet; a revert before the first reply deleting the session and starting fresh; a revert of a fork into its source's turns leaving the source alone; deletion closing and deleting, not a source's; paging out only closing; usage on failed and cancelled rounds; the stop reasons' messages and finish reasons; /compact forwarded and refused; the generated title, the agent's later one, and no title without small_model.

Elicitation (2026-10-24; client protocol 1.25.0, plugin protocol 1.13.0; history format unchanged, two new event types). ACP v1's stable elicitation/create and elicitation/complete, which Claude Code's adapter (0.95.0) uses for its AskUserQuestion tool (a form tied to the tool call: a titled oneOf per question, an array of titled anyOf for a multi-select one, and a free-text question_<n>_custom beside each) and for an MCP server's sign-in (a URL), and Codex's adapter for its elicitations. Before, cookie advertised neither mode and these degraded.

  • Capabilities. initialize declares clientCapabilities.elicitation: {form: {}, url: {}}.
  • Routing (crates/engine/src/runtime/acp/elicitation.rs). A session-scoped elicitation/create goes to its session's runner like a permission request. During a prompt round it becomes a question of the run; between rounds, after the round's answer, after a cancel, for a session no turn runs in, and when request-scoped (requestId, no sessionId), it is answered cancel. That includes a question asked while the agent opens its session (an MCP server of the agent's own that wants a sign-in while session/new or session/resume runs): the session is not routed, or its round has not started, yet. A mode other than form and url, or a URL question without a url, is refused with -32602, as ACP asks.
  • Cookie's model of a question is a new client protocol concept, not an approval: approvals are tool-call operations with fingerprints, evaluations, grants, and the reviewer, none of which apply, and a form's answer carries values. elicitation_requested (run-bound) records the question: elicitation_id (cookie's own UUID), agent, the cookie tool_call_id the agent's toolCallId is shown as (when the agent reported that call), message, and a form or a url. The form's properties become typed fields: string → text (minLength, maxLength, pattern, format, default), string with oneOf, or with enum (titled by enumNames when present) → choice, array with items.anyOf/items.enum → multi_choice (minItems, maxItems, default), number, integer, boolean; required from the schema; any other type is kept as an unknown input (Open::Unknown) that no client can fill in. Field order: the runtime relay carries the agent's messages as parsed JSON and the daemon's serde_json keeps no member order, so the order of the schema's properties is lost before the engine sees them; fields are sorted in natural order of their names (question_2 before question_10), which keeps Claude Code's forms in its order. Keeping the agent's order would need the relay to carry raw text (a runtime protocol change).
  • Answers. elicitation.respond (session_id, elicitation_id, action, content) hands the user's answer to the waiting question; an accepted form is checked against its fields first (required, type, bounds, choices, formats email, uri, date, date-time; pattern is shown, not checked: the protocol crate has no regex engine), and a refused answer (elicitation_answer_invalid) leaves it waiting. A question no run waits on is elicitation_not_pending. elicitation_resolved records action, an accepted form's content, answered_by, and the daemon's reason, before the run's end; the agent gets {action, content?}.
  • No rule or mode answers a question (task decision: it is the agent asking the user, not an action), with these daemon answers, each recorded: a session whose tree's permission mode is auto_approve_n (a cron run's default, and the mode that already answers escalated approvals for an absent user) declines at once (unattended); a headless cookie run declines what waits in its tree on its approval tick (unattended, "a headless cookie run has no one to answer"); the run's cancel answers cancel at once, and the round's end cancels what still waits (run_ended); a form with a required input of an unknown type declines (unsupported). Questions do not expire: [approval] timeout_ms (30 s by default) suits a yes/no, not a form. Yolo, auto-approve, and auto-approve(Y) sessions still ask, since someone who chose not to be asked about permissions may still want the agent's questions.
  • URL completion. Each agent process keeps its URL questions by the agent's elicitationId; an elicitation/complete for one still waiting accepts it (completed), and an unknown or answered ID is ignored, as ACP asks.
  • Clients. The client state keeps a session's waiting questions (SessionState.questions) until elicitation_resolved or the run's end, and shares the form draft, field hints, URL host and warnings, and resolution words (cookie_agent_client_state::elicitation); a resolved question is an info event row. The TUI docks a question panel where the approval panel goes (an approval stays on top), keyboard-only, with the approval hotkey grace before an answer; the web client shows a card above the composer, says waiting for your answer in its bottom bar and on a subagent's delegate row (tree::Activity::WaitingForAnswer, ahead of a waiting approval). Both show who asks, the message, a form's fields with their hints and the first field that does not fit, or a URL with its host and warnings, and Submit/Done, Decline, and Cancel.

Tests (elicitation): the fixture's elicit form|url|url-complete and elicit-wait; an AskUserQuestion-shaped form answered (fields, the call it belongs to, a refused answer that leaves it waiting, the accepted values reaching the agent, elicitation_not_pending after, the initialize capability); a declined URL question and one the agent completes (after an unknown ID); a cancel that answers a waiting question cancel before the run finishes; an auto_approve_n session declining at once and a headless driver declining a waiting one; the schema conversion (natural order, choices from oneOf, enum, and enumNames, multi-choices, defaults, unknown types), the ACP answer shape, the protocol's answer checks and formats, the client state's draft, hints, URL warnings, and reducer; and the TUI panel (rendering, keyboard, a required field, a URL question, Esc and the grace); the web client's helpers and the acp_questions browser scenario (a form refused for its required field, then answered; a URL question's host and link, declined).

Checked by hand against Claude Code (elicitation; adapter 0.95.0 on local of a scratch daemon, driven over the client protocol): asked to use AskUserQuestion, the agent announced the call ("Asking for your input"), then sent a form tied to it, recorded as question_0 (a choice of Red and Blue, each with its description, titled "Color") and question_0_custom ("Other", text), with the question as the message. Accepting {"question_0": "Blue"} ended the call and the agent replied "You chose Blue."; declining another made it reply "You skipped.".

Document models and picker IDs (2026-10-24; no wire change, history format unchanged):

  • models in an ACP document. The top-level models of a document with an acp block is a fallback chain over the agent's own values: each entry's model is a value of its model option (category model, else ID model), its variant a value of its effort option (category thought_level), null or absent for the agent's default effort, and a plain string an entry without a variant. The loader reads it into AcpDocumentSettings::models (AcpModelChoice), so AgentFrontmatter::models stays empty and no native code sees it; entries are ACP labels (1–256 bytes, no control characters), each model once, at most 256, with no cache (strict, so a hard error).
  • At session start (apply_starting_options): the mode, then acp.config without the model and effort options when models has an entry naming a value, then the first entry whose model the agent offers (options::pick_model), then its variant against the effort option as the model change left it, then the session's starting options. No offered model, no model option, or a variant the effort option does not take is a session notice (The agent document's models was skipped there: ...), as an unknown acp.config value is, and the agent keeps its own value. AgentRuntime.options (a draft's) applies the same choice (options::starting_view), so the chip shows what the session starts with.
  • Configuration diagnostics (ResolvedAgents::diagnostics, recomputed from the published agents like the delegation ones): an entry naming a variable (${default_model}, ${small_model}, ${parent_model}, any ${...}) is skipped, with agent <id> skips a models entry: <variable> names one of cookie's models, ..., rather than failing the load, as an entry naming an unset default_model does; and an acp.config key for the model or effort option of a document whose models name a value gives ... models takes precedence .... The option IDs are those the agent last offered on any runtime; before it offered any, only model is known to be the model option.
  • IDs in the pickers (no wire change: the IDs are the descriptors' model keys, variant IDs, and option values[].value). Every model and variant picker shows, dimmed after each row's name, the ID a models entry writes (cookie_agent_client_state::document_id, None when the name is the ID, which then shows once): a native model's full key, a native variant's ID (base for the base), and an ACP agent's model and effort values. The TUI's rows (pickers::document_id_row: the name and its (current) or (default), then the ID in the theme's internal style, the model picker's key style, truncated first with an ellipsis) stay PickerRow targets, so hover and click cover the ID; /model's variant step and /options' value step now render styled rows. The web client's rows put the ID on a muted line under the name, its chips beside the name, each data-doc-id, truncated so a phone's sheet does not scroll sideways.

Attachments in the first prompt (2026-10-25; user decisions of the same day; no wire change, history format unchanged):

  • The block. The first prompt's context carries, after the skills listing and before the memory snapshot, the block on the session's attachments that a model run's system prompt carries (runtime_notes::runtimes_prompt, through Engine::runtimes_block, which compose_runtimes_prompt now uses too, so the wording is one): with at most one attachment besides global, its working directory and machine; with several, the several-attachments text and the <machines> listing that explains <attachment>_<tool> names; the Project: line or the project attribute of a session in a project. Every attachment is listed, including one whose tools hide_tools hides. Before, an agent with several attachments saw bridge tools such as labpc_read with nothing explaining them, and never learned its project.
  • Where the built-in tools run. The harness's own file and shell tools run on the runtime that hosts the agent's process, on its machine, in the cwd of session/new (acp_cwd: the first workspace attachment on that runtime, else the runtime's home). With several attachments, the attachment that serves that cwd (the one whose workspace it is, else the runtime's first) is marked builtin_tools="true" in the listing, and a sentence after it names it, its runtime, its machine when known, and the working directory, says the built-in tools act on that machine and workspace only, and that cookie's tools from the cookie MCP server act on the attachment their description or <attachment>_ prefix names. With one attachment there is only one place the tools can run, so the block is exactly a model run's, with no sentence and no marker (user decision of 2026-10-25).
  • When. With the rest of the context: the first prompt of every new ACP session, a lost session's replacement included, and not a resumed, loaded, or forked one.

Tests (attachments): the exact block for one attachment (a model run's, with and without a project) and for several (the marker on the attachment whose workspace is the agent's cwd, not its runtime's first; the sentence; a runtime home's attachment marked; a runtime no attachment belongs to named alone); the parts in order (tool instructions, skills, attachments, memory, body); several attachments of one runtime listed with every tool hidden, and not sent again on resume; a lost session's replacement getting them again; the project line.

docs.title: Addendum (2026-10-25): a steer waits until the agent takes it
docs.text:
User decision: a message steered into an ACP agent's running turn shows as a model run's steered input does, with no mark of its own.

  • The input stays waiting while it is offered. The runner commits the turn so far, holds the session's pending user inputs (no client can take them back meanwhile: session.recall_input answers gone for a held input), and sends them with the producer messages it promotes and claims as before in _session/steering.
  • injected or startedNewTurn promote exactly the held inputs where the turn stands (user_input_submitted, then user_input_applied), and acp_session_updated.steered records their submitted sequence numbers as before.
  • Anything else releases them: they are still pending, any client can take them back, and the next round takes them as any pending input. Producer messages the agent did not take go with the next round as before. The notice for a failed steer stays.
  • Clients no longer mark steered messages: the TUI's and the web client's ↪ steered into the agent's running turn are gone. The steered record stays in the session log.

docs.title: Addendum (2026-10-25): documents as templates over a declaration
docs.text:
Status: implemented (2026-10-25; client protocol 1.32.0); see the implementation notes at its end.

User request: one ACP agent declaration (claude) serves several agent documents, each with its own cookie permissions, mode, and body. User decisions of the same day: the key is acp.agent; a declaration with no document of its own ID stays an agent with the default document.

# ~/.cookie-agent/agents/claude-review.md
---
description: Claude Code, read-only reviewer
mode: subagent
acp:
  agent: claude          # a [runtimes.*.acp.agents.claude] declaration
  mode: plan
permissions:
  read: allow
  write: deny
  bash: { "git diff *": allow, "*": ask }
---
You review the change you are given and report findings; you do not edit.
  • acp.agent names the declaration the document runs: the key of a [runtimes.<id>.acp.agents.<agent>] table. It follows the agent ID grammar; anything else fails the load (acp.agent, strict like the block's other fields). Absent, it is the document's own ID, so claude.md with acp: {} keeps meaning what it means today.
  • It names a declaration, never a document. acp.agent: claude runs the runtimes' claude whether or not claude.md exists; settings are not inherited from it, and documents cannot chain.
  • The document's ID is the agent's ID. claude-review is listed, picked, delegated to, and scheduled by that ID; its synthetic model is acp/claude-review, and an ACP session record's agent is it while runtime_agent is the declaration (claude).
  • Bare declarations stay agents. A declared ID with no document of that ID is the agent of that ID with the default document, as now. A claude.md with enabled: false hides it, and the templates over claude are unaffected.
  • Shadowing (user decision of the same day: a diagnostic, not a failed load). A document whose ID a runtime declares wins over the declaration as before. With an acp block naming another declaration (claude.md with acp.agent: codex), the claude declaration is no agent of its own and ConfigStatus.diagnostics says so, as for a document without an acp block.
  • Offers and placement. A document's offers are the runtimes that declare its acp.agent (the engine's AcpOffers, relabelled with the document's ID). Placement, the refusals, availability, and the one-offering-runtime rule for runtime.attach are unchanged, judged against those runtimes.
  • One process per declaration and runtime. ProcessKey already names the runtime and the declaration, so claude and claude-review share one agent process, each cookie session with its own ACP session. Everything a template sets is per ACP session already: the starting mode and config options, models, hide_tools (the MCP bridge is started per session), permissions, and the first prompt's body.
  • Switching agents in a session from one template to another starts a new ACP session: resume and load take the latest record of the session's current agent, and only when its runtime_id and runtime_agent are the ones that run the agent now (a document whose acp.agent changed starts afresh, with the diagnostic a move between runtimes gives).
  • What the agent reports is the declaration's. acp-agents.json (the last options and input media) is keyed by declaration and runtime, not by the cookie agent: KnownAgents::update is called with RuntimeAgent::agent instead of RuntimeAgent::id. Existing entries are valid as they are, since every one has the two equal. Every template's AgentRuntime.options is that state with its own acp.mode, acp.config, and models applied; the option IDs the configuration diagnostics use are the declaration's.
  • Undeclared. A document whose acp.agent no runtime declares yet is accepted provisionally with the diagnostic of today, which clears once a runtime reports that declaration; delegation targets resolve the same way.
  • Out of scope. command and env stay with the declaration, and the templates share its process, so a template cannot change them (a different CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR is a second declaration).

Protocol. No schema change. AgentRuntime.agent already carries the declaration's key; it now differs from the agent's ID for a template, and its documentation says so. Client protocol minor bump, for clients that show it: the TUI's and the web's agent pickers and list_agents name the declaration when it differs ([claude on local], acp agent: claude). Plugin and runtime protocols unchanged; the history format is unchanged (AcpSessionRecord already has runtime_agent).

Docs. The ACP agents guide gets a Several documents over one agent section with the example above; the agent document reference in agents lists acp.agent.

Tests. Two documents over one declaration: both listed, each with its own permissions deciding the agent's requests and its own hide_tools in the bridge, one process serving both sessions; options reported in one session shown on the other's draft with its own acp.mode applied; a bare declaration beside its templates, and hidden by enabled: false; a document naming another declaration shadowing its own ID's (the diagnostic); acp.agent not an agent ID refused at load; an undeclared acp.agent provisional until a runtime reports it; switching a session between two templates starting a new ACP session, and a changed acp.agent refusing resume; an old acp-agents.json read unchanged.

Implementation notes (2026-10-25):

  • AcpDocumentSettings::agent (acp.agent) and declaration(id). The registry groups declarations by RuntimeAgent::agent, runs each document with an acp block over its declaration's offers relabelled with its ID, then gives every declared ID no document has the default document; AcpOffers::declaration names the key.
  • KnownAgents is updated by RuntimeAgent::agent. The runner's resume and branch check compares runtime_agent with the placed declaration besides runtime_id (The agent's earlier session is of ACP agent fixture, and its document now runs second ...); an eager fork refuses the same way.
  • ConfigStatus.diagnostics: ACP agent fixture of runtime local is ignored: the agent document fixture runs ghost (acp.agent) ..., and agent fixture runs ACP agent ghost (acp.agent), which no runtime declares yet ... for a document naming an undeclared one.
  • Clients: cookie_agent_client_state::acp::declaration; runtime_note gives claude on local or claude · needs local attached.
  • Bridged tools in the transcript (same day, user report): an ACP turn now records model_tools_published with each attempt, the names the bridge's tools/list gives (bridged_tool_definitions: the run's tool definitions without hide_tools), skipped when the latest record matches, as a model run's request tools are. The tools row of the TUI and the web client titles them cookie tools · N offered to the agent while the latest run is the session's ACP agent (rows::model_tools_summary). No wire change.
  • Tests: crates/engine/src/runtime/tests/acp_templates.rs, a_turn_records_the_tools_the_bridge_offers_for_the_clients, the config test an_acp_document_names_the_declaration_it_runs, and the client note and summary tests.

docs.title: ACP v2: the port, self-wakes, subagent sessions, and background work
docs.text:
Status: implemented (2026-10-26), every phase. Phase 1 (v2 only) implemented 2026-10-26 (04b4b0e4d); phase 2 (self-wakes) implemented 2026-10-26, client protocol 1.38.0 and plugin protocol 1.20.0 (0aacfd74b); phase 3 (subagent sessions) implemented 2026-10-26, client protocol 1.39.0 and plugin protocol 1.21.0 (222198de1); phase 4 (background work) implemented 2026-10-26, client protocol 1.40.0.

The user decided on 2026-10-26:

  • port cookie's ACP client to ACP v2 completely and drop v1;
  • accept the agents' subagent sessions.

The earlier decisions of this draft (then "background tasks and self-wakes", D1 to D7) carry over where v2 leaves them meaningful (section 13).

Builds on ACP agents, background tool calls, external producers, and held sessions.

docs.title: 1.1 Agents work without a prompt, and cookie drops it
docs.text:
An ACP agent can start work with no prompt from cookie. Claude Code does it when something it started in the background finishes:

  • a background shell;
  • a Monitor event;
  • a background subagent;
  • a scheduled wakeup.

Its adapter streams that work as ordinary session updates.

Cookie's v1 client drops it. acp_round treats what arrives between rounds as metadata:

  • text, tool calls, and usage are lost;
  • permission requests, questions, and calls to cookie's MCP bridge are refused.

On 2026-10-26 a Claude Code session twice reported finished background work that the user never saw.

ACP v1 has no way to say when such work ends. Covering it on v1 needed three workarounds: heuristics (Claude's usage _meta, a quiet period), and an IDE vendor's extension for task reports.

ACP v2 makes this part of the protocol. A session's foreground work is reported as state: running, requires_action, and idle, the last with a stop reason. The schema says so directly: work "can start with a prompt or be agent-initiated, for example to pursue an ongoing goal or follow up on a completed background task … Agent-initiated work does not require a prompt request or a synthetic user message."

docs.title: 1.2 v1 limits elsewhere
docs.text:
• A turn's end is the prompt's answer. Steering needs the Claude adapter's _session/steering extension.
  • Subagents. Claude's Task subagents show flat, as tool calls (ACP bridge gaps, item 7). v2 makes subagent sessions part of a client's baseline.
  • Terminal output relies on an adapter _meta extension. v2 has agent-owned terminals.

docs.title: 1.3 Background work dies early
docs.text:
• The agent's process stops after [acp] idle_shutdown_ms (5 minutes) with no cookie run.
  • An evicted session sends session/close.

Both end the agent's background shells.

docs.title: 2. Scope
docs.text:
1. v2 only. Cookie initializes every ACP agent with protocol version 2 and speaks only v2. An agent that answers otherwise is refused (section 3). All v1 paths go (section 11).
  2. Turns end by state. A run ends at the agent's idle. session/prompt only says the prompt was taken in.
  3. Steering is v2's own: a prompt sent while the agent works.
  4. Self-wakes become runs, started by a producer message from the agent itself (sections 6 and 7).
  5. Subagent sessions become cookie child sessions under the parent (section 8).
  6. Background work:
  7. the agent's still-running terminals are shown;
  8. background work and open wake runs keep the process and the session alive (section 9).
  9. Cookie's own tools show once. A bridged call is shown as cookie's call. The v1 fix of 2026-10-26 already does this; on v2 the match uses the tool call's standard name (section 10).

Out of scope:

  • v1 agents (Gemini CLI unless it adds v2, hand-written v1 agents);
  • providers/*;
  • auth/logout.

docs.title: 3. Handshake
docs.text:
• The request: initialize with:
  • protocolVersion: 2;
  • info: cookie's name and version;
  • capabilities: elicitation (form and URL) and _meta.

v2 has no client file system or terminals. Notices, compaction, boolean options, plans, and subagents are baseline. - The response must carry protocolVersion: 2 and info. - Its capabilities.session gives what the session supports: fork, delete, resume, additionalDirectories, prompt content, and MCP transports. - Its authMethods drive auth/login. - Refusal. Any other version, or an initialize error, stops the process. The agent's runs fail with " speaks ACP v; cookie needs ACP v2. Update its adapter, or start it in v2 mode." The agent is reported unavailable in the runtime's agent list, as an agent whose process failed to start is today. - Adapters. The official ACP organisation's Claude and Codex adapters serve v2 (the user, 2026-10-26). - Verified for Claude: @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp 0.97.0 serves both versions, and CLAUDE_AGENT_ACP_PROTOCOL=v2 pins v2. - The starter kit and the ACP agents guide name these packages.

docs.title: 4. Methods
docs.text: v1 v2 initialize (clientCapabilities, clientInfo) initialize (capabilities, info) authenticate auth/login session/new, session/resume, session/close, session/delete, session/list unchanged names, v2 shapes session/load (with replay) gone: session/resume only. An agent without resume gets a new session, as when resume fails today session/fork with _meta.jetbrains.air.fork session/fork (unstable in the schema), with the same _meta fork point (section 4.1) session/prompt, answered at the turn's end session/prompt, answered at insertion with the user message's messageId session/cancel session/cancel; then idle with cancelled session/set_mode, current_mode_update gone: the mode is a config option session/set_config_option unchanged session/request_permission, elicitation/create, elicitation/complete unchanged; requests name their session, which may be a subagent's (section 8) _session/steering (Claude's extension) gone: steering is a prompt during work (section 5.2)

docs.title: 4.1 Forking at a point
docs.text:
v2's session/fork forks a whole session. Its request has sessionId, cwd, additionalDirectories, mcpServers, systemPrompt, and _meta, and no fork point.

Cookie keeps the fork point it sends today:

_meta.jetbrains.air.fork = { version: 1, messageId: <agent message ID> }

It works over v2, checked against @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp 0.97.0:

  • The _meta reaches the fork. The v2 surface hands session/fork to the agent's v1 fork (v1ForkSessionRequest), which drops only mcpServers and systemPrompt. The fork code reads the point from _meta.jetbrains.air.fork (forkPoint in fork-session.js).
  • The message IDs are the same. v2 requires a messageId on every message chunk, and the v2 surface passes v1's through unchanged. So the agent message IDs cookie records are the IDs the fork point names. :segment:<n> suffixes resolve as before.
  • The probe still works. An unknown point is refused with invalidParams (-32602), and JSON-RPC errors pass through the v2 surface. So cookie's once-per-process probe (probe_fork_point) carries over unchanged. An agent that ignores the point forks whole and is handled as such, as today.
  • The fork is ready. The forked session is started by the agent and can be prompted at once, with its config options and commands in the response.

The point stays a vendor extension until v2 names one. Agents without it fall back to cookie's existing whole-session handling.

docs.title: 5.1 A prompted run
docs.text:
1. Cookie sends session/prompt. Its answer is the insertion: the prompt's messageId, and the claim on its input is released as at a commit today.
  2. The run records updates (section 5.3) until the session's state_update says idle. A prompt the agent rejects fails the run with its error.
  3. idle's stopReason ends the run:
  4. end_turn completes it;
  5. cancelled cancels it;
  6. max_tokens, max_turn_requests, and refusal fail it with that reason;
  7. error fails it with the error's message;
  8. a missing or unknown reason completes it.
  9. requires_action is recorded as the session waiting on the user. The run stays open; clients show the approval or question as today.
  10. usage_update gives usage and context as today.

A running with no prompt of cookie's open is a self-wake (section 7). A repeated idle (a resume snapshot) ends nothing.

docs.title: 5.2 Steering and queueing
docs.text:
• Steer: cookie sends session/prompt while the run's work is running.
  • The prompt is steered once its answer (insertion) arrives, as the 2026-10-25 addendum's "a steer waits until the agent takes it".
  • The same run goes on until idle.
  • A cancel before insertion leaves the input pending for the next run.
  • Queue: cookie waits for idle, then sends the prompt as a new run's.

docs.title: 5.3 Updates
docs.text: v2 update Cookie user_message, user_message_chunk the inserted prompt's echo, matched by messageId and not recorded twice; outside a prompt of cookie's, a wake's body (section 6) agent_message, agent_message_chunk assistant text; a whole agent_message replaces its chunks, by messageId agent_thought, agent_thought_chunk thinking, the same way tool_call_update upsert by toolCallId. The first update shows the call; name is the tool's own name (in place of Claude's _meta.claudeCode.toolName) tool_call_content_chunk appends one content item to the call terminal_update, terminal_output_chunk the agent's terminal, shown in the call whose content names it (type: terminal). This replaces the _meta terminal extension; a still-running terminal is background work (section 9) plan_update, plan_removed the checklist block, by plan ID state_update section 5.1 subagent_update, session_message, session_message_chunk section 8 usage_update, notice, compaction_update, compaction_summary_chunk, available_commands_update, config_option_update, session_info_update as today unknown kinds ignored, as today

docs.title: 6. The wake producer
docs.text:
A run cookie did not prompt is recorded as started by a producer message from the agent itself. Clients, push notifications, held sessions, and subagent reports then treat it like any automatic run.

  • Owner: a new ProducerOwner variant, acp_agent { agent: AgentId }.
  • It is engine-derived.
  • The owner enum is closed but sits in the open EventPayload. An older client reads the event as an unknown payload.
  • The message: ProducerMessageAccepted with:
  • mode: steer;
  • a fresh id as the idempotency key;
  • description: "woke on its own";
  • body: the cause when the agent says one, else "The agent started work on its own."

v2 names no cause. A user_message the agent inserts first, or a cause in the running update's _meta, becomes the body when present. - Never sent to the agent. The runner leaves acp_agent messages out of prompts. - Clients show it as a producer row: "◷ Claude woke on its own · …".

docs.title: 7. Self-wakes
docs.text:
• Listening between runs. A listener reads each live session's update channel while no run holds it. Metadata updates apply as today.
  • Start. running or requires_action with no run open starts a wake run:
  • the engine accepts the wake message and starts the run at once;
  • run admission does not apply, because the agent is already working;
  • the listener hands over the updates that follow.
  • Requests (permission, elicitation, bridge calls) that arrive with no run open start a wake run too. They are no longer refused.
  • Inside. A wake run records updates and answers requests exactly as a prompted run does (section 5).
  • Stop sends session/cancel, and the session is held as after any Stop. It does so even when the stop lands before the run's first round, and it drops the wakes still waiting, so the stopped work does not start another run.
  • User input steers into it (section 5.2).
  • End. idle, by its stop reason (section 5.1).
  • Ending a run never stops the agent. After idle the process idle timer runs as after any run (section 9).
  • What follows is as for any run:
  • session status;
  • a push notification when a root settles;
  • a <subagent_report> to the parent of a delegated session;
  • the failure count of held sessions.

A self-wake while the session is held is still recorded.

docs.title: 8. Subagent sessions
docs.text:
v2 reports an agent's subagents (Claude's Task and Agent subagents) as child sessions.

  • The parent's stream carries subagent_update:
  • the child's sessionId;
  • title and description;
  • capabilities (cancel);
  • a mirror of the child's state.
  • The child's stream carries its own updates under the child's sessionId.

The subagents part of the schema is marked unstable.

docs.title: 8.1 Cookie child sessions
docs.text:
• Creation. The first subagent_update for a new child creates a cookie session under the parent's tree. It records origin delegated:
  • root_session_id, parent_session_id, and parent_run_id are the parent's run;
  • parent_tool_call_id is the call that spawned it, when the update's _meta names one (Claude: the Task call), else none;
  • invocation_id and depth are as for a delegation.

SessionOrigin is closed, and a new variant would break older clients' session lists. So the child reuses delegated and carries an additive SessionMeta.acp_subagent: true. - Fields. The child's agent is the parent's ACP agent. Its title is the update's title, else its description. Its ACP session id is the child's sessionId, recorded like any ACP session's. - Clients nest it under its parent as they nest delegated children. The subagent tree shows it running from its mirrored state.

docs.title: 8.2 The child's work
docs.text:
• Runs. The child's own state_updates make its runs, each a wake run of the child (section 7):
  • the first: "◷ started this subagent: ";
  • later ones: "woke on its own".

    • Its updates, permission requests, and questions are recorded and answered in the child's session, under the child's rules, which are the parent's agent document. - Stop. Allowed only when the child's capabilities.cancel is present. It sends session/cancel with the child's id. Sending the child input is not offered: v2 grants no prompt capability to a child. - Not cookie's delegation. The engine's delegation machinery stays off for these children: - no <subagent_report> to the parent, because the parent agent gets the child's result itself; - no handle and no send_message; - no cascade.

    The marker acp_subagent selects this. - Messages. session_message and session_message_chunk (between parent and child) are recorded as producer rows of the receiving session, owner acp_agent, described "message from ". They are never sent to the agent. - Lifetime. - A child lives in the parent's ACP process. - Its session stays resident while the parent's does. - Ending or deleting the parent ends it. - After a restart, its history stays in cookie, but it is not resumed: it was the parent agent's.

docs.title: 9. Background work and keeping it alive
docs.text:
v2 has no background-task report. Claude's v2 surface refuses the async-task updates of the IDE extension that v1 could opt into (it throws on update kinds it does not translate). So this draft's earlier D2 is dropped.

What v2 does report is the agent's terminals.

  • Agent terminals. A terminal still running after the tool call that started it ended (no exitStatus) is background work:
  • It is listed by session.background.list and background.changed as a background call, with a new additive agent_task: true. Its display is the terminal's command, and its tool call is the call that shows it.
  • It leaves the list when the terminal exits.
  • Its end is recorded where it arrives (client protocol 1.50.0, acp_session_updated.background_ended): its tool call, tool, command, when it moved to the background, and the exit code or signal when the agent reports one (Claude's adapter reports none). Clients show it as a background call's report. Between runs it is recorded before the wake it may start, whose row still says only that the agent woke on its own: v2 names no cause. Added 2026-10-28 at the user's request.
  • It has no Stop: v2 gives clients no terminal kill.

Phase 1 checks that Claude's adapter keeps a backgrounded command's terminal open until it exits. If it does not, background shells stay invisible, and only wakes report their end. - Process idle shutdown treats a process as busy while any session of it has: - an open run, wake runs included; - a running agent terminal; - work in running or requires_action. - Session eviction pins a session in the same cases, like "work about to happen" (background tools, section 13). - Daemon restart (daemon.restart, cookie daemon restart) waits for them as for background calls. A forced restart ends them, and the session records that.

docs.title: 10. Cookie's tools through the bridge
docs.text:
The 2026-10-26 fix applies unchanged:

  • the agent's report of its call of a cookie tool is held back while cookie's call through the bridge stands for it;
  • it is shown only when it ends without reaching cookie.

On v2 the tool is read from the call's name (mcp__cookie__<tool> for Claude). The title and raw-input forms remain for adapters that leave name out.

docs.title: 11. What goes
docs.text:
• The v1 wire code:
  • clientCapabilities and its v1 markers (notices, compaction, boolean options);
  • the v1 update kinds (tool_call, plan, current_mode_update);
  • session/load and its replay handling;
  • authenticate;
  • mode handling (session/set_mode, the modes-to-option shim).
  • Claude-only extensions: _session/steering, the terminal _meta keys, and _meta.claudeCode.toolName as the only name source.
  • Draft rules made moot by state: the v1 end rules of this draft's earlier version (Claude's usage _meta, [acp] wake_quiet_ms). Their config key is never added.
  • The ACP fixture agent of the engine tests is rewritten to speak v2 (section 14).

Sessions created under v1 keep their history. Their next run resumes the same ACP session with v2 session/resume; the agent keeps its own storage.

docs.title: 12. Protocols and storage
docs.text:
• Client protocol, next minor, additive:
  • ProducerOwner::acp_agent { agent };
  • BackgroundCall.agent_task;
  • SessionMeta.acp_subagent;
  • no new methods.
  • Events: none new.
  • Wakes are producer messages and runs.
  • Children are SessionCreated with origin delegated and their runs.
  • A run's stop reason uses the existing outcomes.
  • Plugin protocol: a minor bump, for the new owner in events.
  • Runtime protocol: unchanged; the relay carries every ACP line.
  • Configuration: none new.

docs.title: 13. Decisions
docs.text:
Made by the user on 2026-10-26:

  • v2 only, drop v1. Agents that cannot speak v2 are refused with a clear error.
  • Accept subagent sessions as cookie child sessions (section 8).
  • D1. Owner: a new acp_agent { agent } owner.
  • D2. The IDE task extension: dropped. It is not usable over v2 (section 9); agent terminals stand in for it where the adapter keeps them open.
  • D3. Self-wakes while held are recorded.
  • D4. Input during a wake run steers into it.
  • D5. Background work and open runs keep the process and the session alive, with no cap.
  • D6. Daemon restart waits for them.
  • D7. The quiet fallback: dropped. idle ends work.

docs.title: 14. Tests
docs.text:
The engine's ACP fixture agent (crates/engine/tests/fixtures/acp_agent.py) is rewritten as a v2 agent, keeping its commands. It adds:

  • work it starts on its own;
  • a subagent;
  • a backgrounded terminal;
  • a v1-only mode for the refusal test.

Handshake:

  • v2 is accepted;
  • an agent answering version 1 is refused with the message of section 3;
  • auth/login follows authMethods.

Turns:

  • a prompt's run ends at idle with each stop reason;
  • requires_action keeps it open;
  • an error stop fails it with its message;
  • a resume snapshot's idle ends nothing.

Steering:

  • a prompt during work is steered at insertion;
  • a cancel before insertion leaves the input pending;
  • Queue waits for idle.

Updates:

  • whole messages replace their chunks;
  • tool_call_update upserts, and tool_call_content_chunk appends;
  • terminals show in their call;
  • plan_update and plan_removed work.

Wakes:

  • running with no run open starts a wake run with an acp_agent producer row, and idle ends it;
  • a permission request, an elicitation, and a bridge call inside one are answered;
  • Stop cancels and holds the session;
  • a wake while held is recorded.

Subagents:

  • subagent_update creates a nested child session;
  • the child's updates and requests land in it;
  • its Stop is offered only with cancel;
  • no <subagent_report> goes to the parent;
  • session_message rows appear.

Background work:

  • a terminal running past its call is listed, and leaves the list at exit;
  • no idle shutdown or eviction while one runs or a run is open.

Bridge: cookie's tools show once, matched by name.

Browser e2e (acp group): a wake row and its output live; a subagent nested under its parent; a background terminal in the background bar.

Manual (Claude Code on yunhao-labserver, v2):

  1. Start sleep 30 && echo done in the background and end the turn. See the terminal in the background bar, then the wake row, the report, and a push.
  2. Ask for a Task subagent. See it nested and live.

docs.title: 15. Phases
docs.text:
1. Wire v2 (one phase, since v1 goes with it):
  2. the handshake and refusal;
  3. the methods and updates of sections 3 to 5;
  4. turns ending by state;
  5. native steering;
  6. the bridge match by name;
  7. the fixture agent rewritten;
  8. the v1 code removed.

Phase 1 also checks: - whether Claude keeps background terminals open; - Codex's v2 surface. 2. Self-wakes: - the between-run listener; - wake runs and the acp_agent owner; - requests inside wake runs; - the producer row in the TUI and the web client. 3. Subagent sessions: section 8, with the nesting and the child's Stop in both clients. 4. Background work: - agent terminals as background calls; - the idle, eviction, and restart rules of section 9. 5. Docs: - the ACP agents guide (v2 only, which adapters, what wakes and subagents look like); - the reference Claude Code document; - the starter kit's adapter packages.

docs.title: 16. Open questions
docs.text:
• Unstable parts. Some of v2 is marked unstable and may change:
  • the subagent part (subagent_update, session_message);
  • session/fork, whose fork point is a vendor _meta (section 4.1). Cookie follows the SDK version the official adapters use, and treats unknown fields and kinds as today.
  • Codex. Its v2 surface, including what it reports of subagents and background work, is checked in phase 1.

docs.title: 17. Implementation notes
docs.text:
Phase 1 (2026-10-26, 04b4b0e4d):

  • A whole agent_message or agent_thought adds only what its chunks did not already stream (the agents in use stream chunks); it does not replace them.
  • A plan sent as Markdown or as a file shows as a one-entry checklist.
  • The round reads insertion from the user_message echo in the update stream. The prompt's answer and the updates travel apart, so the echo orders them.

Phase 2 (2026-10-26, client protocol 1.38.0):

  • What starts a wake. Only what v2 defines as starting foreground work: running, requires_action, or a request to answer. Output between runs with no such state is kept, and the next run records it.
  • Clients. They show the wake's message as they show any producer message, labelled <agent>, on its own with the description "Woke on its own"; the approval reviewer reads it as [<agent> started work on its own].
  • Holds. A wake starts its run past any hold. A Stop records a hold only when the session could otherwise wake (held sessions, section 2), so a wake after a Stop is the case that needs this.

Phase 3 (2026-10-26, client protocol 1.39.0):

  • The marker. A child is marked as the agent's own by its log, not by SessionMeta.acp_subagent: its first acp_session_started has the new how: subagent. The engine uses it to send no <subagent_report>, to list the child without a delegation record (session.children), and to refuse prompts and turns once the agent's process is gone. Clients use it to refuse sending (AcpSessionView::refusal).
  • The title. The child's title is a runless delegated_set title change, keyed by the child's invocation.
  • The link to the parent. The child's parent_tool_call_id names no cookie call: the agent's own Task call is replaced by the session_message that carries the task.
  • Requests that come early. The process marks a child announced by subagent_update as expected. Requests for it wait for its route instead of being answered cancelled at once.
  • The task. A session_message to the child before its work starts becomes the wake's body ("Started with a task"). Messages during a run show as notices; since client protocol 1.41.0 they are acp_session_updated.session_message instead (direction, peer, the other session as named then, text), shown on both sides as producer messages are. The task a subagent's run starts with shows there once, as that run's message.
  • Cookie's tools. A subagent's calls of cookie's tools go through its parent's bridge and show in the parent's session.

Phase 4 (2026-10-26, client protocol 1.40.0):

  • Checked against the adapter. With claude-agent-acp 0.97.0, a backgrounded command's terminal stays open after its call completes and exits (exitStatus: {}) when the command ends; Claude Code then starts work on its own to report it.
  • When a command counts. A command is background work from the end of its call while its terminal has not exited. Its exit, between runs or in a run, ends it, and so does the end of the agent's process.
  • Keeping work alive. Each such command holds a use of the agent's process, so the process does not idle out, and pins its session against eviction. An idle daemon.restart counts it among background_calls. While one runs, the session waits on a background_call (SessionMeta.waiting_on, 2026-10-27), as on one of cookie's, so the clients mark it waiting.
  • Stop. session.background.stop refuses it, naming the agent as the one to ask. Clients show "run by the agent" in place of Stop.

docs.title: Agent Messaging (Subagent-to-Subagent Communication)
docs.text: Status: implemented. This page is the governing contract for agent-to-agent messaging through the send_message tool. User-facing settings live in Agent Messaging [messaging]; the tool contract is summarized in the tool reference.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Let any agent in a delegation tree send a durable message to any other agent in the same tree (parent ↔ child, sibling ↔ sibling, child → grandparent).
  • Delivery semantics: all delivery is producer-backed. The recipient receives the message either steered into its next safe model-request boundary (if running) or queued durably (if idle or queued). Messaging an idle or finished agent wakes it through the producer reconcile path: the message is admitted durably and the session resumes with it as input.
  • Model-visible tool surface, permission-gated, observable by the TUI and plugins.

docs.title: Non-Goals (v1)
docs.text:
• Cross-daemon / cross-process agent mesh. The engine is in-process; one daemon owns all sessions.
  • Arbitrary cross-session messaging outside the delegation tree. No discovery or authorization basis exists for that yet.
  • Request/response RPC between agents. Async mail only; replies are new messages.
  • Broadcast topics / pub-sub. Can be layered later on the same envelope.

docs.title: Addressing
docs.text:
send_message accepts either a full session UUID or the recipient's short handle (explore_1a2b3c4d) — the same raw-session addressing model the removed steer_subagent tool used. A non-UUID reference is resolved as a handle against the sender's tree only; if it matches no live tree peer the send fails with a self-repairing candidate list, and a handle from another tree never resolves. No labels, aliases, or special targets (parent, root).

There is no discovery mechanism. An agent learns a peer's session ID only because the parent disclosed it — in the delegation prompt, in a steering message, or via delegation tool results (a parent naturally knows its children's IDs from delegate_subagent). The parent therefore controls the communication graph: siblings can only talk if the parent chose to introduce them, and an agent cannot enumerate the tree to find targets on its own.

Every inbound message envelope carries the sender's handle when one exists, so a recipient can reply directly with send_message. Older sessions without a handle use the full sender UUID in the reply hint. Mail from a parent to its own child is the exception: every turn a child finishes already reaches its parent as a <subagent_report> (or as the foreground delegation's result), so the child answers in its final answer, and a send_message reply would arrive twice.

docs.title: Message Envelope
docs.text:
The durable body (ProducerMessageAccepted.body) is readable text rendered into the recipient prompt as a user-turn materialization (repo convention: tool-emitted system input materializes as a user turn):

<agent_message from="explore_1a2b3c4d">
Message written by the sending agent

[use `send_message(to="explore_1a2b3c4d", ...)` to reply]
</agent_message>

Mail from the recipient's parent carries this hint instead, whether or not the recipient can send messages:

<agent_message from="main">
Also check the tests

[reply in your final answer: it reaches `main` when this turn ends]
</agent_message>

The from attribute identifies the sender in every variant. The send_message hint appears only when the recipient's send_message tool is exposed. The original body is preserved as written; the engine adds only the envelope and optional hint. The recipient is implicit — the envelope only ever appears in the session it was delivered to. Message IDs, sender UUIDs, agent hop counts, and other delivery metadata remain in the durable event record and are not rendered into the model-facing body.

docs.title: Tool Surface
docs.text:
MessageToolProvider (provider id builtin.message), modeled on DelegateToolProvider, is registered via try_register_tool_provider in crates/cookie_agent/src/main.rs after engine open.

Tool Args Behavior send_message to: <handle or session_id>, body, mode? (steer/queue, default steer) Resolve the recipient reference (UUID, or handle within the sender's tree), check permission, register/find the sender's agent-producer on the recipient session, send with idempotency key derived from (sender session, run, tool_call) (same derivation pattern as invocation_id)

Model-facing arguments are exactly to, body, and mode; the argument object is strict. The recipient argument is named to; it was renamed from recipient_session_id during implementation with no alias — see Migration notes.

Delivery is fully described by mode: steer (default) joins the recipient's in-flight run at the next safe boundary through producer delivery; queue admits the message durably and it is claimed into the recipient's prompt at the next safe boundary. There is no inbox tool — agents never need to poll.

docs.title: Results, errors, and retries
docs.text:
A successful send_message result means durably accepted (decided): the ProducerMessageAccepted event is persisted in the recipient's event log, so delivery survives a daemon restart. It does not mean the recipient has seen or consumed the message. The result carries:

  • message_id — the durable producer message ID,
  • mode — the effective delivery mode,
  • recipient_state — the recipient's state at send time (running, queued, waking_finished).

Failures are explicit tool errors with stable codes in the send_message: namespace, one per case, so the sending model can react predictably (retry, give up, or report to its parent):

  • send_message:disabled — [messaging] enabled = false, even when permission rules allow the send,
  • send_message:invalid_arguments — missing, unknown, or wrongly typed arguments, including the removed recipient_session_id spelling,
  • send_message:invalid_body — empty or over max_body_bytes,
  • send_message:unknown_session — a well-formed session UUID that names no session,
  • send_message:not_tree_peer — a well-formed session UUID whose root_session_id differs from the sender's,
  • a non-UUID recipient is treated as a subagent handle: a handle that matches no live peer in the sender's tree fails with the self-repairing unknown subagent reference … tool error, whose candidate list renders each addressable peer as handle — description — status (session_id <uuid>) (pre-handle peers print their UUID once),
  • send_message:self_send — sender targeted its own session,
  • send_message:inbox_full — recipient has max_pending_per_session pending agent messages (see Configuration),
  • send_message:max_hops_exceeded — the hop guard rejected the send (see Guards),
  • send_message:inflight_full — the per-pair in-flight window is full (see Guards),
  • send_message:engine_shutdown — send raced daemon shutdown.

Permission failures are not messaging-specific: a denied send follows the generic permission-denied flow, and an ask rule routes through the existing approval flow instead of erroring.

Retries are safe: the idempotency key derives from (sender session, run, tool_call), so a retried call returns the original message_id instead of delivering twice (existing producer dedup behavior).

docs.title: steer_subagent removal
docs.text:
send_message is a strict superset of the removed steer_subagent tool (decided): steering a running child is send_message(mode=steer); steering a queued child durably accepts the message and it is claimed when the child's run starts; finished children, unreachable by steer_subagent, are reachable via wake. The model-visible steer_subagent tool is removed from DelegateToolProvider; delegate_subagent and get_subagent_result remain. (cancel_subagent remained too until 0975445c1 removed it; stop_background given a subagent's handle now stops its turn.) The engine's steer_subagent method is gone too; user steering (run.steer) keeps its own admission path, which send_message does not use. Consequences:

  • Parent→child authority is expressed entirely through message permission rules on the child relationship (e.g. "child": allow in the agent doc).
  • Intentional breaking change (decided): combined with deny-by-default, the out-of-box default agent can delegate subagents but cannot steer them until the user adds message: { "child": allow } to their agent doc. This is accepted as-is; see Migration notes. There is no built-in exemption.
  • Agent docs, prompt sections, and guides were updated in the same change.

send_message uses bounded result truncation and ToolConcurrency::Parallel; guard checks and acceptance are serialized inside the recipient actor.

docs.title: Engine Behavior
docs.text:
1. ProducerOwner::Agent { session_id } variant (protocol/src/producer.rs). Additive payload change; the versionless, best-effort event log tolerates it and old readers degrade gracefully.
  2. Authorization predicate beside ensure_subagent_owned: ensure_tree_peer(sender, recipient) — both sessions are tree peers iff their stored SessionOrigin metadata carries the same root_session_id. That is the entire contract (decided): no live-registry walk, no ancestry or taint validation. Known, accepted limitation: after a parent reverts history, "ghost" sessions from the reverted branch remain reachable by agents that hold their session IDs. Sender identity is always derived from the executing tool context, never from model-supplied arguments. The recipient may be in any state, including finished. Running recipients get steer/queue delivery; Queued/idle recipients get a durable admission claimed at start; Finished/Completed recipients are woken.
  3. Engine API: engine.send_agent_message(invocation) -> AgentMessageHandle in messaging_api.rs, internally accepting the message atomically on the recipient's session actor. Sender-side auto-registration of its Agent producer on the recipient mirrors how background monitors register ProducerOwner::Delegation on parents.
  4. Wake and delivery are producer-backed everywhere. Idle and finished recipients wake through the producer reconcile path — the same reconcile that restarts delivery of accepted-but-unconsumed producer mail after idle eviction or restart — never through user steering or a runless UserInputAdmitted. Messaging an idle-evicted actor therefore reuses the existing producer wake machinery (spawn_actor) with no special casing.
  5. Guards — see Guards.

docs.title: Guards
docs.text:
Two loop-safety guards reject sends at send time; both are opt-out:

  • Hop guard. The engine tracks an internal hop count per message chain, carried in producer metadata and never rendered in the agent-visible envelope. A send that would exceed messaging.max_hops fails with send_message:max_hops_exceeded. The default is unlimited: max_hops <= 0 disables the guard.
  • Per-pair in-flight window. At most max_inflight_per_pair unacknowledged messages per directed pair (default 4) to stop ping-pong storms between two agents. A pair message is unacknowledged while it is accepted, admitted, claimed, or released, and acknowledged once it is consumed or discarded. A full window rejects the send with send_message:inflight_full. max_inflight_per_pair = 0 disables the guard.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
A dedicated PermissionAction::Message gates send_message (decided) — messaging is not overloaded onto Delegate, so steering a child and messaging an agent remain independently controllable.

Rule shape (agent-doc frontmatter):

permissions:
  message:
    "child": allow      # my delegated children
    "parent": allow     # the agent that delegated me
    "sibling": ask      # other children of my parent
    "*": deny           # any other same-tree peer (grandparent, uncle, ...)
  • The permission resource label is the recipient's relationship to the sender: parent, child, sibling, or * (catch-all for any other same-tree peer). The label is derived from stored SessionOrigin metadata at send time and matched by the existing PermissionPipeline + WildcardPattern. This is purely a labeling step — there is no relationship-based authority check anywhere; permissions alone decide.
  • Deny by default, including built-in agents. Built-in agent definitions ship without message rules, so deny-by-default applies and the send_message tool is not even visible to the model (tool_visible requires an allow/ask rule). Messaging is strictly opt-in: an agent doc must declare rules for the tool to appear.
  • ask routes through the existing approval store and TUI approval flow.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
[messaging]
enabled = true
max_hops = 0                  # <= 0 disables the hop guard (default); hop counting is internal metadata
max_body_bytes = 32768        # tighter than the 256 KiB plugin cap; agent mail should be terse
max_pending_per_session = 32  # pending agent mail per recipient; overflow → send rejected
max_inflight_per_pair = 4     # 0 disables the per-pair in-flight window

Inbox overflow (decided): max_pending_per_session counts only pending agent mail (accepted, admitted, claimed, or released, but not yet consumed or discarded) — plugin, delegation-notification, and goal producer messages do not count against it, and no agent message is ever discarded to make room. When the cap is reached, send_message fails with the send_message:inbox_full tool error and the new message is not admitted; the sender may retry later. No silent drops.

docs.title: Observability, TUI, Plugins
docs.text:
• TUI: message lifecycle events are durable, so events.subscribe already delivers them. Both delivery modes surface as producer events — steer and queue sends alike appear as ProducerMessage* rows (owner == Agent) in the transcript, so users see steering and queueing exactly like existing producer traffic.
  • Plugins: zero new hooks — plugin/event observes all mail traffic; tool_before_call can gate/audit sends; plugin/producer/send already lets external systems inject into any session (precedent for external→agent mail).
  • Audit: bodies are durable in the recipient's event log, so full mail history is reconstructable per session.

docs.title: Migration notes
docs.text:
There is no separate changelog; these notes are the migration record for the messaging rollout.

  1. steer_subagent is removed. The model-visible tool no longer exists. Its replacements:
Former call Replacement Steer a running child send_message { to, body, mode: "steer" } (the default mode) Steer a queued child send_message { to, body }; the message is durably accepted and claimed when the child's run starts Reach a finished child Newly possible: send_message wakes finished sessions through producer reconcile

Parent→child authority moves from the delegate action to the message action with relationship labels. Agents that previously steered children need an explicit rule such as message: { "child": allow }; the default agent ships without one, so out-of-box subagent steering is denied until the rule is added. User steering through run.steer is unchanged. 2. Recipient argument renamed without an alias. The send_message recipient argument is to; the earlier recipient_session_id spelling is not accepted and fails with send_message:invalid_arguments. Because tool argument objects are strict, old calls fail closed, and prepared-operation grants issued under the old argument identity do not carry over — a previously granted "allow for the session tree" must be approved again under the new identity. 3. Protocol version 19. ProducerMessageAccepted gained the optional, internal agent_hop field in live RPC responses and durable events, so PROTOCOL_VERSION was bumped and the TS/JSON-schema bindings regenerated in the same change, per the repo's version-bump ritual.

docs.title: Resolved Decisions
docs.text:
1. Scope: tree-only, equality check only. Two sessions are tree peers iff their stored SessionOrigin.root_session_id values are equal. No live registry walk, ancestry validation, or taint reconciliation; sessions left over from a reverted branch remain messageable by agents holding their IDs. Any-session addressing is out of scope (it would need a global agent registry and new ownership rules) and conflicts with the no-discovery model.
  2. Permission action: dedicated Message action. Messaging gets its own PermissionAction variant rather than reusing Delegate, so messaging permissions are controlled independently of delegation.
  3. Finished agents are messageable. Sending to a Finished/Completed session wakes it through the producer reconcile path: the message is admitted durably and the session resumes with the message as input, enabling follow-ups without the parent re-delegating with resume_session_id.
  4. steer_subagent is removed. send_message is a strict superset: it covers steering running and queued children and additionally reaches finished children (wake), siblings, and ancestors. Only the model-visible tool is removed; the engine's steer machinery stays for user steering. Parent→child authority moves to Message permission rules.
  5. Permissions: relationship labels, deny by default. The message resource label is the recipient's relationship to the sender (parent, child, sibling, *), matched by ordinary wildcard rules — no relationship-based authority checks in the engine. Built-in agents ship without message rules: deny-by-default hides the tool entirely, so messaging is opt-in per agent doc. Combined with decision 4, the default agent loses out-of-box subagent steering until the user adds message: { "child": allow } — an accepted breaking change, documented in Migration notes.
  6. Send result = durably accepted. Success means the message is persisted (ProducerMessageAccepted) and returns message_id, effective mode, and recipient_state; failures are explicit send_message:-namespaced tool errors plus the generic permission-denied flow; retries return the original message_id via idempotency dedup.
  7. Inbox overflow rejects the sender. max_pending_per_session counts pending agent mail only (including claimed and released mail until it is consumed or discarded); overflow fails the send with send_message:inbox_full and nothing is admitted or silently discarded.
  8. Guards are enforced and opt-out. The hop guard (max_hops) and the per-pair in-flight window (max_inflight_per_pair) reject overshooting sends with send_message:max_hops_exceeded and send_message:inflight_full. max_hops <= 0 and max_inflight_per_pair = 0 disable their guard. Hop counting is internal metadata, never part of the delivered envelope, and a pair message counts as unacknowledged from acceptance until it is consumed or discarded.

docs.title: Phased Rollout
docs.text:
• Phase 1 (implemented): ProducerOwner::Agent, send_message with both steer (default) and queue modes, tree-scoped auth, relationship-labeled Message permissions (deny-by-default, tool hidden without rules), steer_subagent tool removal with doc/prompt migration. TUI read-only visibility.
  • Phase 2 (implemented): the hop guard and per-pair in-flight window are enforced with the semantics under Guards; ask approvals use the existing approval flow.
  • Phase 3 (future): plugin mediation recipes, optional broadcast-to-children (to: "children"), cross-daemon story if it ever becomes real.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
The implementation is correct when all of the following hold, covered by tests:

  1. An agent with message: { "child": allow } can send_message a running child (steer joins the next safe boundary) and a queued child (durable admission claimed at run start); an agent without message rules does not see the tool.
  2. Sibling→sibling and child→parent sends work when rules allow them; parent/child/sibling/* labels resolve correctly from origin metadata.
  3. A message to a finished session wakes it through producer reconcile: the session resumes with the message as input; the completed delegation is untouched.
  4. Tree authorization: equal root_session_id succeeds; mismatched roots fail with send_message:not_tree_peer; self-send fails with send_message:self_send.
  5. Result contract: success returns message_id, effective mode, and recipient_state; a retried tool call returns the original message_id and delivers once; restart before delivery still delivers.
  6. Limits and guards: send_message:invalid_body at size boundaries, send_message:inbox_full at max_pending_per_session (agent mail only), send_message:max_hops_exceeded and send_message:inflight_full at their configured limits with max_hops <= 0 / max_inflight_per_pair = 0 disabling each guard, and deny-by-default visibility.
  7. steer_subagent is gone from the tool surface; docs, prompt sections, and guides no longer reference it; the breaking change is in Migration notes.
  8. TUI renders steer and queue deliveries as ProducerMessage* mail rows in both live and replayed streams.
  9. PROTOCOL_VERSION bumped to 19; check-bindings.sh and docs stay in sync.

docs.title: Implementation Notes
docs.text:
Deliberately shallow — the mechanisms already exist; do not re-specify them:

  • Wake lifecycle: waking an idle or finished session reuses the producer reconcile path: accepted-but-unconsumed mail makes the session deliverable, the actor is spawned if evicted, and a fresh run starts on the same session with the message as input. No user steering or runless UserInputAdmitted is involved. The completed delegation is not reopened; no new completion notification fires unless the woken agent sends one.
  • Delivery semantics: steer and queue follow the existing producer machinery unchanged in all recipient states. Races with completion or compaction resolve the same way they do for other producer traffic.
  • Revert and fork: mail events follow the event log's existing revert and fork behavior. No special handling, no cross-branch dedup or wake suppression.
  • Hop counting: meaningful only when max_hops > 0; the count travels as internal producer metadata between chained sends and is rejected at send_message:max_hops_exceeded when it would exceed the limit.
