With the generated set at 1.0.0 against the 0.52.0 baselines, every rule enforced, the check found nothing to reject: no information type is closed any more, and a major bump covers every change. The regenerated baselines changed only their version files. The pre-freeze mode (exact-equality baselines, unenforced findings) is removed from check-compat.py, whose every surface is 1.x now; the mutation test's pre-freeze case became a check that a 0.x set is refused against a 1.x baseline, and the update is checked to leave a corpus/ directory beside the surfaces alone. The named fixture roots were unchanged. Experiments (reverted): an optional member added to ContextResult without a bump fails (runtime: the changes need a minor bump from 1.0.0); with RUNTIME_PROTOCOL_VERSION at 1.1.0 it passes; ContextResult.skipped removed with only that minor bump fails (needs a major bump ... field 'skipped' removed or renamed).
  • Golden logs. crates/engine/tests/fixtures/history/1/ holds six scenarios (about 800 KB), recorded by the ignored test record_golden_history (COOKIE_GOLDEN_HISTORY_OUT=<new dir>; it refuses a directory that exists) against fake OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, and OpenAI Responses endpoints, the in-process coding runtime over the runtime protocol, the fake plugin, and the Python reference plugin: coding (reads of a file, a directory, an image, and a missing file; bash with SGR on both streams, a non-zero exit, a background job and its report, and output cut to the budget with full; a plugin tool's json, link, code, and key_value blocks; an edit approved once, a write rejected, a webfetch granted for the tree and then allowed by the grant, a skill; user input with an image and a video upload; the approval reviewer; a summary compaction and a run after it), delegation (foreground, background, and resumed delegation, get_subagent_result, send_message queued and steered, subagent reports, a goal whose pending reminder is discarded when the checklist completes, the reference plugin's tool, a call its hook blocks, its queued producer message, and user input steered into a running run and queued behind it), replay (signed Anthropic thinking replayed natively), native-compaction and native-compaction-fallback (OpenAI's compaction window, and the summary when it fails), and revert-fork (a fork, then a revert of the source). Every display-block kind occurs in a stored result. Each scenario is the session store's root directories as written (artifacts, children, caches; no lock files) and snapshot.json: per session the metadata, usage, model history (full and assembled), and the events as a client of this version receives them, recorded only where they differ from the stored record (a stored display range), so the snapshot does not repeat the log. Indented down to the sessions' members, one line per event. golden_history_reads_as_recorded opens a copy of every scenario of every format directory read-only (the tree's lock held elsewhere; the copy must stay byte-identical) and owned (Engine::resume), and compares: every member the snapshot records must read the same, members a newer build adds are allowed, and arrays keep their lengths. It writes nothing; a failure names the JSON paths and says the logs are frozen. golden_history_tolerates_what_a_newer_build_adds rewrites copies of coding and delegation as a newer build of format 1 could have written them (unknown envelope, payload, and result members, a display block of an unknown kind, and a final record of an unknown type): they read as recorded, the unknown block is not sent to clients, a skippable unknown record is skipped, a fork copies every unknown member and the unknown record, and an unknown state record opens the logs render-only (run.start refused) with one skipped event reported. The recorder's COOKIE_GOLDEN_HISTORY_ONLY names one scenario while a recorder is being written.
  • Not covered by the golden logs. Quarantine needs records a writer never produces, so phase D's synthetic tests keep covering it; raw preservation is covered by the future-data test. The goal tools are not called by the model: on the base layer, goal_get and goal_update declare path actions (read, write) on the relative resource goal:current, which no rule can match without a workspace, so policy denied them whatever the agent allowed; the recorder completes the goal through the API. (Since resolved: the goal tools now declare no permission: they are published only while the user's goal is active or paused, and act on it alone.) MCP tools are not recorded (their blocks are kinds the plugin tool covers).
  • A fork of a session that delegated is refused as a corrupt log ("delegation reservation ownership is invalid"): the fork copies the delegation_reserved records, whose parent_session_id names the source, and validates them against the fork's own ID. This predates the compatibility work (the delegation journal moved into parent events earlier) and is left as an open follow-up, since what a fork should make of its source's children is a design question; the future-data test forks coding, which has no delegations. (Since resolved in client and plugin protocol 1.1.0: a fork leaves its source's subagents behind, replacing each delegation record with a skippable record_omitted at its sequence, and the future-data test forks delegation too. The events baseline's EventPayload root was recorded closed, so the checker called a new event type major; it is now the open event set, as readers take it, so a new type is the minor addition section 3.3 says it is.)
  • Corpora. crates/protocol/compat/corpus/{client,runtime}/1.0.0/ were recorded in one TUI-like session against an in-process daemon with a scripted OpenAI-compatible model and the local coding runtime behind the runtime protocol (the ignored server test record_the_client_and_runtime_corpora, COOKIE_RECORD_CORPUS=<root>): the handshake, the catalog, session creation and listing, a subscription, an image upload, run.start with a text and a file part, a bash call held for approval while session.submit_input and run.steer arrive, approval.list and approval.respond, artifact.read, and every reply and notification; on the runtime side runtime/initialize, capability/open, runtime/context, tool/prepare, tool/revalidate, tool/execute with tool/detachable and tool/progress, and runtime/shutdown. plugin/1.0.0/ is the reference plugin's conversation, recorded with check_reference_plugin.py --record (whose scripted tool_call_terminated now carries a real result: a completed outcome with a null result passes the schema but is nothing a daemon sends). Every line is {from, message}, and each version directory's SHA-256 is pinned in cookie_agent_protocol::corpus::FROZEN (behind test-support), so a rewrite fails every replay; a new minor records its own directory. The replays run where the readers live: requests against a fresh daemon (the server, with IDs taken from the replay's own replies; unix only, as the recorded call runs printf), replies and notifications through their types and a real Client (protocol), the daemon's messages through an SDK plugin and the coding runtime (corpus::play), and peer messages through RuntimeClient's handshakes and readers (engine). Each also re-reads the recorded information with an unknown member in every object. Hand-written newer-peer messages live in corpus/future/{client,plugin,runtime,daemon}.json with a test beside each reader; the SDK's inline newer-daemon test moved there. tool/release and tool/cancel are covered only by the future runtime messages, since the recorded execution consumes its prepared call.
  • Approval records read tolerantly. The corpora found that ApprovalRecord, ApprovalInternalDecision, and ApprovalFinalDecision checked the coherence of status, decision, source, and reason when read, so a value a newer build added (a status deferred, read as cancelled without a final decision) failed an older client's whole approval.list and the history records holding them. Their readers now check coherence only when every one of those values reads as itself; the writers still validate, and known values that contradict each other are still refused.
  • Converters. events/convert/mod.rs describes adding v1_to_v2.rs: bump HISTORY_FORMAT, write the step over format-1 JSON lines (storage encodings included), register it in CONVERTERS for good, record history/2/, and keep history/1/ read through the converter.
  • Policy and docs. AGENTS.md has a Compatibility section (the four surfaces follow this spec, every wire change passes the checker with the right bump, the frozen corpora and golden logs are never regenerated, converters are the only migrations) beside the unchanged strict configuration rule. reference/compatibility.md states sections 3 to 8 as contributor rules and is in the nav; protocol.md, runtime-protocol.md, development/plugins.md, schemas.md, architecture.md, and events.md describe the frozen versions, the storage encoding, and the golden logs.

docs.title: Cron jobs
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-23): the engine and the protocol (phase 1), the TUI, web, and CLI (phase 2), and the docs (phase 3). See Implementation notes and the user guide, Scheduling prompts. Builds on background tool calls (sections 12 and 13: what keeps a parent waiting, and producer waits that let a session page out), projects, and the memory spec (its permission defaults).

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
You and agents can schedule prompts: once after a delay, or on a cron schedule. Each fire either goes into an existing session or starts a new session. The daemon keeps the jobs, fires them while it runs, and records what each fire did.

The design draws on a survey of Claude Code (in-session CronCreate and /loop, Desktop scheduled tasks, cloud routines), OpenClaw (automations) and Hermes Agent (cronjob). From Claude Code it takes "each run is a session" for new-session jobs and "a fire waits its turn" for in-session ones.

Decided 2026-10-22:

  • You and agents can create, list, edit, and delete jobs. A job is an id, a prompt, a schedule, and a target.
  • Schedule: a 5-field cron expression, or a one-shot delay such as in 200s. The only other schedule option is max_runs, default 1 (added 2026-10-22). Cron times are the daemon host's local time. There are no self-paced loops (an agent can already wait on a background command).
  • Payload: a prompt, nothing else (no shell commands, no scripts).
  • Target, chosen when the job is created:
  • a session: you can name any session, and /cron in the TUI or web command panel targets the current one. An agent can target its own session or one of its subagents' sessions, nothing else;
  • a new session per run, from a template: the creator picks the agent and may add permission rules, so a job can do more than its creator. Only you can set a job's permission mode; every job, an agent's or yours, starts in auto_approve_n.
  • Firing into a session: the creator picks steer or queue. The fire runs with the session's current agent.
  • Subagents may use the cron tools when their rules allow it; cron has no default for delegated runs, so it is hidden unless granted. Root runs default to cron: allow.
  • Agents can manage every job. The cron permission's resource is the target kind (session, subagent, or new), and one action covers reading and changing jobs.
  • No expiry: a job with max_runs: "unlimited" runs until it is deleted or disabled. A job that reaches max_runs is deleted if an agent created it and kept, disabled as finished, if you did.
  • No catch-up: a fire missed while the daemon was down is recorded as skipped and not run.
  • Failures: a job is disabled after [cron] max_consecutive_failures failures in a row (default 3), which a job can override. Skips do not count and do not reset the count.
  • Overlap: a fire is skipped while the job's previous fire is still undelivered, or, for a new-session job, while its previous run is still running.
  • Results: run sessions appear in the session list, marked with the job that started them. Notifications are designed later.
  • A subagent with an enabled job that has a next fire time keeps its parent waiting. A session whose only pending thing is a job can page out; the fire reloads it.
  • Deleting a session deletes the jobs that target it.
  • The global runtime gains a list_agents tool, offered whenever delegate_subagent or cron is, so a model can choose an agent, and the rules to add, from what each agent is (section 8.1).

Out of scope: notifications, catch-up runs, self-paced loops, shell or script payloads, time zones other than the host's, webhooks and event triggers.

docs.title: 2. Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Job A scheduled prompt with an id, a schedule, and a target. Fire One moment a job's schedule comes due. Run What a delivered fire leads to: a run in the target session, or a new session's first run. In-session job A job whose target is an existing session (session or subagent). New-session job A job whose target is new: each fire creates a root session from the job's template.

docs.title: 3. The job
docs.text:
{
  "id": "k3v9q2xa",
  "name": "Nightly dependency check",
  "prompt": "Check for outdated dependencies and open a summary.",
  "schedule": { "cron": "0 3 * * *" },
  "max_runs": "unlimited",
  "target": { "new": { "agent": "builder", "project": "cookie-agent", "...": "..." } },
  "delivery": null,
  "permission_mode": "auto_approve_n",
  "max_consecutive_failures": null,
  "enabled": true,
  "created_by": { "agent": { "agent": "default", "session": "…" } },
  "created_at": "2026-10-22T18:00:00Z"
}
  • id: eight lowercase letters and digits, unique among the daemon's jobs, assigned by the daemon.
  • name: optional, at most 80 characters, shown in lists and run titles. Without one, lists show the start of the prompt.
  • prompt: 1 to 32 KiB of text.
  • schedule: one of:
  • {"cron": "<expr>"}: five fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week), with *, lists, ranges, and steps; day of month and day of week combine with OR, as in Vixie cron. Evaluated in the host's local time zone. An expression with no next match (0 0 30 2 *) is refused.
  • {"in": "<duration>"} on create and update: a whole number with s, m, h, or d, from 1s to 365d. The daemon turns it into {"at": "<RFC 3339 time>"} at once and stores that; it fires once.
  • max_runs: cron schedules only: a whole number from 1, or "unlimited". Default 1, so a job fires once unless told otherwise. A job that has run max_runs times:
  • created by an agent: is deleted;
  • created by you: stays, disabled with the reason "finished", until you delete or re-arm it.
  • target: one of:
  • {"session": "<session id>"}: a root session;
  • {"subagent": "<session id>"}: a delegated session;
  • {"new": <template>}, section 3.1.
  • delivery: steer or queue for in-session jobs, default queue; absent for new-session jobs.
  • permission_mode: new-session jobs only. Default auto_approve_n. Only you can set it (section 7); an agent's create or update cannot name it.
  • max_consecutive_failures: optional override of the config value.
  • enabled, and when disabled a disabled_reason: finished, failed <n> times in a row, or disabled by <user or agent>.
  • created_by: user, or {"agent": {agent, session}}.

docs.title: 3.1 The new-session template
docs.text:
Field Meaning When an agent creates the job When you create it agent The agent, and optionally its preset Any agent; default the creating run's agent Any; default the current session's model A model selection Not settable: the agent's own model chain Optional pin permission_rules Rules added to the run, as a session overlay Any Any runtimes, global, cwd Attachments, as session.create takes them Default the creating session's Default the current session's, or the project's project The project the run sessions belong to Default the creating session's Default the current session's

A template is checked when it is saved, as session.create would check it (the agent exists and is enabled, the runtimes are known), and again at each fire.

docs.title: 3.2 Job state
docs.text:
The daemon keeps, per job:

  • next_fire: the next due time, or none for a disabled or finished job;
  • runs: fires that were delivered or started a session, counted against max_runs (skips do not count);
  • consecutive_failures;
  • last_fire;
  • the run history: the last [cron] history fires (default 20), oldest dropped first. Each entry has:
  • the scheduled time and the actual fire time;
  • the session it went to (the new session for a new-session job) and the run it started or steered into;
  • the outcome: delivered, skipped with a reason (previous fire not delivered, previous run still running, daemon was down, interrupted), or failed with the error;
  • for a run the fire started or that it steered into, how that run ended (completed, failed, cancelled) and when.

docs.title: 4.1 The scheduler
docs.text:
• One scheduler task in the daemon, started and stopped like the residency janitor. It sleeps until the earliest next_fire or until jobs change, and fires every due job.
  • Exactly once. A fire is keyed by job id and scheduled time. Before it delivers, the daemon writes the fire to the job's history; a restart that finds a fire written but neither delivered nor started records it as skipped (interrupted).
  • Missed fires. At start, a job whose next_fire has passed gets one history entry, skipped (daemon was down), naming the first missed time and how many fires were missed, and next_fire moves to the next future match. A one-shot that passed is finished the same way.
  • The kill switch: [cron] enabled = false stops firing; jobs, RPCs, and tools keep working.

docs.title: 4.2 In-session fires
docs.text:
• The prompt arrives through the same producer path subagent reports use, so it is persisted, survives restarts, and is delivered exactly once:
  • queue: the session's next run starts with it when the session is idle, or after the current turn when it is busy;
  • steer: into the current turn when one is running; on an idle session it starts a run.
  • It runs with the session's current agent, model, and permission mode.
  • The model sees it marked as a scheduled job, never as the user:
<scheduled_job id="k3v9q2xa" name="Nightly dependency check" fired_at="2026-10-23T03:00:00+02:00">
Check for outdated dependencies and open a summary.
</scheduled_job>

A fire is not user input: it never answers an approval and never counts as consent. - Skipped while the job's previous fire is still undelivered. - A fire into a subagent's session wakes it like any producer message; its turn reports to its parent as every subagent turn does. - A fire into a session that has paged out reloads it.

docs.title: 4.3 New-session fires
docs.text:
• Each fire creates a root session from the template, in the template's project, with the job's permission mode and the template's rules as its overlay, and submits the prompt (marked as in section 4.2) as its first input.
  • Title: <name, or the prompt's start> · <local time of the fire>.
  • The session records its job: SessionMeta::cron = {job_id, fired_at}, so clients can mark and filter run sessions. The session is otherwise ordinary; it stays when the job is deleted.
  • A new-session job's agent must be one that can run as a root (primary or all mode). A subagent-mode agent reaches a job only through an in-session job targeting a subagent's session.
  • Skipped while the job's previous run session is still running.

docs.title: 4.4 Failures and finishing
docs.text:
• A failure is a run the fire started that ends failed, or a fire that cannot start: the agent is missing or disabled, no model is available, a runtime is offline, or session creation fails.
  • A fire's outcome is the run its prompt lands in. Steering into a busy turn is not a failure: the fire succeeds or fails with the turn it joined. A queued fire succeeds or fails with the run that takes it. While that prompt is still waiting, a new fire is skipped (section 4.2), so its outcome is the earlier prompt's.
  • A run that completes resets consecutive_failures to 0. A cancelled run and a skip change nothing.
  • At max_consecutive_failures the job is disabled with the reason. Enabling it again resets the count.

docs.title: 5. Waiting and residency
docs.text:
• Waiting. A session with an enabled in-session job that has a next fire time lists a new WaitingOn::ScheduledJob. It plugs into live_waiting_kinds (background tools section 12), so a subagent with such a job keeps its parent waiting, up the tree. Disabled and finished jobs count for nothing.
  • Residency. A job never keeps a session in memory (background tools section 13); the fire reloads it. The jobs live in the cron store, not in the session.

docs.title: 6. Deleting
docs.text:
• Deleting a session deletes the jobs that target it or any session in its tree.
  • Deleting a project deletes its sessions, so their jobs go too. New-session jobs whose template names the project are deleted as well.
  • A job's run sessions are ordinary sessions: deleting the job keeps them.

docs.title: 7. Permissions
docs.text:
• The action: cron. Its resource is the target kind of the job a call touches: session, subagent, or new. One action covers listing, creating, editing, enabling and disabling, and deleting.
  • Defaults (each applies only when the agent document has no cron key):
Run Default Root, any non-internal agent cron: allow Delegated none: the tools are hidden Internal none
  • What a call checks:
  • create: the new job's target kind;
  • update: the job's current and, when it changes, new target kind;
  • delete, enable, disable: the job's target kind;
  • list: shows only jobs whose target kind the rules allow or ask for.
  • Which sessions an agent may target: its own session, or one of its subagents' sessions (any session below it in its tree). Anything else is refused whatever the rules say. You can target any session.
  • Permission mode: the tools have no permission-mode parameter. Only a client (crons.create, crons.update) can set it.

docs.title: 8. Model tools
docs.text:
The cron provider, builtin.cron, offers five tools, each gated by cron:

Tool Arguments Result cron_create prompt, schedule ({cron} or {in}), max_runs?, name?, target? ("self", the default; a session handle; or {new: {agent?, permission_rules?, runtimes?, project?}}), delivery? The job: id, next fire time in local time and UTC cron_list target? (a kind, to filter) Each job the rules let it see: id, name, schedule, next fire, target, enabled, the last fire's outcome cron_update id, any field of cron_create, enabled? The updated job cron_delete id Confirmation cron_run id, background? Runs the job now as a delegated subagent of the caller (section 8.2)
  • target (simplified 2026-10-22) defaults to "self" when omitted (decided 2026-10-23). It is "self" (the calling session), a session handle as delegate_subagent names subagents, or {new: …}. A handle that is not a session below the caller is refused in the tool result. The permission resource still comes from the session: session for a root, subagent for a delegated session, so "self" from a subagent is subagent.
  • Descriptions say: schedules are in the host's local time; a fire is marked as a scheduled job; prefer updating a job to creating a near duplicate; max_runs defaults to 1, and "unlimited" runs until deleted.

docs.title: 8.1 list_agents
docs.text:
A tool of the global runtime (provider builtin.agents), so a model picking an agent for a delegation or a new-session job sees what each agent is and which permissions it starts with.

  • Visibility: offered exactly when the run is offered delegate_subagent or any cron tool. It has no permission action of its own, as it reveals nothing the caller could not use.
  • Arguments: for?: delegate or cron, to list only the agents that use allows. Without it, both.
  • Which agents:
  • for delegate: the run's delegation targets (enabled subagent and all agents its delegate rules allow), at its remaining depth;
  • for cron: every enabled primary or all agent, the ones a new-session job may run (amended 2026-10-23; it first listed every non-internal agent, subagent ones included, which cron_create refuses).
  • Each agent: its id, description, mode, presets, the models of its default chain (provider/model and variant), and its permission rules as a run of it would have them: each key its document declares in full, with ${agent_id} written as the agent's ID, then one defaults: line naming the actions it names no key for, whose rules are the daemon's defaults. Memory and cron defaults are those of a root run, the delegated ones for a delegation; an agent usable for both shows each block, with its own defaults: line, when they differ.
  • After the agents, once per result: the defaults section, generated from the default-rule functions themselves, listing the defaults for a root run and for a subagent (only the kinds the listed agents need), the ones only some modes get, that internal agents get none, and what ${session_machine}, ${session_project}, and ${workspace_dir} stand for. The result ends with Actions not listed are denied.
  • Example result:
builder (primary) — Primary agent for building features and implementing code changes directly.
  models: deepseek/deepseek-flash (high)
  usable for: cron
  permissions:
    read: allow
    write: ${workspace_dir}/* allow; * ask
    bash: allow
    webfetch: allow
    mcp: my_chrome_* allow
    defaults: list_runtimes, memory, memory_write, cron

Defaults (for actions an agent document names no key for):
  as a root run:
    list_runtimes: allow
    mcp: ask
    memory: allow
    memory_write: user://* allow; agent://<agent id> allow; machine://${session_machine}/* allow; project://${session_project}/* allow
    cron: allow
  Internal agents get none.
  Variables: ${session_machine} is each machine the session's attachments run on; ${session_project} is the session's project; ${workspace_dir} is the session's workspace.

Actions not listed are denied.

docs.title: 8.2 cron_run
docs.text:
Added 2026-10-22. An agent runs a job now the way it delegates:

  • A delegated subagent of the caller. For a new-session job, the child session uses the job's template (agent, permission rules, attachments) and the prompt as its first input, under the caller's session, not as a new root.
  • Foreground or background, like delegate_subagent: foreground waits and returns the result; background returns the child's handle at once, and the caller reads the result with get_subagent_result or receives the usual background report.
  • The child counts against the caller's delegation depth and its resident subagents, like any delegated child.
  • The job's agent need not be a delegation target. A new-session job's agent may be primary-only; cron_run is the one exception to "only subagent and all agents are delegated to", since the job already names the agent (decided 2026-10-22).
  • An in-session job fires into its target session, exactly as a scheduled fire would (section 4.2), with its steer or queue; no child is created.
  • In the job's state: a run-now is recorded in the job's history as run now, but counts toward neither max_runs nor the failure count. The same holds for crons.run.

docs.title: 9. Client protocol
docs.text:
• RPCs:
  • crons.list → every job with its state and history;
  • crons.create, crons.update (any field, permission_mode included), crons.delete;
  • crons.run: fire a job now, as a scheduled fire would (a new root session for a new-session job). It is recorded in the history as run now, counts toward neither max_runs nor the failure count, and moves nothing else;
  • crons.changed: notification, empty, coalesced like projects.changed.
  • Additions: SessionMeta::cron, WaitingOn::ScheduledJob (an open enum), the RPCs above.
  • Delivery's owner. ProducerOwner is a closed enum, so a new variant would be a major bump. The implementation must find an additive encoding, for example an existing owner shape or a new optional field, and record its choice.
  • Client protocol minor, plugin protocol minor (plugins see events and SessionMeta). Runtime protocol and history format unchanged.

docs.title: 10. Configuration
docs.text:
[cron]
enabled = true                 # false stops firing; jobs stay
max_consecutive_failures = 3   # a job can override it
history = 20                   # fires kept per job

docs.title: 11. Storage
docs.text:
• <data_root>/crons.json, one versioned file (version: 1), written atomically like machines.json (temporary file, sync, rename) under the daemon's state lock, with a watch channel for crons.changed.
  • Unknown fields are refused, as in machines.json.

docs.title: 12. Clients
docs.text:
• TUI:
  • /cron opens a panel: jobs with name, schedule (and its plain reading, such as "every day at 03:00"), next fire, target, and last outcome; the selected job's details and history; actions to create, edit, enable or disable, run now, and delete. Every action is also a button with its own hover.
  • In the command panel, /cron creates a job targeting the current session.
  • Run sessions show a clock mark in the session list.
  • Web:
  • a Cron view behind a new icon in the left rail, with the same list, details, history, and actions;
  • the ⋮ menu's "Schedule a prompt" creates a job for the current session;
  • run sessions show a clock mark in the session list, linking to their job.
  • CLI: cookie cron list | show <id> | create | edit <id> | rm <id> | enable <id> | disable <id> | run <id>, through the daemon like cookie memory, with the token inline (--token <token>) for a remote daemon.

docs.title: 13. Tests
docs.text:
• Schedules: cron parsing and next-match boundaries with explicit times (month ends, Vixie OR, DST changes in an explicit zone), in units and limits, refused expressions.
  • Firing: queue and steer into idle and busy sessions; the <scheduled_job> marking; exactly-once across a restart between the history write and delivery; a missed fire recorded as skipped (daemon was down) with no catch-up; skips on an undelivered fire and on a still running new-session run; a paged-out target reloaded by its fire.
  • New sessions: template defaults from the creating session; the permission mode auto_approve_n unless a client set another; an agent's call cannot set the mode; SessionMeta::cron; a subagent-mode agent as a job's agent.
  • Failures: the count across failures with skips between them, reset on completion, unchanged on cancel, disable at the threshold with a per-job override.
  • list_agents: offered with delegate_subagent or a cron tool and never otherwise; the agents per use; rules marked document or default, with root and delegated defaults where they differ.
  • Permissions: root default, hidden for delegated runs without a key, target kinds checked on create, update and delete, list filtered, targets outside the caller's subtree refused.
  • Waiting: a subagent's job keeps the parent waiting; disabling it releases the parent.
  • Deleting: session and project deletion take their jobs.
  • Clients: TUI and web panels, the clock mark, cookie cron.

docs.title: 14. Phases
docs.text:
1. Engine and protocol: the store, scheduler, in-session and new-session firing, failures, waiting, permissions and the tools, list_agents, the RPCs and notification, config.
  2. Clients: TUI, web, CLI.
  3. Docs: a scheduling guide, the permissions and configuration pages, the protocol changelog.

docs.title: 15. Open questions
docs.text: None.

docs.title: 16.1 Phase 1: engine and protocol (2026-10-23)
docs.text:
Landed: the store, the scheduler with exactly-once fires, missed-fire and interrupted-fire records, and the kill switch; in-session fires (queue and steer, the <scheduled_job> marking, the skip while undelivered); new-session fires (the template, auto_approve_n by default, SessionMeta::cron, the title, the skip while the previous run runs); failure counting and auto-disable; max_runs; deletion with sessions and projects; WaitingOn::ScheduledJob and the parent's wait; the cron permission with its root default and hard limits; the five tools and list_agents; crons.list/create/update/delete/run and crons.changed; and [cron]. Client protocol 1.15.0, plugin protocol 1.7.0; the runtime protocol and history format 1 are unchanged. The TUI, web, and CLI only compile against it; their UI is phase 2.

Where it is:

  • Wire types: crates/protocol/src/cron.rs (CronJob, CronSchedule, CronTarget, CronTemplate, CronFire, the params and results, SessionCron), CronJobId in identity.rs, WaitingOn::ScheduledJob and SessionMeta::cron in event.rs, PermissionAction::CRON in agent.rs, the cron_* error codes in errors.rs.
  • Store and schedules: crates/engine/src/crons.rs (CronStore, crons.json) and crates/engine/src/crons/schedule.rs (the five-field parser and the delays). No dependency was added: the parser is about 250 lines over jiff, which the engine already uses.
  • Requests: crates/engine/src/runtime/cron_api.rs; firing: runtime/cron_fire.rs (scheduler, fires, runs now, start-up reconciliation, run outcomes); cron_run: runtime/cron_run.rs.
  • Tools: crates/engine/src/cron_tools.rs (builtin.cron) and crates/engine/src/agents_tool.rs (builtin.agents). Both are providers of the global runtime bound to the engine like the memory tools and list_runtimes, so they reach a session only with global attached.
  • Defaults: cron_default_rules in crates/engine/src/permissions.rs, beside memory_default_rules; run_default_rules gathers every default.
  • Daemon: the routes in crates/server/src/service/routes.rs, the notification in runtime_notifications.rs, the error mapping in crates/server/src/rpc.rs; [cron] in crates/config/src/runtime.rs.

Decisions taken where the spec left room, and deviations:

  • Delivery's owner (section 9). A fire's prompt is a producer message owned by ProducerOwner::External { source: "cron:<job id>", name: "scheduled" }. ProducerOwner keeps its shape; ProducerSource already admits any lowercase kind, and cron is the daemon's own: every connection's source is plugin: or runtime:, so none can claim it. The engine accepts a cron: owner only without a connection epoch, keeps its short-lived registration through reconciliation, and counts it for nothing in live_waiting_kinds (the store adds scheduled_job). Older readers show it as an external producer named cron:<id> · scheduled.
  • SessionMeta::cron is folded from an optional cron member of session_created, which earlier readers ignore (an additive member, not a new event, so no older reader opens such a log render-only). A cron run's child session records it too.
  • The run session's title is committed with the session's creation as user_set, with the client rename ID cron:<job id>:<fired at>: a root session's only runless title change, and one that keeps automatic titles away. The user can rename it as usual.
  • The fire's key is <job id>:<scheduled time> for a scheduled fire and <job id>:now:<UUIDv7> for a run now; it is the producer idempotency key and identifies the history entry.
  • Exactly once. The claim (job enabled, next_fire equal to the scheduled time, no entry for that time) and the pending entry are written before delivery, under the store's lock: section 11's "state lock" is the memory lock (memory/.lock), which machines.json and the projects already take, and every change rereads the file under it. At start, a pending entry whose session holds a message with its owner and key becomes delivered (and counts toward max_runs); a run session that records the job and fire time but has no prompt gets the prompt then; anything else becomes skipped (interrupted).
  • Two daemons sharing a data root both read crons.json, and the claim under the memory lock makes each fire happen once. A daemon whose session store (working directory) lacks a target session fails that fire.
  • Missed fires are counted up to a million per entry; the entry's fired_at is the daemon's start. A fire made late while the daemon runs (a suspended host) fires once and moves to the next match after now, with no record of the matches in between.
  • The kill switch records each due fire as skipped with the reason firing_disabled, a value added to the open skip reasons, and moves the job on, so turning firing back on does not fire a backlog. Runs now (crons.run, cron_run) are explicit and ignore it.
  • Runs now obey the skips of scheduled fires (a run now of an in-session job whose previous prompt still waits is recorded as skipped, and crons.run returns no session_id). A run now never moves next_fire, runs, or the failure count; its run's end is still recorded.
  • Finishing. A job with no next fire after a fire, delivered, skipped, or failed, is finished: kept disabled as finished when you created it, deleted when an agent did. This is how a one-shot ends. A failed fire does not count toward max_runs, so a cron job keeps trying until it has delivered max_runs times or reaches the failure limit. Enabling a finished job resets its runs; enabling a one-shot whose time passed is refused until it gets a new schedule.
  • Outcomes. A fire's run is the run that admitted or consumed its prompt, recorded when that run ends. A message admitted to a run that is cancelled and later taken by another run keeps the first run's end. An interrupted run (a restart) counts for nothing, like a cancelled one. A run session that fails to start (the agent is gone, no model, a runtime is offline, creation fails) records the fire as failed with the error and counts a failure.
  • Schedules. Cron fields accept the three-letter month and day names and 7 for Sunday besides numbers. a/n runs from a to the field's end. A spring-forward gap fires at the instant it jumps to; a fall-back fold fires at the first occurrence only. An expression is refused when no month has one of its days (0 0 30 2 *); restricting the day of week too makes it reachable (Vixie OR). crons.create and crons.update also take {at}, which must be in the future; max_runs other than 1 with a one-shot schedule is refused.
  • Validation details. A name is trimmed, non-blank, at most 80 characters, without control characters; a prompt is non-blank and at most 32 KiB. delivery on a new-session job and permission_mode on an in-session job are refused. A new schedule or target, or enabling, computes next_fire from now. A template's runtimes must be known to the daemon (a template or a remembered dial-in runtime); they are started only at a fire.
  • Agents' requests. The tools never pass a mode or a model, and the engine refuses an agent's request that names either; an agent's update may keep a mode or a pin you set. created_by and disabled by name the calling run's agent and session.
  • Template defaults (section 3.1). An agent's {new: {}} takes the calling run's agent, the calling session's preset, its attachments as explicit runtimes and global (so a fire attaches what the session had when the job was made), and its project (a delegated session's root's). project may be given by name or ID.
  • Permissions. The resource is the target kind; cron_update that changes the kind is one call with two resources, the strictest deciding. cron_list declares no permission of its own: it is published only next to another cron tool and filters jobs by whether the rules allow or ask for their kind. A job's target sessions are checked only when the agent sets one: an agent may change or delete any job its rules allow.
  • list_agents is published exactly when the run's tools include delegate_subagent or a cron tool other than cron_list; its prepared operation names no permission. For a run offered the cron tools it lists every enabled primary or all agent of the run's preset. An agent usable for both shows its rules as a root run and as a subagent when they differ. As first landed it listed subagent agents for cron too and marked each default rule (default) in full; amended 2026-10-23 (section 8.1): only agents a job can run, default-only actions collapsed into one defaults: line per block, ${agent_id} expanded in an agent's own block, a defaults section generated from the default-rule functions (mode, memory, and cron defaults) after the agents, which also explains ${session_machine}, ${session_project}, and ${workspace_dir}, and a closing Actions not listed are denied.
  • cron_run of a new-session job goes through delegate_subagent's path: the call's template (rules, attachments, job) waits in DelegationRuntimeState::cron_runs by tool call ID while the child is admitted, which lets the job's agent through whatever the caller's delegation targets are (any agent but an internal one), uses the caller's delegation depth (or [delegation] max_depth when the caller delegates to nothing), attaches the template's runtimes, and writes the template's rules as the child's overlay with its creation. The child counts against depth and residency like any child. The model pin is not applied: the child takes the agent's own chain, as every delegated child does. The agent is resolved in the caller's preset. Recovery treats a pending cron_run like a pending delegate_subagent; a cron_run interrupted by a restart is not redelivered. get_subagent_result exists only for a caller that can delegate; a background cron_run's child still reports its turns. Its history entry is delivered with the child's session.
  • cron_run is background-capable, so stop_background is offered next to it.
  • Deletion. The jobs of every session a delete or a revert removes are deleted with it. A project's delete first deletes the new-session jobs naming it, then its sessions with their jobs.
  • crons.list also says whether the daemon is firing.
  • Corpora. No 1.15.0 corpus was recorded, as for 1.9.0 to 1.14.0.
  • Tests (crates/engine/src/runtime/tests/crons.rs) also cover a queue fire into a busy session, which waits unadmitted behind the turn and starts the next run, and a steer fire, which the running turn takes and whose outcome is that run's; and the prepared resources of each cron tool, cron_update across kinds checking both, with a rule that allows session and denies new refusing the change.

What phase 2 and 3 need: the TUI and web panels and the clock mark (from SessionMeta::cron and crons.list), cookie cron, the TUI's and web's labels for scheduled_job (the shared waiting_label already names it), and the scheduling guide and the permissions page. The protocol reference, changelog, tools reference, error reference, and the [cron] configuration page are up to date.

docs.title: 16.2 Phase 2: clients (2026-10-23)
docs.text:
Landed: the /cron panel in the TUI, the Scheduled prompts view in the web client, and cookie cron, each on a daemon of client protocol 1.15 or later only, and each refetching crons.list on crons.changed. No wire change.

  • Shared rules live in crates/client_state/src/cron.rs: daemon_has_crons (minor 15), a job's title (its name or the first 48 characters of its prompt's first line), schedule_reading and cron_reading (the plain reading, section 12), target, state, and outcome labels, detail_lines, and CronDraft, the job form as crons.create and crons.update take it. A form's schedule is a cron expression, in <delay>, or at <RFC 3339 time>; an edit sends only the members it changed, and one that changes nothing sends nothing.
  • Plain readings cover the shapes people write: one minute with a list of hours, */n minutes, */n hours, single days of the month, weekday lists and ranges, and named months, such as every Monday to Friday at 09:00 or on the 1st of every month at 08:00. Anything else (0 9-17 * * *) reads as cron <expression>. A cron schedule's reading adds its run limit (, once, , 4 runs); a one-shot reads once at <local time>. Cron times are not converted: they are the host's, which the forms say.
  • TUI (crates/tui/src/ui/app/cron_panel.rs): Modal::Cron lists the jobs with the selected job's details and history beneath; e/Enter, n, t, r, and d (with a y confirmation) edit, create, enable or disable, run now, and delete, each also a button (PointerTarget::CronRow, PointerTarget::CronAction). The TUI takes slash commands only from the command palette, so section 12's "/cron in the command panel creates a job" is the palette entry /cron new, listed while a session is on screen (not a read-only one); /cron opens the panel. The form is a key: value text with the prompt after ---, edited in $VISUAL or $EDITOR through the /memory handoff; a form the daemon refuses is kept to edit again. Run sessions show 🕒 in the session picker, since ⏰ already marks waiting sessions.
  • Web (crates/web/src/views/cron.rs, workspace/cron.rs, cron.rs): the rail's clock icon opens Scheduled prompts, one column with a job's details, history, and actions expanding under its row, so it serves phones without another layer (every target at least 44 px). The ⋮ menu's "Schedule a prompt" opens the form for the open session, as a subagent target in a delegated one. The form reads the schedule live under its field. Times are the browser's, from Date.getTimezoneOffset at each instant, since jiff's system zone is unavailable in the page. A run session's clock mark before its title says which job started it and opens it.
  • New-session template from a client: the agent and preset of the current session's selection (else the preset's first root agent), its project (a delegated session's root's), and no runtimes, so a fire attaches what session.create would; the TUI also sets cwd to its own directory. A model pin and a permission mode are the user's to add.
  • cookie cron (crates/cookie_agent/src/cron_command.rs): create takes --session (root or delegated, read from session.get) or --agent for a new session per fire, with --model, --permission-mode, and --project for the latter; edit takes the same options and applies them to the job's form, so it is scriptable rather than an editor session. list prints two lines per job, show the details, prompt, and history.

docs.title: 16.3 Phase 3: docs (2026-10-23)
docs.text: Scheduling prompts is the user guide, under Working with sessions. The cron action, its resources, defaults, hard limits, and list_agents are in Cron permissions and on the Permissions concept page; the clients' pages have a Scheduled prompts section each and cookie cron its reference.

docs.title: Default models, the starter kit, and onboarding
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-23); see implementation notes.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
• Default models. Two configuration fields, default_model and small_model, that agent documents reach as ${default_model} and ${small_model}, so one edit retargets every agent that uses them.
  • The starter kit. A default config.toml and default agent documents, shipped with each release as a downloadable asset, not bundled in the binary.
  • Onboarding. cookie onboard (or the TUI or web client) connects a provider, sets the models, and can install the kit; clients offer it while the daemon's configuration is not set up.

Decided 2026-10-23:

  • ${default_model} and ${small_model} carry a model and its variant together, as ${parent_model} carries the parent's; any agent may use them.
  • A variant written beside ${default_model}, ${small_model}, or ${parent_model} overrides the variant it carries (new for ${parent_model}, which refused one).
  • A models entry may be a plain string: - ${default_model}.
  • The approval and title agents use ${small_model}, then ${parent_model}. Compaction stays on ${parent_model}, which keeps the session's prompt cache warm.
  • The built-in default agent uses ${default_model}.
  • The starter kit is a release asset; no GitHub Pages copy.
  • Whether the daemon is set up comes from its configuration, not a marker file (decided 2026-10-23): it is set up when the requirements below hold, and clients offer onboarding only while they do not.
  • Onboarding requires a connected provider, default_model, and small_model (decided 2026-10-23): it completes only once at least one model provider is connected and both fields name available models of the connected providers (they may name the same model). The kit stays optional.
  • Any client can onboard (decided 2026-10-23): everything onboarding does is a daemon RPC (section 8), so the TUI, the web client, cookie onboard, and any third-party client do it the same way, with no client-side file access and nothing that depends on the kind of client.
  • The kit's agents: primary, and the subagents explore and worker.

Out of scope: more model slots than these two, per-project default models, fetching the kit without being asked.

docs.title: 2. The two fields
docs.text:
# config.toml
default_model = { model = "anthropic/claude-opus-5-5", variant = "high" }
small_model   = "deepseek/deepseek-flash"      # a bare key: its default variant
  • Shape: a model key string, or a table { model, variant }. Both optional. Unknown keys in the table are errors, as everywhere in the configuration.
  • Validation: the model key must parse; whether the model is available is a runtime matter (section 3), so a configured model whose provider is disconnected does not fail the load.
  • Clients: /config, the web configuration view, and cookie config show and set both, with model pickers.

docs.title: 3. The variables in agent documents
docs.text:
models:
  - ${default_model}                               # model and variant from config
  - { model: "${small_model}", variant: "max" }    # the variant overridden
  - deepseek/deepseek-flash                        # a plain model key
  • Where: any models entry of any agent document, built-in or authored. ${parent_model} stays limited to internal agents, as today.
  • Resolution: when the agent registry compiles (at start and on every configuration reload), so changing a field retargets every agent that uses it without touching documents.
  • Variants: an entry's variant overrides the variable's; without one the variable's variant applies, and a variable without a variant means the model's default variant. The same now holds for ${parent_model}.
  • Unset: an entry naming an unset variable is skipped, with a configuration diagnostic naming the field ("small_model is not set"). Later entries still apply. An agent with no entry left is unavailable, and its reason names the field to set.
  • Duplicates: the existing rule against duplicate entries compares the entries as written, so ${default_model} and the key it currently names may both appear.

docs.title: 4. Plain-string entries
docs.text:
• A models entry may be a string instead of a mapping; the string is the entry's model, with no variant override. Strings and mappings mix freely.
  • YAML reads - ${default_model} as a string without quotes; only an entry starting with { or [ needs them.
  • Any other entry shape (a number, a mapping with unknown keys) stays an error.

docs.title: 5. Built-in agents
docs.text:
Agent models default (built in, when no document replaces it) ${default_model}, then the first available model as today approval (internal) ${small_model}, then ${parent_model} title (internal) ${small_model}, then ${parent_model} compaction (internal) ${parent_model} (unchanged)
  • For an ACP session, which has no model of its own, the approval reviewer runs on ${small_model}; without it, ask requests go to the user as now.

docs.title: 6. The starter kit
docs.text:
• Source: defaults/ in the repository:
defaults/
  config.toml        # commented: default_model, small_model, [server], [memory], [cron], an MCP example
  agents/primary.md  # mode primary, models: [${default_model}]
  agents/explore.md  # mode subagent, read-only exploring, models: [${default_model}] (changed 2026-10-24: `${small_model}` is left to the approval and title agents)
  agents/worker.md   # mode subagent, does a delegated task, models: [${default_model}]
  manifest.json      # kit version, the cookie version it was built for, each file's sha256
                     # skills are not in the kit (section 13)
  • Agents: primary is the root agent (the daemon already falls back to an agent named primary); it may delegate to explore and worker. explore reads and searches and never writes; worker carries out a task with the same tools as primary. Permissions (decided 2026-10-23): primary allows read, write, webfetch, skill, memory with the related memory_write rules (user://*, agent://${agent_id}, machine://${session_machine}/*, project://${session_project}/*), and delegate to explore and worker; bash asks except read-only commands (ls *, cat *, rg *, git status*, git diff*, git log*, …); mcp asks, cron and list_runtimes as their defaults. worker has primary's read, write, and bash rules; explore stays read-only. Every permission is written explicitly, the defaults included, each line with a YAML comment saying whether it equals the daemon's default and what the default would be without the key, and why a non-default line is there.
  • Skills (decided 2026-10-23, then moved by section 13): the kit first carried two skills, customize-cookie-agent (pointers for an agent asked to change cookie itself: where things live, the cookie commands to prefer over editing files, and the docs of each topic) and add-cookie-runtime (adding a machine as a runtime over ssh or by dialing in, short and pointing at the docs, with what to ask the user first). Both are now official skills (section 13), kept honest by cookie skills check.
  • Release asset: the release workflow packs defaults/ as cookie-agent-defaults.tar.gz and uploads it with the binaries, as it does cookie-agent-web.tar.gz. Prereleases carry it too.
  • Kept valid: a test loads every kit file with the build's own configuration and agent parsers (strict), so a release cannot ship defaults its binary rejects.

docs.title: 7. cookie onboard (one client of the onboarding API)
docs.text:
cookie onboard [--from <file>] [--diff] [--yes]
               [--default-model <key[:variant]>] [--small-model <key[:variant]>]
               [--url <url>] [--token <token>]
  • Where the kit comes from: the release asset of the binary's own version; when the binary is not a release build, or its release has no kit, the latest release's. --from takes a local archive instead. The manifest's hashes are checked before anything is written.
  • Installing: cookie onboard itself writes nothing: it calls the daemon's onboarding API (section 8), which writes under the daemon's ~/.cookie-agent, local or remote. A file that does not exist is written; one that exists and differs is left alone and the kit's version is written beside it as <name>.new; an identical one is skipped. --diff prints what would change and writes nothing.
  • Steps: connect a provider when none is connected (the existing provider.connect, with its auth methods), choose default_model from the connected providers' available models, then small_model the same way (both required), then optionally install the kit. The flags answer the questions; with --yes and no --default-model or --small-model it refuses rather than guess.
  • Running it again on a set-up daemon works: it shows the current provider and models, and offers the kit again.

docs.title: 8. The daemon's onboarding API
docs.text:
Client protocol minor, additive. These calls are the only way onboarding happens: every client uses them, the daemon does the work (downloading, checking hashes, writing files and configuration), and it never branches on the kind of client asking.

  • onboarding.get → { ready, missing, providers_connected, default_model?, small_model? }, computed from the live configuration and runtime: ready is missing being empty, and missing lists provider (no provider connected), default_model, and small_model (unset, or naming a model no connected provider offers). Nothing is stored for it, so setting things up by hand (config.apply, provider.connect, editing config.toml) counts just the same, and disconnecting the last provider makes the daemon not ready again. The kit is not part of readiness.
  • onboarding.preview { source? } → the kit's version and, per file, what installing would do (write, skip as identical, write_new beside a changed file) with a diff for changed files. source is release (default: the binary's version, else the latest release) or an uploaded archive (an upload lease, as attachments use). It downloads and checks the kit but writes nothing; the daemon keeps it briefly for the run that follows.
  • onboarding.run { install_kit, source?, default_model?, small_model? } → the files written, skipped, and written as .new, and the configuration fields set. Model values use the configuration's shapes and are checked like config.apply. It refuses (error onboarding_incomplete, naming what is missing) when, after applying its own fields, no provider is connected or default_model or small_model does not name an available model; nothing is written then, kit included.
  • Providers are connected with the existing provider.connect and provider.disconnect; onboarding adds no provider call of its own.
  • No dismiss call: there is nothing on the daemon to dismiss. A client may remember "not now" locally (the browser's storage, the TUI's own state) and ask again later; the daemon's answer stays what its configuration says.
  • onboarding.changed notification whenever onboarding.get's answer would change: a configuration reload or apply, a provider connected or disconnected, or a model becoming available or not.
  • The models to choose from come from the existing model listing, so a client needs nothing onboarding-specific for the pickers.

docs.title: 9. Clients
docs.text:
Every client walks the same four steps, using only the RPCs of section 8 and provider.connect; each step starts from what is already configured.

  1. Provider (required while none is connected): the known providers, the connected ones marked with their count of available models; choosing one offers its auth methods (API key, browser login) and connects it, errors shown in place with a retry. Several may be connected.
  2. Default model (required): a searchable list of the connected providers' available models, grouped by provider, with context size and price where the catalog has them; choosing one offers its variants, preselecting the model's own default variant.
  3. Small model (required): the same list, with no suggestion (decided 2026-10-23). Its variant picker preselects the model's first listed variant: models list their variants in increasing effort, so the first is the cheapest, and no variant names are hard-coded. The same model as the default is allowed.
  4. Starter kit (optional): onboarding.preview per file, new, same as yours (skipped), or differs → written as .new with a diff on request; install, skip, or use a downloaded archive.

Finish calls onboarding.run; it is disabled, with the reason, while missing is not empty. The summary lists the files and settings written and offers a first session on primary.

  • cookie onboard: the steps as numbered questions in the terminal (section 7), with / to search lists and hidden key entry.
  • TUI: on connecting to a daemon that is not ready, a notice line offers "Set up" or "Not now" (remembered for the machine); /onboard opens it any time. The panel shows the four steps as tabs with a check on each done step, reusing the provider connect panel and the model picker; every clickable has its hover (AGENTS.md).
  • Web: a first-run sheet with a four-step stepper, Back and Next, and "Not now" (remembered in the browser); Settings has "Set up Cookie" to reopen it. Provider cards reuse the Settings connect forms (browser logins use the page as the redirect), model steps a searchable list with variant chips, the kit step status badges with expandable diffs and "Use a downloaded kit…". Full screen with touch-sized controls on a phone. Finish ends on "Start your first session", a new-session draft.
  • Every connected client follows onboarding.changed: finishing in one tab closes the sheet in the others.

docs.title: 10. Tests
docs.text:
• Configuration: both field shapes, unknown keys, defaults absent.
  • Variables: resolution, variant overrides for all three variables, unset skipping with diagnostics, an agent left with no entry, string entries, reload retargeting.
  • Built-ins: the approval and title chains, compaction unchanged, the default agent.
  • Kit: every file loads with the build's parsers; the manifest's hashes.
  • Onboarding: install into an empty root, .new beside a changed file, identical files skipped, --diff, hash mismatch refused, ready following the configuration (set up by hand, a provider disconnected, a model gone), onboarding.changed, onboarding.run refused without a provider or an available default_model or small_model (and writing nothing), missing in onboarding.get, onboarding.get/preview/run from a plain protocol client (no TUI or web code), an uploaded archive as the source, the TUI notice, the web sheet.

docs.title: 11. Phases
docs.text:
1. Engine and configuration: the fields, variables, string entries, built-ins.
  2. The kit and the release asset.
  3. Onboarding: the RPCs, cookie onboard, the TUI and web offers.
  4. Docs: the configuration reference, the agents page, a getting-started page built around cookie onboard.

docs.title: 12. Open questions
docs.text: None.

docs.title: 13. Addendum 2026-10-23: official skills kept up to date
docs.text:
Status: implemented (2026-10-23); see the implementation notes.

The starter kit is installed once, so skills added in later releases would never reach a daemon that already onboarded. Skills are cookie's own instructions about cookie; agent documents and config.toml are the user's. So skills leave the kit and are fetched from a versionless official source that every daemon keeps current.

Decided 2026-10-23:

  • A repository, cookie-agent/skills, served by GitHub Pages at https://cookie-agent.github.io/skills/, holds the official skills; its URL carries no version.
  • Daemons use them by default ([skills] official = true) and refresh them at start and then daily.
  • The kit keeps config.toml and the agent documents; its skills (customize-cookie-agent and the runtime setup skill) move to the repository.

docs.title: 13.1 The source
docs.text:
• index.json: { "version": 1, "skills": [ { "name", "version", "requires_cookie", "files": [ { "path", "sha256" } ] } ] }. requires_cookie is a semver range (">=0.4.0") matched against the daemon's own version.
  • <name>/SKILL.md and any other files a skill lists.
  • CI in the repository runs the latest release's cookie skills check on every push and nightly: each skill parses, names only cookie subcommands that exist, and links only to documentation pages that exist (/doc/dev/ paths until a stable release carries the current docs, then /doc/latest/). A failing skill does not publish.

docs.title: 13.2 The daemon
docs.text:
• Managed skills live in <data_root>/official_skills/<name>/ (~/.cookie-agent/official_skills/ by default), written only by the daemon.
  • Refresh: at start and then every 24 hours; the index first, then the files whose hashes changed, each checked against the index before it replaces the cached copy. Skills the index no longer lists, or whose requires_cookie this version does not satisfy, are removed from the official skills folder. Network failures keep the cached copies and are reported as a configuration diagnostic; offline daemons keep working.
  • Discovery: the official skills folder is one more skill root with the lowest precedence: a user or project skill of the same name wins.
  • Configuration: [skills] official = true (default) or false, which stops refreshing and leaves the official skills folder unused.
  • Trust: the source URL is fixed to the official one, over HTTPS, with every file hash-checked. Skills grant no tools; permission rules still decide every call.

docs.title: 13.3 Commands and clients
docs.text:
• cookie skills update refreshes now (through the daemon); cookie skills list shows each skill with its origin (user, project, official) and, for official ones, its version.
  • cookie skills check <dir> validates skills: parsing, cookie subcommands, documentation links (used by the repository's CI and by anyone writing skills).
  • Clients' skill lists mark official skills.
  • Onboarding needs no step for them: they are on by default.

docs.title: 13.4 Tests
docs.text: The refresh against a local fixture server (new, changed, removed, a hash mismatch refused, a requires_cookie range not met, offline with a cache), precedence against a user skill of the same name, official = false, cookie skills check passing and failing cases.

docs.title: 14. Implementation notes
docs.text:
Implemented 2026-10-23 in four phases on one branch.

Versions. Client protocol 1.22.0, plugin protocol 1.10.0 (the events carry the ${parent_model} variant), runtime protocol 1.8.0 (the skill source official), history format unchanged: the frozen ParentModel fallback gained an optional variant that is omitted when absent, so earlier logs read as before.

Engine and configuration.

  • default_model and small_model are ConfiguredModel { model, variant } on EngineConfig, decoded from a key string or a strict table; the top-level key allowlist names both.
  • AgentModelRef has DefaultModel and SmallModel; a models entry deserializes from a string or a strict mapping. ${parent_model} takes a variant override (still internal-only); the override is frozen into run_started and applied by binding the parent's model in that variant, skipping the entry when the variant is not available.
  • An entry naming an unset field is skipped; the agent lists the field in AgentDescriptor.unset_models, and an authored agent reports it in ConfigStatus.diagnostics (which landed meanwhile for ACP agents): "agent x skips a models entry: small_model is not set", or "has no model" when nothing is left. Built-in agents report no diagnostic, since their fallback to ${parent_model} is by design.
  • Deviation: a resolved chain keeps the first entry per model. The protocol refuses a chain naming one model twice, so ${default_model} followed by the key it names resolves to one entry rather than two.
  • The built-in default agent resolves ${default_model} (when set and available), then the first available model when that is another model. Its permissions are unchanged and differ from the kit's primary: it asks before writes, commands, and delegation and has no webfetch.

The kit and the release.

  • defaults/ holds config.toml, the three agents, and manifest.json (kit_version and each file's SHA-256; scripts/pack-defaults.sh --update-manifest refreshes the hashes). The release workflow's build-web job packs it with scripts/pack-defaults.sh <tag>, which checks the hashes and writes cookie_version into the archive's manifest, and uploads cookie-agent-defaults.tar.gz with the other artifacts, prereleases included.
  • Kit files are configuration documents only (config.toml, agents/…); a skill path in a kit is refused. The engine reads the archive in memory (gzip plus a small ustar/pax reader, no new dependency), refuses unlisted, missing, unsafe, or mismatched files, and loads the kit alone with this build's configuration and agent parsers before comparing it with the user root.
  • Tests load defaults/ with those parsers, check its manifest, load config.toml with every commented example uncommented, read a GNU tar archive packed by the script.

Onboarding.

  • The release source tries, in order: <releases>/download/v<version>/… (this build's release); the newest release in one unauthenticated page of the GitHub releases API (prereleases included, drafts skipped) whose tag's major.minor.patch is this build's version and which carries the kit, since nightlies are tagged v<version>-alpha.<n> while the crate version is a plain <version>; then <releases>/latest/download/…, the latest stable release. A rate limit or any other failure of the list moves on to the next step, and the list is not asked for again for a minute; a list over 4 MiB is a failure. When every step fails the kit is unavailable, with each step's reason. The base URL is injectable (Engine::set_releases_url; a non-GitHub base serves its list at <base>/api) and tests serve kits and lists from a local HTTP server. A downloaded kit is kept ten minutes for the run after a preview, then dropped.
  • Deviation: an uploaded archive travels inline, base64 in the source ({"type": "archive", "data": …}, at most 1 MiB), not through an upload lease: upload leases belong to a session's tree and accept only attachment media, while onboarding runs before any session exists.
  • onboarding.run edits the configuration under the configuration lock: new kit documents and the model fields go into one candidate tree, which is validated, checked for readiness against the current models, and only then written; .new files and skills follow. A refusal is onboarding_incomplete with missing; a kit that cannot be used is onboarding_kit_unavailable; a model value the configuration refuses is config_apply_refused, as for config.apply.
  • onboarding.changed is sent per connection after any runtime publication that changes the answer (configuration applies and reloads, provider changes, and catalog refreshes all publish one).
  • "Connected providers" are those offering at least one available model.
  • Readiness before a run is checked against the models compiled now; a run whose candidate configuration changes providers is not recompiled first, and its result reports the state after it applied.
  • cookie onboard reuses cookie connect's provider flow and the shared rules in client_state::onboarding; without --yes or --diff it needs a terminal.
  • TUI: while the daemon is not ready, a notice in the background bar's row (background calls take precedence) says what is missing, with Set up and Not now. Not now is kept in ~/.cookie-agent/tui-state.json until the missing set changes. /onboard opens a panel of four clickable step tabs with checks; step 1 opens the connect panel, steps 2 and 3 the model picker in an onboarding mode, step 4 the kit preview (d diff, i install, o a local archive path); f finishes. Four new pointer targets hover visibly. The kit preview is fetched on reaching its step.
  • Web: a first-run sheet (full screen with 44px targets on a phone, a dialog on wider windows) opens on connecting to a daemon that is not ready, unless Not now is stored (cookie.onboarding_not_now in localStorage; the page's origin is the daemon's, so it is per daemon). It reuses Settings' connect forms, closes in every tab when the daemon becomes ready, and Settings has "Set up Cookie". The browser suite's main daemon now sets both model fields so the sheet stays out of the other scenarios; a new scenario covers the sheet on an empty daemon. The kit step is not browser-tested, since previewing the release kit would reach GitHub. Deviation: the model lists show context size but no price: the catalog view's model descriptors carry none.
  • Deviation: /config, the web configuration view, and cookie config edit default_model and small_model as config.toml text (cookie config set default_model …); the model pickers are the onboarding panels', which run again on a set-up daemon.

Official skills (section 13).

  • The skills live in cookie-agent/skills (index.json, one <name>/SKILL.md each, scripts/update-index.py for the hashes, and a CI workflow that installs the latest release and runs cookie skills check . on every push and nightly, with the newest release, prereleases included). Both start at version 1.0.0 with requires_cookie = ">=0.4.0-alpha.0": the 0.3.0 nightlies have no fetcher.
  • The engine keeps them in <data_root>/official_skills/ with its record of what it keeps in .index.json there; entries starting with . are skipped by discovery. A refresh downloads a skill's changed files, checks every hash and that SKILL.md loads, and only then writes them (each through a temporary file and a rename), so a refused skill keeps its cached copy whole. requires_cookie takes comparators (>=, >, <=, <, =, a bare version, *) separated by commas or spaces, compared by plain semver precedence, pre-releases included (not Cargo's rule that a pre-release only matches a comparator with a pre-release on the same version): nightlies are tagged 0.4.0-alpha.<n>, below 0.4.0, so the skills ask for >=0.4.0-alpha.0. The daemon compares its own crate version, which is a plain 0.4.0 for nightlies and stable builds alike (the tag's pre-release is not in it). A range that does not read refuses the skill.
  • The refresh loop runs in the daemon binary beside the catalog's (at start, then every 24 hours, stopped with it). The source URL is fixed in release builds; tests call Engine::set_official_skills_url, and debug builds under the binary's test switch (COOKIE_AGENT_TEST_BUNDLED_CATALOG) stay off the network unless COOKIE_AGENT_TEST_OFFICIAL_SKILLS_URL names a source.
  • Beyond the spec: a refresh that changes the official skills reloads the global runtime's skills (user skills included) for new sessions, so a freshly started daemon offers them without a restart. official = false stops refreshing at once; whether the folder is offered follows at the next start, when skills load.
  • Protocol: the skill source official (client 1.22.0, runtime 1.8.0), an official skill's version on SkillDescriptor, skills.update, and skills.list without a session for the daemon's own skills (which cookie skills list uses; permission_effect is then ask and visible says whether the skill wins its name).
  • cookie skills check (decision): links are fetched from the published site by default, which the skills repository's CI uses; --docs <dir> checks them against a docs/site checkout instead, as the tests do. It also checks an index.json against the files beside it.
  • The TUI's skill picker labels official skills and its detail line shows official <version>; the web page's skill list shows the same badge.

docs.title: Deferred tools in cookie
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-27, in six phases; see section 14 for where the code differs). Builds on deferred tool loading in oven-sdk (implemented, oven-sdk b875054) and carries out the cookie-side decisions in its section 10.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
Any tool can be sent to the model deferred. On a model that loads tools natively, cookie sends the tools its deferral policy picks as deferred tools. It offers two loader tools, tool_search to find them and tool_load to load them, and tells the model which tools it can load. The policy starts with MCP and plugin tools (section 4). Everything else in this spec works for whatever the policy picks.

Today every MCP and plugin tool costs its full definition in every request. Adding or removing one rewrites the prompt cache from the tools onward, and on the user's gateway it is a thinking-binding 400 that native_replay_cut recovers from. Deferred tools stay out of the cached prefix (oven spec, section 3).

Decided 2026-10-27 (oven spec, section 10):

  1. No loader tools without native loading. A model whose capability is Unsupported gets every tool up front, and neither tool_search nor tool_load.
  2. The clients show provided and searchable tools apart.
  3. A failed MCP server is reconnected before a loaded tool is dropped.
  4. Deferral is tried on Anthropic-compatible endpoints, and falls back on rejection.
  5. The loadable set is announced by appending changes.
  6. MCP and plugin tools are always deferred where supported, with no threshold.
  7. There is an opt-out per server, per plugin, and per tool.
  8. Compaction folds loaded tools into the eager prefix: after an internal summary, and before an OpenAI native compaction.

Decided 2026-10-27, after the first draft:

  1. The loader tools appear only when a tool is deferred. A session with no deferred tool, for example one with no MCP servers or plugins, never sees it (section 4).
  2. Tools change only between rounds. The eager tools are fixed at a session's first request and again at each compaction. Between those points, a tool that joins is deferred, and an eager tool that leaves stays declared (section 8).
  3. Deferral is generic. One policy decides which tools are deferred. Everything else keys on whether a tool is deferred, never on where it came from: the loader tools, announcements, rounds, compaction, the record, and the clients. MCP and plugin tools are the policy's default today, and which tools are hidden is decided later (section 4).

Out of scope: - deciding which other tools to hide; the policy's default may widen later; - hosted search; - Kimi Code's /models declaration (kimi-for-coding uses the Anthropic adapter, so it is attempted; section 3).

docs.title: 2. The oven-sdk pin
docs.text:
Bump to oven-sdk b875054: core 0.8.0, anthropic 0.9.0, and the matching adapters. This is phase 1 and changes no behavior. It fixes what the new types break:

  • oven_capabilities (crates/models/src/manager/mod.rs, the OvenCapabilities literal) gains deferred_tools. Section 3 sets its value; phase 1 sets Unsupported.
  • The OpenAiCompatibleChatSettings literal (crates/models/src/compiler/executable.rs) gains deferred_tools, Unsupported for now.
  • Exhaustive matches on oven_sdk::ToolContent gain a LoadTools arm:
  • persist_tool_content (model_history.rs) persists it as PersistedToolContent::Text(text). A provider-executed result in an assistant turn never loads tools, so there is no new persisted variant.
  • FitToolContent (runtime/compaction.rs) and the hook views (plugin/hook_views.rs) treat it as its text.
  • The release-integrity test and deny.toml comment name the new revision. Publish the crates to crates.io before the next cookie release.

docs.title: 3. Which models defer
docs.text:
Cookie's ModelCapabilities (crates/models/src/model_types.rs) gains deferred_tools: DeferredToolsSupport:

Value Meaning Oven capability Section 9 retry unsupported No deferral: every tool up front, no loader tools Unsupported — native Verified to load natively Native Only on an error oven classifies as Unsupported attempted Tried without verification Native On any 400 or 422

compile_executable (crates/models/src/compiler/executable.rs) decides it next to the compaction capability, in this order:

  1. A per-model override wins. Managed models take deferred_tools = "native" | "unsupported" in their model override; custom models take the same key in their capabilities. There is no attempted value: it is only ever a default.
  2. models.dev's dynamically_loaded_tools: true gives native. It is read as an optional bool in parse_model (crates/models/src/catalog/parser.rs) and stored as a defaulted Option<bool> on CatalogModelRecord. No model carries it yet; Kimi Code reads the same field.
  3. A Claude model that supports tool search, on Anthropic's own endpoint, gives native (decision 3, option B). That means api.anthropic.com, or Claude Platform on AWS. The models are Claude Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 4.5 and later, Fable, and Mythos (the oven spec's section 2 table), matched on the wire model ID. The same model through any other endpoint, the user's gateway included, falls to rule 5, attempted, as Claude Code treats a gateway behind ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. The adapter cannot decide this: the user's anthropic provider resolves to the Anthropic-compatible adapter even through the gateway.
