A session whose agent or preset disappeared follows the existing fallback rules at its next run (the preset falls back to the shared agents, the agent to primary or the first runnable one); an explicit selection of a missing agent or preset is refused, as today. Title generation for runs recorded before internal agents were frozen falls back to the built-in title agent instead of failing.

docs.title: 5. Protocol
docs.text:
Client protocol bump; additive schema check updated.

Method Params Result config.get {} {revision, documents: [{path, text, fingerprint}], status} config.apply {expected_revision, changes: [Change]} {revision, status} config.reload {} {revision, status}
  • Change is one of:
  • {"put": {path, text, expected_fingerprint?}}: create or replace a document; expected_fingerprint is absent for a new one and required otherwise.
  • {"delete": {path, expected_fingerprint}}: remove a document. Removing the last document of a preset removes its directory.
  • {"set": {key, value}}: set one key of config.toml. key is the path of table and key names (["context_compaction", "threshold"], ["mcp", "servers", "docs", "command"]); value is JSON mapped to TOML (string, integer, float, boolean, array, or object as an inline table), and null removes the key. The edit goes through toml_edit, so the rest of the file, comments included, is untouched. A set and a put of config.toml in one change set are refused.

path is config.toml, agents/<id>.md, or agents/<preset>/<id>.md; anything else is refused. - Atomic as a set. The daemon builds the candidate tree with every change, validates it whole (so deleting a subagent and editing its delegator go together), then writes. Each file is written with the existing secure commit (0600 temp file, compare against what was read, rename, directory fsync); if a later write fails, the earlier ones are restored from their originals. The engine applies the new generation only after every write succeeded. - Conflicts. expected_revision and each expected_fingerprint are checked against disk under the configuration lock; a mismatch is config_conflict and nothing is written. A client then refetches and merges. - config.reload re-reads the tree from disk, for edits made by hand, and applies it like config.apply does. - status: {applied_revision, restart_required: [part], error?}. error is the last failed reload's message when disk and the applied generation differ. - Notification. RuntimeSnapshotV1 gains config_revision; every applied change publishes runtime.changed with config_reloaded / agent_reloaded (reasons that exist today but are never sent), so other clients know to refetch. - Trust. Documents travel as they are on disk, including ${env:NAME} placeholders and any literal values in [providers.*], the daemon token in [server], and MCP headers. Anyone holding the daemon token is already a fully trusted client. - MCP methods stay. mcp.server.* keeps its runtime overlay; mcp.server.persist writes through config.apply's commit path, and persisting a removal now deletes the server's table from the file.

docs.title: 6. Clients
docs.text:
• TUI /config. A panel lists config.toml, every preset with its agents, and the shared agents, with the configuration status (last error, restart-required parts). Enter opens the document in $VISUAL/$EDITOR (the TUI suspends, as for an external editor), then sends it with config.apply; a validation error reopens the editor on the same text with the error shown. n creates an agent (in the selected preset or shared), d deletes one, r runs config.reload. Because the text travels over the protocol, this works against a remote daemon.
  • CLI. cookie config edit [<path>] (default config.toml) does the same in the terminal; cookie config set <dotted.key> <TOML value> and cookie config unset <dotted.key> send a single set; cookie config reload and cookie config status report the status.

docs.title: 7. Phases
docs.text:
Each phase lands as its own commit, with every gate, docs, and tests.

  1. Provider connect fixes (section 2), including the safe_to_project removal.
  2. Generations: load_from_tree, the swappable generation with run capture, apply_configuration for the live parts, restart-required status, config.reload, config_revision. The MCP writer's validation moves from a temporary directory to load_from_tree.
  3. Writes: config.get / config.apply (put, delete, set) with the set-atomic commit and rollback; mcp.server.persist on the same path, including removals.
  4. Clients: TUI /config and cookie config.

docs.title: 8. Tests
docs.text:
• Config crate: load_from_tree agrees with loading the same files from disk; every validation boundary that applies to files applies to the tree.
  • Engine: a run in progress keeps its settings and agent across an apply; the next run sees the new ones; a failed candidate leaves the generation and the published runtime unchanged; removing a preset falls queued work back as documented; restart-required parts are reported only when they differ.
  • Protocol: conflicts on revision and fingerprint, a change set that is only valid as a whole, rollback when a write fails, refused paths; set keeps comments and other keys, removes with null, and is refused for a value that fails validation.
  • Provider fixes: per-provider task slots, the retry on a catalog conflict, each error code, and that the server wipes received credentials.

docs.title: 9. Review
docs.text:
Decided 2026-10-17:

  1. Edit unit: whole documents and single-key set edits of config.toml, both in config.apply.
  2. Hand edits: explicit config.reload; no file watcher.
  3. runtimes and plugins: restart required for now; live in a follow-up.
  4. TUI editing: $VISUAL/$EDITOR.

docs.title: 10. Implementation notes
docs.text:
Landed in four commits: the provider fixes (client protocol 46), reloading (47: config.reload, config_revision), reading and writing (48: config.get, config.apply), and the clients. Where it differs from the sections above:

  • What a run keeps. A run keeps what it captures at admission: its agent and delegated children's registry, result limits, retry policy, and delegation depth. Other settings (approval timeout, loop warning, compaction, delegation concurrency, messaging) apply from their next use, also inside a run in progress, rather than the run holding a whole configuration generation.
  • Revisions. config_revision is part of runtime_revision, so a settings-only change publishes a new runtime revision.
  • config.reload answers {status}; a configuration that fails validation is reported in status.error rather than as an RPC error. config.get also lists empty_presets.
  • Errors. A refused config.apply is JSON-RPC error -32040 with data {code: conflict | invalid_configuration | invalid_change, message}.
  • A refused TUI edit is not reopened at once: the panel shows why, marks the document not applied, and Enter reopens the rejected text. cookie config edit asks whether to edit again.
  • cookie config remove <path> was added for parity with the TUI's delete.
  • Writer. write_tree writes the changed documents in path order and restores the earlier ones when a later write fails; the old temporary validation directory is gone, so write_server_token and every write validate in memory with the agent documents.
  • Persisting MCP servers drops the runtime-layer entry once the file holds it, so the server's source becomes the user file.
  • Runtime changes stay off the async workers (2026-10-23). A runtime change (a catalog refresh, a config.apply or reload, a provider connect or disconnect, a provider-store reload) holds the engine's runtime mutation lock while it recompiles, which takes seconds in a debug build. The catalog refresh and provider connect/disconnect already ran on the blocking pool, and runtime.snapshot.get answers with the published runtime instead of waiting (2026-10-23, commit 42eb99ad3). The paths that must still wait for the change, so a run or session started mid-change uses the runtime it publishes, now wait on the blocking pool too (Engine::reconcile_provider_store_off_worker): session.create, run start, session.select_model, session.goal.set and session.goal.lifecycle with a selection, and session.permission.preview. The configuration apply recompiles there as well. Only the in-process cookie run session creation keeps waiting on its own worker.

docs.title: 11. Addendum 2026-10-23: clients restart the daemon
docs.text:
Status: implemented (2026-10-23); see 11.5.

config.status already reports restart_required parts (server, plugins, runtimes) that only a restart applies, but no client can restart the daemon. This addendum adds that, so a change made outside a client (an edited config.toml, a new binary on disk) can be applied from the TUI, the web client, or the CLI.

Decided 2026-10-23:

  • A plain "Restart daemon" waits until no run is active; restarting now, interrupting running turns, is an explicit choice.
  • A daemon that cannot relaunch itself refuses the call.

docs.title: 11.1 Protocol
docs.text:
Client protocol minor, additive:

  • daemon.restart { when: "idle" | "now" } → { scheduled, active_runs }. when defaults to idle. A second call while one is scheduled updates its when (now wins).
  • daemon.restarting notification { when, active_runs, reason? }, sent to every client when a restart is scheduled and as the wait progresses.
  • New error restart_unsupported ("this daemon can't restart itself") for a daemon not started by cookie daemon, such as one embedded in a test harness or another program.
  • Any client holding the daemon's token may call it; the token already grants full control.

docs.title: 11.2 Behaviour
docs.text:
• idle: the restart waits until no run is active in any session. Meanwhile new runs are refused with "the daemon is restarting" (cron fires are recorded as skipped for that reason), producers' messages queue as usual, and clients show why.
  • now: running turns end as interrupted, as after any stop; recovery closes them out when the daemon comes back.
  • The restart: the daemon finishes in-flight replies, flushes session logs and its stores, stops its runtimes and plugins as on shutdown, closes client connections with a restarting close reason, and relaunches its own executable with the same arguments and environment:
  • Unix: an in-place exec, keeping the process ID, so systemd and launchd see no change.
  • Windows: it starts a new process with the same command line and exits; the new process waits for the listening port to free before binding.
  • The executable is re-read from disk, so a restart after an upgrade runs the new build; clients already notice a changed daemon build when they reconnect.
  • Afterwards: clients reconnect as after any dropped connection; dial-in runtimes reconnect as they already do. Sessions are on disk; nothing is lost.

docs.title: 11.3 Clients
docs.text:
• Banner: while config.status lists restart_required parts, the TUI and the web client show "Restart needed to apply: plugins, runtimes · Restart daemon".
  • Always available: TUI /restart; web Settings → "Restart daemon"; cookie daemon restart [--now] [--url <url>] [--token <token>].
  • Confirmation: "Restart when idle" (the default) or "Restart now (interrupts N running turns)".
  • While waiting: "Restarting when idle…" until the connection closes, then the client's ordinary reconnecting state.

docs.title: 11.4 Tests
docs.text:
• idle waits for an active run and refuses new runs meanwhile; now interrupts and the next start recovers the runs; a second call switching to now; restarting notifications; restart_unsupported from an embedded engine.
  • The relaunch itself, in an integration test that starts cookie daemon, restarts it through the RPC, and reconnects (Unix; Windows in CI).
  • The TUI and web banner, buttons, and confirmation.

docs.title: 11.5 Implementation notes
docs.text:
Landed in client protocol 1.19.0 (the protocol, the engine and server, the cookie daemon relaunch and cookie daemon restart, the TUI, and the web client, each its own commit). Where it differs from or adds to the sections above:

  • The hook. The engine schedules the restart and decides when it is due (Engine::schedule_restart, Engine::set_restart_hook); only cookie daemon installs the hook, so an engine embedded anywhere else, cookie --standalone included, answers restart_unsupported. ServerProtocol::restart_daemon refuses by default.
  • What idle waits for. Runs active or starting in any session. A run's delegated children still start, since they are part of a turn the restart waits for; every other start (run.start, session.submit_input on an idle session, queued input, a producer's wake) is refused with the new error daemon_restarting. Queued input stays queued and starts when a client next opens its session on the restarted daemon. crons.run is refused too; a scheduled fire is skipped with the new reason daemon_restarting.
  • Background calls (2026-10-26, client protocol 1.35.0). idle also waits for every background call that has not committed its result: one still running, or one that ended and is committing. The first implementation counted only runs, so a restart scheduled while a backgrounded bash ran after its turn ended was due at once and the shutdown killed the call without a report. daemon.restart and daemon.restarting carry the count as background_calls. ACP agents' own background shells are not cookie background calls and stay invisible to the wait.
  • scheduled is false when a restart was already scheduled and the call only changed its when.
  • daemon.restarting goes to every connection, a new one included, whenever the when or the number of active runs changes and once the restart is due; its reason says what it waits for ("waiting for 2 running turns to finish") or "restarting now".
  • The sequence. The daemon shuts the engine down first (runs end as cancelled, plugins, MCP servers, ACP agents, and runtimes stop, the logs and stores are flushed) while clients are still connected, so they see the turns end; then it closes every client connection with WebSocket close code 1012 (Service Restart) and the reason restarting, which both clients read as "the daemon is restarting". Any server shutdown now sends the frames a connection has queued and a close frame before it closes, and the daemon waits up to 2 seconds for every client connection to finish closing before it exits or relaunches, so the close frame is not cut off.
  • Relaunch. The daemon captures its executable (current_exe at start, so an upgrade replacing the file runs the new build), arguments, environment, and directory before it changes any of them. On Unix it marks every descriptor above standard error close-on-exec and execs in place with the original argv[0]; on Windows it spawns the same command line and exits 0. The relaunched process finds COOKIE_DAEMON_RESTARTED, removes it from its environment, and retries binding a port still in use for up to 30 seconds. The listening line names the process ID, which a Windows user needs to stop the new process outside its scheduled task.
  • Clients. The banner needs the configuration status, so both clients fetch config.get on connect and on runtime.changed with config_reloaded (and resync). The confirmation counts the running sessions the client knows. The TUI's /config panel has Reload from disk (r) and Restart daemon (R) buttons, the latter highlighted while a part waits for a restart; the web client's Settings → Configuration has the same pair. The confirmation returns to the panel it opened over.
  • Token fix. A daemon started without [server] token writes one at start; that write used to read as a server change needing a restart. The daemon now tells the engine the token it serves with (Engine::note_served_server_token).
  • Tests. Engine tests for the idle wait, refused starts, kept queue, now overriding idle and the shutdown interrupting the run, the cron skip, and the missing hook; a server test over a real WebSocket for restart_unsupported, daemon.restarting, and the 1012 close; an integration test (crates/cookie_agent/tests/daemon_restart.rs) that starts the real cookie daemon on a scratch home and a free port, restarts it through the RPC, and reconnects on the same port with the same token (same PID on Unix, a new one on Windows); TUI tests for /restart, the /config buttons, and the hover sweep; and the restart_daemon browser scenario.

docs.title: External Producers
docs.text: Status: implemented (decisions of 2026-10-16; both code phases landed 2026-10-16). This document is the governing specification for letting plugins and runtimes register any number of named producers and send messages into sessions. Section Decisions records what review settled.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
A producer puts messages into a session's model input from outside a user turn: a background call's result, a subagent's report, agent mail, a goal reminder, or a plugin's message. The durable model (accepted, admitted, claimed, consumed, and discarded messages, deduplicated on (session, owner, idempotency key)), the steer and queue delivery modes, and waking an idle session are already generic over the owner.

What is not generic is who may produce from outside the daemon, and as whom:

  • One identity per plugin. A plugin produces as plugin { plugin }. It cannot run several distinct producers, such as a CI watcher and a file watcher, each with its own label and its own idempotency namespace.
  • Runtimes cannot produce. The runtime protocol has no producer methods (runtimes spec section 9 deferred them). A remote runtime's tool therefore cannot use reports_itself: once detached, it has no channel to report on.
  • No body bound. A plugin's body is limited only by the 4 MiB frame.
  • Plugin-only readiness. Recovery state and the goal-readiness gate know only plugins.

After this work, any plugin or runtime can register any number of named producers, for the sessions it may reach, under one owner kind the daemon derives from the connection.

Out of scope: clients as producers (a later client:<id> source fits the same owner), a model-facing envelope around external bodies, and changes to the engine's own producers (delegation, goal, goal_control, agent, tool, subagent).

docs.title: 2. The external owner
docs.text:
ProducerOwner::Plugin { plugin } is replaced by:

{ "type": "external", "source": "runtime:local", "name": "ci-watcher" }
  • source says who is producing. The daemon derives it from the authenticated connection, never from request parameters:
  • plugin:<configured plugin name> for a plugin;
  • runtime:<attachment name> for a runtime, the name the instance reports in runtime/initialize and sessions attach it under.
  • name is a free-form label the sender chooses when it registers, one of [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_.-]{0,63}. One source may register under any number of names, and several registrations may share a name.

The owner is part of the deduplication key, so two names of one source never collide on an idempotency key, and a sender that restarts and registers the same name again replays its earlier sends instead of duplicating them.

The engine's own owners stay as they are. Nothing in the engine, the projection, or a client branches on the source prefix: every external owner gets the same treatment, and a client shows it as <source> · <name>.

Stored logs. A stored plugin { plugin } owner decodes as external { source: "plugin:<plugin>", name: "default" }, and the plugin SDK registers under default when the plugin names nothing, so a plugin upgraded across this change keeps deduplicating against its earlier sends.

docs.title: 3. Registration and authority
docs.text:
The four producer operations are the same for every source:

Operation Params Result register session_id, name producer_id send session_id, producer_id, mode, idempotency_key, description, body message_id unregister session_id, producer_id {} discard session_id, message_id {}
  • A registration belongs to one connection. Its authority is the connection's source and its connection epoch; it ends when the connection does (a plugin exits, a runtime instance stops or reconnects), and the sender registers again on its next connection.
  • Send needs a live registration of the calling connection, as today. Everything else about send is unchanged: the receipt follows durable acceptance, and an identical retry returns the original message_id.
  • Discard addresses a message, not a registration: the caller's source must match the message owner's source, whatever the name. The other discard rules are unchanged.
  • Body. The body is sent to the model as is, as today. It must be non-empty and at most [producers] max_body_bytes (section 6).

docs.title: 4. Plugins
docs.text:
Extension protocol 0.0.8:

  • plugin/producer/register gains name (required on the wire; the SDK's register_producer defaults it to default).
  • Everything else is unchanged: the plugin declares producer_messaging, the operator enables plugins.<name>.producer_messaging, and a plugin may target any session the daemon can load.

docs.title: 5. Runtimes
docs.text:
Runtime protocol 4 adds producer messaging to runtimes.

Change Message Added producer_messaging (boolean, default false) in the runtime/initialize result. Added producer/register, producer/send, producer/unregister, producer/discard (runtime → daemon, requests), with the params and results of section 3. Added producer/recovery/start (daemon → runtime, notification) and producer/recovery/complete (runtime → daemon, request, outcome ready or failed { message }), as for plugins.
  • Scope. A runtime may register for, send to, and discard in only the sessions attached to its instance. A session that detaches it, or is deleted, drops the runtime's registrations there; a send to a session it is not attached to is rejected.
  • Grant. No configuration switch: attaching a runtime to a session is the grant, and the runtime opts in by declaring producer_messaging.
  • Recovery. When a runtime declares producer_messaging, the daemon sends producer/recovery/start after runtime/initialize; the runtime restores whatever external work it tracks and answers producer/recovery/complete. Until then its source is starting (section 7).
  • Self-reporting tools. A runtime tool may now detach with reports_itself and report its own results later as producer messages, as delegate_subagent does in the daemon.
  • On the runtime side, runtime_api gains ProducerChannel (register, send, unregister, discard), which a runtime's tools receive as ToolExecutionContext::producers; the coding runtime's protocol server (coding_runtime::server) implements it with these requests when started with ServeOptions::producer_messaging, and reports its recovery ready at once since it tracks no work of its own.
  • A runtime may send producer requests only after producer/recovery/start; earlier ones are rejected.
  • A runtime's call that detaches with reports_itself is not cancelled when the daemon stops waiting for it; it keeps running and reports through its producers.

docs.title: 6. Configuration
docs.text:
[producers]
max_body_bytes = 65536
Key Type Default Description max_body_bytes integer 65536 Largest body an external producer may send, in UTF-8 bytes. A larger or empty body fails the send. Must be 1..=4194304.

The limit applies to external producers only; the engine's own producers and agent mail ([messaging] max_body_bytes) keep their own bounds.

docs.title: 7. Readiness
docs.text:
PluginRecoveryState { plugin, status } becomes ProducerSourceState { source, status }, with the same statuses (starting, ready, failed, disabled).

  • session.producers returns sources: the state of every producer-capable plugin, and of every producer-capable runtime attached to the session.
  • A goal's reminders wait until every source in that list is ready, where today they wait for every producer-capable plugin. A source that fails or is disabled records a runless producer_diagnostic { source, kind, message } (recovery_failed or recovery_disabled), once per session. The plugin_diagnostic event stays for the plugin host's other diagnostics; its recovery_failed and recovery_disabled kinds are no longer written.
  • A live external registration in a session still holds back goal reminders, as a plugin registration does today.
  • External messages stay outside the agent-mail caps (max_pending_per_session, max_inflight_per_pair, max_hops), as plugin messages are today.

docs.title: 8. Client protocol
docs.text:
Change Where Changed ProducerOwner: plugin { plugin } replaced by external { source, name }. Changed session.producers result: plugin_recovery replaced by sources (ProducerSourceState). Added producer_diagnostic { source, kind, message } event for a producer source's failed or disabled recovery.

Client protocol 43. The TUI labels an external producer <source> · <name> and its notices name the source.

docs.title: 9. Phases
docs.text:
Each phase lands as its own commits with every gate green, and is pushed.

  1. External owner and plugins. The external owner and legacy decoding; named registrations; source-matched discard; [producers] max_body_bytes; ProducerSourceState and the generalized readiness gate; extension protocol 0.0.8 and the SDK; client protocol 43 and the TUI.
  2. Runtimes. Runtime protocol 4: the capability, the four producer requests scoped to attached sessions, recovery, dropping registrations on detach and reconnect; the runtime_api producer handle; a remote self-reporting tool test.
  3. Documentation. Plugins guide, goal-mode producer sections, the protocol, runtime protocol, and events references, the runtimes spec's deferral note; this spec marked implemented.

docs.title: 10. Decisions
docs.text:
Decided 2026-10-16:

  • One generic external { source, name } owner for producers from outside the daemon, with a daemon-derived source and a sender-chosen name.
  • A runtime produces only for the sessions attached to it.
  • External bodies reach the model raw, as today; only a size bound is added.
  • Clients do not register producers in this work.

Defaults confirmed in review:

  • The name charset [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_.-]{0,63}.
  • Stored plugin { plugin } owners decode as name default, and the SDK registers under default by default.
  • Discard matches the caller's source, not its name.
  • Runtimes need no configuration switch; attaching is the grant.
  • [producers] max_body_bytes defaults to 64 KiB.

docs.title: Goal Mode and Producer Messaging (Design Spec)
docs.text:
Status: implemented; approved product contract. This document is the governing specification for session goal mode and the unified producer messaging registry. The prerequisite compaction, permissions, and symlink work was reviewed and pushed as commits 4cf56157 and 9ccf8fa6 before implementation began. See Staging plan.

This spec does not reopen the approved product decisions. Where a genuine ambiguity or contradiction remains, it is listed under Open technical risks instead of being silently resolved here.

Non-goals: no inferred goals, no goal inheritance into subagents, no deadlines/watchdogs/expiry for producers, no Codex-style extra budgets, blocker counters, or additional goal states, no new public scheduler priorities, no mandatory third message queue.

docs.title: 1.1 Activation
docs.text:
Goal mode is activated explicitly only, by the user choosing /goal in the root session's TUI command palette and entering an objective in its follow-up prompt (see crates/tui/src/ui/slash.rs, COMMANDS). The engine never infers a goal from prompt content. Only root sessions can have a goal; the palette refuses the command in a delegated/child session with an explanatory status instead of prompting.

A session whose ACP agent offers its own goal command has no goal mode: the clients list the agent's /goal in its place, and the agent keeps its goal itself (ACP agents spec section 10).

  • Activation errors if a goal is already active or paused (the user must cancel or complete the current goal first). An empty objective is refused in the prompt.
  • Pause (active -> paused), Resume (paused -> active), and Cancel (active|paused -> cancelled) are the goal bar's controls, reachable by mouse or by F6 focus and the keyboard. There are no typed lifecycle commands. A persistent one-line goal bar sits above the message composer whenever the selected session has a goal. It is hidden when no goal exists and remains visible with read-only status for completed or cancelled goals. Clicking the objective description opens a detail modal containing the full objective, checklist, and lifecycle status. This is a read-only checklist view, not an editor; the root maintains checklist items through goal_update { items }.

The producer queue strip remains separate, above the goal bar and composer. This persistent goal surface replaces command-generated status reports and ephemeral goal progress in the general status row. Internal goal IDs, revisions, and lifecycle RPC identity/concurrency checks are unchanged.

Lifecycle states are exactly: active, paused, completed, cancelled. completed and cancelled are terminal. The user owns the objective and the lifecycle; the model cannot change either through tools (see 1.3).

docs.title: 1.2 Durable goal state
docs.text:
Goal state is durable session event history (crates/protocol/src/event.rs) and is independent of summaries and compaction: compaction (crates/engine/src/runtime/compaction.rs, ContextCheckpointCommit) never elides goal events from the projection, and the goal projection is rebuilt from events, not from summary text. The objective and the full checklist are re-injected into goal-continuation reminders (4.3), so compaction cannot strand the goal.

New events (additive; event history is versionless and read best-effort per AGENTS.md):

  • GoalActivated { goal_id, objective, revision }
  • GoalChecklistRevised { goal_id, items: Vec<GoalItem>, revision }
  • GoalLifecycleChanged { goal_id, status, revision }

GoalItem = { description, finished }; checklist items have no IDs. GoalState.revision is an engine-owned, strictly increasing per-goal counter for durable state, user lifecycle controls, and reminder identity. Each activation has a distinct durable goal_id; replacing a terminal goal cannot make an old lifecycle RPC or reminder valid again merely by reusing a revision number. Model checklist updates are not bound to a goal ID.

docs.title: 1.3 Model tools: goal_get and goal_update
docs.text:
After activation, the root run's tool set gains two tools. They are root-only: delegated child sessions never see them and there is no goal inheritance. Because tool prompt sections are composed only at run admission and frozen into run_started (AGENTS.md; crates/engine/src/runtime/tool_prompts.rs), the tools appear/disappear at the next safe run admission after a lifecycle change — never mid-run.

  • goal_get — returns objective, status, revision, and the full checklist.
  • goal_update { items } — replaces the entire ordered checklist of the current/latest session goal when the engine actor accepts the update. Each item contains only description and finished. The session actor serializes replacements; the last accepted update wins. The model supplies neither goal_id nor expected_revision, and there is no model-facing lost-update protection. An update from an older run can intentionally replace the checklist of a newly activated active or paused goal. Updates reject if the current goal is absent or terminal, even from tools still present in an already-admitted run.

User lifecycle RPC controls retain SessionGoalLifecycleParams.goal_id and expected_revision; a stale lifecycle request is rejected. These checks are separate from model checklist replacement.

Rules:

  • The model cannot set, pause, resume, or cancel through tools. Lifecycle transitions are user-only, except the completion rule below.
  • When goal_update leaves the checklist non-empty and every item finished, the engine records completed (via GoalLifecycleChanged) with the new revision. An empty checklist is never vacuous completion: it is accepted as a revision but preserves the current active or paused lifecycle state. An active goal with an empty checklist remains eligible for a reminder that asks the root to establish the checklist.
  • Paused behavior (explicit design judgment): while paused, goal_get and goal_update remain available at the next admission and updates are preserved, including an all-finished update that records completed. Refusing writes would add a new user-facing feature surface; recording is the minimal behavior. Recording completion while paused schedules no continuation — pause and completion both suppress goal wakes (4.2), so there is nothing to resume. The model still cannot unpause or cancel.
  • Tool guidance (system-prompt/tool-description text) instructs the model that evidence and audit are root-authoritative: the root should verify work directly or via subagents before marking items finished, and the root checklist is the authoritative record over any subagent's self-report.

docs.title: 2.1 Model
docs.text:
The engine owns a per-session producer registry: a runtime-only, inspectable vector of registration records. Nothing about registrations is durable; restart semantics are in section 5.

Operations (separate calls, mode is per send, not per registration):

  • register(session) -> producer_id
  • send(producer_id, message, mode: steer | queue) -> ack
  • unregister(producer_id)
  • discard(session, message_id) (owned accepted message, not registration)

Semantics:

  • Registering and unregistering without any send is valid.
  • send to a closed (unregistered) or foreign (wrong owner / wrong session) registration is rejected.
  • A registered producer may send after its turn ends; sending to an idle session wakes it (section 3). Sending to a session being evicted/closed is rejected. (Since 2026-10-22 a registration no longer keeps its session in memory; a send to an evicted session reloads it and is accepted, see background tools section 13.)
  • There are no deadlines, watchdogs, or expiry. Producers are good-faith owners of their registration lifecycle; a leaked registration only affects goal-readiness evaluation (4.2) and is surfaced in inspection.

docs.title: 2.2 Ownership and authorization
docs.text:
Every registration has one authenticated owner. Durable ProducerOwner variants are External { source, name } (a plugin's or a runtime's named producer; stored Plugin { plugin } owners decode as External with name default), Delegation { invocation_id }, Goal { goal_id }, GoalControl { goal_id }, Agent { session_id }, Tool { tool_call_id }, and Subagent { session_id } (crates/protocol/src/producer.rs). Plugin connection authority remains runtime-only. GoalControl identifies engine-authored lifecycle steering, separate from the goal controller's continuation reminders. The destination is fixed at registration and checked on every send.

Plugins declare the producer_messaging capability to register producers (see Plugin development). Only live, owned registrations authorize post-turn model-message sends. plugin/emit publishes to the bus only; content that enters model history requires an explicitly supplied live producer registration, and the engine never creates an implicit registration to authorize an emission.

docs.title: 2.3 Message persistence and acknowledgment
docs.text:
Message registrations are volatile; accepted messages are durable.

  • send returns its ACK only after the engine appends a durable ProducerMessageAccepted { message_id, producer_owner, mode, idempotency_key, body } event to the session log. Senders must treat a missing/failed ACK as commit-uncertain and retry with the same idempotency_key (a stable sender-chosen message ID); the admission path deduplicates on (session, stable_producer_owner, idempotency_key). The stable owner identifies the specific plugin, delegation invocation, or goal, not just its kind or volatile registration ID. A retry requires a live owned registration; identical retries return the original receipt, while reuse with different content or mode is rejected. This is a modest at-least-once design; the engine makes no exactly-once claim about external side effects or model execution.
  • unregister does not remove accepted, unconsumed messages.
  • After a crash, accepted-but-unconsumed, undiscarded messages are recovered and admitted independently of whether their producer re-registers (5.4).

docs.title: 2.4 Owned-message discard
docs.text:
discard(session, message_id) authorizes against the authenticated caller's ownership of the durable accepted message, not a live registration. An owner can discard its own waiting message even after unregistering. Cross-owner discard is rejected; a retry for an owned already-discarded message succeeds idempotently. This is separate from unregistering or recalling user input.

Only unclaimed waiting messages can be discarded, including admitted messages not yet claimed. The actor serializes discard against durable claim acquisition before request preparation/dispatch: consumed or claimed messages reject discard, even if no provider request has been sent yet. A claim is a reservation, not proof of provider dispatch. It remains held through compaction, hooks, streaming, and model commit. Failed or cancelled attempts release claims; recovery releases surviving claims. Once all claims are released, unconsumed, undiscarded messages return to waiting. In-flight input cannot be retracted, and discard cannot undo model or external actions. See crates/engine/src/runtime/producer_claims.rs.

Successful discard is durable through ProducerMessageDiscarded, for real producer messages as well as goal reminders. Discarded messages no longer participate in delivery or pending-work readiness and are removed from the queue strip; replay must not restore them as pending. Goal reminder invalidation continues to check reminder identity and never discards another owner's work.

docs.title: 3. Delivery modes and admission
docs.text:
The existing machinery — the per-session actor mailbox (crates/engine/src/actor.rs), UserInputAdmitted / UserInputSubmitted / pending_inputs (crates/engine/src/runtime/mailbox.rs), and the residency rule that forbids runless pending inputs while a run is active (crates/engine/src/runtime/residency.rs, has_runless_pending_inputs) — retains its existing user-input rules. Producer delivery extends it with separate events:

  • ProducerMessageAccepted durably stores the body and delivery mode, even when a run is active.
  • ProducerMessageAdmitted references that message from a particular run. Its sequence participates in committed model input coverage.
  • ProducerMessagesClaimed reserves admitted messages; its event sequence identifies the claim. ProducerMessagesReleased releases that reservation.
  • ProducerMessageConsumed records committed consumption; ProducerMessageDiscarded records generic owned-message discard, including pending goal reminder invalidation.

User-input event shapes are unchanged. Producer messages do not enter the user composer restoration lane or become void merely because a run ends. Pending and admitted producer steer/queue messages do appear in the existing auto-show/hide queue strip above the goal bar and composer. Visibility does not grant user composer recall. Claimed entries are hidden until release returns them to waiting, unless already consumed or discarded.

docs.title: 3.1 STEER
docs.text: A steer message is inserted into the next safe model API request, including within an active run's tool loop: it joins the existing pending steer lane and is promoted per PromotePendingInputs (crates/engine/src/runtime/mailbox.rs). It never cancels an in-flight API request and never splits a tool-call/tool-result pair. A steer sent to an idle session starts a normal run.

docs.title: 3.2 QUEUE
docs.text: A queue message starts a subsequent normal run. While a run is active it is accepted and persisted but not delivered mid-run; when the session is idle it starts a normal run. This requires additive events plus an admission extension: today runless admits are forbidden while active, so queue admits during an active run must be recorded as accepted-but-deferred rather than rejected or voided (void_runless_pending_inputs, crates/engine/src/runtime/delegation.rs). Both modes wake generically — this is not goal-specific machinery.

docs.title: 3.3 Subagent results
docs.text: Subagent results are always steer. Background delegation completions register a producer before starting the async work, send(.., steer) on finish, then explicitly unregister. Foreground (blocking) delegation keeps its tool result as the single result channel and must not additionally emit a separate message. The result must be materialized exactly once: the former delegate_finished_v2 projection path (crates/engine/src/runtime/delegation.rs, crates/engine/src/model_history.rs) is unified with producer steer delivery so a background completion cannot appear both as a tool-style result and as a steered message.

docs.title: 4.1 Registration
docs.text: While a goal is active, the goal controller holds a producer registration on the root session. When evaluating readiness (4.2), the controller excludes only its own registration ID — any other live producer blocks the wake.

docs.title: 4.2 Readiness condition
docs.text:
A goal continuation reminder is armed when all hold:

  1. goal is active and the checklist is empty or has unfinished items;
  2. the session is recovered and the root is idle (no active run);
  3. no pending real steer, queue, or user messages exist;
  4. no other live producer registration exists;
  5. no goal reminder is already pending.

The check-and-enqueue is atomic inside the session actor and is rechecked at run admission (crates/engine/src/runtime/admission.rs), so real work that arrives between arming and admission always wins. An active goal run can still receive real steer messages normally.

docs.title: 4.3 Reminder identity and content
docs.text:
The reminder message carries the full objective and the entire checklist (finished and unfinished items, with revision). Reminders have an internal identity (goal_id, revision) allowing coalescing and invalidation of a pending reminder — no public scheduler priority and no mandatory third queue. Reconciliation is triggered on: run end, message send/consume, producer unregister, goal activation/resume, and session recovery. A consumed reminder does not block another reminder for the same revision after its run ends: making no checklist edit is not completion. Durable send idempotency uses a fresh message ID for each continuation attempt, distinct from the pending reminder's coalescing key.

GoalReminderIdentity.kind distinguishes Started from Continuation (wire values started and continuation). The initial message begins "Goal started. Pursue the new root objective below." Subsequent messages begin "Continue the root goal." Both retain the full state, checklist bootstrap instruction when needed, and evidence-verification guidance.

A same-goal reminder must be consumed through committed model-input coverage before subsequent messages become continuations. Acceptance, admission, claims, discarded messages, and GoalControl notifications do not establish this fact. The projection therefore preserves the distinction across restart and resume and resets it for a new goal ID. Missing kind in legacy stored reminders defaults to Continuation; coalescing remains keyed by goal ID and revision.

docs.title: 4.4 Pause / cancel / complete
docs.text:
pause, cancel, and completed each unregister the goal producer and invalidate any pending reminder, stopping future goal continuations.

User pause/cancel also durably queues a root notification in steer mode before the relevant producer registration closes if any of these hold:

  • the root has an active run;
  • the root has other live producer registrations, excluding the goal's own registration, including producers for pending subagent results;
  • the root has queued real messages (not goal reminders).

The notification enters the next safe model API request, without cancelling an in-flight request or splitting tool-call/tool-result pairs. It tells the model that the goal was paused or cancelled, to stop autonomous pursuit of that old goal, and to follow the user's directions. Closing the registration does not remove the accepted notification. Its accepted owner is ProducerOwner::GoalControl { goal_id }, not Goal; it is not a reminder and survives goal-controller teardown and reminder invalidation.

For an idle root waiting on other producers or queued real messages, ordinary steer semantics can wake a normal root run. This does not resume goal reminders: the goal remains paused or cancelled. A fully idle root with no other live producers and no queued real messages persists the lifecycle change without an announcement run; the goal's own registration or pending reminder alone does not qualify for notification. Steering does not abort an active run or delegations, and cannot undo actions already emitted. The separate interrupt/cancel-run path (/cancel, RunCancelled, RunInterrupted) is unchanged. This notification adds no run binding to goal_update { items }: updates still target the current session goal at actor acceptance.

docs.title: 5. Restart and recovery
docs.text:
1. Registrations vanish on restart. Durable goal state and accepted messages are restored from the event log; delegations are reconciled by the existing recovery path (crates/engine/src/runtime/recovery.rs).
  2. Producer-capable plugins reconstruct their pending work during their recovery/init phase from their own storage or the external services they front, then register fresh runtime IDs. Logs alone are currently live-only, and this spec deliberately adds no general replay API, no engine-managed durable producer records, and no plugin recovery blobs (both rejected at product level).
  3. Plugin recovery uses an explicit engine request/callback with an explicit completion notification — no timers. The engine tracks per-plugin startup readiness statuses (starting, ready, failed, disabled). Session adoption stays lazy so engine↔plugin callbacks cannot deadlock.
  4. Readiness barrier: a producer-capable plugin may register during restoration without waiting for goal readiness, but the goal controller holds its auto-registration/wake until the readiness barrier completes (all tracked producer-capable plugins report ready). Failed or disabled tracked producers hold goal readiness and are diagnosed rather than being interpreted as completed external work. An inactive (paused/completed/cancelled or absent) goal needs no barrier. Accepted messages from before the crash are recovered and admitted independently of any producer re-registering.
  5. Failed/disabled plugins must not silently prove work done. If a producer-capable plugin ends failed or disabled, the engine surfaces that status (diagnostic event + TUI notice) and goal readiness treats unrecovered external work as unknown rather than complete. Documented limitation: the engine cannot distinguish "plugin had no pending work" from "plugin lost its state" — this is weaker than the user-facing assumption that restarts are transparent, and it is called out in the user docs.

docs.title: 6. Durable events, projection invariants, and history transforms
docs.text:
Events (all in crates/protocol/src/event.rs, with corresponding entries in docs/site/reference/events.md and generated schemas):

Event Payload (summary) GoalActivated goal_id, objective, revision GoalChecklistRevised goal_id, items, revision GoalLifecycleChanged goal_id, status, revision ProducerMessageAccepted message_id, producer_owner, mode, idempotency_key, body, optional reminder ProducerMessageAdmitted message_id; enclosing event carries the destination run_id ProducerMessagesClaimed Nonempty message_ids; run-scoped, envelope seq identifies the claim ProducerMessagesReleased Positive claim_seq; run-scoped to the same run as the referenced claim ProducerMessageConsumed message_id, run_id ProducerMessageDiscarded message_id; optional producer_owner, optional reminder

Projection invariants:

  • Goal revision strictly increases per activation and is assigned by the engine. Model checklist replacements are actor-serialized, last accepted update wins for the current goal at actor acceptance, with no model goal ID or expected-revision check. Updates reject absent or terminal current goals; user lifecycle RPCs still reject stale goal IDs and expected_revision values.
  • completed requires a non-empty, all-finished checklist.
  • Every ProducerMessageAccepted is consumed at most once; consumed messages are excluded from pending_inputs. Consumption is durable only when a committed model turn records that message in its input coverage, not merely when it is selected for an API request. Recovery reconciles a committed turn whose consumption marker was not yet appended. An uncommitted API attempt can be repeated after a crash; this is not an exactly-once guarantee for provider calls or external effects.
  • Reminder coalescing never reorders or drops real (non-reminder) messages.
  • Durable discard is distinct from consumption. Discarded messages are excluded from delivery, pending-work readiness, and the queue strip. Ownership checks survive unregister; eligibility is checked atomically against claim acquisition, not inferred merely from the absence of a consumption marker. Claimed messages are nondiscardable and hidden from the waiting strip, including before dispatch.
  • Claims reference unique accepted/admitted, unconsumed, undiscarded messages belonging to the claim's run. Release identifies a claim by envelope sequence and must match that run. Release removes only that reservation; when all claims are gone, unconsumed, undiscarded messages return to waiting. It does not undo committed consumption or prove that a provider request did or did not execute.
  • Discard projection strictly matches a supplied owner against the accepted message and any supplied reminder against its identity. Historical discards without an owner require a matching reminder; a wrong supplied owner cannot use that legacy fallback. Both forms reject consumed or claimed messages.

History transforms:

  • Compaction (ContextCheckpointCommit): goal events and unconsumed ProducerMessageAccepted events survive compaction in the projection; the reminder re-injects objective+checklist so the model never depends on pre-compaction goal text.
  • Fork: a forked session copies the goal projection and, for an active goal, creates a fresh goal producer registration; runtime registrations never cross the fork. Unconsumed accepted messages are forked with the log; consumed or durably discarded ones are not replayed as pending. Compaction likewise preserves the discard projection alongside accepted-message state.
  • Revert (log truncation): goal and message events after the revert point are removed per the existing contract, which may resurrect an earlier goal state or unconsumed messages. Goal and delegation-owned registrations are reconciled with the surviving projection; plugin registrations cannot be reconstructed from history and remain subject to explicit plugin lifecycle handling. Revert retains the engine's existing active-run restrictions; it does not gain permission to rewrite active execution merely because goal pause is non-interrupting.

docs.title: 7. APIs, permissions, and surfaces
docs.text:
• Protocol/SDK: the plugin protocol's producer capability, the producer/register, producer/send, producer/unregister, producer/discard, and producer/recovery/complete requests, and the deadline-free producer/recovery/start notification, shared with the runtime protocol. The SDK exposes explicit producer handles. See Plugin development for the public contract.
  • Permissions: goal_get/goal_update declare no permission. They are root-only by construction and published only while the session has an active or paused goal, which the user set; they act on that goal alone, so setting the goal is the grant. They are not configurable capability surface. The producer capability is off by default for plugins.
  • Run-freeze integration: tool set and tool-prompt changes apply only at run admission; goal lifecycle events never mutate history[0] (AGENTS.md rules; crates/engine/src/runtime/tool_prompts.rs).
  • TUI (crates/tui/src/ui/slash.rs, crates/tui/src/state): explicit activation through the palette's /goal objective prompt, plus a persistent one-line goal bar above the composer. Its clickable objective opens a detail modal with the full checklist and status, without checklist editing. Pause/Resume and Cancel buttons are the primary lifecycle controls; terminal goals retain a read-only bar and detail view, while absent goals hide the bar. Notifications for goal completion and failed/disabled producer sources remain separate from this persistent surface. Pending/admitted producer steer and queue messages share the existing queue strip above the goal bar and composer, using its existing automatic show/hide behavior. Claimed entries are hidden until release restores waiting, unless consumed or discarded. Discarded entries are removed/hidden; producer messages cannot be recalled into the user composer. Discard is an owner-authorized producer API, not a new composer recall action.
  • Inspection: runtime snapshot exposes the producer registry records (owner kind, session, age) for debugging; this is read-only.

docs.title: 8. Testing and acceptance matrix
docs.text:
Engine tests (crates/engine/src/runtime_tests.rs), protocol round-trips (crates/protocol/src/tests.rs), TUI tests, and docs build (./scripts/build-docs.sh, strict) must cover at minimum:

  1. /goal grammar: explicit objective activation; bare /goal shows objective usage without a status report; /goal status is rejected without activation. Retained lifecycle shortcuts, child-session rejection, and activation conflicts remain covered.
  2. Lifecycle: pause/resume/cancel transitions; terminal-state rejection of further transitions; user-only lifecycle enforcement against tool calls.
  3. Checklist: items contain only description and finished; full ordered replacements take only items, and the last accepted update wins for the current goal. An older run's update can affect a newly activated active or paused goal. Engine revisions still increase; stale user lifecycle goal IDs and revisions, and updates with no current active/paused goal, are rejected. An empty checklist never completes or unpauses a goal, and can bootstrap an active goal; all-finished completes.
  4. Pause semantics: updates preserved while paused; all-finished-while-paused records completion with no continuation; no future continuations after pause/cancel. Each notification condition independently qualifies: an active root run, another live producer (excluding goal self), or queued real messages. Steering is durable before the producer registration closes and enters the next safe model request; idle roots with other producers or real messages can wake a normal run without resuming goal reminders. A fully idle root persists lifecycle without an announcement run; goal self/reminders alone do not qualify. In-flight requests and delegations are not aborted, tool pairs remain intact, and already-emitted actions are not undone. Notification guidance stops autonomous old-goal pursuit without adding run binding to checklist updates.
  5. Tools appear/disappear only at run admission (freeze).
  6. Producer registry: zero-send unregister; closed/foreign send rejection; post-turn send wakes idle session; mode is per-send.
  7. Persistence: ACK-after-durable-accept; retry with same idempotency key dedupes; crash recovery admits accepted-unconsumed messages without a live producer; unregister keeps queued messages.
  8. Delivery: steer lands mid-tool-loop without splitting tool pairs or cancelling in-flight API; queue-while-active is persisted and deferred; idle queue starts a run.
  9. Subagent results: background completion steered exactly once (no delegate_finished_v2 duplication); foreground result not duplicated.
  10. Goal readiness: each readiness conjunct individually blocks; own registration excluded; atomic check + admission recheck; reminder coalescing/invalidation by goal ID and revision; real work ahead of reminders; repeated reminders at an unchanged unfinished revision.
  11. Restart: registrations gone; goal restored; readiness barrier holds auto wake; failed/disabled plugin surfaced and does not complete goal items; lazy adoption does not deadlock.
  12. Compaction/fork/revert invariants from section 6.
  13. Producer discard: owned waiting messages can be discarded before or after unregister, including admitted-but-unclaimed messages; own already-discarded retries are idempotent. Reject cross-owner, consumed, and claimed/in-flight messages, including claims before provider dispatch. Race discard against claim acquisition; replay durable discard without redelivery or a stale pending-work blocker.
  14. Queue strip: pending/admitted producer steer and queue messages appear in the existing strip above the goal bar and composer, participate in automatic show/hide, and disappear on discard. Producer entries cannot be recalled into the user composer. Claims hide entries; release restores only unconsumed, undiscarded waiting entries after all claims end. In-flight input cannot be retracted. Cover failed/cancelled attempts and recovery release.
  15. Goal bar: persist one line while the selected session has a goal; hide when absent and retain terminal read-only status. Clicking the objective opens the full checklist/status modal without editing controls. Pause/Resume and Cancel buttons invoke the existing lifecycle controls with identity/revision checks. Session switching and narrow layouts keep the queue strip, goal bar, and composer separate, without overlap or ephemeral status-row substitution.

docs.title: 9. Staging plan
docs.text:
The prerequisite compaction/permissions/symlink work was reviewed, committed, and pushed before these implementation stages:

  1. Protocol events + projection (section 6) with tests; no behavior change.
  2. Producer registry core + admission extension (sections 2–3) including queue-while-active persistence; plugin capability + SDK surface.
  3. Delegation integration: background completions via registry, single materialization of results (3.3).
  4. Goal mode: durable state, tools, slash commands, wake controller (sections 1, 4, 7).
  5. Recovery/readiness barrier + TUI progress/notifications (sections 5, 7).
  6. Docs: events reference, plugin development, user guide; bindings regen.

docs.title: 10. Open technical risks
docs.text:
1. Queue-while-active admission is the deepest change: the residency invariant (has_runless_pending_inputs, void_runless_pending_inputs) currently forbids or voids runless admits during an active run, and the run-end path voids still-pending steered inputs (crates/tui/src/state/mod.rs mirrors this). Queue messages must be exempted from voiding without weakening the user-input invariants.
  2. Single materialization of background results: merging the delegate_finished_v2 path with producer steer delivery risks either duplicate model-history content or a lost result on the crash boundary between "accepted" and "materialized"; the ACK/consume events must be the single source of truth.
  3. Plugin emit migration: routing existing emit_session model-bound content through registrations is a breaking extension-protocol change for current plugins; the bypass must close without stranding non-model uses.
  4. Readiness barrier vs. plugin latency: holding goal auto-wake until plugin recovery completes can delay continuations arbitrarily if a plugin hangs in starting; the no-timers decision means the engine cannot force a timeout, only surface the status.
  5. Revert/compaction interaction for accepted-but-unconsumed messages relies on best-effort reading of versionless history; malformed or partially reverted message events need defined discard behavior (reuse the existing DiscardedInvalidPayload pattern).
  6. Paused-completion judgment (1.3) is recorded as minimal behavior; if product later wants "paused blocks completion", that is a new decision, not a bug fix.
  7. Historical checklist decoding: treatment of older stored items that contain an id is pending verification of the core implementation. This spec does not promise a particular compatibility decoder or migration; session history remains subject to the versionless best-effort contract.

docs.title: Addendum (2026-10-29): goals the agent sets
docs.text:
Decided by the user on 2026-10-29, with the stable prompt prefix (section 3):

  • The agent can start a goal. A third tool, goal_set { objective, items? }, activates a goal as /goal does, when the root has no active or paused goal, and sets its first checklist when it gives one. The user may also ask for a goal in their own words. Lifecycle stays the user's: the agent cannot pause, resume, or cancel.
  • The goal tools are offered to every root run, not only while a goal is active or paused (this replaces section 1.3's "after activation"). On a model that loads deferred tools they are deferred, so they cost a name in an announcement. An ACP agent's root session keeps the old rule.
  • A goal the agent started is reminded, continued, and completed like the user's. Its first reminder is a started one, as for any goal.

docs.title: Held sessions: stopped and failing automatic runs
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-26; client protocol 1.34.0, plugin protocol 1.19.0); see the implementation notes at the end.

docs.title: 1. Problem
docs.text:
A session starts runs of its own for producer messages: subagent reports, agent mail, plugin and runtime producers, cron fires into the session, and goal reminders. On 2026-10-25 a session looped: its run failed at once with a non-retryable 400, the failure released the subagent report it carried, and the next reconcile started a new run with it, about twice a second, 16,000 events in fifteen minutes. The user's Stop cancelled one run and the next started at once.

[model_retry] bounds the retries of one model attempt inside a run; nothing bounded the runs a producer message starts. A bound alone is not enough either: an engine-made goal reminder is a new producer message, so counting failures "since the last message" lets goal mode retry forever.

docs.title: 2. The rule
docs.text:
A session is held when its automatic runs have stopped:

  • Stopped: the user cancelled its run (Stop in a client, run.cancel; user decision of 2026-10-25: Stop also stops what would start next).
  • Failing: its runs failed more than [model_retry] standard_retries times in a row (negative: never held for failures). The count is of consecutive failed runs since the last run that completed or the user's last input or resume; producer messages, goal reminders included, never reset it. Each retry before the hold waits the model retry backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, ... up to backoff_ceiling_ms).

The bound and the refusals follow the user's proposal of 2026-10-26: producers are refused while a session holds failed messages, as cron skips, and the user clears the state with a Resume in place of Send.

A run interrupted by a daemon restart is neither: it resumes once, as now, and a failure of that run counts.

While a session is held, nothing starts a run on its own, and nothing new is accepted for it, as a cron fire is skipped while the job's previous fire is still undelivered:

Producer While held Plugin and runtime producers (producer.send) Refused with the error session_held (its reason in data); the producer may send again after a resume. Agent mail to the session From the session's parent: a resume (section 4). From any other agent: refused to the sender's tool call, the session is held (<reason>); it takes mail once the user or its parent resumes it. A cron fire into the session Skipped, recorded as skipped (session held); a skip is not a failure (cron spec section 4.4). A subagent's completion report Deferred, not refused: it stays with the delegation and is delivered on resume, as the engine already re-sends a report its parent has not accepted. Goal reminders Not made; the goal stays active and its reminders continue after a resume.

Messages accepted before the hold stay pending in the log and go with the resume. Nothing is lost and nothing is sent until the user acts.

docs.title: 3. Recording it
docs.text:
Two additive events, so the hold survives restarts and clients show it:

  • automatic_runs_held { reason }: appended when the session becomes held. reason is open: stopped, or failing with failures (the count) and error (the last run's model error summary).
  • automatic_runs_resumed {}: appended by a resume (section 4), with the user's origin.

The session is held while its latest of the two is automatic_runs_held. SessionMeta carries held: { reason } | null, so session lists badge it.

docs.title: 4. Resuming
docs.text:
session.resume { session_id, content? }: clears the hold (automatic_runs_resumed) and starts one run with every pending producer message and, when given, content as the user's input. The failure count starts over. Refused when the session is not held (session_not_held) or is running.

  • A plain message while held (run.start, session.input, an older client) resumes the same way: it is the user acting.
  • No discard (user decision of 2026-10-26): Resume always sends the pending messages.
  • The parent resumes a held subagent (user decision of 2026-10-26): its delegate_subagent with the child's resume_session_id, or its send_message to the child, clears the child's hold as the user's message does, with the parent's prompt or mail as the input. Only the session's own parent can; other agents in the tree are refused. A held subagent's turn reports to the parent as failed, with the hold's reason in the report (status="held"), so the parent can decide.

docs.title: 5. Clients
docs.text:
• Web: while the viewed session is held, the composer's Send and Queue buttons are replaced by Resume, which sends the composer's text, if any, with the held messages. A line in the transcript says why: Stopped by you or Failed 4 times: Anthropic request failed (400) ..., with the pending messages counted (2 messages waiting).
  • TUI: the same line; Enter in the composer resumes (the hint row says Enter resume), and a Resume button in the line, with its hover, does the same.
  • Session lists badge a held session (held).
  • Push (user decision of 2026-10-26): a notification when a root session becomes held for failures (: stopped after 4 failed runs</em>), none for a stop, which the user did.</li> </ul> <h2 id="6-protocols-and-history">6. Protocols and history<a class="headerlink" href="#6-protocols-and-history" title="Permanent link">¶</a></h2> <ul> <li>Client protocol minor bump: the two events, <code>SessionMeta.held</code>, <code>session.resume</code>, and the errors <code>session_held</code> and <code>session_not_held</code>. An older client sees the events as unknown records; its plain message still resumes.</li> <li>Plugin and runtime protocols minor bump: <code>producer.send</code> may answer <code>session_held</code>.</li> <li>History format: additive events, no conversion.</li> </ul> <h2 id="7-tests">7. Tests<a class="headerlink" href="#7-tests" title="Permanent link">¶</a></h2> <ul> <li>A run failing with a non-retryable error: <code>standard_retries</code> retries with their backoff, then <code>automatic_runs_held { failing }</code>, and no run after it; a pending goal does not keep the session going.</li> <li>A goal whose runs fail after consuming their reminder: held at the budget, no new reminders.</li> <li>Stop: held at once; the pending report goes with the resume.</li> <li>While held: <code>producer.send</code> refused, agent mail refused, a cron fire skipped, a subagent report deferred and delivered on resume.</li> <li>A restart: an interrupted run resumes; a held session stays held.</li> <li><code>session.resume</code> with and without content, and refused when not held; a plain message resumes.</li> <li>A held subagent: its report to the parent says <code>held</code>; the parent's <code>delegate_subagent</code> resume and its <code>send_message</code> clear the hold; a sibling's mail is refused.</li> <li>A push for a hold for failures, none for a stop.</li> <li>Clients: the Resume button in place of Send and Queue, the transcript line, the TUI's Enter and button hover.</li> </ul> <h2 id="8-decisions">8. Decisions<a class="headerlink" href="#8-decisions" title="Permanent link">¶</a></h2> <p>All of 2026-10-26, by the user:</p> <ol> <li>No Discard: Resume always sends the pending messages.</li> <li>A push when a session becomes held for failures, none for a stop.</li> <li>The parent resumes a held subagent with <code>delegate_subagent</code> (<code>resume_session_id</code>) or <code>send_message</code>; other agents cannot.</li> </ol> <h2 id="9-implementation-notes-2026-10-26">9. Implementation notes (2026-10-26)<a class="headerlink" href="#9-implementation-notes-2026-10-26" title="Permanent link">¶</a></h2> <p>Where the implementation differs from the text above, this section wins.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Method name.</strong> <code>session.resume</code> already opens a session, so the resume is <code>session.held.resume { session_id }</code> → <code>{ resumed }</code>. It is idempotent: a session that is not held answers <code>resumed: false</code>, and there is no <code>session_not_held</code> error. With text in the composer, the clients send it as a normal message, which clears the hold.</li> <li><strong>Refusals reuse existing codes.</strong> A plugin's or runtime's <code>producer.send</code> gets <code>producer_rejected</code> with <em>the session is held (...)</em> as its detail, instead of a new <code>session_held</code> error, so the plugin and runtime error surfaces are unchanged. Agent mail fails with <code>send_message:recipient_held: the session is held (...)</code>.</li> <li><strong>The engine's own producers are accepted and wait.</strong> Subagent turn reports, delegation completions, background tool results, and goal controls are recorded while held and go with the resume, which the hold already guarantees. Goal reminders are not made.</li> <li><strong>A stop</strong> is a <code>run_finished</code> <code>cancelled</code> whose envelope origin is a client or the user. A cancel the engine makes (shutdown, a parent stopping its subagent) does not hold. A stop holds only when something could start a run on its own: a pending producer message, an active goal, or a live producer registration (a background call, a subagent, a plugin or runtime). With nothing such, there is nothing to hold, and the composer keeps Send.</li> <li><strong>A revert</strong> that leaves producer messages waiting from before the cut holds the session as a stop does, so the next run is the user's; what arrives later (a surviving background call's result) wakes it as before.</li> <li><strong>The failure count</strong> runs back from the latest event to the last <code>completed</code> run, <code>user_input_submitted</code>, or <code>automatic_runs_resumed</code>; <code>interrupted</code> runs are skipped, and producer messages never reset it. The held state is that walk's result, so it survives restarts.</li> <li><strong>Subagent reports keep their status.</strong> A report is rendered at the child's run end, before the hold is recorded, so it says <code>failed</code> or <code>cancelled</code> as before rather than <code>held</code>, and a hold sends no report of its own (one would wake the parent, which could undo the user's stop).</li> <li><strong>Clients.</strong> The transcript records each hold as a warning row and each resume as an info row. The web composer shows <strong>Resume</strong> in place of Send and Queue, with a <em>Held — ...</em> status line after the transcript. The TUI draws a banner on the conversation's last row with a <em>resume</em> button (<code>PointerTarget::HeldResume</code>), and Enter in an empty composer resumes. Session lists show a held session as <code>SessionActivity::Held</code>, sorted with the active ones: a pause before its title on the web (red when held for failures, <code>held: <reason></code> as its tooltip), and <code>⏸</code> in the TUI (added 2026-10-26).</li> <li><strong>Tests:</strong> <code>crates/engine/src/runtime/tests/held_sessions.rs</code> (failures to the budget and a resume, a stop, a goal that keeps failing, the parent's and a sibling's mail, the push), the cron skip in <code>tests/crons.rs</code>, the updated delegation and producer tests, <code>client_state::held</code>, the web's composer buttons, and the TUI's pointer sweep.</li> </ul>

docs.title: MCP tool filters
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-23); see Implementation notes. Builds on permission consolidation and the MCP scope work in the runtimes spec.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
An MCP server publishes every tool it lists, each as <server>_<tool>. Two things are missing:

  • No way to drop a server's tools. A server that offers 40 tools, of which three are useful, costs every agent the other 37 in its tool list.
  • Permissions gate calls, not the tool list. With mcp: {"my_chrome_*": allow}, an agent may call only my_chrome_* tools, but it is offered every MCP tool of every server, because a tool is offered when any merged mcp rule allows or asks (MergedRules::offers). Calls to the others are denied, wasting turns.

Decided 2026-10-23:

  • Each MCP server takes include_tools and exclude_tools, patterns over the server's own tool names with * and ?, applied before its tools are published (section 2).
  • An MCP tool is offered only when the merged rules do not deny its published name (section 3, confirmed 2026-10-23).

Out of scope: filtering prompts or resources, renaming tools, per-agent server lists (permissions cover that, section 3).

docs.title: 2. Per-server filters
docs.text:
[mcp.servers.my_chrome]
url = "https://example.test/mcp"
include_tools = ["browser_*"]          # default: every tool
exclude_tools = ["browser_install"]    # applied after include_tools
  • Where: every place an MCP server is configured: [mcp.servers.<name>], [runtimes.<id>.mcp.servers.<name>], and the [runtimes.local.mcp] servers a dial-in runtime reads from its own machine.
  • What they match: the tool's name as the server lists it (browser_click), not the published <server>_<tool> name, so a filter survives a server rename. Patterns use * (any characters) and ? (one character), as permission patterns do; a pattern without either is an exact name.
  • Order: a tool is published when it matches include_tools (every tool when the field is absent) and matches no exclude_tools pattern.
  • When: to the server's tools/list result and to every refresh after notifications/tools/list_changed. Filtering happens where the server runs (the daemon, a runtime template's runtime, or a dial-in runtime), so no protocol carries the filters.
  • Validation: an empty pattern, or an include_tools that is present but empty, is a configuration error, so a server cannot silently publish nothing.
  • Status: the server's status reports how many tools were filtered out (12 tools, 30 filtered). McpServerStatus gains an optional filtered_tools count (client protocol minor, additive).
  • Clients: the TUI and web MCP server editors gain both fields; the MCP sheet shows the filtered count.

docs.title: 3. MCP tools offered by their permission
docs.text:
• The rule: an MCP tool is offered only when the run's merged rules (permission consolidation section 3) do not deny mcp for its published name, on the tool's runtime. allow and ask offer it; deny, or no matching rule, hides it.
  • Example: mcp: {"my_chrome_*": allow} offers only the my_chrome_* tools; with the default mcp: {"*": ask}, every MCP tool is offered and asks.
  • Why only MCP: an MCP tool's permission resource is its own name, known when the tool list is built. Other actions' resources (a path, a command, a URL) are known only from a call's arguments, so they stay offered by action.
  • Grants: an "allow for this session" grant offers a tool its pattern covers, unless the merged rules deny it, as grants do today.
  • Composition: the per-name check runs when tools are composed for a model request, after the per-server filters, so the tool list changes when a session override changes.

docs.title: 4. Compatibility
docs.text:
• Configuration gains two optional fields per MCP server.
  • McpServerStatus.filtered_tools: optional, client protocol minor.
  • Section 3 is a behaviour change with no wire change: agents with narrow mcp rules see fewer tools. Noted in the protocol changelog.

docs.title: 5. Tests
docs.text:
• Filters: include only, exclude only, both (exclude wins), exact names, ?, a server rename keeping the filter, a list-changed refresh filtered, the filtered count, configuration errors; the same for a runtime template's server and a dial-in runtime's local server.
  • Per-tool offering: narrow allow offers only matching tools; ask offers; a deny pattern hides one tool of an allowed server; a session override changes the list; grants.

docs.title: 6. Docs
docs.text:
• docs/site/extend/mcp.md: the two fields with an example, and that narrow mcp rules now also narrow the tool list.
  • The configuration reference for the MCP server table.
  • The protocol changelog.

docs.title: 7. Phases
docs.text: One phase: config and filtering in cookie_agent_mcp, the status count, per-tool offering in the engine, the clients' editor fields, docs.

docs.title: 8. Open questions
docs.text: None.

docs.title: 9. Implementation notes
docs.text:
Landed 2026-10-23 in one phase, as section 7 planned. Client protocol 1.16.0, runtime protocol 1.6.0; the plugin protocol and history format 1 are unchanged.

  • Configuration. McpServerConfig (crates/config/src/runtime.rs) gains include_tools: Option<Vec<String>> and exclude_tools: Vec<String>, both omitted when written back unset, and publishes_tool(name), which matches with the permission patterns' simple_wildcard_match. validate refuses an empty pattern and a present but empty include_tools; every place a server is configured already runs it (top-level servers, runtime templates including [runtimes.local], /mcp add and edit, and the coding runtime parsing the tables the daemon or a dial-in runtime's own configuration hands it), so no protocol carries the filters.
  • Filtering. ServerRuntime::publish_tools_before_commit (crates/mcp/src/lib.rs), the one path both the first listing and every list_changed refresh go through, drops the tools the filters reject before converting and claiming names, so a filtered tool cannot collide either. The count is kept per server, reset when the server fails, and a relist that changes only the filtered tools updates the status without republishing.
  • Status. The registry's McpServerStatus.filtered_tools; on the wire it is McpServerInfo.filtered_tools (the client protocol's status type, which section 2 calls McpServerStatus) and McpServerReport.filtered_tools in the runtime protocol, which carries runtimes' server statuses. Both are optional and absent when nothing was filtered.
  • Editors.
