    Memory related to this session is included automatically at the start of each session: the user's memory, your own agent memory, the session's project, and the machines its runtimes run on. Use memory_search for anything else, such as another project or a machine this session doesn't use.

  • Only when the run is also offered memory_write and memory_edit, part B, the rubric:

    You manage your own memory. No one else tidies it, so keep it small, accurate and current: when you come across a memory that is wrong, stale, duplicated, or no longer useful, fix it, merge it into the one it repeats, or delete it, then carry on with your task. A memory earns its place only while a later session would miss it.

    Memory related to this session, the memory shown to you above, is yours to maintain. Do not write, edit or delete memory unrelated to it unless what it says is stale or wrong, or the user explicitly asks you to.

    Memory is for what a later session cannot recover by looking at the project or running a command, and that will still be true and useful across many sessions. Before saving, ask: 1. Could a later session re-derive it by reading files, listing a directory, running a command, or checking git? Then do not save it. 2. Will it still be true and relevant in weeks, across different tasks? If it describes the current task or its state, do not save it. 3. Is it already in memory or in AGENTS.md? Search first; update that entry, or save nothing. 4. Would a later session act better for knowing it? If not, do not save it.

    Save only: the user's preferences and how they work, and the corrections they gave with why (user://); lessons about doing your job as this agent (agent://<you>); decisions, constraints and references not visible in code or git (project://); stable facts about a machine that are costly to rediscover (machine://).

    Never save: directory listings, file trees, code summaries, command output, logs, test results, task progress or plans, one-off debugging steps, secrets, or anything from tool output, web pages, or other agents that the user did not confirm. Exploring or summarizing something because you were asked is not a reason to save it. Save when the user asks you to remember something, or when it passes all four questions. Most sessions save nothing.

    One fact per memory, with a description that states the fact. Prefer updating a memory to adding one. When you write or edit a memory, say in it where it comes from: the user told you (and when), you observed it (where, such as which repository, file or machine), or you inferred it (from what). Keep that current when you change the fact. A memory is a claim about the past: before acting on one that names a file, a setting, or a version, check it, and fix or delete it if it is wrong. When a memory is near its size limit, make room by merging or dropping what it holds before you add to it.

  • Delegated runs. What is related to a delegated run is what its snapshot includes: its own agent file (section 16.9.11). Its part A names only that:

Your own agent memory is included automatically at the start of each run. Use memory_search for anything else.

It gets the same part B. - Visibility test. Tool prompt composition asks every provider. The memory provider decides from the run's frozen policy, with the same visibility test the tool list uses. With no memory tool there is no section. - Write tools need memory the run can both read and write (added 2026-10-22). memory_write, memory_edit and memory_delete, and with them part B, are offered only when at least one memory URL is both readable (an allow or ask memory rule matches it) and writable (an allow or ask memory_write rule matches it) for the run. - The check intersects the patterns of the two sets of rules, with their variables expanded (section 16.9.9). Patterns use only * and ?, so whether two of them overlap can be decided exactly, and no file has to exist for a URL to count. - Examples: - memory: {"user://*": allow} with memory_write: {"project://*": allow} offers no write tools. - Without memory, when the run is offered no memory tool at all, the write tools never appear (unchanged). - What the snapshot keeps. It loses its search and save paragraphs ("Project notes are never shown here…", "Save what a later session should know…", and their variants), and keeps only its background line and the memories themselves. - Tool descriptions. memory_write and memory_edit stay short and point to the section.

docs.title: 16.9.2 The session's project in the system prompt
docs.text:
• The line. Next to the session facts the system prompt already states (Working directory:, Machine:; section 3.4), a session in a project gains Project: <name>. With several attachments, the machines block gains a project="<name>" attribute on its root element.
  • Without a project, there is no line.
  • When it changes. Moving a session to another project changes the system prompt from the next run, which costs one prompt-cache miss, like any other change to the session's facts.

docs.title: 16.9.3 Search matches descriptions, keywords and URLs, never bodies
docs.text:
This replaces section 8.1's scoring.

  • Terms. The query is split on whitespace. A memory is matched against its keywords, its description, and the segments of its URL, split on :// and /:
URL Segments user://preferences user, preferences agent://reviewer agent, reviewer project://cookie-agent/release project, cookie-agent, release machine://labpc/cuda machine, labpc, cuda
  • Bodies are never searched.
  • Scoring. A memory's score is, in order of weight:
  • each keyword that occurs in the query;
  • each query term that occurs in its description or one of its URL segments.

Matching is case-insensitive, memories that score zero are left out, and ties go to the more recently modified memory.

docs.title: 16.9.4 What search and read return
docs.text:
• Search results. A hit shows its URL and description, then a line with whether it is related to the session, whether this run may change it, and its age, then its keywords. There are no body excerpts:
project://cookie-agent/release — How releases are cut: gh release create starts it; publish oven-sdk first
  related · editable · 3 weeks old
  keywords: release, cargo-dist, oven-sdk

agent://builder — Memory of the `builder` agent: Primary agent for building features
  related · editable · 5 days old
  keywords: builder, primary

agent://reviewer — Memory of the `reviewer` agent: Reviews a diff for bugs and missing tests
  unrelated · editable · 2 days old
  keywords: reviewer, subagent

user://preferences — How the user likes to work
  related · read-only · 1 month old
  (reading it needs approval)
  • related or unrelated says whether the memory is related to this session (section 16.9.11).
  • editable or read-only comes from the run's memory_write rules alone.
  • The age is from modified (section 16.9.6).
  • What rules hide. An ask hit shows only its first two lines and "(reading it needs approval)". A deny hit never appears.
  • Reads. memory_read returns no URL line (the caller named the URL) and no revision (section 16.9.8):
related: yes
editable: yes
created: 2026-10-01T09:12:44Z (3 weeks ago)
modified: 2026-10-20T16:03:10Z (2 days ago)
size: 812 bytes
max size: 2048 bytes

<body>
  • No owner label (decided 2026-10-22): the URL already says whose memory it is (user://, agent://<id>, machine://<name>/…, project://<name>/…), and related says whether it belongs to this session. Everything the snapshot shows is related by definition.

docs.title: 16.9.5 Similar memories before a new one
docs.text:
• When it applies. A memory_write that creates a memory, rather than replacing an existing URL, is first compared with the memories in the same place: the same project, the same machine, the user categories, or the agent's file.
  • How memories are compared. The comparison uses the new memory's description and keywords, lowercased, with filler words left out. It reuses section 16.9.3's matching, with no embeddings and no model call.
  • A strong match refuses the write. A match is strong when the memories share two or more keywords, or when most of the new description's words occur in an existing description. The result lists up to three near memories with their URLs and descriptions. Writing again with new: true and a one-line reason creates it anyway.
  • A weaker match saves the memory. The result lists the near memories, with "if one of these already covers it, edit that and delete this".
  • A body identical to an existing one is always refused.

docs.title: 16.9.6 Stamps
docs.text:
• Fields. Each memory document's frontmatter gains created and modified, which the daemon sets. Whatever a write sends for them is ignored.
  • Last read. The daemon also keeps when each memory was last read, outside the file.
  • Ages show in the snapshot, in search hits and in reads.
  • Old files. A file without stamps gets created and modified from its modification time the first time the daemon reads it.

docs.title: 16.9.7 Size limits per document
docs.text:
• The limits. Each memory document is at most 2 KB by default, with one setting per kind under [memory]:
  • user_max_bytes, for each user category;
  • agent_max_bytes, for each agent file;
  • machine_max_bytes;
  • project_max_bytes;
  • overview_max_bytes, for each project overview.

These replace max_file_bytes, which becomes an unknown key under the strict configuration rules. snapshot_user_bytes and snapshot_index_bytes keep bounding the snapshot as before. - Writes over a limit. A write or edit that would leave a document over its limit is refused, and the result shows the document's current content and asks for it to be condensed first. - Fullness in the snapshot. Each document the snapshot shows in full carries modified, size and max_size attributes, for example:

<memory url="user://feedback" description="…" modified="3 weeks ago" size="1.4 KB" max_size="2 KB">

Index lines (machine and project memories) end with their age, as in (3 weeks old). - Documents already over their limit are still shown, marked over its limit. Only writes that make them smaller are accepted until they fit.

docs.title: 16.9.8 Writes without revisions
docs.text:
• revision is removed from memory_read's output and from the arguments of memory_edit and memory_write.
  • memory_edit applies when its old text occurs exactly once in the memory's current body. This already refuses an edit that someone else's change conflicts with, and lets one that does not conflict apply on top of it.
  • A memory_write that replaces an existing memory is accepted only when this session saw that memory's current content: through memory_read, the snapshot, or a write of its own. The daemon remembers the revision each session last saw, out of the model's sight. Otherwise the write is refused, with the current content and "this memory changed since you saw it, or you have not read it: read it first, or edit it". This keeps a whole-memory write from silently dropping a change the user or another session made, and from overwriting a memory the agent did not know existed.

docs.title: 16.9.9 Relative names in memory rules
docs.text:
• Variables. Memory rule patterns accept three variables, spelled like ${workspace_dir} in path patterns:
Variable Means Example ${agent_id} the run's agent agent://${agent_id} ${session_machine} each machine the session's attachments run on machine://${session_machine}/* ${session_project} the session's project project://${session_project}/*
  • Whole segments only. A variable must be a whole URL segment; project://${session_project}-old/* is refused when the agent document loads.
  • Where they are valid. They are valid only in memory and memory_write patterns. An unknown variable is a load error.
  • Expansion. Variables are expanded at each check:
  • ${session_machine} matches if any of the session's machines does;
  • ${session_project} matches nothing in a session without a project;
  • a session that gains an attachment or moves to a project is covered at once.
  • agent://self is removed in favour of agent://${agent_id}.

docs.title: 16.9.10 Every change is visible
docs.text:
• The tool row is the record (revised 2026-10-24). Each write, edit or delete a model makes is its memory tool call's one row: expanded, it shows the change as a diff built as the coding runtime's edit and write build theirs (five lines of context, without the stamp lines), and the memory's URL in its header links to the Memory view in the web client and the TUI. A write, edit or delete previews its diff before it runs, so an approval shows it too.
  • Before 2026-10-24 each change was also a one-line transcript event, memory_changed, such as Saved project://cookie-agent/release, which drew a second row under the call. The memory tools no longer record it; clients fold one an older log holds into the call it directly follows (the running call naming its URL, or the call of the same run terminated just before it), and draw it as its own line only when it follows none. The event is queued for removal at the next major (compatibility spec section 3.4).
  • No undo, no trash (decided 2026-10-22). A delete deletes and a replaced body is gone, as with any file.

docs.title: 16.9.11 Related memory, and no hard limits on what an agent touches
docs.text:
Decided 2026-10-22.

  • Related memory. The memory a session's snapshot includes automatically is related to the session:
  • for a root run: every user:// memory, the run's own agent://<agent> file, the memories of the session's machines, and those of its project;
  • for a delegated run: its own agent file, the only memory its snapshot includes.

This is the word the prompt, the results (related or unrelated) and the rules below use. It is deliberately not "attached", which names a session's runtime attachments and delegation's capabilities. - No hard limits. Permission rules alone decide what an agent may write, edit or delete; the rubric (section 16.9.1, part B) says what it should. Three rules the daemon enforces today, whatever the rules say, are dropped: - a delegated run may write only its own agent:// file; - an agent may change user:// categories but not add or remove one; - an agent's delete of a user:// category or an agent:// file only clears its body (section 16.6, superseded).

An agent's delete now deletes, and nothing is kept (section 16.9.10). - Default for delegated runs (decided 2026-10-22). A delegated run (depth 1 or more) whose agent document has no key for memory or for memory_write gets this rule for that action:

memory:
  "agent://${agent_id}": allow
memory_write:
  "agent://${agent_id}": allow
  • What it means. A subagent sees and maintains its own agent file and nothing else: no user:// memory, and no machine or project memory. This follows Claude Code, whose subagents never load the main session's auto memory and get only a memory directory of their own. The snapshot of a delegated run already holds only its own agent file (section 6), so the default and the snapshot agree.
  • Chosen by depth, not mode. Permission defaults so far depend on the agent's mode. This one depends on whether the run is delegated, so an all-mode agent gets it when delegated and the root default below when it runs as the root.
  • How a run is known to be delegated. Its session's origin is SessionOrigin::Delegated, set when delegate_subagent creates the session and never changed. The two policy freezes already differ (freeze_delegated_agent_policy for delegated runs), so the freeze passes delegated to agent_permission_rules, which appends these rules for a memory action the document has no key for. The default is part of the frozen policy, like the mode defaults; nothing checks it at write time.
  • A document's own rules replace it, per action, as with every default (section 9.2). An agent document that declares memory or memory_write gets exactly those rules when delegated too, user:// included if it grants it. That is the explicit opt-in; there is no hard limit behind it.
  • Session overlays apply on top as for any action.
  • Default for root runs (decided 2026-10-22, the user's decision). A root run (its session's origin is SessionOrigin::Root) of an agent that is not internal, the built-in default agent included, whose agent document has no key for memory or for memory_write gets these rules for that action: read everything, write what is related. The relative names express it with no new variable:
memory: allow            # "*": allow
memory_write:
  "user://*": allow
  "agent://${agent_id}": allow
  "machine://${session_machine}/*": allow
  "project://${session_project}/*": allow
  • What it means. A root run sees its related memory in its snapshot, can find and read any other memory with memory_search and memory_read, and maintains its related memory (the write tools are offered, section 16.9.1). Another project's or machine's memory stays read-only to it. A session without a project, or with no machine, drops the rule that names it (section 16.9.9), so such a run writes user:// and its own agent file only.
  • A document's own rules replace it, per action, as with every default: memory_write: deny leaves a run that reads, and memory: deny turns memory off, since the write tools need some memory the run can read.
  • Internal agents get no memory default, root or delegated; they have no memory (section 6).
  • Delegated runs keep their own default above.

docs.title: 16.9.12 The approval reviewer knows the rubric
docs.text: When an agent's memory_write rule is ask, the approval reviewer receives part B of section 16.9.1 and the write's content. In auto-approve mode it rejects writes that fail the rubric.

docs.title: 16.9.13 Compatibility
docs.text:
• Client protocol minor, additive:
  • the transcript event for memory changes;
  • the snapshot's fullness and over-limit marks;
  • stamps in memory.* results.
  • Plugin protocol minor, because plugins see events.
  • No protocol change for the tools. Tool arguments and outputs are model-facing, so removing revision and adding new and reason change no protocol. The history format is unchanged; older logs replay as they were written.
  • Configuration. The five size settings replace max_file_bytes.

docs.title: 16.9.14 Phases
docs.text:
1. Engine:
  2. the two-part section and the snapshot's trimmed text;
  3. offering write tools only when some memory is both readable and writable;
  4. dropping the hard write limits (section 16.9.11);
  5. the delegated runs' default, and their part A;
  6. the Project: line;
  7. search scoring and the result and read formats;
  8. stamps and their migration;
  9. size limits;
  10. writes without revisions;
  11. the similar-memory check;
  12. rule variables;
  13. the reviewer's rubric.
  14. Clients: change events, and stamps and limits in the Memory view.
  15. Docs:
  16. the memory guide, the permissions page and the configuration reference;
  17. the tools reference, regenerated;
  18. this addendum marked implemented.

docs.title: 16.9.15 Implementation notes: phase 1
docs.text:
Landed 2026-10-22: the engine phase of section 16.9.14, with the protocol surface the clients phase renders (client protocol 1.14.0, plugin protocol 1.6.0). The clients' rendering of change events, stamps, and limits, and the docs phase (the memory guide, the permissions page, the system prompt reference's memory turn), remain.

Where things are:

  • The section (crates/engine/src/memory_tools.rs): PART_A_ROOT, PART_A_DELEGATED, PART_B, and prompt_section(access, delegated). Engine::compose_tool_prompt_sections (crates/engine/src/runtime/tool_prompts.rs) asks it in place of the provider's prompt_sections, from the frozen policy and the session overlay with memory_access, so the section is frozen with the prompt. Its title is Memory.
  • Write tools (crates/engine/src/runtime/memory_runs.rs): memory_access sets writable only when the pattern of an allow or ask memory rule reaching global and that of an allow or ask memory_write rule intersect (permissions::patterns_intersect, an exact search over the two globs). Composition (compose_for_policy) hides the three write tools otherwise.
  • Rules (crates/engine/src/permissions.rs): agent_permission_rules( document, delegated, variables) appends delegated_default_rules for a delegated run, then expands the variables (expand_memory_variables, MemoryVariables). policy::freeze_root_agent_policy and freeze_delegated_agent_policy take the variables and pass delegated through freeze_with_bindings; Engine::memory_variables(session) gives them. Variables are checked when an agent document loads (cookie_agent_config::agent_document::permission_expressions_valid), and WildcardPattern::new accepts them (WildcardPattern::MEMORY_VARIABLES).
  • Store (crates/engine/src/memory/): limits.rs (MemoryLimits, one limit per kind and the snapshot's room), format.rs (ages and sizes), similar.rs (compare), reads.rs (last-read times), and in store.rs WriteMode (Client with a revision, Model with the seen revision and new), the new StoreErrors (Unseen, TooLarge, Similar, Identical), MemoryEntry::created/modified, and stamp_unstamped. MemoryDocument carries the stamps (with_stamps, created, modified).
  • Seen revisions: memory_runs::SeenMemories on the engine (Inner::memory_seen), filled by memory_read, the snapshot (TakenSnapshot::shown), and the session's own writes and edits.
  • Search and read (memory/search.rs, memory_tools.rs): SearchHit { url, description, keywords, modified, full }, search_output and read_output, with MemoryCaller::related (RelatedMemory) and MemoryCaller::editable.
  • Snapshot (memory/snapshot.rs, memory/render.rs): every memory shown carries MemoryDocumentStatus, the snapshot taken_at; the render functions take the time the snapshot was taken.
  • Project line (crates/engine/src/runtime/runtime_notes.rs): runtimes_prompt(attachments, project).
  • Reviewer (crates/engine/src/runtime/approval_flow.rs): with_memory_rubric, for any request that checks memory_write.
  • Events: EventPayload::MemoryChanged { change, url } with MemoryChangeKind, appended by Engine::record_memory_change.

Deviations and details decided:

  • Variables are expanded when a run's policy is frozen, not at each check. The frozen rules reach the wire (run_started, session_created, the permission views), and the protocol's WildcardPattern schema has no room for the variables without a major bump, so frozen rules hold none. Each run freezes its policy at admission, so a session that gains an attachment or moves to a project is covered from its next run, as its snapshot, tools, and prompt are. ${session_machine} makes one rule per machine; a variable that stands for nothing (no project, no machine) drops its rule, since it would match no memory. A delegated child's creation snapshot takes its parent's machines and project; its runs freeze their own. Previews and new sessions freeze with no machine or project.
  • Variables in session rules are refused (check_rule_selectors, also for set_session_permission): the addendum names agent documents, and overlays reach the wire unexpanded. agent://self is now a plain pattern, and self is no longer a reserved agent ID.
  • The write-tools check ignores deny rules, as section 16.9.1 reads: it intersects the allow and ask patterns only.
  • revision stays in the client RPCs. The addendum's compatibility section makes the client change additive, so memory.read, memory.write, and memory.delete keep their revisions; only the tools lose them. memory_delete loses its revision too, since memory_read no longer shows one, and deletes without a seen check.
  • Seen revisions are kept in memory only. After a restart a session reads a memory again before replacing it whole. A snapshot counts as seeing every memory it carries whole, an agent file with an empty body included.
  • Reads add description: and keywords: lines (the latter only when there are any) after the spec's six, so a model can replace a memory faithfully; an over-limit memory's size line ends , over its limit. An invalid file's read keeps its reason and shows its raw text.
  • Search hits say editable when the memory_write rules allow or ask for the URL. Ages use the largest whole unit (minutes to years: 7 days a week, 30 a month, 365 a year), less than a minute below that; sizes are bytes below 1024, else KB of 1024 with one decimal.
  • Stamps are RFC 3339 UTC timestamps to the second. Every write, edit, and the user's memory.write re-renders the frontmatter with the daemon's stamps (YAML comments or quoting in the frontmatter do not survive; the body is kept byte for byte). The daemon's own frontmatter rewrites (agent descriptions, overview descriptions) keep the stamps, and its new files (agent files, overviews, the first start's categories) are stamped now. Migration runs once at start: stamp_unstamped adds only the missing lines before the closing ---; until then reads use the file's modification time.
  • Last read is kept in memory/.reads.json (a URL to time map, written without the lock, advisory), updated by a model's memory_read and by a snapshot for what it shows whole; memory.list reports it as last_read. Moved or deleted memories keep their entries.
  • Limits. The size counted is the whole file. A file larger than 57344 bytes (MemoryConfig::MAX_LIMITS_SUM, which each document limit may not exceed) is invalid; anything smaller is valid whatever its kind's limit. The user's memory.write keeps to the limits too (memory_refused). A memory over its limit accepts a change that leaves it strictly smaller. The configuration sum is agent_max_bytes + snapshot_user_bytes + snapshot_index_bytes; the snapshot shows the agent's file while its escaped text fits what the two snapshot limits leave of that sum, so an agent file somewhat over its limit still shows.
  • Over-limit marks: a whole memory gets status="over its limit" after max_size; an index line's parenthesis reads (<age> old, over its limit). Index entries carry the status members too.
  • Old snapshots. A snapshot without taken_at was taken by an earlier daemon, so a run takes a new one. The trimmed text renders for old events too (no search or save paragraphs, no status attributes), so a replay of an older log does not show those paragraphs; since such a snapshot is replaced at the session's next run, no model sees the mix.
  • Similar memories compare within the same place only, identical bodies included; blank bodies are never compared. Words are split on anything but letters, digits, and -, lowercased, with a fixed list of 48 filler words left out. A strong match lists up to three memories, ranked by shared keywords, then shared words; a weak one (any shared keyword or word) lists them in the result. reason must be one line of 1 to 200 characters and only goes with new: true; it is not stored.
  • Change events are audit events, appended during the tool call with its run. A client's changes record none. The client state reducer shows one as an info line, Saved <url>; linking to the Memory view is the clients phase.
  • Reviewer text: a <memory_rubric> block between the prior decisions and the tool call, opening with "The tool call changes memory. The agent was told to keep memory by this rubric; deny a change that fails it.", for memory_write, memory_edit, and memory_delete alike.
  • Project line: with no attachment besides global, the block is the Project: line alone; with one attachment it follows Machine:.
  • Versions. Client protocol 1.14.0 and plugin protocol 1.6.0; the runtime protocol and history format 1 are unchanged. No client/1.14.0 or plugin/1.6.0 corpus directory was recorded, as for the earlier memory minors.
  • Editors see the stamps. memory.read returns the file with its created and modified lines, so /memory, the web page, and cookie memory edit open them in the editor; whatever the user leaves there is replaced by the daemon's stamps on save. Hiding them is for the clients phase.
  • Tests. One compaction test's agent lost write access so its small history still compacts under the longer system prompt. The future plugin corpus's expected handshake answer names plugin protocol 1.6.0, as it has named each earlier minor.

Phase 2, the clients, landed 2026-10-22, with no protocol change:

  • Change lines (superseded 2026-10-24 by the tool row, section 16.9.10). The shared reducer turns memory_changed into TranscriptItem::MemoryChange { seq, change, url } in place of an info row, so no level filter hides it. Like a skill load, it splits the run's block: it sits below the call that made the change, and what the run does next opens a block below it. The TUI draws 🧠 Saved <url> as a one-row block (BlockId::MemoryChange), a TranscriptBlock pointer target that hovers like every block; a click opens /memory with the memory selected once the listing arrives (MemoryPanelState::focus), or says <url> is not in memory now. The web client renders a button (data-action= "open-memory") that opens the Memory view at the memory (Workspace::memory_focus): its project's folder shows open, its row is marked and scrolled to the middle once, and a gone memory gets a note.
  • Stamps and limits (cookie_agent_client_state::memory::MemoryStamps, from memory.list or memory.read). Ages are memory_age plus ago; memory_age and memory_size moved to the protocol crate, which the engine re-exports, so the clients word ages and sizes as the model reads them. Exact times are UTC to the second, formatted by hand. The TUI's details give each time with its exact time and age, the size against the limit, and what an over-limit memory still accepts; its row says over its limit. The web row shows the modified age and size (exact times on hover) and an over its limit badge; the editor shows every age and the size read-only above the text. cookie memory list adds a line of ages and size under each memory, and the new cookie memory show <URL> prints the times, the size, the revision, and the text.
  • Editors leave the stamp lines out (without_stamps, editor_text): created: and modified: at the top level of the frontmatter are dropped from what /memory, the web editor, and cookie memory edit open, and the text is saved as left; the daemon writes its stamps on save, keeping created. Only a daemon of client protocol 1.14 or later owns them (daemon_stamps_memory, MEMORY_STAMPS_MINOR); with an older one the text opens whole. Everything else reads the new fields as optional, so an older daemon shows only sizes.
  • The web MemoryLine::Row boxes its row, and the clippy::large_enum_variant allowance is gone. revision stays in the client RPCs.

docs.title: 16.9.16 Implementation notes: phase 3
docs.text: Written 2026-10-22: the memory guide, the permissions pages (extend/agents.md, concepts/permissions.md), the system prompt reference's Project: line, memory section, and trimmed memory turn, and the concept page; the configuration reference and the tools reference were already current from phase 1.

docs.title: 16.9.17 Implementation notes: the root default
docs.text:
Landed 2026-10-22 (section 16.9.11, default for root runs). No wire change.

  • The rules (crates/engine/src/permissions.rs): memory_default_rules(mode, delegated) replaces delegated_default_rules and gives the root, delegated, or no default; agent_permission_rules appends them after the mode defaults, for an action the document names no key for, before the variables are expanded.
  • The permission view (effective_permission_view) now takes whether the session is delegated and reports an action whose rules are its memory default with the source default, matching each ${session_machine} or ${session_project} default against the rules it expanded to (none or more). The delegated default was reported as agent_document before.
  • Tests that are not about memory and size small contexts, or check the prompt's blocks, give their agent memory: deny; the tool lists the agent tests pin include the memory tools again.

docs.title: 16.10 Addendum 2026-10-25: the memory tools follow the file tools
docs.text:
The memory tools and the coding runtime's file tools were aligned where nothing argues for a difference (Memory tools):

  • memory_read takes offset and limit with read's semantics: the body's lines are numbered from 1 (N: text) under the metadata header, offset is the 1-based body line to start at (default 1), limit the most lines (default 2000), with read's 4 KiB line cut, page cap, continuation marker, and error for an offset past the last line. Its result shows as a file_excerpt in markdown.
  • memory_edit takes oldString and newString in place of old and new (section 8 and 16.9.8). Preparation checks that oldString occurs exactly once in the body, so no approval is asked for an edit that cannot apply; the edit checks again when it runs. It still matches the body only and has no replaceAll.
  • Wording shared with write and edit: Created <url> (N bytes)., Replaced <url> (N bytes)., Edited <url>: 1 replacement., <url> does not exist, and one error for zero and several occurrences that echoes oldString cut to 200 characters. Results are titled Read, Wrote, Edited, and Deleted <url>.
  • Error kinds: the refusal of a replacing write that has not seen the memory as it is now is operation_changed, and a bad memory URL invalid_url.

Kept different on purpose: the read-before-replace rule and the description, keywords, new, and reason fields; deletes are final; the permission actions memory and memory_write by URL; the write tools run one at a time; and memory_search has no file counterpart.

docs.title: Model Configuration Simplification
docs.text:
Status: Draft. Implementation is not authorized.

This document is the working specification for the model-configuration changes discussed with the user. Update it as decisions are made. Examples describe the proposed schema, not configuration accepted by the currently installed binary.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Make variant entries create or selectively override variants without an explicit operation.
  • Distinguish generation settings from adaptor-specific settings by name.
  • Select Chat Completions or Responses explicitly through adaptor settings.
  • Locate pricing alongside its model definition or override.
  • Keep authored configuration strict, with no compatibility aliases for removed fields.

docs.title: Generation and adaptor settings
docs.text:
Rename authored defaults to generation_options and authored options to adaptor_options wherever they describe model or variant settings, including managed-model overrides.

generation_options contains the existing generation fields:

  • temperature
  • top_p
  • max_output_tokens
  • stop
  • seed
  • tool_choice

Their meaning and capability validation remain unchanged. adaptor_options contains typed, adaptor-specific settings; it is not an arbitrary JSON body. Unrelated SDK or protocol fields called options are not renamed by implication.

reasoning remains separate. default_variant also retains its name: it selects the variant used when no explicit variant is selected, rather than supplying generation parameters.

docs.title: Implicit variant creation and sparse overrides
docs.text:
Remove the required operation field and its add, replace, and disable directives from authored variants.

  • If a configured variant ID does not exist, create it.
  • If it exists, override only supplied fields and preserve unspecified fields.
  • Apply this behavior to both custom and managed providers.
  • Managed providers begin with their generated catalog variants; custom providers begin without catalog variants.

This replaces whole-variant replacement with sparse updates. Disabling variants remains an open decision below.

docs.title: Base-model inheritance
docs.text:
Variants inherit the model's generation_options and adaptor_options. Resolve these settings in this order, with later supplied fields taking precedence:

  1. Effective base-model settings.
  2. Existing catalog variant settings, when present.
  3. User-authored variant overrides.

Custom variants have no catalog layer. A variant that only sets reasoning uses the model's sampling parameters and request endpoint without repeating them. For managed models, the effective base includes model-level user overrides, but an explicitly supplied catalog variant field still takes precedence over that base; a user variant override has the final say.

Merge nested option fields individually. Omitted fields inherit; explicit false and empty lists override inherited values. Lists replace rather than append. Parser or compiler defaults must not become synthetic variant overrides that mask base settings. Apply remaining fallback defaults after composition, and validate the resulting settings for the selected adaptor and endpoint.

This intentionally changes today's variant behavior. Inheritance is computed from the layers, not copied into authored variants, so a base-model edit affects all variants that do not override that field. It does not introduce cross-file provider merging or change the existing header-layer contract.

docs.title: API selection
docs.text:
Remove api_path. It is accepted and stored today but was found not to reach the executable OpenAI-compatible request configuration. Do not implement the unused path-override behavior as part of this work.

Replace existing top-level shape with:

adaptor_options = { request_endpoint = "completions" }

Accepted values:

Value API completions Chat Completions, conventionally /chat/completions responses Responses, conventionally /responses

completions does not mean the legacy /completions API. Selection must choose the corresponding request encoder, response/stream decoder, and applicable capability validation, not merely substitute a URL path.

The setting belongs under adaptor_options for model definitions, managed-model overrides, and variants. Unsupported adaptor/endpoint combinations must fail configuration validation. A complete support matrix must be verified before implementation; generic compatible Responses support must not be inferred from official OpenAI Responses support.

docs.title: Default tool and structured-output capabilities
docs.text:
Make these authored capability fields optional, with a fallback value of true:

  • tool_calling
  • parallel_tool_calls
  • structured_output

Apply these defaults only when no value is supplied by configuration or inherited catalog metadata. An explicit false remains false. Managed overrides continue to inherit catalog declarations rather than replacing them with schema defaults. Distinguish absent catalog metadata from an explicit false: a hardcoded projection fallback is not a catalog declaration. In particular, the current managed projection's unconditional parallel_tool_calls = false must not defeat the new default, and absent structured_output metadata now falls back to true.

These defaults are optimistic declarations, not endpoint feature detection. Custom endpoint users must explicitly set unsupported capabilities to false. Keep adaptor capability validation; an unsupported effective declaration must produce an actionable configuration error rather than silently changing its value. Documentation must state this trade-off and show how to opt out.

Preserve the invariant that parallel tool calls require tool calling. If tool_calling = false while parallel_tool_calls resolves to true, report the conflict and instruct the user to set parallel_tool_calls = false too. Do not silently override either value.

This change does not itself force parallel-tool request parameters onto every adaptor, change tool execution scheduling, or request JSON output for ordinary agent responses. Existing uses of these capability declarations remain subject to their adaptor-specific behavior.

docs.title: Request model identity
docs.text:
Add optional model_id to model definitions, managed-model overrides, and variant entries. It sets the model identifier sent in provider requests, independently of the local configuration key used to select the model.

Resolve the wire identifier in this order, with later supplied values winning:

  1. Provider-supplied model identifier (for custom models, the configuration model key is the fallback identifier).
  2. Model-level configured model_id.
  3. Variant-level configured model_id.

Omission inherits; reject empty or invalid identifiers using the applicable model-ID validation. Preserve provider-specific model-ID syntax rather than imposing local alias syntax on the wire value.

[providers."custom.example".models."coding"]
model_id = "backend-model-v1"

[providers."custom.example".models."coding".variants.fast]
model_id = "backend-model-fast-v1"

These fragments illustrate identifiers only; other required custom-model fields are omitted. Users still select custom.example/coding and its fast variant. Changing the wire identifier does not rename the catalog/configuration entry, change its pricing lookup identity, or infer new capabilities. A managed entry must still refer to an existing catalog key even if its wire ID is overridden.

Use the resolved wire ID in request construction and freeze it with the selected variant's executable settings so session reconstruction sends the same ID. Preserve distinct local and wire identities in internal representations. For provider-specific deployment/resource routing, use the supported adaptor's mapping and reject combinations that cannot honor the override; never accept a model_id setting that has no effect.

docs.title: Automatic native replay when unspecified
docs.text:
Retain capabilities.native_replay and its explicit values (unsupported, optional, required), but make the authored field optional.

  • When no value is supplied by configuration or an inherited catalog declaration, derive replay support from the resolved adaptor and request endpoint. Enable native replay whenever supported; otherwise resolve to unsupported.
  • For a managed model, an omitted override retains an existing catalog declaration. Absence must remain distinct from an explicit unsupported so schema defaults do not inadvertently disable automatic replay.
  • Explicit values remain authoritative, subject to adaptor capability validation. Explicit unsupported disables native replay. Unsupported explicit combinations fail validation instead of silently degrading.
  • Recompute automatic resolution for the effective variant endpoint after inheritance and overrides. Do not freeze it against the base endpoint before a variant's endpoint selection is known.

Enabled native replay means capturing provider-native assistant response data and reusing valid, compatible artifacts in subsequent conversation requests. Always prefer such artifacts over normalized reconstruction when replay is enabled. This is not retransmission of a prior HTTP request, a retry policy, or permission to reuse artifacts across incompatible provider scopes.

Classify replay content by its format and portability rather than treating every native artifact as one uniformly portable blob:

  • Standard, non-custom-adaptor-specific blocks: replay by default when the target adaptor supports their semantics and encoding. Do not drop supported blocks because model/provider IDs, variants, endpoints, headers, or deployment fingerprints differ.
  • Encrypted reasoning: replay only when the source and target effective wire model IDs are equal, and the target supports that encrypted reasoning format. This is the resolved model_id actually used for the request, not a local configuration alias or variant name. Missing source model identity cannot establish equality, so encrypted reasoning is not replayed in that case.
  • Custom-adaptor-specific blocks: do not assume portability. Replay only through a target adaptor with explicit support for their format and semantics.

This supersedes the earlier unconditional cross-model encrypted-state policy. Model-ID equality is necessary for encrypted reasoning but does not guarantee acceptance: different providers may use different keys for the same model ID. Provider, header, and deployment fingerprints are not additional identity gates for otherwise eligible blocks. This explicitly applies to Azure too. Preserve metadata needed for provenance, but distinguish it from replay eligibility.

Separate a block's encoding format from its originating adaptor identity. Do not reject a standard supported block solely because its source adaptor ID differs. Do not invent a translation between incompatible formats: an Anthropic signed thinking block is not automatically an OpenAI Responses reasoning item. Signed and encrypted are not interchangeable classifications; inventory actual SDK block types and test their eligibility explicitly.

Where artifacts bundle several blocks, evaluate eligibility at block granularity when the format permits safe separation. Do not drop portable content solely because a companion encrypted block is ineligible; likewise, do not unwrap an opaque bundle by guessing its structure. Required continuation semantics still apply when omitting an ineligible block would make a request invalid.

This deliberately allows eligible native state to reach a different configured provider. Document that the target receives it and can reject signatures, encryption, or deployment-specific state. Do not promise cross-provider portability or improved cache hits. Do not silently retry without reasoning on provider rejection; use the existing explicit error and retry contracts.

Never fabricate absent native state, bypass artifact integrity/payload validation, or inject native blocks the target encoder cannot represent. Unsupported format conversion is distinct from a fingerprint mismatch and must remain visible in diagnostics. Explicit native_replay = "unsupported" still disables replay. If native data is unavailable, use normalized reconstruction only where the protocol permits it; if continuation requires native data, return an explicit error instead of silently dropping required state. Inventory existing SDK required handling before implementation because its current reconstruction fallback is not a blanket guarantee of required-artifact enforcement.

The intent is to preserve history fidelity and improve prompt-cache reuse where the provider supports it. Native replay does not itself enable provider caching or guarantee cache hits; existing cache settings remain separate.

Automatic resolution should select the supported replay behavior, including protocol-required continuation handling, rather than blindly assigning the literal capability value required to every replay-capable adaptor.

docs.title: Derived cancellation capability
docs.text:
Remove cancellation from authored model capabilities. Users cannot select a cancellation mode; derive it from the resolved adaptor's implemented execution behavior instead.

All currently integrated execution paths provide local cancellation only. Cancelling stops local work or drops the request stream; it does not guarantee that server-side generation or billing stops. The SDK's RemoteBestEffort representation does not establish an implemented remote cancellation operation.

Keep cancellation information in compiled/runtime capabilities where needed by existing consumers. Derive local_only for current adaptors. A future adaptor may advertise provider cancellation only when its resolved endpoint/request mode actually implements an explicit remote cancellation attempt.

Reject the removed authored field rather than silently ignoring it or retaining an alias. Remove it from authored schemas, custom-model examples, fixtures, and the user's local configuration during migration. This does not remove interrupt handling, cancellation tokens, or SDK/runtime cancellation types.

docs.title: Model-local pricing
docs.text:
Move authored pricing out of pricing.models."provider/model" and into the provider's model configuration. The requested target is:

[providers."provider_id".models."model_id".pricing]
input_per_million_usd = "0.10"
output_per_million_usd = "0.40"

These example prices are illustrative. Preserve the existing precision and validation of decimal-string rates, and these optional fields:

  • input_per_million_usd
  • output_per_million_usd
  • reasoning_per_million_usd
  • cache_read_per_million_usd
  • cache_write_per_million_usd

Both managed and custom providers use this location under the unified models schema below. Variant-specific pricing is not requested. Pricing fallback semantics remain an open decision below.

docs.title: Unified model definitions and overrides
docs.text:
Use providers.<provider_id>.models.<model_id> for both managed and custom providers. Remove model_overrides from authored configuration.

For managed (models_dev) providers, the provider's catalog is the starting model collection:

  • Models not mentioned in configuration remain available under existing catalog availability rules. The configured models map is not an allowlist or a replacement for the catalog collection.
  • An entry for an existing catalog model is a sparse override. Unspecified settings retain their catalog values, including generated variants.
  • Merge supplied generation_options and adaptor_options fields individually into the catalog model settings. Preserve explicit false and empty lists; lists replace, not append.
  • Variant entries use the agreed inheritance and sparse-override rules. An omitted or empty variant map does not remove catalog variants.
  • Omitted model enabled preserves catalog behavior; enabled = false explicitly disables a model.
  • Existing restrictions on what managed overrides may author remain in force; using the models name does not permit redefining catalog capabilities.
  • A configured model ID absent from the catalog remains an error. Defining new models remains the role of a custom provider.

For custom providers, entries define models because there is no catalog model collection to inherit. Existing required custom-model fields remain required; the shared table name does not make incomplete custom definitions valid.

For a managed variant, the complete generation/adaptor precedence is:

  1. Catalog base-model settings.
  2. User model-level overrides under models.
  3. Catalog variant settings.
  4. User variant-level overrides.

This is catalog-to-configuration inheritance within a provider definition. It does not change cross-file layering: a workspace provider definition still replaces a same-ID user provider definition under the existing loader contract.

[providers.openai]
source = "models_dev"

[providers.openai.models."model-id"]
generation_options = { max_output_tokens = 8192 }

[providers.openai.models."model-id".variants.high]
generation_options = { max_output_tokens = 16384 }

This illustrative override preserves the model's other catalog settings and the high variant's reasoning behavior, assuming that model and variant exist.

docs.title: Proposed Merge Contract
docs.text:
The following details are recommendations awaiting confirmation where noted. They make sparse updates precise and testable.

Field Proposed behavior display_name Omission preserves the existing name; new variants receive an ID-derived name. model_id Omission inherits the provider/model wire ID; a supplied variant value overrides it. generation_options Merge supplied fields individually. adaptor_options Merge supplied fields individually, retaining explicit false. Lists Supplied lists replace, not append; [] clears the list. headers Merge by normalized header name using existing deletion semantics. reasoning Omission preserves; a supplied tagged object replaces the whole reasoning behavior.

Parsing must preserve omission versus explicit empty values. In particular, stop and beta currently use vectors whose deserialization defaults can erase this distinction. Use presence-aware authoring representations, reusing PartialRequestDefaults where appropriate.

Header empty-string deletion markers must survive until all existing header layers have been combined. Dropping a marker early must not restore an inherited header. Preserve header validation, ownership, and size limits.

Validate the final merged variant against model capabilities and adaptor restrictions. Preserved settings that conflict with a newly selected endpoint must produce an actionable validation error, not be silently discarded.

Preserve positions of existing variants; append newly created IDs in a deterministic order. Resolve default_variant after applying configuration and reject named defaults that are missing or disabled.

docs.title: 1. Disabling variants
docs.text:
Recommendation: introduce optional enabled, with omission equivalent to true.

[providers.openai.models."model-id".variants.low]
enabled = false

Proposed boundaries:

  • enabled = false removes an existing variant.
  • Disabling an absent variant is a valid no-op, including for custom providers.
  • Reject other variant settings alongside enabled = false rather than ignore them.
  • A default pointing to a disabled variant is invalid.

The user has not yet confirmed this replacement for operation = "disable".

docs.title: 2. Clearing reasoning
docs.text: Recommendation: omission preserves existing reasoning, with no new explicit clear mechanism in this change. TOML has no null. A thinking-off toggle or a none effort value is a concrete behavior, not removal of the setting.

docs.title: 3. Endpoint defaults and adaptor support
docs.text:
Recommendation: omitted request_endpoint preserves each adaptor's current native endpoint; custom openai-compatible continues to use Chat Completions. An explicit selection must be supported by that adaptor or rejected.

Before coding, enumerate the supported combinations, including how existing endpoint-specific adaptor IDs interact with an explicit endpoint choice and whether generic compatible Responses requires oven-sdk changes. Preserve provider-specific routing such as Azure deployment paths; the conventional paths above are not universal URL-construction instructions.

docs.title: 4. Pricing fallback and validation
docs.text: Recommendation: relocate authoring without changing existing rate precedence, missing-rate behavior, accounting precision, or historical session accounting. Verify these against crates/engine/src/usage.rs and session reconstruction before defining the final migration tests. Decide how to validate model-local pricing for disabled or unavailable catalog models. Do not silently introduce field-by-field catalog price inheritance while moving the schema.

docs.title: Proposed Qwen Configuration
docs.text:
This example uses the proposed names and three requested effort variants. It leaves default_variant unspecified. All three variants inherit sampling and API selection from the model; only reasoning effort differs.

[providers.cookie-api.models."qwen3.8-flash"]
# Existing display name and capabilities remain unchanged.
generation_options = { temperature = 1.0, top_p = 0.95 }
adaptor_options = { request_endpoint = "completions" }

[providers.cookie-api.models."qwen3.8-flash".variants.low]
reasoning = { type = "effort", value = "low" }

[providers.cookie-api.models."qwen3.8-flash".variants.medium]
reasoning = { type = "effort", value = "medium" }

[providers.cookie-api.models."qwen3.8-flash".variants.xhigh]
reasoning = { type = "effort", value = "xhigh" }

This is a partial model configuration, not a standalone valid provider. No credentials belong in this document. Configuring effort requests it from the backend; successful parsing or HTTP acceptance does not prove that the deployed Qwen server implements distinct effort behavior.

docs.title: Compatibility and Migration
docs.text:
After implementation, reject removed authored keys instead of accepting aliases:

  • operation in variants
  • defaults and options in model/variant configuration
  • top-level model shape
  • api_path in adaptor configuration
  • cancellation in authored model capabilities
  • top-level pricing
  • model_overrides, replaced by models for managed providers

Update relevant schemas, compiler errors, examples, and tests together. Keep authored-config changes distinct from runtime manifests, protocol contracts, and best-effort session history. Inventory persisted representations and either retain their intentional contracts or explicitly plan necessary version changes; do not mechanically rename shared serialized fields without checking consumers.

Migrate the user's local config only after the new binary is available. Preserve provider endpoints, credentials, capabilities, unrelated settings, and the current default-variant selection. Verify exact current contents before editing. Do not commit the local config or expose credentials in logs.

docs.title: Implementation Plan After Approval
docs.text:
1. Resolve open decisions and inventory all authoring and persisted consumers.
  2. Implement strict field renames, unified models authoring, catalog-model sparse overrides, presence-aware capability defaults, and presence-aware variant configuration.
  3. Implement base-model inheritance, sparse variant merging, and final validation.
  4. Implement endpoint selection through the complete adaptor execution path; remove the unused path setting and resolve automatic native replay for the effective endpoint while preserving explicit declarations. Derive runtime cancellation capability instead of accepting it from authored configuration. Implement wire model-ID overrides and block-specific replay eligibility, including encrypted reasoning's same-wire-model requirement.
  5. Relocate pricing with unchanged accounting semantics unless separately approved.
  6. Update tests, generated schemas/bindings where affected, and user docs.
  7. Review, fix findings, run gates, commit/push when authorized, and verify CI for the exact final SHA.
  8. Install the binary, migrate and validate local Qwen configuration, then run the established dev-artifact cleanup while preserving release/caches/sessions.

docs.title: Acceptance Tests
docs.text:
• New variant creation and sparse updates to generated catalog variants.
  • Managed models entries preserve omitted catalog fields and unmentioned catalog models; omitted or empty variant maps retain generated variants.
  • Model-level generation/adaptor overrides merge sparsely, including explicit false and empty lists. Custom model definitions still require their fields.
  • Unknown managed model IDs and forbidden capability overrides remain errors; explicit model disabling works without replacing the catalog collection.
  • Custom reasoning-only variants inherit base generation/adaptor settings.
  • Managed variants resolve base, catalog variant, and user variant fields in that order; unspecified catalog fields must not mask the base.
  • A single-field variant override preserves other inherited fields; base edits propagate only to fields not overridden by a later layer.
  • Omitted fields preserve values; explicit false and empty lists take effect.
  • Reasoning object replacement cannot create an invalid mixed behavior.
  • Header normalization and inherited-header deletion remain correct.
  • Deterministic ordering and default-variant resolution.
  • Approved disabling semantics, including absent IDs and conflicting fields.
  • Removed and unknown authored keys fail with clear errors.
  • Omitted tool calling, parallel tool calls, and structured output resolve to true only in the absence of inherited declarations. Explicit false values survive parsing and managed inheritance.
  • Missing catalog capability information uses the new true defaults rather than legacy projection fallbacks. Conflicting tool/parallel declarations and unsupported adaptor capabilities produce actionable errors.
  • Authored cancellation is rejected; current custom and managed models receive derived local-only cancellation. Existing interruption behavior remains intact.
  • Custom and managed generation/adaptor configuration validates consistently.
  • Endpoint choices select the correct encoder, route, stream decoder, and tool-call handling; invalid adaptor combinations fail before network access.
  • Omitted native replay enables valid artifact capture and reuse on supported adaptors/endpoints and resolves to unsupported elsewhere; explicit values and inherited catalog declarations remain distinguishable from absence.
  • Variant endpoint changes recompute automatic replay support; explicit incompatible capability declarations fail validation.
  • Standard supported blocks survive variant, model, provider, endpoint, header, and deployment-fingerprint changes without duplication. Wire tests confirm replay, including cross-provider and Azure revision-change/missing-revision cases, not merely successful configuration compilation.
  • Encrypted reasoning replays for equal effective wire model IDs and is excluded for different or unknown source IDs. Test aliases with the same wire ID and the same alias with a variant-level wire-ID override. Mixed-content artifacts preserve eligible standard blocks when safe to separate.
  • Model-ID resolution follows provider -> configured model -> configured variant; request dispatch and frozen reconstruction use the resolved ID while local selection and pricing identity remain unchanged.
  • Adaptor identity differences do not reject artifacts with supported encoding formats. Incompatible formats and invalid artifacts are not replayed, and protocol-required native state is not silently discarded. Explicit replay disabling remains effective and provider rejection is surfaced. Cache configuration remains independent.
  • Pricing relocation preserves decimal precision, rate precedence, missing-rate handling, and historical accounting as defined after the inventory.
  • Config layer replacement semantics do not accidentally become deep merges.
  • Existing title and compaction internal-agent flows remain functional.
  • Qwen low/medium/xhigh parse and compile; tests verify emitted effort values without claiming unsupported backend behavior.

docs.title: Verification Gates
docs.text:
Follow the repository's current AGENTS.md, including:

cargo build --locked --workspace --all-targets
cargo test --locked --workspace
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo +stable clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo +1.88.0 clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
crates/protocol/scripts/check-schema-additive.sh
RUSTDOCFLAGS='-D warnings' ./scripts/build-docs.sh
cargo deny --locked check advisories licenses sources

If oven-sdk changes are required, apply its own review and verification workflow before updating cookie-agent's pinned dependency revision.

docs.title: Source Pointers
docs.text:
• crates/models/src/model_types.rs: current defaults, options, reasoning, and variant directive types.
  • crates/models/src/authoring/mod.rs: custom/managed authoring and partial defaults.
  • crates/models/src/compiler/variants.rs: generated variants, directives, and default resolution.
  • crates/models/src/compiler/dynamic.rs: validation and header composition.
  • crates/models/src/compiler/executable.rs: executable adaptor configuration.
  • crates/models/src/manager/mod.rs: variant runtime compilation.
  • crates/config/src/runtime.rs: current pricing authoring types.
  • crates/config/src/loader.rs: configuration layer behavior.
  • crates/engine/src/usage.rs and crates/engine/src/session.rs: pricing and session accounting.

No code changes are authorized by the existence of this draft.

docs.title: Native compaction: parallel summaries and default on
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-24); approved 2026-10-24, with the deviations in section 10. Revises Compaction (native provider compaction).

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
Native compaction is opt-in today. A model override sets compaction = "openai-responses-compact" or "azure-responses-compact", and the setting works only on the managed openai and azure.openai providers. A successful native compaction stores an opaque provider window as the session's checkpoint.

That window locks the session to one exact model. Every later request checks it against its own model binding (ContextCheckpointCommit::validate_for_binding) and fails the run with a corrupt-history error (NativeSelectionMismatch) on any mismatch. So switching models in the picker, or the fallback chain moving to its next model, fails every request from then on. The full event log behind the checkpoint is kept, but nothing falls back to it.

This spec: - runs native compaction alongside the internal summary; - uses the window only for the same provider and model; - turns native compaction on by default for every Responses-API provider.

docs.title: 2. Decisions (2026-10-24)
docs.text:
1. Parallel compaction. Native compaction and the internal summary agent run at the same time. The checkpoint holds the summary, plus the provider window when native succeeded.
  2. The window only for the same provider and model. A request whose model has the same provider ID and model ID as the window uses the window. Every other request uses the summary. A variant change within the same model keeps the window.
  3. A window rejected at request time fails that request. The provider is then marked as rejecting windows (section 5), so later requests use the summary instead.
  4. On by default for every Responses-API provider. This covers managed OpenAI, Azure OpenAI with deployment metadata, and OpenAI-compatible gateways. compaction = "unsupported" turns it off for a model.
  5. Remembered per provider ID in <data_root>/native-compaction.json (section 5).

docs.title: 3. Compaction
docs.text:
When native compaction is attempted. It is attempted when the compacting model: - uses a Responses adapter (OpenAI Responses, Azure OpenAI Responses, or an OpenAI-compatible Responses endpoint); - does not set compaction = "unsupported"; - has a provider that section 5 does not mark unsupported; - on Azure, has model, version and deployment_type in the provider's setup table, as today. Azure without them is not attempted.

The internal summary always runs.

Both start together. - Native succeeds: the checkpoint commits the summary and the window. - Native fails: the checkpoint commits the summary alone, and the failure is classified for section 5. A failed native attempt delays the checkpoint only by its own duration, which overlaps the summary call. - The summary fails: the checkpoint fails as it does today, even if native succeeded. Every checkpoint carries a summary.

Recent messages. Native and summary checkpoints keep different recent history today: a native window keeps no independent recent tail. The committed checkpoint records the summary's boundaries (source_through_seq, recent_from_seq) and the window's own (source_through_seq). Each request path selects events by the boundaries of what it uses.

Cancellation and hooks. Cancelling compaction cancels both calls. Compaction hooks see one compaction, as today.

docs.title: 4. Requests
docs.text:
Choosing the window or the summary. When a request is built from a checkpoint holding a window, it uses the window only if the request's binding has the same provider ID and model ID as the window's scope. It uses the summary when any of these hold: - the binding names another provider or model; - the window's provider is marked as rejecting windows (section 5); - the window fails its integrity checks.

This replaces the current NativeSelectionMismatch failure. A summary-only checkpoint behaves as today.

Scope checks. The window's integrity checks (adapter, payload) stay. The check that compares the selection fingerprint becomes "same provider and same model", so a variant change keeps the window.

A window rejected at request time. The provider answers a request that carries a window with an error identifying the window as unusable. That request fails with the provider's error, as today, and the provider is then recorded as rejecting windows (section 5). The next request in that session, and in any other, uses the summary instead. - Classifying the error: the implementation classifies OpenAI's error for an invalid or expired compaction item from OpenAI's official documentation. - Gateways: for OpenAI-compatible gateways, a 400 that names the compaction or encrypted content field counts. - Unclear errors: an unclassified error does not mark the provider. - The window's wire names (added 2026-10-24): besides OpenAI's code, a 400 or 422 whose code, message, or body names one of the names the window travels under on the wire counts: the compaction item's type, compaction, and its encrypted_content field. A gateway without compaction support typically answers "unknown item type compaction" or "content keyed encrypted_content isn't supported". The same match on the compact call's own answer marks the provider unsupported. The names are defined once in oven-sdk (oven_sdk::provider_support), where the OpenAI and Azure window validators read them too, so the list cannot drift from what is sent.

docs.title: 5. The provider record
docs.text:
<data_root>/native-compaction.json holds one entry per provider ID:

{
  "providers": {
    "openrouter": {
      "state": "unsupported",
      "since": "2026-10-24T12:00:00Z",
      "reason": "compact endpoint answered 404",
      "config_digest": "…"
    },
    "my-gateway": {
      "state": "rejects_windows",
      "since": "…",
      "reason": "…",
      "config_digest": "…"
    }
  }
}

States: - unsupported: native compaction is not attempted, and only the summary runs. - rejects_windows: native compaction is not attempted, and stored windows from that provider are ignored in favour of the summary.

What marks a provider: - unsupported comes only from a definitive answer to the compact call: - HTTP 404, 405 or 501; - an error explicitly naming compaction as unsupported; - an adapter that cannot build the compact request. - rejects_windows comes from section 4. - Never: transient errors (timeouts, 429, 5xx other than 501, network errors) and authentication errors mark nothing.

Expiry: - An entry expires after 7 days. - An entry is dropped when that provider's configuration changes: the entry stores a digest of the provider's compiled definition, and a different digest drops it.

Writes and reads: - Writes are atomic: a temporary file, then a rename. - A missing or unreadable file counts as empty and is rewritten on the next change. - The daemon holds the record in memory and writes it on change.

Status: config status lists marked providers, with their state, reason and age.

docs.title: 6. Configuration
docs.text:
• compaction on a model override takes:
  • "unsupported": never attempt native compaction;
  • "openai-responses-compact" and "azure-responses-compact": still accepted, now meaning the default, so existing configurations keep loading. The docs mark them redundant.
  • The limit to managed providers is lifted. Any provider on a Responses adapter qualifies, compatible gateways and credential-less endpoints included.
  • No option to force native compaction past the record. Deleting the file, or changing the provider's configuration, clears it.

docs.title: 7. History format
docs.text:
All changes are additive under the 1.x freeze: - the summary-and-window checkpoint stores the window beside the summary in the existing summary checkpoint, as a new optional field, not as a new checkpoint variant; - older readers see a summary checkpoint; - existing native-only checkpoints, written before this change, still read.

Old native-only checkpoints have no summary. A request on another provider or model then has nothing to fall back to. - When that happens, the engine runs an internal compaction of the covered range from the preserved log before the request, and commits it as a new summary checkpoint. This is a one-time cost per old session. - The request proceeds on that new checkpoint.

docs.title: 8. Testing
docs.text:
• Parallel compaction: native and summary both succeed (the checkpoint holds both); native fails (summary only, failure classified); summary fails (the checkpoint fails).
  • Request selection:
  • same provider and model uses the window;
  • another model on the same provider uses the summary;
  • another provider uses the summary;
  • a variant change keeps the window.
  • The labpc-style regression: compact natively, switch models, and the run continues on the summary. This fails today.
  • Rejection at request time: the request fails, the provider is marked rejects_windows, and the next request uses the summary.
  • The record:
  • unsupported marked only for definitive answers, not for 429, 5xx or timeouts;
  • 7-day expiry;
  • a configuration digest change drops the entry;
  • atomic writes;
  • an unreadable file counts as empty.
  • Defaults: a compatible Responses gateway attempts native compaction with no override, and compaction = "unsupported" skips it.
  • Old checkpoints: a native-only checkpoint plus a model switch triggers a one-time internal compaction.

docs.title: 9. Docs
docs.text: sessions/compaction.md, extend/providers.md (the compaction setting), the configuration reference for the record file, and a troubleshooting entry: "native compaction stopped being used for a provider".

docs.title: 10. Implementation notes
docs.text:
Implemented 2026-10-24 in client protocol 1.29.0 and plugin protocol 1.17.0, with oven-sdk 342a029 (native compaction on compatible Responses endpoints, and the window's wire names with error_names_responses_native_context). Where it differs from, or makes concrete, the sections above:

Classifying OpenAI's error (section 4). OpenAI's documentation does not list an error for an invalid or expired compaction item: the compaction guide (developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/compaction), the conversation state guide, the /responses/compact reference, the reasoning guide, and the error codes guide (developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/error-codes) describe the item as opaque and name no failure. The API has been observed to answer an unusable compaction item with HTTP 400, type invalid_request_error, and code invalid_encrypted_content ("The encrypted content for item cmp_... could not be verified"), reported in OpenAI's own Codex tracker (github.com/openai/codex/issues/36704). The implementation does not rely on that code alone: it matches the window's wire names, and invalid_encrypted_content contains encrypted_content. A reasoning item's encrypted content refused on a request that also carried a window marks the provider too; the cost is the summary until the mark lifts.

Compaction (section 3). - Durable elision stays native's. When the native call's input would exceed the model's limit less the compaction output allowance, bulky tool outputs are still elided in the saved log before both calls, as native compaction did before; the summary otherwise keeps its private pruning retry. - The summary builds on the latest summary. A window alone (section 7) is passed over: the summary path summarizes from the latest checkpoint that has a summary, or the whole log, so the one-time summary of an old native-only checkpoint is an ordinary compaction. Its source_from_seq follows the summary it replaces; prior_checkpoint_seq still names the latest checkpoint of any kind. - The window's boundaries. native.source_through_seq is the checkpoint's input_through_seq; a window the boundaries cannot hold is dropped and the summary commits alone. - "The adapter cannot build the compact request" is the adapter's supports_compaction refusing the prepared request; it marks unsupported. A compact call that carried the previous window and is refused naming the window marks rejects_windows instead.

Requests (section 4). - Integrity checks. Besides the adapter, provider, and model, the request asks the adapter to validate the window before any I/O; a window whose scope (endpoint, account, compaction setting) it refuses serves no request, and the summary does. - A window alone that a request cannot use makes the request compact first (forced, summary beside native), then rebuild; if that fails, the run fails with "the session's latest checkpoint is a provider window this model cannot use, and it has no summary". - unsupported keeps windows. Only rejects_windows stops stored windows from serving; unsupported stops new native calls.

The record (section 5). The configuration digest covers what defines the provider rather than one model: its source (the managed recipe and its fingerprint, or the custom definition's fingerprint), endpoint, provider recipe, setup, and authentication method and parameters, not credentials. The configuration status carries each entry as NativeCompactionMark (provider_id, state, reason, age_seconds) in a new optional ConfigStatus.native_compaction; clients show them as notes.

Configuration (section 6). - Custom models. A custom model's capabilities.compaction became optional: omitted, a Responses adaptor compacts natively; "unsupported" opts out and stays the only value accepted. - Variants. A variant that switches request_endpoint compacts natively when its own adaptor does and the base model's setting allows it; the frozen binding's native check reads the selected adaptor, not the base model's protocol recipe. - Azure. Native compaction needs model, version, and deployment_type in the provider's setup; the azure.openai identity is no longer checked separately, since Oven requires it of every Azure model. - Replay scopes change once. The official OpenAI adapter's replay scope includes its compaction setting, so turning native compaction on by default gives every OpenAI Responses model a new scope: reasoning replayed from turns before the upgrade is omitted once. Compatible endpoints keep their scope.

History (section 7). The window is native (CheckpointNativeWindow: window, source_through_seq) on the internal_summary checkpoint. The native_window checkpoint is read, never written.

docs.title: Permission consolidation
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-23); see Implementation notes.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
A run's permissions come from three levels: the defaults the daemon supplies, the agent document, and the session's overrides. Today the engine combines them in three different ways, depending on what it is deciding:

  • which tools are offered: any rule at any level that allows or asks;
  • whether a call runs: a matching session rule beats every document rule, whatever their patterns;
  • what /permissions shows: a merged table, where a session * rule hides the document's rules for that action.

So the table can show cron * deny (session) while the cron tools are still offered and every call is refused. A session override cannot turn off a tool that a default allows (memory, cron, list_runtimes, mcp).

This spec merges the three levels into one rule list per run, and makes every decision read that list.

Decided 2026-10-23:

  • Session overrides the agent document, which overrides the defaults.
  • Document over defaults stays per action: a document that names an action replaces that action's defaults entirely (unchanged).
  • Session over document is per rule (option B): a session rule replaces the rule with the same action, runtime selector, and pattern, and every other rule is kept.
  • The merged list decides the tools offered, every call, the memory snapshot, and what /permissions shows.
