Out of scope: new permission actions, changing defaults, approval grants ("allow for this session"), which keep their current role (section 4.4).

docs.title: 2. The levels today
docs.text:
• Defaults: mode_default_rules, memory_default_rules, and cron_default_rules in crates/engine/src/permissions.rs, chosen by the agent's mode and whether the run is delegated. Each applies only to an action the document names no key for.
  • Agent document: its permissions frontmatter. The document's rules plus the defaults are frozen into the run's policy (agent_permission_rules).
  • Session overrides: SessionPermissionOverlay, a list of single rules. /permissions and the web panel add or remove one rule at a time (set_session_permission, clear_session_permission), identified by action, runtime selector, and pattern. It starts empty and holds only what was changed.

docs.title: 3.1 Building it
docs.text:
For a run, the merged list is built in three steps:

  1. Defaults for each action the document names no key for.
  2. The document's rules. Steps 1 and 2 are today's frozen policy.
  3. The session's rules. A session rule whose identity (action, runtime selector, pattern) equals a rule from steps 1–2 replaces it. Any other session rule is added.

Each rule keeps its source: default, agent_document, or session_overlay. The list is ordered defaults, document, session, which matters only for ties (section 3.2).

Identity compares patterns as written, after the memory variables are expanded (the policy already holds them expanded) and ~/ paths are resolved the way matching resolves them. bash@labpc and bash are different identities.

docs.title: 3.2 Deciding with it
docs.text:
• Is a tool offered? It is offered when some rule in the merged list for its action, applying to its runtime, allows or asks. Nothing else counts.
  • Is a call allowed? The most specific matching rule wins: more literal characters, then fewer wildcards, then a runtime selector, then the later rule in the list. This is today's rule within a document, applied to the merged list. A session rule wins a tie because it comes last.
  • Checks without a resource (an action checked by name only) use the merged list's * rules, a runtime-selected one over a bare one.
  • Memory: the write tools' readable-and-writable test (memory spec section 16.9.1) and the snapshot's read rules use the merged list.
  • /permissions shows the merged list: per action, its * row and its patterns, each with its source. A session * rule replaces only the * row; the document's other patterns stay listed.

docs.title: 3.3 Examples
docs.text: Session override Document and defaults Merged Tool A call cron: deny default cron: "*": allow "*": deny (session) hidden — memory: {"user://*": deny} default memory: "*": allow "*": allow (default), "user://*": deny (session) offered user:// denied, the rest allowed bash: {"cargo test *": allow} bash: {"*": ask} both offered cargo test runs, the rest asks bash: {"*": allow} bash: {"*": ask, "git push *": deny} "*": allow (session), "git push *": deny (document) offered git push denied, the rest runs bash: {"git push *": allow} as above "*": ask, "git push *": allow (session) offered git push runs mcp: deny default mcp: "*": ask "*": deny hidden —

docs.title: 4.1 Session rules no longer win by level alone
docs.text: Today any matching session rule beats the document. With the merged list, specificity decides, so a broad session rule no longer overrides a narrower document rule: the fourth row of section 3.3 denies git push, where today it runs. To change a document's rule for a session, the session overrides that exact rule, which is what the per-row editing in /permissions and the web panel already does.

docs.title: 4.2 A session can turn tools off
docs.text: A session deny that replaces every allowing rule hides the tool, as the first and last rows of section 3.3 show. The docs' note that turning memory or cron off "has to happen in the agent document" is removed.

docs.title: 4.3 The table matches the engine
docs.text: A session * rule no longer hides the document's patterns in /permissions; they stay listed with their source, because they still apply.

docs.title: 4.4 Grants are unchanged
docs.text: An approval answered "allow for this session" records a grant, which still turns an ask into allow for what it covers and can still make a tool offered, but never overrides a deny of the merged list (tool_visible_with_grants). Grants are invalidated when a session change makes an action stricter, as today, with "stricter" judged on the merged list.

docs.title: 4.5 Running and frozen runs
docs.text: A session override already applies to the next decision without re-freezing the run. The merged list is computed from the frozen policy and the current overlay at each decision, so that stays true. Tools offered are recomputed at every model request, as today.

docs.title: 5. Compatibility
docs.text:
• No wire change. EffectivePermissionAction and its rule sources already describe a merged table; only which rules it lists changes (section 4.3).
  • Behaviour change (section 4.1) noted in the protocol changelog and the permissions docs, with no version bump: no message or field changes.
  • History: recorded approvals and decisions replay as they were written.

docs.title: 6. Tests
docs.text:
• Building: replacement by identity across levels; runtime selectors as distinct identities; ~/ patterns; expanded memory variables; sources.
  • Visibility: a session deny hides a default-allowed tool (memory, cron, mcp, list_runtimes); a narrower session deny leaves it offered; a session allow offers a document-denied tool.
  • Decisions: every row of section 3.3, including specificity across levels and a tie won by the session.
  • Name-only checks with session * rules, with and without selectors.
  • Memory: the write tools' test and the snapshot follow the merged list.
  • /permissions: a session * rule keeps the document's patterns listed.
  • Grants: a grant never overrides a merged deny; invalidation on a stricter session change.

docs.title: 7. Docs
docs.text:
• docs/site/concepts/permissions.md and docs/site/extend/agents.md: the three levels, how they merge, and the behaviour change, with the examples of section 3.3.
  • The memory and scheduling guides: drop "turning it off has to happen in the agent document".
  • The protocol changelog: the behaviour change.

docs.title: 8. Phases
docs.text: One phase: the merged list in the engine and every caller (permissions, tool composition, skills, messaging, memory, cron, list_agents, the view), tests, then docs.

docs.title: 9. Open questions
docs.text: None.

docs.title: 10. Implementation notes
docs.text:
Landed 2026-10-23 in one phase, as section 8 planned.

  • One function builds the list. MergedRules (crates/engine/src/permissions.rs) takes the frozen policy's rules, the session overlay, and the home of the runtime being decided for, and holds each rule with its source. offers, decide, and decide_name_only are the three decisions of section 3.2; the old overlay-first paths (effective_permission_with_overlay and effective_loose_permission_with_overlay consulting the overlay before the policy, and tool_visible chaining both levels) are gone, and the remaining entry points are thin wrappers over the list. Callers: the call pipeline (decide_operation_with_overlay and _with_grants), tool composition and call preparation (tool_visible_with_grants, now also given the tool's runtime home), skills, send_message visibility, memory_access (memory and the write tools' readable-and-writable test), the memory tools' and snapshot's read rules (MemoryCaller), the cron tools' cron_list filter, list_agents, grant invalidation (rule_effects), and the /permissions view.
  • Order. The frozen policy lists the document's rules before the defaults. The two never share an action, so section 3.1's order (defaults, then document) and the frozen order rank every tie the same; the list keeps the frozen order.
  • Sources. Telling a default from a document rule needs to know whether the run is delegated, which only the view does. So the view relabels policy rules (MergedRules::label_defaults, the same per-action test as before), while a decision trace keeps labelling every policy rule agent_document, as recorded history already does; a rule an overlay rule replaced no longer appears among a trace's candidates.
  • Identity without a home. Visibility checks that have no runtime home at hand (send_message, list_agents, memory on global) and the view compare ~ patterns as written; the call pipeline and tool composition compare them expanded against the tool's runtime home.
  • The memory snapshot's rules fingerprint still hashes the agent's and the overlay's memory rules separately. The merged list is a function of both, so the fingerprint changes exactly when it can.
  • Clients. The TUI and web client already rendered the view's rows as given, without assuming a session * hides the document's patterns; only the TUI's explanation line changed, from "checked before the agent's rules" to "replaces the agent's rule with this pattern, and the most specific rule wins".
  • Tests. The examples of section 3.3 are one test each, beside the building, visibility, name-only, view, and grant tests, in crates/engine/src/permissions/tests/merged.rs; memory's in crates/engine/src/runtime/memory_runs/tests.rs. Five older tests encoded the overlay-first behaviour and were changed: a broad overlay rule over a narrower agent rule now loses to it, and an overlay deny of the agent's own pattern now hides the tool.
  • cookie run --allowed-tools adds "*": allow overlay rules, so it now replaces only the agent's * rule: a narrower agent rule such as delegate: {reviewer: ask} still decides what it matches. Two headless tests relied on --allowed-tools delegate beating that rule; their agent now writes delegate: ask, and the CLI page says so.

docs.title: Plugins: Tools, Hooks, Events, and Producers
docs.text: Status: implemented (decisions of 2026-10-16). Section Implementation notes records where the code settled details differently. This document is the governing specification for cleaning up the plugin protocol, host, SDK, and configuration: plugin tools speak the runtime protocol's tool messages, the host runs on the runtime stack, and dead or half-built parts go. This spec was written while there were no plugin implementations outside this repository, so every part of the plugin protocol could change. The compatibility spec now governs how the plugin protocol changes: it is versioned by semver, and plugins written for one major keep working with every daemon of that major. Section Decisions records what review settled.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
A plugin does four things: it declares tools, intercepts engine hooks, streams session events and a bus, and produces messages. Runtimes (runtimes spec) do tools far better than plugins do today: a prepare step with the tool's own approval identity, progress, background, cancellation, media, collision and concurrency choices, tools_changed, and prompt sections, where a plugin tool is one plugin/tools/call under a shared plugin:<label> permission. The plugin host also carries its own process supervisor, JSON-RPC loop, framing, and SDK, none of which shares the runtime stack's stderr capture, restart, or status reporting.

After this work a plugin is a trusted, local, daemon-wide extension that declares tools the way a runtime does, intercepts hooks, watches events, publishes to the bus, and produces messages to any session, over the runtime stack's transport and process handling.

Out of scope: remote plugins, hooks in runtimes, event replay and filters, plugin resources, and a runtime SDK.

docs.title: 2. Plugin tools speak the runtime tool messages
docs.text:
A plugin declares and runs tools with the runtime protocol's tool messages, unchanged, over its own connection (runtime protocol):

Message Direction As in the runtime protocol tools in the plugin/initialize result plugin → daemon tools and prompt_sections of RuntimeTools, each tool a ToolDeclaration runtime/tools_changed plugin → daemon the plugin's tool list changed tool/prepare, tool/revalidate, tool/release daemon → plugin the plugin prepares calls and reports their approval identity, normalized arguments, and presentation tool/execute, tool/progress both execution with streamed output and media tool/cancel daemon → plugin cancellation reaches the plugin tool/detachable plugin → daemon background calls and reports_itself
  • Declarations are the runtime's: an optional, free-form permission action (a plugin tool may need none, or name its own action such as browse), collision, concurrency, result_truncation, output, background, and background_default. primary_resource_param goes: the plugin computes its permission resource in tool/prepare.
  • The daemon reuses its runtime tool client for a plugin's tools, so approval, progress, background, cancellation, media retention, and tools_changed behave exactly as for a runtime's.
  • Publication. Plugin tools stay in the global runtime, but each plugin is its own source when names are composed, so its prefix is the plugin's name rather than global. When a plugin tool's name is taken by another tool (another plugin's, an MCP server's, global's own, or any attached runtime's), its declared collision decides:
  • prefix (the default): it is published as <plugin>_<tool>, the other tool keeps its name, as runtime tools are prefixed with their attachment name today;
  • override, a new collision value: it takes the bare name, and the tool it overrides is published under its own source's prefix (or hidden, if that tool is fallback). Two override tools with one name are both prefixed, with a diagnostic. Base-layer names stay reserved: no plugin or runtime tool takes them. override is part of the shared ToolCollision, so a runtime tool may declare it too. The MCP crate no longer knows about plugins.
  • Removed: plugin/tools/call, ExtensionToolDeclaration, ExtensionToolCallParams, ExtensionToolCallResult, the tools capability (declaring tools is the capability), [plugins.<name>] tool_timeout_ms (a runtime call has no per-call timeout; a tool bounds its own work), the plugin permission action and every plugin: special case (permission-name mapping and rule matching, the CLI's --allowed-tools plugin and plugin:<name>, the TUI's "plugin tools" row), and the MCP crate's plugin claims (claim_plugin_tools, plugin_owns_tool, release_plugin_tools, the collision handler, and MCP preempting a plugin). A stored rule naming plugin stays a valid free-form label.
  • Shared types. The runtime protocol's tool wire types (ToolDeclaration, the prepare, execute, progress, and detach params and results, and the JSON-RPC peer and line transport) move from runtime_api into the Apache-2.0 protocol crate, so the Apache-2.0 plugin SDK can use them; runtime_api re-exports them.
  • SDK. The plugin SDK's tool builder takes the runtime declaration and gives an execute closure progress, detach, cancellation, and producers; the echo example is updated.

Hooks, events, and producers stay daemon-wide: a session that detaches global loses plugin tools, as it loses every global tool, and keeps its hooks, events, and producers.

docs.title: 3. Protocol cleanup
docs.text:
The plugin protocol keeps its own methods but takes the runtime protocol's shape where they meet.

Version. An integer, starting at 1 (today's string "0.0.8" goes), checked as the runtime protocol checks its version.

Removed as dead:

Item Why resources and publish_session_events capabilities Never implemented; publishing is always rejected. ExtensionEmitResultParams.durable Always rejected; emit_result reports the bus outcome only. The engine capability flags other than producer_messaging Always true. ExtensionToolAfterResultResult.note Never read. ExtensionAgentBeforeStartResult.addendum Duplicates append_to_system_prompt. ExtensionMessageEndParams.role Always assistant. plugin/ping Used only by tests; liveness is the connection itself. provider_before_headers hook The model adapters do not expose request headers, so it can neither see nor change them. headers of provider_after_response Always empty; the hook keeps status.

Renamed: ExtensionModelSelectSource::FallbackRestore becomes fallback, which is when the engine sends it.

Shared with runtimes. The producer params and results (ExtensionProducer*, ExtensionRecovery*) move to neutral names (ProducerRegisterParams, …, RecoveryCompleteParams) in the protocol crate, used by both protocols. The plugin methods become producer/register, producer/send, producer/unregister, producer/discard, producer/recovery/start, and producer/recovery/complete, the runtime protocol's names.

Hook payloads. tool_before_call and tool_after_result gain the call's origin: { "kind": "runtime", "attachment": "<name>", "runtime_id": "<id>" } for a runtime's or plugin's tool, { "kind": "base" } for a daemon base tool, so a hook can tell local's bash from a remote runtime's.

docs.title: 4. Host fixes
docs.text:
• Per-hook contexts. Each hook invocation gets its own context ID. Today one ID is shared by the four hooks of a model attempt, so a plugin's plugin/emit from the second hook on is rejected as spent.
  • Typed hook failures. A hook failure is classified once, by kind (timeout, crashed, disconnected, rejected, malformed), instead of by matching error strings in five places, so a malformed reply is no longer recorded as a timeout.
  • Engine diagnostics are not plugin diagnostics. Automatic compaction's "disabled after 3 failures" notice gets its own runless event instead of a plugin_diagnostic under the made-up plugin name engine:auto-compact.
  • Dead code. PluginConfig::validate and ConfigError::Plugin, the plugin-origin self-exclusion of streamed events, the EventParamsRef and BusEventParamsRef duplicates of the protocol structs, and plugin_statuses outside the new status RPC.
  • Old logs. plugin_event_added and the recovery_failed and recovery_disabled kinds of plugin_diagnostic are never written; they stay decodable and rendered for old session logs.

docs.title: 5. Host on the runtime stack
docs.text:
The plugin host drops its own process and transport code and uses the runtime stack's:

  • Process. Started like a runtime process: an argv, env, cwd, its own process group (a job object on Windows), and stderr captured into a bounded diagnostic tail instead of inherited, which today can corrupt the TUI's screen.
  • Transport. The runtime protocol's JSON-RPC peer and line transport, with its 48 MiB frame bound, replacing the hand-rolled reader, writer, pending-request table, and 4 MiB bound.
  • Restart. A plugin that exits or drops its connection is restarted with the runtime reconnect policy (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, then failed until the user retries). A restarted plugin gets a new connection epoch; its producers register again and recover as on first start.
  • Status. Client RPCs plugins.list (name, state, capabilities and hooks, last failure with the stderr tail) and plugins.restart, a plugins.changed notification, and a TUI plugins view (/plugins) next to the runtimes view.

docs.title: 6. Configuration
docs.text:
[plugins.audit]
command = ["python3", "audit.py"]
env = { AUDIT_LOG = "~/audit.log" }
cwd = "~/plugins"
enabled = true
producer_messaging = false
interception_timeout_ms = 2000
startup_timeout_ms = 10000
shutdown_grace_ms = 3000
  • command becomes an argv array, as in [runtimes.<id>]; args goes.
  • tool_timeout_ms goes with plugin tools.
  • Plugins still run hooks in the order the file lists them.

docs.title: 7. Phases
docs.text:
Each phase lands as its own commits with every gate green, and is pushed.

  1. Clean the protocol. Section 3 and 4: dead fields, capabilities, and hooks removed, shared producer types and producer/* method names, integer version 1, origins in tool hooks, and the host fixes; the SDK and fixtures follow.
  2. Runtime stack and status. Section 5 and 6: process, transport, restart, stderr capture, plugins.list / plugins.restart / plugins.changed, the TUI view, the command array.
  3. Plugin tools. Section 2: the wire types moved to the protocol crate, plugin tools over the runtime tool messages and the daemon's runtime tool client, each plugin its own composition source with prefix and the new override collision, the plugin action and the MCP crate's plugin claims removed, the SDK's tool builder.
  4. Documentation. The plugin guide and development pages rewritten (dropping the crate-internal sections and stale versions), goal-mode and runtime references; this spec marked implemented.

docs.title: 8. Decisions
docs.text:
Decided 2026-10-16:

  • Plugins keep tools, hooks, events, the bus, and producers.
  • Plugin tools speak the runtime protocol's tool messages, and the daemon runs them with its runtime tool client.
  • Plugins may produce to any session.

Confirmed in review 2026-10-16:

  • Remove provider_before_headers rather than wire headers through the model adapters.
  • Remove plugin/ping.
  • Restart crashed plugins with the runtime reconnect policy.
  • Rename the producer methods to producer/* and share their types.
  • Move the runtime protocol's tool wire types and JSON-RPC peer into the Apache-2.0 protocol crate for the plugin SDK.
  • Drop tool_timeout_ms; a plugin bounds its own tool work, as a runtime does.
  • A colliding plugin tool is prefixed with its plugin's name, or, when it declares collision: override, takes the bare name and pushes the other tool to its prefix.

docs.title: 9. Implementation notes
docs.text:
Landed 2026-10-16, with phases 1 to 3 in one change because the host's tests would otherwise have been rewritten twice.

  • The status RPCs are plugins.list and plugins.restart, matching runtimes.list and runtimes.reconnect. They, the engine_diagnostic event, and the removed plugin action are client protocol 44.
  • Hook failures are timeout, disconnected (not connected, or the connection ended during the hook, recorded as interception_crash), rejected (an error answer), and malformed; the last two record the new interception_rejected diagnostic. unsupported_capability is kept only for old logs.
  • EventParamsRef and BusEventParamsRef stay: they borrow the event so it is serialized once for every subscribed plugin, and a test pins them to the protocol structs' wire form.
  • A plugin's first failed start is reconnecting like a later drop, and is failed once the reconnect policy is exhausted.
  • Plugin request IDs are integers, as the shared peer requires.
  • Every plugin's tool provider shares the reserved provenance ID plugin.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-21), in three phases (section 14). Builds on the memory spec, the runtimes spec, and the web client spec.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
Today a project exists only as a memory folder, ~/.cookie-agent/memory/projects/<project>/. Nothing links it to sessions: the model is told to search memory for the project a task belongs to. This spec makes a project something the daemon knows and sessions belong to.

Decided 2026-10-21:

  • A session may belong to one project. It is chosen at session.create, and the session can later move to another project or out of any project. Projects can be created, renamed, and deleted.
  • A project carries default attachments, a default agent and agent preset, its own AGENTS.md, and its memory folder.
  • Choosing a project in a client's New session prefills the runtime cards from the project's defaults, which stay editable. A session.create that names a project and omits runtimes gets the defaults from the daemon, so the TUI and the CLI get them too. The default agent and preset prefill the draft's agent selection in every client (added 2026-10-21, section 4). Moving a session into a project never changes its attachments or its agent.
  • Sessions in a project see its memory in the snapshot: the reserved project://<name>/overview in full, and an index (URL, description, keywords) of every other memory in the project.
  • Deleting a project deletes its sessions, its memories, its AGENTS.md, and its defaults, after a confirmation that counts them.
  • The web session list groups sessions under collapsible project sections, then "No project". The workspace filter goes away.
  • Users can rename sessions from the TUI and the web client. The protocol already has session.rename; no client calls it yet.
  • Web session rows show where a session runs as machine badges with stable colours (section 9).

Out of scope: nesting projects, a session in several projects, sharing a project between daemons, and per-project permission rules.

docs.title: 2. Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Project A named body of work the daemon keeps: an ID, a name, an optional emoji, default attachments, an AGENTS.md, and a memory folder. Project ID An opaque string the daemon generates. Sessions refer to a project by ID, so a rename never rewrites session logs. Project name The project's name in URLs, folders, and clients. It follows the memory name rule (memory spec section 4.2): a lowercase letter or digit, then up to 63 lowercase letters, digits, or -. Overview The memory project://<name>/overview, loaded in full into every session of the project.

docs.title: 3. Storage
docs.text:
~/.cookie-agent/
  projects/<project-id>/
    project.toml       name, created, default attachments
    AGENTS.md          optional
  memory/projects/<name>/
    overview.md        created empty with the project
    <memory>.md        …
  • project.toml:
name = "cookie-agent"
emoji = "🍪"
created = "2026-10-21T18:00:00Z"

[defaults]
preset = "rust"
agent = "builder"
global = true
runtimes = [
  { runtime_id = "local", capability = "coding", workspace = "/home/u/src/cookie-agent" },
  { runtime_id = "labpc", workspace = "/home/u/cookie-agent" },
]

emoji is optional. When set, it is exactly one emoji: a single extended grapheme cluster of at most 32 bytes that Unicode marks as an emoji. It cannot be ASCII, whitespace, or a control character. global and runtimes in [defaults] have the shape of session.create's fields of the same names. agent and preset name an agent and its preset, as in RunSelection; both are optional, and an agent without a preset is one from the shared registry. A project with no [defaults] gets the daemon's usual defaults. - Each project file carries a revision, as memory files do, and every change is compare-and-swap on it. - The memory folder stays where it is, so project:// URLs, the memory tools, and memory.* keep working. The project's name is its memory folder's name. - First start after the upgrade: every valid folder under memory/projects/ that has no project gets one, with no defaults and no AGENTS.md. Memory projects and daemon projects are then the same set. - Writing to an unknown project: a model write to project://<name>/… for a name that is no project is refused. The message names the existing projects and says that projects are created from a client. Writes from the user's memory.write are refused the same way. Today the first write creates the folder. - The daemon creates overview.md empty when it creates a project. Like agent memory files (memory spec section 16.7), its description is the daemon's: Overview of the `<name>` project, loaded in full into its sessions. An empty overview renders nothing.

docs.title: 4. Sessions in a project
docs.text:
• session.create gains project: Option<ProjectId>. An unknown ID is refused before anything is attached.
  • Membership is event-sourced. A new durable event, session_project_set { project: Option<ProjectId> }, records it. The creation writes one when project is set. SessionMeta.project is its fold, so a cache rebuild keeps it.
  • A session tree has one project. Only root sessions record the event; delegated children take their root's project.
  • session.project.set { session_id, project: Option<ProjectId> } moves a root session into a project or out of one, and is refused for a child. It is allowed while the session runs and takes effect at the next root admission. The move announces sessions.changed upserted.
  • Defaults at creation: when project is set and runtimes is omitted, the daemon attaches the project's [defaults]. An explicit runtimes, even an empty one, wins.
  • Default agent.
  • session.create always carries a RunSelection, so the daemon never replaces it. Clients apply the project's agent and preset when a project is chosen for a draft: the web project picker, the TUI picker, and cookie --project.
  • The model is the agent's own default model, as when the user switches agents. The selection stays editable before the first message.
  • If the agent no longer exists or cannot run as root, the client keeps its usual default and says so.
  • project.update refuses an agent the daemon does not list in that preset, or one that cannot run as root. An agent removed later produces no error until a client tries to use it.
  • session.list gains project: Option<ProjectFilter>, which is a project ID or "none". A session whose project no longer exists lists as having none.

docs.title: 5. Project operations
docs.text:
New client requests (client protocol 1.8.0):

Method Params Result projects.list — { projects: [ProjectInfo] } project.get { project } { project: ProjectInfo, agents_md: { text, revision }? } project.create { name, emoji?, defaults? } { project: ProjectInfo } project.update { project, revision, name?, emoji?, defaults?, agents_md? } { project: ProjectInfo } project.delete { project, revision } { deleted_sessions, deleted_memories }
  • ProjectInfo is { id, name, emoji?, revision, defaults?, has_agents_md, sessions, memories }, where sessions counts root sessions.
  • A projects.changed notification announces any change. Clients refetch projects.list on it.
  • Rename.
  • The new name must be valid and free.
  • The daemon renames the memory folder, holding the memory lock, before it writes project.toml. If the folder move fails, nothing changes.
  • Old project://<old>/… URLs in transcripts no longer resolve.
  • Sessions keep the ID, so their logs are untouched. Their next snapshot shows the new name (section 7).
  • Delete.
  • The daemon refuses while any session of the project is running, and names those sessions.
  • Otherwise it deletes every session tree of the project, as session.delete does, then the whole memory folder (non-memory files too, since the user asked for the project to go), then projects/<id>/.
  • Clients confirm first and show the counts from ProjectInfo.
  • Edits. agents_md replaces the file, and an empty string removes it. emoji is set to a value or cleared with null. defaults is validated like session.create's runtimes, except that the runtimes need not be connected.

docs.title: 6. Project AGENTS.md
docs.text:
• At every root admission, the daemon reads the project's AGENTS.md, alongside the workspace files the coding runtimes return. This needs no runtime: the file lives in the daemon's data directory.
  • It comes first in the AGENTS.md turn, before every workspace's files: general before specific, so a workspace's AGENTS.md still has the last word. It renders as <contents from="project:<name>/AGENTS.md">.
  • It follows [agent_md] enabled and an agent's agent_md frontmatter, as workspace files do. It does not need global.
  • It is recorded in agent_md_loaded, with a new optional project source (an additive event field), so a replay renders what the model saw.
  • The size cap is the same as for workspace files.

docs.title: 7. Memory in the prompt
docs.text:
• memory_loaded gains an optional project entry (additive):
project: {
  project: <name>,
  overview: { description, keywords, body }?,
  memories: [ { url, description, keywords } ],
  omitted: <count>
}
  • Root runs of a session in a project get it. Delegated runs do not, matching the machine index.
  • The overview is whole, or absent when empty or missing. Its rendered size counts toward [memory] snapshot_user_bytes.
  • The index lists every other memory in the project, newest first. It shares [memory] snapshot_index_bytes with the machine index.
  • A new snapshot is taken (additions to memory spec section 7.2) when:
  • the session's project changed since the latest snapshot;
  • the project's name changed since then.

Either costs one prompt-cache miss. - Rendered text. A session in a project gets a section after "Machines in this session":

## Project cookie-agent
This session belongs to the cookie-agent project.

<memory url="project://cookie-agent/overview" …>
…overview body…
</memory>

Other memories of this project (read with memory_read):
- project://cookie-agent/release: How releases are cut …

The paragraph "Project notes are never shown here…" becomes: "This session's project notes are listed below. Search memory (memory_search) for other projects only when the task reaches into them." Sessions outside a project keep today's text.

docs.title: 8. Session titles
docs.text:
• No protocol change. Clients call session.rename with Set, Clear, or Reset.
  • TUI:
  • /rename <title> sets the title.
  • /rename with no argument opens an input prefilled with the current title.
  • /rename --auto resets it to the generated title.
  • In the session picker, Ctrl+R renames the highlighted session.
  • Web:
  • Clicking the title in the title bar edits it in place. Enter saves and Escape cancels.
  • ⋮ menu › Rename does the same.
  • Session rows. A pencil button sits to the left of the delete button. Both show on hover on desktop and on long-press on a phone, with the delete button's layout (centred, the row's hover colour at rest, one step darker on hover). The pencil turns the row's title into a field in place; Enter saves and Escape cancels.
  • An emptied field offers "Use the automatic title" (Reset).

docs.title: 9. Session badges
docs.text:
Web session rows replace the folder-and-paths line with badges. Badges show machines, never runtime IDs (changed 2026-10-21: an ID such as local says nothing a user needs). The global attachment is ignored for all of these rules:

Session's attachments Badges None besides global No badge One [machine] badge, then the workspace as ~/… Several, all on one machine [machine] badge, then the workspaces, comma-joined, truncating On more than one machine One [machine] badge per machine, in attachment order
  • The machine comes from runtimes.list, via the attachment's runtime's machine. A runtime with no known machine counts as its own machine: its runtime ID shows in a machine badge.
  • Colours are stable. Each badge takes one of eight hues, chosen by a hash of the machine name (or, for a runtime of no known machine, its ID). Each hue has a light-theme pair and a dark-theme pair that meet contrast. Colours mean machines everywhere: a runtime's dot on the runtime cards and in the bottom bar takes its machine's hue.
  • Machine badges carry the machine's OS icon, as on the Machines view.
  • A machine's name is never cut (added 2026-10-21). When the line runs out of room, the workspaces shrink first, down to …, and then leave the line; when the machine badges alone still do not fit, the line shows as many whole machine badges as fit, then a final +N badge whose tooltip names the rest. This holds for session rows and project headers; the bottom bar names no machine, only workspaces after their machines' dots.
  • Badges give way before the time does. The row's tooltip keeps the full list, each attachment with its machine, runtime ID, and full path.

docs.title: 10.1 Web
docs.text:
• Sidebar.
  • Project sections are collapsible and remembered per browser.
  • Projects are ordered by their latest session's activity, and "No project" comes last. (Changed 2026-10-26, user decision: projects are ordered by creation, oldest first, in projects.list and the clients.)
  • Each section orders its own sessions (added 2026-10-21). Active sessions come first: running, or waiting on a producer such as an active goal or background calls. Every other session follows. Each group is ordered by last activity, newest first.
  • Each header shows the project's emoji (a folder icon when it has none) and its name, with no count. When the project has default attachments, a second line shows them as badges, by the session-row rules of section 9 (added 2026-10-21). The header also has:
    • + for a new session in the project, always visible;
    • a pencil, then a delete button, shown like the session rows' buttons (on hover on desktop, on long-press on a phone).
  • The pencil opens the project editor. Delete asks for confirmation, with the counts of sessions and memories that go (section 5).
  • "No project" has neither button.
  • Moving sessions. Drag a session row onto a project header. This uses the pointer-event drag of the Machines view: long-press then drag on touch. For keyboards, a third row button, "Move to project…", sits left of the pencil and opens a project picker. On a phone, a long press released without moving shows the three row buttons.
  • New session.
  • A project picker sits above the runtime cards. It starts at the section whose + was used, else "No project".
  • Picking a project prefills the cards from its defaults, and the agent chip from its default agent and preset.
  • A "New project…" entry opens the project editor, empty.
  • Project editor. A right-side panel on desktop, the same width as the model picker's, and a full-height sheet on a phone. It holds:
  • name;
  • emoji, chosen with an emoji picker (section 10.3);
  • default attachments, edited with the same runtime cards;
  • default agent and preset, chosen with the agent picker, or "None";
  • an "Use this session's attachments" shortcut;
  • an AGENTS.md editor;
  • a link to the project's folder in the Memory view.

Save sends one project.update with the editor's revision. If the project changed meanwhile, the editor says so and offers to reload it. Closing with unsaved edits asks first. The "New project…" entry opens the same editor, empty, and saves with project.create. - Memory view. Project folders and projects are the same set. A folder's "Delete project" becomes project.delete, with the session count in its confirmation.

docs.title: 10.2 TUI and CLI
docs.text:
• Wherever the TUI names a project (the bottom bar, the picker, session rows), the emoji comes before the name. Its width is measured as two cells.

  • Session picker:

  • Rows show the project.
  • Ctrl+P cycles the filter: all, a project, then no project. This sits beside the existing Ctrl+A directory scope.
  • Project in the bottom bar.
  • The bottom-left label starts with the project's name, before the runtime and workspaces, whenever no run is active. That covers both a loaded idle session and a new draft; a draft with no project shows "no project".
  • Clicking the name opens a project picker: the projects, "No project", and "New project…".
  • For a loaded session, the picker moves the session with session.project.set. Its attachments never change.
  • For a draft, the picker sets the project the session will be created in. If that project has defaults, the draft takes them, and the label shows their workspaces before anything is sent. Otherwise the draft keeps the TUI's usual attachments. The draft also takes the project's default agent and preset, if set.
  • /project opens the same picker from the keyboard.
  • Starting in a project. A new session belongs to no project unless one is chosen. cookie --project <name> starts in that project, and nothing is ever picked from the current directory.
  • cookie project has list, create <name>, rename <old> <new>, delete <name> (with a confirmation unless --yes), and edit <name>, which opens AGENTS.md in $EDITOR. Defaults are set from the web client, or with cookie project defaults <name> --from-session <id>.

docs.title: 10.3 Emoji picker
docs.text:
• The web client has its own picker, with no JavaScript library. It shows a grid of a few hundred common emoji, bundled as a static list and grouped by category, with a search box that filters by each emoji's Unicode name.
  • A free-text field also takes any single emoji, so the OS emoji keyboard works too, including on phones. The daemon validates either path the same way.
  • "No emoji" clears it.
  • On a phone the picker is a bottom sheet.
  • The bundled list must keep the web bundle well under its 10 MB budget. It is names and code points only, with no images, and emoji render with the system font.

docs.title: 11. Protocol and compatibility
docs.text:
• Client protocol 1.8.0 (additive):
  • session.create.project, SessionMeta.project, session.list.project;
  • session.project.set, the project.* methods (with the project emoji), projects.list, and projects.changed.
  • Events (additive):
  • the session_project_set event;
  • memory_loaded.project;
  • agent_md_loaded's project source.

These need a plugin protocol minor, since plugins see events. The history format stays 1, and older logs read as having no project. - Clients below 1.8 see sessions without projects and cannot manage them. A project's AGENTS.md and memory still reach those sessions' prompts, because the daemon renders them.

docs.title: 12. Phases
docs.text:
1. Store and protocol:
  2. projects on disk and the migration from memory folders;
  3. the project.* methods and projects.list;
  4. session_project_set, session.project.set, and defaults at creation;
  5. delete;
  6. refusing writes to unknown projects.
  7. Prompt: the project AGENTS.md, the overview, the project index, and the snapshot triggers.
  8. Clients:
  9. web sections, moving sessions, the project picker and project editor with the emoji picker, badges, and rename;
  10. TUI rename, /project, and the picker filter;
  11. cookie project and --project.
  12. Docs: a projects concept page, the memory and AGENTS.md pages, the web and TUI guides, and the protocol changelog.

docs.title: 13. Open questions
docs.text: None. The user approved the spec on 2026-10-21, including the choices first proposed with it: - an ID plus a name that follows the memory name rule; - the memory folder staying where it is; - refusing writes to unknown projects; - the place of the project's AGENTS.md; - root runs only; - refusing a delete while a session runs; - hashed badge colours.

docs.title: 14.1 Phases 1 and 2: store, protocol, and prompt (2026-10-21)
docs.text:
Landed: the project store and the upgrade from memory folders, the project.* methods and projects.list, projects.changed, session_project_set and session.project.set, defaults at creation, delete, the refusal of writes to unknown projects, the project AGENTS.md, the overview and the project index in the snapshot, the snapshot triggers, and, from phase 3, cookie project and cookie --project. Client protocol 1.8.0, plugin protocol 1.3.0, history format 1. The web client and the TUI pickers are phase 3.

Where it is: crates/engine/src/projects.rs (ProjectStore), crates/engine/src/memory/projects.rs (the memory folder and the overview), crates/engine/src/runtime/project_api.rs (the requests, membership, and the project's AGENTS.md), crates/protocol/src/project.rs (the wire types), and crates/cookie_agent/src/project_command.rs.

Decisions taken where the spec left room, and deviations:

  • Revision. A project's revision is the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of project.toml, then, when it exists, of AGENTS.md, so an edit of either file by hand, or by another client, makes a stale project.update fail. project.get's agents_md.revision is the file's own digest, for display.
  • The upgrade runs at every start, not only the first: it adopts every valid folder under memory/projects/ that has no project, and it is idempotent. While a project folder does not read, it adopts nothing, and project.create refuses, since that project could have the name. It also makes sure every project's overview exists with the daemon's description, which is how a rename's new description lands even after a crash.
  • Defaults at creation apply when the project's defaults name runtimes or leave out global. Defaults that only name an agent or a preset leave a new session the usual attachments, so adding a default agent never takes the local runtime away. project.update clears the defaults or the emoji with null.
  • The overview's description is the daemon's, as an agent file's is; its keywords are the writer's. memory_write may leave the description out for an overview, and memory_edit keeps the daemon's.
  • Refused writes cover memory_edit as well as memory_write and memory.write; deletes of an unknown project's files stay allowed. A project's folder now stays when its last memory goes: the folder belongs to the project. The model-facing tool descriptions say so.
  • agent_md_loaded's project source is project: { id, name }; the event's attachment, a required member older readers rely on, is global, where the file lives. The rendered <contents> of a project file has no runtime attribute, and adding a project never adds one to a lone workspace's files.
  • Snapshot limits. The overview is measured against snapshot_user_bytes before the user categories and the project index against snapshot_index_bytes before the machines: the session's own project matters most. An overview too long for the user limit is listed first in the index instead of being dropped silently. The snapshot compares the project by name, which is all the event records; a session whose project was deleted is deleted with it.
  • project.delete's result is two counts: root sessions deleted, each with its tree, and memory files deleted. Delete, and ProjectInfo.sessions, reach the sessions of the daemon's own session store, the sessions of its working directory; a second daemon sharing the data root with another working directory keeps its sessions, which then list as having no project.
  • SessionMeta.project of a delegated session is its root's, filled in when the daemon serves session.get and session.list; delegated sessions record nothing. sessions.changed carries the metadata as stored.
  • ProjectFilter spells "no project" as the string none. Project IDs are UUIDv7 strings, so no project has that ID.
  • Emoji validation uses unicode-segmentation and unicode-properties (both already in the dependency tree): one extended grapheme cluster, at most 32 bytes, not all ASCII, no whitespace or control character, made of characters with Emoji or Emoji_Component, at least one of them Emoji. A project file whose emoji does not pass reads as unreadable.
  • cookie --project works with plain cookie, through a running daemon or standalone: the TUI starts on a new session in the project, with the default agent and preset when they resolve; the project applies to that first session only. cookie project defaults --from-session takes the session's agent and preset as well as its attachments.
  • Corpora. The 1.8.0 client corpus and the 1.3.0 runtime corpus are recorded and pinned, with the session created in a project. The recorder now writes the runtime's host name, the machine name derived from it, and its home directory as placeholders.

docs.title: 14.2 Phase 3: the clients (2026-10-21)
docs.text:
Landed: the web client's project sections, moving sessions by drag and with Move to project…, the project editor with its emoji picker, New session's project picker, and project.delete from the sidebar and the Memory view; the TUI's project in the bottom bar, its picker and /project, and the session picker's project filter. Session rename and badges landed beforehand (the rename-badges work), and the waiting clock on web rows with client protocol 1.9.0. No protocol change.

Where it is: crates/client_state/src/projects.rs (sections, the picker's choices, the emoji check, defaults to and from attach requests, the default agent), badges::project_badges, crates/web/src/views/projects.rs and crates/web/src/workspace/projects.rs, crates/web/src/emoji.rs with the list scripts/web-emoji.py writes, and crates/tui/src/ui/app/projects.rs.

Decisions taken where the spec left room, and deviations:

  • Gating. Everything shows from a daemon of client protocol 1.8 or later (projects::daemon_has_projects). An older daemon keeps the web client's workspace filter and the Memory view's per-memory delete, and the TUI names no project.
  • "No project" has a + too, for a new session outside every project; it has no pencil or trash. An open section with no sessions says so, and every header, "No project" included, takes a dropped session.
  • Session counts. projects.changed announces changes to projects, not to their sessions, so the web client reads projects.list again when a session moves, is created in a project, or is removed, and when memory changes: the delete's confirmation then counts what goes.
  • Conflicts. Reloading the editor after project_changed also refreshes the list's revision; a delete refused with project_changed reads the list again and asks for the delete once more.
  • Defaults from the editor keep every picked runtime, one not listed now included, and each workspace as typed (~/…): the coding runtime resolves it when a session attaches it. A project's defaults are sent only when they changed, and null when they say nothing beyond the daemon's usual defaults.
  • Drag. The session rows use the Machines view's gesture: a mouse drags once it moves 4 px (only where there are headers to drop on), a finger after a half-second press, which let go in place reveals the row's Move, Rename, and Delete. A header's own long press shows its pencil and trash. Over a hovered row, the three buttons cover the middle of a 288 px sidebar row; the browser scenarios click rows by their title.
  • Emoji picker. 503 emoji in nine categories (Emoji 13.0 or older, fully qualified, no skin tones, no zero-width joiner sequences, no country flags), with their CLDR names from Unicode's emoji-test.txt. The search matches every word of the query against the name, or the emoji itself. The check is unicode-segmentation and unicode-properties, as the daemon's; client_state now depends on them.
  • New session's project picker is a native <select>, which phones show with their own picker; "New project…" opens the editor and picks the project it creates.
  • TUI. The project leads the bottom bar, before the daemon's address. /project and a click on the name open the same picker; "New project…" asks for a name over it. Ctrl+P in the session picker also has a button on its action row, which names the filter. A draft whose project defaults name runtimes drops runtimes edited with /runtime and shows the defaults' workspaces; the daemon attaches them at creation.
  • Ordering. rows::order_sessions counts a session that waits on a producer (client protocol 1.9) as active, so it leads its section with the running ones.
  • Badges show machines (section 9 as changed on 2026-10-21): badges::session_badges and project_badges follow the new table, and badges::hue_key gives the runtime cards' and the bottom bar's dots their machine's hue. The web client fits each badge line after it draws and whenever it changes size (a ResizeObserver), leaving out whole machine badges for the +N from the end.

docs.title: Push notifications
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-25); approved 2026-10-25 with the user's decisions in section 14, implemented with the deviations in section 16.2. Extends the web client (section 9, installable app), cron jobs, background tool calls (waiting_on), the approval reviewer, and ACP agents (elicitation), and changes the default of [approval] timeout_ms (section 4.4).

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
Today a phone learns nothing until it is opened. The web client is an installable app with a network-only service worker (web client spec, section 9), but a turn that ends, or an approval that waits, while the phone is in a pocket or the tab is in the background goes unnoticed until the user looks.

This spec has the daemon send a Web Push notification to the user's phones and browsers on two occasions:

  • A root session settles (section 3): its run ended and nothing will start another one without the user. Concretely:
  • a root session's run ends completed or failed;
  • no user input and no producer message (steer, queue, goal reminder) is waiting to start the next run;
  • nothing the session waits on will wake it: no running background call, no subagent that runs or can still wake, no external producer registration, no active goal, and no one-time cron job aimed at it. Recurring cron jobs do not count: a session with a nightly job would otherwise never notify.
  • A run needs the user (section 4): an approval escalates to the user, or an ACP agent asks a question (elicitation), in the root session or in any subagent below it.

In scope:

  • the engine's settle rule and its signals (sections 3 and 4);
  • a Web Push sender in the daemon: VAPID keys, RFC 8291 payload encryption, delivery and cleanup (section 6);
  • subscriptions over the client protocol (section 7);
  • suppressing a push while the user is looking at the session (section 8);
  • the web client: turning notifications on, the service worker's push and notificationclick handlers, and opening the session from a notification (section 9);
  • [notifications] configuration (section 10);
  • approvals that wait for the user until answered, by default (section 4.4).

Out of scope:

  • notifying a delegated session's settling on its own: its turns reach the root, which notifies when it settles (its approvals and questions do notify, section 4);
  • answering an approval from the notification itself (Approve and Deny buttons): the service worker has no daemon token, and iOS shows no notification actions; the click opens the approval instead;
  • native mobile apps, email, or third-party relays (ntfy, Pushover);
  • desktop notifications from the TUI.

docs.title: 2. Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Root session: a session whose origin is not delegated, including ACP-agent sessions and sessions a new-session cron job created.
  • Tree: a root session and every session delegated below it.
  • Settled: a root session with no active run, nothing waiting to start one, and nothing in its wake set (section 3.2).
  • Armed: a root session whose last run ended in a way that should be reported once it settles (section 3.1).
  • One-time job: an enabled cron job aimed at the session (in-session target) with an at schedule (what in becomes), or a cron schedule with max_runs = 1 (the default). The agent waking itself later through one is the agent still at work, so it holds the push back. Recurring job: any other enabled job with a next fire time, a cron schedule with max_runs above 1 or "unlimited", judged by its definition and never by how many runs it has left.
  • Needs you: an approval whose approval_step is escalated (it waits for the user), or an ACP elicitation that is requested and not resolved.
  • Subscription: a browser's PushSubscription (endpoint, p256dh, and auth keys) registered with the daemon, with a label.
  • Push service: the browser vendor's relay the endpoint points at (fcm.googleapis.com, web.push.apple.com, updates.push.services.mozilla.com, …).

docs.title: 3.1 Arming and disarming
docs.text:
The engine keeps, per root session and in memory only, whether it is armed.

  • Armed when a run of the session ends completed or failed.
  • Not armed by cancelled (someone stopped it, so someone is there) or interrupted (the daemon went down; the restart says nothing).
  • Disarmed when a run starts, when user input is admitted, when the notification is sent (or suppressed, section 8), and when the session is deleted.

A restart forgets every armed flag. Nothing is written to the session log; session history is unchanged.

docs.title: 3.2 The settle rule
docs.text:
An armed root session settles when all of these hold, checked inside the session actor:

  1. no run is active and none is being admitted;
  2. no pending user input, and no accepted, undiscarded, unconsumed producer message (steer or queue, goal reminders included);
  3. its wake set is empty.

The wake set is what live_waiting_kinds and the fold's Goal report as waiting_on, with one difference: recurring jobs count for nothing, here and in every subagent below the root. So:

The session, or a subagent below it, has… Wake set an active goal goal a running background call background_call an ACP agent's own command still running after its call ended, or one that ended between runs less than 5 s ago (its wake grace: the agent's follow-up, such as Claude Code's, starts within it; a run starting ends it) background_call a subagent turn running, a background delegation queued or running, or a child that can still wake subagent a live external producer registration (plugin or runtime) external_producer a one-time job aimed at it scheduled_job only recurring jobs aimed at it (nothing)

The last two rows need a second view of the tree, because today a subagent with any cron job makes its parent wait as subagent (refresh_live_waiting, crates/engine/src/runtime/producers.rs). refresh_live_waiting computes, beside waiting_on, a wakes_once flag per session: what wakes the session counting only one-time jobs, and a child counting for its parent only while its own wakes_once holds. It is carried up the tree under the same waking_children discipline, in a second map. waiting_on and what clients see do not change.

Crons::waits_on gains a companion, waits_on_once(session), true when a one-time job is aimed at session.

docs.title: 3.3 When the rule is checked
docs.text:
The engine checks an armed session:

  • after a run's RunFinished is committed and the actor has decided whether queued input or producer messages start the next run at once, so a queued message never yields a notification for the turn before it;
  • whenever refresh_live_waiting changes the root's wakes_once, so a turn that ended while a subagent or external producer was still live notifies when that producer goes away without sending (a producer that does send starts a run, which disarms and re-arms the session);
  • when a one-time job aimed at the session, or below it, is deleted, disabled, or becomes recurring through crons.update.

When the rule holds the engine disarms the session and publishes a SessionSettled signal (section 5).

docs.title: 3.4 Examples
docs.text:
• The root answers a question: run completed, nothing waits: notify.
  • The root delegates in the background and ends its turn: wake set subagent, no push. The subagent's report starts a run; that run ends with nothing waiting: notify once, for the final turn.
  • The root ends its turn with a job in 2h aimed at it: no push. Two hours later the fire runs a turn; it ends with nothing waiting: notify.
  • The root ends its turn and has a nightly job with max_runs = "unlimited": notify now, and after each nightly run that settles. A cron job with max_runs = 3 behaves the same, its last run included.
  • The user cancels a run: no push.
  • Goal mode keeps continuing: no push until the goal completes, pauses, or is cancelled and the last run ends.

docs.title: 4. When a run needs the user
4.1 Approvals
docs.text:
• Trigger: an approval_step of type escalated is committed in any session of the tree. Approvals the internal pipeline or the approval reviewer decide (evaluated) never notify, so auto_approve_y and auto_approve_n sessions notify only for what they hand to the user.
  • Content: the tool's display name and one-line summary from the call's tool_call_started presentation (bash: cargo test -p engine), the session the approval is in (the subagent's handle when it is not the root), and the expiry time when the escalation carries expires_at.
  • Several at once: escalations in one tree within 1 second of each other (parallel tool calls) go out as one push, 3 approvals waiting, naming the first.
  • The window. By default an approval waits until it is answered (section 4.4). When [approval] timeout_ms is set, a push for an approval with less than 5 seconds left is not sent.

docs.title: 4.2 Agent questions (elicitations)
docs.text:
ACP agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI) ask questions through elicitation (ElicitationRequested, answered by elicitation.respond; ACP agents spec, elicitation round of 2026-10-24).

  • Trigger: an ElicitationRequested in any session of the tree.
  • Content: the agent's name and the first 160 characters of its message, flattened to plain text; Sign-in requested for a URL elicitation without a message.
  • Grouped with approvals in the same 1-second window.

docs.title: 4.3 What it does not change
docs.text: A needs-you push never arms or disarms the settle rule: the run is still running. When the approval is answered, expires, or the question resolves, the run goes on, and its end arms the root as usual. The settle push uses the same tag (section 5.2), so it replaces the needs-you push on the phone.

docs.title: 4.4 Approvals wait until answered by default
docs.text:
[approval] timeout_ms defaults to 30 seconds today, counted from the escalation, so a push would reach the phone with seconds left (user decision, 2026-10-25: no expiry by default).

  • timeout_ms becomes optional, with no default, and accepts any integer. Absent, or any value <= 0, an escalated approval never expires: its escalated step carries no expires_at, and it waits until a client answers it, the run is cancelled, or the daemon goes down (which interrupts the run, as today). A value <= 0 is the explicit way to write "never", since TOML has no null (user decisions, 2026-10-25). A positive number of milliseconds expires as today.
  • Engine. ApprovalConfig::timeout_ms becomes Option<i64>; the "must be positive" check in crates/config/src/runtime.rs goes, and approval_expiry returns None for None and for any value <= 0. The rest already handles an approval without an expiry: approval_expiry_wait waits without end, and approval_deadline_exhausted is false.
  • Clients. The TUI and the web client already treat a missing expires_at as no countdown and no expiry (crates/client_state/src/lib.rs, crates/tui/src/ui/app/approvals.rs). No wire change: expires_at is already optional.
  • What waiting longer means:
  • the run stays running, so its session stays in memory, its root's tree stays busy, and a parent waiting on it keeps waiting;
  • a new-session cron run (default permission mode auto_approve_n) whose call escalates now waits for the user instead of being denied by expiry after 30 seconds; the job's later fires are skipped as previous run still running until it is answered or cancelled, and the push tells the user;
  • an in-session fire into a session blocked on an approval queues behind that run, as it does behind any running turn.
  • Docs. The approval page (docs/site/engine/approval.md) and the configuration reference describe the optional key and values <= 0; tests cover absent, 0, and -1 (no expiry) and 1 (expiry), not the default.

docs.title: 5.1 Engine signals
docs.text:
The engine publishes on a broadcast channel, beside subscribe_index_changes. These are daemon-internal, not protocol messages.

pub enum PushSignal {
    Settled {
        root: SessionId,
        run_id: RunId,
        outcome: SettledOutcome, // Completed { final_text } | Failed { error }
        title: Option<SessionTitle>,
        project: Option<ProjectId>,
        cron: Option<SessionCron>,
        at: Timestamp,
    },
    NeedsYou {
        root: SessionId,
        session: SessionId,           // where the approval or question is
        handle: Option<String>,       // the subagent's short id, when not the root
        item: NeedsYouItem,           // Approval { approval_id, tool, summary, expires_at }
                                      // | Question { elicitation_id, agent, message }
        title: Option<SessionTitle>,  // the root's
        at: Timestamp,
    },
}

docs.title: 5.2 The payload
docs.text:
The daemon sends a small JSON payload; the service worker renders it.

{
  "v": 1,
  "kind": "settled",
  "root": "01JB…",
  "session": "01JB…",
  "title": "Fix the flaky cron test",
  "body": "The test now waits on the fire's history entry instead of…",
  "outcome": "completed",
  "at": "2026-10-25T14:02:11Z"
}
  • kind: settled, approval, question, or test.
  • title: the root session's title, else Session <short id>. A new-session cron run's title already names its job. For approval and question, prefixed Approval · or Question ·.
  • body:
  • settled, completed: the first 160 characters of the run's final text, Markdown markers and line breaks flattened to plain text, with … when cut; Finished. when the run ended with no text;
  • settled, failed: Failed: and the run's safe error message, cut the same way;
  • approval and question: section 4, with in <handle> when the item is in a subagent and expires 14:03 when it has an expiry.
  • session: where the click goes: the root for settled, the approval's or question's session otherwise.
  • The service worker shows it with:
  • tag: "session:<root>" and renotify: true, so a newer notification for the same tree replaces the older one;
  • requireInteraction: true for approval and question where the browser supports it;
  • data: { session }, for the click (section 9.3);
  • the app icon and badge already in the bundle.
  • A payload kind or version the service worker does not know is shown with its title and body as they are; it never shows nothing (section 9.2).
  • The encrypted record stays under the 4096-byte limit push services set: the payload is cut to at most 3 KiB before encryption.

docs.title: 6. Sending: Web Push in the daemon
6.1 VAPID keys
docs.text:
• On first use the daemon generates a P-256 key pair and stores the private key in <data_root>/push/vapid.pk8 (PKCS#8, mode 0600). It is never sent to a client; its public key (uncompressed point, base64url) is what notifications.get returns.
  • Rotating it is deleting the file: every subscription is then bound to a key the daemon no longer has, so the daemon drops them all, and each browser resubscribes on its next connect (section 9.1).
  • The VAPID JWT (RFC 8292, ES256) carries aud = the endpoint's origin, exp = now + 12 h, and sub = the contact below. Tokens are cached per audience until an hour before exp.
  • The contact is derived, not asked for. sub is the repository URL the binary was built from, env!("CARGO_PKG_REPOSITORY") (https://github.com/cookie-agent/cookie-agent; the server crate takes repository.workspace = true for it). It passes every push service's check, needs no setup, and sends nothing about the user. Rejected sources:
  • the daemon's own URL (the page origin, usually a *.ts.net name): unreachable for a push service, and it would tell Google, Apple, and Mozilla the tailnet's host names;
  • the user's email (git user.email, memory): personal data sent to third parties without asking.

[notifications] contact overrides it for a user who wants to be the one contacted. - What the push services check (checked 2026-10-25): - RFC 8292: aud and exp are required, exp at most 24 hours ahead; sub is optional and SHOULD be a mailto: or https: contact for the application server's operator. - Apple (Sending web push notifications in web apps and browsers) answers 403 BadJwtToken when the subject claim is not a URL or mailto:, the audience is not the push service's origin, or the expiry is more than a day ahead, and asks for a JWT refreshed no more than once an hour. It needs no Apple Developer Program membership. So sub is always sent. - Nothing verifies the contact: Apple checks only its form. It is whom a push service would write to about this sender, so a user who wants to be that contact sets their own mailto:.

docs.title: 6.2 Encryption
docs.text: RFC 8291 aes128gcm content encoding: an ephemeral P-256 key per message, ECDH with the subscription's p256dh, HKDF-SHA-256 with its auth secret, one AES-128-GCM record. Everything comes from aws-lc-rs, already in the dependency tree through rustls (agreement::ECDH_P256, hkdf, aead::AES_128_GCM, signature::ECDSA_P256_SHA256_FIXED_SIGNING), and HTTP from reqwest, already in the tree through oven-sdk; the server crate takes both as direct dependencies. No new crate is downloaded. (proposed; the alternative is the web-push-native crate, which brings the RustCrypto P-256 stack.)

docs.title: 6.3 Delivery
docs.text:
For each signal that passes the configuration (section 10) and presence (section 8) checks, the notifier task in the server sends one POST to every subscription, concurrently:

Header Value Authorization vapid t=<jwt>, k=<public key> Content-Encoding aes128gcm TTL 86400 (a phone offline for a day still gets it); for an approval that expires, the seconds left of its window, at least 1 Urgency high for approval, question, and a failed run; normal otherwise Topic 22 base64url characters hashed from the root's id, so the push service replaces an undelivered notification for the same tree

Responses:

  • 201: delivered to the push service; last_sent_at updated.
  • 404 or 410: the subscription is gone; the daemon deletes it and announces notifications.changed.
  • 429 and 5xx: up to three retries with backoff (honouring Retry-After), within one minute, and never past an approval's expiry.
  • Any other status, or a network error: last_error records it (status and the first 200 bytes of the body); the subscription stays.

The sender never blocks the engine: signals go through a bounded channel, and when it is full the oldest signal is dropped with a warning.

The daemon needs outbound HTTPS to the push services. A daemon with no route to the internet keeps working; its sends fail into last_error.

docs.title: 6.4 Storage
docs.text:
<data_root>/push/subscriptions.json (mode 0600), written atomically like crons.json:

{
  "subscriptions": [
    {
      "id": "p7c2m9qk",
      "endpoint": "https://web.push.apple.com/QG…",
      "p256dh": "BN…",
      "auth": "x3…",
      "label": "iPhone · Safari",
      "created_at": "2026-10-25T13:40:00Z",
      "last_sent_at": "2026-10-25T14:02:12Z",
      "last_error": null
    }
  ]
}

The file is strict like configuration: unknown fields are an error.

docs.title: 7. Client protocol
docs.text:
Additive, a minor client protocol bump.

Method Direction Params → result notifications.get request {} → { public_key, enabled, subscriptions: [Subscription] } notifications.subscribe request { endpoint, p256dh, auth, label } → { subscription } notifications.unsubscribe request { id } → {} notifications.test request { id } → { status: "sent" \| "gone" \| "failed", detail? } notifications.changed notification daemon → client: { subscriptions } client.presence notification client → daemon: { session: SessionId \| null } (section 8)
  • Subscription as clients see it: id, label, push_service (the endpoint's host), created_at, last_sent_at, last_error. The endpoint and keys are never sent back.
  • subscribe is idempotent by endpoint: the same endpoint updates the keys and label and keeps its id. The endpoint must be https://; the label is 1 to 80 characters.
  • test sends a fixed payload (kind: "test") to that subscription now, ignoring presence and enabled.
  • The methods work whatever [notifications] enabled says, so a user can set up devices before turning sending on.

No plugin, runtime, or session-history change.

docs.title: 8. Not notifying the user who is watching
docs.text:
A push for the session the user is looking at is noise (user decision, 2026-10-25). Clients tell the daemon what they show:

  • client.presence { session } names the session the client shows and that the user is there; { session: null } says the user is not.
  • Web client: the page sends the viewed session while document.visibilityState is visible and the window has focus, and null when it hides, blurs, or has seen no pointer, key, or touch input for 2 minutes. It resends on reconnect and on switching sessions.
  • TUI: the same with the terminal's focus events (crossterm FocusGained/FocusLost) and the same 2-minute idle rule; a terminal without focus reporting never reports presence, so its user still gets pushes.
  • A connection's presence ends with the connection.

The notifier suppresses a signal when any connection reports presence on a session of the same tree: for settled, the engine then disarms the root as if it had sent. Presence on another tree does not suppress: the user may be in a different session on the desktop and still want the phone to buzz.

docs.title: 9.1 Turning notifications on
docs.text:
Settings › Notifications (its own section since 2026-10-25, section 16.4), decided by pure logic beside crates/web/src/install.rs, in these states:

State What it shows No PushManager, or not a secure context Needs HTTPS (as the install offer says) iOS or iPadOS, not running from the Home Screen Add to Home Screen first (iOS 16.4 and later push only to installed web apps) Permission denied Notifications are blocked in the browser's site settings Not subscribed Turn on notifications Subscribed with this daemon's key On; Send test, Turn off, the label (editable) Subscribed with another key Subscribed to another daemon or an older key; Switch to this daemon
  • Turn on runs from the click (browsers require a user gesture): Notification.requestPermission(), then registration.pushManager.subscribe({ userVisibleOnly: true, applicationServerKey }) with the daemon's public key, then notifications.subscribe. The default label is the device and browser from the user agent (Pixel · Chrome, iPhone · Safari).
  • The subscribed daemon. Turning on, switching, and resubscribing on connect store that daemon's WebSocket URL in the page's storage (push_daemon_url), beside the URLs and tokens it already keeps; a click uses it (section 9.3).
  • Turn off unsubscribes in the browser, calls notifications.unsubscribe, and forgets push_daemon_url.
  • Switch unsubscribes the old subscription and subscribes again. A browser holds one subscription per service worker, bound to one key, so a page origin can receive pushes from one daemon at a time; Settings says so.
  • On every connect, when permission is granted and a subscription exists with this daemon's key, the page sends notifications.subscribe again, so an endpoint the browser rotated (pushsubscriptionchange) or a daemon that lost its file catches up.
  • Below, Devices lists every subscription from notifications.get with its push service, last sent time, and last error, each removable.
  • After installing on a phone, the one-time install banner's place offers Turn on notifications once, dismissible the same way.

docs.title: 9.2 The service worker
docs.text:
sw.js stays network-only (no Cache Storage; the fetch handler is unchanged) and gains two handlers:

  • push: parses the payload and calls registration.showNotification(title, options) inside event.waitUntil. It always shows a notification, falling back to Cookie Agent with no body for a payload it cannot parse: Safari revokes subscriptions that receive pushes without one, and Chrome shows its own "updated in the background" instead.
  • notificationclick: closes the notification, then focuses a window of the app within the worker's scope and posts it { type: "open-session", session }; with none open, it opens ./#session=<id>.

The section 9 note in the web client spec and the the_service_worker_is_network_only test are updated: the worker still caches nothing.

docs.title: 9.3 Opening a session from a link
docs.text:
The page reads #session=<id> at launch, beside #token=, removes it from the address bar the same way, and opens that session once connected (or says it no longer exists).

The session belongs to the daemon that sent the push, which is the one in push_daemon_url (section 9.1), not necessarily the one the page last connected to: the page may have connected to another daemon since. So a #session= launch connects to push_daemon_url instead of the remembered URL, with the token stored for it; a running page connected elsewhere switches its connection there first, as the connect screen does. With no token stored for that URL, the connect screen opens with it filled in. The daemon's own URL is not in the payload: a daemon does not know the address the page reaches it by. A subagent's session opens in its root's tree, where its approval or question waits. The open-session message does the same in a running page.

When the daemon cannot be reached, the page shows its normal connection error and forgets the session it was asked for: nothing is kept pending for a later connection (user decision, 2026-10-25).

When the page shows a tree, it closes that tree's notifications (registration.getNotifications({ tag })), so a stale approval does not stay on the phone after it was answered on the desktop. Nothing is pushed to retract a notification: a push that shows nothing is what section 9.2 avoids.

docs.title: 10. Configuration
docs.text:
[notifications]
enabled = true        # false stops every push; subscriptions and RPCs keep working
preview = "reply"     # "reply": the start of the final text or question; "status": only what happened
approvals = true      # notify for approvals and agent questions waiting for the user
cron_sessions = true  # notify when a root session a new-session cron job created settles
contact = "mailto:me@example.com"  # optional VAPID `sub` override; absent: the repository URL
  • With preview = "status" the body says only Finished., Failed., Approval waiting, or Question waiting.
  • cron_sessions = false drops only the settle push of those sessions; their approvals and questions still notify, since a run is blocked.
  • Strict like all configuration: unknown keys, wrong types, a preview other than the two values, and a contact that is not https: or mailto: are errors.
  • Live: config.apply and config.reload take effect for the next signal.
  • The configuration reference documents the section; tests cover unknown fields and the boundaries, not the default values.

docs.title: 11. Security and privacy
docs.text:
• Only an authenticated client can add a subscription; the daemon token is as powerful as ever, and nothing new is reachable without it.
  • The daemon POSTs only to https:// endpoints a client registered. An authenticated client can already run commands, so the endpoint is not restricted to known push services (new browsers would break an allowlist).
  • Payloads are end-to-end encrypted to the browser (RFC 8291); push services see the size, the time, the Topic hash, and the endpoint. The lock screen shows the title and preview, an approval's command line included: preview = "status" keeps them off it.
  • A notification never answers anything: approving still takes an authenticated client.
  • The VAPID private key and subscriptions are files of mode 0600 under the data root; neither is in a protocol response.
  • The service worker has no token and makes no daemon request.

docs.title: 12. Documentation
docs.text:
• The web client guide (docs/site/clients/web.md): a Phone notifications section: HTTPS (for example tailscale serve), installing on iOS first, turning on, testing, what triggers a push, and the approval window.
  • The configuration reference: [notifications].
  • The protocol reference and changelog: the notifications.* methods and client.presence.
  • The web client spec: an addendum pointing here from section 9.
  • The specs index: this page, under drafts until implemented.

docs.title: 13.1 Tests
