  • With capabilities: the child gets the root's global by the rule above, so memory, MCP, and plugin tools stay. It also gets each listed runtime, in the order given, attached with the usual names (<runtime>_<workspace basename>, with _2 added for duplicates).
  • Two or more workspaces get tool prefixes, exactly as for any session.
  • The same runtime may be listed twice with different workspaces.
  • Without capabilities: the child inherits the root's attachments, as today.
  • Starting the runtimes. The daemon starts each runtime before it creates the child, as session.create does: a template runtime is started, and a dial-in runtime must be connected. If any runtime fails to start or is refused, the call fails, nothing is created, and the error names the runtime and the reason.
  • The prompt. The child's own system prompt describes its attachments: one workspace, or the machines block when there are several. This is unchanged.

docs.title: 2.3 Deeper children
docs.text:
• At depth 1 and below, delegate_subagent has no capabilities parameter. A call that passes one anyway is refused as an unknown argument (deny_unknown_fields).
  • A child at depth n + 1 inherits the attachments of its parent at depth n. Today it inherits the root's. The two are the same until a depth-1 child is given its own runtimes, which is what this spec adds.
  • A runtime attached or detached on the root later does not reach existing children. New children of the root see it.

docs.title: 3. Permissions
docs.text:
• Rules. The existing action@runtime selector applies to delegate:
  • delegate@labpc: deny keeps the root from delegating to labpc;
  • delegate@labpc: ask asks first;
  • a plain delegate rule covers every runtime.

As with other selectors, the most specific rule wins. - Checking a call. Each runtime listed in capabilities is checked as delegate@<runtime id>. A denied runtime refuses the whole call. An ask runtime puts the call through the usual approval, which shows the runtimes and workspaces. - Inheriting. A call without capabilities is checked as today: plain delegate, with no runtime selector. - The child's own rules still decide what it can do on that runtime, including any bash@labpc-style selectors.

docs.title: 4. list_runtimes
docs.text:
A tool of the global runtime that takes no arguments. It is offered only where global is attached, and only when the run's agent may use it.

  • Permission. The new action list_runtimes controls it. An agent document with no list_runtimes key gets a default rule by its mode, as the memory actions do (memory spec section 9.2):
Mode list_runtimes primary, all allow subagent, internal none

Subagents cannot choose runtimes, so by default they do not see the list. An agent document can grant it with list_runtimes: allow, or turn it off with deny. Session overlays apply on top, as for any action.

  • Live. Every call reads the daemon's current state, from the same sources as runtimes.list and machines.list.
  • Untruncated. It opts out of [tool_output] truncation. Its single output is bounded only by the event size limit, so a daemon with thousands of instances fails with a resource-limit error rather than being cut silently.
  • Output. Tags, grouped by machine and then by runtime (format settled 2026-10-21):
<runtimes>
  <!-- global is attached to this session's root, so every subagent in this tree has it, whether or not its capabilities list it. -->
  <global/>
  <machine name="yunhao-labserver" platform="linux">
    <runtime id="local" connected="true" home="/home/u">
      <capability name="coding" takes_workspace="true" description="Read, write, edit, and run commands in a workspace"/>
      <attachment name="local_cookie_agent" capability="coding" workspace="/home/u/src/cookie-agent" status="ready"/>
    </runtime>
  </machine>
  <machine name="labpc" platform="linux">
    <runtime id="labpc" connected="false" starts_on_use="true" home="/home/u">
      <capability name="coding" takes_workspace="true" description="Read, write, edit, and run commands in a workspace"/>
    </runtime>
  </machine>
  <unplaced>
    <runtime id="roamer" connected="false" message="runtime `roamer` disconnected: the other end closed the connection"/>
  </unplaced>
</runtimes>
  • global is never listed as a runtime, because it cannot be named in capabilities. A single <global/> element, with the comment above it, appears exactly when the root session of the caller's tree has global attached. It is left out otherwise.
  • <capability> carries the capability's own description, from the description the runtime reports for each capability (as in runtimes.list).
  • starts_on_use="true" marks a template runtime that is not running and that the daemon starts when a session needs it. It replaces a lifetime attribute: whether a runtime is built in, spawned, or dials in tells the model nothing more it can act on.
  • <attachment> elements are the calling session's own attachments, and nothing else (decided 2026-10-21). Instances that other sessions have open are left out: they say nothing about where this session can work, and they would show other sessions' workspaces. Any runtime can still be named in delegate_subagent's capabilities, opened or not.
  • Paths are absolute. home is printed so the model can relate a path to the machine's home directory.
  • Attributes with no value (home, platform, message, starts_on_use) are left out. Values are XML-escaped.
  • A runtime with no known machine goes under <unplaced>.
  • Timing. Its result describes the daemon at call time. A runtime that dials in or drops out later shows from the next call. delegate_subagent checks its capabilities against the same live state when it is called.

docs.title: 5.1 Web
docs.text:
Superseded on 2026-10-23: the draft shows its cards above the composer and has no chip (see the addendum).

  • New session opens on the composer with only global attached. The first message creates the session with runtimes: [] and global: true.
  • A "Runtimes…" chip in the bottom bar, shown on drafts, opens the runtime cards as a sheet. A selection there attaches those runtimes at creation, as the cards do today. The chip shows the selected runtimes as badges, or "global only".
  • Projects. A project with default attachments prefills the draft's selection, and the chip shows them. Choosing a project still never changes a running session.
  • The browser no longer remembers a selection across New session. Each new draft starts global-only, or from its project's defaults.

docs.title: 5.2 TUI
docs.text: • No change. Plain cookie attaches global and local at the current directory, /runtime edits a draft's attachments, and project defaults apply as in the projects spec.

docs.title: 5.3 Where a session works: badges from its subagents
docs.text:
Added 2026-10-21. A root with only global shows no badges, yet its subagents work on labpc and in ~/api. The session's badges should say so.

  • The union. A root session's badges are built from its own attachments together with every direct child's attachments, with duplicates (same runtime, capability, and workspace) removed and global ignored as before. The usual badge rules then apply (projects spec section 9): one machine shows [machine] and its workspaces, and several machines show their machine badges.
  • Depth 1 is enough. Only depth-1 children can be given capabilities (section 2), and deeper children inherit from their parent (section 2.3). So the direct children's attachments already cover the whole tree, and nothing deeper is read.
  • Kept with the root, not computed per listing. session.list stays metadata-only (tree-local sessions spec), so the union cannot be built by reading the children at listing time. When a child is created, the daemon adds any of its attachments the root does not yet record to a new SessionMeta.delegated_attachments, which is folded from a durable event on the root's log. A cache rebuild keeps it, and the change is announced with sessions.changed upserted. The cost is one small event per child that brings new attachments, and none when a child only inherits.
  • Order. The root's own attachments come first, then delegated ones in the order children brought them. Machine badges follow that order.
  • It only grows. A child that finishes or is evicted leaves its attachments in the union: the badges say where the session has worked. A detach on the root removes only the root's own attachment.
  • A child's own row in the subagent tree shows badges from its own attachments only.
  • The TUI uses the same union for the project and workspace label in its session picker rows.

docs.title: 6. Prompt
docs.text:
• A root with only global. Its system prompt has no working directory and no machine line, as today. Instead, the delegate tool's prompt section adds a short paragraph: this session has no workspace; work that needs files or commands goes to a subagent with capabilities; and list_runtimes shows what exists.
  • Every other prompt is unchanged.

docs.title: 7. Bringing a runtime in from a subagent
docs.text:
No new mechanism is needed for the pattern of a root that has a daemon coding subagent bring a remote machine in temporarily:

  1. The root delegates to a coding subagent on local.
  2. That subagent runs a background bash call that dials the remote runtime in: ssh <host> cookie runtime serve --daemon <url> --id <id> --token <token>. Alternatively, it adds a [runtimes.<id>] template to config.toml.
  3. The root calls list_runtimes, sees the new runtime, and delegates to it with capabilities.
  4. Stopping the background call (stop_background) ends the dial-in connection, and the runtime shows as disconnected.

Security. The subagent needs the daemon's token, which is [server] token in config.toml. Any agent that may read or bash on the daemon's machine can already read it. This spec gives no new access, but the docs say so plainly. Users who want to prevent it deny reads of ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml in that agent's rules. A config edit takes effect only after config.reload or a daemon restart, which a subagent cannot trigger through a tool. The dial-in path is therefore the one the docs show.

docs.title: 8. Protocol and compatibility
docs.text:
• Tools. The tool schemas are model-facing, so the delegation changes need no protocol version. Children record their attachments with the existing runtime_attached events.
  • Client protocol minor (additive), for section 5.3: SessionMeta.delegated_attachments and the root event it is folded from. The event is also a plugin protocol minor, since plugins see events. Older daemons send nothing, so clients show the root's own attachments, as today.
  • Old logs. Children that inherited the root's attachments keep them. Replay reads attachments from each child's own events.
  • docs/site/reference/tools.md is regenerated for list_runtimes and the new parameter.

docs.title: 9. Phases
docs.text:
1. Engine:
  2. first, the registry remembering where runtimes ran (memory spec section 16.8), so offline runtimes keep their machine in list_runtimes, badges, and the Machines view;
  3. the capabilities parameter and its per-session schema;
  4. starting runtimes for a child;
  5. parent inheritance;
  6. delegate@runtime checks;
  7. list_runtimes;
  8. the prompt paragraph;
  9. tests;
  10. the tools reference.
  11. Web: a global-only New session, the "Runtimes…" chip and sheet, project prefill through the chip, and badges from the union of the root's and its subagents' attachments (section 5.3). The daemon's delegated_attachments belongs to phase 1.
  12. Docs:
  13. the runtimes concept page and delegation guide;
  14. the pattern in section 7, with its security note;
  15. the web guide.

docs.title: 10. Open questions
docs.text:
None. The user approved the spec on 2026-10-21, including: - the list_runtimes permission defaults; - resume_session_id excluding capabilities; - the web client forgetting the selection; - the dial-in pattern in section 7.

A delegated child keeps copying its parent's cwd_identity.

docs.title: 11. Implementation notes
docs.text:
Implemented 2026-10-21 in three phases: the engine, daemon, and protocol (client protocol 1.10.0, plugin protocol 1.4.0), the clients, and the docs (Delegating to runtimes). The registry remembering where runtimes ran (memory spec section 16.8) landed first.

Where things are:

  • The parameter and its checks: crates/engine/src/base_tools/delegate.rs (the per-session schema, check_capabilities, the prompt paragraph) and crates/engine/src/runtime/runtime_delegation.rs (CapabilitiesParam, parse_capability, check_delegated_capabilities, open_delegated_capabilities, inherited_attachments, record_delegated_attachments, and list_runtimes_text).
  • list_runtimes: crates/engine/src/runtimes_tool.rs, a provider of the global runtime bound to the engine like the memory tools.
  • Per-runtime permission checks: PreparedTool::with_permission_runtimes (crates/runtime_api) and strictest_decision in crates/engine/src/runtime/tool_execution.rs.

Deviations and readings of the spec:

  • The parameter is capabilities, as decided; the schema block in section 2.1 still shows the earlier name.
  • Absent means refused as unknown. delegate_subagent keeps one argument type, so a call that passes capabilities where the schema has none is refused by the provider with serde's unknown-field wording.
  • Checks against the live listing cover what the daemon knows: a runtime that has never connected lists no capabilities yet, so its capability and workspace are checked only by starting it. A missing workspace for a capability that takes one, and a workspace for one that takes none, are refused before anything starts.
  • Runtimes start before the admission lock and the reservation. A slow template does not hold up other delegations, and a runtime that does not start leaves no reservation. The capabilities are not part of the durable delegation reservation: a redelivered call computes them again from its arguments, and a child that already exists keeps the attachments it recorded.
  • Deeper children inherit their parent's attachments other than global, plus the root's global attachment when the root has one now, so that global follows the root at every depth.
  • Permission evaluation. Each runtime a call names is evaluated as the agent's delegate rules with that runtime as the scope, and each resource takes the strictest of the runtimes' evaluations, so the approval request keeps one evaluation per resource. The request names no runtime; the runtimes and workspaces show in the call's presentation, as a runtimes entry. delegate@<runtime> became an accepted permission key; message and skill still take no selector.
  • list_runtimes lists runtimes.list's runtimes: the built-in and configured ones and the dial-in runtimes that connected since the daemon started. A dial-in runtime remembered from before a restart is in machines.list but not in list_runtimes until it connects, since it cannot be delegated to before then. Machines are ordered with the daemon's own first and the rest by name, runtimes by ID within a machine; a machine whose runtimes report different platforms puts the platform on each runtime. An attachment whose instance is not open reports status="stopped". The output is also shown to clients as a Markdown code block.
  • Delegated attachments. The root event is delegated_attachments_added { child_session_id, attachments }, a runless state event; attachments are RuntimeAttachments as the child named them, at least one. The fold keeps one entry per runtime, capability, and workspace. A fork leaves the event behind with its source's subagents, as record_omitted. A child is checked again on a redelivery, so a crash between creating the child and recording its attachments is repaired by the redelivery.
  • The TUI uses the union through RuntimeHomes::session_place in its session picker, which shows the delegated workspaces only for a root with no workspace of its own; its machines view lists remembered runtimes, as machine_entries now does for both clients.
  • The web client names the sheet's button Use these runtimes rather than Start. A draft without runtimes of its own in a project whose defaults attach runtimes is created with runtimes omitted, so the daemon attaches the project's defaults; the chip and the draft line show them. A draft whose sheet deselected global shows no runtimes.

docs.title: Addendum 2026-10-22: offline runtimes are refused, connections are checked
docs.text:
An incident showed two gaps in "a dial-in runtime must be connected" (section 2.2). A root delegated to a dial-in runtime on a PC that had gone away without closing its WebSocket. The daemon still counted the runtime as connected, so the first call waited 30 s for capability/open, and the second reused an instance opened earlier over the same dead connection: its child started, prepared a call with tool/prepare, and waited for the answer until the daemon restarted 17 minutes later. Decided and implemented:

  • Never create, attach, or delegate with an offline runtime (user decision). A dial-in runtime that is not connected is refused at once, for capabilities as for session.create, session.runtime.attach, and a project's default runtimes, with runtime `<id>` is not connected (last seen <time>); a runtime the daemon remembers from before a restart is refused the same way rather than as unknown. A template runtime is started and must be online, initialized and its capability opened, before the child exists; a start that fails or times out fails the call and creates nothing.
  • An instance is handed out only over a live connection. Reusing an open instance checks its connection first: one heard from in the last 15 s passes, another must answer runtime/ping within 10 s or it is ended. A dial-in runtime is then refused as not connected; the daemon waits up to 2 minutes for a template runtime it restarts.
  • Liveness and deadlines (runtime protocol 1.4.0, see Liveness): the daemon pings a connection quiet for 15 s and ends one silent for 45 s; tool/prepare, tool/revalidate, and runtime/context fail as runtime_unavailable after 30 s and mark the connection suspect (checked within 10 s); tool/execute is bounded by liveness. A dial-in runtime pings its end over WebSocket and dials in again after 45 s of silence.

docs.title: Addendum 2026-10-23: the web draft shows its cards, and the first message creates the session
docs.text:
Requested by the user and implemented the same day; it replaces the chip and sheet of section 5.1 and the Use these runtimes button of section 11.

  • No Start button. A new session shows its runtime cards where its transcript will be, with the composer under them, so the first message is drafted right away with everything the composer offers (files, agent, model, preset, permission mode, and rules). The "Runtimes…" chip and the cards' sheet are gone, and Runtimes in the ⋮ menu points at the cards while a session is drafted.
  • The first message creates the session. It calls session.create with the selected cards, at the workspaces as typed, plus global when selected; the daemon starts every runtime that is not running (templates included) and creates nothing if one fails. A draft still on its project's defaults omits runtimes, so the daemon attaches them. The message is submitted to the new session; files attached to the draft wait in the page and are uploaded into the session first.
  • A refusal keeps the draft. No session is made, the cards stay, and the message and its files go back into the composer. The error shows on the card of the runtime it quotes (`id`, as the daemon names runtimes), with a line above the composer; an error that names no runtime shows in that line. A message the created session refuses comes back to that session's composer, as any refused submit does.

docs.title: Managing Runtimes from Clients
docs.text: Status: in progress (2026-10-26); every decision in section 9 made by the user on 2026-10-26. Phase 1 implemented 2026-10-26 (client protocol 1.36.0, runtime protocol 1.9.0); phase 2 implemented 2026-10-26: 2a (dial-in tables, runtime/settings_changed, dial-in machines without [runtimes.local]) in runtime protocol 1.10.0, ${NAME} in env deferred; 2b (the panels' editors, mcp.server.rename, runtimes.agents.*) in client protocol 1.37.0, renames not rewriting templates (section 4.2). Builds on runtimes, runtime capabilities, ACP agents, MCP tool filters, web MCP OAuth, and the daemon restart of engine configuration section 11.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
Clients manage every connected runtime from the machines panel, not only the daemon's own global runtime:

  1. Read and change any runtime's configuration: its MCP servers and ACP agents.
  2. Sign in to OAuth MCP servers that run on any runtime. The credentials stay on the daemon's machine. Both the TUI and the web client run the flow.
  3. In the machines panel, expand a runtime to:
  4. list its MCP servers and each server's tools; add, remove, rename, and configure servers; leave out single tools and take them back;
  5. list its ACP agents; add, remove, rename, and configure them; open or create the agent's document;
  6. (proposal, section 5) configure MCP servers and ACP agents once for every runtime of a kind;
  7. restart a template runtime, or a dial-in runtime that can relaunch itself.

Out of scope: runtime protocol changes for plugins, and model-provider sign-ins.

docs.title: 2. Today
docs.text:
• config.get/config.apply cover only the daemon's config.toml and agent documents. A template runtime's MCP servers and ACP agents are in that file ([runtimes.<id>.mcp], [runtimes.<id>.acp]) and reach the runtime once, in runtime/initialize (RuntimeSettings). Editing them only lists runtimes under restart_required. Nothing restarts one template.
  • A dial-in runtime (cookie runtime serve --daemon) reads [runtimes.local] from its own machine's config.toml. The daemon sends it no MCP servers (DialInTemplate::connect). The runtime polls ACP agents every 5 s and reads MCP servers once at startup. The daemon shows those servers as source: machine with no definition, and cannot change them. When RuntimeSettings carries servers or agents, the runtime uses them in place of its own (coding_runtime initialize), with no merge.
  • mcp.server.add/edit/remove/set_enabled act on global only. Only mcp.server.reconnect takes runtime_id. McpServerInfo carries tool counts, not names, though the runtime reports names (McpServerReport.tools). Filtered-out names are not reported.
  • MCP OAuth runs in the daemon, for global servers only. Its store is <data_dir>/mcp-oauth.json, keyed server:sha256(resource URL). A runtime refuses a server with oauth enabled, and maps NeedsAuth to Failed. mcp.auth.* take a server name only.
  • ACP agents reach clients as AgentDescriptor.runtimes. No RPC edits a runtime's agents.
  • RuntimeLifetime is builtin | dial_in | spawned. It does not tell a persistent cookie runtime serve apart from a TUI-embedded runtime. No RPC restarts a runtime.

docs.title: 3. Configuration: the daemon owns every runtime's settings
docs.text: Decided 2026-10-26 (D1, D2): every runtime's MCP servers and ACP agents live in the daemon's config.toml. A dial-in machine keeps no runtime settings of its own, only how to reach the daemon.

docs.title: 3.1 On the daemon
docs.text:
[runtimes.labpc]            # a dial-in runtime: no `command`
[runtimes.labpc.mcp.servers.playwright]
command = ["npx", "@playwright/mcp"]
exclude_tools = ["browser_install"]
[runtimes.labpc.acp.agents.claude]
command = ["claude-code-acp"]
  • A [runtimes.<id>] table without command is valid for any id. It holds the settings of the dial-in runtime of that id, as [runtimes.local] already does for the built-in one. A dial-in id that matches a table with a command is still refused, as today.
  • The daemon sends a dial-in runtime its settings in runtime/initialize, as it does for templates. No table means no MCP servers and no ACP agents.
  • Live settings. A new runtime-protocol notification, runtime/settings_changed { settings }, carries the full RuntimeSettings whenever they change. The runtime diffs by name: it starts added servers and agents, stops removed ones, and restarts changed ones; unchanged ones keep running. A runtime that is not connected gets them at its next runtime/initialize, and so does a runtime older than this protocol minor, after which the panel says a restart applies them. restart_required then no longer lists runtimes for MCP or ACP edits; it still does for command, env, and the timeouts.
  • Clients edit through config.apply, with Set on ["runtimes", <id>, "mcp", "servers", <name>] and so on. The typed RPCs in section 4 wrap it for the panel. No runtime_id is added to config.get or config.apply: there is one configuration, the daemon's.
  • Secrets (deferred, not implemented). env values in these tables may be ${NAME}, expanded on the runtime from its own environment. A token can then stay on the machine that uses it, as it did when the machine declared the server. A plain value is sent as written.

docs.title: 3.2 On a dial-in machine
docs.text:
• The machine's configuration holds only the connection, [server] url and [server] token, which cookie runtime serve --daemon and the TUI's embedded runtime already read. --daemon <url>, --token, and --id still override them.
  • cookie runtime serve --daemon and the TUI's embedded runtime stop reading [runtimes.local]. [runtimes.local] stays what it is in a daemon's own configuration: its built-in runtime's settings.
  • A dial-in runtime started on a machine whose configuration has [runtimes.local.mcp] or [runtimes.local.acp] entries warns once at startup that a dial-in runtime ignores them, and names the daemon table to move them to ([runtimes.<id>]). It does not migrate them.
  • Removed: watch_local_acp_agents and its 5-second poll. Every runtime's servers come from the daemon's configuration, with full definitions; McpConfigSource::Machine stays for a dial-in runtime older than runtime protocol 1.10.0, which still hosts its own machine's.

docs.title: 4. Machines panel
docs.text: Each runtime row in the TUI /runtime → Machines tab and the web Machines page gets a disclosure with two sections. The TUI uses a detail pane with tabs, and every new target gets a PointerTarget and a hover.

docs.title: 4.1 MCP servers and tools
docs.text:
• List. Each server shows its state, where it is declared ([runtimes.<id>], or profile <name>, section 5), scope, and message. Expanded, it lists every tool: offered tools first, then filtered-out ones dimmed.
  • Client protocol 1.36.0: McpServerInfo.server_tools: Vec<McpServerTool { name, filtered }>, using the server's own names. It is omitted when empty.
  • Runtime protocol 1.9.0: the same server_tools on McpServerReport, beside the existing tools (published names).
  • Leave out or take back a tool. A per-tool toggle edits the server's filters:
  • Leaving a tool out adds its exact name to exclude_tools.
  • Taking it back removes the name from exclude_tools. When an include_tools list or a pattern is what filters it, the toggle adds the exact name to include_tools instead and says so.
  • Patterns are never rewritten.
  • Add, edit, remove, rename, and enable. The existing mcp.server.add/edit/remove/set_enabled gain an optional runtime_id, defaulting to global. A new mcp.server.rename { runtime_id?, name, new_name } moves the table and its OAuth credential key in one configuration edit. For a runtime other than global, they edit [runtimes.<id>.mcp.servers] and runtime/settings_changed applies the edit live.

docs.title: 4.2 ACP agents
docs.text:
An ACP agent's ID is its declaration's key on every runtime, as today: the claude that two runtimes declare is one agent, with one document, agents/claude.md, and a session runs it on the attached runtime that offers it. Templates over a declaration (acp.agent) resolve the same way. The panel follows that:

  • List. Under each runtime, the agents it declares: key, where the declaration comes from ([runtimes.<id>] or profile <name>), whether it is available (its command was found), enabled, its description, and the other runtimes that declare the same key.
  • A new runtimes.agents.list { runtime_id } returns [AcpAgentEntry { agent, source, declaration, available, enabled, description, documents }].
  • documents are the agent documents that run the declaration: the one of its own ID, and every template whose acp.agent names it.
  • Add, edit, remove, rename, and enable. runtimes.agents.add/edit/ remove/rename edit [runtimes.<id>.acp.agents.<agent>] (command, env, description, enabled) and apply it live.
  • Rename (D6) renames the declaration on that runtime. When no other runtime or profile still declares the old key, the same config.apply also moves agents/<old>.md to the new key. Templates whose acp.agent names the old key are not rewritten (implemented 2026-10-26: rewriting their front matter by hand is fragile); the result lists them and the clients say which to edit. When another one still does, the documents stay with the old key, which those runtimes go on offering, and the confirmation says so. Existing sessions keep the agent ID they recorded. Where it is gone, they resume with the default agent, as for a removed agent today, and the confirmation says so.
  • Documents. Open opens one of documents in the client's existing document editor: TUI /config, web Settings › Configuration. Create document writes agents/<agent>.md from the built-in template for an ACP agent (an acp: block, description, and permissions), and New template writes agents/<name>.md with acp.agent: <agent>. Both are shared by every runtime that declares the key.

docs.title: 4.3 Restart
docs.text: See section 6. The row shows Restart only when the runtime reports that it can.

docs.title: 5. Every-runtime MCP servers and ACP agents (question 3.3)
docs.text:
Answer: yes. It fits the design of section 3. The daemon already computes each runtime's settings before runtime/initialize. A profile is one more layer in that computation:

[runtime_profiles.coding]
match = { capabilities = ["coding"] }   # or runtimes = ["labpc", "unicorn*"]
[runtime_profiles.coding.mcp.servers.context7]
url = "https://mcp.context7.com/mcp"
[runtime_profiles.coding.acp.agents.claude]
command = ["claude-code-acp"]
[runtime_profiles.coding.acp.agents.codex]
command = ["codex-acp"]
  • Layers, last wins by name: the profiles that match, in name order, then [runtimes.<id>]. A runtime turns one entry off with enabled = false in [runtimes.<id>], or leaves a profile with [runtimes.<id>] profiles = [] (D4).
  • Matching is on free-form labels the user writes: capability names the runtime reports, and runtime id globs. The daemon compares strings and never branches on a particular kind, so this keeps the rule that kinds are labels. global never matches.
  • When it applies: at runtime/initialize, and through runtime/settings_changed when a profile changes. A runtime that connects later gets the profile at once, which is the "automatically configured" part.
  • Machines that lack the command. Each runtime spawns its own copy, so a machine without npx or claude-code-acp reports that server or agent as failed or unavailable, in the panel. Nothing else breaks.
  • Secrets. ${NAME} in env expands on each runtime (section 3.1), so no secret travels from the daemon. HTTP servers that need OAuth share one sign-in (section 7, D3).
  • Agent documents (D5). A profile's ACP agent is one agent with one document, agents/<agent>.md, whichever runtimes the profile adds it to, and so are the templates whose acp.agent names it. Which runtime a session runs it on is decided by the runtime capability the session attaches, as for any ACP agent.
  • local too. A profile matches the daemon's built-in local runtime like any other.
  • Where it does not fit. An HTTP MCP server that does not need the machine is better in global: one connection instead of one per runtime. The editor says so when a profile adds a URL server.
  • UI: a "Profiles" section above the machines in the panel, with the same MCP and ACP editors as section 4. Each runtime's entries name the profile they come from.

docs.title: 6. Restarting runtimes
docs.text:
runtimes.restart { runtime_id, when: "idle" | "now" } → { scheduled, active_runs, background_calls }. The semantics mirror daemon.restart, scoped to one runtime:

  • What idle waits for:
  • runs whose session has an attachment on the runtime or runs one of its ACP agents;
  • background calls executing on the runtime.

Meanwhile, new tool calls on that runtime wait, and calls elsewhere carry on. now ends those calls and the runtime's ACP agent processes. ACP sessions are reopened by the next turn, as after a runtime drop. - Template runtimes: the daemon sends runtime/shutdown and waits the grace period, then starts the template again under a new generation. It re-reads command and env, so restart_required: runtimes clears for that runtime. - Dial-in runtimes: a new runtime-protocol request, runtime/restart. cookie runtime serve answers, closes its connection, and relaunches its own executable with the same arguments: an in-place exec on Unix, keeping the PID for systemd and launchd, and a new process on Windows, as the daemon does. The new binary on that machine runs, so this is also how a machine picks up an upgrade. The daemon then waits for it to dial in again. - Which runtimes offer it (D7). InitializeResult.can_restart: - true for cookie runtime serve, whether it runs as a service or in a terminal: both can exec; - false for a runtime a client embeds (the TUI's or the web's), and for plugins' runtimes.

`RuntimeListing.can_restart` exposes it, and the panel shows **Restart**
only then.
  • global and local restart with the daemon, so they show no Restart.

docs.title: 7. MCP OAuth on any runtime
docs.text:
The daemon runs the whole OAuth flow and keeps the credentials. The runtime only ever holds an access token, in memory.

  • Flow.
  • mcp.auth.begin/complete/cancel gain runtime_id? (default global) and workspace? for workspace-scoped servers.
  • The daemon runs discovery, PKCE, and the code exchange with its existing oauth code, from its own network.
  • Redirects are unchanged: the TUI's loopback listener or paste on the TUI's machine, and the web page as redirect. So both clients work for a server on any machine.
  • Token delivery. Two new runtime-protocol messages:
  • runtime → daemon request mcp/token { server, resource_url, force_refresh } → { access_token, expires_at } or needs_auth. The runtime asks before it connects, near expiry, and after a 401.
  • daemon → runtime notification mcp/auth_changed { server } after a sign-in, a sign-out, or a refresh another process made, so the runtime reconnects.

The refresh token never leaves the daemon. Refresh uses the store's existing cross-process claim. - Runtime side. A server with oauth is accepted. Its transport gets an auth provider that calls mcp/token. A needs_auth answer reports NeedsAuth (no longer Failed), and the panel's Sign in button appears for it. - Credential key (D3). It stays server:sha256(resource URL), plus the client binding the store already checks. One sign-in serves every runtime that has the same server name and URL, which is what profiles want. - Network reach. Discovery and the token exchange run from the daemon. A server whose authorization server only the runtime's network reaches is not supported, and the begin error says so. Relaying the daemon's OAuth HTTP through the runtime is possible later. - Sign out: a new mcp.auth.forget { runtime_id?, name }, missing today, deletes the credential and sends mcp/auth_changed.

docs.title: 8. Protocol and phases
docs.text:
Client protocol minor and runtime protocol minor, all additive on the wire. Dropping a dial-in machine's [runtimes.local] is a behaviour change for its configuration, not for the protocol: an older dial-in runtime still reads its own file, and the daemon still accepts its servers as reported.

Phase Content 1 Tool names and filtered names on the wire (McpServerInfo.server_tools, McpServerReport.server_tools); read-only lists of each runtime's tools and ACP agents in both clients, the agents from the catalog's AgentDescriptor.runtimes 2 runtimes.agents.list; dial-in [runtimes.<id>] settings sent at initialize, dial-in machines ignoring [runtimes.local] with a warning, ${NAME} in env, runtime/settings_changed; runtime_id on mcp.server.*, mcp.server.rename, runtimes.agents.*; the editors, tool toggles, and document links in both clients; the guides moved to the daemon tables 3 runtimes.restart, runtime/restart with self-exec, can_restart 4 Runtime MCP OAuth: mcp/token, mcp/auth_changed, runtime_id on mcp.auth.*, mcp.auth.forget, Sign in on any machine in both clients 5 [runtime_profiles], if approved

Each phase is its own commit series, with the configuration reference, the protocol references and changelogs, and the TUI and web pages updated. Tests cover:

  • strict parsing of the new tables;
  • profile merge order and overrides; a dial-in runtime ignoring [runtimes.local] and warning;
  • the live settings diff, so that unchanged servers are not restarted;
  • tool toggle edits against include_tools, exclude_tools, and patterns;
  • rename moving documents and credentials;
  • restart waits, refusals, and the exec relaunch in an integration test;
  • the token relay, including a refresh after a 401;
  • the panel targets' hover sweep.

docs.title: 9. Decisions
docs.text:
All made by the user on 2026-10-26.

  • D1 Per-runtime settings live in the daemon's config.toml.
  • D2 A dial-in machine drops its runtime settings and keeps only the connection ([server] url and token); see section 3.2.
  • D3 OAuth credentials are shared by server name and URL across runtimes.
  • D4 Build profiles (section 5), with opt-out by enabled = false or profiles = [].
  • D5 A profile's ACP agent has one shared document, like every ACP agent: its ID is the declaration's key on every runtime, and templates over it (acp.agent) resolve to whichever runtime the session attaches.
  • D6 Renaming an ACP agent moves its documents when nothing else declares the old key (section 4.2); old sessions fall back to the default agent.
  • D7 Restart is offered for every cookie runtime serve, not only ones run as a service, since both can exec.

Not yet confirmed, with the defaults this spec assumes: ${NAME} in env expands on the runtime (section 3.1); profiles match local (section 5); labpc's own [runtimes.local] entries move into the daemon's [runtimes.labpc] only when the user asks.

docs.title: Runtimes: Daemon, Global Runtime, and Coding Runtimes
docs.text:
Status: implemented (all four phases, product decisions approved 2026-10-15); the manual end-to-end check against labpc that phase 4 names passed on 2026-10-20: an ssh template and a dial-in runtime, the daemon built from 85710393d and the remote runtime from the b2ddb9e72 musl release build. This document is the governing specification for splitting tool execution and workspace context out of the engine into attachable runtimes. Section Open questions lists anything still undecided.

The runtime capabilities spec later changed parts of this one: a runtime offers capabilities over one connection that serves every workspace (runtime protocol 5), instances are keyed by (runtime ID, capability, workspace), templates no longer substitute {workspace}, runtimes can dial in, and the daemon serves sessions of any directory. Where the two differ, that spec governs.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
Cookie Agent aims to cover both coding-agent use (opencode) and personal assistant use (openclaw). Both need the agent's tools to live somewhere other than the process that runs the model loop: a session may work in a repository on another machine, in several workspaces at once, or with no workspace at all.

Today the daemon is a workspace. EngineOptions.cwd locates the session store, roots permission paths, resolves relative tool paths, feeds the <working_directory> prompt block, finds AGENTS.md and project skills, and selects the workspace configuration layer. The built-in tools are constructed once for that directory.

After this work the processes split three ways:

clients (TUI, CLI, later others)
   │  client protocol (WebSocket / in-memory)
daemon = gateway
   │  config, agents, sessions, model loop, permissions, approvals,
   │  delegation, goals, messaging, compaction, artifacts
   │  base layer tools · global runtime (in-process)
   │  runtime protocol (stdio / in-memory)
coding runtimes, one per workspace (local in-process, remote via a command)

In scope (the milestone): the runtime seam, session attachments, the runtime protocol, and remote coding runtimes launched by command. The milestone ends when a session on the local daemon works in a repository on another machine (labpc over ssh) end to end.

Out of scope: a persistent or discoverable daemon, runtimes that dial in, channel adapters (chat apps), schedulers and other openclaw-style triggers, web clients, and runtime kinds other than coding. Producer messages are the only notification path, and in this milestone they stayed a daemon-side plugin feature; runtime protocol 4 later opened them to runtimes (see external producers).

docs.title: 2. Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Daemon Today's daemon, unchanged in process model: plain cookie runs it in-process, cookie daemon serves it over WebSocket. It is the gateway. Its working directory now only locates the session store and stamps cwd_identity. Base layer Tools the daemon implements itself for its own orchestration. Always present, never detachable. Runtime A source of tools, workspace context, and producer messages. Runtime kind A free-form label a runtime declares for itself in runtime/initialize, such as global or coding; templates do not declare it. The daemon only displays it: behaviour follows from what a runtime reports (its workspace, tools, and skills), never from its kind, so runtimes of new kinds need no daemon change. Runtime template A configured way to start runtimes: [runtimes.<id>]. The <id> is the runtime ID. Runtime instance A running runtime: one per (runtime ID, canonical workspace). Shared by every session attached to it. Attachment A durable session fact binding a session to a runtime instance under a session-unique attachment name. Attachment name The name the runtime instance reports for itself in runtime/initialize; used as the tool prefix on collisions. Model-facing text calls this an attachment (see the memory spec). Machine The computer a runtime runs on; the daemon groups runtimes into machines. Added by the memory spec.

docs.title: 3. Layers
docs.text:
Layer Runs in Tools Context Base layer daemon delegate_subagent, get_subagent_result, send_message, skill, goal_get, goal_update, read_artifact (new), stop_background none Global runtime (global) daemon process, in-process trait calls top-level [mcp] servers and [plugins], webfetch (declared Fallback), memory tools (memory spec) user skills (~/.agents/skills, ~/.cookie-agent/skills), memory snapshot Coding runtime (coding) built-in local instance in the daemon process; others in child processes read, write, edit, bash, webfetch, plus MCP servers from its template workspace root, platform, AGENTS.md, project skills

Plugins exist only on the daemon, hosted by the global runtime. Hosting MCP servers is up to each runtime, not part of the runtime contract: coding runtimes host them, and a runtime that does not rejects a template that lists some. No runtime hosts plugins.

Rules:

  • The global runtime never offers read, write, edit, or bash. Those exist only where a coding runtime is attached.
  • Every daemon always has the local coding runtime template for its own working directory. There is no flag to disable it.
  • New sessions attach global and local (the daemon's working directory) by default. A session may detach either. A session with no coding runtime is valid: it has the base layer and whatever the global runtime offers.
  • Artifact reads move from read to the base layer's read_artifact { artifact, stream?, offset, limit }, so a session with no coding runtime can still page through retained output. artifact is the 64-hex digest and stream an optional stream name; the model-facing artifact://<digest>[/<stream>] URI form is removed. Truncation hints read read_artifact(artifact="<digest>", stream="stdout", offset=…). read becomes filesystem-only. The persisted artifact://sha256/<digest> form in ArtifactReference is internal and unchanged.
  • read_artifact needs no permission rule: it can only reach the session tree's own artifacts. The read: {"artifact://*": allow} pattern and the artifact:// pass-through in permission resource resolution go away.

docs.title: 4.1 Templates
docs.text:
[runtimes.labpc]
command = ["ssh", "labpc", "cookie", "runtime", "coding", "--stdio", "--workspace", "{workspace}"]
env = { }                     # additions to the inherited environment
startup_timeout_ms = 10000
shutdown_grace_ms = 3000

[runtimes.labpc.mcp.servers.rust_analyzer]
command = "rust-analyzer-mcp"
  • Runtime IDs match [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31} because they become tool-name prefixes. global and local are reserved.
  • [runtimes.local] may exist without command; it only carries the mcp table for the built-in local coding runtime. Any other template requires a nonempty command. Templates accept no plugins table.
  • Templates do not declare a kind. The command decides what runs, and the runtime reports its kind in runtime/initialize, so there is one source of truth. The mcp table is still parsed strictly when the configuration loads; a runtime that hosts no MCP servers rejects a nonempty one at initialize.
  • A template whose command contains {workspace} needs a workspace: attach and session creation require one. A template without the placeholder takes none, and supplying one is an error.
  • {workspace} is substituted as one whole argv element, with no shell interpretation by cookie. A command that reaches a remote shell (ssh) is responsible for quoting; the reference docs must say so.
  • The child inherits the daemon's environment plus env, because ssh needs SSH_AUTH_SOCK and similar variables.
  • Template MCP servers are sent to the runtime in runtime/initialize and run on the runtime's machine. MCP OAuth stays global-runtime-only (its credential store is the daemon's mcp-oauth.json); a template server with oauth enabled fails validation. Static-header HTTP servers are allowed.
  • Top-level [mcp] and [plugins] keep their current meaning and belong to the global runtime.
  • Plugin environment changes: plugins, like MCP servers and runtimes, now inherit the daemon's environment, and env adds to it instead of replacing it. This drops today's env_clear(), so a plugin also sees provider API keys that the daemon reads from its environment.

docs.title: 4.2 Removed
docs.text:
• The workspace configuration layer: <cwd>/.cookie-agent/config.toml and <cwd>/.cookie-agent/agents/ are no longer read. Configuration is the user layer only. config_paths.workspace, workspace_mcp_servers, McpConfigTarget::WorkspaceFile, the TUI's "project config.toml" MCP target, and AgentDocumentSource::Workspace go away.
  • BuiltinTools::new(workspace): coding tools take their workspace from the runtime instance.
  • The lazy MCP server setting and the lazy-not-connected status. Every enabled server connects eagerly (section 6.4); an authored lazy key is an unknown field.

No migration or compatibility decoder is added (see AGENTS.md). A leftover workspace file is ignored silently because it is simply never opened; the docs say so. AGENTS.md files under .cookie-agent/agents/ are context, not configuration, and keep working (section 8).

docs.title: 5.1 Events (additive, versionless)
docs.text:
• RuntimeAttached { name, runtime_id, kind, workspace } where workspace is the canonical path the runtime reported (absent for global).
  • RuntimeDetached { name }.

A session's attachment set is the fold of these events. SessionCreated stays as it is; creation writes one RuntimeAttached per initial attachment in the same append. A session whose log holds no RuntimeAttached or RuntimeDetached event at all was created before this change and is read as attached to global and local.

docs.title: 5.2 Operations
docs.text:
• Attach and detach are accepted only while the session has no active run (SessionRunning otherwise), so the set is fixed for every run.
  • Creating a session or attaching a runtime connects it eagerly (section 6.4). Attach waits for the instance to start and for runtime/initialize; failure rejects the attach and records nothing.
  • The runtime chooses its attachment name and returns it from runtime/initialize; clients do not supply one. The global runtime returns global. A coding runtime returns <runtime ID>_<workspace basename>, with the basename lowercased, every character outside [a-z0-9_] replaced by _, repeats collapsed, and the result capped at 32 bytes: labpc in ~/cookie-agent is labpc_cookie_agent. Because the name is fixed per instance, it is the same in every session that attaches that instance.
  • If a session already has an attachment with the returned name (two workspaces with the same basename), the daemon appends _2, _3, and so on for that session.
  • Delegated children inherit the parent's attachments. delegate_subagent accepts an optional runtimes list of the parent's attachment names that narrows the child's set. The child's log records its own RuntimeAttached events so the child is self-describing. Changed 2026-10-17: the runtimes argument is gone; every delegated child inherits the root session's attachments.
  • Reopening a session in a daemon that does not have its instances running (after a restart, or a session created by another daemon) connects them when the session is opened, with the same rules as creation.

docs.title: 6. Tool composition
docs.text: The model's tool list should change as rarely as possible: every change costs the provider's prompt cache and can confuse a model that has already called a tool by name.

docs.title: 6.1 Minimal change, not frozen
docs.text:
The tool set is not frozen. As today, published_tool_definitions recomputes it on every model turn. Instead, the sources of change are reduced so that the list only changes when something really appeared or went away:

  • no lazy connections: everything a session can use is connected when the session is created or opened (section 6.4);
  • short disconnects are bridged by reconnecting before any tool is dropped (section 6.4);
  • only real collisions rename tools (section 6.3).

What remains is the user attaching or detaching a runtime, an MCP server or runtime that cannot be reached at all, and an MCP server changing its own tool list.

docs.title: 6.2 Collision enum
docs.text:
Every runtime tool declares collision: prefix | fallback (default prefix).

  • prefix: on a collision the tool is published as <attachment>_<name>.
  • fallback: on a collision the tool is hidden. The global runtime's webfetch uses this.

Base layer names are reserved: a runtime tool with a base name is always treated as colliding.

docs.title: 6.3 Collisions
docs.text:
Names are computed from the current tool set every time it is composed:

  • A name offered by exactly one source is published bare.
  • When several prefix tools offer one name, the bare name is removed and each of them is published as <attachment>_<name>. Attaching labpc at ~/api to a session whose local runtime is at ~/web therefore turns bash into local_web_bash and labpc_api_bash; detaching labpc turns local_web_bash back into bash.
  • A runtime tool that collides with a base layer name is published as <attachment>_<name>; the base tool keeps its name.
  • An override tool keeps the bare name, and the other tools of that name are prefixed (or hidden, if fallback). Several overrides of one name are all prefixed, with a diagnostic. An override never takes a base layer name. Each plugin composes as its own source, prefixed with the plugin's name (see the plugins spec).
  • fallback tools are hidden whenever a non-fallback tool offers the same name. When both declare the same parameters schema, as both webfetch tools do, the model sees no change.
  • A published name longer than 64 bytes is dropped with a diagnostic.
  • Delegated children compose the same way from their own attachments.

Inside one runtime, names are unique; that runtime enforces it with today's MCP claim rules. MCP tools inside a runtime keep the <server>_<tool> form, so a prefixed one reads <attachment>_<server>_<tool>.

docs.title: 6.4 Connection policy
docs.text:
The same rules apply to MCP servers (in the global runtime and in coding runtimes) and to runtime instances.

  • Eager connect. When a session is created or opened, the daemon makes sure every attached runtime instance is started and every enabled MCP server in it has finished its connection attempt before the session's first run. Instances and servers already up are reused; the global and local instances start with the daemon.
  • Failure at connect. A server or runtime that fails to connect publishes no tools, and every client viewing the session gets an error message naming it and the reason. It is retried the next time a session that uses it is created or opened, and on demand from the /mcp or /runtime panel.
  • Disconnect. When a connected server or runtime drops, the daemon reconnects (restarting the process for stdio servers and runtimes) up to 3 times with 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s backoff. While it reconnects, its tools stay published and calls fail fast with runtime_unavailable, so a brief drop never changes the tool list. If every attempt fails, its tools are dropped and clients get an error message.

docs.title: 6.4.1 Addendum 2026-10-22: MCP server scope and working directory
docs.text:
A runtime template's MCP server takes scope = "workspace" (the default, the hosting described above) or scope = "runtime"; a top-level [mcp] server takes none and fails validation with one.

  • Start. A runtime-scoped server starts once per runtime process, when the runtime accepts runtime/initialize. The reply does not wait for it; every capability/open waits for its first attempt, bounded by its timeout_ms, and reports it before replying. It reconnects with the policy above and stops with the runtime.
  • Tools. Its tools are the runtime's own, outside any instance (runtime/tools_changed, prepared without an instance). A session composes them once per runtime, after the first attachment of that runtime, under the runtime's ID as their composition source, so a collision publishes <runtime>_<server>_<tool>; they run with an origin of the runtime without a workspace.
  • Listing. The runtime reports every configured server at initialize and with runtime/mcp_changed: the runtime-scoped ones live, the workspace-scoped ones as configured. mcp.server.list shows a runtime-scoped server once without a workspace and a workspace-scoped one no instance hosts as "starts when a workspace opens", so a connected runtime's servers are visible before any workspace opens.
  • Working directory. A stdio server without cwd starts in the instance's workspace (workspace-scoped), in the runtime user's home (runtime-scoped), or in the daemon user's home (top-level); a relative cwd resolves against the same directory. Before, it inherited the process's directory, which for a Windows runtime started by Task Scheduler is C:\Windows\System32.
  • Compatibility. Runtime protocol 1.5.0 and client protocol 1.13.0, additive. A runtime hosts every server per workspace for a daemon older than 1.5.0.

docs.title: 6.5 Routing
docs.text: The name map resolves a published name to (attachment, runtime tool name). Preparation, permission decision, and execution keep today's sequence; Arc::ptr_eq publication checks become (attachment, instance generation, spec) equality, so a runtime restart between publication and preparation fails with the existing OperationChanged path.

docs.title: 7. Permissions and approvals
docs.text:
• Rules gain an optional runtime selector written as an action suffix in agent documents and session overlays: bash@labpc, read@local. A plain action with no selector applies on every runtime and to the base layer, so existing agent documents keep working unchanged. A qualified rule is more specific than an unqualified one at the same resource specificity.
  • The selector matches the runtime ID, not the attachment name, so it is stable across sessions.
  • Permission actions are free-form labels a tool declares ([a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}), so a runtime can introduce its own, such as browse. An action no rule names is denied, so a new runtime's tools stay hidden until an agent or the session overlay grants their action. The daemon gives meaning only to the actions of its own tools: read and write take file paths (${workspace_dir}, workspace-relative resources), and delegate, message, and skill belong to the base layer. Every other action matches plain wildcard patterns. A tool may also declare no permission at all (see background tool calls).
  • ${workspace_dir} and relative resources resolve against the workspace of the runtime that prepared the call. Base layer and global tools have no workspace; path-relative patterns never match them.
  • Approval grants and tree grants record the runtime ID. A grant only applies to calls on the same runtime ID. Grant events written before this change have no runtime ID and are read as local.
  • The approval classifier's prompt names the runtime and its workspace instead of "the workspace".

docs.title: 7.1 Addendum 2026-10-22: the mcp default
docs.text:
An action no rule names stays denied and hidden, with the mode default of list_runtimes (runtime delegation spec section 4) as the exception. mcp joins it: when an agent document, the synthesized built-in default included, has no mcp key in any form (mcp@<runtime> included), the daemon supplies mcp: {"*": ask} for the primary, all, and subagent modes; internal agents get none.

Mode mcp primary, all, subagent "*": ask internal none
  • A declared mcp key replaces the default entirely, as for list_runtimes: an agent with only "my_chrome_*": ask is offered only those tools, and mcp: deny hides them all. A key with only a runtime selector counts as declared, so mcp@labpc: allow leaves the other runtimes' MCP tools hidden.
  • The default rule is part of the frozen agent snapshot like the others, so tool visibility, call evaluation, and approvals treat it as any rule. A snapshot frozen before this change has no default and keeps its rules.
  • session.permission.get and the session preview report an action whose agent rules are exactly its mode default with the source default (the list_runtimes default too, which was reported as agent_document before); the TUI's and the web client's /permissions panels show it so. No wire change: default is an existing PermissionRuleSource value. A document that spells out the default rule itself reads the same.
  • The same day the memory actions lost their mode defaults (memory spec section 9.2, note of 2026-10-22): memory and memory_write are denied unless the agent document or the session overlay names them. Later that day they gained defaults chosen by whether the run is delegated, not by mode (memory spec section 16.9.11), which the view reports with the source default as well.

docs.title: 8. Workspace context
docs.text:
At admission, for each attached coding runtime, the daemon asks the runtime for its context (runtime/context):

  • Workspace block. <working_directory> is replaced by one <runtimes> block listing each attachment's name, kind, workspace, platform, and whether its tools are prefixed. It is frozen like today's block. Changed 2026-10-17: global is left out; with one other runtime the prompt gives only its working directory and platform, and with several it lists them and each of their tools' descriptions names its runtime (see System prompt).
  • AGENTS.md. The admission request carries the run's preset. Each coding runtime applies today's lookup to its own workspace: the preset's .cookie-agent/agents/<preset>/AGENTS.md, else .cookie-agent/agents/AGENTS.md, then <workspace>/AGENTS.md, under the existing size rule. Presets themselves are still defined only by the daemon's user layer. AgentMdLoaded gains an attachment field; one event per runtime that returned a file. Replay and compaction pinning treat the latest event per attachment as current.
  • Skills. The global runtime contributes user skills; each coding runtime contributes project skills found from its repository root down to its workspace (today's discovery, run on the runtime's machine). Bodies and the supporting-file sample travel in the context reply; ${COOKIE_SKILL_DIR} expands to the absolute path on the runtime's machine. Project skills shadow user skills as today. Same-named project skills from two attachments follow the prefix rule. A skill's allowed-tools grants apply to the tools of the attachment that contributed it; user skills' grants are unqualified.

Skills are read once when an instance initializes, matching today's "no hot reload". AGENTS.md is read at every root admission, as today.

docs.title: 9. Runtime protocol
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line over stdio, or frames over an InProcessStream. The protocol version is an integer starting at 1 and must match exactly; a mismatch fails initialize with both versions in the diagnostic. The local coding runtime speaks this protocol over the in-memory transport so the local and remote paths are one code path. The global runtime does not; it is called in-process through the same Rust trait.

Method Direction Purpose runtime/initialize daemon → runtime Version, runtime ID, requested workspace (when the template takes one), and settings: tool_output and agent_md limits and the template's MCP servers. A runtime rejects settings it does not support. Reply: version, kind, attachment name, and tool declarations and skills; when they apply, canonical workspace and platform. runtime/tools_changed runtime → daemon Tool list changed; the daemon re-lists before the next model turn (section 6.1). runtime/context daemon → runtime Per-admission context for the run's preset: AGENTS.md. tool/prepare daemon → runtime Name, arguments, session, run, turn context. Reply: prepared ID, operation identity, permission resource, policy labels, presentation, display argument, serialization key, concurrency. tool/revalidate, tool/execute, tool/release daemon → runtime Execute or discard a prepared call. execute replies with the terminal result and inline media (bounded by today's attachment budget). tool/progress runtime → daemon Display deltas and output chunks under today's 64 KiB / 8-stream bounds. The daemon owns capture and artifact retention. tool/cancel daemon → runtime As the call's cancellation token. tool/detachable runtime → daemon An executing call reached its detach point. Superseded tool/stdin and the job/* messages in runtime protocol 3 (see background tool calls). mcp/changed runtime → daemon The status of the template's MCP servers and the ones that failed (section 6.4), merged into mcp.changed. mcp/reconnect daemon → runtime Reconnect one MCP server, or retry the failed ones when a session that uses the instance is created or opened. runtime/shutdown daemon → runtime Graceful stop, then termination after shutdown_grace_ms.

ToolPreparationContext.cwd and workspace_root disappear from the daemon side; the runtime fills them from its own workspace.

Runtime protocol 4 adds producer messaging for runtimes: a runtime that declares it may send producer messages to the sessions attached to it (see external producers).

docs.title: 10. Lifecycle and failure
docs.text:
• The global and local instances start with the daemon. Other instances start when a session that attaches them is created or opened, or when they are attached, and stay up until the daemon exits.
  • Connection, reconnection, and failure follow section 6.4.
  • Runtime stderr is captured into bounded diagnostics, as plugin stderr is.
  • When a runtime drops, calls in flight, backgrounded ones included, fail with a new runtime_unavailable failure code. Tool calls are never retried transparently.
  • Instance status (starting, ready, reconnecting, failed, stopped) is visible to clients (section 11).

docs.title: 11. Client protocol
docs.text:
Protocol 39 → 40 (one bump per phase that changes the wire; phase 1 already used 39 for removing AgentDocumentSource::Workspace).

  • session.create gains runtimes: [{ runtime_id, workspace? }] and global: bool. Omitted means local at the daemon's directory plus global.
  • New session.runtime.attach { session_id, runtime_id, workspace } and session.runtime.detach { session_id, name }.
  • New runtimes.list: templates and live instances with status. New runtimes.changed notification on instance status changes. mcp.changed covers servers in every runtime.
  • Connection failures and drops from section 6.4 reach clients as these notifications with the failure reason; the TUI shows them as an error notice in each affected session.
  • The TUI gains a /runtime panel (attached runtimes with status, attach by template and workspace path, detach) and shows attachment names in the session status line. The MCP panel shows servers from every runtime and edits global-runtime servers only.

docs.title: 12. Crate changes
docs.text:
This lands open review item 9 (extract tool_api into a leaf crate):

  • runtime_api (new leaf crate): the tool trait, prepared-tool types, ToolSpec with collision, progress and stdin abstractions that do not depend on OutputHub, OutputCapture, or ArtifactRouter, and the runtime protocol types. Depends on protocol (or identity) only and knows nothing about MCP.
  • mcp (new crate, from engine/src/mcp.rs): the MCP client and registry, shared by the global runtime in the daemon and by coding_runtime. OAuth stays on the daemon side.
  • coding_runtime (from today's tools): read, write, edit, bash, webfetch, fs_cap, runtime-side MCP hosting, skills and AGENTS.md discovery, and the protocol server loop.
  • engine: base layer tools (delegate, message, skill, goal, read_artifact) move in or into an engine-side module; it gains the runtime registry, attachment fold, composition, and the protocol client.
  • cookie_agent: cookie runtime coding --stdio --workspace <path>. The subcommand needs no provider configuration and exits on stdin EOF.

docs.title: 13. Phases
docs.text:
Each phase lands with all gates green and updates the user-facing docs it changes (architecture.md, configuration, protocol, tools, system prompt).

  1. Runtime seam, in-process (protocol 39 only for removing the workspace agent source). Extract runtime_api; split the base layer, the global runtime, and the local coding runtime behind one engine-side runtime abstraction. Move every workspace-semantics use of store.cwd() to the call's runtime: working_directory.rs, agent_md.rs, tool_execution.rs (preparation context, decisions, visibility), skills.rs visibility, permissions.rs overlay effects, approval_flow.rs text, and the MCP/plugin context digests. Remove the workspace configuration layer. Add read_artifact. Plugins inherit the daemon's environment. Done when the only store.cwd() reads left are the store location and cwd_identity.
  2. Attachments and composition (protocol 40). Events, RPCs, defaults, collision prefixing, eager MCP connection with reconnect and drop notices (removing lazy), runtime-qualified permissions and grants, per-attachment AGENTS.md and skills, delegation narrowing, TUI panel. Tests attach two fake in-process coding runtimes with colliding tools.
  3. Runtime protocol. Wire types, server loop in coding_runtime, client in engine; the local instance switches to it over InProcessStream. Background jobs cross the protocol.
  4. Remote runtimes. [runtimes.<id>] templates, cookie runtime, eager start at session creation, reconnect and drop handling (section 6.4), template MCP servers, instance status. Verified by a test that launches cookie runtime as a real child process, then manually against labpc (installing on labpc needs the author's go-ahead).

docs.title: 14. Open questions
docs.text: None. Every choice this draft made was reviewed on 2026-10-15.

docs.title: The user's shell environment for runtimes
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-28; runtime protocol 1.12.0; notes in section 14). The user decided on 2026-10-28 that capture is a configuration setting that is on by default, and that the default capture is an interactive shell (section 13). Builds on runtimes, runtime capabilities (the persistent daemon), ACP agents, plugins, and live engine configuration.

docs.title: 1. Problem
docs.text:
A daemon run as a service starts with the service manager's environment, not the user's shell's. Everything the daemon's runtimes start inherits that environment: the bash tool and its background calls, stdio MCP servers, ACP agents, plugins, and the commands of [runtimes.<id>] templates. On a machine whose setup lives in the shell's rc files, the local runtime is then close to unusable.

Observed on yunhao-labserver on 2026-10-28:

  • The cookie-daemon systemd user unit's process has only HOME, USER, LOGNAME, SHELL, LANG, PATH, XDG_*, DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS, SSH_AUTH_SOCK, and systemd's own variables. Its PATH is a hand-copied Environment=PATH=... drop-in, the workaround Persistent daemon recommends. The copy has already gone stale once: it names a versioned Node directory.
  • The user's setup is in ~/.bashrc, below Debian's case $- in *i*) ;; *) return;; esac guard: micromamba (MAMBA_EXE, MAMBA_ROOT_PREFIX, the micromamba shell function, alias conda=micromamba), cargo, nvm, bun, the coding-config variables (OPENCODE_IMAGE_GEN_*), a Node PATH entry, and the synced_utils aliases.
  • The bash tool runs bash -c <command> (crates/coding_runtime/src/bash.rs), which is neither interactive nor a login shell. A login shell does not help either: ~/.profile sources ~/.bashrc, which stops at the guard.

From an empty environment like systemd's:

Shell micromamba BUN_INSTALL OPENCODE_* cargo bash -c (the bash tool today) no no no no bash -lc no no no yes (~/.profile) bash -lic yes (function) yes yes yes

The same holds for runtimes on other machines: cookie runtime serve started by an ssh template runs from sshd's non-interactive shell, which returns at the same guard.

docs.title: 2. Goal and scope
docs.text:
Every process a runtime starts gets the environment the user has in a new terminal on that machine. The bash tool also gets the user's shell functions and aliases, so micromamba activate, conda, and nvm work in a command the way they do at a prompt.

In scope: the coding runtime, wherever it runs (the daemon's local, cookie runtime serve over ssh or dial-in, and a client's offered runtime); the daemon's own launches (plugins and template runtime commands); configuration; refresh; failure reporting.

Out of scope:

  • Windows. Windows has no rc-file convention: a service started by Task Scheduler at logon already has the user's environment, and Git Bash's rc files are rarely where the setup lives. The setting is accepted and has no effect there.
  • A persistent shell per session, where cd or export in one command carries over to the next. Each command still starts a fresh shell.
  • The daemon's own process environment, which stays as the service manager started it (section 6).

docs.title: 3. Prior art
docs.text:
• VS Code resolves the login shell's environment once at startup by running $SHELL -i -l -c with a marker around the printed environment and a 10-second timeout. Its output is used as the environment of terminals, tasks, and extensions.
  • Zed does the same when it starts the project's language servers and tasks.
  • Claude Code writes a shell snapshot (options, functions, and aliases from the user's rc file) once per session and sources it before every Bash tool command.
  • Codex runs commands through the user's login shell (bash -lc) and filters the variables with shell_environment_policy.

This spec does what VS Code and Zed do for the environment, and what Claude Code does for functions and aliases.

docs.title: 4. Configuration
docs.text:
[shell_environment]
# "interactive": $SHELL -l -i, the environment of a new terminal.
# "login": $SHELL -l only; misses rc files that return early when not interactive.
# "off": the runtime's own environment, as before this spec.
capture = "interactive"
# How long a capture may take; 0 or less waits indefinitely.
timeout_ms = 10000
# The shell to capture with; $SHELL when empty, else /bin/sh.
shell = ""

The top-level table applies to every runtime and to the daemon's own launches. [runtimes.<id>.shell_environment] overrides any of its keys for one runtime. The default capture is "interactive". Every key applies live: a change reaches each runtime as a settings change and sets off a new capture (section 8). No restart is needed.

The configured env of an MCP server, ACP agent, plugin, or runtime template still overrides captured variables (section 6). That env stays the way to set something just for one process. It is no longer needed for what the shell already sets.

docs.title: 5. Capture
docs.text:
A runtime captures once when it starts, in the background. A process start that needs the result, such as the first bash call or the first MCP server, waits for it, bounded by timeout_ms.

  1. Run <shell> -l -i -c <script> (-l only for "login") with stdin from /dev/null, in a new session (setsid, so there is no controlling terminal and nothing can read from one), in the user's home directory, and with the runtime's own environment. The shell's job-control warnings ("no job control in this shell") go to stderr, which is discarded.
  2. The script prints a random per-capture nonce, then env -0, then the nonce again, so text that rc files print before or after (banners, fortune, a conda notice) cannot be mistaken for variables. For a bash shell it also writes the snapshot (section 7). The script uses only printf, env, and ;, so it runs unchanged in sh, bash, zsh, and fish.
  3. Parse the NUL-separated entries between the two nonces, reading only until the second one arrives: a process an rc file starts in the background may hold the output open. A shell that exits without printing both nonces, or runs past timeout_ms, is a failed capture. When the capture ends, whatever is still running in its session is killed.
  4. Drop the variables that describe that shell rather than the user's setup: PWD, OLDPWD, SHLVL, _, PS1–PS4, PROMPT_COMMAND, COLUMNS, LINES, HISTFILE, TERM, and any COOKIE_* (cookie's own variables always come from the runtime's environment).

The result is the runtime's shell environment: the captured variables in place of the runtime's own, plus the dropped names where the runtime had them. Variables an rc file unsets stay unset.

The capture shell starts from the runtime's own environment, not a clean one, so what was active where the daemon or runtime was started carries over. A daemon started from a terminal with a conda environment or a virtualenv active runs every command in it. This is intended (section 13).

On yunhao-labserver a capture takes about 0.1 s and yields 24 variables (prototype, 2026-10-28).

A failed capture falls back to the runtime's own environment, as before this spec, and is reported (section 10). The next attempt is at the next refresh, not on every process start.

docs.title: 6. What gets it
docs.text:
The shell environment is the base environment of every process a runtime or the daemon starts for the user's work:

Process Where it is started Today bash tool commands and background calls coding_runtime::bash inherits stdio MCP servers mcp inherits + env ACP agents coding_runtime::acp_host inherits + env plugins engine::runtimes::process inherits + env [runtimes.<id>] template commands (ssh host cookie runtime serve) engine::runtimes::process inherits + env

Precedence, lowest first: the runtime's own environment, the shell environment, then the process's configured env. A process is found through the resulting PATH. std::process::Command already looks a program up in the child's PATH once the child's PATH is set, so an MCP server that names npx finds the user's Node.

The daemon process and the runtime process keep their own environment untouched. Three reasons:

  • cookie daemon restart re-executes with the environment the daemon started with (daemon_restart.rs), and that environment should stay the service manager's.
  • The user's secrets, such as the API keys exported from rc files, reach only the processes started for the user's work. The daemon's logs and panic reports cannot include them.
  • A refresh replaces the shell environment without touching the process.

Plugins and template commands are started by the daemon on its own machine, so the daemon keeps a shell environment of its own machine, shared with its in-process local runtime.

docs.title: 7. The bash snapshot
docs.text:
Variables cannot carry shell functions or aliases: micromamba activate needs the micromamba function, and conda is an alias. When the capture shell is bash, the capture script also writes a snapshot file:

shopt -s extdebug
{ shopt -p; alias -p; <functions>; } > "$snapshot"
  • Shell options come first. Functions from bash-completion use extended globs (--!(no-*)dir*)). Without shopt -s extglob ahead of them, sourcing the snapshot stops at a syntax error and loses every function after it. The prototype hit exactly this.
  • Completion functions are left out. <functions> prints declare -f for each function except those whose source file (declare -F under extdebug) lies under /usr/share/bash-completion/ or /etc/bash_completion*. Completion functions are never needed outside a prompt and make up most of the snapshot: 58 KB with them on yunhao-labserver.
  • The snapshot holds no variables, only options, aliases, and functions. Variables travel in the process environment (section 6).

The snapshot is a mode-0600 file in a private mode-0700 temporary directory that the runtime owns and removes when it stops, the same as the ACP bridge's socket directory. Each capture replaces it.

The bash tool then runs:

bash -c "source '<snapshot>' 2>/dev/null
<command>"

The command goes on its own line because bash expands an alias only in commands it parses after the alias is defined; the snapshot's shopt -p turns expand_aliases on. Error messages from the command report its line numbers one higher than before. $0 and the positional parameters are unchanged. The snapshot adds about 45 ms to a command on yunhao-labserver, most of it parsing the functions. The approval prompt, the permission check, and the transcript all show the command as written, without the prefix.

Activation does not carry from one command to the next. Each command is a fresh shell, so micromamba activate ucma in one call is gone in the next. This is expected (the user, 2026-10-28), and the bash tool's description does not mention it: models already assume a fresh shell per command.

With a non-bash capture shell (zsh, fish) there is no snapshot: their functions and aliases are not bash, and the bash tool still gets the captured variables.

docs.title: 8. Refresh
docs.text:
