A root whose last event is now another one is refused, so a delete never removes a turn the user has not seen, such as one another client just added. Only the root's log is compared. A change elsewhere in the tree happens during a run, and a running tree is refused anyway.
  • Params are strict like every command: an unknown member is unknown_field.

The result names every session that was deleted, the root first:

{ "deleted": ["<root session ID>", "<subagent ID>", "…"] }

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
All are -32000 registry errors with message, hint, and detail. Three codes exist already, and three are new in 1.5.0:

data.code Fields When session_not_found session_id No such session, or it was already deleted not_a_root_session (new) session_id, root_session_id The session is a delegated subagent. The hint says to delete its root session_tree_running (new) session_id, optional running_session_id A session of the tree has an active run, a compaction, or a subagent waiting for a slot. The hint says to wait for it or cancel it session_owned_elsewhere session_id Another cookie process holds the tree's owner.lock session_changed (new) session_id, current_last_seq expected_last_seq is no longer the root's last event. The hint says to look at the session again engine_error none The tree could not be moved aside on disk. Nothing was deleted, and detail says why

session_running is not reused: its message and hint speak of starting a run, which a delete does not do.

docs.title: What the daemon does
docs.text:
1. Checks. It resolves session_id: an unknown session is session_not_found, a delegated one not_a_root_session.
  2. Ownership. A tree this daemon holds is deleted on the root's session actor, which orders the delete after every request already queued for the root. A tree it does not hold is not adopted: adoption would repair the tree and append events first. The daemon takes the tree's owner.lock for the deletion itself, which fails with session_owned_elsewhere when another process holds it. Neither path writes an event.
  3. Busy and stale checks. In a held tree it refuses with session_tree_running when:
  4. a run of any of the tree's sessions is active;
  5. a compaction holds one of them;
  6. a delegated child waits in the delegation queue;
  7. or a resident session's status is running.

A tree whose lock was free has no live run. A running status there is what a crashed process left, so it does not refuse. Then expected_last_seq is compared with the root's last event: session_changed. 4. Quiescing. The tree's background calls are stopped without a report. Its uploads in progress are dropped. Every resident log of the tree closes its append handle, so no handle stays open in the directory (Windows cannot rename a directory with an open file). 5. Commit. Under the session store's exclusive mutation lock, the root directory sessions/<workdirkey>/<root>/ is renamed in place to a tombstone, sessions/<workdirkey>/.deleted-<root>-<uuid>, and the work directory is synced. The rename is the commit point: from then on no listing, lookup, or tree load finds the tree. A rename that fails changes nothing and is engine_error. On Windows it is retried while another program briefly holds a file open. 6. Forgetting. The daemon drops what it holds for each session of the tree. In the session store: - locations; - the lazy tree-load state and queued load products; - resident projections, evicted summaries, and deferred metadata tips; - ownership (the tree's entry, which drops its lock and write authority, and each session's writable or adopting entry); - live tails; - cached read-only logs; - per-tree gates.

In the engine: - session actors, whose queued requests then fail with session_not_found; - producers and the goal and producer projections; - skill grants and pending skill invocations; - compaction state; - delegation records and queue entries; - delegation recovery claims; - pending approvals; - the tree's permission mode; - the tree's grant journal, after which the visible tree grants are rebuilt; - the tree's artifact store handle; - upload leases; - fork idempotency keys whose source or fork was deleted; - steer ordering.

Queued inputs and the goal live in the log, so they go with it. 7. Unlocking. The tree lock is released. On Unix it is inside the tombstone. On Windows it is the sidecar <root>.owner.lock beside the tree, which is then removed. 8. Telling clients. A sessions.changed removed change goes to every connection for each deleted session, the root first. 9. Removal. The tombstone is removed with everything in it. A failure is logged and leaves only the tombstone. SessionStore::open removes every .deleted-* entry of its work directory, so a daemon that crashed between the rename and the removal cleans up at its next start.

What is removed on disk is the root directory and everything in it:

  • events.jsonl and metadata;
  • owner.lock on Unix;
  • grant-invalidations.jsonl;
  • artifacts/: uploads, retained tool output, and attachments;
  • subagents/index.json;
  • subagents/<child>/ with each child's events.jsonl and metadata;
  • any temporary files.

On Windows the <root>.owner.lock sidecar goes too. The work directory's own files (cwd, layout.json, and the runtime revision index) are shared by every session and stay. A fork made earlier is not touched: it hard-linked its artifacts into its own tree.

docs.title: Subscribers
docs.text:
sessions.changed removed is the only signal. No events.subscription message is added. When a tree is deleted:

  • the daemon drops the live tails of its sessions;
  • each connection forgets its subscriptions to them, so it sends nothing further for them, and events.unsubscribe answers false;
  • a client viewing a deleted session treats removed as "this session is gone": it leaves the view and drops the session's state.

A connection that fell behind gets resync as before, and the deleted sessions are then absent from session.list.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text:
• Only from 1.5. A client sends session.delete only to a daemon whose handshake protocol_version has minor 5 or later. To an older daemon it shows "The daemon is too old to delete sessions." without sending anything. A -32601 it gets anyway reads the same way.
  • Shared helpers. cookie_agent_client_state provides:
  • whether the daemon's version supports deleting;
  • the call that builds the params from the SessionMeta the user confirmed;
  • the outcome the TUI and the web client show.
  • TUI. The confirmation names the session's title and says how many subagents go with it. Refusals show their registry message and hint.

docs.title: 16.3 Commands, the subagent tree, and the mode picker
docs.text:
Decided by the user, 2026-10-21 (web only; the TUI is unchanged):

  • No slash commands in the web composer. / parsing and the completion popup are gone: text that starts with / (say /compact) is sent as a message. The placeholder is "Message". Every session command is in the title bar's ⋮ menu; the commands with another place keep it (the bottom bar's agent, model, and mode pickers and approvals badge, the composer's attach and Stop, the sidebar's New session, and the rail's views).
  • The ⋮ menu lists each command by a readable name with an icon and a one-line description, never slash syntax (since 2026-10-27 a session's ACP agent's commands follow, by their /name with an agent badge, under a filter for the whole menu; see the ACP agents spec section 10), and each opens a sheet (a side sheet on desktop, a bottom sheet on phones) with labelled fields and a main button:
  • Compact context: an optional Focus and Compact (session.compact with the focus); while it compacts, Cancel compaction, as the composer's Stop and Escape do;
  • Goal: the goal with Pause, Resume, and Cancel as the goal bar offers them, and a New objective field with Set the goal;
  • Skills: a search and the picked skill's arguments with Run;
  • Background calls, Runtimes, Permission rules, Usage, Diagnostics, and Agent preset open their existing sheets (the background sheet says so when no call runs in the background).
  • /agent-panel is gone, with its menu entries. Only the open session's row has a subagent tree, in one of two states; a click on the open session's own row switches them (a click on another session still opens it), and the browser keeps the state per session in localStorage (cookie.tree:<session id>):
  • collapsed (the default): the running subagents at any depth, and the subagent the page shows; a running subagent's ancestors that do not run show dimmed, only to place it; with nothing running, nothing shows;
  • expanded: the whole hierarchy, finished subagents included, each foldable by its chevron.

The nodes keep their rendering (status, agent, handle, task, a click opens the child) and the child's breadcrumb stays. - Permission mode picker. The mode chip no longer cycles modes or shows a toast: like the agent and model chips, it has a chevron and opens a picker (the side sheet on desktop, a bottom sheet on phones). The picker lists every mode with its shield, its name, and a line from the permissions guide, checks the current one, and sets the one clicked (session.set_permission_mode); a footnote says deny rules and the loop guard hold in every mode. The web client names the modes as the guide does: auto-approve, auto-approve-n, auto-approve-y, ask, yolo. - The message menu. A user message's ⋯ shows only while a mouse or pen is over the message's row (the whole band at the bubble's height) or the keyboard is in it; its room is kept, so the bubble never moves. A touch screen has no ⋯: a long press on the bubble (500 ms, cancelled by moving or scrolling, without the browser's callout) opens the same menu. - The composer's padding for its in-box buttons is static CSS chosen by which buttons show, so the text clears them from the first render (it was measured after a render, and missed the attach buttons that appear once the model's media are known).

docs.title: 16.4 The Agents, Machines, and Memory views
docs.text:
Decided by the user, 2026-10-21 (web only; the TUI is unchanged; no protocol change):

  • Agents gets a sidebar like Chat's sessions: the agent documents (the shared agents, then each preset's) on the left with an icon for each agent's mode, the open agent's editor on the right. The sidebar button and its remembered pinning are shared with Chat (cookie.sidebar); below 1024 px the agents slide over, and a phone's drawer carries them beside the rail, as it carries the sessions in Chat. New agent and Reload from disk sit above the list; Apply, Close, and Delete (behind a confirmation) at the editor's foot. Settings › Configuration keeps only config.toml.
  • Machines shows each machine as a card with its runtimes, with icons for the machine's operating system, each runtime's lifetime (built in, spawned from a template, dialled in), and its status. Moving a runtime is a pointer-event drag onto another machine's card: a mouse drags once it moves 4 px; a finger after a 500 ms long press (moving sooner scrolls), during which a non-passive touchmove listener keeps the page still, and a long press let go in place opens Move to…. Every row keeps a Move to… button for the keyboard, which picks another machine or names a new one. A drop on its own machine does nothing; runtimes the machine registry places nowhere (never connected) show under "On no machine yet" and can be dropped onto a machine to pin them.
  • Add a runtime in Machines: an ssh form (runtime ID, host, optional --root) that writes the runtimes guide's template with one config.apply set of ["runtimes", <id>] (retried once when the revision moved, refused when runtimes.list or config.toml already has the ID); the cookie runtime serve --daemon <url> [--id <id>] --token "<the daemon's token>" command with a copy button, whose URL is the page's own unless it is a loopback address (then <daemon host>); and links to the guides of the released documentation.
  • Memory: project folders fold, folded by default, and the browser keeps an opened one in localStorage (cookie.memory_project:<project>, value open; storage that fails leaves folders folding for the page's lifetime only). Delete project confirms, then sends memory.delete for each memory of the project at its listed revision; files that are not memories stay, and so does the folder when there are any.
  • Agent memory files (added the same day, after the daemon took over their description and first keywords, client protocol 1.6.0): the web editor shows an agent:// file's description read-only and its daemon-owned keywords (the agent's ID, then its mode) as fixed, with the other keywords in a comma-separated field and the body in the text area. A save writes the whole file with the description and keywords as read, the extra keywords, and the body; unchanged parts write nothing. memory.write's optional notice follows "Saved …" in the status line, as the TUI shows it; MemoryWriteOutcome::Saved in client_state carries it, and both clients word the status with saved_status.

docs.title: 17. Implementation notes
docs.text: Filled in as phases land.

docs.title: Phase L (2026-10-19)
docs.text:
Landed as specified, with no wire change and no configuration key.

  • Where it lives. crates/cookie_agent/src/local_daemon.rs holds the probe and the runtime choice; main.rs keeps the wiring thin. cookie attach and plain cookie with a found daemon share one function, run_daemon_tui, after their different connects.
  • Probe. The TCP connect runs on its own under the 500 ms deadline, so "nothing listens" is told apart from "answered but unusable". The WebSocket upgrade then runs over that same connection through a new Rust API, Client::connect_websocket_over in the protocol crate, and it shares the 2 s deadline with the handshake. The configuration is loaded once: the in-process daemon composes from the same load, so a broken configuration still fails before the probe, as it did before.
  • Decision as pure functions. The decision is two pure functions, one per section, rather than one:
  • Probe and its notice() cover the rows of 13.1;
  • choose_runtime covers the steps of 13.2.

runtime_for reads runtimes.list and machines.list only when the machine IDs differ. A daemon that cannot list them gets a dial-in. - Step 2 details. - Own ID excluded. Step 2 never picks the runtime ID this client dials in as (client_<host>). That runtime belongs to another TUI on this machine, which limits it to that TUI's directory, and it goes away when that TUI quits. Dialing in again under the same ID retries until that TUI leaves. - Facts only. The exclusion is by runtime ID, a reported fact, not by kind. - Several workspace capabilities. A runtime that offers more than one capability taking a workspace uses the first in runtimes.list order. - Not only coding. SessionPlacement gained a capability, so a chosen runtime's workspace capability need not be named coding. - Notices (deviation). The notices render as NOTICE rows below the transcript, not in the one-line status row: - the status row truncates the address and the suggestions at narrow widths; - the first action overwrites it.

They stay for the TUI's lifetime, like goal notices. The connection label leads the bottom bar: the daemon's address (127.0.0.1:7419, with wss:// kept), or standalone. cookie attach shows it too. - Version notice. It compares the daemon's engine_version (the server crate's version) with this binary's package version, not with cookie --version, whose git hash would always differ. cookie attach shows it too. - --standalone. - Before a subcommand, main_result refuses it with a clap usage error (exit code 2). - After a subcommand's name, clap rejects it as an unknown argument. - Tests. - Unit. The pure functions are tested over every row and step. - Against a real daemon. crates/cookie_agent/src/tests.rs runs a listening daemon, with a scratch [server] pointing at it. It covers: connect and create a session through it; no token; nothing listening; a wrong token; a listener that closes; a silent listener and the handshake deadline; and a dial-in for another machine ID, whose session attaches client_<host> at the directory. - Binary. crates/cookie_agent/tests/local_daemon.rs runs the real binary against a listener at the scratch home's [server] port that counts connections. Plain cookie dials once. Without a token, and for --standalone and cookie run, nothing dials. - Not tested end to end. - The TUI over a pty. "Plain cookie creates its session through the daemon" is covered by session.create over the probed connection, not by driving a TUI over a pty. - Step 2 against a real daemon. A test daemon reports the test process's own machine ID, so it cannot place a runtime on another machine. The pure function covers step 2.

docs.title: Phase W0a (2026-10-19)
docs.text:
The first half of W0: the protocol client on wasm32 (section 4). The client_state extraction and the markdown choice follow in W0b. There is no wire change.

  • Gating. On wasm32 the crate builds as the wire types and the Client. Gated out by target:
  • the server (session/server*);
  • paths and peer (the stdio peer and its codecs);
  • StopSignals, oauth_callback, and the test corpus;
  • RuntimeMachine::this_machine.

Tokio there is sync and macros only, in a target section of crates/protocol/Cargo.toml, as are gloo-timers, wasm-bindgen(-futures), web-sys, and the js features of uuid and jiff. No getrandom is pulled in. oven-sdk (unchanged pin) and cookie_agent_identity build for wasm32 as they are. - Executor shim. session/rt.rs provides spawn, timeout, sleep, and interval: - natively it is tokio, with the old Delay missed-tick behaviour; - on wasm, spawn_local and gloo-timers, with no Send bound.

The client's logic, limits, and tests stay one copy. - Browser transport. BrowserWebSocketTransport keeps the web_sys::WebSocket in one local task that talks to the transport over channels. - Size limit. A text message over MAX_WEBSOCKET_MESSAGE_BYTES ends the transport with an error. - Entry points. A page calls Client::connect_browser_websocket(url), then the new Client::handshake_with_token. That sends the token in ClientHello.token, serialized from wiping buffers like other secrets. - Refusals before the handshake. A socket that closes before it opens fails with the new ClientError::ConnectionRefusedBeforeHandshake { code, reason }. That covers a refused upgrade, such as an origin allowed_origins does not list, and nothing listening. - Firefox reports code 1006 and no HTTP status, so the client cannot tell an origin refusal from other refusals. - The page shows the allowed_origins hint for this whole error (section 7.2). - URLs. - The browser side checks the new validate_page_websocket_url: ws:// or wss://, with a path ending in /ws (wss://abc.efg/cookie/ws). - Native clients keep validate_websocket_url, which requires the path to be exactly /ws. - Both moved to session/daemon_url.rs. - Tests. - crates/protocol/tests/browser.rs runs in headless Firefox. It covers: - handshake with the token, and a wrong token; - an origin that is not allowed, and nothing listening; - an invalid endpoint, and a subpath endpoint; - a reconnect that keeps the identity and origin; - a reconnect that replays across a gap in which another client renamed the session. - scripts/test-wasm-client.sh runs them against two real cookie daemons in scratch homes: one allowing "*" and one allowing no origin. It passes their URLs and token in at compile time. - Built without them, each test passes without connecting. - Natively, a test covers handshake_with_token against a token-requiring serve, and another covers the URL rules. - CI. A wasm job checks the crate for wasm32 and runs clippy over it with websocket and its tests. The browser tests are not run in CI: they need Firefox, geckodriver, and wasm-bindgen-test-runner.

docs.title: Phase W0b (2026-10-19)
docs.text:
The second half of W0: the shared client state (section 5). There is no wire change, and the TUI's behaviour and tests are unchanged, except for paths that moved.

  • New crate. crates/client_state (cookie_agent_client_state) is published with the other library crates, after cookie_agent_protocol.
  • It depends on cookie_agent_protocol and plain crates only: pulldown-cmark, foldhash, jiff, serde_json, base64, and web-time. web-time gives the replay watchdog an Instant that works in a browser, where std's panics.
  • Nothing in it renders, and it builds for wasm32.
  • The TUI's state module is now a re-export of it.
  • Visibility. SessionState's bookkeeping fields became public, because the TUI's tests build it with struct-update syntax.
  • Test helpers. The few helpers the TUI's tests use sit behind a test-support feature.
  • Moved.
  • The reducer, StateStore, SessionState, the runtime snapshot chain, model display names, and their tests.
  • The markdown parse (client_state::markdown).
  • ownership: classifying a session.resume result, with "owned by another process" meaning a read-only snapshot.
  • model_draft: the 300 ms publish debounce as a generation check, and yielding to a live session_model_selected from another origin.
  • subscriptions:
    • the eight-tree recency set with its eviction;
    • SessionState::is_settled;
    • the 2 s retry wait;
    • the redial backoff, 500 ms to 10 s.
  • uploads: the model's accepted media, the chunked artifact.upload.* exchange, and its refusal messages.

No timer runs in the crate: it returns the delays, and the client sleeps them. - Stayed in the TUI. - The subscription state machine (subscribing, live, recovering, resubscribe-after-ownership). Its transitions start the TUI's RPC tasks. It shares the ownership sets with the view, and it holds the watch the session switch waits on. Moving it needs a command interface better shaped with the web client as a second user (W2). - The ownership bookkeeping. The generation map and the owned and read-only sets are read across the view. - The draft's reset intent and fallback resets. - Upload file handling. Reading the file and sniffing its content with runtime_api's validate_upload stay in the TUI, because that crate is not a plain dependency. The web client needs its own sniffing or a move of that function. - Everything section 5 lists as staying. - Markdown: measured. The release-mode transcript_perf harness ran on 150 runs: 632 items, 12,814 lines, 300 code blocks, 419 KB of reply markdown. Before and after the move it measured: - unchanged redraw: 0.60 ms (0.59 ms with descendant rows), the same as before; - streaming text delta and redraw: 1.06 ms; - first draw: 1.7 to 1.8 s, the same within noise; - resize: 92 ms.

Two further measurements: - Parsing all 419 KB of reply markdown from source takes 1.26 ms, twice an unchanged redraw. - Streaming an eight-run reply in 909 deltas costs 1.16 ms when only the open tail is re-parsed, and 33.9 ms when the whole reply is re-parsed after every delta. - Markdown: chosen. The state keeps the source plus pulldown-cmark events per top-level block, parsed incrementally, as the TUI already did. - A source-only state would make each client re-implement the incremental open-tail parse, about 30 times cheaper per streamed delta than parsing the whole reply. - It would also make each client cache its parse to keep redraws at 0.6 ms. - The ratatui styling, the syntax highlighting, and the TUI's per-block render and highlight caches stay in crates/tui/src/markdown.rs. They live in each block's RendererCache, a slot that clones of a block share, so no redraw re-renders what it did not before. - CI. The wasm job also checks cookie_agent_client_state and runs clippy over it.

docs.title: Phase W1 (2026-10-19)
docs.text:
Landed as specified, with no wire change and no configuration change.

  • Leptos and MSRV. Leptos 0.8.22 is the current stable release; 0.9 is a release candidate. It declares rust-version = 1.88, and its dependencies build on 1.88, so the workspace MSRV is unchanged.
  • crates/web (cookie_agent_web, not published) is the client-side rendered Leptos page.
  • It contains:
    • the connect screen (URL fill, #token= handling, paste box, "Forget this daemon", automatic connect, the origin hint after a refusal before the handshake);
    • the connected state, showing the daemon's address and versions;
    • redial with client_state's backoff under the tab's identity, kept in sessionStorage;
    • a check on visibilitychange;
    • the theme toggle.
  • It compiles natively, where only the browser connect is a stub. Native tests cover connect (URL fill, fragment, auto-connect, hint) and theme.
  • Styling.
  • Trunk's rel="tailwind-css" asset runs Tailwind 4.3.3, pinned in Trunk.toml with wasm-bindgen 0.2.126 (Cargo.lock's) and wasm-opt version_131.
  • style/main.css defines the landing palette as @theme colour tokens, @sources src, and makes dark: follow a dark class set from the system setting or the stored override.
  • JetBrains Mono (regular and bold, with its OFL licence) is bundled through Trunk's copy-dir.
  • Build. scripts/build-web.sh checks the pinned trunk (0.21.14) and wasm-bindgen versions, then builds with a new web cargo profile (opt-level = "z", fat LTO, panic = "abort") and wasm-opt -Oz.
  • It copies the result to crates/web_assets/bundle/ and prints sizes.
  • wasm-opt needs the feature flags current Rust emits (bulk memory and others), passed in index.html.
  • W1's bundle is 3.24 MB, 1.24 MB gzipped. Most of it is the 3.0 MB wasm, mainly the protocol crate's types.
  • The daemon serves it uncompressed. Precompressed serving and a size budget are left for W2, which section 10 allows.
  • crates/web_assets embeds the bundle through a build script that writes a table of path, content type, immutability, ETag, and bytes.
  • It falls back to a placeholder index.html.
  • It is published with the bundle through include. Cargo counts the git-ignored bundle as uncommitted, so the release publishes this one crate with --allow-dirty.
  • Server. A fallback route serves the page, with /ws and /runtime explicit and so taking precedence. Anything else, or a method other than GET or HEAD, is a 404.
  • Caching (deviation). Spec 7.1 assumed every bundle file has a hashed name, but Trunk does not hash files copied with copy-dir (here, the fonts). So a file is sent immutable only when its name carries Trunk's hash, and no-cache with an ETag otherwise, like index.html.
  • Headers. Every file carries nosniff.
  • No origin special case. The page's own /ws connection follows allowed_origins.
  • Ready line. The machine-readable daemon-ready line is unchanged, because its format is pinned for supervisors. The page's address and the empty-allowed_origins warning follow it as human log lines.
  • cookie web. It prints <page>#token=<token>, resolving the daemon like cookie attach. --open runs xdg-open, open, or start. cookie_agent_server::page_url derives the page from the client URL, for this command and the ready lines.
  • CI and release.
  • A web CI job:
    • installs trunk through install-action;
    • caches ~/.cache/trunk;
    • runs wasm32 clippy on cookie_agent_web;
    • runs scripts/build-web.sh, with the sizes in the job summary.
  • The release workflow:
    • builds the bundle once (build-web);
    • hands it to every dist build job and to publish-crates;
    • attaches cookie-agent-web.tar.gz to the release.
  • AGENTS.md lists the wasm clippy gate and the build script.
  • Tests.
  • Server:
    • every page path, its content type, cache rule, and ETag revalidation;
    • 404s for other paths and methods;
    • /ws and /runtime precedence;
    • the page's origin refused without an allowed_origins entry and accepted with one.
  • CLI: cookie web derivation and the ready-line page lines.
  • Browser: scripts/test-web-page.sh runs two real daemons, one allowing the page's origin and one allowing none, and drives headless Firefox through geckodriver. It passes:
    • the page connects by itself from the cookie web link, shows the connected state, removes the fragment, and stores the token;
    • against the refusing daemon, it quotes its exact origin as the entry to add.
  • Not in CI. The browser test is not a CI job yet, because it needs Firefox and geckodriver; W5's end-to-end suite adds them.

docs.title: Phase W2 (2026-10-20)
docs.text:
Core chat landed as specified, with no wire change.

  • Moved into cookie_agent_client_state.
  • The subscription state machine (subscriptions::Subscriptions). It covers subscribing, live, and recovering, a resubscribe once ownership arrives, the recent-tree release, and recovery after a failure.
    • Its methods return the events.subscribe requests to send (a Subscribe with its attempt), and the client reports each outcome back (finish, note_replay_end, release, recovery_failed). The client owns the clock and the RPCs.
    • The TUI drives it from ui/app/subscriptions.rs. The watch its session switch waits on stays in the TUI, keyed by session.
    • The TUI's tests are unchanged except that app.next_subscription_attempt reads app.subscriptions.last_attempt().
  • session_actions, also switched over in the TUI:
    • installing an approval.list into the store;
    • the permission-mode cycle and its labels;
    • toggling and finishing the complete content of a cut block (toggle_full_content, finish_full_content, FullContentState::of_read, block_full).
  • Ownership bookkeeping stayed in each client (deviation). The generation map and the owned and read-only sets stayed, because the TUI's tests read and write those HashSets and HashMaps directly. The web client keeps the same small bookkeeping over the shared ownership::classify_session.
  • The page (crates/web/src/{workspace,views}.rs):
  • Sessions: a list with a directory filter fed by the sessions' cwd_identity (all directories by default) and live sessions.changed.
  • New session: a draft whose first message creates the session. It attaches global and local's coding at the named directory, or takes the daemon's defaults, and applies the draft's mode.
  • Ownership: read-only snapshots for sessions another process owns.
  • The shared reducer, fed by every delivery, with voided input restored to the composer.
  • Composer:
    • Enter, Alt+Enter, Shift+Enter, Ctrl+J, Escape, and Up, mapped by the pure keys::composer_action;
    • Send, with a long press or the ▾ menu to queue;
    • the queue strip with recall;
    • run.cancel;
    • one session.submit_input per message.
  • Approvals: answered at their revision and fingerprint, refreshed on approvals_changed.
  • Pickers: agent, model and variant, and preset, from the runtime.snapshot.get / runtime.changed chain. The draft is published after 300 ms and yields to another client's pick.
  • Status bar: the permission mode and its cycle, the cost (from session.usage, debounced 250 ms as in the TUI), the /usage panel with the session and its tree, and the context size.
  • /events: the level filter, kept in localStorage.
  • Commands: the TUI's names and aliases for W2's commands (/new, /sessions with /resume, /load, /continue, /agent, /model, /preset, /usage, /cancel, /events), plus two with no TUI command of the same name: /approvals (the TUI docks approvals over the composer) and /mode (the TUI cycles the mode from its bottom bar). The ☰ menu lists them all.
  • Transcript HTML (crates/web/src/render/): pure functions, tested natively.
  • Markdown comes from MarkdownBlock events. Raw HTML becomes text; links are kept only for http, https, mailto, and relative URLs, and open in a new tab without an opener; images become links.
  • Display blocks: every kind has its own renderer, and none branches on a tool name.
    • Diffs number lines from the hunks' starts.
    • Terminal SGR becomes spans: classes for the 16 standard colours in both palettes, inline styles for 256-colour and RGB.
    • Media blocks are read with artifact.read into Blob URLs.
    • A block of a kind this build does not know renders nothing, as in the TUI. The daemon already turns a newer kind into its text fallback for an older client.
  • Interaction. Interactive parts carry data-action attributes, which one click handler dispatches.
  • Re-rendering. The page re-renders only items whose item_key (the item's version, its tools' revisions, expansion, and the level filter) changed.
  • Highlighting. highlight.js 11.12.0 is vendored with its BSD-3-Clause licence and checked against the npm sha512 integrity, with no CDN.
  • It is copied by Trunk and loaded on the first code block that names its language, through js_sys calls.
  • Its token colours come from the palette, light and dark.
  • Serving.
  • web_assets' build script gzips each compressible file. The daemon sends that copy when Accept-Encoding takes gzip, with Vary: Accept-Encoding and an ETag of its own. Brotli is left out: it would need another crate, and gzip covers every browser.
  • CSP. Every response carries a Content-Security-Policy:
    • script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval' plus a hash of Trunk's inline loader, computed at build time;
    • connect-src 'self' ws: wss:;
    • img-src and media-src with blob:;
    • style-src 'unsafe-inline', which inline terminal colours need;
    • no objects, base URI, framing, or form targets.
  • Size. The bundle is 4.28 MB, 1.65 MB gzipped. Of that, the wasm is 3.88 MB (1.40 MB gzipped), highlight.js 43 KB gzipped, and the fonts 187 KB.
  • scripts/build-web.sh now fails over a budget of 1,900,000 bytes gzipped, which CI enforces in the web job.
  • Tests.
  • Native web tests:
    • every block kind's HTML;
    • markdown sanitization (raw HTML escaped, javascript: links neutralized, images as links, code language classes);
    • SGR to spans;
    • diff line numbers;
    • the composer key mapping and the slash commands;
    • the event-level filter and item keys.
  • client_state tests: every transition of the subscription machine, and the mode cycle.
  • Server tests: gzip negotiation and revalidation of the compressed copy, and the CSP on every response.

  • scripts/test-web-page.sh. It now runs a scripted OpenAI-compatible model (scripts/web-e2e/mock-model.py) behind a daemon whose agent asks before bash. scripts/web-e2e/scenarios.py drives headless Firefox through:

    • connecting from the cookie web link;
    • a new session with streamed, highlighted markdown;
    • a tool call approved from the approvals sheet, with its terminal output;
    • steering a slow run, queueing behind it with Alt+Enter, and cancelling it with Escape, after which the unsent messages return to the composer;
    • a 375 px window with no sideways scroll and the sessions sheet;
    • the origin hint from a daemon that allows no origin.

    All pass, and the screenshots were checked. - Not in CI yet. The browser scenarios still need Firefox and geckodriver in CI (W5).

docs.title: Phase W3 (2026-10-20)
docs.text:
Session depth landed as specified, with no wire change.

  • Moved into shared crates.
  • cookie_agent_protocol::media_sniff. Recognizing and validating media from its content (validate_upload, the image, PDF, audio, and video checks, the caps) moved out of runtime_api::media, which re-exports it. The page sniffs a file exactly as the daemon will.
  • client_state::permissions: the /permissions table rows (permission_rows, permission_actions, the effect and source labels) and a draft's rules (set_draft_rule, remove_draft_rule). The TUI uses them.
  • client_state::uploads. upload now returns an UploadFailure whose too_large carries the limits a media_too_large refusal names (RefusedLimits), so the page can offer a downscale to them. The TUI keeps showing the message.
  • SessionState::user_files: the files each user message attached, by its sequence, for inline display.
  • The page (crates/web/src/workspace/, views/depth.rs):
  • Subagents. The Agents panel in the sidebar (and the sessions sheet) shows the viewed session's session.tree, foldable per session, with /agent-panel show|hide|auto as in the TUI: auto shows it while a delegate is live or a child is viewed.
    • The tree is re-read on tool_call_linked, run_finished, delegation_progressed, delegation_finished, delegate_child_terminated, and a finished replay of any session in it.
    • Its live sessions are subscribed, sharing the root's ownership.
    • A session_ref or tree row opens the child. Its root comes from the shown tree, the session list, or session.get's origin.
  • History edits. A user message's ⋯ menu copies it (navigator.clipboard, else the text is selected), reverts to before it (session.revert with expected_last_seq, confirmed first; the rewound notification rebuilds the transcript and the text returns to the composer; stale_revert is explained), or forks at it (session.fork with a client_fork_id, then opens the fork). /compact [focus] compacts; Escape and /cancel cancel a compaction outside a run (session.compact.cancel).
  • Goal. The goal bar shows the root's goal with the actions its status allows. /goal <objective> sets it with the draft's selection; /goal pause|resume|cancel reads session.goal.get and changes it at its revision. Goals are root-only and read-only snapshots offer none. Only goal_* events change the bar.
  • Background. A running call with backgroundable offers "⇲ background" (run.tool_background). session.background.list is read after each subscribe and background.changed keeps it current. The bar and the /background sheet list the calls with their age and stop one (session.background.stop); the sheet closes with the last call.
  • Media. /attach and 📎 open a file input whose accept lists the selected model's input_media types; 📷 (narrow screens, image models only) opens one with capture. Drop and paste attach too. Nothing is offered for a model without input media.
    • Each file is sniffed and checked against the model (attach::assess), then uploaded at once through the shared chunked upload (a new session is created first, as in the TUI), and shown as a chip.
    • An image over the model's or the daemon's limits, or refused by the daemon as media_too_large, is offered "Downscale and attach?". It is decoded and redrawn through a canvas, as JPEG when the model takes it (else PNG), at the size attach::downscale_target computes, and smaller again until it fits. Video is never re-encoded.
    • Attachments of user messages and media_file parts of assistant messages render inline through the same artifact.read → Blob placeholders as media blocks.
  • Skills. /skills [search] lists skills.list, ranked as the TUI ranks them (skills::matching_skills). Running one checks it with skills.get, then submits encode_skill_submission.
  • Permissions. /permissions shows the effective rules by action with their source. An effect click or the new-rule form sets an override (session.permission.set), and × clears one. While a new session is composed, the same table edits the draft's rules, previewed with session.permission.preview and sent as permission_rules on session.create.
  • /events default. The level the page starts with is the TUI's (EventLevel::DEFAULT_MINIMUM, warnings), so [I] rows are hidden by default; a stored choice still wins.
  • Fixes found on the way.
  • Item keys include the session. Item IDs repeat across sessions, so switching between two sessions of the same shape showed the first one's cached rows.
  • Following the transcript. It stops only when the user scrolls up (wheel, touch, or the scrollbar), not when a re-rendered row or a new bar briefly moves the scroll position.
  • Deviations.
  • /goal pause|resume|cancel are typed arguments. The TUI's palette asks only for an objective and puts the controls on the bar; the page has both.
  • The skill arguments, compaction focus, and goal objective are typed after the command (/skills gre, /compact keep the API notes), or in the sheet, instead of a palette step.
  • Fork and revert are offered on any user message the session's owner can edit, child sessions included, as the daemon decides what is allowed.
  • Size. Profiled with twiggy on an unstripped web build, the wasm was mostly serde code, plus two things the page never needed:
  • regex, used only for the control-character table in diagnostics. It is now a hand-written table, checked against the regex in a native test.
  • Runtime schema generation, used by open_enum! to list a tagged enum's tags. The tags are now listed in each open_enum! and checked against the schema in a native test.

Together they were about 1 MB of the wasm: before W3 it was 3.88 MB (1.40 MB gzipped), and without them 2.85 MB (1.06 MB gzipped). With all of W3 it is 3.19 MB (1.20 MB gzipped), and the bundle 3.60 MB (1.45 MB gzipped). The budget in scripts/build-web.sh is now 1,600,000 bytes gzipped (from 1,900,000). - Tests. - Native: tree rows and folding and the auto panel; /goal arguments and the bar's actions; skill ranking; the accept list, the assessment of a file (attach, downscale, refuse), downscale targets and refused-limit tightening; attachment names; the permission rows and draft rules; user_files; session-scoped item keys; the slash commands with arguments. - scripts/test-web-page.sh now gives the daemon a model that takes images, a helper subagent, a greet skill, an image in the workspace, and a session made by cookie run before the daemon started. The scenarios add: - a delegation shown in the Agents panel (/agent-panel show), its session_ref opening the child, and folding; - a fork at the first message and a revert of the last, with its text back in the composer; - /compact with a focus; - /goal set, then paused from the bar; - a slow bash call approved, moved to the background, listed with /background, and stopped; - an image attached from the file input, and one too large downscaled on acceptance, both shown inline in the sent message; - a read of an image whose media block shows inline; - /skills search and run; - a session permission override added and removed, and a draft rule previewed for a new session; - the cookie run session, whose owner lock the scenario holds as another process would, opening as a read-only snapshot.

All pass, and the screenshots were checked.

docs.title: Phase W4 (2026-10-20)
docs.text:
Management landed as specified, with no wire change.

  • Moved into cookie_agent_client_state, with the TUI switched over:
  • runtimes: attachment rows matched to their instances, a new session's draft runtimes, the attach choices and their search, the attach and retry requests, the machines view's rows, the machine actions each row offers, the changes they make, and their status lines.
  • mcp: the server order, which servers mcp.server.* edits, a server form as text and the definition it makes (McpFields), and the labels.
  • providers: a provider row's state, the model-availability and catalog lines, the setup values and credentials a connect sends, and the store-contention policy. Credentials are serialized once from the caller's buffers into a zeroized buffer (credential_values), as the TUI did.
  • config: the document rows, a new agent's template and path rules, and what an apply or reload answered and what the panel says about it.
  • memory: the rows by layer and group, a new memory's template and URL rules, what a write answered, and a refused delete's message.
  • plugins: a plugin's state and details, and its events' status line.
  • tool_header and rows: a tool call's header text, which drops an argument its title already names, the hint icons, and the producer and goal row labels.
  • The page (crates/web/src/workspace/manage.rs, crates/web/src/views/manage.rs):
  • /runtime: the session's attachments with their status, attach (search, then a workspace when needed), detach, and retry (runtimes.reconnect). In a new session, the draft's runtimes start as global and local's coding at the chosen directory (else where the daemon's own coding instance works, from runtimes.list). Each opens at once, and session.create attaches them. The Machines tab renames, merges, forgets, assigns, and unassigns. The panel re-reads runtimes.list and machines.list every second while open, as the TUI polls, and on runtimes.changed and machines.changed.
  • /mcp: the servers in the TUI's order with state, tools, source, and error, and add, edit, enable or disable, remove, reconnect, and persist. A server that needs authorization says to run cookie mcp auth <server> or use the TUI (since 2026-10-21 it offers Sign in; see web MCP OAuth). Polled every second while open, and on mcp.changed.
  • /connect: the catalog's providers with their state, a connect form per auth method with password fields for credentials, and disconnect with its confirmation. Connects go through connect_provider_retrying, and disconnects retry once on store contention, as in the TUI.
  • /config: the documents, an in-page monospace editor, config.apply at the revision and fingerprint read, refused edits kept to fix, conflicts dropped and reloaded, new agent documents, delete, and config.reload.
  • /memory: the memories by layer, an in-page editor, writes at the revision read, the invalid and changed outcomes with their choices (edit again, reload, overwrite, drop), create, and delete with its revision. It refreshes on memory.changed and machines.changed.
  • /plugins: state and details, restart, plugins.changed, and events.plugin status lines for the viewed session.
  • From the W3 review: producer messages (goal control and reminders, background-call and subagent reports) render as the TUI renders them. A claimed or consumed one is a folded line with its summary that opens to its owner, delivery, and body. A pending or admitted one does not show yet, and a discarded one shows only at the debug level. Goal activations show as their /goal action and goal states as the objective, status, and checklist. Plugin messages, AGENTS.md, loaded skills, and compactions fold as in the TUI. Tool titles use the TUI's header text, so a title that names its argument does not repeat it.
  • Size. Client::call now serializes its parameters before awaiting one shared request future instead of one per parameter type, which saved 16 KB gzipped. The wasm is 3.63 MB (1.37 MB gzipped), and the bundle 4.04 MB (1.62 MB gzipped). Most of the W4 growth is each RPC's request and answer code. The budget in scripts/build-web.sh is raised to 1,700,000 bytes gzipped, with that reason recorded beside it.
  • Deviations.
  • Editors are in the page. /config and /memory edit in a text area (section 6) instead of $EDITOR. A refused config edit stays open in the editor rather than reopening on the next edit.
  • Provider rows say their state in words, without the TUI's key hints.
  • The TUI's copy changed slightly where it now shares the web's text: a refused config edit says "Not applied; edit config.toml again.", and an existing new-agent or new-memory path says "exists; edit it instead".
  • Tests.
  • Native: client_state tests for the runtime, machine, config, memory, MCP, and provider rules, the producer summary, and the tool header; web tests for the folded producer rows and the new commands.

  • scripts/test-web-page.sh now configures a runtime template that never starts ([runtimes.box]) and the reference plugin. The scenarios add:

    • a draft runtime that fails, is retried, and is removed;
    • a session's local coding attachment detached and attached again;
    • a machine renamed;
    • an MCP server that cannot start added, disabled, and removed;
    • a provider connected with an API key (which never shows on the page) and disconnected;
    • a config edit with an unknown key refused, then a valid edit applied;
    • a memory refused as invalid, created, overwritten after a change on disk, and deleted;
    • the reference plugin restarted;
    • goal-control and background-report rows folded, and one opened.

    All pass, and the screenshots were checked.

docs.title: Phase W5 (2026-10-20)
docs.text:
Phone polish, the home screen, the end-to-end suites in CI, and the documentation. There is no wire change.

  • Phones. A new audit in scripts/test-web-page.sh opens every view and sheet (the transcript, sessions, every picker, and every panel) at 360 × 640 and 390 × 844 portrait and 844 × 390 landscape. It fails on sideways scroll, a control the screen's edge cuts off, or a target under 44 px. Firefox windows are at least 500 px wide, so a narrower screen is that window with the page zoomed in, which needs geckodriver's --allow-system-access. It found, and the page now fixes:
  • the composer's Send button cut off at 360 px: the text field could not shrink. The composer now wraps its buttons below the field when the field would be narrower than 12rem;
  • buttons narrower than 44 px (attach, camera, the command menu, the send menu, the permission effects): every button has a 44 px minimum width;
  • session rows squeezed into each other in a short landscape sidebar: rows no longer shrink;
  • the header wrapping its title and buttons over three lines: shorter labels ("Forget", the theme's name) below the sm breakpoint.
  • The on-screen keyboard. The page keeps --app-height at the visual viewport's height, which a phone's keyboard shrinks while 100dvh may not, and sizes its frame and sheets from it; the viewport meta asks for interactive-widget=resizes-content and viewport-fit=cover, and the frame pads by the safe-area insets. Firefox cannot raise a keyboard, so this is checked by reading, not by a scenario.
  • Background tabs. A scenario pauses the daemon (SIGSTOP), hides and shows the tab, sees the page give up on the silent connection, resumes the daemon, and sees the page reconnect and restore its session.
  • Home screen. crates/web/assets/manifest.webmanifest (display: standalone, relative start_url and scope), icons drawn from the logo by scripts/web-icons.py (any and maskable 192 and 512 px PNGs, the SVG, and an Apple touch icon, palette-reduced to 22 KB together), and theme-color for light and dark. Trunk copies them under their own names; the daemon serves them with no-cache, and the CSP's default-src 'self' already covers the manifest. A scenario checks the manifest's content type and that every icon it names is served.
  • CI. The web job now also installs Firefox 157.0.1 (browser-actions/setup-firefox), geckodriver 0.37.1 (checked by SHA-256), and wasm-bindgen-test-runner 0.2.126 (install-action, matching Cargo.lock; the suite checks the match), then runs scripts/test-wasm-client.sh and scripts/test-web-page.sh, uploading the scenario screenshots when a step fails. release_integrity pins these gates, and AGENTS.md lists the two suites.
  • Size. The bundle is 4.07 MB, 1.64 MB gzipped, within the 1.7 MB budget; the manifest and icons add 23 KB.
  • Docs. clients/web.md is the complete guide (phones, the home screen, and what the page does not do, besides every panel and command); engine/server.md, daemon/persistent.md, architecture.md, and the README describe the web client as it is; sections 1 to 14 of this spec now match what landed.

docs.title: Deviations across the phases
docs.text:
• Notices of plain cookie render as rows below the transcript, not in the status row (L).
  • Refused connections cannot be told apart in a browser (close code 1006, no HTTP status), so every refusal before the handshake shows the allowed_origins hint (W0a, W1). Since 2026-10-21 it is a plain hint to check the daemon URL and that the daemon is running.
  • Browser tests run in Firefox only, not Chrome (W0a, W5).
  • Caching: only files whose names carry Trunk's hash are immutable; copied files are revalidated (W1).
  • The ready line is unchanged; the page address and the empty-allowed_origins warning follow it as log lines (W1). The warning went with the allowlist on 2026-10-21.
  • Gzip only, no Brotli (W2).
  • Shared code: the subscription machine, panel rules, and labels moved to client_state over the phases; the ownership bookkeeping stayed in each client (W2–W4).
  • Commands: /approvals and /mode exist only in the page; /goal pause|resume|cancel and typed arguments replace palette steps (W2, W3).
  • Editors are in-page text areas, and a refused config edit stays open (W4).
  • The budget was 1.9 MB gzipped in W2, 1.5 MB after W3's size work, then 1.6 MB with W3's features and 1.7 MB with W4's panels, each raise with its reason recorded (W2–W4). After the UI polish of 2026-10-21 the release build (Rust 1.88.0) measured 1.75 MB, and the budget was raised to 10 MB, a backstop against runaway growth rather than a target.

docs.title: 18. Addendum (2026-10-21): canonical paths and runtime homes
docs.text:
Status: implemented (2026-10-21): runtime protocol 1.3.0 and client protocol 1.7.0 in the protocol, the daemon, and the TUI, then the web client's display and its runtime cards (section 18.3).

The web client's directory filter listed one directory twice: the page sent the ~/x the user typed as cwd, which the daemon stored verbatim because it canonicalized on its own machine and kept the text when that failed, while the TUI sent /home/ada/x. Runtimes already resolved and reported the canonical workspace, and nothing reported a home, so permission rules written ~/… never matched either.

docs.title: 18.1 Decisions (2026-10-21)
docs.text:
1. Paths are stored canonical and absolute, and shown as ~/… everywhere a client shows them.
  2. A session's directory identity (cwd_identity) is its first workspace attachment's canonical workspace, as the runtime reported it, never the client's typed text.
  3. It is decided once, in session.create, after the attachments have opened and before the creation event is written: the first attachment in attach order whose capability reported a workspace. The daemon does not branch on the attachment's kind; in practice it is the first coding attachment.
  4. A session with no workspace attachment keeps the old rule: cwd canonicalized on the daemon's machine, or the raw text when that fails (the daemon's working directory without cwd).
  5. Existing sessions keep what they stored: there is no migration.
  6. Delegated children copy their parent's identity, as before.
  7. Runtimes may report their home directory: an optional home in the result of runtime/initialize, a canonical absolute path on the runtime's machine (runtime protocol 1.2.0 → 1.3.0).
  8. It is on the result, not on RuntimeMachine: one machine runs runtimes of several users, and the machine ID is the operating system's.
  9. A reader takes an absolute POSIX or Windows path of at most 4096 bytes without control characters (runtime_protocol::is_valid_home) and reads anything else as unreported.
  10. cookie runtime serve reports its user's home, canonicalized; the built-in global and local report the daemon's. A runtime that reports none is fine: clients show its paths absolute.
  11. The client protocol exposes homes and attachments (client protocol 1.6.0 → 1.7.0; decided as 1.5.0 → 1.6.0, but memory.write's notice took 1.6.0 first):
  12. RuntimeListing.home in runtimes.list. Only there, not on RuntimeAttachment: the home belongs to the runtime, and attachments are folded from the persisted runtime_attached events, so a home on them would need a history change or go stale. A client maps an attachment's runtime_id to its listing.
  13. SessionMeta.attachments: the session's RuntimeAttachments now (name, runtime_id, capability, kind, workspace), so session lists show and filter by runtime and workspace without a session.get each.
  14. The daemon keeps them current on attach and detach: the metadata cache is written through and sessions.changed upserted goes out. Metadata an older build wrote decodes with none until the session records an event.
  15. Clients gate on minor 7: the TUI fetches homes only from a 1.7 daemon (client_state::paths::daemon_reports_runtime_homes).
  16. Permission rules: a pattern ~ or ~/… expands against the home of the runtime the tool runs on, when that runtime reported one.
  17. Without a home (the base layer included) it stays literal and so matches no absolute label; ~user/… never expands.
  18. A Windows home is spelled with /, as path labels are.
  19. Expansion is pure and allocation-free when it does not apply. It is used wherever a pattern is matched or ranked: agent and overlay rules, specificity, skill grants, and the stricter-overlay check.
  20. action@runtime selectors apply as before.
  21. The coding runtime expands a path argument's ~ against the same canonical home, so labels and rules agree.
  22. A shared display helper: client_state::paths::display_path(path, home) gives ~ for the home itself, ~/rest under it, and the absolute path otherwise.
  23. A Windows path keeps its separators (~\src) and matches its home ignoring case and either separator. There is never a ~ without a home, or for a root home.
  24. RuntimeHomes collects the homes from runtimes.list and names a session's directory under the home of the runtime whose attachment has that workspace.
  25. The TUI uses them in the bottom bar's runtime label (replacing its shorten_home, which used the client's home and mislabelled remote runtimes), the session picker's directory labels (now ~/… rather than the basename), and the /runtime panel's workspaces.

docs.title: 18.2 What the web client does next
docs.text:
• Fetch runtimes.list on connect and on runtimes.changed and machines.changed from a 1.7 daemon, and keep RuntimeHomes.
  • Show every path through display_path or RuntimeHomes: the sessions list's directory names and filter labels (session_directory), the session panel's runtimes, and the runtime cards' workspaces.
  • Filter and group sessions by cwd_identity as before; it now agrees across clients for new sessions. Runtime cards read SessionMeta.attachments to show which sessions use a runtime and workspace.
  • Keep sending what the user typed as cwd and workspace; the daemon and the runtime resolve it.

docs.title: 18.3 The web client's paths and runtime cards (implemented 2026-10-21)
docs.text:
Paths. The page reads runtimes.list when it connects and on runtimes.changed and machines.changed, keeps RuntimeHomes, and shows every path through it:

  • session rows list where a session works, ~/web, labpc:~/api (a runtime other than local is named), or "no workspace";
  • the sessions filter is by cwd_identity, as before, labelled with RuntimeHomes::session_directory and the runtime whose workspace it is (labpc · ~/api);
  • the bottom bar shows the session's (or the draft's) workspaces;
  • the /runtime sheet's attachments;
  • a tool row's title names its runtime's paths under that runtime's home.

From a daemon older than client protocol 1.7, which lists no attachments, a session's place is its cwd_identity, absolute.

New session = runtime cards (approved plan, 2026-10-21). New session opens cards in place of the transcript (a phone's fill the screen under the title bar, in one column, Start pinned at the foot):

  • Groups by machine from runtimes.list (this daemon's machine is local's, with global), first; then the others by name, then runtimes of no known machine. A header folds its group to "name · N runtimes · N ready · N selected"; this daemon's machine and a machine with a selected card start open, and the browser keeps each machine's choice (cookie.machine_open:<machine>).
  • Cards: global, then local, then each other runtime's capabilities that take a workspace, by runtime ID; a runtime that has not said what it offers is one card that asks for a workspace and becomes its capability's card once it connected, keeping its selection. States: ready (connected or built in), starts on use (a template), offline (a dial-in runtime that is not connected; it cannot be selected). A click anywhere on a card but its fields selects or deselects it.
  • Workspaces: a selected card has a field per workspace (more with "another workspace": the same runtime at another directory), suggesting this browser's recent workspaces on that runtime (cookie.recent_workspaces:<runtime>) and the sessions' attachments there, as ~/…; the text typed is sent, and the runtime resolves it. Start waits for every field. With two workspaces or more a note says tools get prefixes, naming the first as <runtime>_<last component>_bash.
  • Start sends runtimes.reconnect for every selected workspace at once. A refusal shows on its card and nothing is created; once all open, the draft composes with them, in card order, at the canonical workspaces they reported, plus global when selected (session.create's runtimes and global; cwd is the first workspace, or none).
  • Defaults: the open session's attachments; else the browser's last selection (cookie.new_session); the first time, global and local with an empty, focused field. The old "the daemon's own directory" field is gone, and nothing falls back to the daemon's directory.

Follow-ups: a subagent's handle truncates before its agent's name, and the open session's row has a chevron that turns with its tree.

docs.title: 19. Addendum (2026-10-21): session row status icons
docs.text:
Client protocol 1.9.0 adds SessionMeta.waiting_on: what will start a session's next run without the user, kept current by sessions.changed upserted (see What a session waits on). Session rows show one status icon, from cookie_agent_client_state::activity::session_activity:

  • Running (status is running): the running icon. It takes precedence: a running session shows as running whatever it waits on.
  • Waiting on a producer (not running, waiting_on not empty): the waiting icon, for an active goal, a background call, a subagent's turn, or an external producer. Its tooltip names the kinds.
  • Completed or idle with nothing to wait on: no icon.
  • A failed, cancelled, or interrupted last run with nothing to wait on is a Problem to the helper; rows keep showing it as they do today.

A daemon before 1.9 sends no waiting_on (activity::daemon_reports_waiting), so its sessions never show the waiting icon. The TUI's session picker marks rows ⏳ (running) and ⏰ (waiting) after the title; the web rows take the icons when they are reworked.

docs.title: MCP OAuth from the web client
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-21), in client protocol 1.11.0; section 7 records how it landed. It closes the one parity gap the web client spec left open ("MCP OAuth, whose redirect must reach a loopback listener").

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
The protocol already splits OAuth between client and daemon:

  • the daemon holds the PKCE verifier and exchanges the code;
  • the client gives mcp.auth.begin a redirect_uri, and hands the URL the browser lands on to mcp.auth.complete.

The TUI binds a loopback listener for this (OAuthCallbackListener). The web client cannot, and the daemon accepts only loopback redirects, so the web client has no sign-in for MCP servers.

This spec lets the web client use its own page as the redirect. It covers both the daemon serving the page and the page hosted anywhere else.

Out of scope: model-provider sign-ins. Providers whose client IDs are fixed to a localhost redirect need a device-code or paste-back flow of their own.

docs.title: 2. Daemon
docs.text:
• Redirect URIs. mcp.auth.begin accepts, besides today's loopback form:
  • https:// URIs, with a host, no user info and no fragment; any path and query are allowed;
  • http:// to a loopback IP literal or localhost, with any path and query, since the page may itself be served from loopback.

Everything else is refused as today, with a message naming the accepted forms. - Safety. Only a client holding the token can call begin, and the code is single-use. The verifier never leaves the daemon, so a code sent to an unexpected URI cannot be exchanged by anyone else. The state check in mcp.auth.complete is unchanged. - Client registration. - With dynamic client registration, the daemon registers the redirect the flow uses. - When a stored dynamic registration was made for a different redirect, the daemon registers again instead of reusing it. - A configured client_id is used as is. If its server refuses the redirect, the error reaches the client unchanged, and the docs explain that the redirect must be allowed on the server's side. - Protocol. Accepting more values is additive, but older daemons refuse them, so this is a client protocol minor bump. The web client offers sign-in only from that minor on.

docs.title: 3. Web client
docs.text:
• The redirect is the page itself. The URI is the page's own URL with ?oauth=callback, for example https://yunhao-labserver.tail34018a.ts.net/?oauth=callback. The OAuth server appends code and state.
  • Starting. The MCP server's "Sign in" button:
  • calls mcp.auth.begin;
  • records the pending server in sessionStorage and localStorage (cookie.oauth_pending), keyed by state with a 10-minute expiry;
  • opens authorization_url in a new tab.

If the browser blocks the new tab, it navigates the current tab instead. - Finishing. When the page loads with oauth=callback: 1. it removes code and state from the address bar at once (history.replaceState); 2. it connects as usual; 3. it calls mcp.auth.complete for the pending server with the full callback URL; 4. it shows the result, "Signed in to <server>" or the daemon's error.

If another tab of the page started the flow, the callback tab passes the URL to that tab over a BroadcastChannel (cookie-oauth) and closes itself. The original tab completes the flow and refreshes the MCP list. With no other tab listening, the callback tab completes the flow itself. - Paste fallback. While a sign-in is pending, the MCP sheet shows "Paste the address you landed on". This covers the system browser on a phone, which on iOS does not share storage with the installed app, and any other case where the callback lands somewhere the flow cannot continue from. Pasting calls mcp.auth.complete with the pasted URL. - Cancel calls mcp.auth.cancel and clears the pending entry. - HTTPS note. When the page is on plain http at an address that is not loopback, the sheet warns that most OAuth servers refuse such redirects. It suggests tailscale serve or another HTTPS front, and links to the remote-access guide. The button stays available, since some servers allow it.

docs.title: 4. Tests
docs.text:
• Daemon: redirect validation cases. Accepted: https with a path and query, loopback http, and localhost. Refused: https with user info or a fragment, a non-loopback http, and other schemes. Also a dynamic registration redone for a new redirect, and an end-to-end flow against the existing mock OAuth server with an https-style redirect.
  • Web, browser suite: against a mock OAuth server in the scenario daemon's config, three flows:
  • sign in through a new tab with the BroadcastChannel handoff;
  • sign in in the same tab;
  • the paste fallback.

Also check that the address bar is cleaned and that a stale or mismatched state is refused.

docs.title: 5. Docs
docs.text:
• The web guide: signing in to MCP servers.
  • The MCP page: web sign-in, the redirect a configured client must allow, and HTTPS.
  • The protocol changelog: the minor bump.
  • The web-client spec: the parity line updated.

docs.title: 6. Open questions
docs.text: None.

docs.title: 7. Implementation notes (2026-10-21)
docs.text:
Implemented as specified, in client protocol 1.11.0. The daemon side is client_redirect_uri and is_callback_for in crates/mcp/src/oauth.rs; the page's rules are crates/web/src/oauth.rs, its calls crates/web/src/workspace/oauth.rs, and its version gate cookie_agent_client_state::mcp::daemon_accepts_page_redirects. Details the spec left open, and the few additions:

  • Registration per flow. The daemon never reuses a dynamic registration across sign-ins: every mcp.auth.begin clears the server's stored credential and registers a client for its own redirect. A stored registration for another redirect therefore cannot be reused, which section 2 asks for; a test pins it.
  • application_type. A dynamic registration declares native for a loopback redirect and web for an https one (OIDC Dynamic Client Registration allows only loopback or custom-scheme redirects for native clients). It used to be native always.
  • The callback's query. mcp.auth.complete also checks that the callback carries every query parameter of the redirect itself, so oauth=callback must be there. A loopback redirect no longer needs a port (section 2 allows any loopback address with any path and query).
  • The tab that started. It is the tab whose sessionStorage holds the state. The browser copies sessionStorage into a tab a script opens, so the page empties the new tab's copy; the tab that comes back is then a client of its own. The new tab is opened blank during the click and sent to the authorization URL once mcp.auth.begin answers, so popup blockers let it through. Its opener is cleared before it leaves.
  • Handoff. The callback tab posts {kind: "callback", state, url} on cookie-oauth and waits 1.5 s for {kind: "taken", state}. One channel object per page, so a tab never hears itself.
  • One sign-in per server. The daemon runs one flow per server, so a new pending entry for a server replaces an older one. A completion that fails forgets the entry only when the daemon's flow ended (a mistaken address leaves it waiting); Cancel forgets it at once.
  • Refused callbacks. A callback whose state this browser does not know (or that already finished) is not completed, and the page shows its address with Copy the address, since the address bar no longer has it: that is how the paste fallback reaches the installed app on iOS. An expired entry is forgotten and the page says to start again.
  • While waiting. The server's row says it waits and offers Open the sign-in again (mcp.auth.begin with the same redirect returns the same URL). A server's needs_auth message shows muted, not as an error; the outcome of a sign-in shows above the servers.
  • Tests. The browser suite's mock is scripts/web-e2e/mock-oauth.py (registration, an authorization endpoint that approves at once and refuses unregistered redirects, PKCE-checked token exchange, a minimal Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint), behind three servers (oauth-tab, oauth-same, oauth-paste) in the scenario daemon's config; the scenario is mcp_sign_in. The blocked new tab is simulated with window.open returning null, and the paste flow with a stand-in tab whose URL the scenario follows itself. The HTTPS warning is checked at a non-loopback name that Chrome maps to the daemon's loopback.

docs.title: tui.toml
docs.text:
The terminal client reads ~/.cookie-agent/tui.toml independently of the engine. Every setting is optional. This is a complete file:

minimum_event_level = "warning"
theme = "auto"
transcript = "reduced"

There is no workspace layer, upward search, environment-selected config path, or environment interpolation. A missing file uses defaults. Unknown keys, wrong types, and malformed values fail with the path and offending key. Engine config.toml settings do not inherit into this file.

Top-level key Purpose Minimum Event Level Filter diagnostic rows Theme Select the terminal palette Transcript Fold agent work into one row per reply, or show all of it

These are scalar keys, not TOML tables. Omitted fields use their individual defaults; the theme's environment and terminal fallbacks are described on its page. Runtime /events palette changes are view-only and never rewrite this file. The TUI writes one key itself: transcript, when /transcript or Ctrl-O changes the mode, leaving the rest of the file as written. See Terminal UI for terminal operation.

docs.title: Minimum Event Level [minimum_event_level]
docs.text:
Choose which diagnostic rows appear in the conversation. Complete tui.toml:

minimum_event_level = "warning"

Accepted strings, from least to most severe, are "debug", "info", "warning", and "error". The default is "warning". Other strings and non-string values are errors. This is a top-level scalar, not a [minimum_event_level] table.

Rows below the threshold remain in the session projection. Lowering the filter to debug with the palette's /events command, or by clicking the filter in the conversation title, reveals them again. Runtime changes do not edit the file or remove events from history. There are no nested fields or workspace overrides; see tui.toml for loading behavior.

docs.title: Theme [theme]
docs.text:
Select a terminal palette. Complete tui.toml:

theme = "dark"
Value Selection "auto" Detect the terminal background, ignoring COOKIE_THEME "default" Light palette "dark" Curated dark palette "mono" Monochrome "high-contrast" Terminal-driven bright ANSI colors

Any file preference takes precedence over COOKIE_THEME, including "auto". When the key is omitted, COOKIE_THEME can select a palette; if that variable is also unset or auto, selection uses automatic detection: OSC 11, the last COLORFGBG field, and finally the light default. NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb force monochrome after selection.

Colour depth is detected separately. COLORTERM=truecolor (or 24bit) selects 24-bit colour; when COLORTERM is unset, Windows Terminal (WT_SESSION, also visible inside WSL) and TERM_PROGRAM values vscode, iTerm.app, WezTerm and ghostty count as 24-bit too. Otherwise a TERM containing 256color selects 256 colours, and anything else 16. Set COLORTERM=truecolor to opt a capable terminal in, for example over SSH, where these variables are not forwarded.

Unknown strings and non-string values fail. There are no nested fields or workspace overrides. Use the scalar theme, not a [theme] table; see tui.toml for file loading.

docs.title: Transcript [transcript]
docs.text:
Choose how the conversation shows an agent's work. Complete tui.toml:

transcript = "reduced"

Accepted strings are "reduced" and "full". The default is "reduced". Other strings and non-string values are errors. This is a top-level scalar, not a [transcript] table.

  • reduced folds each reply's thinking, tool calls, and the text written between calls into one row above the reply. While the agent works, the row reads ▸ Working… 42s · 3 tool calls and the line under it names what it is doing now: the newest step or line of its thinking, or the title of its newest tool call. Once that work ends, it reads ▸ Worked for 1m 23s · 7 tool calls, with · 1 failed when calls failed, or Stopped after … when the run was cancelled or interrupted. Click the row to open the work as the full mode shows it. A call waiting for your approval shows outside the fold until you answer it. A reply with no thinking or tool calls has no row.
  • full shows every thinking block and tool call.

/transcript reduced, /transcript full, and Ctrl-O change the mode in the running TUI and save it here: the TUI rewrites only this key, keeping the file's comments and other keys as written, and creates the file when it is missing. A file that no longer parses is left as it is, and the bottom bar says the mode was not saved; the new mode still applies until the TUI exits. Other running TUIs keep their mode until they start again. See tui.toml for loading behavior.
